few_shot.question:
A previously healthy 39-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a slowly enlarging, painless neck mass that she first noticed 3 months ago. During this period, she has also experienced intermittent palpitations, hair loss, and a weight loss of 4.5 kg (10 lb). There is no personal or family history of serious illness. She appears anxious and fidgety. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 101/min and irregular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a firm, nontender left anterior cervical nodule that moves with swallowing. Laboratory studies show:
TSH 0.4 μU/mL
T4 13.2 μg/dL
T3 196 ng/dL
Ultrasonography confirms the presence of a 3-cm solid left thyroid nodule. A thyroid 123I radionuclide scintigraphy scan shows increased uptake in a nodule in the left lobe of the thyroid gland with suppression of the remainder of the thyroid tissue. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's condition?"

answer_choices.A: Thyroid peroxidase autoantibody-mediated destruction of thyroid tissue
answer_choices.B: Gain-of-function mutations of the TSH receptor
answer_choices.D: Activation of oncogenes promoting cell division

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of weight loss, palpitations, and anxiety, along with her physical examination findings of a thyroid nodule and tachycardia, are suggestive of hyperthyroidism. The thyroid scan findings of a "hot" nodule with suppression of the remainder of the gland are consistent with a toxic adenoma (Plummer disease). Toxic adenomas are autonomously functioning thyroid nodules that produce thyroid hormone independent of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) stimulation. They are typically caused by gain-of-function mutations in the TSH receptor, which lead to constitutive activation of the receptor and subsequent increased synthesis and release of thyroid hormone.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 43-year-old female presents to her primary care physician complaining of a gradually enlarging neck mass. She reports that she first developed a firm nodular midline mass on the anterior aspect of her neck two months ago. She is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. A fine-needle aspiration is performed and a histological sample of the specimen is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The histological sample shows a papillary structure with a fibrovascular core and nuclear changes such as nuclear clearing, grooves, and pseudoinclusions. These findings are characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), the most common type of thyroid cancer. PTC often presents as a painless, firm, solitary thyroid nodule. It is more common in women and in individuals with a history of head or neck irradiation. PTC generally has a good prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate of over 90%.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man presents with a mass on his neck. He says that he first noticed the mass a few weeks ago while taking a shower. Since then, the mass has not increased in size. He denies any pain or difficulty in swallowing. Past medical history is unremarkable. Family history is significant for his father who had his thyroid removed when he was around his age but doesn’t know why. Review of systems is significant for occasional episodes of anxiety that include a pounding headache, racing heart, and sweating. His vital signs include: pulse 88/min, blood pressure 133/87 mm Hg, temperature 37.2°C (99.0°F), and respiratory rate 14/min. He is 183 cm (6 ft 2 in) tall with long extremities. On physical examination, the patient appears cachectic. There is a palpable 4 cm x 4 cm nodule present on the left lobe of the thyroid. Which of the following is the most likely thyroid pathology in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is suggestive of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B). MEN 2B is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytoma, and mucosal neuromas. MTC is a tumor of the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, which secrete calcitonin. It is the most common cause of death in MEN 2B and often presents as a thyroid nodule or mass. Pheochromocytoma can cause episodic hypertension and symptoms such as headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. Mucosal neuromas can cause a characteristic physical appearance, including thickened lips and bumpy tongue. Other features of MEN 2B include a marfanoid habitus (as seen in this patient) and intestinal ganglioneuromas, which can lead to constipation or diarrhea.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of fever, anterior neck pain, and throat swelling. She has no history of serious illness. Her temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F) and pulse is 109/min. Physical examination shows diaphoresis and a fine tremor of the outstretched hands. The thyroid gland is enlarged, firm, and tender to palpation. Serum thyroid stimulating hormone level is 0.06 μU/mL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 65 mm/h. 123I scan shows an enlarged thyroid gland with diffusely decreased uptake. Histologic examination of a thyroid biopsy specimen is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.C: Lymphocytic infiltration with germinal follicle formation
answer_choices.D: Noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, anterior neck pain, and tender thyroid enlargement are suggestive of subacute thyroiditis, also known as de Quervain thyroiditis. This is a self-limited inflammatory disorder of the thyroid that is thought to be caused by a viral infection or postviral inflammatory process. It is often preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection and is more common in women.

Patients with subacute thyroiditis typically present with anterior neck pain that may radiate to the jaw or ears. On examination, the thyroid gland is usually enlarged and exquisitely tender. Patients may also have systemic symptoms such as fatigue, anorexia, and myalgia. Laboratory studies often show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level. Thyroid function tests may show a transient hyperthyroidism due to leakage of preformed thyroid hormone from the inflamed thyroid gland into the circulation. This is followed by a period of hypothyroidism as stores of thyroid hormone become depleted. Most patients eventually return to a euthyroid state.

Histologic examination of the thyroid gland in subacute thyroiditis shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. This is a nonspecific response to tissue injury and is not seen in other thyroid conditions.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 26-year-old woman comes to the clinic for an annual wellness examination. She is healthy with no prior history of significant illness. She exercises 3-4 times a week and eats a plant-based diet with no carbonated drinks. When asked if anything is bothering her, she reports that she has been having recurring episodes of sneezing, congestion, and itchy eyes for the past year. She denies any fever, sick contacts, cough, headaches, chest pain, urinary symptoms, or constipation/diarrhea during these episodes. She is told to take a medication to alleviate her symptoms as needed. What is the likely mechanism of action of the medication in question?

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old woman presents to an urgent care center with progressively worsening cough and difficulty breathing. She has had similar prior episodes since childhood, one of which required intubation with mechanical ventilation. On physical exam, she appears anxious and diaphoretic, with diffuse wheezes and diminished breath sounds bilaterally. First-line treatment for this patient’s symptoms acts by which of the following mechanisms of action?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent episodes of cough and difficulty breathing, along with her physical exam findings of wheezing and diminished breath sounds, are consistent with asthma. Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by bronchial hyperreactivity and variable airflow obstruction. Symptoms include wheezing, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea. The mainstay of acute treatment for asthma exacerbations is inhaled beta-2 agonists (eg, albuterol), which cause bronchodilation and relief of acute symptoms. 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician for evaluation of a 6-month history of persistent rhinorrhea and nasal congestion. She works in retail and notices her symptoms worsen anytime she is exposed to strong perfumes. Her symptoms have worsened since winter began 2 months ago. She has not had fever, nausea, wheezing, itching, or rash. She has no history of serious illness or allergies. She takes no medications. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows congested nasal mucosa, enlarged tonsils, and pharyngeal postnasal discharge. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of chronic rhinorrhea and nasal congestion that worsen with exposure to strong odors (eg, perfumes) are suggestive of vasomotor (nonallergic) rhinitis. Vasomotor rhinitis is a form of nonallergic rhinitis that is triggered by non–immunoglobulin E–mediated stimuli such as changes in weather (eg, cold, dry air), strong odors, and airborne irritants (eg, smoke, pollution). Symptoms include chronic or recurrent nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and postnasal drip. Unlike allergic rhinitis, vasomotor rhinitis is not associated with sneezing, itching, or conjunctival symptoms. The nasal mucosa is typically normal or erythematous with a watery discharge, and there is no evidence of nasal eosinophilia.

First-line treatment for vasomotor rhinitis includes intranasal ipratropium bromide and intranasal corticosteroids. Intranasal ipratropium bromide is an anticholinergic agent that inhibits secretions from serous and seromucous glands lining the nasal mucosa, thereby decreasing rhinorrhea. Intranasal corticosteroids decrease rhinorrhea and congestion by inhibiting cytokine production, adhesion molecule expression, and recruitment of inflammatory cells.

Intranasal antihistamines (eg, azelastine) are also effective in treating vasomotor rhinitis. They are thought to work through their anticholinergic properties, which reduce glandular activity in the nasal mucosa.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman develops progressive difficulty breathing after a long day of chores in a dusty house. These chores included brushing the family dog, vacuuming, dusting, and sweeping. She occasionally gets these episodes once or twice a year and has her medication on hand. Her symptoms are reversed by inhaling a β2-adrenergic receptor agonist. Which of the following chemical mediators is responsible for this patient’s breathing difficulties?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of episodic difficulty breathing, which are reversed by a β2-adrenergic receptor agonist, are suggestive of asthma. Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by bronchial hyperresponsiveness and variable airflow obstruction. It is often triggered by allergens, such as dust and pet dander, as in this patient.

The pathogenesis of asthma involves the release of chemical mediators from mast cells and other inflammatory cells in the airways. These mediators include histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins. Leukotrienes, in particular, cause bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability leading to edema, and mucus secretion in the airways. These effects contribute to the airflow obstruction seen in asthma.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 53-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of wheezing and shortness of breath that began 1 hour after he took a new medication. Earlier in the day he was diagnosed with stable angina pectoris and prescribed a drug that irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 and 2. He has chronic rhinosinusitis and asthma treated with inhaled β-adrenergic agonists and corticosteroids. His respirations are 26/min. Examination shows multiple small, erythematous nasal mucosal lesions. After the patient is stabilized, therapy for primary prevention of coronary artery disease should be switched to a drug with which of the following mechanisms of action?

answer_choices.A: Blockage of P2Y12 component of ADP receptors

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic rhinosinusitis, asthma, and nasal polyps, along with his acute bronchospasm following administration of aspirin, is consistent with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD). AERD is a clinical syndrome characterized by the triad of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis, asthma, and intolerance to aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The exact pathogenesis of AERD is not well understood, but it is thought to involve an imbalance in the metabolism of arachidonic acid. Specifically, inhibition of the cyclooxygenase pathway by NSAIDs leads to overproduction of proinflammatory leukotrienes via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway, leading to bronchospasm and rhinitis.

Patients with AERD who require antiplatelet therapy for coronary artery disease should receive clopidogrel or another P2Y12 inhibitor. These drugs inhibit the P2Y12 component of ADP receptors on the platelet surface, preventing ADP-mediated activation of the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa pathway, a necessary step in platelet aggregation.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of urinary leakage over the last year. She reports involuntarily losing small amounts of urine after experiencing a sudden need to void. She has difficulty making it to the bathroom in time, and only feels comfortable going out into public if she has documented the location of all nearby restrooms. She also has begun to wake up at night to urinate. These symptoms have persisted despite 6 months of bladder training and weight loss and reducing soda and coffee intake. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient is a drug that has which of the following mechanisms of action?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of urgency, frequency, and nocturia are consistent with overactive bladder (OAB), a condition characterized by involuntary detrusor contractions during the bladder filling phase. The detrusor muscle is predominantly innervated by the parasympathetic nervous system, which uses acetylcholine as its main neurotransmitter. Acetylcholine binds to muscarinic receptors on the detrusor muscle to cause contraction. The M2 and M3 subtypes are the most common muscarinic receptors in the bladder, but the M3 receptor is primarily responsible for bladder contraction. Therefore, the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient is a drug that antagonizes muscarinic M3 receptors.

So, the answer is [A].

question:

She has had bloody urine over the last 48 hours but denies any nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She has not traveled anywhere outside her city for the past several years. She appears ill. The temperature is 40.8℃ (105.4℉), the pulse is 108/min, the respiration rate is 20/min, and the blood pressure is 105/50 mm Hg. The abdominal exam reveals hepatosplenomegaly. Lymphadenopathy is absent. Petechiae are seen on the lower extremities. Laboratory studies show the following:
Laboratory test
Hemoglobin 8 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 98 µm3

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia are suggestive of babesiosis, a tick-borne illness caused by the protozoan Babesia microti. Babesiosis is most commonly seen in the Northeast and upper Midwest United States, particularly in the late spring and summer months. The disease is transmitted by Ixodes scapularis, the same tick that transmits Lyme disease and anaplasmosis. Patients often present with fever, fatigue, and hemolytic anemia. The peripheral blood smear typically shows intraerythrocytic ring forms, which can be mistaken for Plasmodium falciparum (the causative agent of malaria). However, the absence of recent travel to a malaria-endemic area makes malaria unlikely in this patient.

Urine dipstick is positive for blood and protein. A blood smear shows schistocytes and normochromic, normocytic cells. In addition to supportive treatment, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes on blood smear, anemia, jaundice), thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury is consistent with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). HUS is most commonly caused by Shiga toxin-producing bacteria (eg, Escherichia coli O157:H7), which are often acquired by eating undercooked beef or other contaminated foods. The toxin inhibits protein synthesis in endothelial cells, leading to cell death and exposure of the subendothelial space. This triggers platelet adhesion, activation, and aggregation, resulting in thrombocytopenia and the formation of platelet-rich thrombi that cause mechanical damage to red blood cells (schistocytes) as they squeeze through the narrowed vessels. The kidneys are particularly susceptible to damage, and renal insufficiency or failure can occur.

The mainstay of treatment for HUS is supportive, including hydration, electrolyte repletion, antihypertensive medications, and transfusion of packed red blood cells for severe anemia. Platelet transfusion is generally avoided unless the patient is actively bleeding or requires an invasive procedure, as it can lead to more platelet aggregation and worsening of the microangiopathic process. Hemodialysis is indicated for patients with severe acute kidney injury, fluid overload, electrolyte abnormalities, or intractable metabolic acidosis, as in this patient.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 26-year-old woman seeks evaluation at an urgent care clinic with complaints of fever and generalized muscle and joint pain for the past 3 days. She also complains of nausea, but denies vomiting. She does not mention any past similar episodes. Her past medical history is unremarkable, but she returned to the United States 1 week ago after spending 2 weeks in southeast Asia doing charity work. She received all the recommended vaccines prior to traveling. The temperature is 40.0°C (104.0°F), the respirations are 15/min, the pulse is 107/min, and the blood pressure is 98/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mild gingival bleeding and a petechial rash over the trunk. Laboratory studies show the following:
Laboratory test
Leukocyte count 4,000/mm³
Platelet count 100,000/mm³
Partial thromboplastin time (activated)  45 seconds
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, myalgias, arthralgias, rash, and thrombocytopenia after returning from Southeast Asia is suggestive of dengue fever. Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne illness caused by the dengue virus, a flavivirus. It is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions around the world, including Southeast Asia. The disease is characterized by high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgias, arthralgias, and a characteristic rash that is often described as "islands of white in a sea of red." Thrombocytopenia is common and can lead to bleeding complications, such as the gingival bleeding seen in this patient.

The other options listed (Ebola virus, leptospirosis, and yellow fever) can also cause similar symptoms, but are less likely given this patient's specific presentation and travel history.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

She recently returned from a trip to India, where she was visiting her family. There is no history of loss of consciousness or respiratory distress. The vital signs include temperature 38.9℃ (102.0℉), respiratory rate 19/min, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, and pulse 94/min (rapid and thready). few_shot.explanation:
The patient's recent travel to India, fever, and jaundice, along with the peripheral smear findings, are suggestive of Plasmodium falciparum malaria. P. falciparum is the most virulent species of Plasmodium and is responsible for the majority of severe malaria cases and malaria-related deaths worldwide. The most severe complication of P. falciparum malaria is cerebral malaria, which is characterized by seizures, loss of consciousness, or abnormal behavior. It is caused by sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in the cerebral microvasculature, leading to cerebral edema and a potentially fatal increase in intracranial pressure.

few_shot.question:
A 33-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a fever and fatigue. He states that he has not felt well since he returned from a hiking trip in Alabama. He is generally healthy and has no other medical conditions. His temperature is 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 127/85 mmHg, pulse is 108/min, respirations are 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Ehrlichiosis is a tick-borne illness caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, which is transmitted by the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum). It is most commonly found in the southeastern and south-central United States. After a bite from an infected tick, the organism infects monocytes within the human host, forming intracytoplasmic morulae. Clinical manifestations typically occur 1-2 weeks following the tick bite and most commonly include fever, malaise, headache, and myalgias. Laboratory abnormalities often include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated aminotransferases. Diagnosis is typically clinical, but can be confirmed with PCR or immunofluorescence assay. Treatment is with doxycycline.

According to his girlfriend, he has had fatigue for the last 3 days and became confused this morning, after which he started having uncontrollable convulsions throughout his entire body. He was unconscious throughout the episode, which lasted about 4 minutes. He has not visited a physician for over 10 years. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 12 years. His girlfriend admits they occasionally use heroin together with their friends. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 93/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation and examination shows normal heart sounds and no carotid or femoral bruits. He appears emaciated and somnolent. There are multiple track marks on both his arms. He is unable to cooperate for a neurological exam. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 3,000/mm3, a hematocrit of 34%, a platelet count of 354,000/mm3, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 27 mm/h. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 84/mm3 (normal ≥ 500). A CT scan of the head is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step considering this patient's CT scan findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, confusion, and seizures in the setting of HIV infection with a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count <100/mm3 is suggestive of cerebral toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasma gondii, an intracellular protozoan, is the most common cause of focal central nervous system disease in patients with AIDS. The organism is often acquired by ingesting tissue cysts in undercooked meat or by exposure to oocysts from cat feces. After ingestion, the organism disseminates and forms tissue cysts, most commonly in the brain, which can reactivate in the setting of immunosuppression. 

On neuroimaging, toxoplasmosis characteristically appears as multiple ring-enhancing lesions. The diagnosis is presumptive, based on clinical presentation and radiographic findings. The most appropriate next step in management is to start empiric treatment with pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin.

few_shot.question:
A 23-year-old female presents to the emergency department complaining of a worsening headache. The patient reports that the headache started one month ago. It is constant and “all over” but gets worse when she is lying down or in the setting of bright lights. Review of systems is significant for low-grade fever, night sweats, cough, malaise, poor appetite, and unintentional weight loss of 12 pounds in the last two months. The patient is sexually active with multiple male partners and reports inconsistent condom use. She has a history of intravenous drug use, and has not been to a doctor in the last two years. The patient’s temperature is 100.4°F (38.0°C), blood pressure is 110/78 mmHg, pulse is 88/min, and respirations are 14/min with an oxygen saturation of 98% O2 on room air. On physical exam, pain is elicited upon passive flexion of the patient’s neck. A CT scan shows ventricular enlargement. A CD4+ count is 57 cells/µL blood. A lumbar puncture is performed with the following findings:

Cerebrospinal fluid:
Opening pressure: 210 mmH2O
Glucose: 32 mg/dL
Protein: 204 mg/dL
India ink stain: Positive

Leukocyte count and differential:
Leukocyte count: 200/mm^3
Lymphocytes: 100%
Red blood cell count: 2

What is the next best step in therapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient’s presentation is consistent with cryptococcal meningitis. Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast that is found in soil and bird droppings. It is a common cause of meningitis in patients with AIDS, especially when the CD4+ count is <100 cells/µL. Patients often present with subacute symptoms of meningitis, including headache, fever, malaise, and, in severe cases, altered mental status. Cryptococcal meningitis is diagnosed by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showing yeast cells on India ink staining and a positive cryptococcal antigen. CSF in cryptococcal meningitis often has a mildly elevated protein, low glucose, and a lymphocytic pleocytosis. Opening pressure is often markedly elevated, which can cause cerebral herniation if not managed appropriately. 

The treatment of choice for cryptococcal meningitis is amphotericin B and 5-flucytosine for at least two weeks, followed by fluconazole for a minimum of eight weeks. Amphotericin B works by binding to ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, leading to the formation of pores and leakage of intracellular contents. 5-Flucytosine is converted to 5-fluorouracil, which inhibits DNA and protein synthesis. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old female with AIDS (CD4 count: 47) presents to the emergency department in severe pain. A lumbar puncture is performed which demonstrates an opening pressure of 285 mm H2O, increased lymphocytes, elevated protein, and decreased glucose. The emergency physician subsequently initiates treatment with IV amphotericin B and PO flucytosine. What additional treatment in the acute setting may be warranted in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with cryptococcal meningitis, a common opportunistic infection in patients with AIDS. The headache and fever are likely due to the infection, while the severe pain is likely due to increased intracranial pressure (ICP). The elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture confirms this. 

The treatment for cryptococcal meningitis is induction therapy with amphotericin B and flucytosine, followed by consolidation therapy with fluconazole. However, in patients with elevated ICP, additional treatment with serial lumbar punctures or a lumbar drain may be necessary to relieve the pressure and associated symptoms. 

Mannitol and acetazolamide, other treatments for elevated ICP, are typically not used in this setting as they have not been shown to be beneficial.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of generalized fatigue and malaise. During this period, she has had a non-productive cough with a low-grade fever. Over the past 6 months, she has had a 13-kg (28.6-lb) weight loss and intermittent episodes of watery diarrhea. She has generalized anxiety disorder and hypothyroidism. She has a severe allergy to sulfa drugs. She is sexually active with 3 male partners and uses condoms inconsistently. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years and drinks 2–3 beers daily. She does not use illicit drugs. Current medications include paroxetine, levothyroxine, and an etonogestrel implant. She is 162.5 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 50.3 kg (110.2 lbs); BMI is 19 kg/m2. She appears pale. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.6°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 100/75 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Examination of the lungs shows bilateral crackles and rhonchi. She has white plaques on the lateral aspect of the tongue that cannot be scraped off. A chest x-ray shows symmetrical, diffuse interstitial infiltrates. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of weight loss, diarrhea, and oral thrush, along with her sexual history, suggest advanced HIV infection. The diffuse interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray and hypoxemia are most consistent with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), the most common opportunistic infection in patients with AIDS. PJP typically presents with fever, nonproductive cough, and dyspnea over weeks, often with little to no physical examination findings despite extensive disease on imaging. The preferred treatment for PJP is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX). However, this patient has a severe sulfa allergy, which is a contraindication to TMP-SMX use. Alternative regimens for PJP in patients with a sulfa allergy include intravenous pentamidine or oral atovaquone. Another option is clindamycin plus primaquine, which is preferred in this patient because it also covers other potential pathogens (eg, bacterial pneumonia) given her physical examination findings (eg, rhonchi, crackles).

Therefore, the answer is [B].

The preferred treatment for PJP is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), which covers both typical and atypical pathogens. few_shot.question: A 39-year-old woman comes to the physician because of recurrent episodes of severe pain over her neck, back, and shoulders for the past year. The pain worsens with exercise and lack of sleep. Use of over-the-counter analgesics have not resolved her symptoms. She also has stiffness of the shoulders and knees and tingling in her upper extremities that is worse in the morning. She takes escitalopram for generalized anxiety disorder. She also has tension headaches several times a month. Her maternal uncle has ankylosing spondylitis. Examination shows marked tenderness over the posterior neck, bilateral mid trapezius, and medial aspect of the left knee. Muscle strength is normal. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and thyroid-stimulating hormone are within the reference ranges. X-rays of her cervical and lumbar spine show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

This patient's chronic, widespread pain; fatigue; and multiple somatic symptoms (eg, headache, paresthesias) are suggestive of fibromyalgia. Fibromyalgia is a disorder of unknown etiology characterized by chronic, widespread musculoskeletal pain and the presence of multiple discrete tender points on examination. It is often associated with poor, nonrestorative sleep, fatigue, morning stiffness, and multiple somatic complaints. Patients may also have a history of psychiatric disorders, including depression and anxiety, as seen in this patient. The diagnosis is clinical, and laboratory and imaging studies are typically normal.

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old Asian woman presents to her primary care physician with joint pain and a headache. She has had intermittent joint and muscle pain for the past several months in the setting of a chronic headache. She states that the pain seems to migrate from joint to joint, and her muscles typically ache making it hard for her to sleep. The patient's past medical history is non-contributory, and she is currently taking ibuprofen for joint pain. Physical exam is notable for an asymmetrical pulse in the upper extremities. The patient has lost 10 pounds since her previous visit 2 months ago. Laboratory values are notable for an elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of headache, jaw claudication, and an asymmetric pulse is concerning for giant cell arteritis (GCA). GCA is a vasculitis that most commonly affects the branches of the external carotid artery, including the temporal artery. The most feared complication of GCA is irreversible vision loss due to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Therefore, patients with suspected GCA should be started on high-dose glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone) immediately to prevent vision loss. A temporal artery biopsy can be performed to confirm the diagnosis, but treatment should not be delayed while awaiting biopsy results.

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old man comes to the physician because of lower back pain that has become progressively worse over the past 2 months. The pain is also present at night and does not improve if he changes his position. He has stiffness for at least 1 hour each morning that improves throughout the day. Over the past 3 months, he has had 3 episodes of acute gout and was started on allopurinol. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows reduced lumbar flexion and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints. Passive flexion of the hip with the knee extended does not elicit pain on either side. Muscle strength and sensation to pinprick and light touch are normal. A pelvic x-ray confirms the diagnosis. The patient is started on indomethacin and an exercise program. Six weeks later, the patient reports no improvement in symptoms. Before initiating further pharmacotherapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's chronic back pain, morning stiffness, and decreased range of motion, along with radiographic evidence of sacroiliitis, are suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis (AS). AS is a chronic inflammatory disease that primarily affects the axial skeleton (ie, spine, sacroiliac joints). Extra-articular manifestations are also common and can include acute anterior uveitis, aortic regurgitation, and apical lung fibrosis.

First-line treatment for AS involves physical therapy and NSAIDs (eg, indomethacin). If patients fail to improve or have frequent flares, the addition of a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor (eg, infliximab, etanercept) is indicated. However, TNF inhibitors increase the risk of reactivation of latent tuberculosis (TB). Therefore, TB screening should be performed before starting a TNF inhibitor. The purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test or interferon-gamma release assay can be used for this purpose.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old woman comes to the physician because of lower back pain that began suddenly 2 weeks ago after getting up from her chair. She has hypertension, chronic bilateral knee pain, and a history of breast cancer 15 years ago that was treated with lumpectomy. Her mother has rheumatoid arthritis. Medications include hydrochlorothiazide and acetaminophen. She appears well. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows tenderness to palpation of the lower spine. Both knees are enlarged and swollen. Neurologic examination shows sensorineural hearing impairment of the left ear. Her gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) is 30 U/L (N: 0–30 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is 310 U/L, and serum calcium is 10.2 mg/dL. A spinal x-ray shows a fracture in the L4 vertebra. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of isolated elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), hearing loss, and bone pain is suggestive of Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans). Paget disease is a common condition that typically presents in older adults. It is characterized by disordered and excessive bone remodeling that results in bone that is larger but weaker and more chaotic in structure. The disease may be asymptomatic or present with bone pain, pathologic fractures, or neurologic complications (eg, hearing loss due to impingement of the cranial nerves at the skull base). The most common laboratory abnormality is isolated elevation of ALP, which is a marker of osteoblast activity. 

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with a concern for joint pain. She states that she often feels minor joint pain and morning stiffness in both of her hands every day, in particular in the joints of her fingers. Her symptoms tend to improve as the day goes on and she states they are not impacting the quality of her life. She lives alone as her partner recently died. She smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day and drinks 2-3 alcoholic drinks per day. Her last menses was at the age of 45 and she works at a library. The patient has a history of diabetes and chronic kidney disease and her last GFR was 25 mL/min. Her temperature is 97.5°F (36.4°C), blood pressure is 117/58 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is within normal limits. Which of the following interventions is appropriate management of future complications in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's age, female sex, postmenopausal status, smoking history, and chronic kidney disease all place her at high risk for osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, leading to enhanced bone fragility and a consequent increase in fracture risk. The most common fractures associated with osteoporosis occur at the spine, hip, and wrist. The goal of pharmacologic therapy in osteoporosis is to reduce the risk of fracture. First-line treatment to prevent fractures in patients with osteoporosis is with antiresorptive therapy, typically a bisphosphonate such as alendronate. Bisphosphonates work by inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, which in turn tips the balance toward bone formation and results in a net gain in bone mineral density.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 3-year-old refugee with increasing pitting edema and abdominal swelling over the past 2 months is brought to the physician. few_shot.question: A 5-year-old child whose family recently immigrated from Africa is brought in for a wellness visit. The boy appears indifferent, doesn’t seem to make eye contact, and keeps to himself. Upon examination, it is noted that his height and weight are below the 5th percentile. Furthermore, his abdomen is protuberant, and there are multiple zones of hyper- and hypopigmentation and desquamation of the skin. Upon palpation of the abdomen, he is found to have hepatomegaly, and lower extremity inspection reveals pitting edema. Which of the following is the cause of this child’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This child's presentation is consistent with kwashiorkor, a form of severe protein malnutrition. Kwashiorkor is characterized by edema, an enlarged fatty liver, skin and hair changes, and apathy. The edema is due to decreased oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia, and the fatty liver results from decreased synthesis of lipoproteins, which are necessary to transport fat from the liver. Skin and hair changes include areas of hyper- and hypopigmentation, desquamation, and a reddish-orange discoloration of the hair. Apathy, irritability, and decreased attention span are also commonly seen.

Kwashiorkor is typically seen in children from developing countries who have been weaned from breast milk and are receiving a diet that, while adequate in calories, is severely deficient in protein.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her parents, who are concerned about an abdominal swelling that they noticed 2 days ago. The family immigrated from Bangladesh to the United States recently. The mother mentions that the girl has never been as active as other children of the same age but has no medical conditions either. Her appetite has declined, and she vomited a few times last week. On physical examination, slight prominence of frontal bosses at the forehead is noticeable with malar prominence and massive splenomegaly. Slight beading at the end of her ribs is evident. She has a dusky complexion, sclerae are anicteric, and oral mucosa is pale. Laboratory results are pending. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the findings seen in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of massive splenomegaly, pallor, and frontal bossing is suggestive of a chronic hemolytic anemia. The most likely cause in this case, given her ethnicity (Bangladeshi), is beta-thalassemia. Beta-thalassemia is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by defective synthesis of the beta-globin chain of hemoglobin, leading to an imbalance in the alpha/beta-globin chain ratio, ineffective erythropoiesis, and hemolysis. 

Frontal bossing and malar prominence are due to expansion of the bone marrow into the skull and facial bones as a result of increased erythropoiesis. The spleen is massively enlarged due to extramedullary hematopoiesis and pooling of red blood cells. 

Hence, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of increasing swelling of his legs and generalized fatigue for 1 month. During this period he has also had a productive cough and shortness of breath. He has been unable to carry out his daily activities. He has a history of recurrent respiratory tract infections and chronic nasal congestion since childhood. He has a 3-month history of foul-smelling and greasy stools. He is at 4th percentile for height and weight. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 23/min, and blood pressure is 104/64 mm Hg. Examination shows clubbing of his fingers and scoliosis. There is 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities. Jugular venous distention is present. Inspiratory crackles are heard in the thorax. Cardiac examination shows a loud S2. The abdomen is mildly distended and the liver is palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin. Hepato-jugular reflux is present. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent respiratory tract infections, chronic nasal congestion, and foul-smelling, greasy stools is suggestive of cystic fibrosis (CF). CF is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by abnormal function of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), a protein that regulates chloride ion transport across epithelial cell membranes. This leads to the production of thick, viscous secretions in multiple organ systems. In the respiratory tract, these secretions cause chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, and recurrent pulmonary infections, often with Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. In the gastrointestinal tract, inspissated secretions can block the pancreatic ducts, leading to malabsorption due to pancreatic insufficiency. This can cause steatorrhea, as seen in this patient.

This patient's physical examination findings of clubbing, inspiratory crackles, and a loud S2 are suggestive of cor pulmonale secondary to chronic hypoxia. Cor pulmonale is right-sided heart failure due to pulmonary disease, and can present with signs of right-sided heart failure such as jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, and hepatomegaly.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of facial swelling that has now progressed to total body swelling. He also complains of nausea and abdominal pain. The child was in his usual state of health a week ago when they first notice swelling around his eyes. A few days later his legs started to swell. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. He is up to date on all vaccines and is meeting all developmental milestones. Today, his blood pressure is 104/60 mm Hg, the heart rate is 90/min, the respiratory rate is 25/min, and the temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F). On examination, he has facial edema, abdominal shifting dullness, and bilateral leg edema up to the knees. Urine dipstick shows 4+ protein and urinalysis shows fatty casts. Serum albumin is 2.2 g/dL. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of facial and leg edema, proteinuria, and hypoalbuminemia is consistent with nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by proteinuria (>3.5 g/24 hr), hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, and hyperlipidemia. The most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children is minimal change disease (MCD). MCD is characterized by effacement of the foot processes of the glomerular epithelial cells (podocytes) on electron microscopy. The pathogenesis of MCD is not completely understood, but it is thought to be related to T-cell dysfunction, which leads to increased glomerular permeability to plasma proteins (especially albumin). The loss of albumin in the urine leads to hypoalbuminemia, which decreases plasma oncotic pressure and leads to the movement of fluid into the interstitial space, causing edema. The liver increases production of lipoproteins in response to low oncotic pressure, leading to hyperlipidemia. Patients with MCD often present with abrupt onset of edema, but are otherwise asymptomatic. They are typically normotensive and do not have hematuria.

So, the answer is [A].

The risk of infection is increased due to urinary loss of immunoglobulins, impaired complement function, and T-cell dysfunction. The most common pathogens are encapsulated organisms (eg, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae).

question: A 33-year-old nurse is referred to an infectious disease specialist after she exhibited a PPD skin test with 17 mm of induration. few_shot.question: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He feels well. He has type 1 diabetes mellitus. His only medication is insulin. He immigrated from Nepal 2 weeks ago . He lives in a shelter. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 5 years. He has not received any routine childhood vaccinations. The patient appears healthy and well nourished. He is 172 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 123/82 mm Hg. Examination shows a healed scar over his right femur. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test is performed. Three days later, an induration of 13 mm is noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test is positive. The PPD test is a screening tool for tuberculosis (TB) infection. A positive test indicates that the patient has been infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, but it does not differentiate between latent TB infection (LTBI) and active TB disease. LTBI is characterized by a positive PPD test, a normal chest x-ray, and the absence of clinical symptoms. Active TB disease is characterized by symptoms of TB (eg, cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss), a positive PPD test, and chest x-ray findings consistent with TB.

This patient is asymptomatic, but he has several risk factors for progression from LTBI to active TB disease, including recent immigration from a country with a high prevalence of TB and type 1 diabetes mellitus. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is to obtain a chest x-ray to evaluate for active TB disease.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old man presents to his family physician for a routine check-up but also states he has been feeling less energetic than usual. His medical history is significant for hypertension and hyperlipidemia, for which he takes enalapril and atorvastatin. The patient has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the last 30 years. His vital signs include the following: the heart rate is 80/min, the respiratory rate is 18/min, the temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), and the blood pressure is 140/84 mm Hg. He appears well-nourished, alert, and interactive. Coarse breath sounds are auscultated in the lung bases bilaterally. A low-dose computerized tomography (CT) scan is scheduled. This patient has a positive tuberculin skin test (TST) and a chest radiograph showing a right upper lobe cavitary lesion. These findings are highly suggestive of active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB). The patient's risk factors for TB include his employment in a healthcare setting and his smoking history. The patient's symptoms of fatigue and the physical examination finding of coarse breath sounds are also consistent with active TB. Although the initial sputum smear is negative, the sensitivity of sputum smear microscopy is only 50%-60%. Therefore, the patient should be started on the standard 4-drug regimen for TB (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) while awaiting sputum culture results. If the sputum culture is positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the 4-drug regimen is continued for 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampin for an additional 4 months. If the sputum culture is negative, the medications can be stopped.

few_shot.question: A 7-month-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her parents with a mild, persistent fever for the past week. The patient’s mother also states she is feeding poorly and has become somewhat lethargic. The patient was born at term and the delivery was uncomplicated. The child’s birth weight was 3.5 kg (7.7 lb) and at 6 months was 7.0 kg (15.4 lb). She is fully immunized. Gastric aspirates are positive for acid-fast bacilli, however, cultures are still pending. Father and daughter are both started on standard antitubercular therapy. few_shot.explanation:
The patient’s mother is at risk for developing tuberculosis (TB) because she is in close contact with two individuals with active TB. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that close contacts of individuals with active TB undergo testing with either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). If the test is positive, it indicates that the individual has been infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis and should be treated with isoniazid for 9 months to prevent progression to active disease. If the initial test is negative, it should be repeated 8-10 weeks after the last exposure to the index case. This is because it can take several weeks for the immune system to mount a response to M tuberculosis after initial infection, and the individual may be in the “window period” during which the test result is falsely negative. If the second test is also negative, the individual is unlikely to be infected and does not require further treatment or follow-up.

DILE is a lupus-like syndrome that occurs in response to various drugs, and it is similar to but distinct from idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The most common drugs associated with DILE are hydralazine, procainamide, and isoniazid. 

Isoniazid is a first-line antitubercular drug that is part of the standard 4-drug regimen for tuberculosis, along with rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. It can cause DILE in addition to other side effects such as peripheral neuropathy (which can be prevented by coadministration of pyridoxine) and hepatotoxicity.

question: A 15-year-old woman presents with fever, altered mental status and a petechial rash on her lower extremities and back since yesterday evening. few_shot.question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the ED with a diffuse, erythematous rash in the setting of nausea, vomiting, and fever for 2 days. Physical exam reveals a soaked tampon in her vagina. Blood cultures are negative. The likely cause of this patient's disease binds to which molecule on T cells?

answer_choices.C: Variable beta portion of the T-cell receptor

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, vomiting, and rash in the setting of tampon use is suggestive of toxic shock syndrome (TSS). TSS is caused by the release of toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) from Staphylococcus aureus. TSST-1 is a superantigen that binds to the variable beta portion of the T-cell receptor and MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells. This interaction bypasses the normal antigen-presenting process, leading to polyclonal T-cell activation and massive cytokine release, which results in the clinical manifestations of TSS.

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of fever, vomiting, rash, and worsening confusion since this morning. The pathogenesis of TSS involves the production of superantigens (eg, toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 [TSST-1] in S aureus) that bypass the normal antigen-presenting process and bind directly to the major histocompatibility complex class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells and T-cell receptors. few_shot.question:

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, myalgias, arthralgias, rash, and thrombocytopenia after returning from Southeast Asia is suggestive of dengue fever. Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne illness caused by the dengue virus, a flavivirus. It is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions around the world, including Southeast Asia. The disease is characterized by high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgias, arthralgias, and a characteristic rash that is often described as "islands of white in a sea of red." Thrombocytopenia is common and can lead to bleeding complications, such as the gingival bleeding seen in this patient.

The other options listed (Ebola virus, leptospirosis, and yellow fever) can also cause similar symptoms, but are less likely given this patient's specific presentation and travel history.

few_shot.question: A 47-year-old man presents to his primary care physician complaining of pain and stiffness in his right index finger and left knee. This patient's history of dandruff (likely scalp psoriasis), dactylitis, nail pitting, and distal interphalangeal joint involvement is suggestive of psoriatic arthritis. Psoriatic arthritis is a chronic inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis. It is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy, meaning that it is not associated with rheumatoid factor or anti-citrullinated protein antibodies. The arthritis can be asymmetric and oligoarticular, as in this patient, or symmetric and polyarticular, similar to rheumatoid arthritis. Dactylitis (ie, "sausage digit"), nail changes (eg, pitting, onycholysis), and enthesitis (ie, inflammation at sites where tendons or ligaments insert into bone) are characteristic. Radiographic findings include periarticular new bone formation and pencil-in-cup deformity of the DIP joints.

few_shot.question: A 59-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of pain and stiffness in her fingers and knees. OA is a degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive erosion of articular cartilage. It is the most common form of arthritis and typically affects the DIP joints, proximal interphalangeal joints, first carpometacarpal joint, hips, knees, and cervical and lumbar spine. Risk factors for OA include age >40, female sex, obesity, and joint injury. Pain in OA is typically worse with use and improves with rest, distinguishing it from the inflammatory arthritides (eg, rheumatoid arthritis), in which pain is worse in the morning and after rest.

few_shot.question: A 39-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-day history of pain and stiffness in her hands and wrists and a nonpruritic generalized rash. Parvovirus B19 infection in adults can cause a nonspecific febrile illness followed by a symmetric polyarticular arthritis that most commonly affects the small joints of the hands. The arthritis is typically self-limited, lasting days to weeks, but can persist for months. A lacy, reticulated rash can also occur.

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old female presents to her primary care provider complaining of pain and stiffness in her hands and knees. She reports that the stiffness is worse in the morning and appears to get better throughout the day. She is otherwise healthy and denies any recent illness. She does not play sports. On examination, her metacarpal-phalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints are swollen and erythematous. Her distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints appear normal. She exhibits pain with both passive and active range of motion in her knees bilaterally. Serological analysis reveals high titers of anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies. Which of the following processes underlies this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.A: Precipitation of monosodium urate crystals in the intra-articular space
answer_choices.B: Post-infectious inflammation of the articular surfaces

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of joint pain and stiffness that is worse in the morning and improves throughout the day, along with the physical exam findings of swollen and erythematous MCP and PIP joints, are suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a systemic, inflammatory disorder that primarily affects the joints. It is characterized by a symmetric, erosive synovitis that often leads to progressive joint destruction, loss of function, and disability. The pathogenesis of RA involves synovial hypertrophy and the formation of a destructive granulation tissue (pannus) at the margins of the articular surfaces and at the bone-cartilage interface. The presence of anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies is highly specific for RA.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

Two days after hospitalization for urgent chemotherapy to treat Burkitt’s lymphoma, a 7-year-old boy develops dyspnea and reduced urine output. He also feels a tingling sensation in his fingers and toes. Blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg, respirations are 28/min, pulse is 100/min, and temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F). The lungs are clear to auscultation. He has excreted 20 mL of urine in the last 6 hours. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 15 g/dL
Leukocyte count 6,000/mm3 with a normal differential serum
K+ 6.5 mEq/L
Ca+ 7.6 mg/dL
Phosphorus 5.4 mg/dL
HCO3− 15 mEq/L
Uric acid 12 mg/dL
Urea nitrogen 44 mg/dL
Creatinine 2.4 mg/dL
Arterial blood gas analysis on room air:
pH 7.30
PCO2 30 mm Hg
O2 saturation 95%
Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.D: No prevention would have been effective

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has tumor lysis syndrome (TLS), a potentially life-threatening condition that can occur after the initiation of chemotherapy, especially in patients with a high tumor burden (eg, Burkitt lymphoma, acute leukemias). TLS results from the rapid release of intracellular contents (eg, potassium, phosphate, nucleic acids) into the bloodstream following lysis of malignant cells. The overproduction of uric acid from the catabolism of nucleic acids can lead to renal vasoconstriction, inflammation, and intratubular precipitation, all of which can cause acute kidney injury. Hyperkalemia can cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias, and hyperphosphatemia can cause secondary hypocalcemia, leading to neuromuscular irritability and seizures.

The cornerstone of TLS prevention is aggressive hydration, which promotes renal excretion of potassium and uric acid. However, allopurinol should also be administered to patients at high risk for TLS (eg, those with high tumor burden or elevated uric acid at baseline). Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that blocks the conversion of xanthine to uric acid, reducing uric acid production.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old college student is diagnosed with acute myelogenous leukemia after presenting with a 3-week history of fever, malaise, and fatigue. He has a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus, multiple middle ear infections as a child, and infectious mononucleosis in high school. He currently smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day, drinks a glass of wine per day, and denies any illicit drug use. The vital signs include: temperature 36.7°C (98.0°F), blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg, heart rate 87/min, and respiratory rate 17/min. On physical examination, his pulses are bounding; his complexion is pale, but breath sounds remain clear. A rapidly progressive form of leukemia is identified, and the patient is scheduled to start intravenous chemotherapy. Which of the following treatments should be given to this patient to prevent or decrease the likelihood of developing acute renal failure during treatment?
few_shot.explanation:
Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is an oncologic emergency that typically occurs following the initiation of cytotoxic therapy, although spontaneous cases have been reported. It is characterized by the rapid release of intracellular contents (eg, potassium, phosphate, nucleic acids) into the systemic circulation, leading to hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, secondary hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia. The latter results from the catabolism of nucleic acids to uric acid by xanthine oxidase. Precipitation of uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals in the renal tubules can cause acute kidney injury.

Allopurinol, a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, is used for prophylaxis in patients at high risk for TLS (eg, those with high tumor burden such as acute leukemias or high-grade lymphomas) to prevent uric acid nephropathy. It reduces the production of uric acid but does not affect preformed uric acid. Therefore, it should be started prior to, or at the time of, initiation of chemotherapy.

So, the answer is [C].

BUN 41 mg/dL
Serum uric acid 28 mg/dL
Potassium 6.9 mEq/L
Which therapy is most likely to reverse the patient’s metabolic abnormalities?

answer_choices.A: Intravenous saline with mannitol with the goal of a daily urinary output above 2.5 L/day

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has tumor lysis syndrome (TLS), a potentially life-threatening complication of chemotherapy, especially in patients with high tumor burden (eg, Burkitt lymphoma, acute leukemias). TLS is caused by the rapid release of intracellular contents (eg, potassium, phosphate, nucleic acids) into the bloodstream following lysis of malignant cells. The nucleic acids are metabolized to uric acid by xanthine oxidase, leading to hyperuricemia. Uric acid can precipitate in the renal tubules, causing acute kidney injury (AKI). Hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia (with secondary hypocalcemia) can also occur.

The management of TLS depends on the severity of the metabolic derangements and the presence of AKI. In patients with severe hyperkalemia (eg, >6.0 mEq/L) or AKI, urgent hemodialysis is indicated. Hemodialysis can rapidly correct hyperkalemia and volume overload, and it can remove uric acid and phosphate.

In patients with less severe TLS, the goal of therapy is to prevent uric acid nephropathy. This can be achieved by maintaining a high urine output (eg, with intravenous fluids) and reducing uric acid levels. Allopurinol can be used to decrease uric acid production, and rasburicase, a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme, can be used to catalyze the conversion of uric acid to allantoin, a more soluble and easily excreted compound.

few_shot.question: A 47-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He states that he has felt fatigued and dizzy on several occasions over the past week. His prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level is 0.3 ng/mL (N < 4.5). An intravenous infusion of para-aminohippurate (PAH) is administered and its clearance is calculated. This patient's laboratory findings of a normal serum creatinine concentration, a low filtration fraction, and a normal effective renal plasma flow are suggestive of a prerenal cause of renal dysfunction. The most likely cause of this patient's prerenal azotemia is NSAID use. NSAIDs inhibit the production of renal prostaglandins, which are important for maintaining renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in states of decreased renal perfusion. Inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis by NSAIDs can lead to unopposed vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole, leading to decreased renal perfusion and GFR. This can lead to acute kidney injury, especially in patients with volume depletion, heart failure, or cirrhosis.

She describes the stools as odorless, watery in consistency, and tea-colored, without blood or mucus. She has not been diagnosed with any specific medical conditions, and there is no history of substance use. Other symptoms can include weakness, nausea, and abdominal cramping. Laboratory findings often include hypokalemia and achlorhydria (due to VIP's inhibition of gastric acid secretion). Pheochromocytoma is the second most common feature of MEN2A and is characterized by episodic hypertension, headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the least common feature of MEN2A and is characterized by hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and elevated parathyroid hormone levels. few_shot.question: A 38-year-old primigravid woman at 34 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of progressive shortness of breath for 3 hours. Her current medications include methyldopa and a multivitamin. She appears anxious. Her pulse is 90/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's shortness of breath?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's hypertension, proteinuria, and pulmonary edema are consistent with preeclampsia with severe features. Preeclampsia is a multisystem disorder characterized by hypertension and proteinuria after 20 weeks' gestation. Severe features include systolic blood pressure ≥160 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure ≥110 mm Hg, thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function, pulmonary edema, and cerebral or visual symptoms. 

Pulmonary edema in preeclampsia can result from either fluid overload (eg, aggressive use of intravenous fluids) or from increased capillary permeability. The latter is due to widespread endothelial dysfunction, which is a key feature of preeclampsia. Endothelial dysfunction leads to vasospasm and increased vascular permeability, which can cause fluid to leak into the interstitial space, including the pulmonary interstitium.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

However, her lack of risk factors for venous thromboembolism (eg, recent surgery, malignancy, immobility, estrogen use, prior history of venous thromboembolism) makes PE less likely. In patients with a low clinical pretest probability of PE, the D-dimer assay is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test. D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product and is typically elevated in the presence of thrombus. The D-dimer assay is very sensitive but not specific for PE, as levels can be elevated in various other conditions (eg, malignancy, infection, surgery, trauma, pregnancy). Therefore, a negative D-dimer assay result can reliably exclude PE in patients with a low clinical pretest probability, but a positive result requires further evaluation with imaging.

One week ago, she returned from a trip to Chile, where she had a 3-day episode of flu-like symptoms that resolved without treatment. Pregnancy and delivery of her first child were uncomplicated. She has no history of serious illness. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 28/min and slightly labored, and blood pressure is 110/76 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 91%. Examination shows jugular venous distention and bilateral pitting edema below the knees that is worse on the left-side. There is decreased breath sounds over the left lung base. The uterus is consistent in size with a 32-week gestation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.A: Decreased fibrinogen levels on serum analysis
answer_choices.B: Depression of the PR segment on electrocardiography
answer_choices.C: Decreased myocardial perfusion on a cardiac PET scan

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, and unilateral leg swelling is concerning for deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE). Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state due to increased levels of procoagulant factors (eg, fibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, X), decreased protein S activity, and venous stasis due to compression of the inferior vena cava and pelvic veins by the enlarging uterus. In addition, this patient has several other risk factors for DVT/PE, including recent long-distance travel and a recent illness with possible transient immobilization. The most appropriate next step in management is to perform ultrasonography of the lower extremities to evaluate for DVT, which is the most common source of PE. If DVT is confirmed, full anticoagulation should be initiated. If the ultrasound is negative, further evaluation for PE should be pursued.

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 35-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a sudden onset of difficulty breathing that began when she woke up that morning. She also reports a dry cough and chest pain that is worse with inspiration. She does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 93% on room air. Physical examination is unremarkable. An ECG shows non-specific ST segment changes. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. In addition to oxygen supplementation, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden onset of dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxemia in the setting of oral contraceptive use is concerning for pulmonary embolism (PE). PE is a common and potentially fatal condition that can be difficult to diagnose because the clinical presentation is often nonspecific. The most common symptoms of PE are dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and cough. Other symptoms can include apprehension, diaphoresis, hemoptysis, and syncope.

The initial step in the evaluation of a patient with suspected PE is to determine the pretest probability of PE, which can be done using a validated clinical prediction rule such as the Wells criteria. If PE is considered likely based on the clinical prediction rule, the next step is to perform diagnostic testing to confirm the diagnosis. The D-dimer assay, which measures fibrin degradation products, is a useful initial test because it has a high sensitivity and negative predictive value for PE. A negative D-dimer result can effectively exclude PE in patients with a low or intermediate pretest probability of PE. However, D-dimer levels can be elevated in many other conditions (eg, malignancy, infection, pregnancy, recent surgery), so a positive D-dimer result is not specific for PE and requires further diagnostic testing with imaging studies.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 41-year-old man presents to the clinic with the complaints of abdominal discomfort and cramping for the past 4 months. He also mentions that he has grossly bloody stool and most of the time an urge to defecate. He has a history of bulimia with laxative abuse several years ago. He admits having lost about 5 lb in the past month. His temperature is 37° C (98.6° F), respiratory rate is 15/min, pulse is 77/min, and blood pressure is 105/86 mm Hg. On physical examination, a mild conjunctival pallor is evident, and the rectum is erythematous, indurated, and tender. Colonoscopy demonstrates continuous mucosal lesions throughout the rectum to the hepatic flexure of the colon. What is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question:
A 24-year-old woman presents to the clinic with chronic abdominal discomfort and cramping. She seeks medical attention now as she is concerned about the diarrhea that she has developed that is occasionally mixed with tiny streaks of blood. Her medical history is significant for lactose intolerance and asthma. She has a family history of wheat allergy and reports that she has tried to make herself vomit on several occasions to lose weight. After counseling the patient about the dangers of bulimia, physical examination reveals the rectum is red, inflamed, tender, and a perirectal abscess is seen draining purulent material. Colonoscopy demonstrates scattered mucosal lesions involving the colon and terminal ileum. A complete blood count is given below:
Hb%:   10 gm/dL
Total count (WBC):   12,500/mm3
Differential count:    
  Neutrophils: 50%
  Lymphocytes: 40%
  Monocytes: 5%
ESR:   22 mm/hr
What is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's chronic abdominal discomfort and cramping, diarrhea, and occasional rectal bleeding are suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The presence of a perirectal abscess and scattered mucosal lesions involving the colon and terminal ileum on colonoscopy are more suggestive of Crohn's disease than ulcerative colitis. Crohn's disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus and is characterized by transmural inflammation, which can lead to the development of fistulas, abscesses, and fissures. In contrast, ulcerative colitis is typically limited to the colon and rectum and causes mucosal inflammation only.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of persistent abdominal cramping, diarrhea, and rectal pain. During the past 2 weeks, she has had up to 4 small volumed, blood-tinged stools with mucus daily. She has also had intermittent fevers and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during this time. She traveled to Southeast Asia 3 months ago and received all appropriate vaccinations and medications beforehand. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 125/80 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft, and there is tenderness to palpation of the left lower quadrant with guarding but no rebound. Bowel sounds are normal. The stool is brown, and a test for occult blood is positive. Flexible sigmoidoscopy shows a granular, hyperemic, and friable rectal mucosa that bleeds easily on contact. Which of the following is this patient at greatest risk of developing?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal cramping, diarrhea, rectal pain, and bloody stools is suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The sigmoidoscopic findings of a granular, hyperemic, and friable rectal mucosa that bleeds easily on contact are consistent with ulcerative colitis (UC), a form of IBD that is limited to the colon and rectum. UC is a chronic, relapsing condition characterized by diffuse mucosal inflammation, which usually begins in the rectum and may extend proximally to involve part or all of the colon. The inflammation is limited to the mucosa and submucosa and is characterized by crypt abscesses and crypt distortion.

Patients with UC are at increased risk for colorectal cancer. The risk is related to the extent and duration of disease, with those having pancolitis for >8-10 years being at greatest risk. Other risk factors include a family history of sporadic colorectal cancer and concomitant primary sclerosing cholangitis. Patients with long-standing extensive UC should undergo surveillance colonoscopy every 1-2 years.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of intermittent lower abdominal cramps associated with diarrhea, bloating, and mild nausea. The presence of a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate and anemia further supports this diagnosis. The two main types of IBD are Crohn disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). CD can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus and is characterized by transmural inflammation, which can lead to complications such as strictures, abscesses, and fistulas. UC, on the other hand, is limited to the colon and rectum and causes mucosal inflammation only. The presence of right-sided colonic inflammation and ulceration on barium enema in this patient is most consistent with CD.

few_shot.question:
A 31-year-old woman visits the clinic with chronic diarrhea on most days for the past four months. She also complains of lower abdominal discomfort and cramping, which is relieved by episodes of diarrhea. She denies any recent change in her weight. Bowel movements are preceded by a sensation of urgency, associated with mucus discharge, and followed by a feeling of incomplete evacuation. The patient went camping several months earlier, and another member of her camping party fell ill recently. Her temperature is 37° C (98.6° F), respiratory rate is 15/min, pulse is 67/min, and blood pressure is 122/98 mm Hg. Her physical examination is unremarkable. A routine stool examination is within normal limits and blood test results show:
Hb%   13 gm/dL
Total count (WBC):   11,000/mm3
Differential count:    
  Neutrophils: 70%
  Lymphocytes: 25%
  Monocytes: 5%
ESR:   10 mm/hr
What is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of chronic diarrhea, lower abdominal discomfort relieved by defecation, urgency, mucus discharge, and a feeling of incomplete evacuation are suggestive of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). IBS is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic or recurrent abdominal pain or discomfort associated with altered bowel habits. The pain or discomfort is typically relieved by defecation and is often associated with a change in stool frequency or form. Other common symptoms include bloating, straining, urgency, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation. The diagnosis of IBS is clinical and is based on the Rome IV criteria, which require recurrent abdominal pain at least 1 day/week in the last 3 months that is associated with two or more of the following: related to defecation, associated with a change in frequency of stool, and/or associated with a change in form (appearance) of stool.
