few_shot.question: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a 2-day history of fever and productive cough. He has had similar episodes sporadically in the past with frequent episodes of thick, discolored nasal discharge. Physical examination shows diffuse crackles and rhonchi. An x-ray of the chest is shown. The most likely cause of recurrent infections in this patient is a dysfunction of which of the following cell types?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent respiratory infections, chronic cough, and thick, discolored nasal discharge are suggestive of primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), also known as Kartagener syndrome when associated with situs inversus. PCD is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by immotile cilia due to a dynein arm defect. This results in dysfunction of ciliated columnar cells, leading to impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Other manifestations include bronchiectasis, conductive hearing loss, and infertility in males due to immotile sperm.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old male with cystic fibrosis is brought to the emergency room by his mother after he had difficulty breathing. He previously received a lung transplant 6 months ago and was able to recover quickly from the operation. He is compliant with all of his medications and had been doing well with no major complaints until 2 weeks ago when he began to experience shortness of breath. Exam reveals a decreased FEV1/FVC ratio and biopsy reveals lymphocytic infiltration. Which of the following components is present in the airway zone characteristically affected by the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of lung transplantation, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, and lymphocytic infiltration on biopsy are suggestive of bronchiolitis obliterans, a form of chronic lung allograft dysfunction. Bronchiolitis obliterans is a late complication of lung transplantation that typically presents with progressive dyspnea and obstructive lung disease (manifested by decreased FEV1/FVC ratio) 6 months to 2 years after transplantation. Histologically, bronchiolitis obliterans is characterized by submucosal inflammation and fibrosis in the small airways (bronchioles), leading to luminal narrowing or complete obliteration.

The bronchioles are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium and do not contain cartilage, goblet cells, or pseudostratified columnar cells, which are characteristic of the larger airways (eg, bronchi).

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 28-year-old woman returns to the clinic to follow up on a recent abnormal cervical biopsy that demonstrated cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) I. The patient is quite anxious about the implications of this diagnosis. Her physical examination is within normal limits. Her vital signs do not show any abnormalities at this time. Her past medical, family, and social histories are all non-contributory. Which of the following is the appropriate management of a newly diagnosed CIN I in a 24-year-old patient?

answer_choices.A: Close observation, pap smear screening at 6 and 12 months, and HPV DNA testing at 12 months

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old G2P2 presents to her gynecologist to discuss the results of her diagnostic tests. She has no  current complaints or concurrent diseases. She underwent a tubal ligation after her last pregnancy. Her last Pap smear showed a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion and a reflex HPV test was positive. Colposcopic examination reveals areas of thin acetowhite epithelium with diffuse borders and fine punctation. The biopsy obtained from the suspicious areas shows CIN 1. Which of the following is an appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.D: Repeat cytology and HPV co-testing in 6 months

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) on Pap smear and positive high-risk HPV test are concerning for high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN 2 or 3). However, her biopsy results show only CIN 1, which is a low-grade lesion. This discrepancy between the cytology and histology results is concerning and could be due to a sampling error during colposcopy and biopsy. Therefore, the next step in management should be a diagnostic excisional procedure (eg, loop electrosurgical excision procedure, cold knife conization) to evaluate for CIN 2 or 3 or invasive cancer.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 56-year-old woman makes an appointment with her physician to discuss the results of her cervical cancer screening. She has been menopausal for  2 years and does not take hormone replacement therapy. Her previous Pap smear showed low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL); no HPV testing was performed. Her gynecologic examination is unremarkable. The results of her current Pap smear is as follows:
Specimen adequacy satisfactory for evaluation
Interpretation low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
Notes atrophic pattern
Which option is the next best step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
The American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP) recommends colposcopy for women of all ages with low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) on cervical cytology. LSIL is associated with productive HPV infection and is usually transient in young women. However, in postmenopausal women, LSIL is more likely to represent a persistent HPV infection and is less likely to regress spontaneously. Therefore, colposcopy is recommended to exclude high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) or cancer.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 39-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist for a routine visit. She has no complaints during this visit. She had an abnormal pap test 6 years ago that showed atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance. The sample was negative for human papillomavirus. On her follow-up Pap test 3 years later, there was no abnormality. The latest pap test results show atypical glandular cells with reactive changes in the cervical epithelium. The gynecologist decides to perform a colposcopy, and some changes are noted in this study of the cervical epithelium. The biopsy shows dysplastic changes in the epithelial cells. Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.C: Follow-up pap smear in one year

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's pap test results show atypical glandular cells, which is a high-risk finding. Atypical glandular cells can be a sign of adenocarcinoma in situ or invasive adenocarcinoma of the cervix or endometrium. The patient's colposcopy and biopsy results show dysplastic changes in the epithelial cells, which is concerning for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) or adenocarcinoma in situ. 

The next best step in the management of this patient is cold knife conization. This procedure involves the removal of a cone-shaped piece of tissue from the cervix, which includes the transformation zone where most cervical cancers arise. The tissue is then examined under a microscope to check for abnormal cells. Cold knife conization is preferred over loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) in this case because it provides a more intact specimen for histologic evaluation, which is important for determining the extent of disease and planning further treatment.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. Her last visit was 3 years ago. She feels well. One year ago, she underwent a tubectomy after the delivery of her third child. She does not take any medications. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A Pap smear shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) is a cytologic diagnosis that includes cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 2 and 3. CIN 2 and 3 are considered precursors to invasive cervical cancer. The appropriate management of HSIL on cytology is immediate colposcopy with endocervical sampling. If CIN 2 or 3 is confirmed on histology, treatment is warranted to prevent progression to invasive cancer. Treatment options include excisional procedures (eg, loop electrosurgical excision procedure [LEEP], cold knife conization) or ablative procedures (eg, cryotherapy, laser ablation). However, ablative therapy is not recommended if the transformation zone or endocervical canal cannot be visualized in its entirety, or if endocervical sampling indicates the presence of CIN. In such cases, an excisional procedure is preferred because it allows for histologic evaluation of the entire lesion and endocervical canal. 

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old woman comes to the physician because she had a positive pregnancy test at home. She reports feeling nauseated and has vomited several times over the past week. During this period, she has also had increased urinary frequency. She is sexually active with her boyfriend and they use condoms inconsistently. Her last menstrual period was 5 weeks ago. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A urine pregnancy test is positive. A pap smear is positive for a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. Colposcopy shows cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade II and III. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.A: Reevaluation with cytology and colposcopy 6 weeks after birth

few_shot.explanation:
This patient is pregnant and has a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) on Pap smear, which is confirmed by colposcopy as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) II and III. CIN II and III are considered precancerous lesions and are usually treated with excisional procedures (eg, loop electrosurgical excision procedure [LEEP], cold knife conization) or ablation (eg, cryotherapy, laser ablation). However, these procedures are associated with risks of cervical stenosis, cervical incompetence, preterm labor, and low birth weight. Therefore, they are avoided in pregnant patients unless invasive cancer is suspected. Instead, colposcopy with biopsy is performed to rule out invasive cancer. If invasive cancer is not identified, definitive treatment is delayed until after delivery. Close surveillance with repeat cytology and colposcopy is performed at 6 weeks postpartum.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 27-year-old man presents to the emergency room complaining of left shoulder pain for several weeks. He says that the pain often worsens when he tries to sleep on his left side. Although he tried several pain medications, none of the pain medications helped. He is an amateur tennis player who practices on weekends. He denies any trauma during his practice sessions. On examination of the shoulder joint, severe tenderness was present localized to the greater tuberosity of the left shoulder joint along with biceps tendon tenderness over the bicipital groove. The range of motion was limited to the left side. An X-ray of the joint showed narrowing of the acromiohumeral space with sclerosis and spurring of the acromion. Routine blood test results are normal except for the rheumatoid factor, which is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old woman presents to her primary care provider for shoulder pain. She reports that she initially thought the pain was due to "sleeping funny" on the arm, but that the pain has now lasted for 4 weeks. She denies trauma to the joint and says that the pain is worse when reaching overhead to retrieve things from her kitchen cabinets. On physical exam, the patient's shoulders are symmetric, and the right lateral shoulder is tender to palpation. The shoulder has full passive and active range of motion, although pain is reproduced on active abduction of the right arm above 90 degrees. Pain is also reproduced on passively internally rotating and then lifting the shoulder. The patient is able to resist elbow flexion without pain, and she otherwise has 5/5 strength. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's shoulder pain, which is worse with overhead activities and is reproduced with passive internal rotation and abduction, is suggestive of rotator cuff tendinopathy. The rotator cuff is a group of four muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis) that stabilize the glenohumeral joint and allow for shoulder abduction and rotation. The supraspinatus muscle is most commonly affected, and patients often report pain with overhead activities or when lying on the affected shoulder. On physical examination, pain is often reproduced with abduction (especially between 60 and 120 degrees, known as the "painful arc") or with maneuvers that compress the supraspinatus tendon against the acromion (eg, Neer impingement sign, Hawkin's impingement sign).

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man presents with pain and a limited range of motion in his right shoulder. He is a collegiate baseball player and says he has not been playing for approx. 1 week because his shoulder hurts when he throws. He also noticed trouble raising his arm over his head. He describes the pain as moderate, dull, and aching in character and worse when he moves his arm above his shoulder or when he lays in bed on his side. He denies any recent acute trauma to the shoulder or other joint pain. The medical history is significant for asthma, which is managed medically. The current medications include albuterol inhaled and fluticasone. He reports a 5-year history of chewing tobacco but denies smoking, alcohol, or drug use. The temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F); blood pressure is 110/85 mm Hg; pulse is 97/min; respiratory rate is 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. The physical examination is significant for tenderness to palpation on the anterolateral aspect of the right shoulder. The active range of motion on abduction of the right shoulder is decreased. The passive range of motion is intact. No swelling, warmth, or erythema is noted. The sensation is intact. The deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. The peripheral pulses are 2+. The laboratory results are all within normal limits. A plain radiograph of the right shoulder shows no evidence of fracture or bone deformities. An MRI of the right shoulder shows increased T1 and T2 signals in the rotator cuff tendon. Which of the following is the best initial course of treatment for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with rotator cuff tendinitis, a common cause of shoulder pain in athletes who perform repetitive overhead activities (eg, baseball pitchers, swimmers, tennis players). The rotator cuff is composed of four muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) that function to stabilize the glenohumeral joint and coordinate shoulder movement. The supraspinatus is the most commonly affected muscle. Patients typically present with a gradual onset of lateral shoulder pain that is worse with overhead activities and often radiates down the arm. Pain may also be present at rest and at night, particularly when lying on the affected shoulder. On examination, there is often tenderness to palpation over the greater tuberosity and a painful arc of motion with shoulder abduction (due to impingement of the rotator cuff tendon between the humeral head and acromion). The initial treatment of rotator cuff tendinitis is conservative and includes rest, activity modification, and NSAIDs for pain control. Physical therapy to strengthen the rotator cuff and shoulder girdle muscles is also beneficial. 

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of severe pain in his left shoulder for several days. He did not fall or injure his shoulder. He has a history of osteoarthritis of both knees that is well-controlled with indomethacin. He spends most of his time at a retirement facility and does not do any sports. There is no family history of serious illness. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows tenderness of the greater tuberosity of the left humerus. There is no swelling or erythema. The patient is unable to slowly adduct his arm after it is passively abducted to 90 degrees. External rotation is limited by pain. Subacromial injection of lidocaine does not relieve his symptoms. An x-ray of the left shoulder shows sclerosis of the acromion and humeral head. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's severe shoulder pain, inability to slowly adduct his arm after passive abduction (positive drop-arm test), and limited external rotation are suggestive of a rotator cuff tear. The rotator cuff is composed of the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis muscles. The supraspinatus muscle is the most commonly affected, and its tendon passes beneath the acromion. Tears are most common in patients >60 years of age and can occur due to age-related degeneration or trauma. This patient's smoking history may have contributed to degeneration of the rotator cuff tendons, as smoking can cause local ischemia.

The diagnosis of rotator cuff tear is suggested by clinical findings and confirmed by musculoskeletal ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging. Ultrasound is highly sensitive and specific for full-thickness rotator cuff tears and is less expensive than MRI.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old woman presents to her primary care provider with a 2-month history of insidious onset of left shoulder pain. It only occurs at the extremes of her range of motion and has made it difficult to sleep on the affected side. She has noticed increasing difficulty with activities of daily living, including brushing her hair and putting on or taking off her blouse and bra. She denies a history of shoulder trauma, neck pain, arm/hand weakness, numbness, or paresthesias. Her medical history is remarkable for type 2 diabetes mellitus, for which she takes metformin and glipizide. Her physical examination reveals a marked decrease in both active and passive range of motion of the left shoulder, with forwarding flexion to 75°, abduction to 75°, external rotation to 45°, and internal rotation to 15° with significant pain. Rotator cuff strength is normal. AP, scapular Y, and axillary plain film radiographs are reported as normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Adhesive capsulitis, also known as frozen shoulder, is a common cause of shoulder pain and disability. It is characterized by a gradual onset of diffuse shoulder pain with progressive limitation of both active and passive range of motion. The etiology is unknown, but it is thought to be due to inflammation and fibrosis of the glenohumeral joint capsule. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, thyroid disease, and prolonged immobilization. The condition is more common in women and in patients aged 40-60 years. The diagnosis is clinical and is supported by normal radiographs of the shoulder. Treatment is conservative and includes physical therapy and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections can be considered for patients with refractory symptoms.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 20-year-old woman college volleyball player presents with left shoulder pain and difficulty elevating her left arm. Her temperature is 37.0℃ (98.6℉), the blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg, the pulse is 66/min, the respiratory rate is 13/min, and the oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. On physical examination, she is alert and cooperative. The left shoulder is normal on the inspection with no swelling or bony deformities. There is point tenderness to palpation of the anterolateral aspect of the left shoulder. Active range of motion of abduction of the left arm is restricted to 70°. Passive range of motion of abduction of the left arm is normal but elicits pain. Strength in the left shoulder is 4/5 and strength in the right shoulder is 5/5. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. The sensation is intact. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.A: IV disk protrusion at the C4-5 level

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of shoulder pain and difficulty elevating her arm, especially after a volleyball game, is suggestive of a rotator cuff injury. The rotator cuff is a group of muscles and their tendons that act to stabilize the shoulder. These muscles are the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis. The supraspinatus muscle is the most commonly injured, as it is used to initiate abduction of the arm. This patient's difficulty with active abduction but normal passive abduction is consistent with a tear of the supraspinatus muscle.

So, the answer is [B].

A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of flank pain, myalgia, and reddish discoloration of her urine for the past 2 days. One week ago, she had a fever and a sore throat and was prescribed antibiotics. She is otherwise healthy and has no history of serious illness. Her temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 128/75 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a soft abdomen and no costovertebral angle tenderness. Examination of the mouth and pharynx shows no abnormalities. There is a faint maculopapular rash over the trunk and extremities. Serum creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows:
Protein 2+
Blood 2+

WBC 12/hpf
Bacteria none
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

This patient's presentation of fever, rash, and acute kidney injury (AKI) following administration of a medication is suggestive of acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). AIN is most commonly due to an allergic drug reaction, especially to antibiotics (eg, beta-lactams, sulfonamides), nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and proton pump inhibitors. Patients typically present with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, rash, and eosinophilia (in approximately 30% of cases), along with renal manifestations of AKI and sterile pyuria (due to the inflammatory nature of the disease). Hematuria can also be seen due to accompanying glomerular inflammation. Diagnosis is confirmed by renal biopsy, which shows an interstitial mononuclear cell infiltrate with tubulitis. Discontinuation of the offending drug typically leads to improvement in renal function.

few_shot.question:
A 27-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for fever and generalized malaise. Her symptoms began approximately 3 days ago, when she noticed pain with urination and mild blood in her urine. Earlier this morning she experienced chills, flank pain, and mild nausea. Approximately 1 month ago she had the "flu" that was rhinovirus positive and was treated with supportive management. She has a past medical history of asthma. She is currently sexually active and uses contraception inconsistently. She occasionally drinks alcohol and denies illicit drug use. Family history is significant for her mother having systemic lupus erythematosus. Her temperature is 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 125/87 mmHg, pulse is 101/min, and respirations are 18/min. On physical examination, she appears uncomfortable. There is left-sided flank, suprapubic, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Urine studies are obtained and a urinalysis is demonstrated below:

Color: Amber
pH: 6.8
Leukocyte: Positive

answer_choices.A: Focal and segmental sclerosis of the glomeruli and mesangium
answer_choices.D: Suppurative inflammation with interstitial neutrophilic infiltration

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, chills, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness in the setting of dysuria and hematuria is consistent with acute pyelonephritis. Acute pyelonephritis is a urinary tract infection that has ascended to the kidneys. It is most commonly caused by gram-negative bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, which is suggested by the positive nitrite test on urinalysis. The pathogenesis of acute pyelonephritis involves bacterial ascent from the bladder into the renal pelvis and then into the renal parenchyma. The infection can cause renal inflammation and subsequent renal scarring if not treated promptly. On histology, acute pyelonephritis is characterized by suppurative inflammation, in which neutrophils infiltrate the renal interstitium and renal tubules, causing patchy necrosis and diffuse interstitial inflammation. Abscesses may form in the renal pelvis, calyces, and medulla.

few_shot.question: A 34-year-old woman presents to her primary care provider after intermittently passing bright pink urine over several days. She is concerned this discoloration is due to blood. Her medical history is unremarkable, she denies being sick in the past weeks and has only taken a couple of diclofenac capsules for pelvic pain associated to her menstrual period. She does not drink alcohol or smoke cigarettes. At the doctor’s office, her blood pressure  is 150/90 mm Hg, pulse is 80/min, respiratory rate is 18/min, and temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F). On physical exam, she has 2+ pitting edema up to her knees. A urinalysis is taken which shows red blood cells, red blood cell casts, and acanthocytes. No proteinuria was detected. Her serum creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL, serum potassium 4.8 mEq/L, serum sodium 140 mEq/L, serum chloride 102 mEq/L. answer_choices.C: Intravenous fluid therapy and electrolyte correction

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypertension, hematuria, and acute kidney injury is suggestive of glomerulonephritis. The presence of red blood cell casts and dysmorphic red blood cells (acanthocytes) on urinalysis is indicative of glomerular hematuria. The most common causes of glomerulonephritis include infection-related (eg, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis), immune-mediated (eg, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis), and vasculitic (eg, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis) processes. The absence of significant proteinuria makes nephrotic syndrome unlikely. The patient's recent use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) could cause acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), but AIN typically presents with white blood cell casts and sterile pyuria, not red blood cell casts. In addition, NSAID-induced nephropathy usually presents with a more subacute or chronic course. Therefore, the next best step in management is to perform a renal biopsy to determine the underlying etiology of this patient's glomerulonephritis.

few_shot.question:
A 33-year-old woman presents to the clinic complaining of yellowish discoloration of her skin and eyes, mild fever, and body aches. She has had this problem for 6 months, but it has become worse over the past few weeks. She also complains of repeated bouts of bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. The past medical history is noncontributory. She takes no medication. Both of her parents are alive with no significant disease. She works as a dental hygienist and drinks wine occasionally on weekends. Today, the vital signs include blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, pulse rate 90/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and temperature 36.6°C (97.8°F). On physical examination, she appears uncomfortable. The skin and sclera are jaundiced. The heart has a regular rate and rhythm, and the lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen is soft with mild hepatosplenomegaly. There is no tenderness or rebound tenderness. The digital rectal examination reveals blood and mucus in the rectal vault. Laboratory studies show:
Serum sodium 140 mEq/L
Serum potassium 3.8 mEq/L
  Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 250 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 170 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 120 U/L
Which of the following antibodies would you expect to find in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and hepatosplenomegaly is suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The presence of jaundice and elevated liver enzymes suggests a hepatobiliary manifestation of IBD, most likely primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). PSC is a chronic, progressive disease characterized by inflammation, fibrosis, and strictures of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. It is strongly associated with IBD, particularly ulcerative colitis (UC), and is often asymptomatic until advanced disease develops. Symptoms of advanced PSC can include fatigue, pruritus, and jaundice. In patients with known IBD, the development of abnormal liver function tests should raise suspicion for PSC, and these patients should undergo additional testing with magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography or endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography.

Perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA) are found in the serum of approximately 60%-70% of patients with UC. Although they are also positive in a number of other autoimmune conditions (including PSC), they can support the diagnosis of UC in the appropriate clinical context.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 25-year-old female is brought to the emergency department by her family. They found her somnolent next to her computer and scattered pill bottles over two hours ago. The family cannot recall the types of pill bottles that they found and did not bring them to the ED. The patient's past medical history is notable for anxiety, obesity, hypertension, and polycystic ovarian syndrome. She is currently not on any medications other than an exercise program with which she is non-compliant. A physical exam is performed and is within normal limits. The patient begins communicating with the physician and states that she did take acetaminophen but it was only a few pills. Her temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), pulse is 82/min, blood pressure is 125/85 mmHg, respirations are 11/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Which of the following is the next best step in management?

few_shot.question:
A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a suicide attempt. Her mother found her next to an empty bottle of acetaminophen in the bathroom. The patient reports that she ingested about twenty-five 500 mg pills. She took the pills 1 hour prior to arrival to the emergency department. She has a history of major depressive disorder. She does not smoke or use illicit drugs. Current medications include fluoxetine. She is oriented to person, place, and time. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL
Leukocyte count 8,000/mm3
Platelet count 150,000/mm3
Serum
Prothrombin time 10.5 sec (INR=1.0)
Na+ 141 mEq/L
K+ 4.2 mEq/L
Cl- 101 mEq/L
HCO3- 25 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen 10 g/dL
Creatinine 0.5 g/dL
Ca2+ 8.8 mg/dL
Total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL
AST 22 U/L
ALT 25 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase 62 U/L
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"
few_shot.explanation:
Acetaminophen overdose is a common cause of acute liver failure. The toxic metabolite of acetaminophen, N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), is normally conjugated with glutathione and renally excreted. However, in the setting of overdose, glutathione stores become depleted, and NAPQI accumulates, leading to hepatocellular necrosis. 

Activated charcoal is an important treatment modality for acetaminophen overdose if administered within 4 hours of ingestion. It adsorbs acetaminophen in the gastrointestinal tract, reducing systemic absorption.

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being found unresponsive on the floor by her boyfriend. Paramedics found several empty pill bottles next to her on the floor. According to her boyfriend, she has a history of insomnia and generalized anxiety disorder and was recently diagnosed with depression. Her temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 64/min, respirations are 10/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 112/75 mm Hg. On examination, she does not open her eyes, makes incomprehensible sounds, and extends her extremities when a painful stimulus is applied. Her pupils are 3 mm and reactive to light. The corneal reflex is normal and gag reflex is absent. There is diffuse hypotonia and decreased deep tendon reflexes. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. She is intubated for airway protection. Mechanical ventilation and an infusion of 0.9% saline are begun. Which of the following would most likely reverse this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of depression, anxiety, and insomnia, along with her presentation of decreased level of consciousness, decreased deep tendon reflexes, and normal vital signs, is suggestive of benzodiazepine overdose. Benzodiazepines are commonly used to treat anxiety and insomnia, and are also a frequent choice in suicide attempts due to their wide availability. Overdose can cause CNS depression, resulting in symptoms ranging from drowsiness to coma. Benzodiazepines can also cause decreased deep tendon reflexes and, in severe cases, respiratory depression.

Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine receptor and can reverse the effects of benzodiazepines. However, it should be used with caution as it can precipitate withdrawal and seizures in patients with long-term benzodiazepine use.

few_shot.question: A man is brought into the emergency department by police. The patient was found somnolent in the park and did not respond to questioning. The patient's past medical history is unknown, and he is poorly kempt. The patient's personal belongings include prescription medications and illicit substances such as alprazolam, diazepam, marijuana, cocaine, alcohol, acetaminophen, and a baggie containing an unknown powder. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's somnolence, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils are suggestive of opioid toxicity. Opioids are commonly used drugs of abuse and are often mixed with other substances, such as benzodiazepines or alcohol, to enhance their effects. Opioid toxicity can cause life-threatening respiratory depression and should be treated immediately with naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist. Naloxone can be administered intranasally or intravenously and has a rapid onset of action. It should be administered to any patient with suspected opioid toxicity who has a decreased level of consciousness or respiratory depression.

few_shot.question:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by fire and rescue after an apparent suicide attempt. She reports ingesting several pills 6 hours prior to presentation but cannot recall what they were. No pills were found on the scene. She complains of severe malaise, ringing in her ears, and anxiety. Her past medical history is notable for bipolar disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, rheumatoid arthritis, obesity, and diabetes. She takes lithium, methotrexate, metformin, and glyburide. She has a reported history of benzodiazepine and prescription opioid abuse. Her temperature is 102.2°F (39°C), blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 26/min. On exam, she appears diaphoretic and pale. Results from an arterial blood gas are shown:

pH: 7.48
PaCO2: 32 mmHg
HCO3-: 23 mEq/L

This patient should be treated with which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with salicylate toxicity. Salicylates are found in aspirin and oil of wintergreen. Symptoms of toxicity include tinnitus, tachypnea, fever, and vomiting. Salicylates directly stimulate the respiratory center in the medulla, leading to hyperventilation and a primary respiratory alkalosis. An anion gap metabolic acidosis can also occur due to several mechanisms, including uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation, which leads to increased conversion of glucose to lactic acid and pyruvic acid. In addition, salicylates inhibit the Krebs cycle, leading to accumulation of ketoacids. The anion gap is calculated as follows: Anion gap = [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]). The normal anion gap is 8-12 mEq/L. 

The treatment of salicylate toxicity includes gastrointestinal decontamination with activated charcoal, which can be repeated to interrupt enterohepatic and enteroenteric recirculation of the drug. Alkalinization of the urine with sodium bicarbonate enhances the ionization and renal excretion of salicylates. Hemodialysis is indicated in severe cases, such as those with altered mental status, pulmonary edema, renal failure, or a significantly elevated salicylate level.

Hence, the answer is [D].

question: A 35-year-old woman arrives to the clinic complaining of progressive urinary leakage that has occurred for the past 1 year. At first, she would notice leakage only during athletic exercise, but now the incontinence occurs even when she laughs or coughs. The patient states that she goes to the bathroom more frequently to try to prevent “wetting myself.” She wakes up once a night to urinate. She denies dysuria, hematuria, abdominal pain, and abnormal vaginal discharge. The patient has bipolar syndrome and takes lithium. She had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery 10 years ago and a cesarean section 4 years ago. She has had no other surgeries. She drinks at least 6 glasses of water a day but may drink more on days she goes for a long run. She also has a large coffee in the morning and another coffee mid-day if she “needs to focus.” The patient denies tobacco, alcohol, and other recreational drug use. Pelvic examination and speculum examination are unremarkable. When that patient is asked to Valsalva, leakage of urine is observed. A urinalysis, including specific gravity, is within normal limits. A beta-human chorionic gonadotropin is negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s symptoms?

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old, multiparous, woman comes to the physician because of urinary leakage for the past 6 months. She involuntarily loses a small amount of urine after experiencing a sudden, painful sensation in the bladder. She has difficulty making it to the bathroom in time, and feels nervous when there is no bathroom nearby. She also started having to urinate at night. She does not have hematuria, abdominal pain, or pelvic pain. She has insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus type 2, and underwent surgical treatment for symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse 3 years ago. Menopause was 6 years ago, and she is not on hormone replacement therapy. She works as an administrative manager, and drinks 3–4 cups of coffee daily at work. On physical examination, there is no suprapubic tenderness. Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities and Q-tip test was negative. Ultrasound of the bladder shows a normal post-void residual urine. Which of the following is the primary underlying etiology for this patient's urinary incontinence?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of urinary urgency, frequency, nocturia, and urge incontinence are suggestive of overactive bladder syndrome (OAB). OAB is caused by involuntary detrusor muscle contractions during the bladder filling phase. These contractions generate a sudden, strong desire to void (urgency) that is difficult to defer, leading to incontinence. The exact etiology of OAB is unknown, but it is thought to involve an interplay of myogenic and neurogenic factors leading to detrusor overactivity. Risk factors for OAB include increasing age, obesity, and conditions that affect the nervous system (eg, stroke, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord lesions). Diabetes mellitus is also a risk factor for OAB, likely due to polyuria and/or diabetic cystopathy (a form of autonomic neuropathy).

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old, multiparous, woman comes to the physician because of urinary leakage for the past 4 months. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's urinary incontinence is characterized by urgency, frequency, nocturia, and urge incontinence (ie, involuntary leakage of urine associated with a sudden, compelling desire to void). These symptoms are suggestive of overactive bladder syndrome, which is caused by increased detrusor muscle activity. Overactive bladder syndrome can be idiopathic or secondary to conditions such as bladder outlet obstruction, neurologic disorders, and bladder stones. In this patient, the most likely cause of overactive bladder syndrome is detrusor overactivity due to her diabetes mellitus. Chronic hyperglycemia can lead to diabetic cystopathy, which is characterized by impaired bladder sensation, increased bladder capacity, and decreased detrusor contractility. However, some patients with diabetic cystopathy may also have detrusor overactivity, which can cause symptoms of overactive bladder syndrome.

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old multiparous woman comes to the physician for the evaluation of episodes of involuntary urine leakage for the past 6 months. She is retired and lives at an assisted-living facility. She has insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus type 2. Her mother received a ventriculoperitoneal shunt around her age. She walks without any problems. Sensation to pinprick and light touch is normal. Which of the following is the primary underlying etiology for this patient's urinary incontinence?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's urinary incontinence is characterized by the involuntary loss of urine during episodes of increased intra-abdominal pressure (eg, laughing, sneezing), which is consistent with stress urinary incontinence (SUI). SUI is caused by urethral hypermobility or intrinsic sphincteric deficiency. Urethral hypermobility is often due to pelvic floor muscle weakness and is common in multiparous women. Intrinsic sphincteric deficiency is due to a weakened or damaged urethral sphincter and is less common.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old female presents to her pediatrician due to lack of menstruation. She states that she developed breasts 4 years ago but has not experienced menses yet. The patient denies abdominal pain and has no past medical history. Her mother underwent menarche at age 13. The patient is a volleyball player at school, is single, and has never attempted intercourse. At this visit, her temperature is 98.3°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 110/76 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 14/min. She is 5 feet 7 inches tall and weighs 116 pounds (BMI 18.2 kg/m^2). Exam shows Tanner IV breasts, Tanner I pubic hair, and minimal axillary hair. External genitalia are normal, but the vagina is a 5-centimeter blind pouch. Genetic testing is performed. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's lack of menstruation, minimal pubic and axillary hair, and blind vaginal pouch are concerning for androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS), also known as testicular feminization. AIS is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by a mutation in the androgen receptor gene. Individuals with AIS are phenotypically female but have a 46,XY karyotype. They have testes, which are often found in the inguinal canal or abdomen, and secrete normal-to-elevated amounts of testosterone. However, due to the androgen receptor defect, tissues are unable to respond to testosterone or dihydrotestosterone. As a result, individuals with AIS have a female phenotype, with scant sexual hair and a blind vaginal pouch. They also have breast development due to peripheral conversion of testosterone to estradiol. The diagnosis is confirmed by finding a 46,XY karyotype on chromosomal analysis.

The best next step in management is gonadectomy to prevent the development of malignancy, which can occur in up to 10% of cases. Gonadectomy is typically performed after puberty to allow for spontaneous breast development. After gonadectomy, lifelong estrogen replacement therapy is required to maintain secondary sexual characteristics and bone health.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has never menstruated. She is at the 15th percentile for weight and 45th percentile for height. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows facial hair, clitoromegaly, and coarse, curly pubic hair that extends to the inner surface of both thighs. She has no glandular breast tissue. Ultrasound shows inguinal testes but no uterus or ovaries. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause for this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's lack of menstruation, presence of facial hair, clitoromegaly, and absence of breast tissue suggest a disorder of sexual development (DSD). The presence of testes and absence of a uterus and ovaries suggest a 46,XY DSD. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is 5-α reductase deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder that impairs the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). DHT is necessary for the development of the male external genitalia in utero. Therefore, patients with 5-α reductase deficiency are often raised as females due to their predominantly female-appearing external genitalia at birth. However, they typically have a marked increase in muscle mass and deepening of the voice at puberty due to the surge in testosterone, which is not affected by this disorder. The testosterone surge can also lead to growth of the phallus (clitoromegaly or micropenis) and increased body hair. Because testosterone can weakly activate the estrogen receptor, patients may also develop small amounts of breast tissue. However, this patient's lack of breast tissue suggests that her testosterone is being converted to estrogen at a very low rate, if at all.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of vaginal bleeding for 2 days. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. There is coarse pubic hair that does not extend to the inner thigh. The remainder of the examination show no abnormalities. An x-ray of the left hand and wrist shows a bone age of 11 years. Her serum luteinizing hormone concentration is 0.1 mIU/mL (N < 0.2 mIU/mL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's vaginal bleeding, breast development, and pubic hair are concerning for precocious puberty, defined as the development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls and age 9 in boys. The most common cause of precocious puberty in girls is idiopathic central precocious puberty (CPP), which is due to premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Other causes of precocious puberty include peripheral precocious puberty (PPP) due to autonomous sex steroid production, and exogenous exposure to sex steroids.

The first step in the evaluation of precocious puberty is to measure basal luteinizing hormone (LH) levels. If the LH level is in the prepubertal range (as in this patient), a GnRH stimulation test should be performed to distinguish between CPP and PPP. In CPP, GnRH will stimulate the release of LH, whereas in PPP, GnRH will have no effect because the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is not involved.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because menarche has not yet occurred. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's obesity, acanthosis nigricans, and amenorrhea are suggestive of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a disorder characterized by hyperandrogenism and chronic anovulation. The exact etiology is unknown, but insulin resistance is thought to play a key role. Hyperinsulinemia stimulates the ovaries to produce androgens, leading to hirsutism, acne, and anovulation. It also decreases hepatic production of sex hormone-binding globulin, leading to increased levels of free testosterone. In addition, insulin resistance leads to acanthosis nigricans, a skin condition characterized by hyperpigmented, velvety plaques in the intertriginous areas.

The diagnosis of PCOS is clinical, based on the presence of hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction. Laboratory studies typically show an elevated LH:FSH ratio (>2:1), but this finding is not necessary to make the diagnosis.

She also complains of pain during sexual intercourse and sometimes after urination. Her past medical history is noncontributory. She takes oral contraceptives and a multivitamin daily. She has had two male sexual partners in her lifetime and uses condoms inconsistently. Today, her vitals are normal. On pelvic exam, she has vulvovaginal erythema and a 'strawberry cervix' that is tender to motion, with minimal green-yellow malodorous discharge. A swab of the vaginal wall is analyzed for pH at bedside. Vaginal pH is 5.8. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of a frothy, yellowish discharge, vulvovaginal erythema, and a 'strawberry cervix' is consistent with trichomoniasis. Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. It is characterized by a purulent, malodorous, yellow-green discharge, and vulvar irritation. On physical examination, a 'strawberry cervix' (punctate cervical hemorrhages) or vulva may be seen. The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of motile trichomonads on a saline wet mount microscopy. The pH of the vaginal discharge is usually elevated (>4.5).

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of vaginal discharge. She has no pain or pruritus. She is sexually active with one male partner and uses condoms inconsistently. Pelvic examination shows a malodorous gray vaginal discharge. Microscopic examination of the vaginal discharge is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's malodorous vaginal discharge and the presence of clue cells on microscopic examination are indicative of bacterial vaginosis (BV). BV is a polymicrobial clinical syndrome that results from the replacement of the normal hydrogen peroxide-producing Lactobacillus species in the vagina with high concentrations of anaerobic bacteria (eg, Prevotella, Mobiluncus), G vaginalis, Ureaplasma, Mycoplasma, and other fastidious or uncultivated anaerobes. Some women with BV are asymptomatic; others may present with a malodorous ("fishy") vaginal discharge. The discharge is typically thin and grayish white. Itching and irritation are usually absent. The diagnosis of BV is confirmed by the presence of at least 3 of the following 4 Amsel criteria: (1) homogeneous, thin, white discharge that smoothly coats the vaginal walls; (2) presence of clue cells on microscopic examination; (3) vaginal fluid pH >4.5; and (4) a fishy odor of vaginal discharge before or after addition of 10% KOH (ie, positive whiff test).

question: An 18-year-old college student presents to the student health clinic complaining of excessive sleepiness. He reports that he goes to bed around 9 p.m. and wakes up for class at 8 a.m.. He naps between classes for a total of 4 hours during the day. Despite this, he wakes up feeling exhausted. He easily falls asleep during class and while studying. This has started to affect both his academics and his social life. On weekends, he can sleep up to 20 hours a day. He reports 2 recent episodes of sudden generalized body weakness along with ptosis and difficulty speaking that occurred after he became angry. Each episode lasted about 10 seconds, but he says he felt back to normal within 15 minutes without any persistent deficits. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 17. few_shot.question: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of generalized fatigue and an inability to concentrate in school for the past 4 months. During this period, she has had excessive daytime sleepiness. While going to sleep, she sees cartoon characters playing in her room. She wakes up once or twice every night. While awakening, she feels stiff and cannot move for a couple of minutes. She goes to sleep by 9 pm every night and wakes up at 7 am. She takes two to three 15-minute naps during the day and wakes up feeling refreshed. During the past week while listening to a friend tell a joke, she had an episode in which her head tilted and jaw dropped for a few seconds; it resolved spontaneously. Her father has schizoaffective disorder and her parents are divorced. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of excessive daytime sleepiness, hypnagogic hallucinations (ie, hallucinations while going to sleep), sleep paralysis (ie, inability to move while awakening), and cataplexy (ie, sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotions) are suggestive of narcolepsy. Narcolepsy is a chronic sleep disorder characterized by overwhelming daytime drowsiness and sudden attacks of sleep. It is thought to be due to a deficiency in hypocretin (orexin), a neurotransmitter that regulates arousal, wakefulness, and appetite. The condition often begins in childhood or adolescence.

The mainstay of treatment for narcolepsy is scheduled naps and medications. Modafinil is a non-amphetamine stimulant that is considered first-line treatment for excessive daytime sleepiness in patients with narcolepsy. It is thought to work by increasing dopaminergic signaling. If modafinil is ineffective or not tolerated, amphetamine-like stimulants (eg, methylphenidate) are second-line treatment.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 63-year-old man presents to his primary care physician complaining of excessive daytime sleepiness. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's excessive daytime sleepiness, loud snoring, and obesity are suggestive of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). OSA is characterized by repetitive episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to recurrent arousals and sleep fragmentation. The most common cause of OSA is obesity, which leads to poor oropharyngeal tone and increased upper airway resistance. This is due to fatty infiltration of the soft tissues surrounding the upper airway, leading to a narrowed airway lumen. The airway is most likely to collapse during sleep, when the muscles surrounding the airway are relaxed. This leads to recurrent episodes of apnea and hypopnea, which can cause hypoxemia and hypercapnia. The hypoxemia and hypercapnia can lead to morning headaches, as seen in this patient. The recurrent arousals lead to nonrestorative sleep and excessive daytime sleepiness. The sleep fragmentation can also lead to mood disturbances, such as depression.

few_shot.question:
A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician for right lower abdominal pain for 6 months. She has multiple non-bloody, watery bowel movements daily and experiences abdominal cramping. Sometimes, she feels sudden palpitations, is short of breath, and her face becomes red. She has lost 7 kg over the past 3 months. She went on a 3-week hiking trip to Cambodia 6 months ago. She has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years. Her temperature is 37˚C (98.6°F), her pulse is 72/min and her blood pressure is 125/70 mm Hg. On physical examination, tiny blood vessels are noted on her face and arms. Lung auscultation shows bilateral wheezing. The abdomen is soft and nondistended. There is localized tenderness to the right lower quadrant, but no rebound tenderness or guarding. Laboratory studies show:
Leukocyte count 4,600 /mm3
Segmented neutrophils 61 %
Eosinophils 2 %
Platelet count 254,000 /mm3
Hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL
Serum
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 110 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 128 IU/L
C-reactive protein 8 mg/dL (N = 0–10)
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of episodic flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing are suggestive of carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid tumors are neuroendocrine tumors that classically originate in the gastrointestinal tract (especially the small intestine) or bronchi. They secrete vasoactive substances such as serotonin, kallikrein, and tachykinins, which can cause symptoms of carcinoid syndrome. However, these substances are metabolized by the liver, so symptoms usually do not occur unless there is hepatic metastasis or the tumor is located in the bronchi, thereby bypassing first-pass metabolism in the liver. This patient's elevated liver enzymes suggest hepatic metastasis.

Carcinoid syndrome is characterized by cutaneous flushing (due to serotonin), diarrhea (due to increased serotonin and bradykinin), and bronchospasm (due to tachykinins). Right-sided valvular heart disease can also occur due to fibrosis from serotonin, leading to tricuspid regurgitation and/or pulmonic stenosis. However, left-sided heart disease is rare because serotonin is metabolized by monoamine oxidase in the lung vasculature.

few_shot.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain, fatigue, and low-volume diarrhea of intermittent frequency for the past 4 months. She also reports weight loss and believes it to be due to a decreased appetite. She has noticed herself being more "forgetful" and she denies seeing any blood in her stool, changes in diet, infection, or recent travel history. Hemoglobin: 10.8 g/dL

Mean corpuscular volume: 118 µm^3

A colonoscopy is performed and demonstrates focal ulcerations with polypoid mucosal changes adjacent to normal appearing mucosa. A biopsy is obtained and shows ulcerations and acute and chronic inflammatory changes. Involvement of which of the following sites most likely explains this patient's clinical presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of right lower quadrant abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss is suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The presence of focal ulcerations with polypoid mucosal changes adjacent to normal appearing mucosa on colonoscopy is consistent with Crohn disease (CD), a form of IBD that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus. CD most commonly affects the terminal ileum and colon, and up to 30% of patients have isolated small bowel disease. The skip lesions seen on colonoscopy (ie, areas of disease separated by normal mucosa) are virtually pathognomonic for CD.

The presence of macrocytic anemia and forgetfulness in this patient is suggestive of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency. Cobalamin is absorbed in the terminal ileum, and deficiency can occur in patients with CD due to inflammation of the terminal ileum. This can lead to decreased absorption of dietary cobalamin or disruption of the ileal receptors responsible for uptake of the cobalamin-intrinsic factor complex.

few_shot.question: A 70-year-old man with a history of chronic constipation presents to the emergency department with a two-day history of left lower quadrant abdominal pain. He is found to have a temperature of 100.8F, BP 140/90, HR 85, and RR 16. On physical examination, he is tender to light palpation in the left lower quadrant and exhibits voluntary guarding. Rectal examination reveals heme-positive stool. Laboratory values are unremarkable except for a WBC count of 12,500 with a left shift. Which of the following tests would be most useful in the diagnosis of this patient's disease?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic constipation, left lower quadrant abdominal pain, and fever is suggestive of diverticulitis. Diverticulitis is an inflammation of the diverticula, which are small, bulging pouches that can form in the lining of the digestive system. They are found most often in the lower part of the large intestine (colon). Diverticula are common, especially after age 40, and seldom cause problems. Sometimes, however, one or more of the pouches become inflamed or infected, causing severe abdominal pain, fever, and a change in bowel habits.

The most useful test in the diagnosis of diverticulitis is an abdominal CT scan, which can show inflamed or infected pouches and confirm a diagnosis of diverticulitis. It can also indicate the severity of diverticulitis and guide treatment.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: An institutionalized 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of abdominal pain and distension for 12 hours. The pain was acute in onset and is a cramping-type pain associated with nausea, vomiting, and constipation. He has a history of chronic constipation and has used laxatives for years. There is no history of inflammatory bowel disease in his family. He has not been hospitalized recently. There is no recent history of weight loss or change in bowel habits. On physical examination, the patient appears ill. The abdomen is distended with tenderness mainly in the left lower quadrant and is tympanic on percussion. The blood pressure is 110/79 mm Hg, heart rate is 100/min, the respiratory rate is 20/min, and the temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F). The CBC shows an elevated white blood cell count. The plain abdominal X-ray is shown in the accompanying image. What is the most likely cause of his condition?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of chronic constipation, use of laxatives, and the presence of a markedly distended sigmoid colon on imaging are suggestive of sigmoid volvulus. This condition occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on its mesentery, leading to bowel obstruction. It is most common in elderly, institutionalized patients with chronic constipation. The classic finding on imaging is the "coffee bean" sign, which represents the grossly dilated sigmoid colon.

The other options, such as acute diverticulitis, intussusception, and colon cancer, can also cause bowel obstruction, but they would not typically present with the imaging findings seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 37-year-old-woman presents to her primary care physician requesting a new form of birth control. few_shot.question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the outpatient OB/GYN clinic as a new patient who wishes to begin contraception. She has no significant past medical history, family history, or social history. The review of systems is negative. Her vital signs are: blood pressure 118/78 mm Hg, pulse 73/min, and respiratory rate 16/min. She is afebrile. Physical examination is unremarkable. She has researched multiple different contraceptive methods, and wants to know which is the most efficacious. Which of the following treatments should be recommended?
few_shot.explanation:
The most effective contraceptive methods are long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs), which include intrauterine devices (IUDs) and the contraceptive implant. These methods have failure rates of less than 1% in the first year of typical use. LARCs are highly effective because they do not depend on patient adherence. 

The contraceptive implant is a single, thin rod that is inserted under the skin of a woman's upper arm. The rod contains a progestin that is released into the body over 3 years.

IUDs are small, T-shaped devices that are inserted into the uterus. They are safe and effective in both nulliparous and parous women. There are two types of IUDs available: copper-containing IUDs, which can be left in place for up to 10 years, and levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs, which can be left in place for 3-5 years.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old gravida 2 para 2 presents to a medical clinic to discuss contraception options. After discussing the various contraceptive methods available, the patient decides to try combination oral contraceptive pills. The use of combination oral contraceptive pills (COCs) is contraindicated in breastfeeding women until at least 6 weeks postpartum. This is because COCs can decrease the quantity and quality of breast milk. After 6 weeks postpartum, the milk supply is well established and COCs are less likely to affect lactation. few_shot.question: A 37-year-old woman presents to the clinic to discuss various options for contraception. The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, Wilson’s disease, and constipation-dominant irritable bowel syndrome. The patient takes rivaroxaban and polyethylene glycol. The blood pressure is 152/98 mm Hg. On physical examination, the patient appears alert and oriented. The heart auscultation demonstrates regular rate and rhythm, and it is absent of murmurs. The lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally without wheezing. The first day of the last menstrual period was 12 days ago. The urine hCG is negative. Given the patient’s history and physical examination, which of the following options form of contraception is the most appropriate?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a history of hypertension and Wilson's disease. The copper IUD is contraindicated in patients with Wilson's disease because it can cause copper toxicity. Ethinyl estradiol is contraindicated in patients with hypertension because it can increase the risk of stroke and myocardial infarction. Depot-medroxyprogesterone acetate is contraindicated in patients with hypertension because it can increase blood pressure. Therefore, the most appropriate form of contraception for this patient is levonorgestrel.

Levonorgestrel is a progestin-only contraceptive that is available in various forms, including oral tablets, intrauterine devices, and subdermal implants. It works by thickening cervical mucus to prevent sperm from reaching the egg, inhibiting ovulation, and thinning the endometrial lining to prevent implantation. It is safe to use in patients with hypertension and does not contain copper, making it a suitable option for this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: An 18-year-old woman presents to the medical clinic 6 days after her boyfriend’s condom broke during sexual intercourse. The most effective method of emergency contraception is the copper intrauterine device (IUD), which can be inserted up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse and can prevent pregnancy by impairing implantation. The copper IUD can also be left in place for long-term contraception for up to 10 years. Other options for emergency contraception include ulipristal acetate and levonorgestrel, which can be used up to 5 and 3 days after unprotected intercourse, respectively. However, these methods are not as effective as the copper IUD.

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician to discuss contraceptive options. She is currently sexually active with one male partner, and they have not been using any contraception. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years. She is allergic to latex and copper. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following contraceptive methods is contraindicated in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
The combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) contains both estrogen and progestin. Estrogen increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), myocardial infarction, and stroke. The risk of these adverse events is further increased in women who smoke, particularly those >35 years of age. Therefore, the use of COCPs is contraindicated in women >35 who smoke. 

The progestin-only pill (POP) is a good alternative for women in whom estrogen is contraindicated (eg, smokers >35 years of age, women with a history of VTE, women with certain types of migraine). The POP works primarily by thickening cervical mucus, thereby inhibiting sperm penetration. 

The diaphragm with spermicide is a barrier method of contraception. It is not contraindicated in smokers. 

The intrauterine device is a long-acting reversible contraceptive that is safe and highly effective. The copper IUD works by causing a local inflammatory reaction toxic to sperm and ova. The levonorgestrel IUD works by thickening cervical mucus, inhibiting sperm penetration, and thinning and atrophying the endometrium. Neither is contraindicated in smokers. 

So, the answer is [D].

question: A 48-year-old woman comes to the physician because of intermittent pain in her neck, right shoulder, and arm, as well as a tingling sensation in her right hand. few_shot.question: A 53-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of intermittent severe left neck, shoulder, and arm pain and paresthesias of the left hand. The pain radiates to the radial aspect of her left forearm, thumb, and index finger. She first noticed her symptoms after helping a friend set up a canopy tent. There is no family history of serious illness. She appears healthy. Vital signs are within normal limits. When the patient extends and rotates her head to the left and downward pressure is applied, she reports paresthesias along the radial aspect of her left forearm and thumb. There is weakness when extending the left wrist against resistance. The brachioradialis reflex is 1+ on the left and 2+ on the right. The radial pulse is palpable bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of neck, shoulder, and arm pain, paresthesias of the thumb and index finger, and weakness when extending the wrist against resistance are suggestive of a cervical radiculopathy. Cervical radiculopathy is most often due to nerve root impingement or inflammation from a herniated disc or osteophyte. The C6 nerve root (C5-C6 disc) is one of the most commonly affected levels. The C6 nerve root contributes to the innervation of the biceps, brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis, and supinator muscles. Therefore, impingement of the C6 nerve root can cause weakness in these muscles, leading to decreased wrist extension and a diminished brachioradialis reflex. Sensory loss occurs over the thumb and index finger. The Spurling test (extension and rotation of the head) can exacerbate nerve root compression and reproduce radicular symptoms.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old man presents with increasing neck pain for several months that does not improve with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The patient says he has had neck pain ever since he was involved in a motor vehicle accident 10 months ago. For the last 2 weeks, he says he has also noticed weakness and numbness in his hands and has difficulty gripping objects. Physical examination reveals a thermal injury that he says he got while holding a hot cup of coffee a week ago when he could not feel the warmth of the coffee mug. Strength is 4/5 bilaterally during elbow flexion and extension and wrist extension. He also has exaggerated deep tendon reflexes bilaterally and decreased sensation symmetrically on the dorsal and ventral surface of both forearms and hands. Which of the following additional findings would you expect to find in this patient?

answer_choices.C: A cavitation in the cervical spinal cord

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of trauma, chronic neck pain, and symptoms of upper extremity weakness and numbness suggest a spinal cord lesion. The presence of both upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia) and lower motor neuron signs (weakness, hyporeflexia) in the upper extremities is characteristic of syringomyelia, a cystic cavitation (syrinx) within the central canal of the spinal cord. The syrinx expands and damages the spinal cord, leading to neurologic deficits. The most common location is the cervical spinal cord.

The earliest and most frequently damaged fibers are the crossing fibers of the spinothalamic tract at the anterior white commissure, which carry pain and temperature sensation from the body. This leads to a "cape-like" bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the upper extremities, while vibration and proprioception sensation (carried in the dorsal columns) are preserved. As the syrinx expands, it can affect other nearby structures, leading to lower motor neuron signs at the level of the lesion (eg, muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, muscle atrophy) and upper motor neuron signs (eg, hyperreflexia, increased muscle tone) below the lesion.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 44-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician’s office with episodes of pain in her right hand. She says that the pain is most significant at night and awakens her from sleep numerous times. When she experiences this pain, she immediately puts her hand under warm running water or shakes her hand. She has also experienced episodes of numbness in the affected hand. Driving and extending the right arm also provoke her symptoms. She denies any trauma to the hand or associated weakness. Medical history is notable for hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She works as a secretary for a law firm. On physical exam, when the patient hyperflexes her wrist, pain and paresthesia affect the first 3 digits of the right hand. Which of the following is the confirmatory diagnostic test for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of nocturnal pain and paresthesias in the first 3 digits of the hand, which are relieved by shaking the hand, are classic for carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). CTS is caused by median nerve compression as it travels through the carpal tunnel. The median nerve provides sensory innervation to the first 3.5 digits and motor innervation to the thenar muscles of the hand. Risk factors for CTS include obesity, female sex, pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, and repetitive activities that involve the wrist (eg, keyboard use).

The diagnosis of CTS is primarily clinical and based on history and physical examination findings. The most sensitive physical examination maneuver is the square wrist sign, which is positive when the anteroposterior and mediolateral dimensions of the wrist are approximately equal. Other physical examination maneuvers include the Tinel test (percussion of the median nerve at the wrist causing paresthesias in the median nerve distribution) and the Phalen test (wrist flexion causing paresthesias in the median nerve distribution).

Electrodiagnostic studies (eg, nerve conduction studies) are the most accurate diagnostic tests for CTS and are typically reserved for patients in whom the diagnosis is unclear or who are being considered for surgery.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 21-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department following a motor vehicle collision. She has significant pain and weakness in her right arm and hand. Physical examination shows multiple ecchymoses and tenderness in the right upper extremity. She is able to make a fist, but there is marked decrease in grip strength. An x-ray of the right upper extremity shows a midshaft humerus fracture. Which of the following structures is most likely injured?
few_shot.explanation:
The radial nerve is the most frequently injured nerve in humeral shaft fractures. It is derived from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and spirals around the humerus in the radial groove, making it susceptible to injury in humeral shaft fractures. The radial nerve provides motor innervation to the extensor muscles of the arm and forearm, which are responsible for wrist and digit extension, and sensation to the posterior arm, forearm, and dorsal hand. Injury to the radial nerve can cause wrist drop, which is the inability to extend the wrist and fingers. This patient's decreased grip strength is due to her inability to extend her wrist; when the wrist is not extended, flexion is weak (unopposed flexion).

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of weakness and intermittent burning pain in her neck, shoulders, and arms. She was involved in a motor vehicle collision 1 year ago. Examination of the upper extremities shows absent reflexes, muscle weakness, and fasciculations bilaterally. Sensation to temperature and pain is absent; vibration and proprioception are preserved. The pupils are equal and reactive to light. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of bilateral upper extremity weakness, fasciculations, and loss of pain and temperature sensation with preservation of vibration and proprioception are suggestive of syringomyelia. Syringomyelia is a condition in which a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) forms within the spinal cord. This syrinx often starts in the cervical region but can extend to other parts of the spinal cord. The syrinx can damage the anterior white commissure of the spinothalamic tracts, leading to loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution. If the syrinx expands, it can affect other structures in the spinal cord, including the anterior horn cells, leading to muscle weakness and fasciculations. Syringomyelia is often associated with Chiari type I malformations but can also be caused by trauma, as in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old man presents to a psychiatrist for management of nicotine dependence. He has been a heavy smoker for the past 20 years. He has unsuccessfully attempted to quit smoking many times. He has seen multiple physicians for nicotine dependence. They prescribed nicotine replacement therapy and varenicline. He has also taken two antidepressants and participated in talk therapy. He asks the psychiatrist whether there are other alternatives. The psychiatrist explains that nicotine replacement therapy, non-nicotine pharmacotherapy, and talk therapy are the best options for the management of nicotine dependence. He tells the patient he can take a second-line medication for non-nicotine pharmacotherapy because the first-line medication failed. Which of the following medications would the psychiatrist most likely use to manage this patient’s nicotine dependence?
few_shot.explanation:
The first-line medications for nicotine dependence are nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), bupropion, and varenicline. NRT is available in many forms, including gum, lozenges, patches, inhalers, and nasal sprays. Bupropion is an atypical antidepressant that inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine. Varenicline is a partial agonist of the α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. It reduces cravings and withdrawal symptoms and decreases the pleasurable effects of tobacco. 

When first-line treatments fail, second-line treatments may be considered. These include clonidine and nortriptyline. Clonidine is an α2 adrenergic agonist that was originally used as an antihypertensive. It can reduce withdrawal symptoms but is less effective than NRT and has a less favorable side effect profile. Nortriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant. It can reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].
