few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his mother complaining of abdominal pain and constipation. She reports that his appetite has been reduced and that he has not had a bowel movement in 2 days. Prior to this, he had a regular bowel movement once a day. She also reports that he has appeared to be more tired than usual. The family recently moved into a house built in the 1940s and have just begun renovations. The child was born via spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks gestation. He is up to date on all vaccinations and meeting all developmental milestones. Today, his blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, heart rate is 95/min, respiratory rate is 25/min, and temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). A physical exam is only significant for moderate conjunctival pallor. A peripheral blood smear shows red blood cells with basophilic stippling. What is the most likely mechanism causing this patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of abdominal pain, constipation, and fatigue, along with the finding of basophilic stippling on peripheral blood smear, are suggestive of lead poisoning. Lead poisoning is a common environmental health hazard in children, especially those living in older homes with chipping lead-based paint. Other risk factors include recent home renovation and exposure to imported goods (eg, toys, cosmetics, jewelry).

Lead inhibits several enzymes in the heme synthesis pathway, including ferrochelatase and delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase. Ferrochelatase catalyzes the insertion of iron into protoporphyrin to form heme. When this step is blocked, zinc is inserted into protoporphyrin instead of iron, leading to increased levels of zinc protoporphyrin. ALA dehydratase inhibition leads to the accumulation of ALA, which is associated with the neurologic symptoms of lead poisoning.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 3-month-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his mother after she notices orange sand–like crystalline material in her child’s diaper. He is not currently taking any medication and is exclusively breastfed. His immunizations are up to date. The doctor tells the mother that her son may have an X-linked recessive disorder. The boy is prescribed a medication that inhibits an enzyme responsible for the production of the crystals seen in his urine microscopy. Which of the following enzymes is the target of this medication?
few_shot.explanation:
The orange sand-like crystalline material in the diaper is suggestive of uric acid crystals, which are seen in conditions that cause hyperuricemia. One such condition is Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a deficiency in hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). This enzyme is involved in the purine salvage pathway, which recycles purines from degraded DNA to synthesize new DNA. In the absence of HGPRT, degraded purines are not recycled and are instead converted to uric acid, leading to hyperuricemia.

The medication prescribed to this patient is likely allopurinol, which inhibits xanthine oxidase, the enzyme responsible for the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. By inhibiting this enzyme, allopurinol reduces the production of uric acid and can help prevent the formation of uric acid crystals.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-hour history of vomiting, lethargy, and confusion. Three days ago, he was treated with an over-the-counter medication for fever and runny nose. He is oriented only to person. His blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Examination shows bilateral optic disc swelling and hepatomegaly. His blood glucose concentration is 65 mg/dL. Toxicology screening for serum acetaminophen is negative. The over-the-counter medication that was most likely used by this patient has which of the following additional effects?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's vomiting, lethargy, confusion, hepatomegaly, and optic disc swelling (papilledema due to increased intracranial pressure) suggest Reye syndrome, a rare and severe illness that typically occurs in children recovering from a viral infection (eg, influenza, varicella). It is characterized by acute encephalopathy and hepatic dysfunction. The exact cause of Reye syndrome is unknown, but aspirin use during a viral illness is a recognized risk factor.

Aspirin is a salicylate that inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 and -2, decreasing the production of prostaglandins and thromboxanes. This leads to its antipyretic, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiplatelet effects. Aspirin also interferes with uric acid elimination in the kidneys, which can lead to hyperuricemia and precipitation of acute gout.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 45-year-old male with a history of diabetes and poorly controlled hypertension presents to his primary care physician for an annual check-up. He reports that he feels well and has no complaints. He takes enalapril and metformin. His temperature is 98.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 16/min. His physician adds another anti-hypertensive medication to the patient’s regimen. One month later, the patient returns to the physician complaining of new onset lower extremity swelling. Which of the following medications was likely prescribed to this patient?

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of swelling of both her feet. It improves a little bit with elevation but is still bothersome to her because her shoes no longer fit. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin and linagliptin. She was diagnosed with hypertension 6 months ago and started treatment with amlodipine. Subsequent blood pressure measurements on separate occasions have been around 130/90 mm Hg. She otherwise feels well. Today, her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 132/88 mm Hg. Cardiovascular examination shows no abnormalities. There is pitting edema of both ankles. Which of the following would have been most likely to reduce the risk of edema in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB) that is commonly used to treat hypertension. It works by inhibiting the L-type calcium channels in arterial smooth muscle, leading to arterial dilation and a reduction in systemic vascular resistance. However, a common side effect of amlodipine and other dihydropyridine CCBs is peripheral edema. This is due to the dilation of the precapillary arterioles relative to the postcapillary venules, leading to a net increase in hydrostatic pressure and fluid extravasation. This effect is not related to the renal function or blood pressure control.

The most effective way to prevent this side effect is to use an alternative antihypertensive medication. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) such as enalapril are a good choice, especially in patients with diabetes, as they have been shown to reduce the progression of diabetic nephropathy.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old man comes to the office due to pain in the lower part of his calves on his afternoon walk to get the mail. The pain is relieved by rest. It started slowly about 6 months ago and has become more painful over time. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and smoking. Medications include hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, metformin, and a multivitamin that he takes daily. The patient does not smoke and only drinks socially. Today, his blood pressure is 145/90 mm Hg, pulse is 75/min, respiratory rate is 17/min, and temperature is 37.6°C (99.6°F). On physical exam, he appears mildly obese and healthy. His heart has a regular rate and rhythm, and his lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Examination of the legs shows atrophic changes and diminished pedal pulses. A measure of his ankle brachial index (ABI) is 0.89. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

answer_choices.C: A recommendation to perform pedal pumping exercises
answer_choices.D: A referral to a supervised exercise program

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of intermittent claudication (ie, exertional calf pain relieved by rest) and diminished peripheral pulses is suggestive of peripheral artery disease (PAD). PAD is caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the lower extremities. Risk factors include advanced age, diabetes mellitus, smoking, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. The ankle-brachial index (ABI), the ratio of systolic blood pressure at the ankle to that in the arm, is used to diagnose PAD. An ABI <0.90 is diagnostic of PAD.

Initial treatment of PAD involves lifestyle modifications (eg, smoking cessation, structured exercise program) and management of atherosclerotic risk factors (eg, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes). Supervised exercise programs are a key component of PAD management and have been shown to improve symptoms of claudication and quality of life. These programs typically involve walking until the onset of moderate claudication pain, resting until the pain resolves, and then repeating the sequence. The goal is to walk for 30-50 minutes at least 3 times per week.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure presents to his cardiologist complaining of mild dyspnea on exertion and swollen ankles. His past medical history is also significant for hypertension and alcohol abuse. He has a 50 pack-year smoking history. He currently takes lisinopril, aspirin, and metoprolol. His temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg, pulse is 85/min, and respirations are 18/min. An echocardiogram reveals an ejection fraction of 35%. His cardiologist adds an additional medication to the patient’s regimen. Two weeks later, the patient notices yellow halos in his vision. Which of the following medications did this patient most likely start taking?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dyspnea on exertion and swollen ankles, along with an ejection fraction of 35% on echocardiogram, are consistent with congestive heart failure. The yellow halos in his vision are a classic symptom of digoxin toxicity. Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside that is used to treat heart failure and certain arrhythmias. It works by inhibiting the sodium-potassium ATPase pump, which leads to increased intracellular sodium. This then leads to increased intracellular calcium via the sodium-calcium exchanger, which increases cardiac contractility. However, digoxin has a narrow therapeutic window and can easily cause toxicity, especially in those with decreased renal function or low potassium levels. Symptoms of digoxin toxicity include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, confusion, weakness, and changes in color vision (eg, yellow halos).

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old man presents for a general follow up appointment. He states that he is doing well and wants to be sure he is healthy. His current medications include metformin, glyburide, lisinopril, metoprolol and hydrochlorothiazide. His blood pressure is 130/90 mmHg and pulse is 80/min. A fasting lipid panel was performed last week demonstrating an LDL of 85 mg/dL and triglycerides of 160 mg/dL. The patient states that he has not experienced any symptoms since his last visit. The patient’s blood glucose at this visit is 100 mg/dL. Which of the following is recommended in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
The American Diabetes Association recommends that all patients with diabetes who are over the age of 40 be started on a statin, regardless of baseline lipid levels. This is because patients with diabetes are at a high risk of developing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Statins have been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in patients with diabetes. Therefore, this patient should be started on a statin.

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old African-American man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination after presenting with elevated blood pressure readings during his last visit. He has no history of major medical illness and takes no medications. He is 180 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2. His pulse is 80/min and blood pressure is 155/90 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
The most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy for this patient with stage 1 hypertension (systolic blood pressure 130-139 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure 80-89 mm Hg) and no compelling indications for other agents is a thiazide diuretic, such as chlorthalidone. Thiazide diuretics are recommended as first-line treatment for hypertension in black patients of any age and in nonblack patients >60 years of age. They are also recommended in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, post-myocardial infarction, and high coronary disease risk. Thiazide diuretics decrease blood pressure by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, thereby promoting natriuresis and reducing plasma volume.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 29-year-old primigravid woman at 35 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. She has no history of serious medical illness. She has had an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her last ultrasound at 22 weeks' gestation was normal. On admission, fetal heartbeats cannot be detected by fetal doppler monitor. Ultrasound shows decreased amniotic fluid levels and no evidence of fetal movement, respiration, or heart activity. The patient gives birth to a 2296 g (5 lb 1 oz) male infant. Physical examination shows no signs of life. There are no visible malformations. The placenta is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.C: Obtain photographs, x-ray imaging, and MRI
answer_choices.D: Obtain consent for parental genetic testing

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, comes for a prenatal visit at 33 weeks' gestation. She delivered her first child spontaneously at 38 weeks' gestation; pregnancy was complicated by oligohydramnios. She has no other history of serious illness. Her blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. On pelvic examination, uterine size is found to be smaller than expected for dates. The fetus is in a longitudinal lie, with vertex presentation. The fetal heart rate is 144/min. Ultrasonography shows an estimated fetal weight below the 10th percentile, and decreased amniotic fluid volume. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of oligohydramnios in a prior pregnancy and current findings of a small-for-gestational-age fetus and oligohydramnios are concerning for chronic uteroplacental insufficiency. This condition is characterized by inadequate uteroplacental perfusion, leading to chronic fetal hypoxia and malnutrition. It is associated with maternal vascular disease (eg, chronic hypertension, systemic lupus erythematosus), maternal metabolic disease (eg, phenylketonuria), and fetal malformations or chromosomal abnormalities. However, in many cases, no cause is identified.

The most appropriate next step in management is antenatal testing to assess for fetal well-being. This typically involves nonstress tests (NSTs) or biophysical profiles (BPPs), which are performed twice weekly. The NST involves monitoring the fetal heart rate for 20-40 minutes. It is considered reactive (normal) if two or more fetal heart rate accelerations (increase of ≥15 beats/min, lasting ≥15 seconds) are noted. A nonreactive NST is followed by a BPP, which includes an ultrasound examination assessing fetal breathing movements, fetal movement, fetal tone, and amniotic fluid volume. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old primigravid woman at 26 weeks' gestation comes to the physician complaining of absent fetal movements for the last 2 days. Pregnancy was confirmed by ultrasonography 14 weeks earlier. She has no vaginal bleeding or discharge. She has a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus controlled with insulin. Vital signs are all within the normal limits. Pelvic examination shows a soft, 2-cm long cervix in the midline with a cervical os measuring 3 cm and a uterus consistent in size with 24 weeks' gestation. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a fetus with no cardiac activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's absent fetal movements and ultrasonographic findings of absent cardiac activity are consistent with intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD). IUFD is defined as fetal death after 20 weeks of gestation but before the onset of labor. The most common causes of IUFD include maternal medical conditions (eg, diabetes, hypertension), placental abnormalities (eg, abruption, infarction), fetal genetic abnormalities, and infections (eg, syphilis, toxoplasmosis). The risk of IUFD is also increased in women with a history of prior stillbirth, cigarette smoking, and advanced maternal age.

Management of IUFD depends on gestational age and maternal stability. In a hemodynamically stable patient, the preferred method of delivery for a nonviable fetus >24 weeks' gestation is typically induction of labor with oxytocin or prostaglandins. Cesarean delivery is not indicated for IUFD unless the mother's life is in danger (eg, placenta previa with bleeding) or the patient is already in labor and vaginal delivery is contraindicated (eg, non-reassuring fetal heart tracing of the living twin, malpresentation). Dilation and curettage is used for IUFD <13 weeks' gestation.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old, gravida 2, nulliparous woman, at 14 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 6-hour history of light vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal discomfort. Eight months ago she had a spontaneous abortion at 10 weeks' gestation. Her pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 134/76 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows no tenderness or masses; bowel sounds are normal. On pelvic examination, there is old blood in the vaginal vault and at the closed cervical os. The uterus is larger than expected for the length of gestation and there are bilateral adnexal masses. Serum β-hCG concentration is 120,000 mIU/ml. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of vaginal bleeding, an enlarged uterus, and elevated β-hCG concentration is suggestive of a molar pregnancy. Molar pregnancies are a type of gestational trophoblastic disease and are characterized by abnormal proliferation of trophoblastic tissue. They can be complete (46, XX and entirely paternal in origin) or partial (69, XXY, XXX, or XYY and usually due to fertilization of a single egg by 2 sperm). Complete moles have a higher potential for malignant transformation into choriocarcinoma.

Transvaginal ultrasound is the most appropriate next step in management to confirm the diagnosis. It would show a uterus filled with a complex, echogenic mass with multiple small cystic spaces (representing swollen, edematous villi) described as a "snowstorm" or "cluster of grapes" appearance. Theca-lutein cysts (due to overstimulation of the ovaries by high levels of β-hCG) can also be seen and may be responsible for the bilateral adnexal masses found on examination.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:

answer_choices.B: Perform an ultrasound examination with nuchal translucency and crown-rump length measurement

Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management would be to recommend chorionic villus sampling with subsequent cell culturing and karyotyping to confirm the diagnosis.

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 36 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a prenatal visit. She feels well. Fetal movements are adequate. This is her 7th prenatal visit. She had an ultrasound scan performed 1 month ago that showed a live intrauterine pregnancy consistent with a 32-week gestation with no anomalies. She had a Pap smear performed 1 year ago, which was normal. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 36-week gestation. Her blood group and type is A negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends that all pregnant women be screened for group B streptococcus (GBS) colonization at 35-37 weeks' gestation. This is done by obtaining a vaginal and rectal swab for culture. GBS is a common cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis, and can also cause pneumonia. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for all women who are GBS positive to prevent transmission to the newborn.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 39-year-old African-American woman presents to the emergency room with hip pain. She has a past medical history significant for sarcoidosis which was recently diagnosed 6 months ago and is currently being treated. She reports that the pain started 2 weeks ago and is localized to the left hip and groin. The pain has been getting progressively more intense. Her temperature is 98.1°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg, pulse is 80/min, respirations are 13/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable for pain with manipulation without restriction of range of motion of the hip. Which of the following is the most sensitive test for this condition?

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy presents with right hip pain for the past 2 days. He reports gradual onset of pain and states it hurts to walk. He had a recent cold last week but is otherwise healthy. His temperature is 98.2°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 107/70 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, respiratory rate is 19/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals no swelling or warmth surrounding the joint. The patient is sitting with the right hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. Passive range of motion of the hip causes discomfort. The patient is able to ambulate but states it hurts. An initial radiograph of the hip is unremarkable. The patient's CRP is 0.10 mg/L. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with transient synovitis, which is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children aged 3-10 years. It is thought to be related to a recent viral infection or trauma. Patients typically present with hip pain and an antalgic gait, and prefer to hold the hip slightly flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. Systemic symptoms (eg, fever) are usually absent. Laboratory studies typically show a normal ESR and CRP, and radiographs are usually normal. Management is supportive, with NSAIDs for pain and rest.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 69-year-old woman presents with pain in her hip and groin. She states that the pain is present in the morning, and by the end of the day it is nearly unbearable. Her past medical history is notable for a treated episode of acute renal failure, diabetes mellitus, obesity, and hypertension. Her current medications include losartan, metformin, insulin, and ibuprofen. The patient recently started taking high doses of vitamin D as she believes that it could help her symptoms. She also states that she recently fell off the treadmill while exercising at the gym. On physical exam you note an obese woman. There is pain, decreased range of motion, and crepitus on physical exam of her right hip. The patient points to the areas that cause her pain stating that it is mostly over the groin. The patient's skin turgor reveals tenting. Radiography is ordered.

Which of the following is most likely to be found on radiography?

answer_choices.A: Loss of joint space and osteophytes

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of hip and groin pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest, along with physical examination findings of decreased range of motion and crepitus, are suggestive of osteoarthritis (OA). OA is a degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive loss of articular cartilage, which leads to pain and stiffness. Risk factors for OA include age, female sex, obesity, and previous joint injury. Radiographic findings in OA include joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis (increased bone density due to increased bone turnover), and osteophyte (bony outgrowth) formation.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy presents to his primary care physician with hip pain that started this morning. The patient claims the pain is severe and is stopping him from skateboarding. The patient recently recovered from a upper respiratory infection that he caught from his siblings but has otherwise been healthy. The patient has a past medical history of obesity. His temperature is 98.1°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 100/55 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On physical exam, you note an obese boy in no acute distress. Cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Inspection of the hip reveals no abnormalities or swelling. The hip exhibits a normal range of motion and physical exam only elicits minor pain. The patient's gait appears normal and pain is elicited when the patient jumps or runs. Which of the following is the best next step in management for this patient's most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with transient synovitis, which is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children aged 3-10. Transient synovitis is a self-limited inflammatory condition that often occurs following a viral infection, as in this patient. Patients typically present with hip pain that may be referred to the thigh or knee, a limp, and decreased range of motion of the hip. Systemic symptoms such as fever and leukocytosis are usually absent. The diagnosis is clinical, and treatment involves rest and NSAIDs (eg, ibuprofen).

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 13-year-old African-American boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-week history of left groin and buttock pain. The pain is worse with activity but also present at rest. He has had many episodes of abdominal, back, and chest pain that required hospitalization in the past. He is at the 20th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), blood pressure is 115/82 mm Hg, and pulse is 84/min. Examination shows tenderness over the lateral aspect of the left hip with no swelling, warmth, or erythema. There is pain with passive abduction and internal rotation of the left hip. Leukocyte count is 8,600/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent episodes of abdominal, back, and chest pain requiring hospitalization, along with his current symptoms, is suggestive of sickle cell disease (SCD). SCD is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a single amino acid substitution in the beta-globin chain of hemoglobin, leading to the production of abnormal hemoglobin S (HbS). HbS polymerizes under conditions of low oxygen tension, leading to the formation of sickle-shaped red blood cells that can cause vaso-occlusion and hemolysis.

Avascular necrosis (AVN) is a common complication of SCD and is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms. AVN occurs due to the occlusion of end arteries, often in the femoral or humeral heads, leading to the death of bone and marrow cells. This can cause severe pain and, if not treated, can lead to the collapse of the bone and loss of joint function.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department for right hip pain 1 hour after she fell while walking around in her house. She has been unable to stand or walk since the fall. She has hypertension and gout. Her sister died of multiple myeloma at the age of 55 years. Current medications include amlodipine and febuxostat. She does not smoke cigarettes. She drinks a glass of wine daily. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 101/min, and blood pressure is 128/86 mm Hg. Examination shows right groin tenderness. Range of motion of the right hip is limited by pain. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A complete blood count and serum creatinine concentration are within the reference range. An x-ray of the hip shows a linear fracture of the right femoral neck. She is scheduled for surgery. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's fracture?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's age, female sex, and low-energy mechanism of injury (fall from standing height) are suggestive of a fragility fracture due to osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is characterized by reduced bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, leading to enhanced bone fragility and a consequent increase in fracture risk. The most common sites of osteoporotic fractures are the vertebral bodies, distal radius (Colles fracture), and proximal femur (hip). Osteoporosis is especially common among postmenopausal women due to decreased estrogen levels. Estrogen deficiency accelerates bone loss by both increasing osteoclastic bone resorption and decreasing osteoblastic bone formation. The balance between the activities of osteoclasts and osteoblasts (coupling) is lost, with the rate of bone resorption exceeding the rate of bone formation. This imbalance is due to both increased osteoclast activity and reduced osteoblast activity, leading to a net loss of bone.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of increasing generalized fatigue for 3 months. He is having more difficulty with keeping up with his activities of daily living and has lost 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) over the past month. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He does not smoke and drinks two to three beers on weekends. His medications include lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and atorvastatin. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 125/73 mm Hg. Examination shows pale conjunctivae. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. His hematocrit is 27.3%, leukocyte count is 4500/mm3, and platelet count is 102,000/mm3. A peripheral blood smear shows numerous blast cells that stain positive for myeloperoxidase, CD33, and CD34. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fatigue, weight loss, and pancytopenia with circulating blasts on peripheral smear are suggestive of acute leukemia. Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a clonal disorder characterized by proliferation of myeloid precursors (myeloblasts) with a reduced capacity to differentiate into more mature cellular elements. AML can occur de novo or as a result of transformation from antecedent hematologic disorders (eg, myelodysplastic syndrome, myeloproliferative neoplasms) or previous cytotoxic chemotherapy or radiation. The median age at diagnosis is 65 years.

Patients with AML can present with symptoms due to anemia (eg, fatigue, dyspnea), neutropenia (eg, fever, infection), or thrombocytopenia (eg, easy bruising, mucosal bleeding). Bone marrow examination shows hypercellularity with >20% myeloblasts. Myeloblasts can be seen on the peripheral smear and are typically large cells with fine chromatin and prominent nucleoli. Auer rods (pink, needle-like inclusions within the cytoplasm) may be seen and are specific for AML. Flow cytometry typically shows expression of myeloid markers (eg, CD13, CD33, myeloperoxidase) and immature cell markers (eg, CD34, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase).

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 72-year-old man goes to his primary care provider for a checkup after some blood work showed lymphocytosis 3 months ago. He says he has been feeling a bit more tired lately but doesn’t complain of any other symptoms. Past medical history is significant for hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He takes lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and atorvastatin. Additionally, his right hip was replaced three years ago due to osteoarthritis. Family history is noncontributory. He drinks socially and does not smoke. Today, he has a heart rate of 95/min, respiratory rate of 17/min, blood pressure of 135/85 mm Hg, and temperature of 36.8°C (98.2°F). On physical exam, he looks well. His heartbeat has a regular rate and rhythm and lungs that are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Additionally, he has mild lymphadenopathy of his cervical lymph nodes. A complete blood count with differential shows the following:
Leukocyte count 5,000/mm3
Red blood cell count 3.1 million/mm3
Hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL
MCV 95 um3
MCH 29 pg/cell
Platelet count 150,000/mm3
Neutrophils 40%
Lymphocytes 40%
Monocytes 5%
A specimen is sent for flow cytometry that shows a population that is CD 5, 19, 20, 23 positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). CLL is a malignancy of mature B cells that is most common in older adults. It is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on routine blood work. Symptoms, when present, are often nonspecific and include fatigue, weight loss, and night sweats. Physical examination may reveal lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, and/or splenomegaly. The peripheral blood smear shows smudge cells and lymphocytosis with mature-appearing lymphocytes. Flow cytometry typically shows a population of cells that are CD5, CD19, CD20, and CD23 positive, which is diagnostic of CLL.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 65-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of muscle weakness. During this period, the patient has had low energy, intermittent nosebleeds, and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. He also reports progressive hearing and vision problems. He has a history of pins-and-needles sensation, numbness, and pain in his feet. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a palpable liver tip 2–3 cm below the right costal margin. There is nontender lympadenopathy in the groins, axillae, and neck. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL
White blood cells 6,300/mm3
Platelet count 98,000/mm3

Serum

Alkaline phosphatase 100 U/L
Lactate dehydrogenase 120 U/L
A serum protein electrophoresis exhibits a sharp, narrow spike of monoclonal IgM immunoglobulin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fatigue, weight loss, and lymphadenopathy, along with the laboratory findings of anemia, thrombocytopenia, and a monoclonal IgM spike on serum protein electrophoresis, are suggestive of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (WM). WM is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma characterized by bone marrow infiltration with lymphoplasmacytic cells, which produce monoclonal IgM. This leads to symptoms of anemia, such as fatigue and weakness, as well as hyperviscosity syndrome due to the large size and quantity of IgM. Hyperviscosity can cause a variety of neurologic and ophthalmologic symptoms, including blurry vision, headache, dizziness, and ataxia. The IgM can also deposit in various tissues, leading to organomegaly and peripheral neuropathy, as seen in this patient.

few_shot.question:
A 59-year-old man comes to the clinic for an annual well-exam. He was lost to follow-up for the past 3 years due to marital issues but reports that he feels fine. The patient reports, “I feel tired but it is probably because I am getting old. I do feel a little feverish today - I think I got a cold.” His past medical history is significant for hypertension that is controlled with hydrochlorothiazide. He reports fatigue, congestion, cough, and night sweats. He denies any sick contacts, recent travel, weight changes, chest pain, or dizziness. His temperature is 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 151/98 mmHg, pulse is 97/min, and respirations are 15/min. His laboratory values are shown below:

Hemoglobin: 13.5 g/dL
Hematocrit: 41%
Leukocyte count:  25,000/mm^3
Segmented neutrophils: 73%
Bands: 8% 
Eosinophils: 1%
Basophils: 2%
Lymphocytes: 15%
Monocytes: 2%
Platelet count: 200,000/mm^3

What diagnostic test would be helpful in distinguishing this patient’s condition from pneumonia?

answer_choices.D: Magnetic resonance imaging of the chest

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, cough, and night sweats, along with leukocytosis and a left shift (ie, increased bands), are concerning for an infection such as pneumonia. However, the markedly elevated leukocyte count with a predominance of mature neutrophils (ie, segmented neutrophils) is also suggestive of a myeloproliferative disorder such as chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). CML is a clonal disorder characterized by overproduction of mature myeloid cells. It is most common in middle-aged adults and typically presents with fatigue, night sweats, and splenomegaly. The peripheral smear shows leukocytosis with a left shift and basophilia. The presence of the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) is diagnostic.

The leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is often used when the diagnosis of CML is considered. LAP is present in the secondary granules of neutrophils and is released during the respiratory burst that accompanies phagocytosis. The enzyme is typically elevated in conditions associated with increased myeloid cell production (eg, infection, malignancy, polycythemia vera) but is low in CML. This is thought to be due to the decreased secondary granule formation seen in CML neutrophils.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 72-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) comes to the physician with a 2-day history of severe fatigue and dyspnea. He regularly visits his primary care physician and has not required any treatment for his underlying disease. His temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 105/min, respiratory rate is 22/min, and blood pressure is 125/70 mm Hg. The conjunctivae are pale. Examination of the heart and lungs shows no abnormalities. The spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. No lymphadenopathy is palpated. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 7 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 105 μm3
Leukocyte count 80,000/mm3
Platelet count 350,000/mm3
Serum  
Bilirubin Total // Direct 6 mg/dL / 0.8 mg/dL
Lactate dehydrogenase 650 U/L (Normal: 45–90 U/L)
Based on these findings, this patient’s recent condition is most likely attributable to which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's severe fatigue, dyspnea, and pallor are consistent with anemia. The elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and indirect bilirubin, along with the absence of red blood cells in the peripheral smear, suggest an intravascular hemolytic process. The elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is likely due to reticulocytosis, which is a response to the hemolysis. The most likely cause of these findings in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), which is the answer [A].

AIHA is a well-known complication of CLL and can occur in up to 10% of patients. It is caused by the production of IgG autoantibodies against red blood cell antigens, leading to extravascular hemolysis by the mononuclear phagocyte system, primarily in the spleen. Patients typically present with symptoms of anemia and jaundice. The direct antiglobulin test (Coombs test) is usually positive for IgG and sometimes complement.

question: A 25-year-old woman presents to her physician with complaints of cyclic vomiting for 3 days. The vomitus is watery and contains undigested food particles. She also complains of feeling tired and having the “sniffles”. She has not felt like eating or drinking since her symptoms started, and she has not taken any medications. Her concern now is that she immediately gets dizzy when she stands up. Vitals signs include: pulse 120/min, respiratory rate 9/min, and blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg. Her eyes are sunken, and her tongue appears dry. Which set of lab values would best correspond to this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.A: pH = 7.5, Pco2 = 50 mm Hg, HCO32- = 38 mEq/L
answer_choices.B: pH = 7.2, Pco2 = 25 mm Hg, HCO32- = 30 mEq/L

answer_choices.D: pH = 7.5, Pco2 = 30 mm Hg, HCO32- = 24 mEq/L

few_shot.question: A 34-year-old female comes to the ED complaining of epigastric pain and intractable nausea and vomiting for the last 24 hours. Her vitals are as follows: Temperature 38.1 C, HR 97 beats/minute, BP 90/63 mm Hg, RR 12 breaths/minute. Arterial blood gas and labs are drawn. Which of the following sets of lab values is consistent with her presentation?

answer_choices.A: pH 7.39, PaCO2 37 , serum chloride 102 mEq/L, serum bicarbonate 27 mEq/L
answer_choices.B: pH 7.46, PaCO2 26 , serum chloride 102 mEq/L, serum bicarbonate 16 mEq/L
answer_choices.C: pH 7.51, PaCO2 50 , serum chloride 81 mEq/L, serum bicarbonate 38 mEq/L
answer_choices.D: pH 7.31, PaCO2 30 , serum chloride 92 mEq/L, serum bicarbonate 15 mEq/L

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting are suggestive of a gastric outlet obstruction, such as pyloric stenosis. This can cause a metabolic alkalosis due to loss of gastric acid (which contains hydrochloric acid) in the vomitus. This leads to an increase in bicarbonate concentration, which would cause the observed increase in pH. The body compensates for this by decreasing the respiratory rate, leading to an increase in PaCO2. However, this compensation is not sufficient to bring the pH back to normal, so the pH remains elevated. The loss of chloride in the vomitus can also lead to hypochloremia.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of weakness and fatigue. She says she caught a “stomach bug” and has not been able to eat anything without vomiting for three days. Past medical history is significant for hyperlipidemia. She takes atorvastatin and a multivitamin daily, except for the last two days due to nausea. Today her heart rate is 106/min, respiratory rate is 16/min, temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F) and blood pressure of 110/70 mm Hg. On physical examination, her oral mucosa is dry and she looks pale and uncomfortable. She is admitted for care and administered ondansetron. An intravenous infusion of normal saline is also initiated. An arterial blood gas is collected. Which of the following results is expected to be seen in this patient?

answer_choices.A: pH: 7.36, pCO2: 42 mm Hg, HCO3-: 22 mEq/L
answer_choices.B: pH: 7.30, pCO2: 36 mm Hg, HCO3-: 17 mEq/L
answer_choices.C: pH: 7.48, pCO2: 44 mm Hg, HCO3-: 29 mEq/L
answer_choices.D: pH: 7.49, pCO2: 33 mm Hg, HCO3-: 18 mEq/L

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of vomiting and physical examination findings of dry oral mucosa are consistent with volume depletion due to gastrointestinal fluid losses. Vomiting leads to a loss of gastric acid (ie, HCl), which results in a primary metabolic alkalosis due to an increase in bicarbonate concentration. The body compensates for this by decreasing ventilation to increase the partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2), a weak acid. However, this compensation is not complete, and the arterial pH increases, resulting in an alkalemia. Therefore, the arterial blood gas of a patient with protracted vomiting will show an increased pH, an increased bicarbonate concentration, and an increased PaCO2.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a headache, vertigo, confusion, and dyspnea. A relevant history cannot be obtained from the patient because she seems confused and gives incoherent responses to questions. Her husband says that she was cleaning the kitchen this morning until the curtains caught on fire earlier this morning from the stove’s flame. Her vitals include: pulse 100/min, respirations 20/min, blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On physical examination, the patient is oriented x 0. The skin has a bright cherry-red color. Laboratory testing shows:
pH 7.35
PaO2 90 mm Hg
pCO2 40 mm Hg
HCO3-  26 mEq/L
SpO2 97%
Blood lactate  11 mmol/L
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of headache, vertigo, confusion, and dyspnea after a house fire is suggestive of cyanide poisoning. Cyanide is a rapidly acting substance that is produced by the combustion of household items such as plastics, silk, and paper. It is a potent cellular asphyxiant that binds to the ferric ion (Fe3+) in cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, thereby halting oxidative phosphorylation and leading to cellular hypoxia and lactic acidosis. The diagnosis of cyanide poisoning is primarily clinical and should be suspected in any victim of a closed-space fire who presents with altered mental status or lactic acidosis. 

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 57-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 4 days. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows:
pH 7.58
PCO2 43 mm Hg
PO2 96 mm Hg
HCO3- 32 mEq/L
The most appropriate next step in diagnosis is measurement of which of the following?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's arterial blood gas analysis shows a primary metabolic alkalosis (increased bicarbonate concentration and increased pH). Metabolic alkalosis can be caused by two main mechanisms: loss of hydrogen ions (eg, vomiting, nasogastric suctioning) or gain of bicarbonate ions (eg, milk-alkali syndrome, alkali administration). The most common causes of metabolic alkalosis are vomiting and diuretic use.

The next step in the evaluation of metabolic alkalosis is to assess the volume status of the patient and to measure the urine chloride concentration. The urine chloride can help distinguish between chloride-responsive (urine chloride <10 mEq/L) and chloride-resistant (urine chloride >20 mEq/L) metabolic alkalosis. Chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis is due to volume contraction and is often due to vomiting or diuretic use. Chloride-resistant metabolic alkalosis is often due to hyperaldosteronism or other mineralocorticoid excess states.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman is admitted to the emergency room with dyspnea which began after swimming and progressed gradually over the last 3 days. She denies cough, chest pain, or other respiratory symptoms. She reports that for the past 4 months, she has had several dyspneic episodes that occurred after the exercising and progressed at rest, but none of these were as long as the current one. Also, she notes that her tongue becomes ‘wadded’ when she speaks and she tires very quickly during the day. The patient’s vital signs are as follows: blood pressure 125/60 mm Hg, heart rate 92/min, respiratory rate 34/min, and body temperature 36.2℃ (97.2℉). Blood saturation on room air is initially 92% but falls to 90% as she speaks up. On physical examination, the patient is slightly lethargic. Her breathing is rapid and shallow. Lung auscultation, as well as cardiac, and abdominal examinations show no remarkable findings. Neurological examination reveals slight bilateral ptosis increased by repetitive blinking, and easy fatigability of muscles on repeated movement worse on the face and distal muscles of the upper and lower extremities. Which arterial blood gas parameters would you expect to see in this patient?

answer_choices.A: PaCO2 = 34 mm Hg, PaO2 = 61 mm Hg
answer_choices.B: PaCO2 = 31 mm Hg, PaO2 = 67 mm Hg
answer_choices.C: PaCO2 = 51 mm Hg, PaO2 = 58 mm Hg
answer_choices.D: PaCO2 = 37 mm Hg, PaO2= 46 mm Hg

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dyspnea, fatigability, and bilateral ptosis are suggestive of myasthenia gravis (MG). MG is an autoimmune disorder characterized by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction, leading to muscle weakness that worsens with repetitive use. The disease often presents with ocular symptoms (eg, ptosis, diplopia) but can progress to generalized weakness. In severe cases, patients can develop a myasthenic crisis, which is a life-threatening condition characterized by weakness of the respiratory muscles, leading to respiratory failure.

Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis in patients with myasthenic crisis typically shows hypoxemia (PaO2 <60 mm Hg) and hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mm Hg) due to inadequate ventilation.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 59-year-old overweight woman presents to the urgent care clinic with the complaint of severe abdominal pain for the past 2 hours. few_shot.question: A 52-year-old woman presents to the urgent care center with several hours of worsening abdominal discomfort with radiation to the back. The patient also complains of malaise, chills, nausea, and vomiting. Social history is notable for alcoholism. On physical exam, she is febrile to 39.5°C (103.1°F), and she is diffusely tender to abdominal palpation. Complete blood count is notable for 13,500 white blood cells, bilirubin 2.1, lipase 842, and amylase 3,210. Given the following options, what is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and elevated lipase and amylase is consistent with acute pancreatitis. The most common causes of acute pancreatitis are gallstones and alcohol use. Gallstone pancreatitis occurs when a gallstone becomes lodged in the ampulla of Vater, blocking the outflow of pancreatic secretions. This can lead to autodigestion of the pancreas by its own enzymes, causing inflammation and pancreatitis. Alcohol-induced pancreatitis is also common, but it usually occurs after many years of heavy drinking. Given this patient's acute presentation and known history of alcoholism, gallstone pancreatitis is the most likely diagnosis.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Given this patient's history of alcoholism, it is possible that either etiology could be responsible for her symptoms. few_shot.question: A 44-year-old obese woman presents with abdominal pain. She says the pain started while she was having lunch at a fast-food restaurant with her children. The pain began shortly after eating and has persisted for 6 hours. She has vomited once. Her vital signs are as follows: HR 88, BP 110/70 mmHg, T 38.5°C (101.3°F). On physical exam, she is tender to palpation in the right upper quadrant of her abdomen. Her skin appears normal. Her liver function tests, amylase, and lipase levels are normal. A right upper quadrant abdominal ultrasound is challenged by her body habitus and is not able to visualize any gallstones. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of postprandial right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting is suggestive of biliary colic, which is most commonly caused by gallstones. Gallstones are formed when substances in the bile (eg, cholesterol, bilirubin) precipitate and form solid particles. Risk factors for gallstone formation include obesity, female sex, and increasing age. The pain of biliary colic typically occurs after meals (especially fatty meals), as cholecystokinin is released in response to fat ingestion, leading to gallbladder contraction and impaction of a gallstone in the cystic duct. The pain usually lasts 1-5 hours and can radiate to the right shoulder or back. 

Although this patient's ultrasound did not visualize any gallstones, the sensitivity of ultrasound for detecting gallstones is decreased in obese patients and those with small stones or a small amount of sludge. Therefore, the absence of gallstones on ultrasound does not rule out gallstone disease in a patient with a high clinical suspicion.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 55-year-old female presents to clinic with recurrent episodes of abdominal discomfort and pain for the past month. She reports that the pain occurs 2-3 hours after meals, usually at midnight, and rates it as moderate to severe in intensity when it occurs. She also complains of being fatigued all the time. Past medical history is insignificant. She is an office secretary and says that the job has been very stressful recently. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), respiratory rate is 15/min, pulse is 67/min, and blood pressure is 122/98 mm Hg. Her BMI is 34. A physical examination reveals conjunctival pallor and mild tenderness over her epigastric region. Blood tests show:
Hb%: 10 gm/dL
Total count (WBC): 11,000 /mm3
Differential count:
Neutrophils: 70%
Lymphocytes: 25%
Monocytes: 5%
ESR: 10 mm/hr
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of recurrent abdominal pain that occurs 2-3 hours after meals and at midnight, along with the presence of conjunctival pallor and anemia, are suggestive of a duodenal peptic ulcer. Peptic ulcers are most commonly caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use. This patient's recent stress and obesity could also be contributing factors. The pain of duodenal ulcers classically presents as nocturnal pain or pain that occurs 2-3 hours after meals, when the stomach is empty. This is because the pyloric sphincter closes after food passes into the duodenum, leaving gastric acid in the stomach where it can irritate the ulcer crater. The pain is often relieved by eating, which buffers the gastric acid, or by antacids. The anemia is likely due to chronic gastrointestinal blood loss from the ulcer.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 50-year-old overweight woman presents to her physician with complaints of recurrent episodes of right upper abdominal discomfort and cramping. She says that the pain is mild and occasionally brought on by the ingestion of fatty foods. The pain radiates to the right shoulder and around to the back, and it is accompanied by nausea and occasional vomiting. She admits to having these episodes over the past several years. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting, especially after eating fatty foods, are suggestive of biliary colic. Biliary colic is caused by the impaction of a gallstone in the cystic duct, leading to increased pressure in the gallbladder as it contracts in response to cholecystokinin release after a meal. The pain of biliary colic is often severe, but it can be mild in some cases. It is typically steady (rather than crampy or colicky) and can radiate to the right shoulder or back. The pain usually lasts for one or more hours and then gradually subsides. Fever and leukocytosis are not seen unless cholecystitis (inflammation of the gallbladder) is also present. The liver function tests are usually normal, but mild elevations in alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases can be seen.

question: A 57-year-old female with a past medical history of alcoholism presents to the emergency room vomiting bright red blood. Vital signs are temperature 37 degrees celsius, heart rate 141 beats per minute, blood pressure 90/60, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. On physical examination, she has splenomegaly and a positive fluid wave. The remainder of her examination is within normal limits. The patient is stabilized with intravenous fluids, and her blood pressure improves. Subsequent emergent upper endoscopy reveals bleeding from the submucosal veins in the lower 1/3 of the esophagus, but no gastric bleed. In the endoscopy suite she also receives IV octreotide. After intervention and resolution of her acute bleed, which of the following pharmacologic agents is indicated?

few_shot.question:
A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with bloody vomiting for the last hour. She had been vomiting for several hours. Additionally, she states she felt a sudden onset of chest and epigastric pain when she noted blood in her vomit. In the emergency room, she endorses feeling lightheaded and denies difficulty breathing or coughing, and the pain is not worse with swallowing. On review of systems, she notes that she has been bruising more easily than usual over the last 3 months. The patient has a long history of alcoholism with recent progression of liver disease to cirrhosis. She has known esophageal varices and is on propranolol for prophylaxis. In the emergency room, the patient’s temperature is 98.2°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 94/60 mmHg, pulse is 103/min, and respirations are 16/min. On exam, she is in moderate distress, and there is frank blood in her emesis basin. Cardiovascular and lung exams are unremarkable, and there is pain on palpation of her epigastrium and chest without crepitus. Initial labs are shown below:

Hemoglobin: 13.1 g/dL
Leukocyte count: 6,200/mm^3
Platelet count: 220,000/mm^3
Creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL

The patient is started on IV isotonic saline, pantoprazole, ceftriaxone, and octreotide. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient presents with hematemesis and epigastric pain after vomiting, which is concerning for a Mallory-Weiss tear. Mallory-Weiss tears are longitudinal mucosal lacerations in the distal esophagus and proximal stomach that are caused by forceful retching or vomiting. Patients often present with hematemesis and may have associated abdominal or chest pain. The diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopy, which also allows for therapeutic intervention if needed. Therefore, the best next step in management is endoscopy.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 54-year-old man with alcoholism comes to the emergency department because of vomiting blood for 6 hours. He has had 3–4 episodes in which he has vomited dark red blood during this period. He has had no epigastric pain or tarry stools. On arrival, his temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 134/min, and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg. He is resuscitated with 0.9% saline and undergoes an emergency upper endoscopy, which shows actively bleeding varices. Band ligation of the varices is done and hemostasis is achieved. He is diagnosed with Child class B cirrhosis. He is concerned about the possibility of recurrence of such an episode. He is asked to abstain from alcohol, to which he readily agrees. In addition to non-selective beta-blocker therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation to prevent future morbidity and mortality from this condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient with alcoholism and cirrhosis presented with hematemesis and hypotension, which are consistent with acute variceal hemorrhage. The most common cause of variceal bleeding is portal hypertension, which is most often due to cirrhosis. The initial management of acute variceal hemorrhage includes hemodynamic resuscitation, prophylactic antibiotics, and vasoactive drugs (eg, octreotide). Definitive therapy is achieved with upper endoscopy, which allows for either band ligation or sclerotherapy of the bleeding varices.

Following recovery from an episode of acute variceal hemorrhage, patients should be started on therapy to prevent recurrence. Nonselective beta blockers (eg, propranolol, nadolol) are the mainstay of therapy for primary and secondary prevention of variceal hemorrhage. They reduce portal pressure by decreasing cardiac output (beta1 receptor blockade) and causing splanchnic vasoconstriction (beta2 receptor blockade). In patients who have recovered from acute variceal hemorrhage, the addition of endoscopic variceal ligation to nonselective beta blocker therapy is the most effective method for preventing recurrent variceal hemorrhage.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 49-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because he is vomiting blood. He has not had any bloody stool, melena, or abdominal pain. He was diagnosed with alcoholic cirrhosis 6 months ago. He drank approximately 1 liter of vodka over the past day, which is typical for him. He takes no medications. He is confused and disoriented to place and time. Physical examination shows ascites. Vital signs are within normal limits. His hemoglobin concentration is 9.5 g/dL. Intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun. He starts to vomit bright red blood again intermittently, which continues for 10 minutes. When vital signs are measured again, his pulse is 95/min and blood pressure is 109/80 mm/Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has alcoholic cirrhosis and is presenting with hematemesis, likely due to bleeding esophageal varices. The initial management of suspected variceal bleeding includes aggressive fluid resuscitation, prophylactic antibiotics, and pharmacologic therapy with a splanchnic vasoconstrictor (eg, octreotide). However, this patient's ongoing hematemesis and altered mental status put him at high risk for aspiration. Therefore, the most appropriate initial step in management is endotracheal intubation to protect the airway.

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's ECG findings are consistent with first-degree atrioventricular (AV) block, which is defined as a PR interval >200 ms. First-degree AV block is often an incidental finding on ECG and is usually asymptomatic. It can be seen in healthy, well-trained athletes and is also associated with increased vagal tone. In addition, it can be caused by medications such as beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, and amiodarone. This patient's use of verapamil, a calcium channel blocker, is likely contributing to her prolonged PR interval. However, first-degree AV block does not typically progress to higher degrees of block and does not require specific therapy. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is observation.

The initial management of suspected variceal bleeding includes resuscitation with intravenous fluids and blood products as needed, discontinuation of any potential offending agents (eg, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), and initiation of pharmacologic therapy with a somatostatin analog (eg, octreotide) and a prophylactic antibiotic (eg, ceftriaxone).

question: A 25-year-old man presents to his primary care provider complaining of several weeks of intense itching, particularly localized around his anus. Of note, the patient denies any recent travel, sexual contacts, fever, dysuria, or diarrhea. His temperature is 98.1°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 65/min, and respirations are 12/min. On exam, the patient demonstrates severe excoriations in his perianal region with slight erythema over the areas that are torn. He does not have any other dermatologic findings. The scotch tape test is positive. The patient has a previous documented allergy to albendazole. Which of the following is an alternative medication that can be used?

few_shot.question: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of itching of the vulva and anal region for the past 2 weeks. She has difficulty sleeping because of the itching. Physical examination shows excoriation marks around the vulva and perianal region. There is minor perianal erythema, but no edema or fissures. Microscopy of an adhesive tape applied to the perianal region shows multiple ova. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of perianal itching, especially at night, and the finding of ova on microscopy are consistent with a diagnosis of enterobiasis (pinworm infection). Enterobiasis is caused by Enterobius vermicularis, a nematode that is the most common helminthic infection in the United States. Humans are the only known host of E. vermicularis. Infection occurs following ingestion of infective eggs, which then hatch in the small intestine. The larvae mature into adult worms in the colon. Female worms migrate out of the anus at night to lay eggs, causing perianal itching. The eggs can then be ingested by the same individual (autoinfection) or another person.

The treatment of choice for enterobiasis is mebendazole or albendazole. Pyrantel pamoate is an alternative for patients who cannot tolerate these medications or for pregnant women.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of abdominal pain and an itchy rash on his buttocks. He also has fever, nausea, and diarrhea with mucoid stools. One week ago, the patient returned from Indonesia, where he went for vacation. Physical examination shows erythematous, serpiginous lesions located in the perianal region and the posterior thighs. His leukocyte count is 9,000/mm3 with 25% eosinophils. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.C: Giardia lamblia antibodies on stool immunoassay
answer_choices.D: Branching septate hyphae on KOH preparation

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recent travel to Indonesia, eosinophilia, and serpiginous, pruritic rash in the perianal region are suggestive of Strongyloides stercoralis infection. S stercoralis is an intestinal nematode that is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. Infection is acquired through skin penetration by filariform larvae present in soil contaminated by human feces. The larvae then migrate through the venous system to the lungs, where they are coughed up and swallowed, allowing them to reach the small intestine. Here, they mature into adult females that live in the mucosa and produce eggs, which hatch into noninfectious rhabditiform larvae. These larvae are passed in the stool or can mature into infectious filariform larvae, which can penetrate the intestinal mucosa or perianal skin and cause autoinfection. This can lead to chronic infection, or hyperinfection in immunocompromised patients. Diagnosis is made by identifying rhabditiform larvae on stool microscopy.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 1, at 25 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of mild itching of the vulva and anal region for 2 weeks. She has a history of 2 episodes of vulvovaginal candidiasis last year that both subsided following 1 week of treatment with butoconazole. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 25-week gestation. There are no signs of vulvar or perianal erythema, edema, or fissures. Microscopy of an adhesive tape that was applied to the perianal region shows multiple ova. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms and the finding of ova on microscopy are consistent with enterobiasis (pinworm infection). Enterobiasis is the most common helminthic infection in the United States. It is caused by the nematode Enterobius vermicularis and is most common in children. Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route, either through direct contact with an infected individual or indirectly through contact with contaminated fomites (eg, bedding, clothing, toys). Adult worms inhabit the cecum, and gravid females migrate to the perianal region to lay eggs, causing perianal pruritus, especially at night. The diagnosis is confirmed by identification of eggs on microscopy of an adhesive tape applied to the perianal region in the morning.

Treatment is with a single dose of albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel pamoate, repeated in 2 weeks. However, these medications are not recommended during pregnancy due to lack of safety data. Therefore, the best management in a pregnant patient is supportive therapy, including good personal hygiene, daily morning bathing, and frequent changing and washing of underclothes and bed linens. This can help remove a large proportion of the eggs and reduce the likelihood of reinfection. Treatment with an anthelmintic agent should be given after delivery.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old man presents to the physician after he discovered a raised, red, string-shaped lesion beneath the skin on his right foot. The lesion seems to move from one location to another over the dorsum of his foot from day to day. He says that the the lesion is extremely itchy and has not responded to over the counter topical treatment. He and his wife recently returned from a honeymoon in southern Thailand, where they frequented the tropical beaches. The physician diagnoses him with a parasitic infection and prescribes albendazole for the patient. With which of the following organisms is the patient most likely infected?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with cutaneous larva migrans, a pruritic, erythematous, serpiginous rash caused by dog and cat hookworms (Ancylostoma braziliense and Ancylostoma caninum). Humans are infected by walking barefoot on sandy soil contaminated with dog or cat feces. The hookworm larvae penetrate the skin and migrate within the epidermis, causing intense pruritus and a visible, snakelike tract that advances a few millimeters to a few centimeters each day. The condition is self-limited because the larvae cannot penetrate the basement membrane and complete their life cycle in humans. However, treatment with albendazole or ivermectin can be used to alleviate symptoms.

So, the answer is [A].

His hemoglobin concentration is 10.2 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume is 63.2 μm3, and platelet count is 450,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this skin condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's skin findings (symmetric, pruritic, blistering rash over extensor surfaces), history of diarrhea, and laboratory findings (microcytic anemia) are suggestive of dermatitis herpetiformis (DH). DH is an autoimmune blistering disorder that is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease). It presents with grouped pruritic vesicles and papules on extensor surfaces. The diagnosis is confirmed by skin biopsy showing granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae. The rash responds dramatically to a gluten-free diet and dapsone, which is thought to work by inhibiting neutrophil function. However, dapsone can cause hemolysis and methemoglobinemia, so patients must be monitored closely.

question: A 42-year-old man presents to a neurologist for evaluation of severe headache. few_shot.question: A 45-year-old-man presents to the physician with complaints of intermittent episodes of severe headaches and palpitations. During these episodes, he notices that he sweats profusely and becomes pale in complexion. He describes the episodes as coming and going within the past 2 months. His temperature is 99.3°F (37.4°C), blood pressure is 165/118 mmHg, pulse is 126/min, respirations are 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. Which of the following would be the first medication given to treat this patient’s most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of severe headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis are suggestive of a pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor that arises from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. The diagnosis is confirmed by elevated levels of plasma free metanephrines or urinary fractionated metanephrines.

Initial management of a pheochromocytoma involves blood pressure control with alpha-adrenergic blockade to prevent a hypertensive crisis. Phenoxybenzamine, a nonselective, irreversible alpha-adrenergic antagonist, is the drug of choice. It is started 10-14 days preoperatively and uptitrated until blood pressure control is achieved. 

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old male presents to the emergency department due to severe headaches and palpitations. He has had previous episodes of sweating and headache, but this episode was particularly disabling. Upon presentation, he appears pale and diaphoretic. His temperature is 99.3°F (37.4°C), blood pressure is 162/118 mmHg, pulse is 87/min, and respirations are 20/min. Based on clinical suspicion, an abdominal CT scan is obtained, which shows a retroperitoneal mass. This patient's increased heart rate is most likely due to a change in activity of which of the following channels?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis, along with hypertension and a retroperitoneal mass, are suggestive of a pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytomas are tumors of the adrenal medulla that secrete catecholamines, leading to symptoms of sympathetic overactivity. The most common catecholamine secreted by these tumors is norepinephrine, which acts on alpha-1, alpha-2, and beta-1 adrenergic receptors. 

The beta-1 adrenergic receptors are found in the heart, where they increase heart rate and contractility. The increase in heart rate is due to an increase in the slope of phase 4 of the action potential in the SA node, which is mediated by hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels. These channels allow the slow inward flow of sodium and potassium ions, which leads to the slow depolarization seen in phase 4. Norepinephrine increases the activity of these channels, leading to a more rapid phase 4 depolarization and an increased heart rate.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician complaining of a several-month history of episodic sweating and heart racing. Her family history is negative for hypertension, endocrinopathies, or tumors. Vital signs reveal a blood pressure of 220/120 mm Hg, temperature (normal) and pulse of 110/min. Fundus examination reveals hypertensive retinal changes. This patient condition is most likely due to neoplasm arising from which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's episodic symptoms of headache, sweating, and tachycardia are suggestive of a pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor that arises from the adrenal chromaffin cells. The adrenal medulla, which is derived from neural crest cells, contains chromaffin cells that synthesize and release catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine) into the bloodstream. Pheochromocytomas can cause sustained or paroxysmal hypertension, and they can be life-threatening if not recognized and treated.

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man presents to his primary care physician complaining of increasingly frequent headaches. He also reports that his hats and wedding ring do not fit anymore. His temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 145/80 mmHg, pulse is 85/min, and respirations are 16/min. Physical examination is notable for frontal bossing, a prominent jaw, and an enlarged tongue. A chest radiograph reveals mild cardiomegaly. Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 levels are significantly elevated. Which of the following conditions is this patient at greatest risk for?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of headache, increased hat and ring size, frontal bossing, prominent jaw, and enlarged tongue are suggestive of acromegaly, a condition caused by excessive growth hormone (GH) secretion. In adults, GH excess leads to an increase in soft tissue growth and bone thickness (as opposed to length). The most common cause of acromegaly is a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma.

Patients with acromegaly are at increased risk for a number of complications, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular disease. They are also at increased risk for carpal tunnel syndrome due to the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the soft tissues, which can cause entrapment of peripheral nerves.

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with 2 weeks of headache, palpitations, and excessive sweating. He has no past medical history and his family history is significant for clear cell renal cell carcinoma in his father as well as retinal hemangioblastomas in his older sister. On presentation his temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 181/124 mmHg, pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 18/min. After administration of appropriate medications, he is taken emergently for surgical removal of a mass that was detected by abdominal computed tomography scan. A mutation on which of the following chromosomes would most likely be seen in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of headache, palpitations, and excessive sweating are suggestive of a pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor that arises from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. His family history of clear cell renal cell carcinoma and retinal hemangioblastomas is suggestive of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by the development of numerous benign and malignant tumors. VHL disease is caused by a deletion in the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3. The VHL gene product is involved in the degradation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, a transcription factor that promotes angiogenesis, erythropoiesis, and glycolysis. In the absence of a functional VHL gene product, hypoxia-inducible factor 1α is not degraded and acts as if the cell is in a state of hypoxia, leading to the development of highly vascular tumors.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of anorexia, nausea, upper abdominal pain, and dark-colored urine. He recently returned from a trip to Belize. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). Physical examination shows scleral icterus and tender hepatomegaly. Serum studies show markedly elevated transaminases and anti-hepatitis A virus antibodies.
