A 27-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use comes to the physician because of anorexia, nausea, dark urine, and abdominal pain for 2 weeks. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and right upper quadrant tenderness. Serum studies show:
Alanine aminotransferase 1248 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase 980 U/L
Hepatitis B surface antigen negative
Anti-hepatitis B surface antibody positive
Anti-hepatitis C antibody negative
Further evaluation shows hepatitis C virus RNA detected by PCR. Without appropriate treatment, which of the following is the most likely outcome of this patient's current condition?"
few_shot.explanation:
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is an RNA virus that is transmitted primarily through blood and blood products. It is the most common cause of chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma in the United States. The natural history of HCV infection is variable. Approximately 15%-25% of patients will spontaneously clear the virus, whereas the remaining 75%-85% will develop chronic infection. Chronic HCV infection is usually slowly progressive, and the majority of patients remain asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic for many years. However, 20% of patients with chronic HCV infection will develop cirrhosis over a 20- to 30-year period. Patients with cirrhosis are at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss over the past 6 months. He experimented with intravenous drugs during his 20s and has hepatitis C. His father died of colon cancer. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and several telangiectasias on the abdomen. The ultrasound image shows a hyperechoic mass in the liver, which is concerning for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). HCC is a common complication of cirrhosis, regardless of the underlying cause (eg, hepatitis B or C, alcohol). The diagnosis of HCC can be suggested by an elevated α-fetoprotein level and confirmed by characteristic findings on four-phase liver CT or dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI.

few_shot.question:
A 28-year-old man presents to the office with complaints of malaise, anorexia, and vomiting for the past 2 weeks. He also says that his urine is dark. The past medical history is unremarkable. The temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), the pulse is 72/min, the blood pressure is 118/63 mm Hg, and the respiratory rate is 15/min. The physical examination reveals a slightly enlarged, tender liver. IgM anti-HBc < 1:1,000
Anti-HBs Negative

HBV DNA 2.65 × 109 IU/L

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of malaise, anorexia, vomiting, and dark urine, along with the physical examination findings of hepatomegaly and tenderness, are suggestive of acute hepatitis. The presence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) in the serum, along with a high viral load (HBV DNA), indicates active viral replication and high infectivity. The absence of IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc) rules out acute hepatitis B infection, as this antibody is typically present in the acute and early convalescent phases of the disease. The presence of antibody to HBeAg (anti-HBe) suggests prior infection with hepatitis B. Therefore, this patient's presentation is most consistent with an acute exacerbation of chronic hepatitis B infection.

few_shot.question: Two weeks after returning from vacation in Mexico, a 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of malaise, nausea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and right upper quadrant tenderness. The liver is palpated 1.5 cm below the right costal margin. A biopsy specimen of this patient's liver would most likely show which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recent travel to Mexico, along with his symptoms of malaise, nausea, vomiting, fever, abdominal pain, and jaundice, suggest acute viral hepatitis, most likely due to hepatitis A virus (HAV). HAV is transmitted via the fecal-oral route, and infection is common in developing countries with poor sanitation. The virus replicates in the liver and is excreted into the bile. 

Histologically, acute viral hepatitis is characterized by ballooning degeneration, in which hepatocytes become enlarged and round with rarified cytoplasm. There is also typically mononuclear inflammation and hepatocellular necrosis, which can be spotty (acidophilic bodies) or bridging (ie, connecting portal tracts and/or central veins). 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

A 22-year-old man is evaluated for abdominal discomfort he has had for the past 6 days and fever for the past 2 weeks. He also notes that his right upper abdomen is bothering him. Hepatitis B surface AB negative

The patient's symptoms, physical examination findings, and laboratory results are consistent with acute hepatitis A infection. The presence of anti-hepatitis A IgM antibodies indicates a recent infection, as these antibodies are produced early in the course of infection and usually disappear within 3-6 months. Anti-hepatitis A IgG antibodies, on the other hand, appear later in the course of infection and persist for life, providing lifelong immunity.

The production of these antibodies requires the differentiation of B cells into plasma cells, a process that is regulated by several transcription factors. One of these is B lymphocyte induced maturation protein 1 (BLIMP1), which is required for the terminal differentiation of B cells into antibody-secreting plasma cells. In the absence of BLIMP1, B cells cannot differentiate into plasma cells, leading to a lack of antibody production.

question:

Her temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), pulse is 105/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 112/82 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"

The presence of altered mental status and hypotension indicates severe disease (Reynolds pentad: fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, altered mental status, and hypotension). This is a medical emergency that requires prompt biliary decompression to prevent progression to septic shock and death. The preferred method of biliary decompression is endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), which allows for both diagnostic visualization and therapeutic intervention (eg, stone extraction, stent placement).

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old female visits the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain and fever of 2-hours duration. She denies alcohol, cigarette, and drug use and reports no other medical problems. Body mass index is 30 kg/m^2. Her temperature is 38.5 degrees Celsius (101.3 degrees Fahrenheit), blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 18/min. Jaundice is present in the sclera and at the base of the tongue. The abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant. Liver function test (LFTs) reveal elevated direct and total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase of 500 U/L. IV Ampicillin-gentamicin is administered, fluid resuscitation is initiated, and over 24 hours the patient’s fever improves. Which of the following is the next step in the management of this patient:
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice (Charcot's triad) is suggestive of ascending cholangitis, a bacterial infection of the biliary tree. The most common cause of ascending cholangitis is choledocholithiasis (ie, gallstones in the common bile duct). The presence of gallstones can cause obstruction of the biliary tree, leading to stasis of bile and bacterial overgrowth. The most common organisms involved are gram-negative enteric bacteria (eg, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species) and enterococci.

The initial management of ascending cholangitis involves hemodynamic resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Once the patient is stabilized, the definitive treatment is to relieve the biliary obstruction. This is typically accomplished via endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), which allows for both visualization of the biliary tree and removal of gallstones.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 44-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 10-hour history of severe nausea and abdominal pain that began 30 minutes after eating dinner. The pain primarily is in her right upper quadrant and occasionally radiates to her back. She has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolemia. Current medications include metformin and atorvastatin. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 91 kg (200 lb); BMI is 34 kg/m2. Her temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 150/76 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows right upper quadrant tenderness with guarding. A bedside ultrasound shows a gall bladder wall measuring 6 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sloughing of the intraluminal membrane, and a 2 x 2-cm stone at the neck of the gallbladder. The common bile duct appears unremarkable. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis and normal liver function tests. Intravenous fluids are started, and she is given ketorolac for pain control. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis after eating, along with ultrasound findings of gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck, is consistent with acute cholecystitis. This condition is caused by obstruction of the cystic duct, usually by a gallstone, leading to gallbladder inflammation. The initial management of acute cholecystitis includes supportive care with intravenous hydration, analgesics, and antibiotics. Antibiotics are used to target the most common pathogens, which include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species, and Enterococcus species. Empiric treatment options include a third-generation cephalosporin, a fluoroquinolone, or ampicillin/sulbactam. After the patient is stabilized, laparoscopic cholecystectomy is performed within 72 hours.

So, the answer is [B].

The pain began after her last meal, is constant, and she describes it as 7 out of 10 in intensity. She has had multiple similar episodes over the past 4 months that resolved spontaneously. She drinks 2 pints of vodka daily. She appears ill. Her temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 165/90 mm Hg. She is alert and fully oriented. Examination shows diaphoresis and multiple telangiectasias over the trunk and back. The abdomen is distended; there is tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant. When the patient is asked to inhale with the examiner's hand below the costal margin in the right midclavicular line, the patient winces and her breath catches. Voluntary guarding and shifting dullness are present. The liver is palpated 3 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL
Leukocyte count 16,300/mm3
Platelet count 150,000/mm3
Prothrombin time 20 sec (INR=1.3)
Serum
Urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL
Glucose 185 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL
Bilirubin (total) 2.1 mg/dL
Albumin 3.1 g/dL
An abdominal ultrasound shows multiple small stones in the gallbladder and fluid in the gallbladder wall with wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid and stranding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has acute cholecystitis, as evidenced by right upper quadrant pain, fever, leukocytosis, and a positive Murphy sign. The ultrasound findings of gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid are also consistent with this diagnosis. However, the presence of ascites and the physical examination findings of shifting dullness and a fluid wave suggest spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) as well. SBP is a common and potentially fatal complication of cirrhosis and is characterized by infection in the ascitic fluid. The diagnosis of SBP is made by paracentesis with ascitic fluid analysis showing an absolute polymorphonuclear leukocyte count >250/mm3. Empiric antibiotic therapy with a third-generation cephalosporin (eg, cefotaxime) should be started immediately after collecting fluid for analysis due to the high risk of death without prompt treatment.

few_shot.question:
A 42-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of intermittent sharp right upper quadrant abdominal pain and nausea for the past 10 hours. She has vomited 3 times. There is no associated fever, chills, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms. She has 2 children who both attend high school. She appears uncomfortable. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb). Her BMI is 32 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. She has mild scleral icterus. On physical examination, her abdomen is soft and nondistended, with tenderness to palpation of the right upper quadrant without guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds are normal. Laboratory studies show the following:
Blood
Hemoglobin count 14 g/dL
Leukocyte count 9,000 mm3
Platelet count 160,000 mm3
Serum
Alkaline phosphatase 238 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase 60 U/L
Bilirubin

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

answer_choices.B: Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan of the biliary tract
answer_choices.C: Supine and erect X-rays of the abdomen

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and abnormal liver function tests is suggestive of biliary tract disease. The most common cause of biliary tract disease is cholelithiasis, or gallstones. Gallstones can cause biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, and gallstone pancreatitis. This patient's lack of fever and normal leukocyte count make acute cholecystitis and cholangitis less likely. The absence of severe, constant abdominal pain and abnormal pancreatic enzymes makes gallstone pancreatitis less likely. Therefore, this patient most likely has biliary colic or choledocholithiasis.

The initial diagnostic test of choice for suspected gallstone disease is transabdominal ultrasonography, which can detect gallstones as well as findings suggestive of acute cholecystitis (eg, gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid). If ultrasonography does not show gallstones but the suspicion for gallstone disease remains high, a hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan can be performed. If gallstones are present but there is a high suspicion for choledocholithiasis (eg, due to abnormal liver function tests, as in this patient), further imaging of the common bile duct, such as endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), should be performed.

So, the answer is [D].

She is up to date on all vaccines and is meeting all developmental milestones. What is the most likely blood disorder?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's petechial rash, easy bruising, and isolated thrombocytopenia are suggestive of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). ITP is an acquired disorder that often occurs following a viral infection, and is caused by the production of autoantibodies against platelets. This leads to increased platelet destruction in the spleen, resulting in thrombocytopenia. The most common presentation is a child with new-onset petechiae, purpura, or easy bruising 1-3 weeks after a viral illness. The remainder of the CBC is normal, and coagulation studies (PT, PTT) are also normal because the coagulation factors are not affected.

ITP is an acquired disorder that commonly occurs in children following a viral infection, as in this patient. It is caused by the production of antiplatelet antibodies (typically IgG) that bind to platelets, leading to their premature destruction by the reticuloendothelial system, especially the spleen. The disease is usually self-limited in children, with bleeding symptoms and platelet counts improving within weeks to months. few_shot.question: A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a swollen and painful knee. He says that he was exploring with his friends when he tripped and hit his knee against the ground. He didn't feel like he hit it very hard but it started swelling and becoming very painful. His mom reports that he has always been prone to bleeding from very minor trauma and that others in the family have had similar problems. Based on clinical suspicion a coagulation panel was obtained showing a prothrombin time (PT) of 10 seconds (normal range 9-11 seconds), a partial thromboplastin time (PTT) of 45 seconds (normal 20-35 seconds), and a normal ristocetin cofactor assay (equivalent to bleeding time). Mixing tests with factor IX and XI do not show complementation, but mixing with factor VIII reverses the coagulation abnormality. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of bleeding from minor trauma, prolonged PTT, and correction of the coagulation abnormality with mixing studies containing factor VIII are suggestive of hemophilia A. Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by deficiency of factor VIII. It is the most common severe bleeding disorder and usually affects males. Patients may present with deep tissue bleeding, easy bruising, or prolonged bleeding after surgery or trauma. Hemarthroses (bleeding into joint spaces) are also common and can lead to debilitating arthropathy.

Hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) is clinically indistinguishable from hemophilia A but is less common. The PTT does not correct with mixing studies containing factor VIII in patients with hemophilia B.

Bernard-Soulier disease and Glanzmann thrombasthenia are platelet disorders that would present with mucocutaneous bleeding symptoms (eg, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia) and a prolonged bleeding time. The PT and PTT are normal in these conditions.

few_shot.question: A 5-year-old girl presents for a routine checkup. The patient’s parents say she has been looking pale and tired lately. Her family history is unremarkable. The presence of a mediastinal mass is highly suggestive of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), which is the most common malignancy in children. T-cell ALL often presents with a mediastinal mass, which can manifest with respiratory symptoms (eg, cough, stridor, dyspnea) due to compression of the trachea and/or superior vena cava.

question: An 80-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of fatigue and lightheadedness. He does not have chest pain, palpitations, or difficulty breathing. few_shot.question: A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of shortness of breath, epigastric pain, and sweating. He has no history of similar symptoms. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications include amlodipine and metformin. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. He appears weak and pale. His pulse is 56/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows normal heart sounds. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The skin is cold to the touch. An ECG is shown. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography shows normal left ventricular function. High-dose aspirin is administered. Administration of which of the following is most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute-onset chest pain, diaphoresis, and dyspnea is concerning for acute coronary syndrome (ACS). The ECG shows sinus bradycardia and inferior ST-segment elevations, consistent with an inferior wall ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Inferior STEMI is most often due to occlusion of the right coronary artery, which also supplies the sinoatrial (SA) and atrioventricular (AV) nodes in most individuals. As a result, inferior STEMI can present with bradyarrhythmias due to ischemia of the SA or AV node. This patient's bradycardia is likely due to increased vagal tone from inferior wall infarction/ischemia.

The initial management of STEMI includes aspirin, anticoagulation, and preparation for immediate reperfusion with percutaneous coronary intervention. However, this patient's hypotension and bradycardia suggest cardiogenic shock, which can be seen in the setting of right ventricular infarction. Right ventricular infarction impairs right ventricular function, leading to decreased right ventricular stroke volume and reduced left ventricular preload. This results in hypotension, elevated central venous pressure, and clear lung fields on examination. The treatment for right ventricular infarction is to optimize right ventricular preload with intravenous fluids, as right ventricular stroke volume in these patients is highly dependent on preload.

few_shot.question: A 70-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month-history of worsening shortness of breath on exertion and bouts of coughing while sleeping. His ECG findings of T wave inversions in leads V1 to V4 suggest a prior anterior wall myocardial infarction, which is a common cause of HFrEF. The mainstay of treatment for HFrEF includes beta blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (or angiotensin receptor blockers), and aldosterone antagonists, as these agents have been shown to decrease mortality. This patient is already on an ACE inhibitor (lisinopril), so the addition of a beta blocker (eg, metoprolol) would be the next best step in management.

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department for squeezing and substernal chest pain. He states that he was at home eating dinner when his symptoms began. The patient has a past medical history of diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. He is currently taking atorvastatin, lisinopril, insulin, metformin, metoprolol, and aspirin. Six days ago he underwent percutaneous coronary intervention. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 197/118 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals an uncomfortable elderly man who is sweating. An ECG is ordered. Which of the following is the best next step in management for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient presents with chest pain, diaphoresis, and a history of recent percutaneous coronary intervention, which is concerning for acute coronary syndrome (ACS). ACS is a spectrum of disease that includes unstable angina, non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The initial evaluation of a patient with suspected ACS includes an ECG and cardiac biomarkers. The ECG can help differentiate between STEMI and NSTEMI/unstable angina, as ST-segment elevation is indicative of transmural infarction (ie, STEMI). Cardiac biomarkers, including troponin and creatine kinase-muscle/brain (CK-MB), are released into the bloodstream from necrotic heart muscle. Troponin is the most sensitive and specific biomarker for myocardial injury and should be measured in all patients with suspected ACS. CK-MB is less sensitive and specific for myocardial injury but can be helpful in certain situations, such as identifying reinfarction in the days following an initial MI. Myoglobin is a nonspecific marker of muscle injury and is not recommended for routine use in ACS.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old man presents to the emergency department with progressive dyspnea for the last 3 weeks. He complains of shortness of breath while lying flat and reports nighttime awakenings due to shortness of breath for the same duration. The patient has been a smoker for the last 30 years. Past medical history is significant for myocardial infarction 7 months ago. Current medications include metoprolol, aspirin, and rosuvastatin, but the patient is noncompliant with his medications. His temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), the blood pressure is 150/115 mm Hg, the pulse is 110/min, and the respiratory rate is 24/min. Oxygen saturation on room air is 88%. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral crackles and an S3 gallop. On physical examination, the cardiac apex is palpated in left 6th intercostal space. Bilateral pitting edema is present, and the patient is in moderate distress. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of the patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and bilateral crackles on lung auscultation is consistent with acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF). ADHF is a common and potentially serious cause of acute respiratory distress. The condition is characterized by the sudden or gradual onset of heart failure symptoms, which typically include dyspnea at rest or with exertion, orthopnea, and lower extremity edema. Physical examination may reveal pulmonary rales, an S3 gallop, and elevated jugular venous pressure. The most common precipitating factors for ADHF include ischemia, uncontrolled hypertension, medication noncompliance, and arrhythmias.

The initial management of ADHF involves measures to relieve congestion (preload reduction) and improve cardiac output. Intravenous loop diuretics (eg, furosemide) are the most effective agents for preload reduction and are typically the first-line treatment for patients with volume overload. Diuretics decrease blood volume, reducing ventricular filling pressures and alleviating pulmonary and systemic congestion.

question: A 32-year-old Caucasian woman is referred to a gastroenterologist by her family physician for 8 months of abdominal pain, foul-smelling diarrhea with floating, bulky stools, weight loss, and macrocytic anemia. few_shot.question: A 43-year-old woman visits her primary care physician complaining of abdominal pain for the past 6 months. She reports that the pain is localized to her lower abdomen and often resolves with bowel movements. She states that some days she has diarrhea while other times she will go 4-5 days without having a bowel movement. She started a gluten-free diet in hopes that it would help her symptoms, but she has not noticed much improvement. She denies nausea, vomiting, hematochezia, or melena. Her medical history is significant for generalized anxiety disorder and hypothyroidism. Her father has a history of colon cancer. The patient takes citalopram and levothyroxine. Physical examination reveals mild abdominal tenderness with palpation of lower quadrant but no guarding or rebound. A guaiac test is negative. A complete blood count is pending. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of abdominal pain that is relieved by defecation and altered bowel habits are suggestive of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). IBS is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic or recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits. It is a clinical diagnosis based on the Rome IV criteria, which require recurrent abdominal pain at least 1 day/week in the last 3 months associated with 2 or more of the following: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, or change in stool form. However, IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion and should only be made after ruling out organic disease, especially in patients >50 years of age or those with alarm symptoms (eg, nocturnal diarrhea, rectal bleeding, weight loss, family history of colon cancer, sudden change in bowel habits after age 50). This patient's family history of colon cancer is concerning, and she should undergo colonoscopy to rule out colorectal cancer.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old Caucasian woman is referred to the outpatient clinic by a physician at a health camp for 6-months of foul-smelling diarrhea with bulky and floating stools as well as significant flatulence which makes her extremely uncomfortable at work and social events. She has concomitant weight loss and recently fractured her wrist in a seemingly insignificant fall from her own height. Vital signs are normal and a physical examination shows grouped, papulovesicular, pruritic skin lesions, as well as areas of hypoesthesia in the hands and feet. Which of the following would be most useful in this case?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's foul-smelling, bulky, floating stools, flatulence, weight loss, and wrist fracture are suggestive of malabsorption. The grouped, papulovesicular, pruritic skin lesions are consistent with dermatitis herpetiformis, which is pathognomonic for celiac disease. Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder that is triggered by the ingestion of gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. It is characterized by inflammation and villous atrophy of the small intestine, leading to malabsorption. Dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely pruritic, chronic, autoimmune, blistering disease that is associated with gluten sensitivity and is characterized by granular deposits of IgA in the dermal papillae. The areas of hypoesthesia in the hands and feet are likely due to peripheral neuropathy, which can occur in celiac disease due to vitamin B12 deficiency. The diagnosis of celiac disease can be confirmed by the presence of anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with a longstanding history of diarrhea. This patient's chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and rash are suggestive of celiac disease, an autoimmune disorder triggered by the ingestion of gluten in genetically predisposed individuals. The rash she describes is likely dermatitis herpetiformis, an intensely pruritic, chronic, papulovesicular rash that is pathognomonic for celiac disease. The rash is typically distributed symmetrically on extensor surfaces (eg, elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp) and is characterized histologically by granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae.

The diagnosis of celiac disease is suggested by positive serologic testing (eg, anti-tissue transglutaminase, anti-endomysial antibodies) and confirmed by small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of abdominal pain and diarrhea for 2 months. The pain is intermittent, colicky and localized to her right lower quadrant. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F), blood pressure 125/65 mm Hg, pulse 75/min, and respirations 14/min. An abdominal examination shows mild tenderness of the right lower quadrant on deep palpation without guarding. Colonoscopy shows small aphthous-like ulcers in the right colon and terminal ileum. Biopsy from the terminal ileum shows noncaseating granulomas in all layers of the bowel wall. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of chronic abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss, along with colonoscopy findings of aphthous-like ulcers in the right colon and terminal ileum, is suggestive of Crohn disease (CD). CD is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus. It is characterized by transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas on biopsy.

The treatment of CD depends on the severity and location of the disease. Mild to moderate ileocecal disease, as in this patient, is typically treated with an oral corticosteroid such as budesonide. Budesonide is a glucocorticoid with high first-pass metabolism that results in less systemic toxicity compared to other corticosteroids. It is used to induce remission in patients with mild to moderate CD involving the ileum and/or ascending colon.

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old woman is brought to her primary care physician by her son who is worried about her weight loss. She forgets phone conversations and often acts surprised when he visits, even though he always confirms his visits the night before. Her medical history includes arthritis, which she admits has been getting worse, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. She takes omeprazole. On physical exam, she has a new systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border. Labs show normocytic anemia. A transesophageal echocardiogram reveals a small mobile mass on the aortic valve with moderate aortic insufficiency. A colonoscopy is obtained with a small bowel biopsy. A periodic acid-Schiff stain is positive for foamy macrophages. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has aortic valve endocarditis with a positive periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain, which is indicative of Whipple disease. Whipple disease is a systemic illness caused by the gram-positive bacillus Tropheryma whipplei. It classically presents with migratory arthralgias, weight loss, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Neurologic symptoms, such as cognitive impairment, are also common. The PAS stain is positive for foamy macrophages in the lamina propria of the small intestine. The disease can also cause endocarditis, which is suggested by the new murmur and the mobile mass on the aortic valve seen on echocardiogram. The treatment for Whipple disease is ceftriaxone or penicillin G for 2 weeks, followed by trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 1-2 years.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 25 minutes after falling and hitting his left flank on a concrete block. AAC is most commonly seen in critically ill patients (eg, severe trauma, burns, sepsis, postoperative state) and is associated with gallbladder stasis and ischemia. The pathogenesis of AAC is multifactorial and includes bile stasis (due to fasting and the use of narcotics), ischemia (due to hypotension or vasospasm), and systemic inflammation (eg, sepsis, major surgery). AAC can lead to gallbladder necrosis and perforation if not treated promptly.

The diagnosis of AAC is suggested by right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis in a hospitalized patient. Abdominal ultrasonography typically shows a distended gallbladder, gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and an absence of gallstones. The Murphy sign (ie, inspiratory arrest during palpation of the right upper quadrant) may also be present.

AAC is initially managed with antibiotics and percutaneous cholecystostomy, especially in critically ill patients who are poor surgical candidates. Cholecystectomy is typically performed after the patient's condition stabilizes.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of shortness of breath and right-sided chest pain for 3 days. The pain is sharp and worsens with deep inspiration. He has also had a fever and a cough productive of yellow sputum for 5 days. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.5°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 132/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dullness to percussion at the bases of the right lung; breath sounds are diminished over the right middle and lower lobes. An x-ray of the chest shows blunting of the right costophrenic angle. Pleural fluid obtained via diagnostic thoracocentesis shows a pH of 7.1 and glucose concentration of 55 mg/dL. In addition to broad-spectrum antibiotics, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of cough productive of purulent sputum, fever, pleuritic chest pain, and unilateral pleural effusion is consistent with parapneumonic effusion (ie, pleural effusion associated with bacterial pneumonia). Parapneumonic effusions can be categorized as uncomplicated or complicated based on pleural fluid analysis. Complicated parapneumonic effusions are associated with more severe infection and are suggested by any of the following: pH <7.2, glucose <60 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase >1000 U/L, Gram stain or culture positive for bacteria. This patient's pleural fluid analysis shows a pH of 7.1 and glucose of 55 mg/dL, consistent with a complicated parapneumonic effusion.

The initial management of a complicated parapneumonic effusion involves prompt chest tube placement for complete drainage of the infected pleural fluid. This is in addition to appropriate antibiotics. Failure to drain the infected fluid can lead to progression to an empyema (ie, frank pus in the pleural space), which may require more invasive interventions such as video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery or open thoracotomy for drainage.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of redness, swelling, and pain of the right leg. He also has fever, chills, and nausea. He has noticed liquid oozing from the affected area on his right leg. He has a history of hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Three months ago, he was hospitalized for treatment of a hip fracture. His current medications include metoprolol, enalapril, and omeprazole. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 106/min, and blood pressure is 142/94 mm Hg. Examination of the right lower leg shows a large area of erythema with poorly-demarcated borders and purulent drainage. The area is nonfluctuant, warm, and tender to touch. Examination of the right groin shows several enlarged, tender lymph nodes. There is mild edema of the ankles bilaterally. Blood and wound cultures are collected. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, erythema, and purulent drainage from the right lower leg is consistent with cellulitis, a skin infection that typically involves the dermis and subcutaneous tissues. The most common pathogens are Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S aureus (MRSA). Risk factors for MRSA infection include recent hospitalization, surgery, dialysis, and residence in a long-term care facility. This patient's recent hospitalization for a hip fracture is a risk factor for MRSA infection. Therefore, empiric antibiotic therapy should include coverage for MRSA, such as vancomycin or daptomycin.

few_shot.question: A 70-year-old man with a recent above-the-knee amputation of the left lower extremity, due to wet gangrene secondary to refractory peripheral artery disease, presents with weakness and dizziness. He says that the symptoms began acutely 24 hours after surgery and have not improved. The amputation was complicated by substantial blood loss. He was placed on empiric antibiotic therapy with ciprofloxacin and clindamycin before the procedure, and blood and wound culture results are still pending. The medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Current medications are metformin and lisinopril. The family history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus in both parents. Review of symptoms is significant for palpitations and a mild headache for the past 24 hours. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F); blood pressure, 120/70 mm Hg (supine); pulse, 102/min; respiratory rate, 16/min; and oxygen saturation, 99% on room air. When standing, the blood pressure is 90/65 mm Hg and the pulse is 115/min. On physical examination, the patient appears pale and listless. The surgical amputation site does not show any signs of ongoing blood loss or infection. Laboratory tests and an ECG are pending. Which of the following is the next best step in management?

answer_choices.A: Administer IV fluids and withhold lisinopril

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of weakness, dizziness, and orthostatic hypotension is suggestive of hypovolemia, likely due to the substantial blood loss during his recent surgery. The most appropriate next step in management is to administer IV fluids to restore intravascular volume. In addition, his antihypertensive medication, lisinopril, should be withheld. This is because ACE inhibitors can exacerbate hypotension by blocking angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone release, leading to arterial and venous dilation and decreased sodium reabsorption in the distal tubules, respectively.

question: A 45-year-old G3P3 presents complaining of the feeling of a foreign body in her vagina that worsens on standing. She does not have urinary or fecal incontinence or any other genitourinary symptoms. She has no known gynecologic diseases. There were no complications with her pregnancies, all of which were full-term vaginal deliveries. She is sexually active with her husband and no longer uses oral contraceptives. She has an 11 pack-year history of smoking. Her weight is 79 kg (174 lb) and her height is 155 cm (5 ft). Her vital signs are within normal limits. The physical examination is unremarkable. The gynecologic examination reveals descent of the cervix halfway towards the introitus. On Valsalva and standing, the cervix descents to the plane of the hymen. The uterus is not enlarged and the ovaries are non-palpable. Which of the following treatments is most reasonable to offer this patient?

few_shot.question: A 53-year-old woman presents with a feeling of pelvic pressure which worsens with prolonged standing, pain on sexual intercourse, and lower back pain. She reports no urinary or fecal incontinence. She is G3P3 with no history of any gynecological disease and is premenopausal. All pregnancies were without complication and resolved with full-term vaginal deliveries. The patient has sex with her husband who is her single sexual partner and uses oral contraceptives. Her vital signs are within normal limits and physical examination is unremarkable. A gynecological examination reveals bulging of the posterior vaginal wall in the lower portion of the vagina which increases in the upright position and Valsalva maneuver. The cervix is in its normal position. The uterus is not enlarged, ovaries are nonpalpable. Damage to which of the following structures might contribute to the patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of pelvic pressure, dyspareunia, and lower back pain, along with the physical examination findings of bulging of the posterior vaginal wall, are suggestive of a rectocele. A rectocele is a type of pelvic organ prolapse that occurs when the rectum herniates into the vagina. This is typically due to damage to the rectovaginal fascia, which normally separates the rectum from the vagina. Risk factors for rectocele include vaginal childbirth, advanced age, and conditions that increase intra-abdominal pressure such as obesity and chronic constipation.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 66-year-old G3P3 presents with an 8-year-history of back pain, perineal discomfort, difficulty urinating, recurrent malaise, and low-grade fevers. These symptoms have recurred regularly for the past 5–6 years. She also says that there are times when she experiences a feeling of having a foreign body in her vagina. With the onset of symptoms, she was evaluated by a physician who prescribed her medications after a thorough examination and recommended a vaginal pessary, but she was non-compliant. She had 3 vaginal deliveries She has been menopausal since 51 years of age. She does not have a history of malignancies or cardiovascular disease. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus that is controlled with diet and metformin. Her vital signs include: blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, heart rate 91/min, respiratory rate 13/min, and temperature 37.4℃ (99.3℉). On physical examination, there is bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness. The urinary bladder is non-palpable. The gynecologic examination reveals descent of the cervix to the level of the introitus. A Valsalva maneuver elicits uterine procidentia. Which pathology is most likely to be revealed by imaging in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections, back pain, and perineal discomfort, which are suggestive of urinary stasis. The physical examination findings of uterine procidentia (ie, total eversion of the uterus) are consistent with stage IV pelvic organ prolapse (POP). POP occurs when the normal support structures of the vagina (eg, levator ani muscles, cardinal-uterosacral ligament complex) become weakened or damaged, allowing descent of the pelvic organs. Risk factors for POP include conditions that increase intra-abdominal pressure (eg, obesity, chronic cough, constipation) and injure the pelvic support structures (eg, pregnancy, childbirth, prior pelvic surgery). This patient's multiple vaginal deliveries and advanced age are likely risk factors for her POP.

Advanced POP can cause obstructive uropathy due to urethral kinking, leading to urinary retention and stasis. This can result in recurrent urinary tract infections and hydronephrosis, which can present with back pain due to urinary obstruction and subsequent distention of the renal capsule. Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 70-year-old woman, gravida 5, para 5, comes to the physician for the evaluation of sensation of vaginal fullness for the last six months. During this period, she has had lower back and pelvic pain that is worse with prolonged standing or walking. The patient underwent a hysterectomy at the age of 35 years because of severe dysmenorrhea. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolemia. Medications include metformin and atorvastatin. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination elicits a feeling of pressure on the perineum. Pelvic floor muscle and anal sphincter tone are decreased. Pelvic examination shows protrusion of posterior vaginal wall with Valsalva maneuver and vaginal discharge. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sensation of vaginal fullness, lower back and pelvic pain, and protrusion of the posterior vaginal wall with Valsalva maneuver are suggestive of a pelvic organ prolapse. The most common type of pelvic organ prolapse is cystocele, which is the herniation of the bladder into the vagina. However, this patient's history of hysterectomy makes an enterocele more likely. An enterocele is the herniation of the small bowel into the vagina, and it is more common in women who have had a hysterectomy. The other options, Bartholin gland cyst, atrophic vaginitis, and infectious vulvovaginitis, would not cause the sensation of vaginal fullness or the protrusion of the posterior vaginal wall with Valsalva maneuver.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 31-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist to be evaluated for her inability to conceive. She is G1P0 who has a 28-day cycle and no menstrual abnormalities. Her single pregnancy terminated early with an elective abortion at the patient’s request. She had several sexual partners before meeting her husband 5 years ago. They have intercourse regularly without the use of contraception and have been tracking her ovulation cycle to try to become pregnant for at least 1 year. She reports a history of occasional malodorous vaginal discharge and mild lower abdominal pain after menses and sexual intercourse, but she notes no such symptoms recently. Her husband’s spermogram was normal. Her weight is 65 kg (143 lb) and the height is 160 cm (5 ft, 3 in). On examination, the patient’s vital signs are within normal limits. The physical examination is unremarkable. On pelvic examination, the adnexa are slightly tender to palpation bilaterally. Which of the following tests is the most reasonable to be performed next in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a history of multiple sexual partners and symptoms of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which is a risk factor for infertility. PID is an ascending infection of the female reproductive tract that can cause tubal scarring and obstruction, leading to infertility. The most common organisms that cause PID are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. The diagnosis of PID is clinical and is based on the presence of lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, and adnexal tenderness. This patient's history of malodorous vaginal discharge and lower abdominal pain after menses and sexual intercourse is suggestive of PID. The most appropriate next step in the evaluation of this patient's infertility is hysterosalpingography, which can evaluate tubal patency and the uterine cavity.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 58-year-old woman presents to the physician’s office with vaginal bleeding. The bleeding started as a spotting and has increased and has become persistent over the last month. The patient is G3P1 with a history of polycystic ovary syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She completed menopause 4 years ago. She took cyclic estrogen-progesterone replacement therapy for 1 year at the beginning of menopause. Her weight is 89 kg (196 lb), height 157 cm (5 ft 2 in). Her vital signs are as follows: blood pressure 135/70 mm Hg, heart rate 78/min, respiratory rate 12/min, and temperature 36.7℃ (98.1℉). Physical examination is unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound reveals an endometrium of 6 mm thickness. Speculum examination shows a cervix without focal lesions with bloody discharge from the non-dilated external os. On pelvic examination, the uterus is slightly enlarged, movable, and non-tender. Adnexa is non-palpable. What is the next appropriate step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has postmenopausal bleeding (PMB), which is defined as any bleeding that occurs 12 months or more after the last menstrual period. PMB is a common problem, occurring in up to 10% of postmenopausal women. The most common cause of PMB is atrophy of the endometrium or vagina due to decreased estrogen levels. However, PMB can also be a sign of endometrial cancer or atypical endometrial hyperplasia, a precursor to cancer. Therefore, all women with PMB should undergo evaluation to exclude endometrial cancer or hyperplasia.

The initial evaluation of PMB includes a transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness. An endometrial thickness ≤4 mm significantly decreases the likelihood of endometrial cancer in a patient with PMB. However, if the endometrial thickness is >4 mm, as in this patient, or if it cannot be adequately measured, an endometrial biopsy should be performed. Endometrial biopsy is an office-based procedure that involves dilating the cervix and passing a small suction catheter into the uterus to obtain a sample of the endometrium. It is the most cost-effective method for evaluating women with PMB and has a sensitivity of approximately 90% for diagnosing endometrial cancer.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 51-year-old man presents to his primary care provider complaining of malaise. He returned from a research trip to Madagascar 2 weeks ago and has since developed a worsening fever with a maximum temperature of 102.2°F (39°C). He also reports some swelling around his neck and groin. He works as a zoologist and was in rural Madagascar studying a rare species of lemur. His past medical history is notable for hypertension and gout. He takes lisinopril and allopurinol. His temperature is 101.9°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 145/85 mmHg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 22/min. On exam, he has painful erythematous cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Black hemorrhagic eschars are noted on his fingertips bilaterally. The pathogen responsible for this patient’s condition produces a virulence factor that has which of the following functions?

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of a 1-day history of fever, shortness of breath, dizziness, and cough productive of purulent sputum. Six days ago, she developed malaise, headache, sore throat, and myalgias that improved initially. Her temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F) and blood pressure is 84/56 mm Hg. Examination shows an erythematous, desquamating rash of the distal extremities. A sputum culture grows gram-positive, coagulase-positive cocci in clusters. The most likely causal organism of this patient's current symptoms produces a virulence factor with which of the following functions?

answer_choices.B: Binding of Fc domain of immunoglobulin G

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, hypotension, erythematous rash, and desquamation are suggestive of toxic shock syndrome (TSS), a toxin-mediated disease caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. The most common cause of staphylococcal TSS is the superantigen toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1). Superantigens are able to bypass the normal major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II processing and presentation of antigens to T cells. Instead, they bind directly to the MHC class II molecule on the antigen-presenting cell and the variable region of the β-chain of the T-cell receptor, leading to polyclonal T-cell activation. This results in massive cytokine release, including interleukin-1, interleukin-2, and tumor necrosis factor-α, which leads to the clinical manifestations of TSS.

The other options listed are virulence factors of other organisms. Degradation of membranous phospholipids is a function of phospholipases, which are produced by organisms such as Clostridium perfringens and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Overstimulation of guanylate cyclase is a function of the heat-stable enterotoxin produced by enterotoxigenic E. coli. Inactivation of elongation factor 2 is a function of the diphtheria toxin produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy presents with fever, sore throat, hoarseness, and neck enlargement. The symptoms started 3 days ago and progressed gradually with an elevated temperature and swollen lymph nodes. His family immigrated recently from Honduras. He was born via spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks after an uneventful gestational period and he is now on a catch-up vaccination schedule. He lives with several family members, including his parents, in a small apartment. No one in the apartment smokes tobacco. On presentation, the patient’s blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg, heart rate is 103/min, respiratory rate is 20/min, and temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F). On physical examination, the child is acrocyanotic and somnolent. There is widespread cervical edema and enlargement of the cervical lymph nodes. The tonsils are covered with a gray, thick membrane which spreads beyond the tonsillar bed and reveals bleeding, erythematous mucosa with gentle scraping. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the target of the virulence factor produced by the pathologic organism infecting this child?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, sore throat, and cervical lymphadenopathy are suggestive of pharyngitis. The presence of a grayish-white pseudomembrane that bleeds upon removal is characteristic of diphtheria, which is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. This organism produces an exotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis in the host cell by catalyzing the ADP-ribosylation of eukaryotic elongation factor-2 (eEF-2). This prevents the translocation step of protein synthesis, leading to cell death. The exotoxin can also cause myocarditis and neuritis.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A previously healthy 32-year-old male comes to the emergency department because of a high-grade fever and malaise for 3 days. He has severe generalized joint and body pains refractory to acetaminophen. He also has a severe stabbing pain behind his eyes. He returned from a trip to Taiwan 1 week ago. He is sexually active and uses condoms inconsistently. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Examination shows nontender inguinal lymphadenopathy. There is a maculopapular rash over the trunk and extremities with some sparing of the skin over his back and groin. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL
Leukocyte count 3,900/mm3
Platelet count 90,000/mm3
Serum
Na+ 136 mEq/L

Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL
Bilirubin

Alkaline phosphatase 40 U/L
AST 130 U/L

Urinalysis is normal. An ELISA test for HIV is negative. Which of the following measures is most likely to have prevented this patient’s condition?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of high fever, severe myalgias, retro-orbital pain, rash, and leukopenia after returning from Taiwan is suggestive of dengue fever. Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne illness caused by the dengue virus, a flavivirus. It is transmitted by the Aedes mosquito and is common in the tropical regions of the world. The virus has 4 serotypes, and infection with 1 serotype leads to lifelong immunity against that serotype but only short-term immunity against the others. Subsequent infection with a different serotype can lead to more severe disease (eg, dengue hemorrhagic fever, dengue shock syndrome).

The most effective preventive measure against dengue fever is mosquito control and use of protective measures to prevent mosquito bites (eg, use of mosquito repellent, protective clothing, staying in air-conditioned or well-screened areas, treating clothing with permethrin).

few_shot.question: A 49-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-hour history of fever, an itchy rash, and generalized body aches. Ten days ago, he received treatment in the emergency department for a snake bite. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 120/84 mm Hg. Physical examination shows multiple well-demarcated, raised, erythematous plaques over the trunk. There is tenderness to palpation and decreased range of motion of the metacarpophalangeal and wrist joints bilaterally. Urine dipstick shows 2+ protein. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, rash, arthralgias, and proteinuria following a recent snake bite is suggestive of serum sickness. Serum sickness is a type III hypersensitivity reaction that occurs following the administration of certain drugs (eg, penicillins, sulfonamides), infections (eg, hepatitis B), or antiserum (eg, antivenom for snake bites). It is caused by the formation of immune complexes that deposit in various tissues, leading to complement activation and an inflammatory response. This can result in symptoms such as fever, rash, arthralgias, and renal involvement (eg, proteinuria). Serum complement concentrations are often decreased due to consumption by the immune complexes.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 35-year-old male nurse presents to the emergency room complaining of fever and malaise. On examination, a generalized maculopapular rash and bilateral conjunctival injection are noted. Laboratory testing reveals the presence of negative sense, singled-stranded linear genetic material with filaments of varying lengths. The pathogen responsible for this patient’s symptoms is most similar to which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fever, malaise, myalgia, and sore throat, along with his recent travel to Liberia, are suggestive of Ebola virus disease. The Ebola virus is a member of the Filoviridae family, which also includes the Marburg virus. These viruses are filamentous, enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses. They are known to cause severe hemorrhagic fever in humans and nonhuman primates. The disease is often severe, with a high case fatality rate and a propensity to spread within healthcare settings.

question: A 27-year-old male presents for emergency surgery to reattach his left arm, severed during a high-speed car accident, and has lost significant amounts of blood. His wife arrives within minutes to the hospital exclaiming that under no circumstance should he receive any blood transfusions during surgery. After reviewing his medical chart, you see also see an annotation indicating no blood transfusions for religious reasons. Knowing that he needs a blood transfusion to save his life, what do you do?

answer_choices.A: Administer a blood transfusion to save the patient's life
answer_choices.B: Call the ethics board of the hospital to discuss the issue
answer_choices.C: Respect the patient's written instructions and do not adminster a blood transfusion

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman is in a high-speed motor vehicle accident and suffers multiple injuries to her extremities and abdomen. In the field, she was bleeding profusely bleeding and, upon arrival to the emergency department, she is lethargic and unable to speak. Her blood pressure on presentation is 70/40 mmHg. The trauma surgery team recommends emergency exploratory laparotomy. While the patient is in the trauma bay, her husband calls and says that the patient is a Jehovah's witness and that her religion does not permit her to receive a blood transfusion. No advanced directives are available. Which of the following is an appropriate next step?

answer_choices.B: Withhold transfusion based on husband's request
answer_choices.D: Obtain a court order for transfusion

In an emergency situation, when a patient is unable to provide consent and no advanced directives are available, the physician should proceed with the treatment that is most likely to save the patient's life. In this case, the patient is in hemorrhagic shock and requires immediate resuscitation, which includes blood transfusion. Therefore, the physician should proceed with the transfusion.

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman is in a high-speed motor vehicle accident and suffers multiple injuries to her extremities and abdomen. The trauma surgery team recommends emergency exploratory laparotomy. While the patient is in the trauma bay it is noted in the chart that the patient is a Jehovah's witness, and you are aware that her religion does not permit her to receive a blood transfusion. No advanced directives are available, but her ex-husband is contacted by phone and states that although they haven't spoken in a while, he thinks she would not want a transfusion. Which of the following is an appropriate next step?

answer_choices.B: Ask ex-husband to bring identification to the trauma bay
answer_choices.D: Obtain a court order for transfusion

few_shot.explanation:
In an emergency situation, when a patient is unable to provide consent for a life-saving intervention, the principle of implied consent applies. This principle assumes that a reasonable person would consent to emergency treatment if they were able to do so. Therefore, in this case, the patient should be given a blood transfusion if it is deemed necessary to save her life.

The ex-husband's opinion is not relevant in this case, as he is not the patient's legal surrogate decision maker. An ethics consult or court order would not be appropriate, as they would delay the necessary treatment.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 15-year-old teenager presents to the emergency department via emergency medical service (EMS) after a motor vehicle accident. The patient is in critical condition and is hemodynamically unstable. It becomes apparent that the patient may require a blood transfusion, and the parents are approached for consent. They are Jehovah’s Witnesses and deny the blood transfusion, saying it is against their beliefs. However, the patient insists that she wants the transfusion if it will save her life. Despite the patient’s wishes, the parents remain steadfast in their refusal to allow the transfusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

answer_choices.A: Give the patient the blood transfusion.
answer_choices.B: Do not give blood transfusion due to the parents’ refusal.
answer_choices.D: Obtain a court order to give blood products.

few_shot.explanation:
In general, parents have the right to make medical decisions for their minor children. However, this right is not absolute and can be limited in certain situations. For example, when a minor is deemed to be a mature minor, they may be able to make their own medical decisions. A mature minor is a person under the age of 18 who has the capacity and maturity to understand and appreciate the nature and consequences of a proposed treatment, including its risks, benefits, and alternatives. In this case, the patient is a mature minor who understands the risks and benefits of a blood transfusion and is able to make her own medical decisions. Therefore, the physician should respect the patient's autonomy and give the blood transfusion.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 12-year-old boy and his mother are brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. The boy was an unrestrained passenger in a head-on collision and was ejected from the front seat. The patient's mother was the driver and she is currently being resuscitated. Neither the child nor the mother are conscious; however, it is documented that the family are all Jehovah's witnesses and would not want a transfusion in an acute situation. The husband/father arrives to the trauma bay and confirms this wish that everyone in the family would not want a transfusion in accordance with their beliefs. The father is confirmed as the official healthcare proxy. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

answer_choices.B: Do not transfuse the boy or the mother
answer_choices.C: Do not transfuse the mother and transfuse the boy

few_shot.explanation:
In the United States, competent adults have the right to refuse medical treatment, including life-saving interventions, for religious or other reasons. However, parents do not have the right to refuse life-saving treatment for their children based on religious beliefs. Therefore, if a blood transfusion is necessary to save the life of the child in this case, it should be administered despite the parents' objections. The mother, as a competent adult, has the right to refuse a blood transfusion, and her wishes should be respected.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 35-year-old man and his 9-year-old son are brought to the emergency department following a high-speed motor vehicle collision. The father was the restrained driver. He is conscious. His pulse is 135/min and his blood pressure is 76/55 mm Hg. His hemoglobin concentration is 5.9 g/dL. His son sustained multiple body contusions and loss of consciousness. He remains unresponsive in the emergency department. A focused assessment of the boy with sonography is concerning for multiple organ lacerations and internal bleeding. The physician decides to move the man's son to the operating room for emergency surgical exploration. The father says that he and his son are Jehovah's witnesses and do not want blood transfusions. The physician calls the boy's biological mother who confirms this religious belief. She also asks the physician to wait for her arrival before any other medical decisions are undertaken. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the physician?

answer_choices.A: Consult hospital ethics committee for medical treatment of the son
answer_choices.B: Proceed to surgery on the son without transfusion
answer_choices.C: Seek a court order for medical treatment of the son
answer_choices.D: Transfuse packed red blood cells to the son but not to father

few_shot.explanation:
Jehovah's Witnesses are a religious group that often refuse blood transfusions due to their interpretation of biblical passages. However, the right to refuse medical treatment based on religious beliefs applies only to competent adults and mature minors. In the case of minors who lack decision-making capacity, parents generally have the authority to make medical decisions on their behalf. However, this authority is not absolute and can be overridden in life-threatening situations if the proposed intervention is likely to prevent significant harm or death. In such cases, medical professionals have a duty to provide life-saving treatment, even if it is against the wishes of the parents. Therefore, in this case, the physician should transfuse packed red blood cells to the son but not to the father.

So, the answer is [D].

question: A 35-year-old man returns to the clinic to follow up for his chronic stomach pain. At the last visit a few months ago, he explained that he had been experiencing discomfort in his upper abdomen for awhile. He had never vomited up any blood and had not had any substantial weight loss. He did not take any medications, did not smoke, and had no family history of gastric cancer. At that time, the doctor empirically started him on a proton pump inhibitor (PPI). Today, despite the PPI, the patient says he is still experiencing discomfort. Hearing this, the doctor decides to order a urease breath test. What is the most likely cause of this patient's chronic stomach pain?

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 37-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of a 8-week history of intermittent burning epigastric pain. During this period, he has also felt bloated and uncomfortable after meals. He has not had weight loss or a change in bowel habits. He has no personal or family history of serious illness. He takes no medications. He does not smoke. He drinks 1–3 beers per week. Vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows mild epigastric tenderness on palpation without guarding or rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are normal. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's epigastric pain, postprandial fullness, and bloating are suggestive of dyspepsia. Dyspepsia is a common condition characterized by chronic or recurrent discomfort or pain centered in the upper abdomen. It is typically classified as either functional (ie, no organic, systemic, or metabolic disease that is likely to explain the symptoms) or secondary to an underlying condition (eg, peptic ulcer disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, malignancy).

In patients <60 years of age with uninvestigated dyspepsia, the most common causes are functional dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease. Because this patient has no alarm features (eg, unintentional weight loss, progressive dysphagia, recurrent vomiting, evidence of gastrointestinal bleeding, family history of gastrointestinal cancers, previous esophagogastric malignancy), the next best step is to test for Helicobacter pylori infection, which is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease. The urea breath test is a noninvasive test that detects active H pylori infection with high sensitivity and specificity.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of upper abdominal pain. During this period, he has also had nausea, heartburn, and multiple episodes of diarrhea with no blood or mucus. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 18 years. He does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. Current medications include an antacid. The abdomen is soft and there is tenderness to palpation in the epigastric and umbilical areas. Upper endoscopy shows several ulcers in the duodenum and the upper jejunum as well as thick gastric folds. Gastric pH is < 2. Biopsies from the ulcers show no organisms. Which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's multiple peptic ulcers, especially those in the jejunum, along with the presence of thick gastric folds, suggest the diagnosis of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES). ZES is characterized by severe peptic ulcer disease, gastroesophageal reflux, and chronic diarrhea due to a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) that leads to gastric acid hypersecretion. The diagnosis of ZES is confirmed by demonstrating an elevated fasting serum gastrin level and positive secretin stimulation test (ie, increased serum gastrin level following administration of secretin).

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 12-month history of upper abdominal pain. The pain is worse after eating, which she reports as 7 out of 10 in intensity. Over the last year, she has also had nausea, heartburn, and multiple episodes of diarrhea with no blood or mucus. Eight months ago, she underwent an upper endoscopy, which showed several ulcers in the gastric antrum, the pylorus, and the duodenum, as well as thick gastric folds. The biopsies from these ulcers were negative for H. pylori. Current medications include pantoprazole and over-the-counter antacids. She appears anxious. Vital signs are within normal limits. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is soft and there is tenderness to palpation in the epigastric and umbilical areas. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. A repeat upper endoscopy shows persistent gastric and duodenal ulceration with minimal bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent peptic ulcers, diarrhea, and negative tests for H. pylori suggest a diagnosis of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES). ZES is characterized by severe peptic ulcer disease, gastroesophageal reflux, and diarrhea due to a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) that leads to gastric acid hypersecretion. The ulcers in ZES are often multiple and can be found in unusual locations such as the distal duodenum and jejunum. The diagnosis of ZES is established by demonstrating elevated fasting serum gastrin levels and positive secretin stimulation test results. The secretin stimulation test is performed by administering intravenous secretin and measuring serum gastrin levels. An increase in serum gastrin level following secretin administration is diagnostic of ZES. However, the initial test in the evaluation of a patient with suspected ZES is the fasting serum gastrin level.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old male patient with a history of recurrent nephrolithiasis and chronic lower back pain presents to the ER with severe, sudden-onset, upper abdominal pain. The patient is febrile, hypotensive, and tachycardic, and is rushed to the OR for exploratory laporotomy. Surgery reveals that the patient has a perforated gastric ulcer. Despite appropriate therapy, the patient expires, and subsequent autopsy reveals multiple ulcers in the stomach, duodenum, and jejunum. The patient had been complaining of abdominal pain and diarrhea for several months but had only been taking ibuprofen for his lower back pain for the past 3 weeks. What is the most likely cause of the patient's presentation?

answer_choices.A: A gastrin-secreting tumor of the pancreas

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of recurrent nephrolithiasis, chronic diarrhea, and multiple peptic ulcers (including jejunal ulcers) is suggestive of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES). ZES is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) that is most commonly located in the pancreas or duodenum. Gastrin stimulates gastric parietal cells to secrete acid, leading to severe peptic ulcer disease. The ulcers in ZES are often multiple and can be found in unusual locations such as the jejunum. Gastrin also stimulates gastric mucosal growth, leading to hypertrophic rugae that may mimic gastric cancer (ie, Menetrier disease). Increased acid production can cause secretory diarrhea and, by overwhelming the buffering capacity of the duodenum, lead to increased absorption of calcium and oxalate, causing hypercalcemia and hyperoxaluria, respectively. This can result in recurrent nephrolithiasis.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old man presents to the office complaining of abdominal pain. He was started on a trial of proton pump inhibitors 5 weeks ago but the pain has not improved. He describes the pain as dull, cramping, and worse during meals. Medical history is unremarkable. Physical examination is normal except for tenderness in the epigastric region. Endoscopy reveals an eroding gastric ulcer in the proximal part of the greater curvature of the stomach overlying a large pulsing artery. Which of the following arteries is most likely visible?
few_shot.explanation:
The greater curvature of the stomach is supplied by the left and right gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) arteries. The left gastro-omental artery arises from the splenic artery, and the right gastro-omental artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery, which is a branch of the common hepatic artery. The left gastro-omental artery runs from left to right along the greater curvature of the stomach, anastomosing with the right gastro-omental artery. The proximal part of the greater curvature of the stomach is supplied by the left gastro-omental artery, and the distal part is supplied by the right gastro-omental artery.

Therefore, the answer is [C].
