few_shot.question: A 47-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 20 minutes after being involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. His pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min and labored, and blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. Physical examination shows ecchymoses over the trunk and abdomen. In preparation for an exploratory laparotomy, atracurium is administered as an anesthetic. Which of the following characteristics is the most likely reason that this drug was chosen over other drugs in the same class?
few_shot.explanation:
Atracurium is a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that is used to induce muscle relaxation during surgery. It is metabolized by ester hydrolysis and Hofmann elimination, which is a temperature- and pH-dependent process that does not require hepatic or renal function. This makes atracurium a good choice for patients with hepatic or renal dysfunction, such as this patient with alcoholic cirrhosis.

So, the answer is [C].

question: A 68-year-old man comes to the physician with a 1-week history of painless hematuria. A CT scan of the urinary tract shows areas of bladder wall thickening. Cystoscopy shows several sessile masses with central necrosis arising from the bladder wall. A biopsy specimen of the bladder masses shows moderately differentiated urothelial cells with abundant mitotic figures and nuclear atypia. The patient most likely has a history of exposure to which of the following?

few_shot.question: A 70-year-old man presents to a medical office with painful micturition for 2 weeks. He denies any other symptoms. The past medical history is unremarkable. He has been a smoker most of his life, smoking approx. 1 pack of cigarettes every day. The physical examination is benign. A urinalysis shows an abundance of red blood cells. A cystoscopy is performed, which reveals a slightly erythematous area measuring 1.5 x 1 cm on the bladder mucosa. A biopsy is obtained and microscopic evaluation shows cells with an increased nuclear: cytoplasmic ratio and marked hyperchromatism involving the full thickness of the epithelium, but above the basement membrane. Which of the following best describes the biopsy findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking and pain on urination (dysuria) along with the biopsy findings are suggestive of urothelial carcinoma-in-situ (CIS). Urothelial CIS is a flat, high-grade, noninvasive lesion that is characterized by cells with an increased nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, hyperchromatic nuclei, and abnormal mitotic figures. The cells involve the full thickness of the urothelium but do not invade past the basement membrane. Urothelial CIS is often multifocal and has a high risk of progression to invasive cancer. Therefore, patients with urothelial CIS are often treated with intravesical immunotherapy (eg, Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) or total cystectomy.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 55-year old man living in Midwest USA comes in complaining of painless hematuria for the past week. He denies dysuria but complains of fatigue and lethargy at work. He has lost about 9.0 kg (20.0 lb) in the past 6 months. He drinks 1–2 beers on the weekends over the past 10 years but denies smoking. He has worked at a plastic chemical plant for the past 30 years and has never been out of the country. His father died of a heart attack at age 62 and his mother is still alive and well. There is a distant history of pancreatic cancer, but he can not remember the specifics. His vitals are stable and his physical exam is unremarkable. Urinary analysis is positive for RBCs. A cystoscopy is performed and finds a pedunculated mass projecting into the bladder lumen. A biopsy shows malignant cells. Which of the following is the most concerning risk factor for this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's painless hematuria, weight loss, and fatigue are concerning for bladder cancer. The most common type of bladder cancer is urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, which is strongly associated with exposure to aromatic amines. Aromatic amines are used in the rubber, dye, and leather industries, and in the production of plastics. This patient's long history of working in a plastic chemical plant is therefore the most concerning risk factor for his bladder cancer.

Other risk factors for bladder cancer include smoking, cyclophosphamide use, and chronic cystitis (eg, due to Schistosoma haematobium infection or long-term indwelling catheters).

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of urinary frequency, dysuria, and blood in his urine. He has also had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss over the past 3 months and has been feeling more fatigued than usual. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years but quit 2 years ago. A urinalysis shows 3+ blood. Cystoscopy shows an irregular mass on the bladder wall; a biopsy is taken. Which of the following histologic findings would indicate the worst survival prognosis?

answer_choices.A: Dysplastic cells extending into the lamina propria
answer_choices.B: Nests of atypical cells in the urothelium
answer_choices.D: Disordered urothelium lined with papillary fronds

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of smoking, weight loss, and hematuria is concerning for bladder cancer. The most common type of bladder cancer is urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, which is strongly associated with smoking and occupational exposure to aniline dyes and aromatic amines.

Urothelial carcinoma can be either papillary or flat. Papillary tumors are often low-grade and have a better prognosis. Flat tumors are usually high-grade and have a worse prognosis. The most important prognostic factor for both types is the depth of invasion. The bladder wall is composed of the mucosa (urothelium + lamina propria), muscularis propria, and adventitia. Tumors that invade the muscularis propria (ie, muscle-invasive) have a much worse prognosis because they have a higher risk of metastasis. Therefore, the worst prognosis would be seen with dysplastic cells extending into the lamina propria, indicating at least stage T1 disease.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of lower back pain. He has had several episodes of painless hematuria over the past 2 months. Physical examination shows localized tenderness over the lumbar spine. A CT scan shows multiple osteolytic lesions in the body of the lumbar vertebrae. Cystoscopy shows a 4-cm mass in the right lateral wall of the bladder. A photomicrograph of a biopsy specimen is shown. Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of painless hematuria and a bladder mass is suggestive of bladder cancer. The biopsy specimen shows cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and hyperchromatic nuclei, which are characteristic of transitional cell carcinoma (TCC), the most common type of bladder cancer. TCC can occur anywhere in the urinary tract lined by transitional epithelium (ie, renal calyces, renal pelvis, ureters, bladder, proximal urethra). The strongest risk factor for TCC is cigarette smoking, which contributes to approximately 50% of cases. Other risk factors include occupational exposure to aniline dyes and aromatic amines (eg, benzidine, naphthylamine), and treatment with cyclophosphamide or phenacetin.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of several episodes of dark urine over the past 2 weeks. He does not have dysuria or flank pain. He works in a factory that produces dyes. Since an accident at work 5 years ago, he has had moderate hearing loss bilaterally. He takes no medications. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 29 years and drinks one alcoholic beverage daily. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. His urine is pink; urinalysis shows 80 RBC/hpf but no WBCs. Cystoscopy shows a 3-cm mass in the bladder mucosa. The mass is resected. Pathologic examination shows an urothelial carcinoma with penetration into the muscular layer. An x-ray of the chest and a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast show a normal upper urinary tract and normal lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: Transurethral resection of tumor with intravesical chemotherapy

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma of the bladder. Risk factors for bladder cancer include smoking, occupational exposure to aromatic amines (eg, dyes, rubber, textiles), and chronic inflammation (eg, recurrent urinary tract infections, long-term indwelling catheter, cyclophosphamide therapy). The most common presenting symptom is painless hematuria. 

The treatment of bladder cancer depends on the depth of invasion. Non-muscle-invasive tumors (ie, those involving the mucosa or lamina propria) are treated with transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT) and intravesical chemotherapy or immunotherapy. However, muscle-invasive tumors (ie, those involving the detrusor muscle) are managed with radical cystectomy (removal of the bladder and pelvic lymph nodes) with urinary diversion. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to cystectomy may be considered in some patients. 

Hence, the answer is [C].

question: A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 6-month history of shortness of breath. He says that he used to enjoy playing golf with his friends but now he cannot walk for long enough to play. The shortness of breath is now starting to complicate his ability to get around in daily life. His past medical history is significant for diabetes, hypertension, and early stage prostate cancer that was removed 10 years ago without recurrence. He has smoked 1 pack per day for the past 55 years and drinks about 6 drinks per week. On presentation he is found to be breathing with pursed lips. Physical exam reveals decreased breath sounds on auscultation, increased chest diameter, and hyperresonance to percussion. Which of the following findings would most likely be seen in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Decreased residual volume and decreased 1 second forced expiratory volume
answer_choices.B: Decreased residual volume and increased 1 second forced expiratory volume
answer_choices.C: Increased residual volume and decreased 1 second forced expiratory volume
answer_choices.D: Normal residual volume and decreased 1 second forced expiratory volume

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department for evaluation of a 2-year history of increasing shortness of breath. He also has an occasional nonproductive cough. The symptoms get worse with exertion. The medical history is significant for hypertension and he takes chlorthalidone. He is a smoker with a 40-pack-year smoking history. On physical examination, the patient is afebrile; the vital signs include: blood pressure 125/78 mm Hg, pulse 90/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. The body mass index (BMI) is 31 kg/m2. The oxygen saturation is 94% at rest on room air. A pulmonary examination reveals decreased breath sounds bilaterally, but is otherwise normal with no wheezes or crackles. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable. A chest radiograph shows hyperinflation of both lungs with mildly increased lung markings, but no focal findings. Based on this clinical presentation, which of the following is most likely?

answer_choices.D: FEV1/FVC of 80% with an FEV1 of 82%

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic dyspnea, cough, and significant smoking history, along with physical examination findings of decreased breath sounds and chest radiograph findings of hyperinflation, are suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is characterized by persistent airflow limitation that is usually progressive and associated with an enhanced chronic inflammatory response in the airways and the lung to noxious particles or gases. The airflow limitation is caused by a mixture of small airway disease (obstructive bronchiolitis) and parenchymal destruction (emphysema), the relative contributions of which vary from person to person. Chronic inflammation causes structural changes and narrowing of the small airways. Destruction of the lung parenchyma leads to the loss of alveolar attachments to the small airways and decreases lung elastic recoil; in turn, these changes diminish the ability of the airways to remain open during expiration. 

Spirometry is required to make the diagnosis in this clinical context; the presence of a postbronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70 confirms the presence of persistent airflow limitation and thus of COPD. 

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents to the physician with a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath. She now has to stop to rest three or four times whenever she climbs the stairs to her apartment on the third floor. She reports chronic, nonproductive cough and wheezing, for which she uses ipratropium inhalers. She has a 25 pack-year smoking history. On examination, the blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, the pulse rate is 95/min, the temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), and the respiratory rate is 26/min. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral crepitations. Cardiac auscultation reveals normal S1 and S2 without murmurs or added sounds. Arterial blood gas analysis shows:

Which of the following would you expect to find in this patient?

answer_choices.B: Decreased diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO)
answer_choices.C: Shift of the flow volume loop to the right

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, chronic cough, and wheezing, along with her physical examination findings of bilateral crepitations, are suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The arterial blood gas analysis shows chronic respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia, which is also consistent with COPD.

In COPD, the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is decreased due to the loss of alveolar walls, leading to a decrease in the surface area available for gas exchange. This is the primary cause of hypoxemia in COPD.

few_shot.question: A 81-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 4-month history of shortness of breath. He says that he has slowly lost the ability to do things due to fatigue and now gets winded after walking around the house. He also says that his cough has been getting worse and seems to be producing more sputum. He has gained about 5 pounds over the last 6 months. His past medical history is significant for hypertension and diabetes. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history and drinks about 3 drinks per week. Physical exam reveals a cyanotic appearing man with 1+ edema in his legs bilaterally. He also has wheezing on lung auscultation with a prolonged expiratory phase. Which of the following would most likely be seen on a chest radiograph in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Calcified pleural plaques surrounding the diaphragm
answer_choices.C: Hyperinflated lungs and loss of lung markings
answer_choices.D: Perihilar mass with unilateral hilar enlargement

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic cough with sputum production, dyspnea, and a significant smoking history is suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is a common, preventable, and treatable disease characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities. It is usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases, most commonly from tobacco smoking in developed countries. The two major forms of COPD are chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as a chronic productive cough for 3 months in each of 2 successive years in a patient in whom other causes of chronic cough (eg, bronchiectasis) have been excluded. Emphysema is defined pathologically as abnormal, permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis. Patients with COPD often have features of both chronic bronchitis and emphysema.

Chest radiograph in patients with chronic bronchitis typically shows cardiomegaly due to pulmonary hypertension and increased bronchial markings due to bronchial wall thickening. In contrast, chest radiograph in patients with emphysema shows hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and decreased lung markings in the lung periphery.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of worsening shortness of breath and dry cough for 6 months. The patient's symptoms get worse when he walks more than about 150 yards. He also reports fatigue and difficulty swallowing solid foods. In cold weather, his fingers occasionally turn blue and become painful. He occasionally smokes cigarettes on weekends. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), and respirations are 22/min, pulse is 87/min, and blood pressure is 126/85 mm Hg. The skin over his trunk and arms is thickened and tightened. Fine inspiratory crackles are heard over bilateral lower lung fields on auscultation. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dyspnea, dry cough, and bibasilar crackles on lung auscultation, along with skin thickening and Raynaud phenomenon, are suggestive of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma). Scleroderma is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, including the lungs. Pulmonary involvement is common in scleroderma and can manifest as interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).

ILD is the most common pulmonary manifestation of scleroderma and is characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung parenchyma, leading to decreased lung compliance (increased elastance) and impaired gas exchange. The fibrosis seen in ILD primarily affects the lung interstitium, which is responsible for gas exchange. This leads to a decrease in the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO), which is a measure of the lungs' ability to transfer gas from inhaled air to the red blood cells in pulmonary capillaries.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 51-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressive shortness of breath, exercise intolerance, and cough for the past 6 months. He is no longer able to climb a full flight of stairs without resting and uses 3 pillows to sleep at night. He has a history of using cocaine in his 30s but has not used any illicit drugs for the past 20 years. His pulse is 99/min, respiratory rate is 21/min, and blood pressure is 95/60 mm Hg. Crackles are heard in both lower lung fields. An x-ray of the chest shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with bilateral fluffy infiltrates and thickening of the interlobar fissures. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, and bibasilar crackles on lung examination, along with the chest x-ray findings of cardiomegaly and bilateral fluffy infiltrates, are consistent with congestive heart failure (CHF). In CHF, the heart is unable to pump blood effectively, leading to a backup of blood into the pulmonary circulation. This causes an increase in pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure and subsequent transudation of fluid into the interstitium and alveoli, leading to pulmonary edema. The presence of fluid in these spaces increases the stiffness of the lungs, leading to decreased lung compliance. This means that a greater change in pressure is required to achieve a given change in lung volume.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: Three days after undergoing an open cholecystectomy, an obese 57-year-old woman has fever, chills, and a headache. She has right-sided chest pain that increases on inspiration and has had a productive cough for the last 12 hours. She had an episode of hypotension after the operation that resolved with intravenous fluid therapy. She underwent an abdominal hysterectomy 16 years ago for multiple fibroids of the uterus. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 17 years. She appears uncomfortable. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. Inspiratory crackles are heard at the right lung base. The abdomen is soft and nontender. There is a healing surgical incision below the right ribcage. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old-woman presents to the emergency room with complaints of fever and abdominal pain. Her blood pressure is 130/74 mmHg, pulse is 98/min, temperature is 101.5°F (38.6°C), and respirations are 23/min. The patient reports that she had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 4 days ago but has otherwise been healthy. She is visiting her family from Nebraska and just arrived this morning from a 12-hour drive. Physical examination revealed erythema and white discharge from abdominal incisions and tenderness upon palpations at the right upper quadrant. What is the most probable cause of the patient’s fever?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's fever, erythema, and white discharge from the abdominal incisions are suggestive of a wound infection. This is a common complication of surgery, especially in the first few days after the procedure. The infection is usually caused by skin flora, such as Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, that contaminate the surgical site. Treatment typically involves antibiotics and sometimes surgical debridement.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: Five days after being admitted to the hospital for an open cholecystectomy, a 56-year-old woman develops difficulty breathing. She also has fevers, chills, and malaise. She has a cough productive of minimal amounts of yellowish-white sputum that started two days prior. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and a history of gallstones. Her current medications include metformin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. Her temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), pulse is 104/minute, blood pressure is 94/68 mm Hg, and respirations are 30/minute. Pulse oximetry on 2 L of oxygen via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Examination reveals decreased breath sounds over the right lung base. Abdominal examination shows a well-healing scar without erythema or discharge in the right upper quadrant. The skin is warm and well-perfused. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10.5 g/dL, leukocyte count is 16,000/mm3, platelet count is 345,000/mm3, and creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL. She is admitted to the ICU and started on IV fluids. Blood and urine for cultures are obtained. X-ray of the chest reveals a right sided pleural effusion. Which of the following is the next best step in management?

answer_choices.A: CT of the chest with contrast

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP), which is defined as pneumonia that occurs 48 hours or more after admission and did not appear to be incubating at the time of admission. HAP is often caused by gram-negative bacilli (eg, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, E coli) and/or Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S aureus (MRSA). Risk factors for HAP include recent surgery, prolonged hospitalization, and severe underlying disease. This patient's fever, cough, leukocytosis, and new lung infiltrate on chest x-ray are consistent with HAP. In addition, she has sepsis, manifested by tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension. Therefore, she should be started on empiric antibiotics with broad gram-negative and MRSA coverage (eg, vancomycin and cefepime) while culture results are pending.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old woman presents to the hospital for an elective right hemicolectomy. She is independently mobile and does her own shopping. She has had type 2 diabetes mellitus for 20 years, essential hypertension for 15 years, and angina on exertion for 6 years. She has a 30-pack-year history of smoking. The operation was uncomplicated. On post-op day 5, she becomes confused. She has a temperature of 38.5°C (101.3°F), respiratory rate of 28/min, and oxygen saturation of 92% on 2 L of oxygen. She is tachycardic at 118/min and her blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg. On chest auscultation, she has coarse crackles in the right lung base. Her surgical wound appears to be healing well, and her abdomen is soft and nontender. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a new-onset confusion, fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia, which are all signs of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). SIRS is a clinical syndrome that is characterized by systemic inflammation and widespread tissue injury. It can be triggered by a variety of conditions such as infection (resulting in sepsis), pancreatitis, ischemia, and multiple trauma. In this patient, the presence of SIRS in the setting of a likely infection (as evidenced by the presence of coarse crackles on lung auscultation, suggesting pneumonia) meets criteria for sepsis.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
Three days after undergoing an open cholecystectomy, a 73-year-old man has fever and abdominal pain. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He had smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years but quit 1 year ago. He does not drink alcohol. Prior to admission to the hospital, his medications included lisinopril, metformin, ipratropium, and tamsulosin. He appears acutely ill and lethargic. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/84 mm Hg. He is oriented only to person. Examination shows a 10-cm subcostal incision that appears dry and non-erythematous. Scattered expiratory wheezing is heard throughout both lung fields. His abdomen is distended with tenderness to palpation over the lower quadrants. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dl
Leukocyte count 19,000/mm3
Serum
Glucose 180 mg/dl
Urea Nitrogen 25 mg/dl
Creatinine 1.2 g/dl
Lactic acid 2.5 mEq/L (N = 0.5 - 2.2 mEq/L)
Urine
Protein 1+
RBC 1–2/hpf
WBC 32–38/hpf
Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's current condition?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, altered mental status, and lower abdominal pain in the setting of a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and recent surgery are concerning for urinary retention with overflow incontinence. Urinary retention can occur in the postoperative period due to the use of medications with anticholinergic effects (eg, ipratropium, tamsulosin), perioperative fluid administration, bed rest, and decreased mobility. In addition, anesthesia can decrease the sensation of bladder fullness and inhibit the voiding reflex. Patients with BPH are at increased risk due to a mechanical obstruction of the bladder outlet by prostatic hypertrophy. 

Urinary retention can lead to bladder distention, which can cause lower abdominal discomfort and suprapubic fullness on examination. If untreated, it can lead to overflow incontinence, autonomic dysregulation, and/or postrenal acute kidney injury. In addition, urinary stasis can lead to urinary tract infection, as suggested by this patient's pyuria.

few_shot.question: A 73-year-old woman visits an urgent care clinic with a complaint of fever for the past 48 hours. She has been having frequent chills and increasing abdominal pain since her fever spiked to 39.4°C (103.0°F) at home. She states that abdominal pain is constant, non-radiating, and rates the pain as a 4/10. She also complains of malaise and fatigue. The past medical history is insignificant. The vital signs include: heart rate 110/min, respiratory rate 15/min, temperature 39.2°C (102.5°F), and blood pressure 120/86 mm Hg. On physical examination, she is icteric and there is severe tenderness on palpation of the right hypochondrium. The ultrasound of the abdomen shows a dilated bile duct and calculus in the bile duct. The blood cultures are pending, and the antibiotic therapy is started. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
Ascending cholangitis is a bacterial infection of the biliary tree that typically occurs secondary to biliary obstruction. The most common cause of obstruction is choledocholithiasis, as seen in this patient. The classic Charcot triad of fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice is seen in only 50%-70% of patients with ascending cholangitis. The presence of sepsis (hypotension and/or altered mental status) in addition to Charcot triad is known as Reynolds pentad. The most common organisms involved are gram-negative enteric bacteria (eg, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species) and enterococci. Empiric antibiotic therapy should be initiated immediately after blood cultures are obtained, and biliary decompression should be performed as soon as possible.

So, the answer is [A].

Current medications include amlodipine, methotrexate, and ibuprofen. He does not smoke. He has a history of chronic alcohol abuse. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 148/86 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor, periorbital edema, 2+ pedal edema, and ascites. His symptoms began shortly after he returned from a trip to Cambodia. He occasionally takes ibuprofen for chronic back pain. He has a history of arterial hypertension and osteoarthritis of both knees. He had an episode of pneumonia 4 months ago. His current medications include lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. He has no history of drinking or smoking. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 101/min, and blood pressure is 135/76 mm Hg. Examination shows pitting edema of the upper and lower extremities. Laboratory studies show:

Serum

Creatinine 2.9 mg/dL

Urine

Protein 4+

Renal biopsy with Congo red stain shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's nephrotic syndrome (edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia) and renal biopsy findings of apple-green birefringence under polarized light with Congo red staining are consistent with renal amyloidosis. Amyloidosis is a disease characterized by extracellular deposition of insoluble fibrils in various tissues and organs. The fibrils are derived from serum proteins that are produced in excess, are mutated, or are prone to misfolding. The most common types of amyloidosis are AL (primary) and AA (secondary) amyloidosis.

AL amyloidosis is associated with plasma cell dyscrasias, such as multiple myeloma, in which there is overproduction of immunoglobulin light chains (AL proteins). The light chains form insoluble fibrils that are deposited in tissues. Patients with AL amyloidosis may have a nephrotic syndrome, restrictive cardiomyopathy, or autonomic neuropathy. The diagnosis is suggested by the presence of a monoclonal protein in serum or urine and is confirmed by tissue biopsy. Rouleaux formation, the stacking of erythrocytes in a manner that resembles a stack of coins on peripheral blood smear, is a common finding in patients with plasma cell dyscrasias, including multiple myeloma.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old African American man presents to his primary care physician with a chief complaint of leg swelling. He says that the swelling began about 2 weeks ago and he cannot recall anything that may have provoked the episode. Otherwise he has had joint pain, headaches, frothy urine, and some tingling in his fingers and toes though he doesn't feel that any of this is related to his swelling. He denies any shortness of breath, back pain, or skull pain. His past medical history is significant for mild rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, and hypertension all of which are well controlled. Physical exam reveals 3+ pitting edema in his legs bilaterally. A chest radiograph reveals mild enlargement of the cardiac shadow. Urinalysis reveals 3+ protein and casts with a cross appearance under polarized light. A renal biopsy is taken with a characteristic finding seen only under polarized light. Which of the following is associated with the most likely cause of this patient's edema?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of bilateral leg swelling, frothy urine, and proteinuria is suggestive of nephrotic syndrome. The presence of casts with a cross appearance under polarized light is indicative of multiple myeloma, which can cause nephrotic syndrome due to deposition of light chains in the glomeruli (light chain cast nephropathy). This is also known as myeloma kidney.

Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell dyscrasia characterized by the proliferation of a single clone of plasma cells, leading to overproduction of a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein). The M protein can be an intact immunoglobulin or a fragment of one, such as the immunoglobulin light chain. The light chains can be toxic to the renal tubules and can also form casts that obstruct the tubular lumen, leading to renal impairment.

Multiple myeloma is associated with elevated levels of IL-6, which promotes the growth of the neoplastic plasma cells. IL-6 also increases osteoclast activity, leading to lytic bone lesions, a common finding in multiple myeloma.

So, the answer is [D].

Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is a common cause of chronic kidney disease and is characterized by sclerosis of the renal arterioles and small arteries, leading to ischemic changes in the glomeruli and tubulointerstitium. The glomeruli may show focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, global glomerulosclerosis, or ischemic collapse. The arterioles and small arteries show hyaline arteriolosclerosis, which is characterized by homogenous, pink, hyaline thickening of the walls with narrowing of the lumen. The patient's elevated blood pressure and elevated serum creatinine are consistent with hypertensive nephrosclerosis.

few_shot.question:
A 52-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department because of bilateral leg swelling and puffiness of both eyes in the morning. His symptoms started about 2 weeks ago. He denies smoking or alcohol use and his family history is noncontributory. Today, his vital signs include a temperature of 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure of 162/87 mm Hg, and a pulse of 85/min. On physical examination, he is jaundiced and there is hepatosplenomegaly and 2+ lower extremity edema up to the mid-thigh. Laboratory results are shown:
Anti-HCV
reactive
Serum albumin
3 g/dL
Urine dipstick
3+ protein
Urinalysis
10–15 red blood cells/high power field and red cell casts
Which of the following is a feature of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of nephrotic syndrome (edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia), microscopic hematuria, red cell casts, and hepatosplenomegaly in the setting of chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is suggestive of type I membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN). MPGN is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults and is often associated with chronic infections (eg, HCV, hepatitis B virus, endocarditis), autoimmune diseases, and monoclonal gammopathy.

Type I MPGN is characterized by subendothelial immune complex deposition with granular immunofluorescence. On light microscopy, there is a "tram-track" appearance on silver stain due to mesangial interposition between the basement membrane and endothelial cells. Electron-dense deposits can be seen in the subendothelial space on electron microscopy.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 41-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of fatigue, worsening abdominal discomfort, and progressive swelling of his legs for 3 months. The swelling is worse in the evenings. His only medication is ibuprofen for occasional joint pain. The patient does not smoke and drinks 2–3 beers each weekend. His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Pulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows a mildly distended abdomen with shifting dullness. The liver is palpated 2–3 cm below the right costal margin. When pressure is applied to the right upper quadrant, the patient's jugular veins become visibly distended for 15 seconds. The 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands are tender to palpation. There is 2+ edema in the lower extremities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's edema?

answer_choices.A: Impaired relaxation of the right ventricle

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, and jugular venous distention that increases with inspiration (Kussmaul sign) is suggestive of constrictive pericarditis. This condition is characterized by a thickened, fibrotic pericardium that prevents diastolic filling of the heart. The impaired relaxation of the right ventricle leads to increased systemic venous pressure, resulting in hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema. The most common cause of constrictive pericarditis in developed countries is idiopathic or viral pericarditis. Other causes include cardiac surgery, mediastinal irradiation, and connective tissue diseases.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 6-year-old Russian boy who recently immigrated to the United States presents to your office with fever and dyspnea. On examination of the oropharynx, you note a grayish-white pseudomembrane and uneven elevation of the soft palate. The patient displays marked enlargement of the cervical lymph nodes. Which of the following describes the organism responsible for this patient's disease?

answer_choices.B: Gram-positive bacteria producing exotoxin that acts via ADP ribosylation
answer_choices.C: Gram-positive cocci with hyaluronic acid capsule
answer_choices.D: Gram-negative encapsulated bacteria producing IgA protease

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old male who recently immigrated to the United States from Asia is admitted to the hospital with dyspnea. Physical exam reveals a gray pseudomembrane in the patient's oropharynx along with lymphadenopathy. The patient develops myocarditis and expires on hospital day 5. Which of the following would have prevented this patient's presentation and decline?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of a gray pseudomembrane in the oropharynx, lymphadenopathy, and myocarditis is consistent with diphtheria, which is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. The bacterium produces an AB exotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis via ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2. This can cause cell death in the heart, nervous system, and adrenal glands. The diphtheria vaccine (a component of the DTaP vaccine) contains diphtheria toxoid, which induces the production of circulating IgG antibodies against the toxin. Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy presents with fever, sore throat, hoarseness, and neck enlargement. The symptoms started 3 days ago and progressed gradually with an elevated temperature and swollen lymph nodes. His family immigrated recently from Honduras. He was born via spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks after an uneventful gestational period and he is now on a catch-up vaccination schedule. He lives with several family members, including his parents, in a small apartment. No one in the apartment smokes tobacco. On presentation, the patient’s blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg, heart rate is 103/min, respiratory rate is 20/min, and temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F). On physical examination, the child is acrocyanotic and somnolent. There is widespread cervical edema and enlargement of the cervical lymph nodes. The tonsils are covered with a gray, thick membrane which spreads beyond the tonsillar bed and reveals bleeding, erythematous mucosa with gentle scraping. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the target of the virulence factor produced by the pathologic organism infecting this child?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, sore throat, and cervical lymphadenopathy are suggestive of pharyngitis. The presence of a grayish-white pseudomembrane that bleeds upon removal is characteristic of diphtheria, which is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. This organism produces an exotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis in the host cell by catalyzing the ADP-ribosylation of eukaryotic elongation factor-2 (eEF-2). This prevents the translocation step of protein synthesis, leading to cell death. The exotoxin can also cause myocarditis and neuritis.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 5-year-old boy presents to your office with his mother. The boy has been complaining of a sore throat and headache for the past 2 days. His mother states that he had a fever of 39.3°C (102.7°F) and had difficulty eating. On examination, the patient has cervical lymphadenopathy and erythematous tonsils with exudates. A streptococcal rapid antigen detection test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?

answer_choices.A: A gram-negative, pleomorphic, obligate intracellular bacteria
answer_choices.C: A gram-positive, beta-hemolytic cocci in chains

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of sore throat, headache, fever, and difficulty eating, along with physical findings of cervical lymphadenopathy and erythematous tonsils with exudates, are suggestive of acute tonsillitis. The negative streptococcal rapid antigen detection test rules out Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus), the most common bacterial cause of tonsillitis.

The next most common cause of tonsillitis in children is adenovirus, a naked, double-stranded DNA virus. Adenovirus can cause a variety of illnesses, including respiratory infections, conjunctivitis, and gastroenteritis. In tonsillitis, it can cause symptoms similar to those of streptococcal pharyngitis, including fever, sore throat, and cervical lymphadenopathy.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of a 2-day history of low-grade fever, headache, nausea, and a sore throat. Examination of the oral cavity shows enlarged, erythematous tonsils with exudates and palatal petechiae. There is cervical lymphadenopathy. Her parents agree to her participating in a study of microbial virulence factors. A culture of the girl's throat is obtained and an organism is cultivated. The physician finds that the isolated organism is able to withstand phagocytosis when placed in fresh blood. The most likely explanation for this finding is the expression of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of fever, sore throat, and headache, along with physical examination findings of pharyngeal erythema, tonsillar exudates, and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, are suggestive of streptococcal pharyngitis. Group A Streptococcus (GAS, S. pyogenes) is the most common bacterial cause of pharyngitis. The M protein virulence factor of GAS inhibits phagocytosis by polymorphonuclear leukocytes and is antiphagocytic even in nonimmune individuals. M protein also contributes to the invasiveness of GAS by binding fibrinogen, which in turn binds neutrophil receptors and blocks their activation.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency room with difficulty breathing after several days of severe sore throat. Further history reveals that his family immigrated recently from Eastern Europe and he has never previously seen a doctor. Physical exam shows cervical lymphadenopathy with extensive neck edema as well as the finding shown in the image provided. You suspect a bacteria that causes the disease by producing an AB type exotoxin. Which of the following is the proper medium to culture the most likely cause of this infection?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of severe sore throat, difficulty breathing, and "bull neck" appearance are suggestive of diphtheria, which is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. This bacterium produces an AB exotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis, leading to cell death. The pseudomembrane shown in the image is composed of dead epithelial cells, white blood cells, and fibrin, and can cause airway obstruction.

C. diphtheriae is a gram-positive rod that is most commonly cultured using tellurite agar or Loeffler medium. On tellurite agar, the bacteria reduce potassium tellurite to metallic tellurite, which gives the colonies a characteristic black color.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question:
A 57-year-old homeless man is brought to the emergency department because of several episodes of hematemesis in the past 24 hours. His vital signs include a temperature of 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse of 95/min, and blood pressure of 85/60 mm Hg. On physical examination, he appears confused and unable to give a complete history. He is noted to have jaundice, palpable firm liver, mild splenomegaly, and shifting dullness consistent with the presence of ascites. Liver function tests are as follows:
Serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  97 U/L
Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 40 U/L
Serum albumin 2.5 g/dL
Total bilirubin 3 mg/dL
Prothrombin time 20 seconds
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's illness?

few_shot.question:
A 48-year-old homeless male presents to the ED because he hasn’t felt well recently. He states that he has been feeling nauseous and extremely weak over the past few days. He has several previous admissions for alcohol intoxication and uses heroin occasionally. His temperature is 100.9°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 127/89 mmHg, and pulse is 101/min. His physical examination is notable for palmar erythema, tender hepatomegaly, and gynecomastia. His laboratory findings are notable for:

AST: 170 U/L
ALT: 60 U/L
GGT: 400 (normal range: 0-45 U/L)
Alkaline phosphatase: 150 IU/L
Direct bilirubin: 0.2 mg/dL
Total bilirubin: 0.8 mg/dL
WBC: 10,500
Serum iron: 100 µg/dL
TIBC: 300 µg/dL (normal range: 250–370 µg/dL)
Serum acetaminophen screen: Negative
Serum AFP: 6 ng/mL (normal range: < 10ng/mL)

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of alcohol abuse, hepatomegaly, and elevated liver enzymes with an AST:ALT ratio >2:1 is suggestive of alcoholic hepatitis. Alcoholic hepatitis is a syndrome of progressive inflammatory liver injury associated with long-term heavy intake of ethanol. The pathologic hallmark is hepatocellular necrosis and inflammation in the perivenular area (zone 3) of the liver acinus. Symptoms include fever, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and evidence of hepatic decompensation (eg, ascites, encephalopathy). Laboratory findings include markedly increased serum aminotransferases (typically <300 U/L, with AST > ALT), and increased serum bilirubin and γ-glutamyltransferase. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 64-year-old man comes to the emergency department complaining of fatigue and abdominal distension. He has a remote history of intravenous drug use. Vital signs include a normal temperature, blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg, and a pulse of 75/min. Physical examination reveals jaundice and a firm liver. Abdominal ultrasonography shows liver surface nodularity, moderate splenomegaly, and increased diameter of the portal vein. Complete blood count of the patient is shown:
Hemoglobin 14 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 90/μm3
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin 30 pg/cell
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 34%
Leukocyte count 7,000/mm3
Platelet count 50,000/mm3
Which of the following best represents the mechanism of low platelet count in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of intravenous drug use, jaundice, and firm liver on examination suggest chronic hepatitis C infection leading to cirrhosis. The ultrasonographic findings of liver surface nodularity, splenomegaly, and increased diameter of the portal vein are consistent with portal hypertension, a common complication of cirrhosis. Thrombocytopenia (platelet count <150,000/mm3) is the most common hematologic manifestation of chronic liver disease. In cirrhosis, thrombocytopenia results from both decreased production of thrombopoietin by the liver and sequestration of platelets in the spleen (secondary to portal hypertension). Although both mechanisms contribute, splenic sequestration is thought to play a greater role in most cases.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 49-year-old man presents to the emergency department with abdominal discomfort, fever, and decreased urination. He has a history of liver cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C infection. His blood pressure is 90/70 mm Hg, pulse is 75/min, and temperature 38°C (100.4°F). On physical examination he is jaundiced, and he has tense ascites with generalized abdominal tenderness. There is pitting edema to the level of his upper thighs. Which of the following excludes the diagnosis of hepatorenal syndrome in this patient?

answer_choices.D: Presence of 30 red cells/high powered field in the urine

few_shot.explanation:
Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a functional renal failure that occurs in patients with advanced liver disease. It is characterized by renal vasoconstriction leading to decreased glomerular filtration rate. The diagnosis of HRS is one of exclusion and requires the presence of advanced liver disease with ascites, low glomerular filtration rate (creatinine >1.5 mg/dL), absence of shock, no current or recent treatment with nephrotoxic drugs, and absence of parenchymal kidney disease (no proteinuria, no hematuria, and normal renal ultrasound). The presence of 30 red cells/high powered field in the urine of this patient suggests intrinsic renal disease and excludes the diagnosis of HRS.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 58-year-old man with liver cirrhosis presents to his primary care physician complaining of increased abdominal girth and early satiety. He drinks 2–4 glasses of wine with dinner and recalls having had abnormal liver enzymes in the past. Vital signs include a temperature of 37.1°C (98.7°F), blood pressure of 110/70 mm Hg, and a pulse of 75/min. Physical examination reveals telangiectasias, mild splenomegaly, palpable firm liver, and shifting dullness. Liver function is shown:
Total bilirubin 3 mg/dL
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 150 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 70 U/L
Total albumin 2.5 g/dL
Abdominal ultrasonography confirms the presence of ascites. Diagnostic paracentesis is performed and its results are shown:
Polymorphonuclear cell count 10 cells/mm
Ascitic protein 1 g/dL
Which of the following best represent the mechanism of ascites in this patients?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of alcohol use, abnormal liver enzymes, and physical examination findings of splenomegaly and a firm liver are consistent with alcoholic cirrhosis. The most common cause of ascites in the United States is cirrhosis, usually due to alcohol or viral hepatitis. The development of ascites in a patient with cirrhosis is an important landmark in the progression of the disease and is associated with a poor prognosis.

The pathogenesis of ascites in cirrhosis is multifactorial and begins with portal hypertension, which leads to increased sinusoidal pressure and movement of fluid into the peritoneal cavity. This is the primary event in the formation of ascites. Sodium and water retention due to increased renal sodium reabsorption also contribute to the formation of ascites, but this is a secondary event.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department when he was found obtunded at the homeless shelter. The patient is currently not responsive and smells of alcohol. The patient has a past medical history of alcohol use, IV drug use, and hepatitis C. His temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 95/65 mmHg, pulse is 95/min, respirations are 13/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. The patient is started on IV fluids, and his pulse decreases to 70/min. On physical exam, the patient has an abdominal exam notable for distension and a positive fluid wave. The patient displays mild yellow discoloration of his skin. The patient has notable poor dentition and poor hygiene overall. A systolic murmur is heard along the left sternal border on cardiac exam. Pulmonary exam is notable for mild bibasilar crackles. Laboratory values are ordered, and return as below:

Hemoglobin: 10 g/dL
Hematocrit: 32%
Leukocyte count: 7,500 cells/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 227,000/mm^3

Serum:
Na+: 125 mEq/L
Cl-: 100 mEq/L
K+: 5.0 mEq/L
HCO3-: 24 mEq/L
BUN: 51 mg/dL
Glucose: 89 mg/dL
Creatinine: 2.2 mg/dL
Ca2+: 10.0 mg/dL
AST: 22 U/L
ALT: 19 U/L

Urine:
Color: Amber
Nitrites: Negative
Sodium: 12 mmol/24 hours
Red blood cells: 0/hpf

Over the next 24 hours, the patient produces very little urine. Which of the following best explains this patient’s renal findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a history of alcohol use and hepatitis C, and presents with jaundice, ascites, and hyponatremia, suggesting cirrhosis. The kidneys attempt to compensate for the decreased effective arterial blood volume seen in cirrhosis by avidly reabsorbing sodium in the proximal tubule, leading to a low fractional excretion of sodium (FENa). This can lead to oliguria and azotemia, as seen in this patient. The patient's urine sodium concentration is low (<20 mEq/L), suggesting that the kidneys are appropriately reabsorbing sodium in response to the decreased effective arterial blood volume. This is consistent with hepatorenal syndrome (HRS), a form of functional renal impairment seen in patients with advanced cirrhosis or acute liver failure.

HRS is thought to occur due to splanchnic arterial vasodilation, leading to decreased effective arterial blood volume and renal hypoperfusion. The renal hypoperfusion triggers the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, leading to sodium and water retention in an attempt to increase the intravascular volume. However, because the fundamental problem is arterial vasodilation and not volume depletion, the kidneys continue to sense a volume deficit, leading to continued sodium and water retention. This can result in dilutional hyponatremia, as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of intermittent chest pain and palpitations. She also complains of dyspnea on exertion and has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss in the past 2 months despite normal appetite. She has no history of serious medical illness. Cardiac examination shows an irregularly irregular rhythm and a grade 3/6, low pitched, rumbling, mid-diastolic murmur heard best over the apex. Diffuse wheezing and bilateral rales are present in the lung bases. A transthoracic echocardiogram shows a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 40% and a mass in the left atrium. A biopsy of the mass is likely to show which of the following?

answer_choices.A: Nonencapsulated groups of well-differentiated skeletal muscle cells
answer_choices.B: Mixture of cells from different germinal layers
answer_choices.C: Encapsulated cluster of mature fat cells

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of mild fever, fatigue, and shortness of breath. She has no history of serious medical illness and takes no medications. Cardiopulmonary examination shows a mid-diastolic plopping sound heard best at the apex and bilateral rales at the base of the lungs. Echocardiography shows a pedunculated, heterogeneous mass in the left atrium. A biopsy of the mass shows clusters of mesenchymal cells surrounded by gelatinous material. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, fatigue, and shortness of breath, along with the finding of a pedunculated, heterogeneous mass in the left atrium, is suggestive of a cardiac myxoma. Cardiac myxomas are the most common primary cardiac tumors in adults. They are typically located in the left atrium and are attached to the interatrial septum by a stalk. On histologic examination, myxomas are composed of scattered cells within a background of mucopolysaccharide stroma. The cells may appear rounded, polygonal, or spindle-shaped, and may form rings or clusters. 

Patients with cardiac myxomas may present with symptoms related to obstruction of blood flow (eg, dyspnea, orthopnea, pulmonary edema, sudden death), embolization of tumor fragments (eg, stroke, myocardial infarction), or constitutional symptoms (eg, fever, weight loss, fatigue, Raynaud phenomenon). The constitutional symptoms are thought to be due to the production of IL-6 by the myxoma cells. IL-6 is a proinflammatory cytokine that can cause fever and stimulate the production of acute phase reactants, leading to an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old woman presents to the clinic complaining of a 9-month history of weight loss, fatigue, and a general sense of malaise. She additionally complains of an unusual sensation in her chest upon rapidly rising from a supine to a standing position. Current vitals include a temperature of 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse of 72/min, blood pressure of 118/63 mm Hg, and a respiratory rate of 15/min. Her BMI is 21 kg/m2. Auscultation demonstrates an early-mid diastole low-pitched sound at the apex of the heart. A chest X-ray reveals a poorly demarcated abnormality in the heart and requires CT imaging for further analysis. What would most likely be seen on CT imaging?

answer_choices.B: Fistula between the right and left atria

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of weight loss, fatigue, and malaise are nonspecific and could be seen in many conditions. However, the presence of an early-mid diastolic sound heard at the apex of the heart (tumor plop) is suggestive of an atrial myxoma. Atrial myxomas are the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults and are typically located in the left atrium. They are usually attached to the interatrial septum by a stalk and can cause symptoms due to obstruction of blood flow, embolization, or constitutional symptoms (eg, fever, weight loss, fatigue). Therefore, a CT scan would most likely show a tumor within the left atria.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 51-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion and fatigue for the past 2 months. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs or bruits. Coarse crackles are heard at the lung bases bilaterally. An ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent p waves. An x-ray of the chest shows globular enlargement of the cardiac shadow with prominent hila and bilateral fluffy infiltrates. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 40%. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, and coarse crackles at the lung bases is suggestive of heart failure. His ECG findings of an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent p waves are consistent with atrial fibrillation (AF). AF is a common cause of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, which can occur in any persistently tachycardic state (heart rate typically >100-120/min). The incessant tachycardia leads to progressive left ventricular dilation and a reduction in systolic function, which can result in heart failure. The mechanism is thought to be cellular changes, including a decrease in the number of myocardial contractile proteins, in response to a high heart rate. AF is the most common cause of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Treatment involves controlling the heart rate (eg, with beta blockers) and/or restoring sinus rhythm (eg, with cardioversion), which can lead to normalization of left ventricular size and function.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 75-year-old woman presents to her physician with a cough and shortness of breath. She says that cough gets worse at night and her shortness of breath occurs with moderate exertion or when lying flat. She says these symptoms have been getting worse over the last 6 months. She mentions that she has to use 3 pillows while sleeping in order to relieve her symptoms. She denies any chest pain, chest tightness, or palpitations. Past medical history is significant for hypertension and diabetes mellitus type 2. Her medications are amiloride, glyburide, and metformin. Family history is significant for her father who also suffered diabetes mellitus type 2 before his death at 90 years old. The patient says she drinks alcohol occasionally but denies any smoking history. Her blood pressure is 130/95 mm Hg, temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), and heart rate is 100/min. On physical examination, she has a sustained apical impulse, a normal S1 and S2, and a loud S4 without murmurs. There are bilateral crackles present bilaterally. A chest radiograph shows a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette. A transesophageal echocardiogram is performed and shows a normal left ventricular ejection fraction. Which of the following myocardial changes is most likely present in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Ventricular hypertrophy with sarcomeres duplicated in series
answer_choices.B: Ventricular hypertrophy with sarcomeres duplicated in parallel
answer_choices.C: Asymmetric hypertrophy of the interventricular septum
answer_choices.D: Granuloma consisting of lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages surrounding necrotic

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, along with physical examination findings of a sustained apical impulse and bilateral crackles, are suggestive of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), also known as diastolic heart failure. This condition is characterized by impaired ventricular relaxation and decreased compliance, leading to increased filling pressures. It is most commonly seen in elderly women with a history of hypertension, as in this patient.

The pathophysiology of HFpEF involves structural changes in the myocardium, including left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), which is a common adaptive response to pressure overload (eg, hypertension). In LVH, the sarcomeres are duplicated in parallel, leading to increased wall thickness. This is in contrast to volume overload (eg, mitral or aortic regurgitation), in which the sarcomeres are duplicated in series, leading to ventricular dilation.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old woman referred to the cardiology clinic for the evaluation of fatigue and dyspnea for 4 months. She also has loose stools (2–4 per day), palpitations, and non-pitting edema up to her mid-calf. On examination, vital signs are unremarkable, but she appears to be flushed with mild bilateral wheezes can be heard on chest auscultation. Cardiovascular examination reveals a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left mid-sternal area, which is louder during inspiration. Basic laboratory investigations are unremarkable. Echocardiography reveals moderate to severe right ventricular dilatation with severe right ventricular systolic dysfunction. A CT of the chest and abdomen reveals a solid, non-obstructing 2 cm mass in the small intestine and a solid 1.5 cm mass in the liver. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of flushing, diarrhea, and right-sided heart disease are suggestive of carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid syndrome is a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with carcinoid tumors, which are neuroendocrine tumors that most commonly originate in the gastrointestinal tract. These tumors secrete vasoactive substances such as serotonin, histamine, and tachykinins, which can cause symptoms of flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm. Over time, the excess serotonin can lead to fibrosis, particularly of the right side of the heart, leading to manifestations such as tricuspid regurgitation (as suggested by this patient's holosystolic murmur that is louder during inspiration) and, less commonly, pulmonic valve disease. The left side of the heart is usually spared because monoamine oxidase in the lungs metabolizes serotonin to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA). The diagnosis can be confirmed by measuring 24-hour urine levels of 5-HIAA.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 81-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after he fell asleep at the dinner table and was not able to be roused by his family. His past medical history is significant for Alzheimer disease though he is still relatively functional at baseline. He has also been taking warfarin over the last 3 months after he suffered a deep venous thrombosis. After he was transported to the ED, his family found that the pills his grandson takes for seizures were missing. On presentation, he is found to be somnolent and physical exam reveals ataxia and nystagmus. After determining the cause of this patient's symptoms, his physicians begin monitoring his international normalized ratio, because they are concerned that it will start trending down. Which of the following treatments would most improve the urinary excretion of the substance likely responsible for these symptoms?

few_shot.question: A 79-year-old man, hospitalized for overnight monitoring after elective surgery, is found on morning rounds to be confused and disoriented. He was recovering well in the post-anesthesia care unit before being moved up to the inpatient floor unit; however, he was found to be delirious and agitated overnight. Therefore, he was given a dose of a drug that affects the opening frequency of a neuronal ion channel. During morning rounds, he is found to have weakness, tremors, uncoordinated muscle movements, blurred vision, and disorientation. Which of the following could be used to reverse the drug that was administered to this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's confusion, disorientation, and agitation are suggestive of delirium, a common condition in hospitalized elderly patients. Delirium is often treated with benzodiazepines, which enhance the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening. This leads to hyperpolarization of the neuron and decreased neuronal firing. However, benzodiazepines can also cause side effects such as weakness, tremors, ataxia, and blurred vision, as seen in this patient. These side effects can be reversed with flumazenil, a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine receptor.

few_shot.question: A 65-year old man comes to the emergency department because of altered mental status for 1 day. He has had headaches, severe nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for 2 days. Management of lithium toxicity involves discontinuation of the drug, management of symptoms, and treatment of the underlying cause of toxicity (eg, volume depletion). few_shot.question: A 76-year-old man is brought to his geriatrician by his daughter, who reports that he has been "losing his memory." NPH is a syndrome of ventriculomegaly that is not associated with increased intracranial pressure. It is thought to be due to decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), leading to dilation of the ventricles and stretching of the periventricular white matter tracts. This can cause the classic triad of symptoms seen in this patient.

The diagnosis of NPH is suggested by clinical presentation and brain imaging showing ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy. A high-volume lumbar puncture (also known as a "therapeutic LP" or "CSF tap test") can be both diagnostic and therapeutic. Removal of a large volume of CSF can lead to rapid (though temporary) improvement in the patient's symptoms. If the patient's symptoms improve after the LP, this would suggest that the patient may benefit from placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, which can lead to more sustained improvement in symptoms.

question:

ICSs are the most effective long-term control medications for persistent asthma of all severity levels. They reduce airway inflammation, decrease airway hyperresponsiveness, and improve symptoms and lung function.

few_shot.question: A 21-year-old man presents to his physician with a cough that has persisted for 4 weeks. His cough is usually nocturnal and awakens him from sleep. There are no signs of respiratory distress, and chest auscultation reveals bilateral wheezing. Which of the following medications is most likely to provide quick relief?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of his asthma, likely triggered by exposure to dust. The most effective treatment for rapid relief of acute asthma symptoms is a short-acting beta2-agonist such as albuterol. Albuterol relaxes bronchial smooth muscle by binding to beta2-receptors, leading to bronchodilation and relief of bronchospasm. It also inhibits mast cell degranulation, which can further help reduce bronchoconstriction and inflammation.

Inhaled corticosteroids (eg, fluticasone) are the most effective long-term control medications for persistent asthma, but they do not provide immediate relief of symptoms. Cromolyn is a mast cell stabilizer that is used as a prophylactic agent in asthma and does not relieve acute symptoms. Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist that is used for long-term control and prevention of symptoms in asthma. It is not used for quick relief.

question: A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of genital lesions. She has no history of serious illness. few_shot.question: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because of painless lesions on the vulva that she first noticed 2 days ago. She does not have any urinary symptoms. She has gastroesophageal reflux disease for which she takes omeprazole. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 10 years. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of multiple, painless, raised, rough-textured vulvar lesions is consistent with condyloma acuminatum, a manifestation of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. HPV is a sexually transmitted infection that is associated with cervical, vaginal, vulvar, anal, penile, and oropharyngeal cancers. HPV types 6 and 11 are responsible for 90% of genital warts. The warts are typically asymptomatic but can cause itching, burning, tenderness, pain, or bleeding. They can be diagnosed clinically, but acetic acid application can be used to help visualize subclinical warts. 

Treatment of genital warts includes patient-applied (eg, imiquimod, podofilox) or provider-administered (eg, cryotherapy, trichloroacetic acid) therapies. Cryotherapy is a provider-administered therapy that involves the use of liquid nitrogen to freeze and destroy the warts. It is safe and effective, and it can be used in pregnant women.

The virus infects the basal layer of the squamous epithelium and causes proliferation of the infected cells, leading to the formation of a papule. As the papule enlarges, the surface can become hyperkeratotic and irregular. The lesions can be found in the anogenital region, including the vagina, cervix, penis, and anus. The application of a dilute solution of acetic acid can turn the lesions white, which can aid in their visualization.

Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors (eg, sitagliptin) are a good choice for patients with T2DM who have a compelling need to avoid hypoglycemia or weight gain. DPP-4 inhibitors block the degradation of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), an incretin hormone that increases insulin secretion, decreases glucagon secretion, and slows gastric emptying. DPP-4 inhibitors have a modest glucose-lowering effect and are weight neutral. They are generally well tolerated, with a low risk of hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy or with metformin.

answer_choices.A: Respect the wife’s wishes and resuscitate the patient
answer_choices.B: Contact the patient’s siblings or other first-degree relatives
answer_choices.C: Respect the patient’s advance directive orders

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's advance directive clearly states that he does not wish to be resuscitated or have any sort of life support. This is a legally binding document and must be respected, regardless of the wishes of the patient's wife or other family members. The patient's autonomy and wishes must be respected above all else.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for the evaluation of severe chest pain for the last hour. The pain travels along the left arm and upper jaw. The patient also reports difficulty breathing and profuse sweating. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the last 35 years. His medications include enalapril and metformin. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. An ECG shows ST elevation in the leads II, III, and aVF. Morphine is administered and oxygen supplementation and fluid resuscitation are begun. Shortly after, the patient becomes unstable. Following emergency resuscitation and stabilization, a written advance directive provided by the patient's primary care physician shows a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order. The patient's wife, who is the power of attorney, disagrees. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

answer_choices.A: Obtain court order to revoke written advance directive

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's ECG findings are consistent with an inferior wall ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The patient's hypotension and tachycardia suggest cardiogenic shock, a complication of STEMI. Cardiogenic shock is a medical emergency that requires immediate intervention, including revascularization (eg, percutaneous coronary intervention, fibrinolytic therapy) and hemodynamic support (eg, vasopressors, intra-aortic balloon pump). However, this patient has a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order, which is a type of advance directive. Advance directives are legal documents that allow patients to convey their decisions about end-of-life care ahead of time. They provide a way for patients to communicate their wishes to family, friends, and health care professionals and to avoid confusion later on. Some people want to receive all available treatments, while others do not. In this case, the patient's DNR order indicates that he does not want to receive cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) or advanced cardiac life support (ACLS). Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is to provide supportive care only.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [D] > [A] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 76-year-old man is brought to the hospital after having a stroke. Head CT is done in the emergency department and shows intracranial hemorrhage. Upon arrival to the ED he is verbally non-responsive and withdraws only to pain. He does not open his eyes. He is transferred to the medical ICU for further management and intubated for airway protection. During his second day in the ICU, his blood pressure is measured as 91/54 mmHg and pulse is 120/min. He is given fluids and antibiotics, but he progresses to renal failure and his mental status deteriorates. The physicians in the ICU ask the patient’s family what his wishes are for end-of-life care. His wife tells the team that she is durable power of attorney for the patient and provides appropriate documentation. She mentions that he did not have a living will, but she believes that he would want care withdrawn in this situation, and therefore asks the team to withdraw care at this point. The patient’s daughter vehemently disagrees and believes it is in the best interest of her father, the patient, to continue all care. Based on this information, what is the best course of action for the physician team?

answer_choices.A: Listen to the patient’s wife’s wishes and withdraw care
answer_choices.B: Listen to the patient’s daughter’s wishes and continue all care
answer_choices.C: Compromise between the wife and daughter and withdraw the fluids and antibiotics but keep the patient intubated
answer_choices.D: Call other family members and consult them for their opinions

few_shot.explanation:
The patient’s wife is the durable power of attorney (DPOA) for the patient. This means that she has the legal authority to make medical decisions for the patient when he is unable to do so. The patient’s daughter does not have this legal authority. Therefore, the physician team should listen to the patient’s wife’s wishes and withdraw care.

So, the answer is [A].
