few_shot.question:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department for the evaluation of diarrhea and vomiting for the last 2 days. During this period, he has had about 12 watery, non-bloody bowel movements and has vomited three times. He came back from a trip to India 3 days ago, where he and his family were visiting relatives. He has not been able to eat anything since the symptoms started. The patient has not urinated since yesterday. He appears pale. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 106/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Examination shows dry mucous membranes. The abdomen is soft with no organomegaly. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 13 g/dL
Serum
Na+ 148 mEq/L
Cl- 103 mEq/L
K+ 3.7 mEq/L
HCO3- 19 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen 80 mg/dL
Glucose 90 mg/dL
Creatinine 2 mg/dL
Intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's abnormal renal laboratory findings?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recent travel to a developing country, along with his symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea, suggest that he has gastroenteritis, likely due to an infectious cause. The resulting volume depletion has caused prerenal azotemia, as evidenced by the elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine levels. Prerenal azotemia is the most common cause of acute kidney injury and is due to decreased renal perfusion. In this case, the decreased perfusion is due to volume depletion from the severe vomiting and diarrhea. Other potential causes of prerenal azotemia include decreased cardiac output (eg, congestive heart failure) and systemic vasodilation (eg, sepsis).

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 19-year-old female college soccer player presents to a sports medicine clinic with right knee pain. One day prior she twisted her right knee and felt a “pop” while chasing after a ball. She has since felt severe throbbing knee pain and noticed a rapid increase in swelling around her knee. She is able to bear weight but feels “unstable” on her right leg. On exam, anterior drawer and Lachman’s tests are positive. The physician informs her that she has likely injured an important structure in her knee. What is the function of the structure that she has most likely injured?

answer_choices.A: Prevent excess posterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur
answer_choices.B: Prevent excess anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur
answer_choices.C: Resist excess valgus force on the knee
answer_choices.D: Provide a cushion between the lateral tibial and femoral condyles

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old professional soccer player presents to the clinic with discomfort and pain while walking. He says that he has an unstable knee joint that started after an injury during a match last week. He adds that he heard a popping sound at the time of the injury. Physical examination of the knee reveals swelling of the knee joint with a positive anterior drawer test. Which of the following structures is most likely damaged in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is one of the four major ligaments of the knee. It originates from the medial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle in the intercondylar notch and extends to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia. The ACL prevents anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur and is most commonly injured during sports that involve sudden stops and changes in direction (eg, soccer, basketball). Patients often report a popping sensation at the time of injury. The anterior drawer test, in which the tibia is pulled forward while the patient is lying supine with hips flexed and knees flexed to 90 degrees, is used to assess the integrity of the ACL. A positive test (ie, increased anterior translation of the tibia compared with the opposite side) suggests ACL tear.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old female college basketball player presents in Sports Clinic after she felt a "pop" in her knee after coming down with a rebound. To examine the patient, you have her lie down on the table with her knees flexed 90 degrees. With your hand around her knee you are able to draw the tibia toward you from underneath the femur. The torn structure implicated by this physical exam maneuver has which of the following attachments?

answer_choices.A: The posterior intercondylar area of tibia and the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femur
answer_choices.B: The anterior intercondylar area of tibia and the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femur
answer_choices.C: The lateral epicondyle of the femur and the head of fibula
answer_choices.D: The medial condyle of the femur and the medial condyle of the tibia

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history and physical exam are consistent with an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. The ACL originates from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia and inserts into the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femur. It prevents anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur (positive anterior drawer sign) and is most often injured with sudden direction changes (twisting or pivoting) with the foot planted, hyperextension, or a sudden deceleration. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her father because of a 1-month history of pain in her right knee. She is a competitive volleyball player and has missed several games recently due to pain. Examination shows swelling distal to the right knee joint on the anterior surface of the proximal tibia; there is no overlying warmth or deformity. Extension of the right knee against resistance is painful. Which of the following structures is attached to the affected anterior tibial area?
few_shot.explanation:
The patellar ligament is a continuation of the quadriceps tendon and extends from the patella to the tibial tuberosity. It is a key component of the extensor mechanism of the knee, along with the quadriceps muscle, quadriceps tendon, and patella. The patellar ligament is responsible for transmitting the force generated by the quadriceps muscle to the tibia, allowing for knee extension. Repetitive stress on the patellar ligament, such as from jumping or kicking, can lead to inflammation and microtearing at its insertion site on the tibial tuberosity. This condition, known as Osgood-Schlatter disease, is a common cause of anterior knee pain in adolescents. It is characterized by pain and swelling at the tibial tuberosity that is exacerbated by activities such as running, jumping, and climbing stairs. Pain may also be elicited by direct pressure (eg, kneeling) or resisted knee extension.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 19-year-old collegiate football player sustains an injury to his left knee during a game. He was running with the ball when he dodged a defensive player and fell, twisting his left knee. He felt a “pop” as he fell. When he attempts to bear weight on his left knee, it feels unstable, and "gives way." He needs assistance to walk off the field. The pain is localized diffusely over the knee and is non-radiating. His past medical history is notable for asthma. He uses an albuterol inhaler as needed. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. On exam, he has a notable suprapatellar effusion. Range of motion is limited in the extremes of flexion. When the proximal tibia is pulled anteriorly while the knee is flexed and the patient is supine, there is 1.5 centimeter of anterior translation. The contralateral knee translates 0.5 centimeters with a similar force. The injured structure in this patient originates on which of the following bony landmarks?

answer_choices.A: Lateral aspect of the lateral femoral condyle
answer_choices.B: Medial aspect of the medial femoral condyle
answer_choices.C: Posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of a twisting injury, feeling a "pop," and subsequent instability of the knee is suggestive of an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. The ACL originates from the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and inserts onto the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia. It prevents anterior translation of the tibia on the femur and is the primary restraint to hyperextension of the knee. The ACL also resists tibial rotation and varus/valgus angulation when the knee is in full extension. The Lachman test, which demonstrates increased anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur, is the most sensitive and specific test for an ACL tear.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain and swelling in his right knee that began 3 days ago when he fell during football practice. He fell on his flexed right knee as he dove to complete a pass. He felt some mild knee pain but continued to practice. Over the next 2 days, the pain worsened and the knee began to swell. Today, the patient has an antalgic gait. Examination shows a swollen and tender right knee; flexion is limited by pain. The right knee is flexed and pressure is applied to proximal tibia; 8 mm of backward translation of the foreleg is observed. Which of the following is most likely injured?
few_shot.explanation:
The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) is the primary restraint to posterior translation of the tibia. It is stronger and less frequently injured than the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). The mechanism of injury for a PCL tear is most often a fall onto a flexed knee with the foot in plantar flexion (eg, dashboard injury in a motor vehicle accident, fall onto a flexed knee). The classic physical examination finding in PCL tear is posterior sag sign, in which the tibia "sags" backward from the femur when the knee is flexed to 90 degrees. The posterior drawer test is another physical examination maneuver used to diagnose PCL tear. In this test, the knee is flexed to 90 degrees and the tibia is pushed posteriorly. Increased backward translation of the tibia compared with the opposite side suggests PCL tear.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 64-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus is referred to a urologist. The patient has had pain when urinating and difficulty starting a stream of urine for over 4 months now. He is bothered because he has to urinate about 9 times every day, including several times when he wakes up at night. A digital rectal examination revealed multiple hard nodules in the prostate gland. A CT scan shows a nodule in the right lung that measures 3 cm. An ultrasound scan of his urinary bladder and prostate shows residual urine of > 200 mL and heterogeneous findings of the prostate gland. Biopsy reveals grade 2 prostate adenocarcinoma. Follow-up 9 months later shows his prostate cancer is well controlled with goserelin. If one considers pulmonary nodules that are the same size as this patient’s, which of the following additional findings on CT scans would most likely prompt the removal of such nodules?

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of nocturia and a weak urinary stream. These symptoms began 1 year ago, but have progressively worsened over the past 6 months. He now wakes up 3–5 times every night to urinate. He has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide and lisinopril. The patient has smoked a half-pack of cigarettes daily for the past 30 years. He appears well. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 77/min, and blood pressure is 128/77 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. His abdomen is soft and nontender. Digital rectal examination shows a diffusely enlarged prostate with a firm nodule in the right posterior lobe. Urinalysis is within normal limits. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level is 6.5 ng/mL (N = 0–4). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.B: Repeat PSA level in one year
answer_choices.D: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's nocturia, weak urinary stream, and diffusely enlarged prostate with a firm nodule are concerning for prostate cancer. Prostate cancer is the most common solid organ malignancy in men and the second leading cause of cancer death. Risk factors include age >60, African American race, and a family history of prostate cancer. The diagnosis is suggested by an elevated or rapidly rising prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level and/or an abnormal digital rectal examination (eg, nodularity, induration, asymmetry). However, these tests are not diagnostic, and the definitive diagnosis of prostate cancer requires a transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy of the prostate. Biopsy is typically performed in men with a PSA level >4.0 ng/mL or an abnormal digital rectal examination, as in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of difficulty initiating urination. He wakes up at least 3–4 times at night to urinate. Digital rectal examination shows a symmetrically enlarged, nontender prostate with a rubbery consistency. Laboratory studies show a prostate-specific antigen level of 2.1 ng/mL (N < 4). Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.A: Hyperplasia of lateral prostatic lobe tissue
answer_choices.C: Hypertrophy of middle prostatic lobe tissue
answer_choices.D: Lymphocytic infiltration of anterior prostatic lobe stroma

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of difficulty initiating urination and nocturia are suggestive of bladder outlet obstruction due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). BPH is a common condition in older men and is characterized by hyperplasia of prostatic stromal and epithelial cells, particularly in the periurethral (ie, transitional zone) region of the prostate. This leads to the formation of large, discrete nodules in the periurethral region of the prostate. The lateral lobes of the prostate are located in the periurethral region, and hyperplasia of these lobes can cause compression of the urethra, leading to the observed symptoms.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of urinary frequency, dysuria, and blood in his urine. He has also had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss over the past 3 months and has been feeling more fatigued than usual. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years but quit 2 years ago. A urinalysis shows 3+ blood. Cystoscopy shows an irregular mass on the bladder wall; a biopsy is taken. Which of the following histologic findings would indicate the worst survival prognosis?

answer_choices.A: Dysplastic cells extending into the lamina propria
answer_choices.B: Nests of atypical cells in the urothelium
answer_choices.D: Disordered urothelium lined with papillary fronds

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of smoking, weight loss, and hematuria is concerning for bladder cancer. The most common type of bladder cancer is urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, which is strongly associated with smoking and occupational exposure to aniline dyes and aromatic amines.

Urothelial carcinoma can be either papillary or flat. Papillary tumors are often low-grade and have a better prognosis. Flat tumors are usually high-grade and have a worse prognosis. The most important prognostic factor for both types is the depth of invasion. The bladder wall is composed of the mucosa (urothelium + lamina propria), muscularis propria, and adventitia. Tumors that invade the muscularis propria (ie, muscle-invasive) have a much worse prognosis because they have a higher risk of metastasis. Therefore, the worst prognosis would be seen with dysplastic cells extending into the lamina propria, indicating at least stage T1 disease.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
An obese 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of 3 episodes of red urine over the past week. He has also had recurrent headaches and intermittent blurry vision during the past month. He has benign prostatic hyperplasia. He works as an attendant at a gas station. The patient has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the last 40 years. He does not drink alcohol. Current medications include tamsulosin. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.4°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 152/95 mm Hg. Examination shows a flushed face. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. Digital rectal examination shows an enlarged prostate with no nodules. Urinalysis shows:
Blood 3+
Glucose negative
Protein negative
WBC 1-2/hpf
RBC 40-45/hpf
RBC casts none
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, obesity, and hypertension, along with his symptoms of recurrent headaches, intermittent blurry vision, and flushed face, are suggestive of paraneoplastic syndrome due to renal cell carcinoma (RCC). RCC is the most common primary renal malignancy and is associated with several paraneoplastic syndromes, including polycythemia due to increased erythropoietin production. Polycythemia can cause symptoms such as headaches, blurry vision, and a ruddy complexion due to increased red blood cell mass. Hematuria, which can be gross or microscopic, is the most common clinical manifestation of RCC.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician because of several episodes of dark urine over the past 2 months. He has had a 6 kg (13.2-lb) weight loss over the past 3 months despite no changes in appetite. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. A CT scan shows a heterogeneous enhancing mass arising from the left renal pelvis. Pathologic examination of the lesion is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.A: Ulcerating tumor comprised of glandular cells within mucinous material
answer_choices.B: Pedunculated tumor comprised of pleomorphic urothelial cells with severe nuclear atypia
answer_choices.C: Bright yellow tumor comprised of polygonal cells filled with lipids and glycogen
answer_choices.D: Grayish-tan tumor comprised of primitive blastemal cells forming abortive glomeruli

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, weight loss, and dark urine (indicating hematuria) is concerning for urothelial carcinoma (also known as transitional cell carcinoma), the most common malignancy of the urinary tract. Urothelial carcinoma can occur anywhere along the urinary tract lined by urothelium, from the renal pelvis to the urethra, but it most commonly occurs in the bladder. Risk factors include smoking, occupational exposure to aniline dyes and aromatic amines, and long-term analgesic abuse.

Grossly, urothelial carcinoma is a papillary and friable tumor, often with areas of necrosis and hemorrhage. Microscopically, the tumor is composed of cells that resemble normal urothelium. However, these cells show significant nuclear atypia and pleomorphism, and can invade the underlying lamina propria and muscularis propria.

So, the answer is [B].

question:
A 50-year-old man presents to his physician with chronic cough, aching joints in his hips and lower back, and malaise over the past 2 months. He describes himself as being “generally healthy” before the cough began. Past medical history includes hypertension. The patient takes clopamide and a multivitamin daily. His parents are both well and living in a senior living facility. He does not smoke and only drinks alcohol occasionally. During a review of symptoms, the patient described a hiking trip in and around the desert near Phoenix, Arizona, 4 months ago. At the office, his temperature is 38.6°C (101.4°F), heart rate is 102/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 120/82 mm Hg. A focused chest exam reveals mild fremetus and dullness with percussion on the right side. A chest X-ray shows a right-sided consolidation of the lower right lung, and a chest CT shows an irregular opacity measuring 3.8 cm x 3.0 cm in the sub-plural region of the right middle lobe, a small right-sided pleural effusion, and mild right-sided hilar adenopathy. A lung biopsy is performed to rule out cancer and reveals necrotic granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and spherules with endospores in the surrounding tissues. The laboratory tests show the following results:
Hemoglobin 12.9 mg/dL
Leukocyte count 9,300/mm3
Platelet count 167,000/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 43 mm/hr
Periodic acid-Schiff and silver methenamine Positive
Acid-fast stain Negative
 Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old man presents to the physician with fever, cough, weakness, night sweats, and poor appetite for the past 6 months. Medical records suggest that he has lost 7.5 kg (16.5 lb) of weight during this period. There is no history of breathlessness, nasal discharge, nasal obstruction, palpitations, chest pain, or symptoms related to digestion. He was released from prison 9 months ago after serving a 2-year sentence. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 122/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows hepatomegaly and generalized lymphadenopathy, and auscultation of the chest reveals diffuse crackles throughout the lung fields bilaterally. On direct ophthalmoscopy, three discrete, yellow-colored, 0.5 mm to 1.0 mm lesions with indistinct borders are seen in the posterior pole. A chest X-ray is shown in the image. Tuberculin skin test with purified protein derivative is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fever, cough, weight loss, and night sweats, along with his history of incarceration, are highly suggestive of tuberculosis (TB). The chest X-ray shows bilateral upper lobe infiltrates, which is a common finding in TB. The yellowish lesions seen on ophthalmoscopy are choroidal tubercles, which are seen in disseminated TB. The negative tuberculin skin test does not rule out TB, as false negatives can occur in patients with disseminated disease due to anergy.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever, malaise, productive cough, and left-sided chest pain for 2 weeks. During this time, he has woken up to a wet pillow in the morning on multiple occasions and has not been as hungry as usual. He was diagnosed with HIV infection 1 year ago. He currently stays at a homeless shelter. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 22 years. He has a history of intravenous illicit drug use. He drinks 5–6 beers daily. He is receiving combined antiretroviral therapy but sometimes misses doses. His temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 106/min, and blood pressure is 125/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Auscultation shows decreased breath sounds over the left base of the lung. There is dullness to percussion on the left lower part of the chest. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 14 g/dL
Leukocyte count 5,000/mm3
CD4+ T lymphocytes 240/mm3 (N > 500)
Serum
Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
γ-Glutamyltransferase (GGT) 65 U/L (N = 5–50)
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 15 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 19 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase 40 U/L
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 50 U/L
An x-ray of the chest shows a left-sided pleural effusion and hilar lymphadenopathy. Analysis of the pleural fluid shows an effusion with lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis, high protein, an LDH of 500 U/L, and high adenosine deaminase. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, cough, and night sweats in the setting of homelessness, alcoholism, and HIV infection is concerning for pulmonary tuberculosis (TB). TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacillus that is spread via respiratory droplets. Risk factors for TB include HIV infection, homelessness, incarceration, and immigration from an endemic area. TB can present with a variety of symptoms, including fever, night sweats, cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss. Chest x-ray may show cavitary lesions, but findings can be atypical in patients with HIV infection. TB can also cause a pleural effusion, which is typically an exudate with lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis. Pleural fluid adenosine deaminase levels are often elevated in TB, and this test can be used to support the diagnosis.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of a productive cough, shortness of breath, and low-grade fever. He works as a farmer in southern Arizona. Physical examination shows multiple skin lesions with a dark blue center, pale intermediate zone, and red peripheral rim on the upper and lower extremities. There are diffuse crackles on the left side of the chest. An x-ray of the chest shows left basilar consolidation and left hilar lymphadenopathy. A photomicrograph of tissue obtained from a biopsy of the lung is shown. Which of the following is the most likely causal pathogen?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of cough, shortness of breath, and fever, along with the finding of left basilar consolidation on chest x-ray, are suggestive of pneumonia. The presence of skin lesions and hilar lymphadenopathy suggest a systemic fungal infection. The patient's occupation as a farmer in southern Arizona and the photomicrograph showing large spherules filled with endospores are characteristic of Coccidioides immitis, a dimorphic fungus found in the soil of the southwestern United States, parts of Mexico, and Central and South America. Coccidioidomycosis (also known as Valley fever) typically presents as a self-limited respiratory illness, but it can also cause more severe disease, including pneumonia, meningitis, and disseminated disease, especially in immunocompromised individuals.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 43-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a fever, nausea, and a nonproductive cough for 7 days. During this period, she has had headaches, generalized fatigue, and muscle and joint pain. She has also had increasing shortness of breath for 2 days. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and osteoarthritis of her left knee. Current medications include insulin and ibuprofen. She had smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 20 years but stopped 10 years ago. Her temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 94/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 132/86 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. There are multiple skin lesions with a blue livid center, pale intermediate zone, and a dark red peripheral rim on the upper and lower extremities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL
Leukocyte count 11,100/mm3
Serum
Na+ 137 mEq/L
K+ 4.1 mEq/L
Cl- 99 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen 17 mg/dL
Glucose 123 mg/dL
Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
An x-ray of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, nonproductive cough, and malaise, along with the chest x-ray findings of diffuse interstitial infiltrates, is suggestive of atypical pneumonia. The most common cause of atypical pneumonia is Mycoplasma pneumoniae, especially in patients <40 years old. Other common causes include Chlamydophila pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila. In contrast to typical pneumonia (eg, due to Streptococcus pneumoniae), which often presents acutely with high fever, productive cough, and lobar consolidation on chest x-ray, atypical pneumonia often has a more indolent course with prominent extrapulmonary findings such as headache, sore throat, and skin rash. The skin lesions seen in this patient are consistent with erythema multiforme, a hypersensitivity reaction to infections (including Mycoplasma pneumoniae) and drugs.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 71-year-old African American man is brought to the emergency department with a worsening productive cough and dyspnea for 2 days. He has had generalized bone pain for 2 months. He was admitted for pyelonephritis last month. He also received outpatient treatment for pneumonia almost 2 months ago. Over the past 2 months, he has been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen for pain as needed. He appears anxious. The vital signs include: temperature 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse 95/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and blood pressure 155/90 mm Hg. The conjunctivae are pale. Crackles are heard in the right lower lobe. The cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. The laboratory studies show the following:
Hemoglobin 9 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 95 μm3
Leukocyte count 13,500/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 75%
Lymphocytes 25%
Platelet count 240,000/mm3
ESR 85 mm/hr
Serum
Na+ 135 mEq/L
K+ 4.2 mEq/L
Cl− 113 mEq/L
HCO3− 20 mEq/L
Ca+ 12.4 mg/dL
Albumin 4 g/dL
Urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL
Creatinine 2.2 mg/dL
A chest X-ray shows a right lower lobe opacity and blurring of the ipsilateral diaphragmatic dome. Skull and pelvic X-rays are performed (see image). Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s recent infections?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent infections, anemia, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, and lytic bone lesions are suggestive of multiple myeloma (MM). MM is a malignancy of plasma cells that primarily occurs in older adults and is more common in African Americans. The disease is characterized by overproduction of a single clone of plasma cells, leading to overproduction of a monoclonal immunoglobulin protein (M protein). The M protein can be an intact immunoglobulin or only a portion of the immunoglobulin (eg, light chains only, also known as Bence Jones protein). The overproduction of this single clone of plasma cells suppresses the production of other normal, polyclonal immunoglobulins, leading to an increased susceptibility to infections, particularly with encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. This is known as hypogammaglobulinemia.

question: A 25-year-old Hispanic male presents with heat intolerance and recent weight loss. Serum analysis shows increased levels of T4 and T3, as well as the presence of thyroglobulin-stimulating immunoglobulins. The patient is found to be tachycardic and has marked edema and waxy discoloration in his legs. Which of the following would be consistent with this patient's disease?

few_shot.question: A 47-year-old Hispanic man presents with complaints of recent heat intolerance and rapid heart rate. The patient has also experienced recent unintentional weight loss of 15 pounds. Physical exam reveals tachycardia and skin that is warm to the touch. A radioactive iodine uptake scan of the thyroid reveals several focal nodules of increased iodine uptake. Prior to this study, the physician had also ordered a serum analysis that will most likely show which of the following?

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with symptoms of heat intolerance, unintentional weight loss, feelings of anxiety, and excessive energy that hinder her from falling asleep at night. few_shot.question: A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presents with a three-month history of weight loss, anxiety, and tremors. question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an acute, painful swelling of the left labia that she first noticed that morning. She also reports some pain while sitting and walking. few_shot.question: A 35-year-old female presents to her gynecologist complaining of vaginal discomfort. Which of the following embryologic precursors gives rise to the affected tissue in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms and physical examination findings are consistent with a Bartholin gland cyst. The Bartholin glands are located bilaterally at the posterior aspect of the vaginal introitus and drain through ducts that empty into the vestibule at the 4 and 8 o'clock positions. These glands secrete mucus to lubricate the vagina. If the duct becomes blocked, a cyst may form. If the cyst becomes infected, an abscess can develop.

The Bartholin glands are derived from the urogenital sinus, as are the bladder, urethra, and lower vagina.

few_shot.question: An 80-year-old woman seeks evaluation at an outpatient clinic for a firm nodular lump on the left side of her labia. She first noticed the lump about 5 months ago. On physical examination, the temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), the blood pressure is 135/89 mm Hg, the pulse is 95/min, and the respiratory rate is 17/min. Examination of the genital area reveals a small nodular lump on the left labium majus with visible excoriations, but no white plaque-like lesions. What is the next best step in management?

Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis that affects the anogenital region in postmenopausal women. It is characterized by intense pruritus and thinning of the skin, which can cause significant architectural distortion (eg, resorption of the labia minora). Patients with lichen sclerosus are at an increased risk for vulvar SCC. Although the absolute risk is small, any new lump in a patient with lichen sclerosus should raise concern for malignancy. A vulvar biopsy is needed to establish the diagnosis.

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 25-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-hour history of sudden severe lower abdominal pain. The pain started shortly after having sexual intercourse. The pain is worse with movement and urination. The patient had several urinary tract infections as a child. She is sexually active with her boyfriend and uses condoms inconsistently. She cannot remember when her last menstrual period was. She appears uncomfortable and pale. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows a palpable, tender right adnexal mass. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dL and her hematocrit is 30%. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 5 x 3-cm right ovarian sac-like structure with surrounding echogenic fluid around the structure and the uterus. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden-onset, severe lower abdominal pain, adnexal mass, and hypotension are concerning for ovarian torsion. Ovarian torsion occurs when the ovary twists around its vascular pedicle, leading to venous obstruction, edema, and eventually arterial obstruction and infarction if not promptly treated. Risk factors include ovarian masses (eg, cysts, tumors) and ovarian hyperstimulation. The pain is typically sudden in onset, severe, and unilateral. Nausea and vomiting are common. On examination, an adnexal mass may be palpated. Ultrasonography often reveals an enlarged ovary with peripheral follicles and may show decreased or absent blood flow on Doppler. However, normal flow does not rule out the diagnosis as it may be present in early or intermittent torsion. Management of ovarian torsion involves prompt surgical intervention to untwist the ovary and preserve function. If the ovary is necrotic, oophorectomy is performed.

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with abdominal and pelvic pain. She states it started 3 days ago and it has been getting gradually worse. She states it is diffuse and is located over her abdomen, pelvis, and inside her vagina. She also endorses vaginal pruritus and a discharge from her vagina. The patient works in an ice cream parlor and is sexually active with multiple different partners. Her temperature is 98.0°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 122/80 mmHg, pulse is 82/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a foul smelling vagina with a thin, white discharge. Her abdomen is diffusely tender. The patient is noted to be itching her vagina during the exam. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, and pruritus is concerning for pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). PID is an infection of the upper genital tract (uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries) that can cause significant morbidity, including chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. It is often polymicrobial, with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis being the most common pathogens. Other organisms associated with bacterial vaginosis (eg, Gardnerella vaginalis, as suggested by the presence of a thin, white, malodorous discharge) can also be involved. Risk factors for PID include multiple sexual partners and inconsistent condom use.

However, before the diagnosis of PID can be made, pregnancy must be ruled out, as the symptoms of PID can mimic those of ectopic pregnancy (eg, lower abdominal pain, adnexal tenderness). Therefore, the most appropriate initial step in management is to check a urine pregnancy test.

question: A 40-year-old obese man with a history of diabetes and chronic kidney disease presents with one day of excruciating pain, swelling, and redness in his greater toe. few_shot.question: A 41-year-old man presents to the office with pain in his right big toe. This patient's acute onset of severe pain, swelling, and erythema in the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is suggestive of gout. Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition in tissues, leading to a severe inflammatory response. It is associated with conditions that increase serum uric acid levels, such as obesity, alcohol use, and chronic kidney disease.

Joint fluid analysis in gout shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the axis of the compensator) crystals.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old man presents to his physician with the complaint of a painful toe joint on his right foot. It is often triggered by conditions that increase serum uric acid levels. Thiazide diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide, are a common cause of drug-induced hyperuricemia and gout. Risk factors for gout include obesity, alcohol consumption, and diets high in purines (eg, red meat, shellfish).

question: A 78-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressively worsening fatigue and headache for 6 months and occasional abdominal pain. He has not had any changes in his weight. He has a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic shoulder pain. Current daily medications include hydrochlorothiazide, metformin, and ibuprofen. He does not drink alcohol and does not smoke. His diet has mostly consisted of potatoes and lean meats since his wife passed away 1 year ago. His pulse is 92/min and blood pressure is 135/80 mm Hg. Examination shows conjunctival and mucosal pallor. Abdominal and rectal examination shows no abnormalities. Neurological exam shows mild postural tremor. few_shot.question:
A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of worsening fatigue. During this time, she has noted a decrease in her exercise capacity and she becomes short of breath when walking briskly. She has had occasional streaks of blood in her stools during periods of constipation. She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus at the age of 24 years and has a history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her current medications include insulin, lisinopril, aspirin, and atorvastatin. Her diet mostly consists of white meat and vegetables. Her pulse is 92/min and blood pressure is 145/92 mm Hg. Examination shows conjunctival pallor. Cardiac auscultation shows a grade 2/6 midsystolic ejection murmur best heard along the right upper sternal border. Sensation to pinprick is decreased bilaterally over the dorsum of her feet. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL
WBC count 7,200/mm3
Erythrocyte count 3.06 million/mm3
Mean corpuscular volume 84 μm3

Reticulocyte count 0.6 %

Serum

Creatinine 3.1 mg/dL

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's anemia, decreased exercise capacity, and elevated blood urea nitrogen and creatinine levels are suggestive of chronic kidney disease (CKD). The most common causes of CKD in the United States are diabetes mellitus and hypertension, both of which are present in this patient. Anemia in CKD is typically normocytic and normochromic with low reticulocyte count, as seen in this patient. It is largely due to decreased production of erythropoietin by the diseased kidneys. Erythropoietin is a glycoprotein hormone that is produced by the kidneys in response to low oxygen tension in the renal blood supply. It acts on erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow to stimulate the production of red blood cells. In CKD, the production of erythropoietin is decreased, leading to decreased stimulation of the bone marrow and subsequent anemia.

This patient's history of polycystic kidney disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, along with his elevated creatinine level, suggest chronic kidney disease (CKD). CKD is associated with a bleeding diathesis due to platelet dysfunction. This is due to impaired platelet aggregation and adhesion, which can lead to mucosal bleeding, such as the gastrointestinal bleeding seen in this patient. The exact mechanism of platelet dysfunction in CKD is not well understood, but it is thought to be due to the accumulation of uremic toxins. This can also cause uremic pruritus, which is suggested by the excoriations on the extensor surfaces of his upper extremities. The flapping tremor (asterixis) is a sign of metabolic encephalopathy, which can be due to uremia in the setting of advanced CKD.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

The most common malignancies associated with hypercalcemia are multiple myeloma, and cancers of the lung, kidney, ovary, and thyroid.

The pathogenesis of analgesic nephropathy is not completely understood, but it is thought to involve inhibition of renal prostaglandin synthesis by NSAIDs. few_shot.question: A 78-year-old man presents with fatigue and exertional dyspnea. The patient says that symptoms onset gradually 4 weeks ago and have not improved. He denies any history of anemia or nutritional deficiency. Past medical history is significant for ST-elevation myocardial infarction 6 months ago, status post coronary artery bypass graft, complicated by recurrent hemodynamically unstable ventricular tachycardia. Current medications are rosuvastatin, aspirin, and amiodarone. His blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg, the pulse is 71/min, the temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), and the respiratory rate is 16/min. On physical examination, patient appears lethargic and tired. Skin is dry and coarse, and there is generalized pitting edema present. A complete blood count (CBC) and a peripheral blood smear show evidence of normochromic, normocytic anemia. Additional laboratory tests reveal decreased serum level of iron, decreased TIBC (total iron-binding capacity) and increased serum level of ferritin. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of the anemia in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's normochromic, normocytic anemia and low serum iron level may suggest iron deficiency anemia. However, the decreased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) and increased ferritin level are inconsistent with iron deficiency, which would present with an increased TIBC and decreased ferritin level. Instead, these laboratory findings suggest anemia of chronic disease (also known as anemia of inflammation). This is a common cause of anemia in hospitalized patients and is associated with chronic illnesses such as infection, inflammatory disorders (eg, autoimmune diseases), malignancy, and chronic kidney disease.

In anemia of chronic disease, inflammatory cytokines (eg, interleukin-6) lead to increased hepcidin production by the liver. Hepcidin decreases iron absorption from the gut and decreases the release of iron from macrophages. This results in decreased iron availability for erythropoiesis, despite adequate iron stores (as indicated by the increased ferritin level). The decreased iron availability leads to decreased hemoglobin production and subsequent anemia.

In this patient, the most likely source of inflammation is his amiodarone use. Amiodarone is associated with a number of adverse effects, including pulmonary toxicity, thyroid dysfunction, and hepatotoxicity. question: A 29-year-old woman presents to the clinic after several months of weight loss. She noticed a 6.8 kg (15 lb) unintentional weight loss over the preceding several months. few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of irritability and frequent bowel movements. During this time, she has had a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss. She has not had a change in appetite or diet. She takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.4°C (99.4°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg. Examination shows moist palms. The thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged; there are no palpable nodules. Serum studies show a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration of 0.2 μU/mL, thyroxine (T4) concentration of 22 μg/dL, and antibodies against the TSH receptor. Which of the following treatment modalities is associated with the lowest rate of recurrence for this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of weight loss, irritability, and tachycardia, along with physical examination findings of a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland and moist palms, are suggestive of hyperthyroidism. The presence of antibodies against the TSH receptor confirms the diagnosis of Graves' disease, the most common cause of hyperthyroidism.

The three main treatment options for Graves' disease are antithyroid drugs (eg, methimazole), radioactive iodine ablation, and surgery. Of these, radioactive iodine ablation is associated with the lowest rate of recurrence. However, it often leads to permanent hypothyroidism, requiring lifelong thyroid hormone replacement.

few_shot.question: A 35-year-old woman presents to the clinic for a several-month history of heat intolerance. This leads to increased synthesis and release of thyroid hormones (triiodothyronine [T3] and thyroxine [T4]). The elevated levels of T3 and T4 provide negative feedback to the anterior pituitary, leading to decreased TSH production. Therefore, the most likely laboratory finding in this patient is a low TSH level.

few_shot.question: A 21-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician at 10 weeks' gestation because of progressive fatigue for the past 3 weeks. This patient's weight loss, increased appetite, anxiety, insomnia, tremor, tachycardia, and systolic murmur are consistent with hyperthyroidism. The diffuse goiter and ophthalmopathy suggest Graves disease, the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in women of childbearing age. Graves disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by circulating immunoglobulins that bind to and stimulate the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, leading to increased synthesis and release of thyroid hormone.

In pregnancy, the preferred treatment for hyperthyroidism is propylthiouracil during the first trimester, then switching to methimazole for the second and third trimesters. Propylthiouracil is preferred initially because methimazole has been associated with a rare congenital anomaly (eg, aplasia cutis, esophageal and choanal atresia). few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman comes to her primary care physician complaining of palpitations. She reports that for the past 2 months she has felt anxious and states that her heart often feels like it’s “racing.” She also complains of sweating and unintentional weight loss. Physical examination reveals symmetrical, non-tender thyroid enlargement and exophthalmos. After additional testing, the patient is given an appropriate treatment for her condition. She returns 2 weeks later complaining of worsening of her previous ocular symptoms. Which of the following treatments did the patient most likely receive?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of palpitations, anxiety, sweating, and weight loss, along with the physical examination findings of a symmetrically enlarged thyroid and exophthalmos, are suggestive of Graves' disease. This is an autoimmune disorder that results in hyperthyroidism and is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in the United States.

The treatment options for Graves' disease include antithyroid drugs (eg, methimazole, propylthiouracil), radioactive iodine, and surgery. Radioactive iodine is often the treatment of choice for most nonpregnant adults. It works by destroying the overactive thyroid cells, thereby reducing the amount of thyroid hormone produced. However, it can also cause a transient exacerbation of hyperthyroid symptoms in the weeks following treatment. This is because the destruction of thyroid cells can cause them to release a large amount of thyroid hormone into the bloodstream.

In addition, radioactive iodine can also cause a worsening of ophthalmopathy, as seen in this patient. This is thought to occur due to an increase in autoantibodies following treatment. For this reason, patients with severe ophthalmopathy are usually treated with antithyroid drugs or surgery instead of radioactive iodine.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 50-year-old woman comes to the physician because of palpitations and irritability. Over the past 4 months, she has had several episodes of heart racing and skipping beats that lasted between 30 seconds and several hours. She has also been arguing with her husband more, often about the temperature being too warm. The patient has also lost 8.8-kg (19.4-lb) over the past 4 months, despite being less strict with her diet. She has mild asthma treated with inhaled bronchodilators. Her pulse is 102/min and blood pressure is 148/98 mm Hg. On physical examination, the skin is warm and moist. A mass is palpated in the anterior neck area. On laboratory studies, thyroid stimulating hormone is undetectable and there are antibodies against the thyrotropin-receptor. Thyroid scintigraphy shows diffusely increased iodine uptake. Two weeks later, a single oral dose of radioactive iodine is administered. This patient will most likely require which of the following in the long-term?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of palpitations, weight loss, and heat intolerance, along with physical examination findings of tachycardia, hypertension, and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland, are suggestive of hyperthyroidism. The presence of thyrotropin-receptor antibodies confirms the diagnosis of Graves disease, an autoimmune disorder that is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism. 

Treatment options for Graves disease include antithyroid drugs (eg, methimazole), radioactive iodine (RAI) ablation, and thyroidectomy. RAI ablation and thyroidectomy are more definitive treatment options and are preferred in patients with a large goiter, severe hyperthyroidism, or inability to adhere to medical therapy. RAI ablation is the most common treatment for Graves disease in adults in the United States. It works by emitting beta particles that destroy the surrounding thyroid tissue. 

The goal of RAI therapy is to ablate the thyroid gland sufficiently to render the patient euthyroid or hypothyroid. Because it is difficult to titrate the exact dose of RAI to make a patient euthyroid, most patients (up to 80%) will become hypothyroid within 1 year of treatment. Therefore, patients who receive RAI therapy require long-term monitoring of thyroid function tests to determine when to initiate thyroid hormone replacement therapy (levothyroxine).

So, the answer is [D].

question: A 27-year-old man with a history of cocaine abuse comes to the physician 2 weeks after undergoing successful arthroscopic repair of a torn medial collateral ligament in his left knee. There were no complications. He was discharged with prescriptions for oxycodone and acetaminophen. few_shot.question: An 83-year-old man with advanced-stage prostate cancer comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of worsening lower back and hip pain. The patient's analgesic regimen includes oxycodone, ibuprofen, and alendronic acid. Physical examination shows localized tenderness over the lumbar spine and right hip. His current pain management requires opioid dose escalation. Which of the following opioid side effects is most likely to remain unaffected by the mechanism underlying this patient's need for a higher drug dose?
few_shot.explanation:
Opioids are commonly used to manage moderate to severe pain in patients with advanced cancer. However, their use is often limited by the development of tolerance and side effects. Tolerance, defined as the need for increasing doses to maintain the same level of analgesia, typically develops to the analgesic, euphoric, sedative, and respiratory depressive effects of opioids. In contrast, tolerance to the constipating effects of opioids usually does not occur. This is because opioids decrease gastrointestinal motility and slow transit time by acting on the myenteric plexus. This effect is mediated by the mu opioid receptor, which is not subject to the same degree of desensitization as the receptors mediating the other effects of opioids.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for left-sided knee pain. The patient has a history of osteoarthritis but states that he has been unable to control his pain with escalating doses of ibuprofen and naproxen. His past medical history includes diabetes mellitus and hypertension. His temperature is 102.0°F (38.9°C), blood pressure is 167/108 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals a warm and tender joint that is very tender to the touch and with passive range of motion. The patient declines a gait examination secondary to pain. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's acute monoarticular arthritis with systemic symptoms (eg, fever) is concerning for septic arthritis, a medical emergency. The most common pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S aureus. Neisseria gonorrhoeae should be suspected in sexually active young adults, especially if there are multiple affected joints, tenosynovitis, or a rash. Risk factors for septic arthritis include age >80, diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, recent joint surgery, and hip or knee prosthesis. The diagnosis is confirmed by arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis showing a white blood cell count >50,000/mm3 with >90% neutrophils. Gram stain and culture of the synovial fluid can identify the causative organism. Blood cultures should also be obtained as they may be positive in up to 50% of cases.

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department for severe pain in his knee. The patient states that the pain began yesterday and has steadily worsened. This patient's presentation of an acutely painful, swollen, and erythematous joint is concerning for septic arthritis, which is a medical emergency. The most common pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S aureus. Neisseria gonorrhoeae should be suspected in sexually active young adults. Although this patient has a history of gout, the presence of systemic symptoms (eg, fever) makes septic arthritis more likely. In addition, his recent skin infection (cellulitis) could have spread hematogenously to seed the joint. Other risk factors for septic arthritis include preexisting joint disease (eg, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis), diabetes mellitus, recent joint surgery, and immunosuppression.

The diagnosis of septic arthritis is suggested by synovial fluid analysis showing a white blood cell count >50,000/mm3 with >90% neutrophils. Gram stain is positive in only 50% of cases. few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of intermittent lower back pain for 1 week. His symptoms began shortly after lifting heavy boxes at work. Acute LBP is a benign, self-limited condition that typically improves over 2-4 weeks with or without treatment. The goal of therapy is to control pain and maintain normal function. First-line treatment includes patient reassurance, maintenance of activity as tolerated, and administration of analgesics as needed. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and acetaminophen are both considered first-line analgesics for acute LBP. However, this patient's history of peptic ulcer disease is a contraindication to NSAID use, as these drugs can exacerbate this condition. Therefore, acetaminophen is the most appropriate choice for this patient.

question: A 78-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of painful enlarging bruises and skin ulceration over his thighs and external genitalia. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus, mitral regurgitation, and atrial fibrillation. Three days ago, he was started on treatment with warfarin. His only other medications are metformin and lisinopril. His temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F), pulse is 108/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 155/89 mm Hg. Examination of the skin shows large purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, and areas of skin necrosis over his anterior legs, gluteal region, and penis. This patient is most likely to benefit from treatment with which of the following?

few_shot.question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever and easy bruising for 3 days. He has had fatigue for 2 weeks. He has no past medical history, and takes no medications. Excessive bleeding from intravenous lines was reported by the nurse. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. The temperature is 38.2°C (102.6°F), pulse is 105/min, respiration rate is 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. On physical examination, he has multiple purpura on the lower extremities and several ecchymoses on the lower back and buttocks. Petechiae are noticed on the soft palate. Cervical painless lymphadenopathy is detected on both sides. The examination of the lungs, heart, and abdomen shows no other abnormalities. The laboratory test results are as follows:
Hemoglobin 8 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 90 μm3
Leukocyte count 18,000/mm3
Platelet count 10,000/mm3
Partial thromboplastin time (activated) 60 seconds
Prothrombin time 25 seconds (INR: 2.2)
Fibrin split products Positive
Lactate dehydrogenase, serum 1,000 U/L
A Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear is shown by the image. Intravenous fluids, blood products, and antibiotics are given to the patient. Based on the most likely diagnosis, which of the following is the best therapy for this patient at this time?

answer_choices.C: Rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP)

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, fatigue, and cervical lymphadenopathy, along with the presence of Auer rods on peripheral blood smear, is suggestive of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). APL is a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia that is characterized by a specific chromosomal translocation, t(15;17), which results in the fusion of the retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARα) gene on chromosome 17 and the promyelocytic leukemia (PML) gene on chromosome 15. This fusion gene product disrupts normal myeloid differentiation and promotes proliferation of immature myeloid cells (ie, promyelocytes).

APL is associated with a high risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which is suggested in this patient by the presence of thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and aPTT, and positive fibrin split products. Therefore, APL is considered a medical emergency and requires prompt treatment.

The treatment of choice for APL is all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), which binds to the altered retinoic acid receptor and allows the promyelocytes to differentiate into mature neutrophils. This leads to rapid resolution of the coagulopathy seen in APL. ATRA is typically combined with an anthracycline (eg, daunorubicin, idarubicin) for induction therapy.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 73-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of skin lesions. Initially, she experienced pain in the affected areas, followed by discoloration of the skin and formation of blisters. Four days ago, the patient was started on a new medication by her physician after failed cardioversion for intermittent atrial fibrillation. She lives alone and does not recall any recent falls or trauma. She has hypertension treated with metoprolol and diabetes mellitus treated with insulin. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 108/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 145/85 mm Hg. Examination of her skin shows well-circumscribed purple maculae, hemorrhagic blisters, and areas of skin ulceration over the breast, lower abdomen, and gluteal region. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing factor for this patient's condition?

answer_choices.D: Formation of antibodies against a platelet antigen

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's skin findings of well-circumscribed purple maculae, hemorrhagic blisters, and areas of skin ulceration are consistent with warfarin-induced skin necrosis (WISN). WISN is a rare complication of warfarin therapy that typically occurs within the first few days of treatment. It is most commonly seen in obese, middle-aged women. The initial lesion is usually painful and erythematous, and it subsequently progresses to a hemorrhagic blister with surrounding erythema and edema. The blister then forms an eschar, which can be complicated by secondary infection or sepsis.

WISN is thought to occur due to a rapid decrease in protein C levels after the initiation of warfarin therapy. Protein C is a natural anticoagulant with a short half-life that is rapidly depleted by warfarin. In contrast, the procoagulant factors (II, VII, IX, X) have longer half-lives and are not decreased as quickly. This transient hypercoagulable state can lead to thrombosis of the dermal and subcutaneous vessels, causing skin necrosis. Patients with protein C or protein S deficiency are at an increased risk of WISN.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old man comes to the emergency department 12 hours after the appearance of tender, purple discolorations on his thighs and lower abdomen. He began taking a medication 4 days ago after failed cardioversion for atrial fibrillation, but he cannot remember the name. Physical examination shows a tender bluish-black discoloration on the anterior abdominal wall. A photograph of the right thigh is shown. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's skin findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with warfarin-induced skin necrosis, a rare but serious complication of warfarin therapy. It typically occurs within the first few days of treatment and is characterized by painful, erythematous macules that progress to a hemorrhagic bullous lesion and then full-thickness skin necrosis. The lesions are often sharply demarcated and can occur anywhere on the body, but they are most common on the breasts, buttocks, thighs, and abdomen.

Warfarin inhibits the synthesis of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors (II, VII, IX, X) and proteins C and S. Protein C has the shortest half-life and is therefore the first to be depleted. Because protein C is an anticoagulant, its depletion can paradoxically lead to a hypercoagulable state. This is thought to be the cause of warfarin-induced skin necrosis.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with leg pain. He states that the pain started suddenly while he was walking outside. The patient has a past medical history of diabetes, hypertension, obesity, and atrial fibrillation. His temperature is 99.3°F (37.4°C), blood pressure is 152/98 mmHg, pulse is 97/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a cold and pale left leg. The patient’s sensation is markedly diminished in the left leg when compared to the right, and his muscle strength is 1/5 in his left leg. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute onset of a cold, pale, and painful leg with decreased sensation and motor function is consistent with acute limb ischemia. This is a vascular emergency that occurs due to a sudden decrease in limb perfusion, most commonly from in situ thrombosis (eg, secondary to severe peripheral artery disease) or embolization (eg, from the heart in a patient with atrial fibrillation). The "six P's" of acute limb ischemia classically include pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesias, paralysis, and poikilothermia (cool skin). However, not all findings may be present, and the absence of one or more does not exclude the diagnosis.

The best initial treatment for acute limb ischemia is anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin to prevent propagation of the clot. This should be started as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, even before imaging, as it has been shown to improve limb salvage rates. Emergent surgical or endovascular intervention is indicated in patients with limb-threatening ischemia (ie, those with rest pain or with motor or sensory deficits). However, anticoagulation should be started first, as soon as the diagnosis is suspected.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of increasing abdominal pain for 6 hours. The pain is dull and diffuse over her abdomen and radiates to her lower back bilaterally. Three weeks ago, she was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation and started on warfarin. Her only other medication is 1 g of acetaminophen daily for osteoarthritis of her knees. Her pulse is 87/min and blood pressure is 112/75 mm Hg. Physical examination shows abdominal tenderness to palpation at both lower quadrants. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a retroperitoneal mass and hazy margins of the surrounding structures. In addition to discontinuation of warfarin, the most appropriate next step in management is administration of which of the following?

answer_choices.B: Factor VIII and von Willebrand factor

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of anticoagulation with warfarin, acute abdominal and back pain, and CT findings of a retroperitoneal mass with hazy margins of the surrounding structures are suggestive of a retroperitoneal hematoma. Retroperitoneal hematomas can occur spontaneously in patients on anticoagulation or those with bleeding disorders. They can also occur due to trauma or rupture of a retroperitoneal structure (eg, aortic aneurysm). In this case, the patient's recent initiation of warfarin therapy is the most likely cause.

The management of serious bleeding in patients on warfarin involves both reversal of warfarin's anticoagulant effects and replacement of clotting factors. Warfarin's effects can be reversed by administering vitamin K (phytonadione), but this may take up to 24 hours. In the setting of serious bleeding, clotting factors should be replaced more urgently using prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC), which contains the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. PCC can reverse the effects of warfarin within minutes.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 35-year-old man presents with a 7 month history of insomnia. The patient admitted to having trouble sleeping from a young age but became more aware of how much this is affecting his health after attending a sleep conference earlier this year. He is worried that his health has suffered because of this, and he is also concerned that he will not be able to pay his bills if he were to get sick. few_shot.question: A 28-year-old man who works as a resident in general surgery presents feeling "burned out" for the last 2 months. He says he has been working extremely long hours under stressful conditions, which makes him irritable, edgy, unfocused, and forgetful. He says he also has severe anxiety about how these symptoms are affecting his performance at work, making it difficult for him to sleep even when he has time off. The patient is referred for counseling and is prescribed some mild sleep aids. At follow-up a few months later, he says he is feeling much improved due to improved staffing at the hospital and a more manageable workload. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of irritability, difficulty concentrating, and insomnia developed in response to a specific stressor (ie, long work hours, stressful work conditions) and resolved when the stressor was removed. These findings are consistent with adjustment disorder, which is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor. Symptoms occur within 3 months of the onset of the stressor and typically resolve within 6 months after the stressor or its consequences have terminated. The stress-related disturbance causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. 

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with complaints of muscle pains, poor sleep, and daytime fatigue. OCPD is a chronic condition that often begins in early adulthood and is characterized by a pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and mental and interpersonal control, at the expense of flexibility, openness, and efficiency. These individuals are often high achievers and feel a sense of urgency about their actions. They may be excessively stubborn and rigid about matters of morality, ethics, or values. They may force themselves and others to follow rigid moral principles and strict standards of performance. They are often miserly with their money and time, not because of a desire to save, but because of a desire to keep everything under control.

In contrast, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by obsessions (recurrent, intrusive thoughts) and compulsions (repetitive behaviors that the person feels driven to perform). Patients with OCD often have good insight and realize that their thoughts and behaviors are not rational, whereas patients with OCPD believe that their thoughts and behaviors are correct and do not have the obsessional or compulsive symptoms seen in OCD.

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old high school student comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of insomnia. This patient's difficulty falling asleep at the desired bedtime, difficulty waking up in the morning, and daytime sleepiness are consistent with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder (DSWPD). DSWPD is a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder characterized by a delay in the timing of the major sleep period relative to the desired sleep and wake times. Patients with DSWPD have a delay in the timing of melatonin secretion, which is normally secreted a few hours before bedtime to promote sleep. As a result, these patients have difficulty falling asleep and waking up at socially acceptable times. However, when they are allowed to follow their preferred sleep schedule (eg, on weekends or during school vacations), they have normal sleep quality and duration. Infection typically occurs following traumatic inoculation into the skin (eg, thorn prick) and is more common in gardeners and agricultural workers. The primary cutaneous lesion is a painless, erythematous, subcutaneous nodule that develops at the site of inoculation 1-4 weeks after exposure. The nodule can subsequently ulcerate and form a painless, granulomatous lesion. Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis, the most common form of the disease, is characterized by the development of nodules along the lymphatic channels proximal to the primary lesion. Pulmonary and disseminated disease can occur but are rare and typically seen in immunocompromised patients.

question: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman presents to the clinic for a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan. few_shot.question: A 66-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. She has no history of serious medical illness and takes no medications. A screening DEXA scan shows a T-score of -1.5 at the femur. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing factor for osteopenia?
few_shot.explanation:
Osteopenia is a condition characterized by low bone mass and is a precursor to osteoporosis. It is diagnosed when the bone mineral density (BMD) T-score is between -1.0 and -2.5. The T-score is the number of standard deviations the BMD is from the mean BMD of a healthy, young adult reference population. A T-score of -1.0 or above is considered normal, while a T-score of -2.5 or below is diagnostic of osteoporosis.

The most important risk factor for osteopenia and osteoporosis is age, as bone mass naturally decreases with age. However, other risk factors include female sex, low body weight, family history of osteoporosis, and certain lifestyle factors. Of the options listed, smoking is a significant risk factor for osteopenia and osteoporosis. Smoking has been shown to decrease BMD and increase the risk of fractures. Other lifestyle factors that increase the risk of osteopenia and osteoporosis include excessive alcohol use and lack of physical activity.

So, the answer is [D].

Other risk factors include low body weight, smoking, excessive alcohol intake, and a sedentary lifestyle.

The best way to prevent osteoporosis is to build strong bone early in life and to maintain bone strength in adulthood. This can be achieved by ensuring an adequate intake of calcium and vitamin D, regular weight-bearing exercise, and avoidance of smoking and excessive alcohol intake.

This patient's history of depression, poor self-care, and decreased BMI suggest inadequate dietary intake as the likely cause of her vitamin D deficiency. 

Patients with osteomalacia often present with diffuse bone pain and muscle weakness. On laboratory examination, patients may have decreased serum calcium and phosphate levels, with a concomitant increase in parathyroid hormone levels as a physiologic response to the low serum calcium. Alkaline phosphatase levels are often elevated due to increased osteoblastic activity.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She has no other history of serious illness. Menopause occurred 1 year ago. Current medications include antirheumatic drugs and hormone replacement therapy. She exercises regularly. A DEXA scan shows a T-score of -1.80, indicating decreased bone density. Which of the following drugs is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of this finding?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's decreased bone density is most likely due to the use of prednisone, a glucocorticoid. Glucocorticoids are commonly used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis due to their potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects. However, they have many adverse effects, including decreased bone density leading to osteoporosis. This occurs due to decreased intestinal calcium absorption and increased renal calcium excretion, leading to secondary hyperparathyroidism. Additionally, glucocorticoids decrease bone formation by inhibiting osteoblast function and increasing osteoblast and osteocyte apoptosis.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [B] > [D] > [A].

question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 3-week history of burning sensation in his mouth. One year ago, a peripheral blood smear performed during workup of fatigue revealed erythrocytes without central pallor. His father had gallstones, for which he underwent a cholecystectomy at the age of 26 years. Examination shows pallor of the mucosal membranes, mild scleral icterus, a swollen, red tongue, and several mouth ulcers. There is darkening of the skin over the dorsal surfaces of the fingers, toes, and creases of the palms and soles. His spleen is enlarged and palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 9.1 gm/dL, mean corpuscular volume of 104 μm3, and a reticulocyte count of 9%. Which of the following would most likely have prevented this patient's oropharyngeal symptoms?

few_shot.question: An 8-year-old boy presents with a 7-day history of fever and abdominal pain for the past 4 days. Past medical history is significant for an exchange transfusion for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and recurrent attacks of pallor during the course of upper respiratory tract infections. His vital signs include: blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse 105/min, respiratory rate 40/min, and temperature 37.0℃ (98.6℉). On physical examination, the patient is ill-looking. Conjunctivae are pale and the sclera is icteric. The liver is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory findings show hemoglobin of 5.9 gm/dL, Hct of 20%, and haptoglobin of 28 gm/dL. A peripheral blood smear shows hypochromic anemia, polychromasia, anisocytosis, and occasional Heinz bodies. The reticulocyte count was 15%. A direct Coombs test was negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, recurrent episodes of pallor during infections, and current findings of anemia, jaundice, and reticulocytosis suggest a chronic hemolytic anemia. The presence of Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) on the peripheral smear is indicative of oxidative damage to the red blood cells (RBCs). This is seen in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, an X-linked disorder that is one of the most common causes of hemolytic anemia worldwide.

G6PD is an enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway that generates NADPH. NADPH is necessary to keep glutathione in its reduced form. Reduced glutathione protects RBCs from oxidative damage. In G6PD deficiency, RBCs are more susceptible to oxidative stress. Oxidative stress can be precipitated by infections, certain drugs (eg, sulfonamides, dapsone, primaquine, nitrofurantoin), and fava beans. The oxidative stress denatures hemoglobin, forming Heinz bodies. Heinz bodies damage the RBC membrane, leading to intravascular hemolysis or bite cells (RBCs with a "bite" taken out of the cell membrane) if the Heinz bodies are removed by splenic macrophages.

So, the answer is [B].
