few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-month history of recurrent retrosternal chest pain that often wakes her up at night. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Upper endoscopy shows hyperemia in the distal third of the esophagus. A biopsy specimen from this area shows non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with hyperplasia of the basal cell layer and neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's findings?

answer_choices.C: Proximal migration of the gastroesophageal junction

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's retrosternal chest pain, especially at night, and the endoscopic findings of distal esophageal hyperemia are suggestive of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). GERD occurs due to the reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, leading to inflammation and damage of the esophageal mucosa. This is often due to transient lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxations, a decrease in LES pressure, or anatomic disruption of the gastroesophageal junction (eg, hiatal hernia). The histologic findings of basal cell hyperplasia and papillary lengthening in the squamous epithelium, along with intraepithelial eosinophils and neutrophils, are characteristic of reflux esophagitis.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of difficulty swallowing for the past 1 year. She was diagnosed with gastroesophageal reflux 3 years ago and takes pantoprazole. She has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 14 years. Examination shows hardening of the skin of the fingers and several white papules on the fingertips. There are small dilated blood vessels on the face. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's difficulty swallowing?

answer_choices.B: Degeneration of neurons within esophageal wall
answer_choices.C: Outpouching of the lower pharyngeal mucosa
answer_choices.D: Demyelination of brain and spinal cord axons

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's skin findings (sclerodactyly, fingertip calcinosis, telangiectasias) and dysphagia suggest a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma). Systemic sclerosis is a connective tissue disease characterized by fibrosis and collagen deposition in the skin and internal organs. The disease is also associated with vascular abnormalities and autoantibodies. The skin is commonly involved, with initial edema followed by induration and tightening. Raynaud phenomenon is often the earliest symptom. Telangiectasias and calcinosis cutis (subcutaneous deposition of insoluble calcium salts) are also common.

Gastrointestinal involvement is seen in the majority of patients with systemic sclerosis and can affect any portion of the GI tract from the mouth to the anus. The esophagus is the most commonly involved portion of the GI tract. Dysphagia in these patients is due to replacement of muscularis with fibrous tissue in the lower two thirds of the esophagus, which leads to aperistalsis. Combined with dysfunction of the lower esophageal sphincter, this can result in severe gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of progressive dysphagia. She initially had symptoms only when consuming solid foods, but for the past 2 months she has also had difficulty swallowing liquids. She describes a feeling of food “getting stuck” in her throat. She was diagnosed with gastroesophageal reflux disease 2 years ago and has had episodic pallor of her fingers since adolescence. She has smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily for 24 years. Her only medication is omeprazole. Her pulse is 65/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 127/73 mm Hg. Examination shows thickening of the skin of her fingers, with small white papules on her fingertips. There are small dilated blood vessels on her face, lips, and tongue. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's dysphagia?

answer_choices.B: Protrusion of thin tissue membranes into the esophagus
answer_choices.C: Esophageal smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis
answer_choices.D: Degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of progressive dysphagia, skin thickening, and Raynaud phenomenon is suggestive of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma). Scleroderma is a connective tissue disease characterized by fibrosis and collagen deposition in the skin and internal organs. The skin findings in this patient (thickening of skin, small white papules on fingertips, dilated blood vessels on face/lips/tongue) are consistent with scleroderma.

Esophageal involvement is the most common visceral manifestation of scleroderma and is seen in the majority of patients. It occurs due to atrophy of the smooth muscle in the esophagus, with replacement by fibrous tissue. This leads to reduced lower esophageal sphincter pressure and dysmotility of the smooth muscle in the lower two thirds of the esophagus, which can cause dysphagia and increase the risk of gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of a painless right-sided scrotal swelling. The swelling started several weeks ago but is not always present. Physical examination shows an 8-cm, soft, cystic nontender right-sided scrotal mass that transilluminates. The mass does not increase in size on coughing and it is possible to palpate normal tissue above the mass. There are no bowel sounds in the mass, and it does not reduce when the patient is in a supine position. Examination of the testis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the mass?

answer_choices.A: Imbalance of fluid secretion and resorption by tunica vaginalis
answer_choices.B: Failure of processus vaginalis to obliterate
answer_choices.C: Extension of abdominal contents through the inguinal canal
answer_choices.D: Dilation and tortuosity of veins in the pampiniform plexus

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 20-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of a painless mass in his left groin that has been gradually increasing in size. Physical examination shows a 3x3-cm oval, non-tender left inguinal mass and a fluctuant, painless left scrotal swelling that increase in size with coughing. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.A: Failure of processus vaginalis to close

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of a painless, gradually enlarging left inguinal mass and scrotal swelling that increases in size with coughing is consistent with an indirect inguinal hernia. Indirect inguinal hernias are the most common type of hernia and are caused by a congenital defect in which the processus vaginalis fails to obliterate. The processus vaginalis is an outpouching of the peritoneum that accompanies the testes as they descend into the scrotum. Normally, the processus vaginalis obliterates during the first year of life. If it remains patent, abdominal contents (eg, small bowel, omentum) can pass through the internal inguinal ring into the inguinal canal and, in males, into the scrotum. This is in contrast to direct inguinal hernias, which are acquired defects that occur medial to the inferior epigastric vessels due to weakness in the transversalis fascia in Hesselbach's triangle.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a right-sided scrotal swelling for the past 2 months. The swelling is intermittent and appears usually after the patient has been taken outdoors in a baby carrier, and disappears the next morning. The patient was born at term without complications and has been healthy. Examination shows a 3-cm, soft, nontender, and fluctuant right scrotal mass that is reducible and does not extend into the inguinal area. A light held behind the scrotum shines through. There are no bowel sounds in the mass. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.C: Ligation of the patent processus vaginalis

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history and physical examination findings are consistent with a communicating hydrocele. The processus vaginalis is an outpouching of the peritoneum that travels with the testis through the inguinal canal during its descent into the scrotum. Normally, the processus vaginalis obliterates by the time of birth, leaving the tunica vaginalis as a closed serous sac surrounding the testis. If the processus vaginalis remains patent, peritoneal fluid can travel from the abdominal cavity to the scrotum, leading to a hydrocele. A communicating hydrocele will change in size throughout the day as the fluid moves back and forth between the abdomen and the scrotum. In contrast, a noncommunicating hydrocele, which results from an imbalance of fluid production versus reabsorption within the tunica vaginalis, will not change in size.

Communicating hydroceles are common in infants and usually resolve spontaneously by age 1 year as the processus vaginalis obliterates. Therefore, the initial management is conservative with observation and reassurance. If the hydrocele persists beyond age 1 year or becomes significantly large or symptomatic, surgical repair is indicated.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician because of right-sided painless scrotal swelling that he noticed yesterday while taking a shower. He is currently sexually active with two female partners and uses condoms inconsistently. He immigrated to the US from Argentina 2 years ago. His immunization records are unavailable. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the last 5 years. He is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 70 kg (154 lb); BMI is 24.2 kg/m2. He appears healthy and well nourished. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 125/75 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is soft with dull lower abdominal discomfort. Testicular examination shows a solid mass in the right testis that is firm and nontender. A light held behind the scrotum does not shine through. The mass is not reduced when the patient is in a supine position. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of a painless, solid testicular mass that does not transilluminate is concerning for a testicular tumor. Testicular tumors are most common in men aged 15-35 years. Risk factors include cryptorchidism, Klinefelter syndrome, and a history of testicular cancer in the contralateral testis. The most common type of testicular tumor is a germ cell tumor, which can be further classified as a seminoma or nonseminoma. Nonseminomas include embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and teratoma. Patients with testicular tumors may present with a painless testicular mass, testicular pain, or symptoms related to metastatic disease (eg, back pain, cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea). Testicular tumors may also produce hormones, leading to gynecomastia or, in prepubertal boys, precocious puberty.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the physician by his father because of swelling of his left hemiscrotum. He has otherwise been healthy and is gaining weight appropriately. Physical examination shows a nontender left scrotal mass that transilluminates. The mass increases in size when the boy cries but is easily reducible. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with a left inguinal hernia. Inguinal hernias are common in infants, especially in premature infants, and are more common in boys than in girls. They are caused by a patent processus vaginalis, which is an outpouching of the peritoneum that normally follows the path of the testes as they descend into the scrotum. The processus vaginalis normally obliterates after the descent of the testes, but if it remains patent, it can allow abdominal contents (usually a loop of bowel or omentum) to enter the inguinal canal and even the scrotum, leading to an inguinal hernia. In this patient, the mass increases in size when he cries due to increased intra-abdominal pressure, and it is easily reducible, both of which are characteristic of an inguinal hernia.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old male presents with primary complaints of a palpable mass in his scrotum and mild testicular pain. Physical exam reveals an abnormal appearing scrotum around the left testis, as depicted in image A. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this presentation?

answer_choices.A: Compression of the left renal vein at the aortic origin of the superior mesenteric artery
answer_choices.B: Neisseria gonorrhoeae Infection of the left testis leading to epididymitis
answer_choices.C: Unilateral failure of the left testis to descend into the scrotum
answer_choices.D: Twisting of the spermatic cord secondary to rotation of the left testis

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's presentation is consistent with a varicocele, which is characterized by a dilated pampiniform plexus of veins in the spermatic cord. This is often described as a "bag of worms" and is usually asymptomatic, but can cause a dull, aching pain in the scrotum. Varicoceles are more common on the left side due to differences in venous drainage. The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left testicular vein is therefore more susceptible to compression between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta, which can cause blood to back up into the pampiniform plexus and result in a varicocele.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after his wife noticed during breakfast that the left side of his face was drooping. He is alert and oriented to time, place and person. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 99/min and blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg. Examination shows equal and reactive pupils. There is drooping of the left side of the face. Muscle strength is decreased in the left upper and lower extremities. Plantar reflex shows an extensor response on the left side. Speech is dysarthric. There is a bruit on the right side of the neck. Fundoscopy shows no abnormalities. A complete blood count, coagulation profile, and serum concentrations of glucose and electrolytes are within the reference range. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 59-year-old man presents with the persistent right-sided facial droop and slurred speech for the past 2 hours. He says he had similar symptoms 6 months ago which resolved within 1 hour. His past medical history is significant for long-standing hypertension, managed with hydrochlorothiazide. He reports a 10-pack-year smoking history but denies any alcohol or recreational drug use. The vital signs include: blood pressure 145/95 mm Hg, pulse 95/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. On physical examination, the patient has an asymmetric smile and right-sided weakness of his lower facial muscles. There is a deviation of his tongue towards the right. Dysarthria is noted. His muscle strength in the upper extremities is 4/5 on the right and 5/5 on the left. The remainder of the physical exam is unremarkable. Which of the following is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.A: CT of the head without contrast

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's acute onset of focal neurologic symptoms is concerning for an ischemic stroke. The first step in the evaluation of a patient with a suspected stroke is a noncontrast head CT to rule out hemorrhagic stroke, which is a contraindication to thrombolytic therapy. If the CT scan does not show hemorrhage and the patient is within the therapeutic window (ie, symptom onset within the last 3-4.5 hours), IV tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) should be administered.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of right-sided weakness and subjective decreased sensation that started 30 minutes ago. The patient reports that his symptoms started to ease 5 minutes after onset and have now completely resolved. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. His current medications include lisinopril, metformin, and sitagliptin. He is 183 cm (6 ft 0 in) tall and weighs 105 kg (220 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m2. He appears well. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 150/88 mm Hg. Neurological examination shows no abnormalities. Cardiac examination shows regular rate and rhythm and a left-sided carotid bruit. Complete blood count, serum glucose, and electrolytes are within the reference ranges. An ECG shows sinus rhythm and left axis deviation. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows no abnormalities. Carotid doppler ultrasound shows 45% stenosis in the left carotid artery and 15% stenosis in the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden-onset, focal neurologic symptoms that completely resolved within 60 minutes are consistent with a transient ischemic attack (TIA). TIAs are often warning signs of an impending stroke, and patients with a TIA are at highest risk for stroke in the first 48 hours after the event. Therefore, rapid evaluation and intervention are necessary to prevent a subsequent stroke.

The ABCD2 score (Age, Blood pressure, Clinical features, Duration of symptoms, Diabetes) can be used to risk-stratify patients with a TIA. This patient's score is 5 (1 point each for age >60, blood pressure >140/90 mm Hg, unilateral weakness, and duration of symptoms >10 minutes; 0 points for absence of speech disturbance), which indicates a moderate risk of stroke in the next 2 days.

The most effective intervention to prevent stroke following a TIA is initiation of antiplatelet therapy (eg, aspirin, clopidogrel). Aspirin is typically used first-line, but clopidogrel is preferred in patients with aspirin allergy or in whom aspirin is contraindicated.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 78-year-old man is brought in to the emergency department by ambulance after his wife noticed that he began slurring his speech and had developed facial asymmetry during dinner approximately 30 minutes ago. His past medical history is remarkable for hypertension and diabetes. His temperature is 99.1°F (37.3°C), blood pressure is 154/99 mmHg, pulse is 89/min, respirations are 12/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Neurologic exam reveals right upper and lower extremity weakness and an asymmetric smile. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's acute onset of slurred speech, facial asymmetry, and right-sided weakness is concerning for an acute ischemic stroke. The most important initial step in management is to determine whether the stroke is ischemic or hemorrhagic, as this will guide further management. Noncontrast head CT is the imaging modality of choice for making this determination, as it can quickly and accurately identify hemorrhage. If hemorrhage is not seen on the initial noncontrast head CT, ischemic stroke is presumed, and the patient can be evaluated for thrombolytic therapy with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). 

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of slurred speech and left facial droop for the past 30 minutes. During this period, she has also had numbness on the left side of her face. She has never had such an episode before. She has hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her father died of lung cancer 1 week ago. The patient has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. She drinks one glass of wine daily. Her current medications include metformin, sitagliptin, enalapril, and atorvastatin. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 30.5 kg/m2. She is oriented to time, place, and person. Her temperature is 37°C (98.7°F), pulse is 97/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows drooping of the left side of the face. Her speech is clear. Examination shows full muscle strength. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. A finger-nose test and her gait are normal. Cardiopulmonary examination shows a right-sided carotid bruit. A complete blood count and serum concentrations of creatinine, glucose, and electrolytes are within the reference ranges. An ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. A noncontrast CT scan of the brain shows no abnormalities. On the way back from the CT scan, her presenting symptoms resolve. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden onset of focal neurologic symptoms (eg, slurred speech, facial droop, facial numbness) that completely resolved within 1 hour is consistent with a transient ischemic attack (TIA). TIAs are brief episodes of neurologic dysfunction resulting from focal cerebral ischemia not associated with permanent cerebral infarction (ie, symptoms completely resolve). They are often described as a "warning sign" or "sentinel event" for stroke, as more than a third of patients who experience a TIA will go on to have a stroke, half of which occur within the first year. This patient's risk factors for atherosclerosis (eg, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking) and the presence of a carotid bruit increase her risk for a cerebrovascular event.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 77-year-old woman is brought by ambulance to the emergency department after she developed weakness of her right arm along with a right-sided facial droop. On physical examination, she is awake and alert but the right side of her mouth is dropping, making it difficult for her to speak clearly. The most important initial step in the management of a patient with a suspected stroke is to obtain a noncontrast CT scan of the brain. This is done to rule out a hemorrhagic stroke, which can present similarly to an ischemic stroke but is managed differently. If the CT scan does not show any hemorrhage, the patient may be a candidate for thrombolytic therapy with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), which can significantly improve outcomes if given within 4.5 hours of symptom onset.

question: A 4-year-old child is rushed to the emergency department after developing sudden abdominal pain followed by nausea, vomiting, and dark, almost black-colored stool. Prior to the onset of symptoms, he was seen playing with his mother’s purse containing a bottle of vitamin supplements, which she takes for chronic microcytic anemia. Which of the following medications is the treatment for this patient's intoxication?

few_shot.question:
A previously healthy 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of abdominal pain and vomiting for 6 hours. His mother immediately brought him after noticing that he had gotten into the medicine cabinet. The mother is 5 months' pregnant. He appears uncomfortable. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 133/min and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg. Examination shows diffuse abdominal tenderness; there is no guarding or rigidity. Digital rectal examination shows dark-colored stools. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL
Leukocyte count 14,100/mm3
Serum
Na+ 136 mEq/L
K+ 3.3 mEq/L
Cl- 105 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL
Glucose 98 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL
Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows:
pH 7.31
pCO2 32 mm Hg
HCO3- 16 mEq/L
Intravenous fluids are administered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"
few_shot.explanation:
This child's presentation of abdominal pain, vomiting, and metabolic acidosis is concerning for iron toxicity, which can occur after accidental ingestion of prenatal vitamins (which contain iron). Iron toxicity is one of the most common causes of poisoning deaths in children. The severity of iron poisoning is determined by the quantity of elemental iron ingested, with ingestion of >60 mg/kg being potentially lethal. Clinical features of iron poisoning occur in 5 stages:

1. Gastrointestinal phase (30 minutes to 6 hours postingestion): Abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and gastrointestinal bleeding due to direct corrosive effects. Metabolic acidosis can occur due to several mechanisms, including increased lactic acid due to poor tissue perfusion, ketoacidosis, and the presence of acid metabolites of iron.
2. Latent phase (6-24 hours postingestion): Apparent clinical improvement.
3. Systemic toxicity phase (12-48 hours postingestion): Circulatory collapse, lethargy, seizures, and coma due to iron's cellular toxicity.
4. Hepatic phase (2-5 days postingestion): Hepatic necrosis.
5. Late phase (2-8 weeks postingestion): Gastric or intestinal scarring or obstruction.

Management of iron poisoning includes resuscitation, administration of deferoxamine (an iron-chelating agent), and whole bowel irrigation for radiopaque tablets visible on abdominal x-ray.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician for generalized fatigue and multiple episodes of abdominal pain and vomiting for the past week. His last bowel movement was 4 days ago. He has been having behavioral problems at home for the past few weeks as well. He can walk up stairs with support and build a tower of 3 blocks. He cannot use a fork. He does not follow simple instructions and speaks in single words. His family emigrated from Bangladesh 6 months ago. He is at the 40th percentile for height and weight. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 115/min, and blood pressure is 84/45 mm Hg. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and gingival hyperpigmentation. His hemoglobin concentration is 10.1 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume is 68 μm3, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin is 24.5 pg/cell. The patient is most likely going to benefit from administration of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This child's symptoms of abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, and behavioral changes, along with the physical examination findings of pallor and gingival hyperpigmentation, are suggestive of lead poisoning. Lead poisoning is a common problem in children, especially those living in older homes with lead-based paint or those who have recently emigrated from countries with less strict regulations on lead. The child's microcytic anemia is also consistent with lead poisoning, as lead inhibits several enzymes in the heme synthesis pathway, leading to anemia.

The treatment for lead poisoning is chelation therapy, which involves the use of agents that bind to lead in the body and promote its excretion. Succimer and calcium disodium edetate are two such agents that are commonly used.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A steel welder presents to his family physician with a one-week history of intense abdominal cramping with nausea, vomiting, constipation, headaches, myalgias, and arthralgias. He claims that the symptoms started about two months after he began work on replacing the pipes in an early 20th century house. Blood was taken and he was found to have a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with basophilic stippling. Which of the following is the best treatment for his symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of abdominal pain, constipation, headaches, myalgias, and arthralgias, along with his microcytic, hypochromic anemia with basophilic stippling, are suggestive of lead poisoning. This is likely due to his work on replacing the pipes in an old house, as lead was commonly used in pipes and paint in the early 20th century.

The treatment of choice for lead poisoning is chelation therapy with EDTA or dimercaprol for severe cases, and succimer for less severe cases. These agents work by binding to the lead ions and promoting their excretion in the urine.

few_shot.question: A 3-year-old boy presents with progressive lethargy and confusion over the last 5 days. He lives with his parents in a home that was built in the early 1900s. His parents report that "his tummy has been hurting" for the last 3 weeks and that he is constipated. He eats and drinks normally, but occasionally tries things that are not food. Abdominal exam shows no focal tenderness. Hemoglobin is 8 g/dL and hematocrit is 24%. Venous lead level is 55 ug/dL. Which therapy is most appropriate for this boy's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This child's symptoms of abdominal pain, constipation, anemia, and neurologic symptoms (eg, lethargy, confusion) in the setting of pica and living in a home built before 1978 (when lead-based paint was banned in residential properties) are concerning for lead poisoning. The diagnosis is confirmed by an elevated blood lead level.

The mainstay of treatment for lead poisoning is removal from the source of exposure. In addition, chelation therapy is indicated for blood lead levels ≥45 µg/dL in asymptomatic children and ≥25 µg/dL in symptomatic children. Succimer is an oral chelating agent used as first-line treatment in children with blood lead levels in these ranges. It binds lead in the bloodstream and enhances urinary excretion.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.explanation:
This child's symptoms of abdominal pain and epistaxis, along with an elevated INR, are suggestive of ingestion of a long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide, such as brodifacoum. These rodenticides antagonize vitamin K, leading to decreased synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) in the liver. This results in a prolonged PT and INR, but a normal PTT. The treatment for ingestion of these rodenticides is vitamin K1, which should be continued for several weeks due to the long half-life of the rodenticides. In patients with active bleeding, fresh frozen plasma should also be administered to replenish clotting factors.

question: A 60-year-old woman presents to a physician for worsening shortness of breath and increasing abdominal distention over the last 3 months. She says that the shortness of breath is worse on exertion and improves with rest. While she could previously walk to the nearby store for her groceries, she now has to drive because she gets ''winded'' on the way. The patient was diagnosed with diabetes 5 years ago and is compliant with her medications. The medical history is otherwise unremarkable. The physical examination reveals gross ascites and visibly engorged periumbilical veins. Bilateral pitting edema is noted around the ankles. The finger-prick blood glucose level is 100 mg/dL. What is the mechanism of action of the anti-diabetic medication this patient is most likely taking?

answer_choices.A: Binding to the alpha subunit of the insulin receptor
answer_choices.B: Closure of ATP-sensitive K-channels in the pancreatic beta-cell

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute onset vomiting, vertigo, throbbing headache, and weakness. She says that the symptoms started when she went to dinner with friends and had a drink of alcohol. Her past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes, and she was recently started on a new medication for this disease. She says that she was warned that she might experiences these symptoms as a side effect of a new medication, but she did not realize how severe they would be. Which of the following describes the mechanism of action for the most likely diabetes drug that this patient started taking?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of vomiting, vertigo, throbbing headache, and weakness after alcohol ingestion are suggestive of disulfiram-like reaction. Disulfiram is a drug used in the treatment of alcohol use disorder that works by inhibiting aldehyde dehydrogenase, an enzyme involved in alcohol metabolism. This leads to an accumulation of acetaldehyde, a toxic metabolite of alcohol, which causes the symptoms seen in this patient.

Several drugs are known to cause a disulfiram-like reaction, including certain cephalosporins, procarbazine, certain oral hypoglycemics, and the over-the-counter weight loss drug orlistat. In this patient with diabetes, the most likely drug to cause these symptoms is an oral hypoglycemic from the sulfonylurea class, which includes glyburide, glipizide, and glimepiride. These drugs work by closing potassium channels in the beta cells of the pancreas. This leads to depolarization of the cells, opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, influx of calcium, and release of preformed insulin.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 43-year-old woman presents to her primary care provider for follow-up of her glucose levels. At her last visit 3 months ago, her fasting serum glucose was 128 mg/dl. At that time, she was instructed to follow a weight loss regimen consisting of diet and exercise. Her family history is notable for a myocardial infarction in her father and type II diabetes mellitus in her mother. She does not smoke and drinks 2-3 glasses of wine per week. Her temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 131/78 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 17/min. Her BMI is 31 kg/m^2. On exam, she is well-appearing and appropriately interactive. Today, despite attempting to make the appropriate lifestyle changes, a repeat fasting serum glucose is 133 mg/dl. The patient is prescribed the first-line oral pharmacologic agent for her condition. Which of the following is the correct mechanism of action of this medication?

answer_choices.B: Closure of potassium channels in pancreatic beta cells
answer_choices.C: Inhibition of alpha-glucosidase in the intestinal brush border

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's fasting serum glucose levels are consistent with a diagnosis of type II diabetes mellitus (DM). The first-line oral pharmacologic agent for type II DM is metformin. Metformin primarily works by inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis and improving peripheral glucose uptake and utilization. It also decreases intestinal glucose absorption. Metformin is the only oral hypoglycemic agent that has been shown to reduce macrovascular complications and mortality in patients with type II DM. It is also weight neutral, making it a good choice for overweight or obese patients.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 51-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of fatigue and increased thirst. She has no history of serious medical illness and takes no medications. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 72 kg (160 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m2. Her fasting serum glucose concentration is 249 mg/dL. Treatment with an oral hypoglycemic agent is begun. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the drug that was most likely prescribed for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fatigue and increased thirst, along with her elevated fasting serum glucose concentration, are suggestive of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). The first-line treatment for T2DM is lifestyle modification (eg, diet, exercise, weight loss). If lifestyle modifications are insufficient or if the patient is significantly hyperglycemic at presentation (as in this patient), pharmacologic therapy should be initiated. Metformin is the initial drug of choice for the treatment of T2DM. It primarily works by decreasing hepatic gluconeogenesis and improving peripheral glucose uptake and utilization. Metformin has been shown to decrease mortality in patients with T2DM and is weight neutral, making it an excellent choice for overweight or obese patients.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 46-year-old woman presents with palpitations, tremors, and anxiety. She says these symptoms have been present ever since a recent change in her diabetic medication. The most recent time she felt these symptoms, her blood glucose level was 65 mg/dL, and she felt better after eating a cookie. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the drug most likely to have caused this patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.A: Block reabsorption of glucose in proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)
answer_choices.C: Blocking of the ATP-sensitive K+ channels

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of palpitations, tremors, and anxiety are suggestive of hypoglycemia. The fact that her symptoms resolved after eating a cookie (which contains glucose) further supports this diagnosis. The most likely cause of her hypoglycemia is her recent change in diabetic medication.

Sulfonylureas (eg, glipizide, glyburide) are oral hypoglycemic agents that stimulate insulin release from pancreatic β cells. They do this by blocking ATP-sensitive potassium channels on the cell membrane of the β cells. This leads to depolarization of the cell membrane, opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, and an influx of calcium. The increased intracellular calcium triggers the release of insulin-containing granules.

A common side effect of sulfonylureas is hypoglycemia, which is what this patient is experiencing.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. One week ago, an oral glucose tolerance screening test showed elevated serum glucose levels. She has complied with the recommended diet and lifestyle modifications. Over the past week, home blood glucose monitoring showed elevated fasting and post-prandial blood glucose levels. Which of the following describes the mechanism of action of the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's elevated fasting and postprandial blood glucose levels despite diet and lifestyle modifications are consistent with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). GDM is defined as carbohydrate intolerance that begins or is first recognized during pregnancy. It is associated with an increased risk of fetal macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, and maternal preeclampsia. 

Insulin is the preferred treatment for GDM when lifestyle modifications are insufficient to maintain euglycemia. Insulin does not cross the placenta and has an excellent safety profile. Insulin binds to tyrosine kinase receptors, leading to autophosphorylation and activation of the receptor. This initiates a cascade of events that ultimately promotes glucose uptake and utilization, glycogen synthesis, and lipogenesis, while inhibiting gluconeogenesis.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of increasing weakness in both legs for 7 days. She also reports a tingling sensation in her legs that is exacerbated by taking a hot shower. She is sexually active with one male partner and does not use condoms. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100.1°F). Physical examination shows decreased muscle strength and clonus in both lower extremities. Patellar reflex is 4+ bilaterally and plantar reflex shows an extensor response on both sides. Abdominal reflex is absent. An MRI of the brain is shown. Which of the following findings is most likely to further support the diagnosis in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Positive antibody response to cardiolipin-cholesterol-lecithin antigen in the serum
answer_choices.B: Oligodendrocytes that stain positive for polyomavirus proteins on brain biopsy
answer_choices.C: Presence of immunoglobulin bands on cerebrospinal fluid immunofixation
answer_choices.D: Identification of gram-positive cocci in groups on blood culture

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of increasing weakness and numbness of her legs for 3 days. She noticed that the weakness was more severe after she had a hot shower that morning. A year ago, she had an episode of partial vision loss in her left eye that resolved within 3 weeks. She is sexually active with 3 male partners and uses condoms inconsistently. She appears anxious. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 108/77 mm Hg. Examination shows spasticity and decreased muscle strength in bilateral lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally. Plantar reflex shows an extensor response bilaterally. The abdominal reflex is absent. Sensation to vibration and position over the lower extremities shows no abnormalities. Tandem gait is impaired. MRI of the brain and spine is inconclusive. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following?

answer_choices.D: Oligoclonal bands in cerebral spinal fluid

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent neurologic symptoms affecting different parts of the central nervous system (CNS) is suggestive of multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by immune-mediated demyelination and axonal damage within the CNS. Symptoms depend on the location of lesions and often include optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and motor, sensory, and cerebellar deficits. Symptoms can be exacerbated by heat (Uhthoff phenomenon), as seen in this patient.

Diagnosis of MS requires evidence of lesions disseminated in time (eg, history of symptom remission and recurrence) and space (eg, symptoms referable to different parts of the CNS). Although MRI is the imaging modality of choice, it may be inconclusive early in the disease course. In such cases, lumbar puncture can be performed to look for oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Oligoclonal bands represent IgG antibodies and are present in approximately 90% of patients with MS. They indicate inflammation within the CNS and support the diagnosis of MS when detected in the CSF but not in the serum.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of progressive tingling and weakness in both of his legs for the past two days. The patient reports that his symptoms interfere with his ability to walk. Two weeks ago, he had an upper respiratory tract infection, which resolved spontaneously. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows weakness in the lower extremities with absent deep tendon reflexes. Reflexes are 1+ in the upper extremities. Sensation to pinprick and light touch is intact. Romberg's test is negative. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 12,000/mm3. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis results show:
Opening pressure normal
Protein 200 mg/dL
Glucose 70 mg/dL
White blood cells 4/mm3
This patient is at increased risk for which of the following conditions?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of ascending weakness and areflexia following a recent infection is suggestive of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). GBS is an immune-mediated polyneuropathy that often presents with rapidly progressive, symmetric weakness that begins in the lower extremities and ascends to involve the upper extremities and, possibly, the cranial nerves and respiratory muscles. The deep tendon reflexes are typically absent or depressed. Sensation is usually preserved, although some patients may experience paresthesias or sensory loss. The diagnosis is supported by the finding of albuminocytologic dissociation (ie, elevated protein with a normal cell count) on cerebrospinal fluid analysis.

The most serious complication of GBS is respiratory failure due to diaphragmatic and intercostal muscle weakness. This can occur in up to 30% of patients and is the most common cause of death. Therefore, all patients with GBS should be monitored closely for signs of respiratory distress (eg, dyspnea, orthopnea, respiratory fatigue, use of accessory muscles, paradoxical abdominal movement). Pulmonary function tests, including negative inspiratory force and forced vital capacity, should be measured serially, and elective intubation should be considered if there is a significant decline.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 51-year-old woman comes to the physician because of numbness of her legs and toes for 3 months. She has also had fatigue and occasional shortness of breath for the past 5 months. She is a painter. Examination shows pale conjunctivae. Sensation to vibration and position is absent over the lower extremities. She has a broad-based gait. The patient sways when she stands with her feet together and closes her eyes. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely to be seen in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fatigue, shortness of breath, and pale conjunctivae suggest anemia, while her neurologic findings (eg, loss of position and vibration sensation, ataxia, positive Romberg sign) suggest a peripheral neuropathy. These findings are characteristic of vitamin B12 deficiency, which can cause a macrocytic anemia and a neurologic syndrome of peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, and loss of position and vibration sense. The neurologic findings are due to the role of vitamin B12 in the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, a step in fat metabolism. When vitamin B12 is deficient, methylmalonyl-CoA accumulates and is converted to methylmalonic acid. This can be detected as elevated methylmalonic acid levels in the blood or urine, which is a sensitive and specific finding in vitamin B12 deficiency.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old woman is referred to a tertiary care hospital with a history of diplopia and fatigue for the past 3 months. She has also noticed difficulty in climbing the stairs and combing her hair. She confirms a history of 2.3 kg (5.0 lb) weight loss in the past 6 weeks and constipation. Past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus. She has a 50-pack-year cigarette smoking history. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 135/78 mm Hg supine and 112/65 while standing, a heart rate of 82/min supine and 81/min while standing, and a temperature of 37.0°C (98.6°F). She is oriented to time and space. Her right upper eyelid is slightly drooped. She has difficulty in abducting the right eye. Pupils are bilaterally equal and reactive to light with accommodation. The corneal reflex is intact. Muscle strength is reduced in the proximal muscles of all 4 limbs, and the lower limbs are affected more when compared to the upper limbs. Deep tendon reflexes are bilaterally absent. After 10 minutes of cycling, the reflexes become positive. Sensory examination is normal. Diffuse wheezes are heard on chest auscultation. Which of the following findings is expected?

answer_choices.B: Incremental pattern on repetitive nerve conduction studies
answer_choices.C: Periventricular plaques on MRI of the brain
answer_choices.D: Thymoma on CT scan of the chest

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of ptosis, diplopia, and proximal muscle weakness is suggestive of myasthenia gravis (MG). MG is an autoimmune disorder caused by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction. These antibodies lead to complement-mediated damage to the postsynaptic membrane, reducing the number of available AChRs and causing defective neuromuscular transmission. The disease is characterized by fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with repetitive use (eg, difficulty climbing stairs, combing hair) and improves with rest. Ocular symptoms (eg, ptosis, diplopia) are often the initial manifestation.

The diagnosis of MG is confirmed by detecting serum AChR antibodies and with electrophysiologic studies. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 2-3 Hz shows a decremental response (ie, progressively smaller amplitudes) due to failure of neuromuscular transmission. Single-fiber electromyography, which measures the variability in neuromuscular transmission, is the most sensitive test.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old woman presents to the office with the complaint of a tingling sensation over her face and distal parts of her lower limbs. Three weeks ago, she had an episode of bloody diarrhea and was successfully treated with erythromycin. She is a full-time radiology technician. Currently, she takes oral contraceptives and zopiclone (1 mg) at bedtime. Her blood pressure is 100/80 mm Hg, her heart rate is 91/min, her respiratory rate is 15/min, and her temperature is 36.7°C (98.0°F). Neurological examination reveals loss of all sensation over the face and in the distal part of her lower limbs. Strength in calf flexor and extensor muscles is diminished bilaterally (4/5 on all of the muscle groups). Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ in the knees and 1+ in the ankles. Plantar reflexes are flexor. What is the most probable mechanism of the pathological findings in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Antibody-mediated destruction of peripheral myelin by cytotoxic cells
answer_choices.B: Granulomatous alteration of the vessels supplying peripheral nerves
answer_choices.C: Radiation-induced oxidative stress in the neurons of dorsal ganglia
answer_choices.D: Failure of Schwann cells to produce myelin

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recent infection and the presence of distal weakness and sensory loss are suggestive of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). GBS is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy that often occurs 1-3 weeks following a gastrointestinal or respiratory tract infection. The most common infectious agents include Campylobacter jejuni, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus. The exact mechanism of nerve injury in GBS is not completely understood, but it is thought to be due to molecular mimicry, in which the immune system mounts an immunologic attack against peripheral nerve components that share structural similarities with a preceding infectious agent. This results in an antibody-mediated destruction of peripheral myelin by cytotoxic cells.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 25-year-old primigravida is admitted to the hospital at 36 weeks gestation after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She is conscious, but lethargic and complains of a headache that started 2 hours prior to the seizure. She denies alcohol intake or drug use. She has no history of convulsive disorders and the antepartum course has been unremarkable. She was compliant with the recommended prenatal care and her last prenatal visit was 2 weeks ago. She has gained 2 kg (4.4 lb) since her last visit. The blood pressure was 160/90 mm Hg, the heart rate was 79/min, the respiratory rate was 14/min, and the temperature was 37.0℃ (98.6℉). The physical examination shows leg and perineal edema. The neurologic examination is significant for symmetric upper and lower extremity hyperreflexia and ankle clonus. Which of the following laboratory findings would be most common in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old gravida 1 is admitted to the hospital after a tonic-clonic seizure at 37 weeks gestation. At the time of presentation, she complains of a severe headache, double vision, and nausea. Her vital signs are as follows: blood pressure, 165/90 mm Hg; heart rate, 91/min; respiratory rate, 9/min; and temperature, 37.0℃ (98.6℉). The rapid dipstick test performed on admission unit shows 3+ proteinuria. The fetal heart rate is 118/min. On examination, the patient is lethargic (GCS 12/15). There is 2+ pitting leg edema. The neurologic examination is significant for left eye deviation towards the nose, paralysis of the left conjugate gaze with a paralytic left eye, and right hemiplegia. Meningeal signs are negative. Which of the following findings would be expected if a head CT scan is performed?

answer_choices.A: Regions of hyperdensity within the cerebellar hemispheres
answer_choices.B: Hyperattenuating material in the subarachnoid space
answer_choices.C: Regions of hyperdensity in the left pons
answer_choices.D: Subcortical hypodense region with surrounding irregular hyperdense margins

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe headache, visual changes, altered mental status, and seizure in the setting of hypertension and proteinuria is consistent with eclampsia. Eclampsia is a severe form of preeclampsia characterized by new-onset grand mal seizures in a preeclamptic patient. The exact pathophysiology of eclampsia is not well understood, but it is thought to be related to cerebrovascular changes (eg, vasospasm, ischemia, hemorrhage) and endothelial dysfunction leading to cerebral edema. 

The patient's neurologic examination is consistent with a brainstem lesion, specifically in the left pons. The pons contains the abducens nucleus, which controls lateral gaze, and the corticospinal tract, which controls contralateral motor function. Therefore, a lesion in the left pons would cause ipsilateral lateral gaze palsy (due to involvement of the abducens nucleus) and contralateral hemiplegia (due to involvement of the corticospinal tract). 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old primigravida is admitted to the hospital at 36 weeks gestation with a severe frontal headache. The initial assessment shows her vital signs to be as follows: blood pressure, 170/90 mm Hg; heart rate, 85/min; respiratory rate; 15/min; and temperature, 36.9℃ (98.4℉). The fetal heart rate is 159/min. The patient’s physical examination is remarkable for pitting edema of the lower extremity. Dipstick urine assessment shows 2+ proteinuria. While being evaluated the patient has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which of the following pharmacologic agents should be used to control the seizures?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of new-onset headache, hypertension, and proteinuria after 20 weeks' gestation is consistent with preeclampsia. The subsequent tonic-clonic seizure meets criteria for eclampsia. Eclampsia is a life-threatening obstetric emergency that requires immediate treatment to prevent maternal death. Initial management includes ensuring a secure airway and administering antiseizure prophylaxis. The drug of choice for eclamptic seizure prophylaxis and treatment is magnesium sulfate. Magnesium sulfate decreases the frequency of eclamptic seizures by an unknown mechanism, possibly through blockade of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, which inhibits the release of excitatory neurotransmitters in the CNS.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: Six hours after giving birth to a healthy 3100 g (6 lb 13oz) girl, a 40-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1 suddenly has a tonic-clonic seizure for 2-minutes while on the ward. She had been complaining of headache, blurry vision, and abdominal pain for an hour before the incident. Her pregnancy was complicated by gestational hypertension and iron deficiency anemia. Her medications until birth included labetalol, iron supplements, and a multivitamin. Her temperature is 37°C (98.7°F), pulse is 95/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 152/100 mm Hg. The cranial nerves are intact. Muscle strength is normal. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ with a shortened relaxation phase. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's headache, blurry vision, abdominal pain, and seizure in the setting of hypertension are suggestive of eclampsia. Eclampsia is defined as the new onset of grand mal seizure activity or unexplained coma during pregnancy or postpartum in a woman with signs or symptoms of preeclampsia. Preeclampsia is a multisystem disorder characterized by hypertension and involvement of one or more other organ systems and/or the fetus. This patient's hypertension, hyperreflexia, and visual symptoms are consistent with preeclampsia. Eclampsia is a life-threatening emergency that can occur antepartum, intrapartum, or postpartum (up to 4 weeks following delivery). The initial management of eclampsia includes stabilizing the mother with airway protection during the seizure, turning the patient to the left lateral decubitus position to prevent aspiration, and administering magnesium sulfate to prevent recurrent seizures. Antihypertensive therapy (eg, hydralazine, labetalol) should be administered to keep systolic blood pressure <160 mm Hg and diastolic blood pressure <110 mm Hg in order to prevent maternal end-organ damage.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 25-year-old primigravida woman at 35 weeks estimated gestational age presents with a headache for the past 5 hours. She describes the headache as severe and incapacitating and showing no response to acetaminophen. In the emergency department, her blood pressure is found to be 150/100 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min, respiratory rate is 30/min, and temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). Her records show that her blood pressure was the same yesterday during her regular antenatal visit. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral crackles along the lung base. Abdominal examination reveals a gravid uterus consistent with a gestational age of 32 weeks and a floating fetus in a cephalic presentation. Pelvic examination is performed which shows a closed firm cervix with no evidence of bleeding or discharge. Moderate pitting edema is noted and neurologic examination shows generalized hyperreflexia. Laboratory findings are significant for the following:
Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL
Platelets 185,000/μL
Serum creatinine 0.4 mg/dL
Spot urine creatinine 110 mg/dL
Spot urine protein 360 mg/dL
AST 40 IU/L
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
Preeclampsia is a multisystem disorder characterized by hypertension and proteinuria after 20 weeks of gestation. It is diagnosed by the presence of hypertension (blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart) and proteinuria (≥300 mg/24 hours or a spot urine protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3). In the absence of proteinuria, preeclampsia can be diagnosed if hypertension is accompanied by thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function, pulmonary edema, or cerebral or visual symptoms. Severe features of preeclampsia include severe hypertension (systolic blood pressure ≥160 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure ≥110 mm Hg), thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function, pulmonary edema, or new-onset cerebral or visual disturbances. This patient's severe headache, hypertension, and pulmonary edema are consistent with preeclampsia with severe features.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician for an initial prenatal visit at 13 weeks' gestation. She has had episodic headaches over the past month. She has no history of serious illness. Her immunizations are up-to-date. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F) and pulse is 90/min. Repeated measurements show a blood pressure of 138/95 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 13-week gestation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis is within normal limits. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, serum ALT is 19 U/L, and platelet count is 210,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely condition in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's blood pressure is elevated (>140/90 mm Hg) before 20 weeks' gestation, which is diagnostic of chronic hypertension. Chronic hypertension is present in about 1-5% of pregnancies and is associated with increased risk of superimposed preeclampsia, preterm delivery, placental abruption, and fetal growth restriction. Chronic hypertension can be differentiated from gestational hypertension, which is diagnosed when hypertension first presents after 20 weeks' gestation in a previously normotensive woman.

question: Thirty minutes after delivery, a 3600-g (7-lb 15-oz) newborn has noisy breathing, bluish discoloration of her lips, and intermittent respiratory distress. She was born at 38 weeks' gestation and required bag-mask resuscitation immediately after delivery. Pregnancy was uncomplicated. Her mother has noticed the bluish lip discoloration worsen when she fed and improve when she cried. The patient's pulse is 163/min, respirations are 62/min, and blood pressure is 60/30 mm Hg. The crying infant's lungs are clear to auscultation. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?

answer_choices.A: Diffuse reticulogranular densities on chest x-ray
answer_choices.C: Passage of a gastric catheter through the mouth not possible
answer_choices.D: Passage of a catheter through the nasal cavity not possible

few_shot.question: One day after a 4700-g (10-lb 6-oz) male newborn is delivered to a 28-year-old primigravid woman, the newborn has bluish discoloration of the lips and fingernails. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 166/min, respirations are 63/min, and blood pressure is 68/44 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 81%. Examination shows central cyanosis. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard over the left lower sternal border. A single second heart sound is present. Supplemental oxygen does not improve cyanosis. An x-ray of the chest shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with a narrowed mediastinum. Further evaluation of the mother is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has transposition of the great arteries (TGA), the most common cause of cyanotic heart disease in the first 24 hours of life. TGA is characterized by the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle, resulting in two parallel circulations. The only communication between the systemic and pulmonary circulations is through a patent foramen ovale and/or patent ductus arteriosus. Clinical findings include profound cyanosis within the first day of life, a single second heart sound (S2), and a systolic ejection murmur due to increased flow across the pulmonary valve. Chest x-ray shows an "egg on a string" appearance, with an enlarged cardiac silhouette and a narrowed mediastinum.

Maternal diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for TGA. Hyperglycemia during the first trimester of pregnancy, when organogenesis occurs, can lead to various congenital malformations, including cardiac defects. Therefore, an elevated hemoglobin A1c, which reflects the average blood glucose level over the past 3 months, is the most likely finding in this patient's mother.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: One day after doctors helped a 28-year-old primigravid woman deliver a 4,700 g (10 lb 6 oz) boy, the newborn has bluish discoloration of the lips and fingernails. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), the pulse is 166/min, the respirations are 63/min, and the blood pressure is 68/44 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 81%. Examination shows central cyanosis. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard over the left lower sternal border. A single second heart sound is present. Supplemental oxygen does not improve cyanosis. An X-ray of the chest shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with a narrowed mediastinum. Which of the following cardiac defects would be associated with this newborn’s diagnosis?

answer_choices.B: Division of aorta and pulmonary artery

few_shot.explanation:
This newborn's central cyanosis, single second heart sound, and holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border are suggestive of a cyanotic congenital heart disease. The chest x-ray findings of an enlarged cardiac silhouette with a narrowed mediastinum ("egg on a string" appearance) are characteristic of transposition of the great arteries (TGA). TGA is the most common cause of cyanosis in the first 24 hours of life. It occurs due to failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral, causing the aorta to arise from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery to arise from the left ventricle. This leads to two parallel circulations (ie, systemic venous blood bypasses the lungs and is pumped into the aorta, and oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is pumped back into the pulmonary artery), which is incompatible with life unless a right-to-left shunt is present to allow for some degree of mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Such shunts can occur at the atrial level (eg, patent foramen ovale), ventricular level (eg, ventricular septal defect), or arterial level (eg, patent ductus arteriosus).

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 2350-g (5-lb 3-oz) male newborn delivered at 28 weeks’ gestation develops rapid breathing, grunting, and subcostal retractions 2 hours after delivery. The mother did not receive prenatal care. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 168/min, respirations are 88/min, and blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. Physical examination shows cyanosis and nasal flaring. Breath sounds are decreased bilaterally. An x-ray of the chest shows diffuse reticulonodular ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this patient's disease?
few_shot.explanation:
This premature infant has respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also known as hyaline membrane disease. RDS is characterized by poor lung compliance and atelectasis due to surfactant deficiency. Surfactant is a lipoprotein complex that reduces alveolar surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse at the end of expiration. It is synthesized by type II pneumocytes and stored in lamellar bodies within these cells. Surfactant production begins at approximately 24 weeks' gestation, but adequate amounts are not produced until 34-36 weeks' gestation. Therefore, premature infants are at risk for surfactant deficiency and RDS. The risk is inversely proportional to gestational age and birth weight. 

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: Two hours after delivery, a 1900-g (4-lb 3-oz) female newborn develops respiratory distress. She was born at 32 weeks' gestation. Pregnancy was complicated by pregnancy-induced hypertension. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 140/min and respirations are 64/min. Examination shows bluish extremities. Grunting and moderate subcostal retractions are present. There are decreased breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation. An x-ray of the chest shows reduced lung volume and diffuse reticulogranular densities. Supplemental oxygen is administered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This preterm infant has respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also known as hyaline membrane disease. RDS is caused by surfactant deficiency, leading to alveolar collapse and ventilation-perfusion mismatch. The disease is characterized by the onset of respiratory distress within minutes to hours after birth, and is associated with hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis. Chest x-ray shows diffuse reticulogranular densities ("ground glass" appearance) and air bronchograms.

Initial management of RDS includes administration of supplemental oxygen and noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (PPV) to prevent alveolar collapse. Nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the preferred mode of noninvasive PPV in preterm infants with RDS. If the infant's condition worsens or does not improve with CPAP, surfactant therapy and intubation should be considered.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: Thirty minutes after delivery, a 1780-g (3-lb 15-oz) male newborn develops respiratory distress. He was born at 30 weeks' gestation via vaginal delivery. His temperature is 36.8C (98.2F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 64/min, and blood pressure is 61/32 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Examination shows pale extremities. Grunting and moderate subcostal retractions are present. Pulmonary examination shows decreased breath sounds bilaterally. Supplemental oxygen is administered. Ten minutes later, his pulse is 148/min and respirations are 66/min. Pulse oximetry on 60% oxygen shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This premature infant has respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also known as hyaline membrane disease. RDS is caused by surfactant deficiency due to lung immaturity. Surfactant is a lipoprotein complex that reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse at the end of expiration. Without surfactant, the alveoli collapse, leading to ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxemia. 

Clinical features of RDS include respiratory distress (eg, tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions) that typically occurs immediately after birth in a premature infant. The infant often requires supplemental oxygen and has a chest x-ray showing diffuse reticulogranular (ground-glass) appearance and air bronchograms.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever, intermittent rigors, and night sweats. She also has a 1-month history of progressive fatigue. Five weeks ago, she was hospitalized and received intravenous antibiotics for treatment of bacterial meningitis while visiting relatives in Guatemala. Her temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse is 130/min, and blood pressure is 105/70 mm Hg. Examination shows pallor and scattered petechiae and ecchymoses. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 9.0 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 1,100/mm3 with 30% segmented neutrophils, and a platelet count of 20,000/mm3 . Blood cultures grow coagulase-negative staphylococci. The patient was most likely treated with which of the following antibiotics?

few_shot.question: An 18-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of severe headache with photophobia and diffuse myalgias. She is a college student and lives in a dormitory in a large urban area. She has not traveled recently. On arrival, she is lethargic. Her temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 88/58 mm Hg. Examination shows scattered petechiae and ecchymoses on the trunk and lower extremities. There is decreased range of motion of the neck. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows a cell count of 1,600/μL (80% neutrophils) and a lactate concentration of 5.1 mmol/L. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, and petechial rash is concerning for meningococcal meningitis. Neisseria meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus that is a common cause of bacterial meningitis in adolescents and young adults. It is transmitted via respiratory droplets, and outbreaks are common in close-quarter living conditions such as college dormitories or military barracks. 

The most effective strategy for preventing meningococcal disease is vaccination. The meningococcal vaccine is a polysaccharide conjugate vaccine that contains antigens to the most common disease-causing serogroups of N meningitidis (A, C, W, Y). The vaccine is recommended for all adolescents at age 11-12 with a booster at age 16. It is also recommended for individuals at increased risk for meningococcal disease, including college freshmen living in dormitories and military recruits.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 59-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of worsening fever, chills, malaise, productive cough, and difficulty breathing. Three days ago, she returned from a trip to South Africa. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and varicose veins. Her current medications include metformin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. Her temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse is 102/minute, blood pressure is 94/68 mm Hg, and respirations are 31/minute. Pulse oximetry on 2 L of oxygen via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 91%. Examination reveals decreased breath sounds and dull percussion over the left lung base. The skin is very warm and well-perfused. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL
Leukocyte count 15,400/mm3
platelet count 282,000/mm3
Serum
Na+ 144 mEq/L
Cl- 104 mEq/L
K+ 4.9 mEq/L
Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL
Blood and urine for cultures are obtained. Intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun. Which of the following is the next best step in management?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, cough, and dyspnea, along with the physical examination findings of decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion, are suggestive of pneumonia. The presence of tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension, and hypoxemia indicate severe pneumonia, and likely sepsis. The most common pathogens in community-acquired pneumonia are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. However, this patient's recent travel to South Africa and her comorbidities (eg, diabetes mellitus) increase her risk for infection with drug-resistant pathogens. Therefore, empiric antibiotic therapy should include coverage for both methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The regimen of choice is an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (eg, piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, imipenem, meropenem) plus MRSA coverage (eg, vancomycin or linezolid).

few_shot.question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the physician with complaints of fever with rigors, headache, malaise, muscle pains, nausea, vomiting, and decreased appetite for the past 3 days. He informs the physician that he had been backpacking on the Appalachian Trail in the woods of Georgia in the month of June, 2 weeks ago, and had been bitten by a tick there. His temperature is 39.0°C (102.3°F), pulse is 94/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 126/82 mm Hg. His physical exam does not reveal any significant abnormality except for mild splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:
Total white blood cell count 3,700/mm3 (3.7 x 109/L)
Differential count  
Neutrophils 85%
Lymphocytes 12%
Monocytes 2%
Eosinophils 1%
Basophils 0%
Platelet count 88,000/mm3 (95 x 109/L)
Serum alanine aminotransferase 140 IU/L
Serum aspartate aminotransferase 80 IU/L
Microscopic examination of a peripheral blood smear stained with Wright-Giemsa stain shows the presence of morulae in the cytoplasm of leukocytes. In addition to drugs for symptomatic relief, what is the most appropriate initial step in the treatment of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of tick bite, fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, and leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and transaminitis is suggestive of human granulocytic anaplasmosis (HGA). HGA is caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum, a gram-negative bacterium transmitted by the Ixodes scapularis tick, which also transmits Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease) and Babesia microti (babesiosis). HGA is most common in the upper Midwest and Northeastern United States, but it can also occur in Northern California and the Southeast. The presence of morulae (mulberry-shaped aggregates of Anaplasma organisms) within granulocytes on peripheral blood smear confirms the diagnosis.

Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for both adults and children with HGA, regardless of the severity of illness. It is also the preferred treatment for other tick-borne illnesses, including Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and ehrlichiosis. Therefore, empiric treatment with doxycycline is recommended in any patient with a febrile illness who has been exposed to ticks, even before the results of diagnostic tests are available.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 22-year-old female is brought to the emergency department by her roommate with a one day history of fever and malaise. She did not feel well after class the previous night and has been in her room since then. She has not been eating or drinking due to severe nausea. Her roommate checked on her one hour ago and was alarmed to find a fever of 102°F (38.9°C). On physical exam temperature is 103°F (40°C), blood pressure is 110/66 mmHg, pulse is 110/min, respirations are 23/min, and pulse oximetry is 98% on room air. She refuses to move her neck and has a rash on her trunk. You perform a lumbar puncture and the CSF analysis is shown below.

Appearance: Cloudy
Opening pressure: 180 mm H2O
WBC count: 150 cells/µL (93% PMN)
Glucose level: < 40 mg/dL
Protein level: 50 mg/dL
Gram stain: gram-negative diplococci

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, headache, neck stiffness, and rash along with the CSF findings of a high opening pressure, elevated WBC count with a predominance of neutrophils, low glucose, and elevated protein are consistent with bacterial meningitis. The gram stain showing gram-negative diplococci suggests Neisseria meningitidis, the most common cause of meningitis in adolescents and young adults. 

The most important first step in management is prompt initiation of empiric antibiotics to cover the most likely pathogens. In this case, ceftriaxone is the drug of choice. 

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: Three days after admission to the hospital following a motor vehicle accident, a 45-year-old woman develops a fever. A central venous catheter was placed on the day of admission for treatment of severe hypotension. Her temperature is 39.2°C (102.5°F). Examination shows erythema surrounding the catheter insertion site at the right internal jugular vein. Blood cultures show gram-positive, catalase-positive cocci that have a low minimum inhibitory concentration when exposed to novobiocin. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) due to Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species. S epidermidis is a common skin commensal and is the most common cause of CLABSI. It is often resistant to methicillin due to the presence of the mecA gene, which codes for an altered penicillin-binding protein with decreased affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics. Therefore, empiric treatment of serious S epidermidis infections should include vancomycin, especially in patients with prosthetic devices or intravascular catheters.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 37-year-old woman with an HIV infection comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Laboratory studies show a decrease in the CD4 count and an increase in the viral load despite ongoing treatment. The patient is switched to a new treatment regimen, including a drug that acts by preventing viral DNA synthesis without undergoing intracellular phosphorylation.
