few_shot.question: A previously healthy 6-week-old infant is brought to the emergency department because of fever, fatigue, and dry cough for the past 24 hours. She has been feeding poorly and has had difficulty latching on when breastfeeding since this started. She has also had nasal congestion. The mother reports that her daughter has not been going through as many diapers as usual. She was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 42 weeks' gestation. Her mother is a cystic fibrosis carrier. The patient has been treated with acetaminophen for the last 24 hours and vitamin D drops since birth. She appears irritable, pale, and lethargic. She is at the 25th percentile for both length and weight; she had the same percentiles at birth. Her temperature is 38.2°C (100.7°F), and the respirations are 64/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Examination shows an ill-appearing infant with a cough and nasal flaring. Mucous membranes are dry. Chest examination shows intercostal and supraclavicular retractions. Expiratory wheezes are heard on auscultation. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
few_shot.explanation:
This infant has signs of bronchiolitis, a common lower respiratory tract infection in children <2 years of age. Bronchiolitis is characterized by acute inflammation, edema, and necrosis of epithelial cells lining small airways, increased mucus production, and bronchospasm. The most common cause of bronchiolitis is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), which is typically seen in epidemics during the winter and early spring. RSV bronchiolitis commonly affects children <2 years of age, with a peak incidence at age 2-6 months. Risk factors for severe disease include prematurity, age <6 weeks, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, and immunodeficiency. Clinically, patients present with 1-3 days of upper respiratory tract symptoms (eg, rhinorrhea, congestion, cough, low-grade fever) followed by signs of lower respiratory tract disease (eg, wheezing, rales, respiratory distress). Diagnosis is usually clinical, but it can be confirmed by identification of the virus in nasal secretions by immunofluorescence or enzyme immunoassay.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 6-week-old infant is brought to the emergency department because of fever, fatigue, and dry cough for one day. She has been feeding poorly and had difficulty latching on to breastfeed since yesterday. She has had nasal congestion. The mother reports that her daughter has not been going through as many diapers as usual. She was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 42 weeks' gestation. Her mother is a cystic fibrosis carrier. The patient has been treated with acetaminophen for the last 24 hours, and vitamin D drops since birth. She appears irritable, pale, and lethargic. She is at the 25th percentile for both length and weight; she had the same percentiles at birth. Her temperature is 38.2°C (100.7°F) and respirations are 64/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Examination shows an ill-appearing infant with a cough and nasal flaring. Mucous membranes are dry. Chest examination shows intercostal and supraclavicular retractions. Expiratory wheezes are heard on auscultation. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
few_shot.explanation:
This infant's presentation of fever, cough, and respiratory distress with wheezing and hypoxia is suggestive of bronchiolitis, a common lower respiratory tract infection in children <2 years of age. Bronchiolitis is most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), especially during the winter months. RSV is transmitted through respiratory droplets and causes inflammation and necrosis of the bronchiolar epithelium, leading to increased mucus production and bronchiolar obstruction. This results in air trapping, atelectasis, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch, which can cause hypoxia. 

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 5-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever and a cough for 3 days. His mother reports that he has had multiple episodes of loose stools over the past 3 months. He has been treated for otitis media 4 times and bronchiolitis 3 times during the past 3 months. He was born at 37 weeks' gestation and the neonatal period was uncomplicated. He is at the 10th percentile for height and 3rd percentile for weight. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 126/min, and respirations are 35/min. Examination shows an erythematous scaly rash over the trunk and extremities. There are white patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa that bleed when scraped. Inspiratory crackles are heard in the right lung base. An x-ray of the chest shows an infiltrate in the right lower lobe and an absent thymic shadow. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent infections, failure to thrive, and chronic diarrhea is concerning for severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). SCID is a group of disorders characterized by defects in both T- and B-cell immunity. The most common form of SCID is X-linked and is due to mutations in the gene encoding the common gamma chain, a component of several interleukin receptors. Defective signaling through these receptors impairs T-cell development and function. Because T cells are necessary for B-cell isotype switching, B-cell function is also impaired, leading to hypogammaglobulinemia. 

Patients with SCID typically present in infancy with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, and severe recurrent infections involving bacteria, viruses, and opportunistic pathogens. Candida infections are common and can cause oral thrush, as seen in this patient. The absence of a thymic shadow on chest x-ray is due to T-cell deficiency. 

Hence, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [D] > [A] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of an increasing productive cough with a moderate amount of white phlegm for the past week. He has been treated for pneumonia with antibiotic therapy four times over the past year. A chest x-ray performed 3 months ago showed no anatomical abnormalities. He has had multiple episodes of bulky greasy stools that don't flush easily. He is at 3rd percentile for height and at 5th percentile for weight. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 132/min, and respirations are 44/min. A few inspiratory crackles are heard in the thorax. The abdomen is soft and nontender. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the best initial test to determine the underlying etiology of this patient's illness?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent pneumonia, malnutrition, and steatorrhea are suggestive of cystic fibrosis (CF). CF is an autosomal recessive disorder that is caused by mutations in the CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene. The CFTR protein is a chloride channel that is present in the epithelial cells of many organs, including the lungs, pancreas, and sweat glands. In CF, the CFTR protein is dysfunctional, leading to decreased chloride secretion and increased sodium absorption. This results in the production of thick, viscous mucus that can obstruct the airways and pancreatic ducts, leading to the symptoms seen in this patient.

The best initial test to diagnose CF is the sweat chloride test, which measures the concentration of chloride in sweat. A high concentration of chloride is indicative of CF.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

question:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency room (ER) by her co-workers after they found her unconscious in her cubicle when they returned from lunch. They tell you that she has diabetes but do not know anything more about her condition. The woman’s vital signs include: pulse 110/min, respiratory rate 24/min, temperature 36.7°C (98.0°F), and blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg. On physical examination, the patient is breathing heavily and gives irrelevant responses to questions. The skin and mucous membranes appear dry. Examination of the abdomen reveals mild diffuse tenderness to palpation. Deep tendon reflexes in the extremities are 1+ bilaterally. Laboratory studies show:
Finger stick glucose 630 mg/dL
Arterial blood gas analysis:
pH 7.1
PO2 90 mm Hg
PCO2 33 mm Hg
HCO3 8 mEq/L
Serum:
Sodium 135 mEq/L
Potassium 3.1 mEq/L
Chloride 136 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL
Serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL
Urine examination shows:
Glucose Positive
Ketones Positive
Leukocytes Negative
Nitrite Negative
RBCs Negative
Casts Negative
The patient is immediately started on a bolus of intravenous (IV) 0.9% sodium chloride (NaCl). Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?

few_shot.question:
A 22-year-old woman with a history of type I diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, and drowsiness for the past day. Her temperature is 98.3°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 114/74 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 27/min, and oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a confused and lethargic young woman. Initial laboratory values are notable for the findings below.

Serum:
Na+: 139 mEq/L
Cl-: 100 mEq/L
K+: 2.9 mEq/L
HCO3-: 9 mEq/L
BUN: 20 mg/dL
Glucose: 599 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL
Ca2+: 10.2 mg/dL
AST: 12 U/L
ALT: 10 U/L

An initial ECG is notable for sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the best initial step in management for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hyperglycemia, anion gap metabolic acidosis, and positive serum ketones is consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA is a medical emergency and treatment should be initiated promptly. The mainstays of therapy are insulin and intravenous fluids. Insulin stops further ketone production and allows glucose to enter the cells. Intravenous fluids are necessary because patients are often volume depleted due to osmotic diuresis.

However, this patient has hypokalemia, which is a contraindication to starting insulin therapy. Insulin promotes the entry of potassium into cells, which can further decrease serum potassium levels and potentially cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Therefore, in patients with DKA who are hypokalemic, potassium replacement should be started before insulin therapy.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [B] > [D] > [A].

few_shot.question:
A 48-year-old woman is transferred from her primary care physician's office to the emergency department for further evaluation of hypokalemia to 2.5 mEq/L. She was recently diagnosed with hypertension 2 weeks ago and started on medical therapy. The patient said that she enjoys all kinds of food and exercises regularly, but has not been able to complete her workouts as she usually does. Her temperature is 97.7°F (36.5°C), blood pressure is 107/74 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, respirations are 15/min, and SpO2 is 94% on room air. Her physical exam is unremarkable. Peripheral intravenous (IV) access is obtained. Her basic metabolic panel is obtained below.

Serum:
Na+: 135 mEq/L
Cl-: 89 mEq/L
K+: 2.2 mEq/L
HCO3-: 33 mEq/L
BUN: 44 mg/dL
Glucose: 147 mg/dL
Creatinine: 2.3 mg/dL
Magnesium: 2.0 mEq/L

What is the next best step in management?

answer_choices.C: Administer isotonic saline 1 liter via peripheral IV

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis is suggestive of primary hyperaldosteronism. This condition is characterized by autonomous production of aldosterone, leading to increased sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal tubules and collecting ducts. This can lead to hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. The metabolic alkalosis is due to increased H+ secretion in the distal tubules and collecting ducts, and contraction alkalosis due to volume contraction from the diuretic effect of aldosterone.

The patient's elevated BUN and creatinine are suggestive of prerenal azotemia, likely due to volume contraction from the effects of aldosterone. Therefore, the next best step in management is to administer isotonic saline to correct the volume contraction.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 19-year-old man with unknown medical history is found down on a subway platform and is brought to the hospital by ambulance. He experiences two episodes of emesis en route. In the emergency department, he appears confused and is complaining of abdominal pain. His temperature is 37.0° C (98.6° F), pulse is 94/min, blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg, respirations are 24/min, oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. His mucus membranes are dry and he is taking rapid, deep breathes. Laboratory work is presented below:

Serum:
Na+: 130 mEq/L
K+: 4.3 mEq/L
Cl-: 102 mEq/L
HCO3-: 12 mEq/L
BUN: 15 mg/dL
Glucose: 362 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.2 mg/dL
Urine ketones: Positive


The patient is given a bolus of isotonic saline and started on intravenous insulin drip. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hyperglycemia, ketonuria, and anion gap metabolic acidosis is consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA is a medical emergency that requires immediate treatment with intravenous fluids, insulin, and electrolyte management. Insulin therapy can lead to a rapid decline in serum potassium levels due to an intracellular shift of potassium. Therefore, all patients with DKA should have their potassium levels closely monitored. If the serum potassium is <3.3 mEq/L, insulin should be held and potassium should be aggressively replaced. If the serum potassium is 3.3-5.2 mEq/L, insulin and potassium should be given simultaneously. If the serum potassium is >5.2 mEq/L, administer insulin alone.

His current medications include naproxen, insulin, atorvastatin, metformin, ibuprofen, omeprazole, and fish oil. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 170/115 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, respirations are 19/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On physical exam, the patient is somnolent and has a Glasgow Coma Scale of 11. Cardiac and pulmonary exams are notable for bibasilar crackles and a systolic murmur that radiates to the carotids. Platelet count: 199,000/mm^3

Ca2+: 9.2 mg/dL

The patient is started on IV fluids. Which of the following represents the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of somnolence, decreased responsiveness, and laboratory findings of an elevated BUN and creatinine are suggestive of acute kidney injury (AKI). The patient's history of diabetes and hypertension, as well as his current blood pressure, suggest that he has chronic kidney disease (CKD). The patient's AKI is likely due to his use of naproxen and ibuprofen, two nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). NSAIDs can cause AKI by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, leading to unopposed vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole and decreased renal perfusion. This is especially likely in patients with CKD, as they often have decreased renal perfusion at baseline. Therefore, the best next step in management is to discontinue the patient's home medications, especially the NSAIDs.

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old female is found by her roommate in her dormitory. The patient has a history of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus and was binge drinking the night prior with friends at a local bar. The patient is brought to the emergency department, where vital signs are as follow: T 97.3 F, HR 119 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 100% on RA. On physical exam, the patient is clammy to touch, mucous membranes are tacky, and she is generally drowsy and disoriented. Finger stick glucose is 342 mg/dL; additional lab work reveals: Na: 146 K: 5.6 Cl: 99 HCO3: 12 BUN: 18 Cr: 0.74. Arterial Blood Gas reveals: pH 7.26, PCO2 21, PO2 102. Which of the following statements is correct regarding this patient's electrolyte and acid/base status?

answer_choices.A: The patient has a primary respiratory alkalosis with a compensatory metabolic acidosis
answer_choices.B: The patient has a metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia from increased total body potassium
answer_choices.C: The patient has an anion gap metabolic acidosis as well as a respiratory acidosis
answer_choices.D: The patient has an anion gap metabolic acidosis with decreased total body potassium

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which is characterized by hyperglycemia, anion gap metabolic acidosis, and ketonemia. DKA is often precipitated by an event that increases insulin requirements (eg, infection, myocardial infarction, stroke, stress, noncompliance with insulin therapy). In this patient, alcohol consumption likely contributed to her DKA. Alcohol increases the ratio of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) to NAD, which inhibits gluconeogenesis and favors formation of ketoacids (eg, beta-hydroxybutyrate). In addition, alcohol can have a direct insulin-like effect that leads to hypoglycemia, which would stimulate glucagon release and thereby worsen ketoacid production.

DKA is also associated with total body potassium depletion due to osmotic diuresis. However, acidemia drives extracellular shift of potassium in exchange for intracellular hydrogen ions, causing hyperkalemia. Insulin promotes the transfer of potassium into cells, so insulin deficiency also contributes to hyperkalemia. Therefore, despite the hyperkalemia, this patient has decreased total body potassium.

So, the answer is [D].

question: A 53-year-old female patient comes to the physician’s office for her annual check-up visit. She has no complaints and her past medical history is notable for diabetes and hypertension. During this visit, the patient undergoes screening procedures per guidelines including a mammogram. On the screening mammogram a spiculated, irregular mass is found on the left breast. Further diagnostic mammography and biopsy reveal ductal adenocarcinoma of the breast in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. few_shot.question: A 56-year-old woman comes to the physician because she palpated a mass in her right breast during self-examination a week ago. Menarche was at the age of 14, and her last menstrual period was at the age of 51. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a nontender, firm and hard mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Mammography shows large, dense breasts, with a 1.7-cm mass in the right upper outer quadrant. The patient undergoes right upper outer quadrant lumpectomy with subsequent sentinel node biopsy, which reveals moderately differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma and micrometastasis to one axillary lymph node. There is no evidence of extranodal metastasis. The tumor tests positive for both estrogen and progesterone receptors and does not show human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) over-expression. Flow-cytometry reveals aneuploid tumor cells. Which of the following factors has the greatest effect on this patient's prognosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The most important prognostic factor in breast cancer is the presence of metastasis, especially to the axillary lymph nodes. The number of positive nodes is directly proportional to the risk of distant metastasis. In this patient, the presence of micrometastasis to one axillary lymph node is the most important factor affecting her prognosis.

Other factors that affect prognosis include tumor size, histologic grade, hormone receptor status, and HER2 receptor status. However, these are less important than nodal status.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for an annual checkup. She reports that she has been feeling well and has no medical concerns. Her past medical history is significant for childhood asthma but she has not experienced any symptoms since she was a teenager. Physical exam reveals a 1-centimeter hard mobile mass in the left upper outer quadrant of her breast. A mammogram was performed and demonstrated calcifications within the mass so a biopsy was obtained. The biopsy shows acinar proliferation with intralobular fibrosis. Which of the following conditions is most likely affecting this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
Sclerosing adenosis is a benign condition of the breast that is characterized by proliferation of acini and intralobular fibrosis. It is often associated with calcifications, which can be seen on mammography. It is a component of fibrocystic changes of the breast, which are common in premenopausal women. Sclerosing adenosis is usually asymptomatic but can present as a palpable mass or as microcalcifications on mammography. It is not associated with an increased risk of breast cancer.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 48-year-old woman comes to the physician for the evaluation of a left breast mass that she noticed 4 weeks ago. It has rapidly increased in size during this period. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows large dense breasts; a 6-cm, nontender, multinodular mass is palpated in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. There are no changes in the skin or nipple. There is no palpable cervical or axillary adenopathy. Mammography shows a smooth polylobulated mass. An image of a biopsy specimen is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Phyllodes tumors are rare fibroepithelial neoplasms that account for less than 1% of all breast tumors. They are most common in women aged 40-50 years. These tumors are similar to fibroadenomas but tend to be larger and grow more rapidly. They are usually solitary and unilateral, and they most commonly occur in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. On physical examination, they present as a large, painless, mobile mass with well-defined borders. On mammography, they appear as a round or lobulated mass with variable density. Histologically, they are characterized by leaf-like projections of tissue (phyllodes means "leaf-like" in Greek). 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old woman presents with changes in her left breast that started 1 month ago. She came to get it checked out because her best friend was just diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma. The past medical history is significant for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, well-managed medically with levothyroxine. The patient has a 30-pack-year smoking history, but she quit over 15 years ago. The menarche occurred at age 11, and the menopause was at age 53. She does not have any children and has never been sexually active. Her last screening mammogram 10 months ago was normal. The family history is significant for her mother dying from a myocardial infarction (MI) at age 68, her sister dying from metastatic breast cancer at age 55, and for colon cancer in her paternal grandfather. The review of systems is notable for unintentional weight loss of 3.6 kg (8 lb) in the past month. The vital signs include: temperature 37.0℃ (98.6℉), blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, pulse 72/min, respiratory rate 15/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. There is no axillary lymphadenopathy noted. Which of the following characteristics is associated with this patient’s most likely type of breast cancer in comparison to her friend’s diagnosis?

answer_choices.D: Mammogram is more likely to demonstrate a discrete spiculated mass

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, lack of sexual activity, and family history of breast cancer are all risk factors for breast cancer. Her physical examination findings of a palpable mass with irregular, poorly defined margins in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast are concerning for malignancy. However, the movable, rubbery nature of the mass is more suggestive of a lobular carcinoma, which is the second most common type of breast cancer after invasive ductal carcinoma. Invasive lobular carcinoma is more likely to present bilaterally and is often multifocal, making it more difficult to detect on physical examination and mammography. It is also more likely to present with architectural distortion rather than a discrete spiculated mass. The prognosis for invasive lobular carcinoma is similar to that of invasive ductal carcinoma.

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician 10 days after noticing a mass in her left breast while bathing. A core biopsy shows foam cells and multinucleated giant cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's breast mass is most likely a fat necrosis. Fat necrosis is a benign, non-suppurative inflammatory process of adipose tissue. It is most commonly seen in obese, postmenopausal women and typically presents as a painless, hard lump that may be associated with skin or nipple retraction. Fat necrosis can occur following surgery, radiation, or trauma to the breast, but it may also occur spontaneously. Mammography often shows calcifications and oil cysts, which are pathognomonic for fat necrosis. Histologically, fat necrosis is characterized by lipid-filled macrophages (foam cells), multinucleated giant cells, and calcifications. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 61-year-old man presents to his primary care provider complaining of abdominal pain and constipation. He reports a 4-day history of steady right lower quadrant pain. few_shot.question: A 74-year-old man presents to the emergency room with abdominal pain. He reports acute onset of left lower quadrant abdominal pain and nausea three hours prior to presentation. The pain is severe, constant, and non-radiating. He has had two maroon-colored bowel movements since the pain started. His past medical history is notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, and rheumatoid arthritis. He takes lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, dabigatran, methotrexate. He has a 60 pack-year smoking history and drinks 1-2 beers per day. He admits to missing some of his medications recently because he was on vacation in Hawaii. His last colonoscopy was 4 years ago which showed diverticular disease in the descending colon and multiple sessile polyps in the sigmoid colon which were removed. His temperature is 100.1°F (37.8°C), blood pressure is 145/85 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, and respirations are 20/min. On exam, he has notable abdominal distention and is exquisitely tender to palpation in all four abdominal quadrants. Bowel sounds are absent. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of atrial fibrillation, recent noncompliance with anticoagulation, and acute onset of severe abdominal pain with "maroon" stools is concerning for mesenteric ischemia due to an embolic event. The superior mesenteric artery is the most common site of acute mesenteric arterial occlusion due to its low takeoff angle from the aorta and its relatively large caliber. The sudden onset of severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings is a classic presentation. Other findings may include nausea, vomiting, and an urgent desire to defecate. Hematochezia or "maroon" stools may be seen if bowel infarction has occurred. The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical presentation and confirmed by CT angiography.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 67-year-old man comes to the emergency department complaining of severe abdominal pain for the last several hours. The pain is cramp-like in nature, constant, 8/10, and has worsened over time. It is associated with bilious vomiting. He gives a history of episodic right upper abdominal pain for the past few months, mostly after consuming fatty foods, radiating to the tip of the right scapula. He reports no change in bowel habits, bladder habits, or change in weight. His past medical history includes diabetes and hypertension, and he takes hydrochlorothiazide, metformin, ramipril, and atorvastatin. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 102/min, respiratory rate is 20/min, and BMI is 23 kg/m2. On physical examination, his abdomen is distended and diffusely tender.
Laboratory test
Complete blood count
Hemoglobin 13 g/dL
WBC 16,000/mm3
Platelets 150,000/mm3
Basic metabolic panel
Serum Na+ 148 mEq/L
Serum K+ 3.3 mEq/L
Serum Cl- 89 mEq/L
An abdominal CT scan is shown. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s current presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of episodic right upper abdominal pain after consuming fatty foods, radiating to the tip of the right scapula, is suggestive of biliary colic due to cholelithiasis. The pain is caused by transient cystic duct obstruction by a gallstone leading to increased pressure in the gallbladder. The current presentation of severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and leukocytosis is suggestive of small bowel obstruction. The abdominal CT scan shows a dilated loop of small bowel with air in the biliary tree (pneumobilia), a small bowel feces sign (intraluminal debris with gas-fluid levels), and a gallstone in the distal ileum. These findings are consistent with gallstone ileus, a rare form of small bowel obstruction caused by impaction of a large gallstone in the ileum after it passes into the bowel lumen through a cholecystoenteric fistula. The fistula forms as a result of an inflamed gallbladder adhering to the adjacent bowel wall, with subsequent pressure necrosis and fistula formation. The gallstone usually impacts at the ileocecal valve, the narrowest part of the small bowel. Gallstone ileus is more common in elderly women and often presents with signs of small bowel obstruction (crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distention) and pneumobilia.

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician with intermittent bloody diarrhea over the past 2 months. He has occasional abdominal pain. His symptoms have not improved over this time. He has no history of a serious illness and takes no medications. His blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 75/min, respirations are 14/min, and temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F). Deep palpation of the abdomen shows mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Colonoscopy shows diffuse erythema with a sandpaper pattern involving the rectosigmoid and descending colon, with normal mucosa of the rest of the colon. Biopsy shows involvement of the mucosal and submucosal layers with distortion of crypt architecture and crypt abscess formation. This patient is most likely to develop which of the following hepatobiliary diseases?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and endoscopic findings of continuous colonic inflammation involving the rectum is consistent with ulcerative colitis (UC). UC is an idiopathic inflammatory bowel disease that is characterized by chronic, relapsing inflammation of the colonic mucosa. Patients with UC are at increased risk for primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), a chronic, progressive disease of the bile ducts characterized by inflammation, fibrosis, and strictures of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. PSC can lead to cholestasis, cirrhosis, and portal hypertension. Patients with PSC often present with fatigue, pruritus, or jaundice, but some patients are asymptomatic and are diagnosed based on abnormal liver function tests. The diagnosis of PSC is confirmed by cholangiography, which shows multifocal stricturing and segmental dilations of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts ("beaded" appearance). PSC is also a risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.

So, the answer is [D].

The most common cause of chronic pancreatitis is alcohol abuse, which can also cause liver disease (as suggested by this patient's nodular liver). few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe abdominal pain, irregularly irregular rhythm, and a history of hypertension and smoking is suggestive of acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) due to an embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). The SMA supplies the small bowel and the proximal colon. The most common source of emboli is the heart, with atrial fibrillation being the most common cause. The pain of AMI is typically out of proportion to the physical examination findings, as the bowel wall is initially spared. The diagnosis of AMI is confirmed by CT angiography, which can show an embolus in the SMA.

The definitive treatment of AMI due to an embolic occlusion of the SMA is emergent surgery, which typically involves embolectomy and revascularization. In some cases, percutaneous balloon angioplasty and stenting may be performed. Anticoagulation with heparin is typically started after the diagnosis is confirmed to prevent clot propagation, but it is not definitive treatment.

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician for follow-up care. One year ago, she was diagnosed with a 3.8-cm infrarenal aortic aneurysm found incidentally on abdominal ultrasound. She has no complaints. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and COPD. Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, glyburide, and an albuterol inhaler. She has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 145/85 mm Hg. Examination shows a faint abdominal bruit on auscultation. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows a 4.9-cm saccular dilation of the infrarenal aorta. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: Adjustment of cardiovascular risk factors and follow-up CT in 6 months
answer_choices.C: Adjustment of cardiovascular risk factors and follow-up ultrasound in 6 months
answer_choices.D: Adjustment of cardiovascular risk factors and follow-up ultrasound in 12 months

few_shot.explanation:
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) are often asymptomatic and are usually detected incidentally on imaging studies. Risk factors for AAA include age >60, smoking, male sex, and a family history of AAA. The risk of rupture is related to the size of the aneurysm, with the risk increasing significantly when the diameter exceeds 5.0-5.5 cm. This patient's AAA has grown from 3.8 cm to 4.9 cm in 1 year, which is a rapid expansion. Given the size of the aneurysm and the rapid expansion, the risk of rupture is high. Therefore, elective repair is indicated to prevent rupture. Endovascular repair is generally preferred over open surgical repair because it is associated with lower perioperative morbidity and mortality.

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of severe abdominal pain radiating to his left flank for 30 minutes. Current medications include enalapril, metoprolol, aspirin, simvastatin, and pantoprazole. He appears ill. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 131/min, respirations are 31/min, and blood pressure is 82/56 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. Examination shows a painful pulsatile abdominal mass. Intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun. answer_choices.C: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

This patient's presentation of severe abdominal pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile abdominal mass is consistent with a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). AAA rupture is a surgical emergency, and this patient should be taken to the operating room as soon as possible. The mortality rate is extremely high, and increases by the hour. The most common presenting symptom of AAA rupture is abdominal or back pain. Syncope may also occur. On examination, a pulsatile abdominal mass may be present. Hypotension, if present, suggests rupture.

few_shot.question: A 74-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset abdominal pain that is most painful around the umbilicus. The pain began 16 hours ago and has no association with meals. He has not been vomiting, but he has had several episodes of bloody loose bowel movements. He was hospitalized 1 week ago for an acute myocardial infarction. He has had diabetes mellitus for 35 years and hypertension for 20 years. He has smoked 15–20 cigarettes per day for the past 40 years. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.42°F), blood pressure is 95/65 mm Hg, and pulse is 95/min. On physical examination, the patient is in severe pain, there is mild periumbilical tenderness, and a bruit is heard over the epigastric area. Which of the following is the definitive test to assess the patient condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden-onset abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and history of atherosclerotic disease are suggestive of acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI). AMI is a life-threatening condition that occurs when blood flow to the intestines is compromised. The most common cause of AMI is embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery, often in patients with atrial fibrillation. However, this patient's history of recent myocardial infarction suggests that his AMI may be due to in situ thrombosis of the mesenteric vessels, which is the second most common cause of AMI.

The definitive test for diagnosing AMI is mesenteric angiography, which can directly visualize the occlusion. However, this test is invasive and not always readily available. Therefore, in many cases, a CT angiogram is performed instead, which is less invasive and can also visualize the mesenteric vessels.

question: A 34-year-old woman presents to the plastic surgery office 3 months following a rhinoplasty procedure. The patient has been recovering well. However, she has noticed a small whistling noise when she respires through her nose, which you appreciate on physical exam. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this phenomenon?

answer_choices.B: A septal hematoma causing a perforation
answer_choices.C: A deviated septum that is now straight, resulting in altered nasal airflow
answer_choices.D: Excessive columellar show resulting in increased nasal airflow

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician because of a whistling sound during respiration for the past 3 weeks. He reports that the whistling is becoming louder, and is especially loud when he exercises. He says the noise is frustrating for him. Six months ago, the patient underwent outpatient treatment for an uncomplicated nasal fracture after being hit in the nose by a high-velocity stray baseball. Since the accident, the patient has been taking aspirin for pain. He has a history of asymptomatic nasal polyps. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following would have prevented the whistling during respiration?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of nasal trauma and subsequent development of a whistling sound during respiration is suggestive of a septal perforation. Septal perforations can occur as a complication of nasal trauma, especially if a septal hematoma forms and is not promptly drained. The hematoma can disrupt the blood supply to the septum, leading to ischemia and necrosis of the septal cartilage, and ultimately resulting in a septal perforation. Therefore, prompt drainage of a septal hematoma following nasal trauma would have prevented the development of a septal perforation and the subsequent whistling sound during respiration.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother with the complaint of increasing bilateral nasal obstruction for the past 5 months. He also complains of continuous bilateral nasal discharge. He adds that he no longer has any sense of smell of foods. Past medical history is significant for growth retardation and chronic bronchitis at the age of 6 years. Anterior rhinoscopy reveals multiple semi-transparent, soft and mobile masses in the middle meatus. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic sinusitis, nasal polyposis, and bronchiectasis is suggestive of cystic fibrosis (CF). CF is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by abnormal function of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator, a protein that regulates chloride transport across cell membranes. This results in the production of thick, viscous secretions in multiple organ systems. In the respiratory tract, these secretions cause chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, and sinusitis. Nasal polyps are seen in up to 48% of patients with CF and are thought to result from chronic inflammation and edema of the sinonasal mucosa. Nasal polyps can cause symptoms of chronic nasal obstruction, discharge, and decreased sense of smell.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with complaints of chronic congestion. She notes that she has always had trouble breathing through her nose, and her new husband has told her that she breathes loudly when she sleeps. She denies frequent infections or allergies. She has no chronic medical problems and takes no medications. Family history is also insignificant. The blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, heart rate is 74/min, and respiratory rate is 14/min. On physical examination, her lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Intranasal inspection reveals a deviated septum. She is referred to an otolaryngologist for surgical evaluation. When discussing the surgical options for this condition, she asks if she will be given propofol for anesthesia. Which of the following forms of anesthesia may utilize intravenous propofol?
few_shot.explanation:
Propofol is a sedative-hypnotic agent used for the induction and maintenance of anesthesia or sedation. It enhances the activity of GABA, the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, leading to a decrease in neuronal activity. Propofol is used in moderate to deep sedation, and general anesthesia. In moderate sedation, the patient can respond to verbal commands, either alone or accompanied by light tactile stimulation. In deep sedation, the patient cannot be easily aroused but can respond to repeated or painful stimulation. The ability to independently maintain ventilatory function may be impaired, and the patient may require assistance in maintaining a patent airway. Cardiovascular function is usually maintained.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician's office by her parents with a complaint of foul-smelling discharge from one side of her nose for the past 2 weeks. There is no history of trauma to the nose and she was completely fine during her well-child visit last month. She was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. She is up to date on all vaccines and is meeting all developmental milestones. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the nose reveals a mucoid discharge oozing out from the left nostril. The girl panics when the physician tries to use a nasal speculum. Palpation over the facial bones does not reveal any tenderness. An X-ray image of the paranasal sinuses shows no abnormality. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this condition?
few_shot.explanation:
The most common cause of unilateral nasal discharge in children is a foreign body in the nose. The discharge is typically mucopurulent and foul-smelling. The foreign body can be any object small enough to fit into the nostril, such as a bead, a small toy, or food. The child may not remember or may not be able to communicate that they inserted the object into their nose. The diagnosis can be confirmed by direct visualization of the foreign body. If the child is uncooperative, as in this case, removal can be performed under sedation or anesthesia.

few_shot.question: Thirty minutes after surgical nasal polyp removal for refractory rhinitis, a 40-year-old man has retrosternal chest tightness and shortness of breath in the post-anesthesia care unit. The surgical course was uncomplicated and the patient was successfully extubated before arrival to the unit. He received 0.5 L of lactated Ringer's solution intraoperatively. The patient was given morphine and ketorolac for postoperative pain. He has a history of obstructive sleep apnea, asthma, hypertension, and sensitivity to aspirin. His daily medications include metoprolol and lisinopril. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. Pulse oximetry shows an oxygen concentration of 97% with support of 100% oxygen via face mask. Bilateral wheezes are heard in both lungs. Breath sounds are decreased. The patient's face appears flushed. ECG shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of asthma and sensitivity to aspirin, along with his new-onset wheezing, flushing, and shortness of breath, is suggestive of a pseudoallergic reaction (ie, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease [AERD]). AERD is characterized by the triad of asthma, nasal polyposis, and hypersensitivity to cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) inhibitors (eg, aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs). The exact pathogenesis of AERD is not well understood, but it is thought to be related to inhibition of COX-1 with a subsequent shunting of arachidonic acid metabolism to the 5-lipoxygenase pathway. This results in overproduction of proinflammatory cysteinyl leukotrienes and underproduction of anti-inflammatory prostaglandins, leading to increased inflammation and bronchoconstriction. The patient's recent administration of ketorolac, a COX-1 inhibitor, likely triggered his symptoms.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 30-year-old man presents to his primary care provider complaining of drowsiness at work for the past several months. However, he often falls asleep during meetings even though he usually gets a good night sleep and has limited his exposure to alcohol and caffeine in the evening. His past medical history is noncontributory. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination is unremarkable. The primary care provider recommends keeping a sleep journal and provides a questionnaire for the patient’s wife. The patient returns one month later to report no changes to his condition. The sleep journal reveals that the patient is getting sufficient sleep and wakes up rested. The questionnaire reveals that the patient does not snore nor does he stop breathing during his sleep. A sleep study reveals mean sleep latency of 6 minutes. Which of the following is the best course of treatment for this patient’s condition?

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old man presents to his primary care physician concerned about excessive sleepiness that has persisted his entire life. He notes that he has been having difficulty with his job as a waiter because he often falls asleep suddenly during the day. He also experiences a sensation of dreaming as he goes to sleep even though he still feels awake. He sleeps about 10 hours per day and still feels tired throughout the day. The patient has even reported driving into a tree once as he fell asleep while driving. The patient often stays up late at night working on the computer. Physical exam demonstrates an obese young man who appears tired. His oropharynx demonstrates high palatal ridges and good dental hygiene. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

answer_choices.A: Continuous positive airway pressure at night
answer_choices.C: Recommend scheduling regular naps and more time for sleep at night
answer_choices.D: Recommend to abstain from activities at night that expose the patient to blue light

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's excessive daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations are suggestive of narcolepsy. Narcolepsy is a chronic sleep disorder characterized by overwhelming daytime drowsiness and sudden attacks of sleep. It is caused by a deficiency in hypocretin (orexin), a neurotransmitter that regulates arousal, wakefulness, and appetite. The most effective treatment for narcolepsy is usually a combination of medications and lifestyle changes. Medications often include stimulants, such as modafinil, and inhibitors of dopamine reuptake, such as methylphenidate.

few_shot.question:
A 19-year-old man is seen by his primary care physician. The patient has a history of excessive daytime sleepiness going back several years. He has begun experiencing episodes in which his knees become weak and he drops to the floor when he laughs. He has a history of marijuana use. His family history is notable for hypertension and cardiac disease. His primary care physician refers him for a sleep study, and which confirms your suspected diagnosis.

Which of the following is the best first-line pharmacological treatment for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's excessive daytime sleepiness and episodes of muscle weakness triggered by strong emotions (eg, laughter) are suggestive of narcolepsy, a chronic sleep disorder characterized by overwhelming daytime drowsiness and sudden attacks of sleep. The muscle weakness, known as cataplexy, is pathognomonic for narcolepsy. Other symptoms can include sleep paralysis and hallucinations.

The first-line treatment for narcolepsy is modafinil, a non-amphetamine stimulant that promotes wakefulness. It is thought to work by increasing the release of monoamines, especially dopamine, from the synaptic cleft. Other stimulants, such as amphetamines and methylphenidate, can be used if modafinil is not effective.

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man is brought to the physician by his wife for the evaluation of abnormal sleep patterns that began 10 days ago. She reports that he has only been sleeping 2–3 hours nightly during this time and has been jogging for long periods of the night on the treadmill. The patient has also been excessively talkative and has missed work on several occasions to write emails to his friends and relatives to convince them to invest in a new business idea that he has had. He has chronic kidney disease requiring hemodialysis, but he has refused to take his medications because he believes that he is cured. Eight months ago, he had a 3-week long period of persistent sadness and was diagnosed with major depressive disorder. Mental status examination shows psychomotor agitation and pressured speech. Treatment of this patient's condition should include which of the following drugs?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's decreased need for sleep, increased talkativeness, and grandiosity are suggestive of a manic episode. His history of major depressive disorder and current manic episode meet criteria for bipolar I disorder. First-line treatment options for acute mania include lithium, valproate, and atypical antipsychotics. However, lithium is contraindicated in this patient due to his chronic kidney disease. Valproate is a good option for this patient because it can be used safely in patients with renal disease. It is hepatically metabolized and undergoes minimal renal elimination. Valproate is also highly protein bound, and free levels can increase in hypoalbuminemic states (eg, nephrotic syndrome). Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 63-year-old man presents to his primary care physician complaining of excessive daytime sleepiness. He explains that this problem has worsened slowly over the past few years but is now interfering with his ability to play with his grandchildren. He worked previously as an overnight train conductor, but he has been retired for the past 3 years. He sleeps approximately 8-9 hours per night and believes his sleep quality is good; however, his wife notes that he often snores loudly during sleep. He has never experienced muscle weakness or hallucinations. He has also been experiencing headaches in the morning and endorses a depressed mood. His physical exam is most notable for his large body habitus, with a BMI of 34. What is the best description of the underlying mechanism for this patient's excessive daytime sleepiness?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's excessive daytime sleepiness, loud snoring, and obesity are suggestive of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). OSA is characterized by repetitive episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to recurrent arousals and sleep fragmentation. The most common cause of OSA is obesity, which leads to poor oropharyngeal tone and increased upper airway resistance. This is due to fatty infiltration of the soft tissues surrounding the upper airway, leading to a narrowed airway lumen. The airway is most likely to collapse during sleep, when the muscles surrounding the airway are relaxed. This leads to recurrent episodes of apnea and hypopnea, which can cause hypoxemia and hypercapnia. The hypoxemia and hypercapnia can lead to morning headaches, as seen in this patient. The recurrent arousals lead to nonrestorative sleep and excessive daytime sleepiness. The sleep fragmentation can also lead to mood disturbances, such as depression.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man presents to his geriatrician due to waking several times during the night and also rising too early in the morning. He says this has worsened over the past 7 months. In the morning, he feels unrefreshed and tired. His medical history is positive for hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has never been a smoker. He denies drinking alcohol or caffeine prior to bedtime. Vital signs reveal a temperature of 36.6°C (97.8°F), blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, and heart rate of 77/min. Physical examination is unremarkable. After discussing good sleep hygiene with the patient, which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's difficulty falling asleep, frequent awakenings, and early morning awakenings are suggestive of insomnia, a common complaint in the elderly. Insomnia is defined as difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or nonrestorative sleep, for at least 1 month. It is often associated with daytime fatigue, impaired concentration, and mood disturbance. Insomnia can be due to many causes, including poor sleep hygiene, medical illness, psychiatric disease, or certain medications. In this patient, no specific cause is identified, so he likely has primary insomnia.

The first-line treatment for insomnia is nonpharmacologic and includes sleep hygiene measures (eg, regular sleep schedule, comfortable sleep environment, avoiding caffeine and stimulating activities before bedtime). If these general measures are ineffective, short-term treatment with a sedative-hypnotic medication may be beneficial. Zolpidem is a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic that is commonly used for the short-term treatment of insomnia. It has a rapid onset of action and a short half-life, with fewer side effects (eg, hangover, dependence) compared to benzodiazepines.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: An 11-year-old boy was brought in by his mother with red tender bumps on his legs. The patient’s mother says that his symptoms started 3 days ago with a low-grade fever, malaise, and joint pain. He began to improve over the next 2 days, but this morning, when he woke up, she noticed multiple painful red bumps on his shins. Past medical history is significant for a recent severe sore throat and fever 1 week ago which resolved without treatment. The vital signs include: temperature 38.0°C (100.4°F), blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse 85/min, and respiratory rate 15/min. Physical examination reveals multiple, firm and tender erythematous nodules with indistinct borders, averaging 4 cm in diameter. Lesions are localized to the anterior surface of the lower legs. No evidence of drainage, bleeding, abscess formation or ulceration. Which of the following is the next best diagnostic step in this patient?

few_shot.question: An otherwise healthy 28-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 14-day history of a painful red nodules on her legs associated with malaise and mild joint pains. She reports that the nodules were initially smaller and distinct but some have fused together over the past 3–4 days and now appear like bruises. There is no preceding history of fever, trauma, or insect bites. Her vital signs are within normal limits. A photograph of the tender lesions on her shins is shown. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Complete blood count and antistreptolysin O (ASO) titers are within the reference range. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 30 mm/h. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management ?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of tender, erythematous nodules on the anterior shins that have coalesced to form bruise-like lesions is consistent with erythema nodosum (EN). EN is a type of panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat) that is often associated with systemic diseases, including streptococcal infections, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and tuberculosis (TB). The absence of preceding fever and negative ASO titers make streptococcal infection less likely. The absence of gastrointestinal symptoms makes inflammatory bowel disease less likely. Therefore, the next step in management should be to evaluate for sarcoidosis and TB, the most common causes of EN. Chest x-ray is the initial test of choice for both these conditions and can show bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in sarcoidosis or apical lung lesions in TB.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 39-year-old woman presents to your office with 4 days of fever, sore throat, generalized aching, arthralgias, and tender nodules on both of her shins that arose in the last 48 hours. Her medical history is negative for disease and she does not take oral contraceptives or any other medication regularly. The physical examination reveals the vital signs that include body temperature 38.5°C (101.3°F), heart rate 85/min, blood pressure 120/65 mm Hg, tender and enlarged submandibular lymph nodes, and an erythematous, edematous, and swollen pharynx with enlarged tonsils and a patchy white exudate on the surface. She is not pregnant. Examination of the lower limbs reveals erythematous, tender, immobile nodules on both shins. You do not identify ulcers or similar lesions on other areas of her body. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
Erythema nodosum is a type of panniculitis (inflammation of the subcutaneous fat) that presents as tender, erythematous nodules on the anterior shins. It is often associated with systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and arthralgias. Erythema nodosum can be idiopathic or associated with various conditions, including streptococcal infections, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and medications (eg, oral contraceptives, sulfonamides). In this patient, the pharyngitis with fever, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar exudate suggest a streptococcal infection as the underlying cause of her erythema nodosum.

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy presents to his pediatrician accompanied by his mother for evaluation of a rash. The rash appeared a little over a week ago, and since that time the boy has felt tired. He is less interested in playing outside, preferring to remain indoors because his knees and stomach hurt. His past medical history is significant for an upper respiratory infection that resolved uneventfully without treatment 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 18/min. Physical exam shows scattered maroon macules and papules on the lower extremities. The abdomen is diffusely tender to palpation. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy or conjunctival injection. Which of the following will most likely be found in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of palpable purpura, arthralgia, and abdominal pain following an upper respiratory infection is suggestive of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura). This is the most common vasculitis of childhood and often presents following a recent infection. It is caused by the deposition of IgA immune complexes in the skin, gut, and glomeruli, leading to a leukocytoclastic vasculitis that affects small vessels. The classic tetrad of symptoms includes palpable purpura (often over the buttocks and lower extremities), arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal disease (hematuria and/or proteinuria). The abdominal pain can be severe and may be associated with intussusception.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother with fever, sore throat, and a rash. The patient’s mother says that her symptoms started 3 days ago with a high-grade fever, sore throat, vomiting, and malaise. Twenty-four hours later, she says a rash appeared on the patient’s neck and, over the next 24 hours, spread to the trunk and extremities. The patient’s mother mentions she had a bad sore throat about a week ago but denies any chills, seizures, or sick contacts. The patient has no significant past medical history and takes no current medications. Her birth was uncomplicated, and she has been meeting all developmental milestones. The patient’s vital signs include: pulse 90/min, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 39.0℃ (102.2℉), and blood pressure 90/50 mm Hg. On physical examination, the patient has a whole-body, erythematous punctate, maculopapular rash, as shown in the exhibit (see image). Oropharyngeal examination shows circumoral pallor and a red tongue. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.D: Serology for IgM and IgG antibodies

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of high fever, sore throat, and a diffuse, erythematous, sandpaper-like rash that started on the neck and spread to the trunk and extremities is consistent with scarlet fever. Scarlet fever is a disease caused by group A Streptococcus (GAS) that produces an erythrogenic toxin, resulting in the characteristic rash. The rash usually spares the palms and soles and is associated with circumoral pallor and a red, "strawberry" tongue. The next best step in the management of this patient is to perform a rapid antigen detection test to confirm GAS pharyngitis. If the rapid test is negative and clinical suspicion for GAS pharyngitis remains high, a throat culture should be obtained, as the rapid test can yield false-negative results.

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 5-day history of fever, malaise, and joint pain. He had a sore throat 4 weeks ago that resolved without treatment. His temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F) and blood pressure is 84/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows several firm, painless nodules under the skin near his elbows and the dorsal aspect of both wrists. Cardiopulmonary examination shows bilateral basilar crackles and a blowing, holosystolic murmur heard best at the cardiac apex. Both knee joints are warm. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 129 mm/h. The immune response seen in this patient is most likely due to the presence of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, migratory polyarthritis, carditis, and subcutaneous nodules are suggestive of acute rheumatic fever (ARF), a delayed immune-mediated complication of group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis. The skin nodules seen in ARF are firm, painless, and measure 0.5-2 cm in diameter. They are typically located over bony prominences or extensor surfaces of joints. The carditis of ARF manifests as a new murmur, pericarditis, and/or congestive heart failure. The arthritis is migratory, involving large joints.

ARF is thought to result from molecular mimicry, in which structural components of GAS resemble molecules in human tissues. GAS M protein, a virulence factor that inhibits phagocytosis, shares antigenic epitopes with human tissues (eg, myocardium, synovium, brain). Antibodies formed against M protein can cross-react with human tissues, leading to inflammation and the clinical manifestations of ARF.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 68-year-old man from California presents for a routine checkup. He does not have any complaints. few_shot.question: A 68-year-old man comes to the physician 3 months after noticing skin changes on his scalp. When he scrapes off the crust of the lesion, it reappears after a few days. Occasionally, his scalp itches or he notices a burning sensation. He had a mole removed on his right forearm 5 years ago. He is a retired winemaker. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows multiple rough patches on his scalp. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of sun exposure and the presence of rough, scaly patches on sun-exposed areas of his skin are consistent with actinic keratosis (AK). AK is a premalignant lesion that can progress to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). It is caused by cumulative sun exposure and subsequent UV radiation-induced DNA damage. AKs are most commonly found in fair-skinned individuals on sun-exposed areas (eg, face, scalp, ears, dorsal hands/forearms). Lesions appear as rough, erythematous papules that may be easier felt (like sandpaper) than seen. Dermatoscopic examination may show a strawberry pattern characterized by a red pseudo-network and prominent follicular openings. 

Hence, the answer is [B].

Actinic keratosis is a common precancerous skin lesion that occurs on sun-exposed areas in fair-skinned, elderly individuals. It presents as a rough, scaly, sand paper-like plaque that is easier felt than seen. The base is usually erythematous. Actinic keratosis is a precursor to squamous cell carcinoma, and therefore, early recognition and treatment are important.

Lesions appear as well-circumscribed, tan, brown, or black papules or plaques with a characteristic "stuck-on" appearance. The surface is often verrucous or velvety, and it may also appear greasy. Although seborrheic keratoses can be found anywhere on the body, they are most commonly located on the trunk, head, and neck. Lesions are usually asymptomatic, but patients may complain of pruritus or irritation, especially if the lesions are traumatically disrupted. Seborrheic keratoses have no malignant potential, but sudden appearance of multiple pruritic seborrheic keratoses (Leser-Trélat sign) can be a cutaneous marker of internal malignancy, most commonly adenocarcinoma of the gastrointestinal tract.

His grandson, who often spends the weekends with him, recently had impetigo. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis of his thumbs. Five months ago, he was treated for a gout attack of his left hallux. Current medications include captopril, hydrochlorothiazide, simvastatin, allopurinol, and ibuprofen. This patient's pruritic rash with tense blisters is consistent with bullous pemphigoid (BP), an autoimmune blistering disorder that typically occurs in elderly patients. BP is characterized by an urticarial or eczematous prodrome that can last for several months, followed by the development of tense bullae. The bullae are typically located on the trunk and flexural surfaces of the extremities, and the oral mucosa is usually spared. The Nikolsky sign (ie, formation of a blister upon lateral pressure to the skin) is negative in BP.

BP is caused by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins BP230 and BP180, which are located on the basement membrane of the epidermis. These autoantibodies activate the complement cascade, leading to an inflammatory response that causes subepidermal blistering. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows a linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane, which is diagnostic of BP.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

The oral mucosa is almost always involved, and the skin lesions are often painful.

The neighbor helped him home, but found him again 1 hour later slumped over on his driveway in a puddle of vomit. He is oriented to self, but not to place or time. His vitals are as follows: temperature, 36.9°C (98.5°F); pulse, 82/min; respirations, 28/min; and blood pressure, 122/80 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination indicates no abnormalities. He is unable to cooperate for a neurological examination. Physical examination reveals muscle spasms involving his arms and jaw. Laboratory studies show:
Na+ 140 mEq/L

The calculated serum osmolality is 294 mOsm/kg. The arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.25 and a lactate level of 3.2 mmol/L. Urine examination shows oxalate crystals and the absence of ketones. What is the most appropriate treatment indicated for this patient experiencing apparent substance toxicity?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with ethylene glycol poisoning. Ethylene glycol is a common component of antifreeze and is often ingested accidentally or in suicide attempts. It is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and is metabolized in the liver by alcohol dehydrogenase to glycoaldehyde, which is then further metabolized to glycolic acid, glyoxylic acid, and finally oxalic acid. These metabolites are responsible for the major toxic effects of ethylene glycol ingestion.

The patient's presentation of altered mental status, vomiting, and muscle spasms is consistent with the early, or neurologic, phase of ethylene glycol poisoning, which occurs within 12 hours of ingestion. This phase is due to the direct effects of ethylene glycol on the central nervous system.

The patient's laboratory findings of an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis, increased osmolal gap, and calcium oxalate crystals in the urine are consistent with the metabolic phase of ethylene glycol poisoning, which occurs 12-24 hours after ingestion. This phase is due to the metabolism of ethylene glycol to its toxic metabolites.

The treatment of ethylene glycol poisoning involves blocking its metabolism to its toxic metabolites. This can be accomplished with either ethanol or fomepizole, both of which inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase. Fomepizole is generally preferred because it has fewer side effects and is easier to administer.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old male with a history of hepatitis C cirrhosis status post TIPS procedure is brought in by his wife to the emergency department because he has been acting disoriented, slurring his speech, and sleeping throughout the day. On arrival the patient is afebrile and his vital signs are pulse is 87/min, blood pressure is 137/93 mmHg, and respirations are 12/min with shallow breaths. Examination reveals a jaundiced male who appears older than stated age. Abdominal exam is positive for a fluid wave and shifting dullness to percussion. You note enlarged breasts, decreased facial hair, 3+ patellar reflexes bilaterally, and the following in the upper extremity (Video A). Paracentesis reveals ascitic fluid with neutrophil counts of < 100 cells/mcL. Serum creatinine is 1.0 and BUN is 15. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of cirrhosis, altered mental status, and asterixis (flapping tremor) is suggestive of hepatic encephalopathy (HE). HE is a potentially reversible metabolic encephalopathy seen in patients with liver disease. Precipitating factors include infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, electrolyte abnormalities, and constipation. However, in many cases, no precipitating factor is identified. The mainstay of treatment for HE is lactulose, a nonabsorbable disaccharide that traps and expels ammonia in the colon. Lactulose is converted by colonic bacteria into lactic acid and acetic acid, which acidify the colonic contents. The acidic environment promotes conversion of ammonia (NH3), which is absorbable, to ammonium (NH4+), which is not absorbable. Lactulose also acts as a cathartic, reducing colonic bacterial production of ammonia.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with esophageal varices, alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatic encephalopathy, portal hypertension, and recent onset confusion. The patient’s husband does not recall her past medical history but knows her current medications and states that she is quite disciplined about taking them. Current medications are spironolactone, labetalol, lactulose, and furosemide. Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), heart rate is 115/min, blood pressure is 105/62 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 12/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. On physical examination, the patient is disoriented, lethargic, and poorly responsive to commands. A cardiac examination is unremarkable. Lungs are clear to auscultation. The abdomen is distended, tense, and mildly tender. Mild asterixis is present. Neurologic examination is normal. The digital rectal examination reveals guaiac negative stool. Laboratory findings are significant for the following:
Basic metabolic panel Unremarkable
Platelet count 95,500/µL
Leukocyte count 14,790/µL
Hematocrit 33% (baseline is 30%)
Which of the following would most likely be of diagnostic value in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, leukocytosis, and new-onset encephalopathy in the setting of tense ascites are concerning for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). SBP is a common and potentially fatal complication of cirrhosis and ascites. It is often associated with gastrointestinal bleeding, which can translocate bacteria from the gut lumen into the bloodstream and then into the ascitic fluid. However, SBP can also occur in the absence of a clear precipitating event. The diagnosis of SBP is made by paracentesis with ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear leukocyte count >250/mm3. Empiric antibiotic therapy with a third-generation cephalosporin (eg, cefotaxime) should be initiated promptly after the paracentesis is performed, without waiting for culture results.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department for fever and altered mental status. The patient was found by his wife in his chair at home. She noticed he responded incoherently to her questions. He has a past medical history of pancreatitis and alcohol abuse and is currently in a rehabilitation program. His temperature is 103°F (39.4°C), blood pressure is 127/68 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 12/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Laboratory values are obtained and shown below.

Serum:
Na+: 139 mEq/L
Cl-: 100 mEq/L
K+: 4.3 mEq/L
HCO3-: 25 mEq/L
BUN: 29 mg/dL
Glucose: 99 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.5 mg/dL
Ca2+: 5.2 mg/dL
AST: 12 U/L
ALT: 10 U/L
1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol: 50 nmol/L

Physical exam notes a diffusely distended and tender abdomen. Which of the following is the most likely symptom this patient is experiencing secondary to his laboratory abnormalities?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of pancreatitis and alcohol abuse, along with his current presentation of fever, altered mental status, and a diffusely distended and tender abdomen, is concerning for acute pancreatitis. The most common causes of acute pancreatitis are gallstones and alcohol abuse. The diagnosis is suggested by the presence of two of the following three criteria: (1) characteristic abdominal pain, (2) serum lipase or amylase level at least three times the upper limit of normal, and (3) characteristic findings of acute pancreatitis on imaging.

This patient's laboratory results show a low calcium level (5.2 mg/dL; reference range 8.5-10.5 mg/dL). Hypocalcemia is a common electrolyte abnormality seen in acute pancreatitis. It is caused by precipitation of calcium soaps in the abdominal cavity (saponification) and hypoalbuminemia. Hypocalcemia can cause a variety of symptoms, including perioral numbness, paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, and laryngospasm. However, the majority of patients with hypocalcemia are asymptomatic, especially if the decrease in calcium levels is chronic or occurs slowly over time.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old woman with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis and recurrent esophageal varices who recently underwent transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) placement is brought to the emergency room by her daughter due to confusion and agitation. Starting this morning, the patient has appeared sleepy, difficult to arouse, and slow to respond to questions. Her temperature is 97.6°F (36.4°C), blood pressure is 122/81 mmHg, pulse is 130/min, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. She repeatedly falls asleep and is combative during the exam. Laboratory values are notable for a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L. The patient is given normal saline with potassium. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of cirrhosis, recent TIPS procedure, and new-onset confusion and agitation are suggestive of hepatic encephalopathy (HE). HE is a reversible syndrome of impaired brain function occurring in patients with advanced liver disease. It can present with a spectrum of neurologic and psychiatric abnormalities, ranging from minimal cognitive deficits to coma. Precipitating factors include medications (eg, sedatives, opioids), infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hypokalemia), and procedures such as TIPS or large-volume paracentesis without albumin replacement.

The mainstay of treatment for HE is lactulose, a nonabsorbable disaccharide that traps nitrogen in the colon by acidifying the gut lumen and converting ammonia to ammonium. This reduces the absorption of ammonia and promotes its excretion. Lactulose also has a cathartic effect, which helps to eliminate nitrogenous substances from the colon.

Therefore, the answer is [B].
