few_shot.question: A 25-year-old woman presents to an urgent care center following a presumed bee sting while at a picnic with her friends. She immediately developed a skin rash and swelling over her arms and face. She endorses diffuse itching over her torso. She denies any episodes similar to this and has no significant medical history. She does note that her father has an allergy to peanuts. Her blood pressure is 92/54 mm Hg, heart rate, 118/min, respiratory rate 18/min. On physical examination, the patient has severe edema over her face and inspiratory stridor. Of the following options, this patient is likely experiencing which of the following hypersensitivity reactions?

answer_choices.D: Mixed type 1 and type 3 hypersensitivity reactions

few_shot.explanation:
This patient is experiencing anaphylaxis, a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction. Anaphylaxis is a type I hypersensitivity reaction, which is an immediate (within minutes to hours) IgE-mediated immune response. Initial exposure to an allergen (eg, bee venom, peanuts, shellfish) stimulates a Th2 response, leading to the production of allergen-specific IgE antibodies. These antibodies bind to mast cells and basophils via Fc receptors. Subsequent exposure to the same allergen cross-links the cell-bound IgE antibodies, leading to degranulation and release of preformed mediators (eg, histamine, tryptase) and newly synthesized mediators (eg, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, platelet-activating factor). These mediators cause increased vascular permeability (leading to edema and hypotension), smooth muscle contraction (causing bronchospasm and increased gastrointestinal motility), and inflammation (leading to urticaria and angioedema).

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old man comes into the urgent care clinic with an intensely itchy rash on the bilateral mid-lower extremities, with a fine linear demarcation approximately an inch above his socks. The rash is arranged in streaks of erythema with superimposed vesicular lesions. The patient states that he recently began hiking in the woods behind his house, but he denies any local chemical exposures to his lower extremities. His vital signs include: blood pressure of 127/76, heart rate of 82/min, and respiratory rate of 12/min. Of the following options, which is the mechanism of his reaction?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's intensely pruritic, linear, vesicular rash on the lower extremities is consistent with contact dermatitis due to exposure to poison ivy, oak, or sumac. These plants contain urushiol, which is a potent antigen that can cause a type IV hypersensitivity reaction in sensitized individuals. This reaction is mediated by T cells and is also known as a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction because it typically occurs 24-72 hours after exposure. The reaction begins when the antigen is taken up by Langerhans cells in the skin, which then migrate to regional lymph nodes and present the antigen to naive T cells. This leads to the activation and clonal expansion of antigen-specific T cells, which then migrate back to the skin and release inflammatory cytokines upon re-exposure to the antigen. This results in the characteristic skin findings of erythema, induration, and vesicle formation.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy is rushed to the urgent care department from a friend’s birthday party with breathing trouble. He is immediately placed on supplemental oxygen therapy. The patient’s father explains that peanut butter treats were served at the event, but he reported not having witnessed his son actually eat one. During the party, the patient approached his father with facial flushing, difficulty breathing, and itching of his face and neck. The patient was born at 40 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. He has met all age-related developmental milestones and is fully vaccinated. His past medical history is significant for peanut allergy and asthma. He carries an emergency inhaler. Family history is noncontributory. The patient’s vitals signs include a blood pressure of 110/85 mm Hg, a heart rate of 110/min, a respiratory rate of 25/min, and a temperature of 37.2°C (99.0°F). Physical examination reveals severe facial edema and severe audible stridor in both lungs. Which of the following types of hypersensitivity reaction is the most likely in this patient?

answer_choices.D: Mixed anaphylactic and cytotoxic hypersensitivity reaction

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of facial flushing, difficulty breathing, and itching of his face and neck are consistent with an anaphylactic reaction. Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction that is rapid in onset. It is most commonly associated with foods (eg, peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish), medications (eg, penicillin), and insect stings. The reaction is due to the release of mediators (eg, histamine, tryptase, platelet-activating factor) from mast cells and basophils, typically through an immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated mechanism. This is known as a type I hypersensitivity reaction.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 62-year-old man with a history of chronic bronchitis comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of worsening shortness of breath and cough productive of thick sputum. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years but quit 5 years ago. Physical examination shows an increased anteroposterior chest diameter and coarse crackles in the lower lung fields bilaterally. Treatment with a drug that directly antagonizes the effects of vagal stimulation on the airways is begun. Which of the following drugs was most likely started?

few_shot.question: A 20-year-old man presents to your office with dyspnea, reporting nocturnal cough. You note expiratory wheezing on auscultation. Chest x-ray reveals increased anteroposterior diameter. Past medical history is significant for multiple episodes of "bronchitis" as a child. Which of the following drugs would be most effective for long-term treatment of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent "bronchitis" and current symptoms of dyspnea and nocturnal cough are suggestive of asthma. Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by bronchial hyperresponsiveness and variable airflow obstruction. Symptoms include wheezing, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea. The diagnosis is confirmed by pulmonary function tests showing reversible airflow obstruction (ie, increase in FEV1 or peak expiratory flow rate ≥12% following bronchodilator administration).

The mainstay of long-term asthma treatment is control of the underlying inflammation. Inhaled corticosteroids (eg, fluticasone) are the most effective anti-inflammatory medications for long-term control of persistent asthma. Regular use decreases airway hyperresponsiveness, inhibits inflammatory cell migration and activation, and blocks late-phase reaction to allergen. Inhaled corticosteroids also decrease airway mucus production and improve symptoms, lung function, and quality of life, and they decrease the frequency of asthma exacerbations and asthma-related mortality.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 20-year-old man comes to the physician because of recurrent episodes of shortness of breath and a nonproductive cough for the past 4 months. He has two episodes per week, which resolve spontaneously with rest. Twice a month, he wakes up at night with shortness of breath. His pulse is 73/min, respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Spirometry shows an FVC of 95%, an FEV1:FVC ratio of 0.85, and an FEV1 of 81% of predicted. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent episodes of shortness of breath and cough are suggestive of asthma. The diagnosis of asthma is supported by the presence of symptoms that vary over time and in intensity, and by the presence of normal lung function between episodes. The severity of asthma is classified based on the frequency of daytime symptoms, nighttime awakenings, interference with normal activity, short-acting β2-agonist use for symptom control, and lung function (FEV1 and FEV1:FVC ratio). This patient's symptoms (ie, daytime symptoms >2 days/week, nighttime awakenings >2 times/month) are consistent with moderate persistent asthma.

The goal of asthma therapy is to achieve good symptom control and to minimize future risk of exacerbations, fixed airflow limitation, and side effects. The Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) recommends that all patients with asthma, even those with the mildest form of the disease, receive a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) to reduce the risk of serious exacerbations and to control symptoms. For patients with moderate persistent asthma, GINA recommends the use of a combination of a low-dose ICS and a long-acting β2-agonist (LABA) as initial therapy. Therefore, this patient should be started on a combination inhaler containing budesonide (an ICS) and formoterol (a LABA).

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 70-year-old man presents to a physician with a cough and difficulty breathing during the last 7 years. He has smoked since his teenage years and regularly inhales tiotropium, formoterol, and budesonide and takes oral theophylline. The number of exacerbations has been increasing over the last 6 months. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), the heart rate is 92/min, the blood pressure is 134/88 mm Hg and the respiratory rate is 26/min. On chest auscultation breath sounds are diffusely decreased and bilateral rhonchi are present. Pulse oximetry shows his resting oxygen saturation to be 88%. Chest radiogram shows a flattened diaphragm, hyperlucency of the lungs, and a long, narrow heart shadow. The physician explains this condition to the patient and emphasizes the importance of smoking cessation. In addition to this, which of the following is most likely to reduce the risk of mortality from the condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, chronic cough, and dyspnea, along with physical examination findings of decreased breath sounds and rhonchi, are suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The chest x-ray findings of hyperlucency, a flattened diaphragm, and a long, narrow heart shadow are consistent with emphysema, a form of COPD. The most effective intervention to reduce mortality in patients with COPD is smoking cessation. However, this patient's resting oxygen saturation of 88% indicates significant hypoxemia, which is an indication for supplemental oxygen therapy. Long-term oxygen therapy has been shown to decrease mortality in patients with COPD who have severe resting hypoxemia (ie, PaO2 ≤55 mm Hg or SpO2 ≤88%).

Therefore, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [C] > [B] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 10-month history of progressive shortness of breath and a cough productive of a small amount of white phlegm. Bilateral end-expiratory wheezing is heard on auscultation of the chest. Pulmonary function tests show total lung capacity that is 108% of predicted, an FEV1 that is 56% of predicted, and an FEV1:FVC ratio of 62%. Which of the following interventions is most likely to slow the decline in FEV1 in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, chronic cough, and dyspnea, along with the presence of wheezing and obstructive findings on pulmonary function tests (eg, decreased FEV1:FVC ratio, increased total lung capacity due to air trapping), are consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The most effective intervention to slow the rate of decline in FEV1 in patients with COPD is smoking cessation. Smoking cessation also decreases the risk of death and improves quality of life in these patients.

So, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department because of difficulty breathing and chest tightness for the last 3 days. He also has a productive cough with excessive amounts of green sputum. He has had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease for the past 10 years, but says that the cough and sputum are different compared to his baseline. He took 2 doses of nebulized albuterol and ipratropium at home, but that did not completely relieve his symptoms. He has a 50 pack-year smoking history and drinks alcohol occasionally. His vital signs include a blood pressure of 110/60 mm Hg, a temperature of 37.2 °C (98.9°F), a respiratory rate of 26/min, an irregular radial pulse at a rate of 110–120/min, and an oxygen saturation of 88%. On physical examination, the patient appears drowsy, crackles are heard on chest auscultation bilaterally, and the heart sounds are irregular. A chest X-ray shows hyperinflation of the lungs bilaterally, and the diaphragm is flattened. An ECG is ordered and shown in the accompanying image. Which of the following is the best initial treatment for this patient’s arrhythmia?

answer_choices.A: Reversing bronchoconstriction and correction of electrolyte abnormalities
answer_choices.C: Catheter ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI)

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) due to a respiratory infection. The ECG shows atrial fibrillation (AF) with a rapid ventricular response, which is a common complication of COPD exacerbations. AF can be caused by a variety of factors in COPD patients, including hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, and increased adrenergic tone. The best initial treatment for AF in this setting is to address the underlying COPD exacerbation, which includes bronchodilator therapy and antibiotics. Additionally, electrolyte abnormalities such as hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, which can be caused by diuretic use and poor nutrition, should be corrected as they can contribute to the development of AF.

So, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

question: A 42-year-old man presents to establish care with a family physician after having progressively worsening back pain. He has recently migrated from Sweden and has not had any checkups in the last 3 years. He first started having back pain 3 years ago, but his pain has begun to be excruciating in the mornings. He is no longer able to get relief with over the counter medications. He also feels stiff every morning and this usually lasts between 30 minutes and an hour. Both of his knees are also very painful, particularly upon standing up from a seated position. His pain improves when he moves around, so he tries to be somewhat physically active. He also reports that he cannot use his hands for long periods of time due to joint pain and stiffness. His father and sister also have joint issues, and his mother was recently diagnosed with osteoporosis. He has been a smoker for 13 years. Upon physical examination, his wrist and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints are warm and swollen. Which of the following is the next best step in management?

answer_choices.A: Testing for serum Ca and PTH
answer_choices.C: Testing for serum ESR and autoantibodies

few_shot.question: A 59-year-old male with history of hypertension presents to your clinic for achy, stiff joints for the last several months. He states that he feels stiff in the morning, particularly in his shoulders, neck, and hips. Occasionally, the aches travel to his elbows and knees. His review of systems is positive for low-grade fever, tiredness and decreased appetite. On physical exam, there is decreased active and passive movements of his shoulders and hips secondary to pain without any obvious deformities or joint swelling. His laboratory tests are notable for an ESR of 52 mm/hr (normal for males: 0-22 mm/hr). What is the best treatment in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's age, symptoms of stiffness and aching in the shoulders and hips, and elevated ESR are suggestive of polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). PMR is an inflammatory disorder of unknown etiology that affects older individuals (age >50) and is characterized by aching and morning stiffness in the shoulders, hip girdle, and neck. Systemic symptoms such as low-grade fever, fatigue, and weight loss are also common. The diagnosis is clinical, and laboratory tests often show a markedly elevated ESR.

The treatment of choice for PMR is corticosteroids, which often result in dramatic improvement of symptoms within a few days. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can be used as adjunctive therapy but are not as effective.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man presents with worsening joint pain and stiffness. Past medical history is significant for rheumatoid arthritis, diagnosed 3 months ago and managed with celecoxib and methotrexate, and occasional gastric reflux, managed with omeprazole. His vitals are a pulse of 80/min, a respiratory rate of 16/min, and blood pressure of 122/80 mm Hg. On physical examination, the left wrist is swollen, stiff, and warm to touch, and the right wrist is red and warm. There is limited active and passive range of motion at the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable. A plain radiograph of the hands shows progressive degeneration of multiple joints. Another drug, etanercept, is added to help control progressive arthritis. Which of the following diagnostic tests should be ordered before starting this new medication in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
Etanercept is a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. TNF is a proinflammatory cytokine that plays a key role in granuloma formation and stabilization. Inhibition of TNF can therefore increase the risk of infections, particularly those caused by intracellular pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis. As a result, patients should be screened for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) prior to starting therapy with a TNF inhibitor. The preferred test in most situations is the interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), but the tuberculin skin test (TST) is an acceptable alternative. If the IGRA or TST is positive, active tuberculosis should be ruled out and treatment for LTBI should be initiated before starting the TNF inhibitor.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [D] > [C] > [B].

few_shot.question:
A 39-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressive pain and swelling of her wrists and hands for the past 2 months. Her hands are stiff in the morning; the stiffness decreases as she starts her chores. She also reports early-morning neck pain at rest for the past 3 weeks. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her sister has systemic lupus erythematosus. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows bilateral swelling and tenderness of the wrists, second, third, and fourth metacarpophalangeal joints; range of motion is limited by pain. There is no vertebral tenderness. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL
Leukocyte count 9,800/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 44 mm/h
Serum
Glucose 77 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL
Total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase 33 U/L
AST 14 U/L
ALT 13 U/L
Rheumatoid factor positive
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symmetric polyarthritis involving the small joints of the hands and morning stiffness lasting >1 hour are suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a systemic, inflammatory disorder that primarily involves the joints but can also affect other organ systems. Extra-articular manifestations of RA include rheumatoid nodules, pulmonary disease (eg, pleuritis, interstitial lung disease), ocular disease (eg, episcleritis, scleritis), and cardiac disease (eg, pericarditis, myocarditis). Cervical spine involvement can also occur and most commonly affects the atlantoaxial joint (C1-C2), leading to atlantoaxial subluxation (AAS). Patients with AAS may be asymptomatic or may present with occipital headache and neck pain, which can be exacerbated by neck movement. Neurologic findings (eg, weakness, hyperreflexia) may be present if there is spinal cord involvement. Because this patient has neck pain, the next best step is to obtain cervical spine radiographs to evaluate for AAS. Flexion views are often necessary to detect instability. If AAS is present, the patient should be referred for neurosurgical evaluation.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old man comes to the physician because of lower back pain that has become progressively worse over the past 2 months. The pain is also present at night and does not improve if he changes his position. He has stiffness for at least 1 hour each morning that improves throughout the day. Over the past 3 months, he has had 3 episodes of acute gout and was started on allopurinol. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows reduced lumbar flexion and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints. Passive flexion of the hip with the knee extended does not elicit pain on either side. Muscle strength and sensation to pinprick and light touch are normal. A pelvic x-ray confirms the diagnosis. The patient is started on indomethacin and an exercise program. Six weeks later, the patient reports no improvement in symptoms. Before initiating further pharmacotherapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's chronic back pain, morning stiffness, and decreased range of motion, along with radiographic evidence of sacroiliitis, are suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis (AS). AS is a chronic inflammatory disease that primarily affects the axial skeleton (ie, spine, sacroiliac joints). Extra-articular manifestations are also common and can include acute anterior uveitis, aortic regurgitation, and apical lung fibrosis.

First-line treatment for AS involves physical therapy and NSAIDs (eg, indomethacin). If patients fail to improve or have frequent flares, the addition of a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor (eg, infliximab, etanercept) is indicated. However, TNF inhibitors increase the risk of reactivation of latent tuberculosis (TB). Therefore, TB screening should be performed before starting a TNF inhibitor. The purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test or interferon-gamma release assay can be used for this purpose.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 51-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and progressive pain and stiffness in her hands for 3 months. She used to play tennis but stopped 1 month ago because of difficulties holding the racket and her skin becoming “very sensitive to sunlight.” Her last menstrual period was 1 year ago. She has diabetes mellitus controlled with insulin. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Vital signs are within normal limits. The patient appears tanned. The second and third metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands are tender to palpation and range of motion is limited. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fatigue, arthralgia, and skin hyperpigmentation are suggestive of hemochromatosis, a disorder characterized by increased intestinal absorption of dietary iron, saturation of iron-binding proteins, and deposition of hemosiderin (iron) in tissues. The iron deposition can lead to multiorgan damage, including cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus (bronze diabetes), restrictive cardiomyopathy, hypogonadism, and arthropathy. The arthropathy of hemochromatosis is typically seen in the metacarpophalangeal joints, especially the second and third joints, and can mimic osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis. The skin hyperpigmentation is due to increased melanin in the skin, which is thought to be due to increased iron stimulating melanocytes. 

The diagnosis of hemochromatosis is initially suggested by elevated serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation (>45%). The diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing for the C282Y mutation in the HFE gene.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

question: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents for difficulty breathing and bluish discoloration of the lips for the past hour. During the past 3 months, the patient has had several upper respiratory tract infections and poor weight gain. Physical examination shows crackles over both lung fields and enlargement of the tonsils and cervical lymph nodes. His serum IgA, IgE, and IgG titers are decreased. An x-ray of the chest shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Methenamine silver staining of bronchial lavage fluid shows disc-shaped cysts. A defect in which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

few_shot.question: A 5-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of difficulty breathing for the past hour. The parents report noisy breathing and bluish discoloration of their son's lips. During the past two months, the patient has had several upper respiratory tract infections and poor weight gain. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. His immunizations are up-to-date. He is at the 20th percentile for length and 5th percentile for weight. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 80/55 mm Hg. Crackles are heard over both lung fields. An x-ray of the chest shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Intubation is performed and methylprednisolone is administered. Methenamine silver staining of bronchial lavage fluid shows aggregates of 2 to 8 cysts with central spores. Serum IgA titers are decreased. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent respiratory infections, failure to thrive, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) are suggestive of a T-cell disorder. The most likely diagnosis is hyper-IgM syndrome, an X-linked disorder caused by a defective CD40 ligand (CD154) on activated T cells. CD40 ligand binds to CD40 on B cells, inducing isotype switching from IgM to IgG, IgA, and IgE. Defective CD40 ligand prevents isotype switching, leading to normal or elevated levels of IgM with decreased levels of IgG, IgA, and IgE. The decreased IgA levels in this patient support the diagnosis of hyper-IgM syndrome.

Patients with hyper-IgM syndrome are susceptible to bacterial sinopulmonary infections due to low IgG. They are also susceptible to opportunistic infections such as PCP due to T-cell dysfunction. PCP presents with fever, tachypnea, and hypoxia, and chest x-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Methenamine silver staining of bronchial lavage fluid shows the characteristic cysts of Pneumocystis.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 12-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents for a 4-week history of fever, malaise, cough, and difficulty breathing. He has had recurrent episodes of gastroenteritis since birth. Cardiopulmonary examination shows subcostal retractions and crackles bilaterally. There is enlargement of the cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes. An x-ray of the chest shows bilateral consolidations. A sputum culture shows colonies of Burkholderia cepacia. A blood sample is obtained and after the addition of nitroblue tetrazolium to the sample, neutrophils remain colorless. A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent infections, including gastroenteritis and pneumonia, and the finding of colorless neutrophils after the addition of nitroblue tetrazolium to a blood sample are suggestive of chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). CGD is an immunodeficiency disorder characterized by a defect in the NADPH oxidase complex, which is responsible for the respiratory burst in phagocytic cells. This respiratory burst is necessary for the destruction of certain bacteria and fungi. The nitroblue tetrazolium test is used to confirm the diagnosis of CGD. In this test, neutrophils are incubated with the dye nitroblue tetrazolium. In normal neutrophils, the respiratory burst converts the yellow dye to a dark blue color. However, in CGD, the neutrophils are unable to produce this respiratory burst, and the dye remains colorless.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [B] > [C] > [A].

few_shot.question: An 11-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with a 2-day history of fever, malaise, and productive cough. On presentation, he is found to be very weak and is having difficulty breathing. His past medical history is significant for multiple prior infections requiring hospitalization including otitis media, upper respiratory infections, pneumonia, and sinusitis. His family history is also significant for a maternal uncle who died of an infection as a child. Lab findings include decreased levels of IgG, IgM, IgA, and plasma cells with normal levels of CD4 positive cells. The protein that is most likely defective in this patient has which of the following functions?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent infections, especially with encapsulated organisms, and decreased levels of all immunoglobulin isotypes suggest a diagnosis of X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA). XLA is caused by a mutation in Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK), a protein that plays a crucial role in B-cell maturation. Affected individuals have normal pre-B-cell populations in the bone marrow but these cells are unable to mature into peripheral B cells, leading to a near-complete absence of all immunoglobulins. BTK is a tyrosine kinase, which functions by phosphorylating proteins.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question:
A 10-month-old boy is referred to the hospital because of suspected severe pneumonia. During the first month of his life, he had developed upper airway infections, bronchitis, and diarrhea. He has received all the immunizations according to his age. He failed to thrive since the age of 3 months. A month ago, he had a severe lung infection with cough, dyspnea, and diarrhea, and was unresponsive to an empiric oral macrolide. Upon admission to his local hospital, the patient has mild respiratory distress and crackles on auscultation. The temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), and the oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. The quantitative immunoglobulin tests show increased IgG, IgM, and IgA. The peripheral blood smear shows leukocytosis and normochromic normocytic anemia. The chloride sweat test and tuberculin test are negative. The chest X-ray reveals bilateral pneumonia. The bronchoalveolar lavage and gram stain report gram-negative bacteria with a growth of Burkholderia cepacia on culture. The laboratory results on admission are as follows:
Leukocytes 36,600/mm3
Neutrophils 80%
Lymphocytes 16%
  Eosinophils 1%
Monocytes 2%
Hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
BUN 15 mg/dL
Which of the following defects of neutrophil function is most likely responsible?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent infections, failure to thrive, and neutrophilia is suggestive of chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). CGD is an inherited disorder of the NADPH oxidase complex that impairs the ability of phagocytes (eg, neutrophils, monocytes) to generate superoxide ions and other reactive oxygen species. This results in an absent respiratory burst, which is a rapid release of reactive oxygen species. The respiratory burst is a critical component of the immune response that is necessary for killing certain types of bacteria and fungi.

Patients with CGD are susceptible to catalase-positive organisms, which include Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus, and Burkholderia cepacia, which was isolated in this patient. The most common presentation is with recurrent infections and granuloma formation in the skin, lungs, and GI tract. The granulomas can obstruct the GI and GU tracts, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea and obstruction.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [D] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician for the evaluation of fever, breathing difficulty, and cough during the past week. In the past year, the patient was diagnosed with four sinus infections, 3 upper respiratory tract infections, and an episode of severe bronchiolitis requiring hospitalization. Since birth, he has had multiple episodes of oral thrush treated with nystatin, as well as chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive. His temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 38/min, and blood pressure is 106/63 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry at room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Pulmonary auscultation shows bilateral crackles and wheezing. Physical examination indicates a prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic nasal wing, a shortened chin, and dysplastic ears. An X-ray of the chest shows hyperinflation of the lungs, interstitial infiltrates, and atelectasis. The patient tests positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in the nasopharyngeal aspirate. This patient most likely has a deficiency of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and oral thrush suggests a T-cell deficiency. The facial abnormalities (prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic nasal wing, a shortened chin, and dysplastic ears) are characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome (DGS), a disorder caused by abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. This results in thymic aplasia or hypoplasia, leading to T-cell deficiency. The thymus is the primary site of T-cell maturation, and its absence in DGS results in decreased T-cell production and disrupted cell-mediated immunity. This leads to increased susceptibility to infections with viruses, fungi, and intracellular bacteria. In addition, because T cells are necessary for B-cell activation and production of specific antibodies, patients with DGS also have impaired humoral immunity, leading to increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated bacteria. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

question: A 27-year-old graduate student is bitten by a coral snake while he was hiking alone through the woods and dies 2 hours later from respiratory failure. His body was discovered 7 hours later by a group of campers who promptly called the police. On arrival, the police found his body to be cold and stiff. Which of the following processes is responsible for the rigidity observed?

answer_choices.A: Activation of muscle contraction by neurotoxins
answer_choices.B: Effect of low temperature on muscle proteins

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of weakness, headache, and vomiting for 40 minutes. He is an amateur chef and his symptoms started 10 minutes after he ingested pufferfish that he had prepared. On arrival, he is lethargic. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 8/min, and blood pressure is 92/64 mm Hg. He is intubated and mechanical ventilation is begun. Intravenous fluid resuscitation is started. The cause of this patient's condition exerts its effect by which of the following mechanisms of action?

answer_choices.A: Decrease in cell membrane permeability to sodium ions
answer_choices.B: Decrease in cell membrane permeability to calcium ions
answer_choices.C: Decrease in cell membrane permeability to potassium ions
answer_choices.D: Increase in cell membrane permeability to calcium ions

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of weakness, headache, and vomiting after ingesting pufferfish are suggestive of tetrodotoxin poisoning. Tetrodotoxin is a potent neurotoxin found in the liver and reproductive organs of several species of pufferfish. It exerts its effects by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve cell membranes, thereby inhibiting the propagation of action potentials. This leads to paralysis, which can cause respiratory failure and death.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father 10 minutes after falling into a frozen lake during ice fishing. He was in the water for less than 1 minute before his father managed to pull him out. On arrival, his clothes are still wet and he appears scared. His body temperature is 36.2°C (97.1°F), pulse is 102/min, blood pressure is 133/88 mm Hg. Which of the following mechanisms contributes most to maintaining this patient's core body temperature?
few_shot.explanation:
Involuntary muscular contractions (shivering) is the most important mechanism for heat production in humans. Shivering is a high-frequency, involuntary muscle contraction that increases metabolic heat production. It is triggered by cold exposure and can increase the metabolic rate 2-5 times the normal rate. This patient's tachycardia is also a response to cold exposure and is mediated by increased sympathetic outflow, which also contributes to heat conservation by causing peripheral vasoconstriction.

The other options listed are less important in maintaining core body temperature. Contraction of arrector pili muscles (goosebumps) is a vestigial response in humans and does not significantly prevent heat loss. Inhibition of the thyroid axis would decrease metabolic heat production and therefore would not be beneficial in this setting. Activation of thermogenin (uncoupling protein) in brown fat is an important mechanism of heat production in infants but is of minimal importance in adults, who have little brown fat.

So, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [D] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A well-dressed couple presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of headache, a sensation of floating, and weakness of arms and legs after eating a plate of shellfish 2 hours ago. They mention that they had experienced tingling of the lips and mouth within 15 minutes of ingesting the shellfish. They also complain of mild nausea and abdominal discomfort. On physical examination, their vital signs are within normal limits. Their neurological examination reveals decreased strength in all extremities bilaterally and hyporeflexia. After detailed laboratory evaluation, the physician confirms the diagnosis of paralysis due to the presence of a specific toxin in the shellfish they had consumed. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the action of the toxin these patients had consumed?

answer_choices.B: Blockade of voltage-gated fast sodium channels
answer_choices.C: Increased opening of presynaptic calcium channels

few_shot.explanation:
The clinical presentation of this couple is consistent with paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP), a foodborne illness caused by the consumption of shellfish contaminated with saxitoxin. Saxitoxin is a potent neurotoxin produced by certain species of marine dinoflagellates, which are ingested by shellfish. The toxin accumulates in the shellfish and is not destroyed by cooking.

Saxitoxin acts by binding to the voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve cell membranes, blocking the influx of sodium ions and preventing the generation and conduction of action potentials. This leads to flaccid paralysis and can cause death due to respiratory failure.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old man presents to the emergency department with unrelenting muscle spasms for the past several hours. The patient’s girlfriend states that he started having jaw spasms and soreness last night but now his neck, back, and arms are spasming. She also states that he stepped on a nail about 1 week ago. Past medical history is noncontributory. The patient's vaccination status is unknown at this time. Today, the vital signs include temperature 39.1°C (102.4°F), heart rate 115/min, blood pressure 145/110 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 10/min. On exam, the patient is in obvious discomfort, with a clenched jaw and extended neck. Labs are drawn and a basic metabolic panel comes back normal and the white blood cell (WBC) count is moderately elevated. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient’s symptoms?

answer_choices.A: A heat-labile toxin that inhibits ACh release at the NMJ
answer_choices.B: A toxin that disables the G-protein coupled receptor
answer_choices.C: An exotoxin that cleaves SNARE proteins
answer_choices.D: An exotoxin that causes ADP-ribosylation of EF-2

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of muscle spasms, trismus (lockjaw), and a history of a puncture wound are suggestive of tetanus. Tetanus is caused by the gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium Clostridium tetani. The bacterium produces a potent exotoxin, tetanospasmin, which is taken up by motor neurons and transported retrogradely to the spinal cord. The toxin then cleaves synaptobrevin, a SNARE protein, which is involved in the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in the spinal cord. This leads to unopposed muscle contraction and spasm.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought by his mother to the emergency room after the child was bitten by a rattlesnake one hour prior to presentation. The child was reportedly playing in the backyard alone when his mother heard the child scream. She rushed out to her child and found a snake with a rattle on its tail slithering away from the child. On examination, the child has a bleeding bite mark and significant swelling over the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He is in visible distress and appears pale and diaphoretic. The child undergoes fluid resuscitation and is placed on supplemental oxygen. He is administered rattlesnake antivenom and is admitted for observation. He is subsequently discharged 24 hours later feeling better. However, 6 days after admission, he presents again to the emergency department with a temperature of 102°F (38.9°C), diffuse wheals, and knee and hip pain. This patient’s condition is caused by which of the following?

answer_choices.A: Antibodies directed against cell membrane antigens
answer_choices.B: Antibodies directed against cell surface receptors

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, urticaria, and arthralgias occurring 5 days after administration of a foreign protein (ie, snake antivenom) is suggestive of serum sickness. Serum sickness is a type III hypersensitivity reaction that occurs when antibodies are formed against foreign proteins. These antibodies form immune complexes with the proteins, which are then deposited in various tissues, including the skin, joints, and kidneys. This leads to an inflammatory reaction that results in the symptoms seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 14-year-old girl comes to the physician with her father for evaluation of her short stature. She feels well overall, but is concerned because all of her friends are taller than her. Her birth weight was normal. Her father reports he had a short stature during his teenage years; he is currently 177 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall. She is at the 2ndpercentile for height and 35th percentile for weight. Breast development is Tanner stage 2. Pubic and axillary hair is absent. An x-ray of the left hand and wrist shows a bone age of 11 years. Which of the following is the most appropriate next best step in management?

few_shot.question: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician for evaluation of her short stature. She was born at term, and her birth length was normal. She has not yet attained menarche. Her mother is 162 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and her father is 177 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall. She is at the 3rd percentile for height and 40th percentile for weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. Breast and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 2. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

answer_choices.A: Measurement of serum insulin-like growth factor concentration
answer_choices.B: Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration
answer_choices.C: X-ray of the hand and wrist

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's short stature with normal birth length and delayed puberty is suggestive of constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), the most common cause of short stature and delayed puberty in males and females. CDGP is a variation of normal development often seen in children who are referred for short stature or delayed puberty. It is typically seen in children with a family history of delayed puberty, often in the father or brother. These children have delayed skeletal maturation (bone age), and their growth plates remain open longer than average during adolescence, allowing for continued linear growth. They therefore have a delayed but otherwise normal pubertal growth spurt and ultimately reach a normal adult height that is appropriate for their family. The diagnosis of CDGP is made by demonstrating a delayed bone age, which is assessed by an x-ray of the left hand and wrist.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician with her father for evaluation of short stature. She feels well overall but is concerned because all of her friends are taller than her. Her birth weight was normal. Menarche has not yet occurred. Her father says he also had short stature and late puberty. The girl is at the 5th percentile for height and 35th percentile for weight. Breast development is Tanner stage 2. Pubic and axillary hair is absent. An x-ray of the left hand and wrist shows a bone age of 12 years. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following sets of laboratory findings?
 $$$ FSH %%% LH %%% Estrogen %%% GnRH $$$
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's short stature, delayed puberty, and delayed bone age are suggestive of constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), the most common cause of delayed puberty in boys and the second most common cause in girls. CDGP is a diagnosis of exclusion, and patients should have an otherwise normal history and physical examination. Patients with CDGP are typically shorter than their peers during childhood and adolescence until their pubertal growth spurt, which occurs later than average. However, they ultimately attain a normal adult height that is appropriate for their family. CDGP is often familial, and many affected patients have a history of delayed puberty in their parents, as seen in this patient.

Patients with CDGP have low sex hormone levels for their age, but GnRH stimulation testing will show a normal increase in LH and FSH, indicating a functioning hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of vaginal bleeding for 2 days. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. She is at the 95th percentile for height and at the 90th percentile for weight. Examination shows enlarged breasts, and the areola and papilla have formed a secondary mound. There is coarse pubic hair that does not extend to the inner thigh. The remainder of the examination show no abnormalities. An x-ray of the left hand and wrist shows a bone age of 11 years. Her serum luteinizing hormone concentration is 0.1 mIU/mL (N < 0.2 mIU/mL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's vaginal bleeding, breast development, and pubic hair are concerning for precocious puberty, defined as the development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls and age 9 in boys. The most common cause of precocious puberty in girls is idiopathic central precocious puberty (CPP), which is due to premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Other causes of precocious puberty include peripheral precocious puberty (PPP) due to autonomous sex steroid production, and exogenous exposure to sex steroids.

The first step in the evaluation of precocious puberty is to measure basal luteinizing hormone (LH) levels. If the LH level is in the prepubertal range (as in this patient), a GnRH stimulation test should be performed to distinguish between CPP and PPP. In CPP, GnRH will stimulate the release of LH, whereas in PPP, GnRH will have no effect because the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is not involved.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. She is at the 90th percentile for height and weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows enlarged breast buds that extend beyond the areola. There is coarse pubic hair that does not extend onto the inner thigh. The remainder of the examination show no abnormalities. An x-ray of the left hand shows a bone age of 10 years. Following GnRH agonist stimulation, serum luteinizing hormone levels increase to twice the median. Which of the following is the most appropriate next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's physical examination findings (breast development, pubic hair) and advanced bone age are consistent with precocious puberty, defined as the development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls and age 9 in boys. The GnRH stimulation test is used to differentiate between central (GnRH-dependent) and peripheral (GnRH-independent) precocious puberty. In central precocious puberty, the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is prematurely activated, and GnRH stimulation will cause an increase in luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels. In peripheral precocious puberty, sex steroid production is independent of GnRH stimulation, and LH and FSH levels will not increase following a GnRH stimulation test.

This patient's increase in LH levels following GnRH stimulation is consistent with central precocious puberty. The most common cause of central precocious puberty in girls is idiopathic, but it can also be due to central nervous system abnormalities such as tumors, congenital anomalies, trauma, or inflammation. Therefore, all girls diagnosed with central precocious puberty should undergo brain imaging, preferably with MRI, to evaluate for an intracranial lesion.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician with her father for evaluation of her tall stature. She is concerned because she is taller than all of her friends. Her birth weight and height were within normal limits. Her father is 174 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall; her mother is 162 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall. She is at the 98th percentile for height and 90th percentile for BMI. She has not had her menstrual period yet. Her mother has Graves disease. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a tall stature with broad hands and feet. There is frontal bossing and protrusion of the mandible. Finger perimetry is normal. The remainder of the examinations shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show a fasting serum glucose of 144 mg/dL. An x-ray of the left hand and wrist shows a bone age of 15 years. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's tall stature, delayed menarche, acral enlargement (broad hands and feet), frontal bossing, mandibular protrusion, and hyperglycemia are suggestive of growth hormone (GH) excess, or acromegaly. In children who are still growing (ie, prior to epiphyseal plate closure), GH excess leads to gigantism, which is characterized by excessive longitudinal bone growth and markedly increased height. After epiphyseal plate closure, GH excess leads to acromegaly, which is characterized by an increase in soft tissue growth and bone growth at sites that remain responsive to GH (eg, hands, feet, jaw). GH-secreting pituitary adenomas are the most common cause of GH excess. Transsphenoidal adenomectomy is the treatment of choice for GH-secreting pituitary adenomas and would have prevented this patient's condition.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 6-day-old male newborn is brought to the physician because he has become increasingly irritable and restless over the past 2 days. During this period, he has had 12 bowel movements. He feeds 10 to 12 times a day. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation and weighed 1800 g (3 lb 15 oz); he currently weighs 1700 g (3 lb 12 oz). His mother has Graves' disease and received propylthiouracil during the last trimester of pregnancy. She has a history of intravenous heroin use. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 180/min, and respirations are 50/min. Examination shows mild diaphoresis and a firm 2-cm midline neck swelling. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 5-day-old, 2200 g (4 lb 14 oz) male newborn is brought to the physician because of poor feeding and irritability. He was born at 36 weeks' gestation after the pregnancy was complicated by premature rupture of membranes. His APGAR scores at delivery were 5 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. He appears lethargic. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 170/min, and respirations are 63/min. Examination shows scleral icterus. Subcostal retractions and nasal flaring are present. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds. Laboratory studies are ordered and an x-ray of the chest is scheduled. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This premature newborn with poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and poor perfusion (prolonged capillary refill time) has signs of sepsis. Newborns, especially those who are premature, have an immature immune system and are at high risk for serious bacterial infections. Risk factors in this patient include prematurity and premature rupture of membranes. The most common pathogens in early-onset sepsis (ie, <7 days of age) are group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli. Empiric antibiotic therapy with ampicillin and gentamicin, which covers these organisms, should be initiated immediately after obtaining blood cultures but before results are available. Ampicillin has the added benefit of covering Listeria monocytogenes, another potential pathogen in early-onset sepsis.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: Two days after delivery, a 4300-g (9-lb 8-oz) newborn has difficulty feeding and has become increasingly lethargic. His cry has become weak. He was born at term. His mother has a history of intravenous drug use. His temperature is 36.4°C (96.5°F), pulse is 170/min, respirations are 62/min, and blood pressure is 70/48 mm Hg. Examination shows midfacial hypoplasia, diaphoresis, and tremor of the lower extremities. Macroglossia is present. There are folds in the posterior auricular cartilage. The left lower extremity is larger than the right lower extremity. Abdominal examination shows an umbilical hernia. The liver is palpated 4 cm below the right costal margin. Neurological examination shows decreased tone in all extremities. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has findings consistent with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS), an overgrowth syndrome characterized by macrosomia, macroglossia, and abdominal wall defects (eg, omphalocele, umbilical hernia). Additional findings can include earlobe creases/pits, neonatal hypoglycemia, and hemihyperplasia. BWS is associated with defects in genomic imprinting, with most cases linked to abnormalities on chromosome 11p15. This region contains growth-promoting genes (eg, insulin-like growth factor 2) that are normally suppressed by imprinting but are overexpressed in BWS.

Neonatal hypoglycemia is common in BWS due to the overexpression of insulin-like growth factor 2, which has insulin-like effects. Hypoglycemia can cause nonspecific findings such as poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, and jitteriness/tremors. Severe or prolonged hypoglycemia can cause seizures or apnea. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is to administer glucose.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 21-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician at 10 weeks' gestation because of progressive fatigue for the past 3 weeks. She reports that she has had a 3.2-kg (7-lb) weight loss after conceiving despite an increase in appetite. She has become increasingly anxious and has trouble falling asleep. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. Medications include folic acid and a multivitamin. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 55 kg (120 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37.4°C (99.4°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 150/70 mm Hg. The globes of the eyes are prominent. The thyroid gland is firm and diffusely enlarged. Neurologic examination shows a fine resting tremor of the hands. There is a midsystolic click at the apex and a grade 2/6 early systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is 0.1 μU/mL. An ECG is normal except for sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's weight loss, increased appetite, anxiety, insomnia, tremor, tachycardia, and systolic murmur are consistent with hyperthyroidism. The diffuse goiter and ophthalmopathy suggest Graves disease, the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in women of childbearing age. Graves disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by circulating immunoglobulins that bind to and stimulate the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, leading to increased synthesis and release of thyroid hormone.

In pregnancy, the preferred treatment for hyperthyroidism is propylthiouracil during the first trimester, then switching to methimazole for the second and third trimesters. Propylthiouracil is preferred initially because methimazole has been associated with a rare congenital anomaly (eg, aplasia cutis, esophageal and choanal atresia). However, propylthiouracil use later in pregnancy is associated with hepatotoxicity, so it is recommended to switch to methimazole after the first trimester.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 2-day-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of irritability and vomiting for two hours. During this period, he has vomited bilious fluid three times. He has not yet passed stool. The mother has breastfed the newborn every two hours. He has wet two diapers during the last two days. He was born at term and was delivered at home. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. The mother had no prenatal care during pregnancy. The patient currently weighs 3100 g (6 lb 13 oz) and is 50 cm (19.6 in) in length. The newborn appears restless. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.14°F), pulse is 166/min, respirations are 60/min, and blood pressure is 60/45 mm Hg. There is no redness or warmth around the umbilical cord stump. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Bowel sounds are sparse. The abdomen is distended. Digital rectal examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the abdomen with contrast shows dilated small bowel loops, a microcolon, a mixture of gas and meconium located in the right lower quadrant. A nasogastric tube is placed and fluid resuscitation is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has bilious vomiting, abdominal distention, and failure to pass meconium, which are concerning for intestinal obstruction. The abdominal x-ray findings of dilated small bowel loops, a microcolon, and a mixture of gas and meconium located in the right lower quadrant are suggestive of meconium ileus, which is often the presenting sign of cystic fibrosis (CF) in the newborn period. Meconium ileus occurs due to abnormally thick and sticky meconium obstructing the terminal ileum. 

The initial management of uncomplicated meconium ileus (ie, no signs of bowel perforation such as pneumoperitoneum or peritonitis) is nonoperative and involves rehydration, electrolyte repletion, and relief of the intestinal obstruction. Hyperosmolar contrast enema with a water-soluble agent (eg, Gastrografin) is both diagnostic and therapeutic. The contrast draws water into the bowel lumen, which can help loosen the thick meconium and relieve the obstruction. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A previously healthy 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of 6 months of progressive fatigue and weight loss. His mother reports that during this time, he has had decreased energy and has become a “picky eater.” He often has loose stools and complains of occasional abdominal pain and nausea. His family moved to a different house 7 months ago. He is at the 50th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 116/min, and blood pressure is 85/46 mm Hg. Physical examination shows tanned skin and bluish-black gums. The abdomen is soft, nondistended, and nontender. Serum studies show:
Na+ 134 mEq/L
K+ 5.4 mEq/L
Cl- 104 mEq/L
Bicarbonate 21 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL
Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
Glucose 70 mg/dL
Intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in treatment?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, and loose stools are suggestive of adrenal insufficiency. His hyperpigmentation (tanned skin, bluish-black gums) is due to increased production of proopiomelanocortin, a precursor of both adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH). In primary adrenal insufficiency, ACTH levels are high due to lack of negative feedback, leading to increased MSH and hyperpigmentation. His hyponatremia and hyperkalemia are due to mineralocorticoid deficiency, and his hypoglycemia is due to glucocorticoid deficiency. His hypotension is due to both mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency.

The most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in children is autoimmune adrenalitis, but this patient's history of moving to a new house 7 months ago raises the possibility of exposure to tuberculosis, which can cause adrenal insufficiency by destroying the adrenal glands. Other infectious causes include fungal infections (eg, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis) and, in patients with AIDS, infections such as CMV and MAI.

Regardless of the cause, the most appropriate initial step in management is to administer glucocorticoids (eg, hydrocortisone) to reverse the life-threatening glucocorticoid deficiency. Mineralocorticoid replacement (eg, fludrocortisone) can be added later.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has been feeling very stressed over the past several months. During this period, she has found it difficult to relax. She states that her head is full of worries. She works at an accountant's office and reports difficulty in concentrating on her work. She has been working longer shifts because one of her coworkers is on vacation and reports feeling more tired than usual. She is married and frequently fights with her husband. The patient states that in order to deal with her stress, she goes shopping. While shopping, she steals small trivial items and feels immediately relieved thereafter. She discards the objects she steals and has feelings of shame and guilt about her actions. Her husband is concerned about her behavior, but she is unable to stop shoplifting. Her vital signs are within normal limits. On mental status examination, she is oriented to person, place, and time. She reports feeling anxious. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

few_shot.question:
A 20-year-old woman is brought in by police for trying to break into a museum after hours. The patient states that she is a detective on the trail of a master collusion scheme and needs the artifacts from the museum to prove her case. Her family reports that she has been acting strangely for the past week. She has been up perusing the internet all night without taking breaks. Her husband states that she has had increased sexual interest for the past week; however, he did not report this to the physician when he first noticed it. The patient is unable to offer a history as she cannot be redirected from her current theory. Her temperature is 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 122/81 mmHg, pulse is 97/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable only for a highly-energized patient. Laboratory studies are ordered as seen below.

Urine:
Color: Yellow
Nitrite: Negative
Bacteria: Negative
Leukocytes: Negative
hCG: Positive
Benzodiazepines: Negative
Barbiturate: Negative
Cocaine: Negative
Acetaminophen: Negative

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's decreased need for sleep, increased energy, grandiosity, and hypersexuality are suggestive of mania. Mania is a psychiatric condition characterized by an elevated, expansive, or irritable mood lasting at least one week, and associated with at least three of the following: inflated self-esteem or grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, increased talkativeness or pressure to keep talking, flight of ideas or racing thoughts, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation, and excessive involvement in pleasurable activities that have a high potential for painful consequences. In this patient, the symptoms have led to significant impairment in her social functioning, as evidenced by her arrest.

The treatment of acute mania involves mood stabilizers (eg, lithium, valproate, carbamazepine) and/or atypical antipsychotics (eg, olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine). However, in patients with severe agitation or psychosis, as in this patient, a typical antipsychotic such as haloperidol can be used for rapid tranquilization.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of worsening insomnia and anxiety. She says that she has an important college exam in the next few weeks for which she has to put in many hours of work each day. Despite the urgency of her circumstances, she states that she is unable to focus and concentrate, is anxious, irritable and has lost interest in almost all activities. She also says that she has trouble falling asleep and wakes up several times during the night. She claims that this state of affairs has severely hampered her productivity and is a major problem for her, and she feels tired and fatigued all day. She denies hearing voices, abnormal thoughts, or any other psychotic symptoms. The patient asks if there is some form of therapy that can help her sleep better so that she can function more effectively during the day. She claims that the other symptoms of not enjoying anything, irritability, and anxiety are things that she can learn to handle. Which of the following approaches is most likely to address the patients concerns most effectively?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's insomnia, anxiety, anhedonia, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating are suggestive of major depressive disorder (MDD). MDD is a common psychiatric disorder characterized by depressed mood or anhedonia (inability to feel pleasure) along with ≥4 of the following symptoms for a duration of ≥2 weeks: sleep disturbance, loss of interest, guilt, low energy, poor concentration, appetite/weight changes, psychomotor changes, or suicidality (mnemonic: SIGECAPS).

Mirtazapine is a tetracyclic antidepressant that is often used in patients with MDD and insomnia. It enhances the release of norepinephrine and serotonin by blocking presynaptic α2-adrenergic auto-receptors and heteroreceptors. It also blocks postsynaptic serotonin type 2 (5-HT2) and type 3 (5-HT3) receptors, enhancing serotonin transmission. In addition, mirtazapine is a potent antagonist of histamine (H1) receptors, which accounts for its sedating properties. The sedation caused by mirtazapine can be beneficial in depressed patients with marked anxiety or insomnia. However, the sedating effects are often dose dependent, with lower doses (eg, 15 mg) generally causing more sedation than higher doses (eg, 30-45 mg). This is because the drug's noradrenergic effects become more prominent at higher doses, counteracting the sedation caused by H1 receptor blockade.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 31-year-old female presents to her primary care physician with mild anxiety and complaints of mood swings lasting several months. The patient reports that the mood swings affect her work and personal relationships. In addition, she complains of increased irritability, breast tenderness, bloating, fatigue, binge-eating, and difficulty concentrating for 10 days prior to her menstrual period. The patient's symptoms increase in severity with the approach of menses but resolve rapidly on the first day of menses. She states that she is very sensitive to criticism of her work by others. She also snaps at her children and her husband. She has tried yoga to unwind, but with limited improvement. She is concerned that her behavior is affecting her marriage. The patient has no past medical history, and has regular periods every 24 days. She has had two normal vaginal deliveries. She uses condoms for contraception. Her mother has major depressive disorder. The physical exam is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in the treatment of this patient?

answer_choices.C: Oral contraceptive and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of mood swings, irritability, and physical symptoms (eg, breast tenderness, bloating) that occur in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle (ie, the week prior to menses) and resolve with the onset of menses are consistent with premenstrual syndrome (PMS). PMS is a common condition, affecting up to 85% of menstruating women. It is diagnosed clinically, and symptoms must occur in the luteal phase and be severe enough to interfere with normal activities and relationships. 

The first-line treatment for PMS is lifestyle modifications, including regular exercise, a balanced diet, caffeine reduction, and smoking cessation. For patients with an inadequate response to lifestyle modifications, as in this patient, second-line treatment includes SSRIs and/or hormonal contraceptives. SSRIs are effective for both the physical and mood symptoms of PMS. Hormonal contraceptives prevent ovulation and can help alleviate the physical symptoms of PMS. 

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can also be used to treat the physical symptoms of PMS, such as breast tenderness and bloating. 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her husband, who is concerned about her ability to care for herself. Three weeks ago, she quit her marketing job to start a clothing company. Since then, she has not slept more than 4 hours per night because she has been working on her business plans. She used a significant portion of their savings to fund business trips to Switzerland in order to buy “only the best quality fabrics in the world.” She has not showered and has eaten little during the past 3 days. She has had 2 similar episodes a few years back that required hospitalization and treatment in a psychiatry unit. She has also suffered from periods of depression. She is currently not taking any medications. She appears unkempt and agitated, pacing up and down the room. She speaks very fast without interruption about her business ideas. She has no suicidal ideation or ideas of self-harm. Toxicology screening is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, and excessive involvement in activities with a high potential for painful consequences (eg, spending sprees) are consistent with a manic episode. The history of recurrent manic episodes and periods of depression suggest a diagnosis of bipolar disorder. 

The mainstay of treatment for bipolar disorder is mood stabilizers, such as lithium, valproate, and carbamazepine. Lithium is particularly effective for classic euphoric mania with hyperactivity, grandiosity, and flight of ideas, as seen in this patient. It is also effective in decreasing the risk of suicide in these patients. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old woman presents to her family doctor requesting sleeping pills. She is a graduate student and confesses that she is a “worry-a-holic,” which has been getting worse for the last 6 months as the due date for her final paper is approaching. During this time, she feels more on edge, irritable, and is having difficulty sleeping. She has already tried employing good sleep hygiene practices, including a switch to non-caffeinated coffee. Her past medical history is significant for depression in the past that was managed medically. No current medications. The patient’s family history is significant for her mother who has a panic disorder. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals a mildly anxious patient but is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most effective treatment for this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's chronic (at least 6 months) excessive worry and anxiety about multiple events or activities, difficulty controlling the worry, and associated symptoms (eg, restlessness, irritability, sleep disturbance) are consistent with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). GAD is a common condition that often coexists with major depressive disorder. Patients with GAD often have muscle tension and a sensation of being "on edge." They may also have fatigue, poor concentration, and sleep disturbances. The diagnosis is clinical and does not require that patients have panic attacks, compulsions, or obsessions.

First-line treatment for GAD includes selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), and psychotherapy (eg, cognitive-behavioral therapy). However, SSRIs and SNRIs can take several weeks to become effective. If immediate symptom relief is necessary, benzodiazepines can be used for a short period. However, they have the potential for tolerance and dependence and can also cause disinhibition, sedation, and psychomotor impairment.

Buspirone, a nonbenzodiazepine anxiolytic, is a good option for patients who need long-term anxiety control but wish to avoid the adverse effects of benzodiazepines. It is a partial agonist of the serotonin 1A receptor and is as effective as benzodiazepines for treatment of GAD. Unlike benzodiazepines, buspirone does not cause sedation or physical dependence and has no potential for abuse. However, it may take 2-4 weeks for buspirone to become effective.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 69-year-old right-handed man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. On questioning, he has had some difficulty speaking for 3 months. During a conversation, he often has difficulty repeating what his interlocutor has said. He has hypertension and takes hydrochlorothiazide. His vital signs are within normal limits. The patient speaks fluently in full sentences and demonstrates normal comprehension. When asked to say the word “kindergarten,” he replies with, “Sintelmarvin… no, that's wrong…kinterflargin, no that isn't it either...kantolargen...no? How about, kindergarten?” The most likely cause of the patient's symptoms is occlusion of a branch of which of the following arteries?

few_shot.question: A 78-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of difficulty speaking. The symptoms began abruptly one hour ago while he was having breakfast with his wife. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease. Current medications include pravastatin, lisinopril, metformin, and aspirin. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 165/90 mm Hg. He is right-handed. The patient speaks in short, simple sentences, and has difficulty repeating sequences of words. He can follow simple instructions. Right facial droop is present. Muscle strength is 4/5 on the right side and 5/5 on the left, and there is a mild right-sided pronator drift. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.A: Occlusion of the right penetrating arteries
answer_choices.B: Occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery
answer_choices.C: Occlusion of the right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
answer_choices.D: Rupture of left posterior cerebral artery malformation

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of acute-onset expressive aphasia and right-sided hemiparesis are suggestive of a stroke. The most likely cause of his symptoms is occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery (MCA). The MCA supplies a large portion of the lateral convexity of the cerebral hemisphere and the lateral aspects of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. Occlusion of the MCA can cause contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss, with the upper limb and face more affected than the lower limb. In addition, occlusion of the left (dominant) MCA can cause global aphasia if the entire MCA is occluded, or expressive aphasia with or without receptive deficits if only the superior division of the MCA is occluded.

Therefore, the answer is [B].
