few_shot.question: A 53-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of intermittent severe left neck, shoulder, and arm pain and paresthesias of the left hand. The pain radiates to the radial aspect of her left forearm, thumb, and index finger. She first noticed her symptoms after helping a friend set up a canopy tent. There is no family history of serious illness. She appears healthy. Vital signs are within normal limits. When the patient extends and rotates her head to the left and downward pressure is applied, she reports paresthesias along the radial aspect of her left forearm and thumb. There is weakness when extending the left wrist against resistance. The brachioradialis reflex is 1+ on the left and 2+ on the right. The radial pulse is palpable bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of neck, shoulder, and arm pain, paresthesias of the thumb and index finger, and weakness when extending the wrist against resistance are suggestive of a cervical radiculopathy. Cervical radiculopathy is most often due to nerve root impingement or inflammation from a herniated disc or osteophyte. The C6 nerve root (C5-C6 disc) is one of the most commonly affected levels. The C6 nerve root contributes to the innervation of the biceps, brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis, and supinator muscles. Therefore, impingement of the C6 nerve root can cause weakness in these muscles, leading to decreased wrist extension and a diminished brachioradialis reflex. Sensory loss occurs over the thumb and index finger. The Spurling test (extension and rotation of the head) can exacerbate nerve root compression and reproduce radicular symptoms.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of episodic tingling and numbness in his right hand for the past 3 months. His symptoms are worse in the evening. There is no history of trauma. He is employed as a carpenter. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the past 10 years. He drinks a pint of vodka daily. He does not use illicit drugs. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows decreased pinch strength in the right hand. Sensations are decreased over the little finger and both the dorsal and palmar surfaces of the medial aspect of the right hand. Which of the following is the most likely site of nerve compression?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of numbness and tingling in the little finger and medial aspect of the hand, along with decreased pinch strength, are suggestive of ulnar nerve compression. The ulnar nerve can be compressed at several sites along its course, including the cubital tunnel at the elbow, the ulnar (Guyon) canal at the wrist, and the thoracic outlet. However, the ulnar nerve innervates the dorsal and palmar aspects of the medial hand and the little finger, and the ulnar nerve is most commonly compressed at the cubital tunnel. This is known as cubital tunnel syndrome, and it is the second most common compression neuropathy after carpal tunnel syndrome. It is often caused by prolonged flexion of the elbow (eg, during sleep) or by repetitive trauma (eg, in a carpenter).

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of pain and weakness in her right forearm and hand for several months. Two years ago, she sustained a fracture of her ulnar shaft with dislocation of the radial head that was treated surgically. Physical examination shows mild tenderness a few centimeters distal to the lateral epicondyle. She has marked weakness when attempting to extend her right middle finger. There is radial deviation on extension of the wrist. Sensation is not impaired. Which of the following nerves is most likely affected in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) is a branch of the radial nerve that supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm. It is purely a motor nerve and does not have any sensory fibers. The PIN is susceptible to injury in the setting of trauma, particularly fractures of the radial head or shaft, or from compression at the radial tunnel. Symptoms of PIN injury include weakness of the extensor muscles of the forearm, resulting in inability to extend the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints and the thumb at the interphalangeal joint. There is also radial deviation of the wrist on extension due to unopposed action of the radial wrist extensors.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of intermittent tingling of his hand. He is an avid cyclist and has recently started training for a cycle marathon. Physical examination shows decreased grip strength in the right hand and wasting of the hypothenar eminence. On asking the patient to grasp a piece of paper between his right thumb and right index finger in the first web space, there is hyperflexion of the right thumb interphalangeal joint. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Inability to flex the index finger at the interphalangeal joints
answer_choices.B: Loss of sensation over the dorsum of the medial half of the hand
answer_choices.C: Loss of sensation over the palmar aspect of the middle finger
answer_choices.D: Inability to extend the little finger at the proximal interphalangeal joints

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of intermittent tingling of the hand, decreased grip strength, and wasting of the hypothenar eminence are suggestive of ulnar nerve entrapment. The ulnar nerve is vulnerable to injury at the elbow (eg, cubital tunnel syndrome) and wrist (eg, Guyon canal syndrome). Cyclists are at risk for ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist due to prolonged pressure on the handlebars (handlebar palsy). The ulnar nerve provides motor innervation to most intrinsic hand muscles, including the hypothenar muscles, interossei, and medial two lumbricals. It also provides sensory innervation to the medial one and a half fingers and the associated palm area. The Froment sign (ie, hyperflexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint when pinching a piece of paper) is indicative of adductor pollicis muscle weakness, which is innervated by the ulnar nerve. The patient compensates for this weakness by flexing the flexor pollicis longus, which is innervated by the median nerve.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 75-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 30 minutes of slurred speech and arm weakness. On the drive over to the hospital, her symptoms have resolved completely. The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, morbid obesity, gout, and vascular claudication. Her temperature is 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 184/111 mmHg, pulse is 88/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals cranial nerves II-XII as grossly intact with normal strength and sensation in the patient's upper and lower extremities. The patient's memory is intact and her speech seems normal and fluent. Her gait is stable with no ataxia. An initial head CT demonstrates diffuse atrophy which is consistent with previous head CT scans. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 78-year-old man is brought in to the emergency department by ambulance after his wife noticed that he began slurring his speech and had developed facial asymmetry during dinner approximately 30 minutes ago. His past medical history is remarkable for hypertension and diabetes. His temperature is 99.1°F (37.3°C), blood pressure is 154/99 mmHg, pulse is 89/min, respirations are 12/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Neurologic exam reveals right upper and lower extremity weakness and an asymmetric smile. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's acute onset of slurred speech, facial asymmetry, and right-sided weakness is concerning for an acute ischemic stroke. The most important initial step in management is to determine whether the stroke is ischemic or hemorrhagic, as this will guide further management. Noncontrast head CT is the imaging modality of choice for making this determination, as it can quickly and accurately identify hemorrhage. If hemorrhage is not seen on the initial noncontrast head CT, ischemic stroke is presumed, and the patient can be evaluated for thrombolytic therapy with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). 

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband due to difficulty speaking and confusion for 1 hour. She was gardening when she suddenly developed these symptoms. She is not able to respond to the questions despite multiple repetitions. She also appears unsteady with her gait and is able to walk with support. The past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and osteoarthritis. The medicine list includes aspirin, atorvastatin, metformin, and chondroitin sulfate. The vital signs include: blood pressure 174/88 mm Hg, heart rate 154/min and irregular, respiratory rate 12/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She is awake, but not following commands. The pupils are equal bilaterally and reactive to light. There is mild facial droop on the right side. The forehead wrinkles are preserved. When the soles of her feet are stimulated with a blunt instrument, the right-sided big toe goes upward, while the left-sided big toe goes downward. The ECG shows variable R-R intervals and absent of P waves. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's acute onset of confusion, dysarthria, and right-sided facial droop is concerning for an acute ischemic stroke. The most important initial step in management is to determine whether the stroke is ischemic or hemorrhagic, as management differs significantly. This is best accomplished with a noncontrast head CT, which can quickly and accurately identify the presence of blood. If no hemorrhage is identified, acute ischemic stroke is diagnosed, and the patient should be evaluated for thrombolytic therapy with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). 

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department for sudden weakness. He was doing mechanical work on his car where he acutely developed right-leg weakness and fell to the ground. He is accompanied by his wife, who said that this has never happened before. He was last seen neurologically normal approximately 2 hours prior to presentation. His past medical history is significant for hypertension and type II diabetes. His temperature is 98.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 177/108 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Neurological exam reveals that he is having trouble speaking and has profound weakness of his right upper and lower extremity. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's acute onset of right-sided weakness and speech difficulty is concerning for an ischemic stroke. The first step in management is to obtain a noncontrast head CT to differentiate between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. Hemorrhagic stroke is a contraindication to thrombolytic therapy, which is the treatment of choice for ischemic stroke if there are no contraindications and the patient presents within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: An 82-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after losing consciousness at her nursing home. She had been watching TV for several hours and while getting up to use the bathroom, she fell and was unconscious for several seconds. She felt dizzy shortly before the fall. She does not have a headache or any other pain. She has a history of hypertension, intermittent atrial fibrillation, and stable angina pectoris. Current medications include warfarin, aspirin, hydrochlorothiazide, and a nitroglycerin spray as needed. Her temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 100/min and regular, and blood pressure is 102/56 mm Hg. Physical exam shows a dry tongue. A fold of skin that is pinched on the back of her hand unfolds after 2 seconds. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.C: Hypodense lesions on CT scan of the head

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of dizziness upon standing, dry tongue, and tenting of the skin on the back of her hand are suggestive of volume depletion. Volume depletion (also known as hypovolemia) refers to a loss of both water and sodium, often due to conditions such as vomiting, diarrhea, or, as in this case, use of diuretics. This can lead to a decrease in effective circulating volume, which can cause symptoms such as dizziness or syncope, especially upon standing (orthostatic hypotension). 

In volume depletion, the kidneys attempt to conserve water and sodium, which can lead to an increase in the blood urea nitrogen (BUN) concentration. This is because urea reabsorption in the proximal tubule is a passive process that is increased when the tubular flow rate is decreased (as in volume depletion). In contrast, creatinine is freely filtered at the glomerulus and is not reabsorbed by the tubules, so its concentration is not significantly affected by changes in tubular flow rate. Therefore, the BUN/creatinine ratio is often elevated (>20:1) in prerenal conditions such as volume depletion.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with complaints of right-sided weakness and slurring of speech for 1 hour. There is no history of head trauma, myocardial infarction, recent surgery, gastrointestinal or urinary bleeding. He has hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation, and a 20 pack-year cigarette smoking history. The medication list includes valsartan and rivaroxaban. The vital signs include: blood pressure 180/92 mm Hg, pulse 144/min and irregular, and temperature 37.2°C (99.0°F). On physical examination, there is a facial asymmetry with a deviation of angle of mouth to the left side on smiling. Muscle strength is reduced in both upper and lower limbs on the right side while on the left side it’s normal. Random blood glucose is 104 mg/dL. A complete blood count is normal. A CT scan of the head is shown in the image. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has an acute ischemic stroke, as evidenced by the sudden onset of focal neurologic deficits and a non-contrast CT scan of the head showing a hyperdense middle cerebral artery (MCA) sign. The hyperdense MCA sign is caused by thromboembolic occlusion of the MCA, leading to increased density of the artery relative to the brain parenchyma and other arteries. This is a poor prognostic sign, indicating a large clot burden and increased risk for significant cerebral edema and hemorrhagic transformation.

The mainstay of treatment for acute ischemic stroke is intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), which must be administered within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. However, tPA is contraindicated in patients with certain conditions that increase the risk for hemorrhagic complications, including current use of direct oral anticoagulants (eg, rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran) within the last 48 hours, regardless of laboratory coagulation studies. Therefore, this patient should be treated with aspirin, which is the treatment of choice for patients with acute ischemic stroke who are not candidates for tPA.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 78-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department by his daughter for sudden onset speech changes. The patient lives with his daughter and was chatting with her when suddenly his speech became distorted with random and disconnected words that made no sense. He seems to be physically frustrated that no one understands him. Physical examination demonstrates weakness of the right arm. Damage to which location would best explain this patient’s symptoms?

few_shot.question: A 78-year-old right-handed male is brought in by ambulance after being found down in his home. After being aroused, the patient has difficulty answering questions and appears to be frustrated by his inability to communicate. He is able to speak his name and a few other words but his speech is not fluent. Subsequent neurologic exam finds that the patient is able to comprehend both one and two step instructions; however, he is unable to repeat phrases despite being able to understand them. He also has difficulty writing despite retaining fine motor control. CT reveals an acute stroke to his left hemisphere. Damage to which of the following sets of structures would be most likely to result in this pattern of deficits?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of non-fluent speech, impaired repetition, and difficulty writing are consistent with Broca's aphasia. This condition is caused by damage to the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, which is the left hemisphere in about 95% of right-handed individuals and 70% of left-handed individuals. The inferior frontal gyrus is also known as Broca's area.

The other options listed are not typically associated with Broca's aphasia. For example, damage to the arcuate fasciculus, which connects Broca's area to Wernicke's area, would cause conduction aphasia, characterized by fluent speech, poor repetition, but intact comprehension. Damage to the watershed zone would cause a variety of symptoms depending on the specific location of the infarct, but would not typically cause Broca's aphasia. Damage to the precentral gyrus would cause contralateral weakness or paralysis, but would not affect speech.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old female patient is brought to the emergency department after her daughter noticed she has been having meaningless speech. When assessing the patient, she calls the chair a table, and at times would make up new words. She does not appear to be aware of her deficit, and is carrying on an empty conversation. Her speech is fluent, but with paraphasic errors. Her repetition is impaired. On physical examination, a right upper quadrant field-cut is appreciated, with impairment in comprehension and repetition. Which of the following structures is most likely involved in this patient’s presentation?

answer_choices.C: Acuate fasciculus, inferior frontal gyrus, and superior temporal gyrus
answer_choices.D: Frontal lobe, sparing Broadmann's area 44 and 45

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fluent speech with paraphasic errors, impaired comprehension, and impaired repetition are consistent with Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia. Wernicke's aphasia is caused by a lesion in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant cerebral hemisphere (usually the left hemisphere). Patients with Wernicke's aphasia often have a right upper visual field cut due to involvement of the optic radiation in the lesion.

The other options listed are not typically associated with Wernicke's aphasia. The inferior frontal gyrus is involved in Broca's (expressive) aphasia, which is characterized by non-fluent speech, intact comprehension, and impaired repetition. The arcuate fasciculus connects Broca's and Wernicke's areas and is involved in conduction aphasia, which is characterized by fluent speech, intact comprehension, and impaired repetition. A lesion in the frontal lobe sparing Brodmann's areas 44 and 45 would not typically cause the symptoms seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: An 82-year-old right-handed woman is brought in by ambulance after being found down in her home. On presentation, she is found to be awake but does not follow directions or respond to questions. She is able to speak and produces a fluent string of nonsensical words and sounds. She does not appear to be bothered by her deficits. Subsequent neurologic exam finds that the patient is unable to comprehend any instructions and is also unable to repeat phrases. CT scan reveals an acute stroke to her left hemisphere. Damage to which of the following structures would be most likely to result in this pattern of deficits?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fluent speech, impaired comprehension, and inability to repeat phrases are consistent with Wernicke's aphasia. This condition is caused by a lesion in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, which is the left hemisphere in about 95% of right-handed individuals and 70% of left-handed individuals. Patients with Wernicke's aphasia are often unaware of their language deficits, a condition known as anosognosia.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 59-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife for a 1-hour history of sudden behavior changes. They were having lunch together when, at 1:07 PM, he suddenly dropped his sandwich on the floor. Since then, he has been unable to use his right arm. She also reports that he is slurring his speech and dragging his right foot when he walks. Nothing like this has ever happened before. The vital signs include: pulse 95/min, blood pressure 160/90 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 14/min. The physical exam is notable for an irregularly irregular rhythm on cardiac auscultation. On neurological exam, he has a facial droop on the right half of his face but is able to elevate his eyebrows symmetrically. He has 0/5 strength in his right arm, 2/5 strength in his right leg, and reports numbness throughout the right side of his body. Angiography of the brain will most likely show a lesion in which of the following vessels?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of sudden-onset right-sided weakness, numbness, and slurred speech are concerning for an acute ischemic stroke. His irregularly irregular heart rhythm suggests atrial fibrillation, a common cause of cardioembolic stroke. The middle cerebral artery (MCA) is the most commonly affected vessel in cardioembolic stroke. Occlusion of the MCA can cause contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss (face and upper extremity > lower extremity), homonymous hemianopia, and, if the dominant hemisphere is involved, aphasia. The facial droop that spares the forehead seen in this patient is characteristic of a central (upper motor neuron) process such as stroke. In contrast, peripheral facial paralysis (eg, Bell palsy) affects the entire half of the face, including the forehead.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of a 2-week history of progressive disorientation and a 1-day history of left-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. The wife reports that the patient had a minor fall 4 months ago, during which he may have hit his head. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He drinks 3–4 bottles of beer daily. He is only oriented to person. Neurological examination shows moderate spastic weakness, decreased sensation, and increased deep tendon reflexes in the left upper and lower extremities. A CT scan of the head is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a minor fall, progressive disorientation, and focal neurologic deficits, along with the CT scan findings, are suggestive of a chronic subdural hematoma (SDH). SDHs are caused by tearing of the bridging veins, which run through the subdural space to drain blood from the surface of the brain into the dural sinuses. The elderly, alcoholics, and patients receiving anticoagulation are at increased risk due to brain atrophy, which stretches and makes these veins more susceptible to tearing. SDHs can have an indolent course and may present weeks to months after a minor fall with nonspecific symptoms such as headache, confusion, and lethargy. Focal neurologic deficits can also occur due to compression of the underlying brain tissue.

So, the answer is [D].

question: A 54-year-old man comes to the clinic for management of his gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). He is currently on cimetidine for his condition and reports that his GERD initially improved. However, following his recent move to Michigan, he is experiencing more frequent episodes of chest pain (4-5 times a week). The pain is described as burning in quality and is concentrated around his epigastric region following food ingestion. It does not radiate anywhere and is alleviated when he takes antacids. A physical examination demonstrates a healthy male with unremarkable findings. He is subsequently prescribed a new medication for control of his symptoms. What is the most likely mechanism of action of this new medication?

answer_choices.B: Irreversible inhibition of H+/K+-ATPase at parietal cells
answer_choices.C: Reversible inhibition of H+/K+-ATPase at parietal cells
answer_choices.D: Reversible inhibition of histamine H2 receptors

few_shot.question: A 47-year-old man with gastroesophageal reflux disease comes to the physician because of severe burning chest pain and belching after meals. He has limited his caffeine intake and has been avoiding food close to bedtime. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy shows erythema and erosions in the distal esophagus. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the most appropriate drug for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of burning chest pain and belching after meals, along with endoscopic findings of erythema and erosions in the distal esophagus, are consistent with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). GERD is caused by the reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, leading to symptoms of heartburn and regurgitation. It is often associated with obesity, hiatal hernia, and certain foods and medications.

The mainstay of treatment for GERD is acid suppression, which can be achieved with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) or histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs). PPIs are more effective than H2RAs and are therefore considered first-line therapy. PPIs (eg, omeprazole, pantoprazole) work by irreversibly inhibiting the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) in gastric parietal cells. This inhibition blocks the final step in gastric acid production, thereby providing potent and long-lasting acid suppression.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of burning epigastric pain, dry cough, and occasional regurgitation. The pain is aggravated by eating and lying down. Physical examination shows a soft, non-tender abdomen. Upper endoscopy shows hyperemia in the distal third of the esophagus. Which of the following drugs is most likely to directly inhibit the common pathway of gastric acid secretion?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of burning epigastric pain, dry cough, and occasional regurgitation are suggestive of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). GERD is caused by the reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, leading to symptoms of heartburn and regurgitation. It can also cause chronic cough, laryngitis, and even asthma due to microaspiration of gastric contents.

The most effective drugs for the treatment of GERD are proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as lansoprazole. PPIs inhibit the H+/K+ ATPase in the stomach, which is the final common pathway for gastric acid secretion. This makes them more effective than H2 receptor antagonists (eg, ranitidine) and antacids (eg, aluminum hydroxide) at reducing gastric acid secretion.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old man comes to his primary care physician complaining of abdominal pain. He describes intermittent, burning, epigastric pain over the past 4 months. He reports that the pain worsens following meals. He had an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy done 2 months ago that showed a gastric ulcer without evidence of malignancy. The patient was prescribed pantoprazole with minimal improvement in symptoms. He denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or melena. The patient has no other medical problems. He had a total knee replacement 3 years ago following a motor vehicle accident for which he took naproxen for 2 months for pain management. He has smoked 1 pack per day since the age 22 and drinks 1-2 beers several nights a week with dinner. He works as a truck driver, and his diet consists of mostly of fast food. His family history is notable for hypertension in his paternal grandfather and coronary artery disease in his mother. On physical examination, the abdomen is soft, nondistended, and mildly tender in the mid-epigastric region. A stool test is positive for Helicobacter pylori antigen. In addition to antibiotic therapy, which of the following is the most likely to decrease the recurrence of the patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a gastric ulcer, which is likely due to Helicobacter pylori infection. H pylori is a gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the gastric mucosa and causes chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, gastric adenocarcinoma, and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma. The bacterium produces urease, which generates ammonia from urea and neutralizes gastric acid, allowing the bacteria to survive in the acidic environment of the stomach. H pylori infection is treated with a combination of a proton pump inhibitor and two antibiotics (eg, amoxicillin, clarithromycin, metronidazole) for 10-14 days.

However, the patient's smoking habit is also a risk factor for peptic ulcer disease. Smoking impairs ulcer healing and increases the risk of ulcer complications (eg, bleeding, perforation) and recurrence. It does so by decreasing mucosal blood flow, bicarbonate secretion, and prostaglandin production, and by increasing gastric acid secretion. Therefore, smoking cessation is the most effective intervention to decrease the recurrence of the patient's symptoms.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 51-year-old man seeks evaluation from his family physician with a complaint of heartburn, which has been gradually increasing over the last 10 years. The heartburn gets worse after eating spicy foods and improves with antacids. The past medical history is benign. He is a security guard and works long hours at night. He admits to smoking 1.5 packs of cigarettes every day. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals several gastric ulcers and regions of inflammation. A biopsy is obtained, which revealed gram-negative bacteria colonized on the surface of the regenerative epithelium of the stomach, as shown in the micrograph below. Which of the following bacterial products is responsible for neutralizing the acidity of the stomach?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of chronic heartburn and endoscopic findings of gastric ulcers and inflammation are suggestive of Helicobacter pylori infection. H. pylori is a gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the stomach and is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastritis. It is also associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma.

H. pylori has several mechanisms that allow it to survive in the acidic environment of the stomach. One of the key mechanisms is the production of urease, an enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide. The ammonia produced can neutralize gastric acid, creating a more favorable environment for the bacteria.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 47-year-old man visits the outpatient clinic with complaints of heartburn and chest pain for the past 6 months. His pain is retrosternal and was initially only associated with intake of solid foods, but it now occurs with liquids as well. Antacids do not relieve his pain anymore. He is worried about the pain as it is getting worse with time. He also had an unintentional weight loss of 2.7 kg (6 lb) during this period. Physical examination including the abdominal examination is normal. Laboratory investigations reveal:
Hgb 10 mg/dL
White blood cell total count 5 x 109/L
Platelet count 168 x 109/ L
Hematocrit 38%
Red blood cell count 4.2 x 1012/ L
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy reveals an exophytic mass in the lower third of the esophagus with ulcerations and mucous plugs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of progressive dysphagia (initially to solids, then to liquids), weight loss, and anemia are concerning for esophageal cancer. The two main types of esophageal cancer are squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and adenocarcinoma. SCC often presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss, and is associated with smoking and alcohol use. It is most common in the upper two-thirds of the esophagus. Adenocarcinoma is most common in the distal esophagus and is associated with Barrett esophagus, a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease. Given this patient's symptoms of heartburn and the location of the mass in the distal esophagus, adenocarcinoma is the most likely diagnosis.

So, the answer is [D].

question: An otherwise healthy 15-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with extreme fatigue and shortness of breath. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), the blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg and the pulse is 100/min. Past medical history is noncontributory and he takes no medication. His father and aunt both suffer from mild anemia. On examination, he is very pale and his spleen is enlarged. His hemoglobin is 5 g/dL and platelet count is slightly reduced. His peripheral blood smear is shown in the picture. Over the next 2 weeks, the patient recovers, and his hemoglobin is 11 g/dL. Which of the following best represents the pattern of inheritance of this patient underlying disorder?

few_shot.question:
A 6-year-old girl comes with her parents to the physician’s office to initiate care with a new physician. The patient was recently adopted and her parents do not know her birth history; however, she has had some issues with fatigue. They were told by the adoption agency that the patient has required blood transfusions for “low blood count” in the past but they are not aware of the reason for these transfusions. Her temperature is 37.8°C (99.8°F), blood pressure is 110/84 mmHg, and pulse is 95/min. Physical examination is notable for conjunctival pallor, pale skin, and mild splenomegaly. A complete blood count is taken in the office with the following results:

Hemoglobin: 6.8 g/dL
Leukocyte count: 5,000/mm^3
Platelet count: 190,000/mm^3

Peripheral smear shows echinocytes and further analysis reveals rigid red blood cells. The most likely cause of this patient's symptoms has which of the following modes of inheritance?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's pallor, fatigue, and splenomegaly are suggestive of anemia. The presence of rigid red blood cells on peripheral smear is indicative of hereditary spherocytosis (HS). HS is the most common inherited disorder of red blood cell membrane proteins. It is most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, but can also be autosomal recessive, especially in cases where there is no family history, as in this patient. The disease is characterized by extravascular hemolysis, which occurs when the spleen destroys structurally abnormal, spherically shaped erythrocytes. 

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: An 8-year-old boy presents with a 7-day history of fever and abdominal pain for the past 4 days. Past medical history is significant for an exchange transfusion for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and recurrent attacks of pallor during the course of upper respiratory tract infections. His vital signs include: blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse 105/min, respiratory rate 40/min, and temperature 37.0℃ (98.6℉). On physical examination, the patient is ill-looking. Conjunctivae are pale and the sclera is icteric. The liver is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory findings show hemoglobin of 5.9 gm/dL, Hct of 20%, and haptoglobin of 28 gm/dL. A peripheral blood smear shows hypochromic anemia, polychromasia, anisocytosis, and occasional Heinz bodies. The reticulocyte count was 15%. A direct Coombs test was negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, recurrent episodes of pallor during infections, and current findings of anemia, jaundice, and reticulocytosis suggest a chronic hemolytic anemia. The presence of Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) on the peripheral smear is indicative of oxidative damage to the red blood cells (RBCs). This is seen in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, an X-linked disorder that is one of the most common causes of hemolytic anemia worldwide.

G6PD is an enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway that generates NADPH. NADPH is necessary to keep glutathione in its reduced form. Reduced glutathione protects RBCs from oxidative damage. In G6PD deficiency, RBCs are more susceptible to oxidative stress. Oxidative stress can be precipitated by infections, certain drugs (eg, sulfonamides, dapsone, primaquine, nitrofurantoin), and fava beans. The oxidative stress denatures hemoglobin, forming Heinz bodies. Heinz bodies damage the RBC membrane, leading to intravascular hemolysis or bite cells (RBCs with a "bite" taken out of the cell membrane) if the Heinz bodies are removed by splenic macrophages.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department due to an episode of lightheadedness. The patient was working at his garage workbench when he felt like he was going to faint. His temperature is 98.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 125/62 mmHg, pulse is 117/min, respirations are 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Laboratory values are ordered as seen below.

Hemoglobin: 7 g/dL
Hematocrit: 22%
Leukocyte count: 6,500/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 197,000/mm^3

The patient is started on blood products and a CT scan is ordered. Several minutes later, his temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 87/48 mmHg, and pulse is 180/min. The patient's breathing is labored. Which of the following is also likely to be true?

answer_choices.A: A past medical history of repeat GI and respiratory infections
answer_choices.B: Autoimmune reaction against red blood cell antigens
answer_choices.C: Diffuse whiting out of the lungs on chest radiograph

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), which is a type of transfusion reaction that occurs within 6 hours of transfusion. It is characterized by acute onset of hypoxemia and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. The pathogenesis of TRALI is not entirely understood, but it is thought to involve the infusion of donor antibodies that react against recipient leukocytes, causing them to aggregate in the pulmonary vasculature. This leads to endothelial damage and capillary leak. The chest x-ray in TRALI shows bilateral infiltrates. Treatment is supportive, with oxygen or mechanical ventilation as needed.

The other options are not consistent with this patient's presentation. A past medical history of repeat GI and respiratory infections could suggest an immunodeficiency, but this patient's leukocyte count and differential are normal. An autoimmune reaction against red blood cell antigens could cause autoimmune hemolytic anemia, but this would not explain this patient's acute decompensation. Sudden rupture of a vessel could cause hemorrhagic shock, but the patient's acute respiratory distress and absence of findings such as abdominal pain or distension make this less likely.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 5-day history of fever, fatigue, and red spots on her body. Her temperature is 38.3°C (101.1°F), pulse is 115/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor and petechiae over the trunk and lower extremities. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 7 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 2,000/mm3, a platelet count of 40,000/mm3, and a reticulocyte count of 0.2%. Peripheral blood smear shows normochromic, normocytic cells. A bone marrow aspirate shows hypocellularity. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's pancytopenia (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and hypocellular bone marrow are consistent with aplastic anemia. Aplastic anemia is a disorder of bone marrow stem cells that results in a loss of blood cell precursors and subsequent pancytopenia. The etiology is often idiopathic, but it can be secondary to radiation, drugs (eg, chloramphenicol, alkylating agents, antiepileptics), chemicals (eg, benzene, toluene), viral infections (eg, hepatitis, EBV, HIV, parvovirus B19), or immune disorders (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus). Patients present with symptoms of anemia (eg, fatigue, pallor), thrombocytopenia (eg, petechiae, easy bruising, mucosal bleeding), and neutropenia (eg, fever, recurrent infections). The diagnosis is confirmed by bone marrow biopsy showing hypocellular marrow replaced with fat.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 13-year-old girl is brought to the outpatient clinic by her parents with a complaint of episodic spasm in her fingers for the past few months. Upon further questioning, her mother notes that the girl has not been doing well at school. She also believes that the girl is shorter than the other children in her class. On examination, her pulse is 72/min, temperature 37.6°C (99.7°F), respiratory rate 16/min, and blood pressure 120/88 mm Hg. The girl has short 4th and 5th fingers on both hands, a round face, and discolored teeth. Her height is 135 cm (4 ft 5 in) and she weighs 60 kg (132 lb). Investigation reports show the following values:
Hemoglobin (Hb%) 12.5 g/dL
White blood cell total count 10,000/mm3
Platelets 260,000/mm3
Calcium, serum (Ca2+) 4.0 mg/dL
Serum albumin 4.0 g/dL
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), serum 15 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST), serum 8 U/L
Serum creatinine 0.5 mg/dL
Urea 27 mg/dL
Sodium 137 mEq/L
Potassium 4.5 mEq/L
Magnesium 2.5 mEq/L
Parathyroid hormone, serum, N-terminal 930 pg/mL (normal: 230-630 pg/mL)
Serum vitamin D 45 ng/dL
Which of the following is the mode of inheritance of the disease this patient has?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's short stature, round face, short 4th and 5th fingers, and discolored teeth are suggestive of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (AHO), also known as pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism. This is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mutation in the GNAS1 gene, which codes for the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein (Gsα). This protein is involved in the signal transduction of several hormones, including parathyroid hormone (PTH). In AHO, there is end-organ resistance to PTH, leading to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. This can cause symptoms such as muscle spasms and seizures. The elevated PTH level in this patient is consistent with this diagnosis.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 53-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of cough and progressively worsening difficulty walking up the stairs in his apartment. He has noticed that it is easier for him to climb the stairs after he has exercised. He has also had a 4.6-kg (10.1-lb) weight loss over the past 6 months. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years. Examination shows dry mucous membranes. The pupils are equal and react sluggishly to light. Muscle strength in the proximal lower extremity is initially 3/5 but increases to 5/5 after repeated muscle tapping. His achilles reflex is 1+. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old woman is referred to a tertiary care hospital with a history of diplopia and fatigue for the past 3 months. She has also noticed difficulty in climbing the stairs and combing her hair. She confirms a history of 2.3 kg (5.0 lb) weight loss in the past 6 weeks and constipation. Past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus. She has a 50-pack-year cigarette smoking history. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 135/78 mm Hg supine and 112/65 while standing, a heart rate of 82/min supine and 81/min while standing, and a temperature of 37.0°C (98.6°F). She is oriented to time and space. Her right upper eyelid is slightly drooped. She has difficulty in abducting the right eye. Pupils are bilaterally equal and reactive to light with accommodation. The corneal reflex is intact. Muscle strength is reduced in the proximal muscles of all 4 limbs, and the lower limbs are affected more when compared to the upper limbs. Deep tendon reflexes are bilaterally absent. After 10 minutes of cycling, the reflexes become positive. Sensory examination is normal. Diffuse wheezes are heard on chest auscultation. Which of the following findings is expected?

answer_choices.B: Incremental pattern on repetitive nerve conduction studies
answer_choices.C: Periventricular plaques on MRI of the brain
answer_choices.D: Thymoma on CT scan of the chest

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of ptosis, diplopia, and proximal muscle weakness is suggestive of myasthenia gravis (MG). MG is an autoimmune disorder caused by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction. These antibodies lead to complement-mediated damage to the postsynaptic membrane, reducing the number of available AChRs and causing defective neuromuscular transmission. The disease is characterized by fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with repetitive use (eg, difficulty climbing stairs, combing hair) and improves with rest. Ocular symptoms (eg, ptosis, diplopia) are often the initial manifestation.

The diagnosis of MG is confirmed by detecting serum AChR antibodies and with electrophysiologic studies. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 2-3 Hz shows a decremental response (ie, progressively smaller amplitudes) due to failure of neuromuscular transmission. Single-fiber electromyography, which measures the variability in neuromuscular transmission, is the most sensitive test.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 54-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of difficulty swallowing of both solids and liquids for 1 month. During the past 5 months, he has also had increased weakness of his hands and legs. He sails regularly and is unable to hold the ropes as tightly as before. Ten years ago, he was involved in a motor vehicle collision. Examination shows atrophy of the tongue. Muscle strength is decreased in the right upper and lower extremities. There is muscle stiffness in the left lower extremity. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ in the right upper and lower extremities, 3+ in the left upper extremity, and 4+ in the left lower extremity. Plantar reflex shows an extensor response on the left foot. Sensation to light touch, pinprick, and vibration is intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.C: Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of progressive weakness, muscle atrophy, and both upper and lower motor neuron signs (eg, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar response) is suggestive of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). ALS is a degenerative disorder that affects upper motor neurons in the motor cortex and lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord. It is characterized by progressive muscle weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations due to loss of lower motor neurons, along with spasticity and hyperreflexia due to loss of upper motor neurons. Bulbar symptoms (eg, dysarthria, dysphagia) due to involvement of the cranial nerves can also occur. Sensation and bowel and bladder function are typically spared.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 19-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of progressive difficulty climbing stairs over the last 2 years. During this period, he has also had problems with running, occasional falls, and standing from a chair. He has not had any vision problems or muscle cramping. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. Neurological examination shows deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally and sensation to pinprick and light touch is normal. Musculoskeletal examination shows enlarged calf muscles bilaterally. He has a waddling gait. Laboratory studies show a creatine kinase level of 1700 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's proximal muscle weakness, waddling gait, and calf pseudohypertrophy are suggestive of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). DMD is an X-linked recessive disorder that affects 1 in 3600 male births. It is caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene, which leads to progressive muscle fiber damage. The onset of symptoms is usually between ages 2 and 5, and affected boys typically become wheelchair-bound by their early teens. The diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing, which can identify deletions or duplications in the dystrophin gene in approximately 60%-70% of patients. If genetic testing is negative, muscle biopsy demonstrating absent dystrophin can confirm the diagnosis.

So, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [C] > [B] > [A].

few_shot.question:
A 50-year-old man arrives to the clinic complaining of progressive weakness. He explains that for 3 months he has had difficulty climbing the stairs, which has now progressed to difficulty getting out of a chair. He denies diplopia, dysphagia, dyspnea, muscle aches, or joint pains. He denies weight loss, weight gain, change in appetite, or heat or cold intolerance. He reports intermittent low-grade fevers. He has a medical history significant for hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He has taken simvastatin and losartan daily for the past 6 years. His temperature is 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 135/82 mmHg, and pulse is 76/min. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, non-distended, and without hepatosplenomegaly. Muscle strength is 3/5 in the hip flexors and 4/5 in the deltoids, biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric. Sensation to pain, light touch, and vibration are intact. Gait is cautious, but grossly normal. There is mild muscle tenderness of his thighs and upper extremities. There is no joint swelling or erythema and no skin rashes. A complete metabolic panel is within normal limits. Additional lab work is obtained as shown below:

Serum:
Na+: 141 mEq/L
Cl-: 100 mEq/L
K+: 4.3 mEq/L
HCO3-: 23 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen: 18 mg/dL
Glucose: 128 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.0 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase: 69 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 302 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT): 210 U/L
TSH: 6.9 uU/mL
Thyroxine (T4): 5.8 ug/dL
Creatine kinase: 4300 U/L
C-reactive protein: 11.9 mg/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 37 mm/h

Which of the following is the most accurate diagnostic test?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's proximal muscle weakness, elevated muscle enzymes (creatine kinase, AST, ALT), and evidence of an inflammatory response (elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) are suggestive of an inflammatory myopathy. Dermatomyositis also presents with proximal muscle weakness but is distinguished by its characteristic skin findings (eg, Gottron papules, heliotrope rash). The diagnosis of polymyositis is suggested by clinical findings and serum elevations in muscle enzymes, but it is definitively diagnosed by muscle biopsy. Biopsy typically shows endomysial inflammation with muscle fiber necrosis.

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with weakness. She states that at the end of the day she feels so fatigued and weak that she can hardly care for herself. She currently feels this way. The patient has had multiple illnesses recently and has been traveling, hiking, and camping. Her temperature is 98.0°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 124/84 mmHg, pulse is 82/min, respirations are 12/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable for 2/5 strength of the upper extremities and 4/5 strength of the lower extremities. Visual exam is notable for mild diplopia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigable weakness that is worse at the end of the day and involves the ocular muscles is suggestive of myasthenia gravis (MG). MG is an autoimmune disorder caused by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction. These antibodies lead to degradation and loss of AChRs, impairing neuromuscular transmission and causing muscle weakness. The weakness in MG is often fatigable (ie, worsens with repetitive use) and classically improves with rest. Ocular symptoms (eg, ptosis, diplopia due to weakness of the extraocular muscles) are often the initial presentation and are seen in the majority of patients. However, the disease can also affect other muscle groups, leading to symptoms such as dysarthria, dysphagia, and limb weakness.

question: A healthy, full-term 1-day-old female is being evaluated after birth and is noted to have a cleft palate and a systolic ejection murmur at the second left intercostal space. A chest radiograph is obtained which reveals a boot-shaped heart and absence of a thymus. few_shot.question: A healthy, full-term 1-day-old female infant is evaluated after birth. She is noted to have a cleft palate and a systolic ejection murmur at the left intercostal space. Low-set ears and micrognathia are also noted on examination. A chest radiograph is obtained which reveals a boot-shaped heart and absence of thymus. Vital signs are unremarkable. Echocardiography is performed which demonstrates a ventricular septal defect, pulmonary valve stenosis, a misplaced aorta, and a thickened right ventricular wall. Family history is non-contributory; not much is known about the father. Of the following, which might the baby likely have?
few_shot.explanation:
This infant has DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome), a disorder associated with abnormal development of the pharyngeal pouch system. The pharyngeal pouches give rise to the thymus and parathyroid glands, among other structures. Therefore, patients with DiGeorge syndrome often have T-cell deficiency due to thymic aplasia and hypocalcemia due to parathyroid aplasia. Hypocalcemia can cause neuromuscular irritability and, in severe cases, seizures. Other findings in DiGeorge syndrome may include congenital heart disease (especially conotruncal abnormalities such as tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, and interrupted aortic arch), characteristic facial features (eg, low-set ears, fish-shaped mouth), and palatal abnormalities.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old woman gives birth to a male infant. During her third-trimester antenatal sonogram, the radiologist noted a suspected congenital heart defect, but the exact nature of the defect was not clear. The pediatrician orders an echocardiogram after making sure that the baby’s vital signs are stable. This reveals the following findings: atresia of the muscular tricuspid valve, pulmonary outflow tract obstruction, open patent ductus arteriosus, a small ventricular septal defect, and normally related great arteries. The pediatrician explains the nature of the congenital heart defect to the infant's parents. He also informs them about the probable clinical features that are likely to develop in the infant, the proposed management plan, and the prognosis. Which of the following signs is most likely to manifest first in this infant?
few_shot.explanation:
The infant has tricuspid atresia, a cyanotic congenital heart defect. In this condition, the tricuspid valve is completely closed, leading to an underdeveloped or absent right ventricle. This prevents the flow of blood from the right atrium to the right ventricle, and hence to the lungs. The only way for the blood to reach the lungs is through an atrial septal defect or a patent foramen ovale, and a ventricular septal defect. The blood then returns to the left atrium, mixes with the oxygenated blood, and is then pumped into the systemic circulation. This leads to cyanosis, which is the earliest sign in tricuspid atresia. The cyanosis is usually noted in the first few days of life, and manifests as a bluish discoloration of the lips and tongue.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 1-month-old baby is brought to the emergency department because he had a coughing spell while feeding and turned blue. The mother says that the blue color went away when she picked the baby up and brought his knees to his chest. The physician orders a chest X-ray which shows a boot-shaped heart and he tells the mother that the baby has a condition that is caused by an anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum. What are the 4 features of the baby’s cardiac condition?

answer_choices.A: Pulmonary stenosis, left ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta
answer_choices.B: Pulmonary regurgitation, left ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta
answer_choices.C: Pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, atrial septal defect, overriding pulmonary artery
answer_choices.D: Pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta

few_shot.explanation:
The baby's symptoms and the chest X-ray findings are consistent with Tetralogy of Fallot, the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease. This condition is characterized by four features:

1. Pulmonary stenosis: This leads to right-to-left shunting of blood through the ventricular septal defect, causing cyanosis.
2. Right ventricular hypertrophy: This is a result of the increased pressure load on the right ventricle due to the pulmonary stenosis.
3. Ventricular septal defect: This allows for the right-to-left shunting of blood.
4. Overriding aorta: The aorta is positioned directly over the ventricular septal defect, allowing for oxygen-poor blood to enter the systemic circulation.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 4-day-old male infant is brought to the physician because of respiratory distress and bluish discoloration of his lips and tongue. He was born at term and the antenatal period was uncomplicated. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 170/min, respirations are 65/min, and blood pressure is 70/46 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 82%. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard over the left lower sternal border. A single S2 that does not split with respiration is present. Echocardiography shows defects in the interatrial and interventricular septae, as well as an imperforate muscular septum between the right atrium and right ventricle. few_shot.explanation:
This infant's cyanosis, respiratory distress, and single S2 are suggestive of a cyanotic congenital heart disease. The echocardiographic findings of an imperforate muscular septum between the right atrium and right ventricle, as well as defects in the interatrial and interventricular septae, are consistent with tricuspid atresia. Tricuspid atresia is a cyanotic congenital heart disease characterized by the absence of the tricuspid valve and a hypoplastic right ventricle. This leads to right-to-left shunting of blood through an atrial septal defect, resulting in cyanosis. The murmur heard in this patient is likely due to blood flow across a ventricular septal defect.

On electrocardiogram, tricuspid atresia is associated with left-axis deviation due to the underdevelopment of the right ventricle and dominance of the left ventricle.

few_shot.question: A 1-day-old infant born at full term by uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery is noted to have cyanosis of the oral mucosa. The baby otherwise appears comfortable. On examination, his respiratory rate is 40/min and pulse oximetry is 80%. His left thumb is displaced and hypoplastic. A right ventricular lift is palpated, S1 is normal, S2 is single, and a harsh 3/6 systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border. Chest X-ray is shown. few_shot.explanation:
This infant has cyanosis, a harsh systolic ejection murmur, and a right ventricular lift, which are suggestive of a right-to-left shunt. The chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart due to right ventricular hypertrophy and decreased pulmonary vascular markings, which are indicative of decreased pulmonary blood flow. These findings are consistent with tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), the most common cause of cyanotic congenital heart disease after the neonatal period. TOF consists of a ventricular septal defect, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (eg, pulmonary stenosis), right ventricular hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta. The degree of right-to-left shunting and cyanosis depends on the severity of the right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The thumb abnormality in this infant is suggestive of Holt-Oram syndrome (heart-hand syndrome), an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by upper limb abnormalities and cardiac defects, most commonly atrial and ventricular septal defects and TOF.

question: A 42-year-old woman with a history of depression and headaches presents to the emergency room with severe, pulsating pain around the crown of her head beginning 12 hours ago. few_shot.question: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because of multiple episodes of headache over the past 3 months. The headaches last the entire day and are unilateral and throbbing. During the headaches, she has severe nausea and is unable to work and perform her daily activities. She has noticed that she becomes unusually hungry prior to the onset of headache. She locks herself in a dark room, takes ibuprofen, and avoids going out until the headache subsides. However, over the past month, the headaches have increased to 2–3 times a week and become more intense. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for long-term prevention of headaches in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's headaches are consistent with migraines, which are characterized by unilateral, pulsating headaches of moderate or severe intensity that last 4–72 hours. Migraines are often associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and/or phonophobia. Many patients also experience premonitory symptoms (eg, food cravings, mood changes, excessive yawning) hours to days before the headache.

The goal of migraine treatment is to reduce the frequency, severity, and duration of headaches and to improve the patient's quality of life. Acute treatment is used to relieve symptoms of ongoing attacks and includes analgesics (eg, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), antiemetics, and migraine-specific drugs (eg, triptans, ergot alkaloids). Preventive treatment is indicated in patients with frequent or severe migraines that interfere with daily activities despite acute treatment, those with contraindications to or failure of acute therapies, and those at risk for medication overuse headache.

Preventive treatment options include beta blockers (eg, propranolol), tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline), antiepileptic drugs (eg, valproate, topiramate), and monoclonal antibodies targeting the calcitonin gene-related peptide pathway. Beta blockers are often used as first-line preventive treatment because they are well tolerated and can be used in patients with common migraine comorbidities (eg, hypertension, as in this patient).

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old obese woman presents with a severe right-sided frontotemporal headache that started 2 days ago. There is no improvement with over-the-counter pain medications. Yesterday, the pain was so intense that she stayed in bed all day in a dark, quiet room instead of going to work. This morning she decided to come in after an episode of vomiting. She says she has experienced 5–6 similar types of headaches each lasting 12–24 hours over the last 6 months but never this severe. She denies any seizures, visual disturbances, meningismus, sick contacts or focal neurologic deficits. Her past medical history is significant for moderate persistent asthma, which is managed with ipratropium bromide and an albuterol inhaler. She is currently sexually active with 2 men, uses condoms consistently, and regularly takes estrogen-containing oral contraceptive pills (OCPs). Her vital signs include: blood pressure 122/84 mm Hg, pulse 86/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) 98% on room air. Physical examination, including a complete neurologic exam, is unremarkable. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain appears normal. Which of the following is the best prophylactic treatment for this patient’s most likely condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's severe, unilateral, pulsating headaches associated with nausea, vomiting, and photophobia are consistent with migraines. Migraines are thought to be due to activation of the trigeminovascular system, which results in the release of vasoactive neuropeptides, causing vasodilation and inflammation. Migraines can be triggered by a variety of factors, including hormonal changes, certain foods, stress, sensory stimuli, changes in sleep pattern, physical factors, changes in the environment, and medications. In this patient, her obesity and use of estrogen-containing oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are likely contributing to the frequency and severity of her migraines.

Migraine prophylaxis is indicated in patients with frequent, long-lasting, or disabling headaches (eg, those that interfere with daily activities or cause significant nausea/vomiting). Prophylactic treatment options include beta blockers (eg, propranolol), calcium channel blockers (eg, verapamil), tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline), and antiepileptic drugs (eg, valproate, topiramate). Given this patient's normal neurologic examination and brain MRI, and the absence of seizures, amitriptyline would be the best prophylactic treatment for her migraines.

few_shot.question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of recurring episodes of headache for the past 5 months. During this period, she has had headaches for approximately 20 days per month. The episodes last for about 2 hours each. She describes the headaches as dull, pressing, and non-pulsating holocranial pain. The symptoms do not increase with exertion. She has no vomiting, nausea, phonophobia, or photophobia. She has two children and has had a great deal of stress lately due to frequent fights with her husband. She appears well. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's headache is chronic (ie, >15 days/month for >3 months) and has at least two of the following characteristics: bilateral location, nonpulsating quality, mild/moderate severity, and not aggravated by routine physical activity. In addition, during the headache, the patient does not have nausea/vomiting or photophobia/phonophobia. These findings are consistent with a diagnosis of chronic tension-type headache (TTH), the most common type of headache. TTH is thought to be associated with pericranial muscle tenderness and stress. The headaches are often described as a "band-like" sensation around the head.

Treatment of TTH depends on the frequency of the headaches. For infrequent TTH, simple analgesics (eg, NSAIDs, acetaminophen) are the treatment of choice. However, medication overuse can lead to chronic TTH or can exacerbate the problem in patients with preexisting chronic TTH. Therefore, patients with chronic TTH should be given prophylactic treatment to reduce the frequency of their headaches. Amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant, is the most effective prophylactic medication for TTH. It is believed to work through antagonism of the 5-HT2 receptor, which results in a down-regulation of the 5-HT2 receptors in the cerebral cortex.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old female presents to her primary care provider for headache. The patient reports that every few weeks she has an episode of right-sided, throbbing headache. few_shot.question: A 66-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a throbbing headache. She states that the pain is worse when eating and is localized over the right side of her head. This patient's headache, jaw claudication, and vision changes in the setting of elevated inflammatory markers are concerning for giant cell arteritis (GCA). The most feared complication of GCA is irreversible vision loss due to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Therefore, patients with suspected GCA should be treated empirically with high-dose glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 40-60 mg/day or equivalent) to prevent vision loss. Temporal artery biopsy should be performed to confirm the diagnosis, but it should not delay treatment.

few_shot.question: A 73-year-old woman visits an urgent care clinic with a complaint of fever for the past 48 hours. She has been having frequent chills and increasing abdominal pain since her fever spiked to 39.4°C (103.0°F) at home. She states that abdominal pain is constant, non-radiating, and rates the pain as a 4/10. She also complains of malaise and fatigue. The past medical history is insignificant. The vital signs include: heart rate 110/min, respiratory rate 15/min, temperature 39.2°C (102.5°F), and blood pressure 120/86 mm Hg. On physical examination, she is icteric and there is severe tenderness on palpation of the right hypochondrium. The ultrasound of the abdomen shows a dilated bile duct and calculus in the bile duct. The blood cultures are pending, and the antibiotic therapy is started. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
Ascending cholangitis is a bacterial infection of the biliary tree that typically occurs secondary to biliary obstruction. The most common cause of obstruction is choledocholithiasis, as seen in this patient. The classic Charcot triad of fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice is seen in only 50%-70% of patients with ascending cholangitis. The presence of sepsis (hypotension and/or altered mental status) in addition to Charcot triad is known as Reynolds pentad. The most common organisms involved are gram-negative enteric bacteria (eg, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species) and enterococci. Empiric antibiotic therapy should be initiated immediately after blood cultures are obtained, and biliary decompression should be performed as soon as possible.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old male presents to your clinic with shortness of breath and lower extremity edema. He was born in Southeast Asia and emigrated to America ten years prior. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with mitral stenosis (MS), which is characterized by an opening snap followed by a mid-to-late diastolic murmur. The murmur of MS is best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. The PCWP is a surrogate for left atrial pressure. In mitral stenosis, the pressure gradient across the mitral valve leads to elevated left atrial pressures, and thus an elevated PCWP. Examination of the lower extremities shows bilateral pitting edema and prominent superficial veins. The skin is warm and there is reddish-brown discoloration of both ankles. Laboratory studies show a normal serum creatinine and normal urinalysis. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's bilateral lower extremity edema, prominent superficial veins, and reddish-brown skin discoloration are suggestive of chronic venous insufficiency (CVI). CVI is caused by venous hypertension, which most commonly results from valvular destruction after deep venous thrombosis or from primary valve incompetence. Venous hypertension leads to the transudation of fibrinogen, which is then polymerized to fibrin. Entrapment of red blood cells in this fibrin meshwork leads to extravasation of red blood cell contents, causing the characteristic reddish-brown skin discoloration (ie, hemosiderin deposition) seen in CVI.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of lower extremity swelling and frothy urine. He has a history of chronic hepatitis C infection. Physical examination shows 3+ pitting edema of the lower legs and ankles. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's lower extremity edema and frothy urine are suggestive of nephrotic syndrome, a kidney disorder characterized by heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/24 hr), hypoalbuminemia, peripheral edema, and hyperlipidemia. The hyperlipidemia is due to both increased synthesis and decreased catabolism of lipoproteins. The liver increases lipoprotein synthesis as a nonspecific response to the hypoalbuminemia. Decreased catabolism occurs because lipoprotein lipase, the enzyme that breaks down triglycerides, is lost in the urine along with the urinary protein.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 2 episodes of loss of consciousness over the past week. She recovered immediately and was not confused following the episodes. During the past 5 months, she has also had increased shortness of breath and palpitations. She has been unable to carry out her daily activities. She also reports some chest tightness that resolves with rest. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She immigrated with her family from India 10 years ago. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 115/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention and pitting edema below the knees. Bilateral crackles are heard at the lung bases. Cardiac examination shows an accentuated and split S2. There is an opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic murmur in the fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation and right axis deviation. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of these findings?

answer_choices.A: Increased left ventricular end diastolic pressure

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and lower extremity edema is suggestive of congestive heart failure. The presence of an opening snap and diastolic murmur at the apex suggests mitral stenosis (MS), most likely due to rheumatic heart disease, which is common in developing countries. In MS, the mitral valve orifice is narrowed, impeding blood flow from the left atrium (LA) to the left ventricle (LV) during diastole. This leads to elevated LA pressures, particularly during exercise when the heart rate increases and the diastolic filling period shortens. The elevated LA pressure is transmitted to the pulmonary vasculature, causing pulmonary congestion and resultant dyspnea, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Atrial fibrillation, the most common arrhythmia in patients with MS, can develop due to chronic LA enlargement. This can lead to decreased cardiac output and/or tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy, both of which can cause or exacerbate heart failure symptoms. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old African American man presents to his primary care physician with a chief complaint of leg swelling. He says that the swelling began about 2 weeks ago and he cannot recall anything that may have provoked the episode. Otherwise he has had joint pain, headaches, frothy urine, and some tingling in his fingers and toes though he doesn't feel that any of this is related to his swelling. He denies any shortness of breath, back pain, or skull pain. His past medical history is significant for mild rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, and hypertension all of which are well controlled. Physical exam reveals 3+ pitting edema in his legs bilaterally. A chest radiograph reveals mild enlargement of the cardiac shadow. Urinalysis reveals 3+ protein and casts with a cross appearance under polarized light. A renal biopsy is taken with a characteristic finding seen only under polarized light. Which of the following is associated with the most likely cause of this patient's edema?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of bilateral leg swelling, frothy urine, and proteinuria is suggestive of nephrotic syndrome. The presence of casts with a cross appearance under polarized light is indicative of multiple myeloma, which can cause nephrotic syndrome due to deposition of light chains in the glomeruli (light chain cast nephropathy). This is also known as myeloma kidney.

Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell dyscrasia characterized by the proliferation of a single clone of plasma cells, leading to overproduction of a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein). The M protein can be an intact immunoglobulin or a fragment of one, such as the immunoglobulin light chain. The light chains can be toxic to the renal tubules and can also form casts that obstruct the tubular lumen, leading to renal impairment.

Multiple myeloma is associated with elevated levels of IL-6, which promotes the growth of the neoplastic plasma cells. IL-6 also increases osteoclast activity, leading to lytic bone lesions, a common finding in multiple myeloma.

So, the answer is [D].

question: A 51-year-old man is brought to the physician by his wife because of a 3-week history of abnormal behavior. His wife reports he has been preoccupied with gambling at the local casino.
