few_shot.question: A 9-month-old male infant is brought to his pediatrician by his mother with lethargy and decreased oral intake for one day. His mother also mentions that he did not sleep well the previous night. A review of the medical record reveals several missed appointments and that the boy was born at 36 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. At the clinic, his temperature is 37.2ºC (99.0ºF), pulse rate is 140/minute, respirations are 44/minute, and blood pressure is 92/60 mm Hg. On physical exam the infant is awake but irritable and the rest of the physical is within normal limits for his age. On ophthalmologic examination, there are multiple retinal hemorrhages that extend to the periphery in both eyes. Which of the following investigations is most likely to be helpful in the management of the infant?
few_shot.explanation:
The presence of retinal hemorrhages in an infant, especially when they extend to the periphery, is highly suggestive of nonaccidental trauma (child abuse), specifically abusive head trauma (formerly known as shaken baby syndrome). This is a form of child abuse that occurs when a child is violently shaken, leading to acceleration-deceleration forces that cause shearing of the bridging veins and subdural hemorrhages. The violent shaking can also cause retinal hemorrhages. The most common presenting symptoms are nonspecific and include vomiting, poor feeding, seizures, and altered mental status, as seen in this patient.

The most appropriate next step in management is to obtain a noncontrast head CT to evaluate for subdural hematomas, cerebral edema, and other intracranial injuries. If abusive head trauma is confirmed, a skeletal survey should also be obtained to evaluate for additional signs of abuse, such as metaphyseal fractures (corner or bucket-handle fractures).

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the emergency room by his mother who reports he has appeared lethargic for the past 3 hours. She reports that she left the patient with a new nanny this morning, and he was behaving normally. When she got home in the afternoon, the patient seemed lethargic and would not breastfeed as usual. At birth, the child had an Apgar score of 8/9 and weighed 2.8 kg (6.1 lb). Growth has been in the 90th percentile, and the patient has been meeting all developmental milestones. There is no significant past medical history, and vaccinations are up-to-date. On physical examination, the patient does not seem arousable. Ophthalmologic examination shows retinal hemorrhages. Which of the following findings would most likely be expected on a noncontrast CT scan of the head?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's lethargy, retinal hemorrhages, and history of being left with a new nanny are concerning for nonaccidental trauma (child abuse). The most common form of child abuse in infants is abusive head trauma (formerly known as shaken baby syndrome). This occurs when a caregiver violently shakes an infant, leading to rapid acceleration-deceleration and rotational forces that cause intracranial injury. The most common findings in abusive head trauma are subdural hematomas, retinal hemorrhages, and encephalopathy (manifesting as seizures, apnea, lethargy, or vomiting). Subdural hematomas are caused by the rupture of the bridging veins that extend from the cerebral hemispheres to the dural sinuses. On noncontrast CT scan of the head, subdural hematomas appear as crescent-shaped, concave hyperdensities along the cerebral convexities that do not cross the midline or the falx.

few_shot.question:
A 6-month-old male presents to the emergency department with his parents after his three-year-old brother hit him on the arm with a toy truck. His parents are concerned that the minor trauma caused an unusual amount of bruising. The patient has otherwise been developing well and meeting all his milestones. answer_choices.B: Complete blood count and coagulation panel

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is concerning for a bleeding disorder. The patient's family history of an unknown blood disorder, pale skin, and blue irises are suggestive of a type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), a group of inherited disorders that affect the connective tissues in the skin, joints, and blood vessel walls. The vascular type of EDS is associated with easy bruising, thin skin with visible veins, and a risk of rupture of blood vessels and organs. The blue irises are a characteristic feature of this type of EDS.

The best initial step in the evaluation of a bleeding disorder is to obtain a complete blood count and coagulation panel. This will help to identify any abnormalities in platelet count, prothrombin time, or partial thromboplastin time, which could suggest a platelet or coagulation factor disorder.

few_shot.question:
A two-month-old female presents to the emergency department for difficulty feeding. The patient was born at 38 weeks gestation to a 29-year-old primigravid via vaginal delivery. The newborn period has thus far been uncomplicated. The patient has been exclusively breastfed since birth. Her parents report that feeding had previously seemed to be going well, and the patient has been gaining weight appropriately. Over the past several days, the patient’s mother has noticed that the patient seems to tire out before the end of the feeding. She has also noticed that the patient begins to appear short of breath and has a bluish discoloration of her lips. The patient’s height and weight were in the 20th and 10th percentile at birth, respectively. Her current height and weight are in the 20th and 15th percentiles, respectively. Her temperature is 98.0°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 60/48 mmHg, pulse is 143/min, and respirations are 40/min. On physical exam, the patient is in no acute distress and appears well developed. A systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur can be heard at the left upper sternal border. Her abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. During the abdominal exam, the patient begins crying and develops cyanosis of the perioral region.

Which of the following is the best initial test to diagnose this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of cyanosis during feeding and crying, along with a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left upper sternal border, is suggestive of tetralogy of Fallot. Tetralogy of Fallot is a congenital heart defect characterized by four anatomical abnormalities: ventricular septal defect, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (usually pulmonary stenosis), overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. The degree of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction determines the severity of the disease. In severe cases, patients may present with cyanosis shortly after birth. In less severe cases, like this one, patients may not present until several weeks or months after birth, when the pulmonary vascular resistance decreases and the right-to-left shunt across the ventricular septal defect increases.

The best initial test to diagnose tetralogy of Fallot is an echocardiogram, which can visualize the anatomical abnormalities and assess the degree of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

His medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, coronary artery disease, stroke, atrial fibrillation, and peptic ulcer disease. Due to his recurrent bleeding peptic ulcers, he does not take warfarin. His surgical history is significant for an appendectomy as a child. His medications include metformin, lisinopril, metoprolol, and omeprazole. He has a 50-pack-year history of smoking. His temperature is 37.6 C (99.7 F), blood pressure is 146/80 mm Hg, pulse is 115/min, and respiratory rate is 20/min. On physical exam, he is in acute distress due to the pain. Pulmonary auscultation reveals scattered wheezes and decreased air entry. His heart rate is irregularly irregular, with no murmurs, rubs or gallops. Abdominal exam is significant for decreased bowel sounds and diffuse tenderness. Initial laboratory evaluation is as follows:

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute abdominal pain, nausea, and elevated amylase in the setting of multiple risk factors for atherosclerosis (eg, age, diabetes, smoking, hypertension, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation) is concerning for acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI). AMI is a condition in which there is inadequate blood flow through the mesenteric vessels, resulting in ischemia and eventual gangrene of the bowel wall. It is a surgical emergency and requires immediate intervention to restore blood flow and prevent bowel necrosis. The most common cause of AMI is embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery, often in patients with atrial fibrillation. Other causes include arterial thrombosis, nonocclusive ischemia due to low flow states, and venous thrombosis. Patients typically present with severe abdominal pain that is out of proportion to physical examination findings. Laboratory studies may show leukocytosis and elevated serum lactate, amylase, and LDH levels.

A 55-year-old female presents to clinic with recurrent episodes of abdominal discomfort and pain for the past month. Peptic ulcers are most commonly caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use. This patient's recent stress and obesity could also be contributing factors. This is because the pyloric sphincter closes after food passes into the duodenum, leaving gastric acid in the stomach where it can irritate the ulcer crater. The pain is often relieved by eating, which buffers the gastric acid, or by antacids. The anemia is likely due to chronic gastrointestinal blood loss from the ulcer.

She reports that she has had a 3.2-kg (7-lb) weight loss after conceiving despite an increase in appetite. She has become increasingly anxious and has trouble falling asleep. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. Medications include folic acid and a multivitamin. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 55 kg (120 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37.4°C (99.4°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 150/70 mm Hg. The globes of the eyes are prominent. The thyroid gland is firm and diffusely enlarged. Neurologic examination shows a fine resting tremor of the hands. There is a midsystolic click at the apex and a grade 2/6 early systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is 0.1 μU/mL. An ECG is normal except for sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's weight loss, increased appetite, anxiety, insomnia, tremor, tachycardia, and systolic murmur are consistent with hyperthyroidism. The diffuse goiter and ophthalmopathy suggest Graves disease, the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in women of childbearing age. Graves disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by circulating immunoglobulins that bind to and stimulate the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, leading to increased synthesis and release of thyroid hormone.

In pregnancy, the preferred treatment for hyperthyroidism is propylthiouracil during the first trimester, then switching to methimazole for the second and third trimesters. Propylthiouracil is preferred initially because methimazole has been associated with a rare congenital anomaly (eg, aplasia cutis, esophageal and choanal atresia). However, propylthiouracil use later in pregnancy is associated with hepatotoxicity, so it is recommended to switch to methimazole after the first trimester.

A 23-year-old primigravida presents to her physician’s office at 12 weeks gestation complaining of increased sweating and palpitations for the last week. In some cases, it can also cause transient hyperthyroidism, as seen in this patient. This is thought to be due to the high levels of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) produced during pregnancy, which can weakly stimulate the thyroid hormone receptor and lead to increased production of thyroid hormone. This is usually a self-limiting condition that resolves as hCG levels decrease later in pregnancy. Treatment is usually supportive, with a focus on correcting dehydration and electrolyte imbalances. Beta-blockers can be used to control symptoms of hyperthyroidism, such as tachycardia and tremors.

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because she has not had her menstrual period yet. She currently takes oral isotretinoin and an oral contraceptive. The patient is at the 97th percentile for height and 50th percentile for weight. A pelvic ultrasound shows ovaries with multiple cysts and a normal uterus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's clitoromegaly, lack of breast development, and cystic ovaries in the setting of maternal virilization during pregnancy are suggestive of a disorder of sex development. The most likely diagnosis is aromatase deficiency. Aromatase is a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of estrogens, catalyzing the conversion of androgens (androstenedione and testosterone) to estrogens (estrone and estradiol). Aromatase deficiency leads to increased levels of androgens (causing virilization) and decreased levels of estrogens. 

In females, lack of estrogen results in lack of breast development and primary amenorrhea despite the presence of a uterus and ovaries. Increased androgens can lead to acne (as seen in this patient) and ambiguous genitalia. Maternal virilization occurs during pregnancy due to the passage of excess androgens from the fetus to the mother, where they are not converted to estrogens due to the fetus's enzyme deficiency. 

This patient's history of fractures is also indicative of low estrogen levels. Estrogen deficiency can lead to decreased bone mineral density and result in fractures.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

She has also noticed an increase in blackheads and pimples on her skin. Her female partner has also recently brought to her attention the deepening of her voice, weight gain, and changes in her external genitalia that generated some personal relationship issues. The patient is frustrated as these changes have appeared over the course of the last 8 months. She claims that she was feeling completely normal before all of these physical changes started. Physical examination shows dark coarse stubbles distributed along her upper lip, chin, chest, back, oily skin, and moderately inflamed acne. Pelvic examination reveals a clitoris measuring 12 mm long, a normal sized mobile retroverted uterus, and a firm, enlarged left ovary. What is the most likely diagnosis of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hirsutism, acne, deepening of the voice, and clitoromegaly is suggestive of virilization, which is a severe form of hyperandrogenism. Virilization is characterized by temporal balding, increased muscle mass, and breast atrophy in addition to the findings in this patient. The most common cause of virilization is a testosterone-secreting ovarian or adrenal neoplasm. The presence of a firm, enlarged ovary on pelvic examination in this patient is suggestive of a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, a sex cord-stromal tumor that secretes testosterone. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors are rare and occur most often in women of reproductive age. They are typically unilateral and often solid, and they range in size from 5 to 25 cm. Most are considered low-grade malignancies, and prognosis is generally good with surgical removal.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of oligomenorrhea and intermittent vaginal spotting for 5 months. Menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals and lasted for 5 days with normal flow. She has also noted increased hair growth on her chin. She is not sexually active. She takes no medications. Physical examination shows temporal hair recession and nodulocystic acne on her cheeks and forehead. There is coarse hair on the chin and the upper lip. Pelvic examination shows clitoral enlargement and a right adnexal mass. Laboratory studies show increased serum testosterone concentration; serum concentrations of androstenedione and dehydroepiandrosterone are within the reference ranges. Ultrasonography of the pelvis shows a 10-cm right ovarian tumor. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, temporal hair recession, nodulocystic acne, clitoral enlargement, and a unilateral ovarian mass is suggestive of a virilizing ovarian tumor. The most common virilizing ovarian tumors are Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors (androblastomas), which are a type of sex cord-stromal tumor. These tumors produce testosterone, leading to the signs of virilization seen in this patient. They are typically unilateral and occur in women of reproductive age. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 3-month-old boy presents to his pediatrician with persistent diarrhea, oral candidiasis, and signs and symptoms suggestive of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) pneumonia. His weight is in the 10th percentile. He is being evaluated for an immunodeficiency disease. Laboratory results for the HIV are negative by PCR. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings in this patient?

answer_choices.B: Grossly reduced levels of B cells

few_shot.question: A 3-month-old boy presents to his pediatrician with persistent diarrhea, oral candidiasis, and signs and symptoms of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) pneumonia. He is very lean with weight in the 10th percentile. His blood pressure is 105/64 mm Hg and heart rate is 84/min. He is being evaluated for an immunodeficiency. Laboratory results for HIV are negative by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Which of the following is the most likely cause of this child’s presentation?

answer_choices.A: An X-linked inheritance of HLA genes
answer_choices.D: Grossly reduced levels of B cells

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of persistent diarrhea, oral candidiasis, and RSV pneumonia is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). SCID is a group of disorders characterized by defects in both T and B cell immunity. The most common form of SCID is X-linked and is due to mutations in the gene for the common gamma chain, a component of several interleukin receptors (eg, IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21). These interleukins are involved in the growth, proliferation, and differentiation of T and B cells. Therefore, defects in the common gamma chain can lead to a severe loss of both T and B cell function.

The other options listed, such as an X-linked inheritance of HLA genes, selective IgA deficiency, and grossly reduced levels of B cells, would not explain this patient's presentation.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [D] > [C] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician for the evaluation of fever, breathing difficulty, and cough during the past week. In the past year, the patient was diagnosed with four sinus infections, 3 upper respiratory tract infections, and an episode of severe bronchiolitis requiring hospitalization. Since birth, he has had multiple episodes of oral thrush treated with nystatin, as well as chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive. His temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 38/min, and blood pressure is 106/63 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry at room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Pulmonary auscultation shows bilateral crackles and wheezing. Physical examination indicates a prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic nasal wing, a shortened chin, and dysplastic ears. An X-ray of the chest shows hyperinflation of the lungs, interstitial infiltrates, and atelectasis. The patient tests positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in the nasopharyngeal aspirate. This patient most likely has a deficiency of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and oral thrush suggests a T-cell deficiency. The facial abnormalities (prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic nasal wing, a shortened chin, and dysplastic ears) are characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome (DGS), a disorder caused by abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. This results in thymic aplasia or hypoplasia, leading to T-cell deficiency. The thymus is the primary site of T-cell maturation, and its absence in DGS results in decreased T-cell production and disrupted cell-mediated immunity. This leads to increased susceptibility to infections with viruses, fungi, and intracellular bacteria. In addition, because T cells are necessary for B-cell activation and production of specific antibodies, patients with DGS also have impaired humoral immunity, leading to increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated bacteria. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever, fast breathing, and difficulty feeding for 2 days. His mother reports that he has had recurrent pneumonia and has been hospitalized for severe dehydration secondary to acute gastroenteritis caused by rotavirus infection three times in the past 4 months. He is at the 3rd percentile for both height and weight. Examination shows a generalized, erythematous, scaly rash and white patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa that bleed when scraped. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates and an absent thymic shadow. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent infections, failure to thrive, and dermatitis is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). SCID is a group of disorders characterized by defects in both T- and B-cell immunity. The most common form of SCID is X-linked SCID, which is due to a mutation in the gene for the IL-2 receptor gamma chain. This chain is shared by several other interleukin receptors (eg, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21), and its absence leads to a severe impairment in both cellular and humoral immunity. 

Affected infants typically present in the first few months of life with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, and severe, recurrent infections with a variety of pathogens, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, and opportunistic organisms. The most common viral infections are caused by respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza, and rotavirus. The most common fungal infections are due to Candida species, which can cause oral thrush, as seen in this patient. 

The diagnosis of SCID is suggested by lymphopenia, markedly reduced T-cell receptor excision circles, and absence of the thymic shadow on chest x-ray. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [C] > [B] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician for the evaluation of fever, difficulty breathing, and coughing for the past week. In the past year, he has had four sinus infections, three upper respiratory tract infections, and an episode of severe bronchiolitis requiring hospitalization. Since birth, he has had multiple episodes of oral thrush treated with nystatin, as well as chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive. His temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 38/min, and blood pressure is 106/63 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Auscultation of the lungs show bilateral crackles and wheezing. Examination shows a prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic wing of the nose, a shortened chin, and dysplastic ears. An x-ray of the chest shows hyperinflation of the lungs, interstitial infiltrates, and atelectasis. A nasopharyngeal aspirate test for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is positive. This patient most likely has a deficiency of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive in the setting of characteristic facial features (prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic wing of the nose, shortened chin, dysplastic ears) is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. DiGeorge syndrome is a congenital disorder caused by the deletion of a small piece of chromosome 22. It results in the poor development of several body systems, including the thymus and parathyroid glands. The thymus gland is necessary for T cell maturation, and thus, patients with DiGeorge syndrome often have T cell deficiency. This leads to an increased susceptibility to viral and fungal infections, as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic because of persistent sinus infections. For the past 5 years, he has had multiple sinus and upper respiratory infections. He has also had recurrent diarrhea throughout childhood. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), the heart rate is 90/min, the respirations are 16/min, and the blood pressure is 125/75 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show abnormally low levels of one immunoglobulin isotype but normal levels of others. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections suggest an immunodeficiency. The most common symptomatic primary immunodeficiency is selective IgA deficiency, which is characterized by decreased levels of IgA with normal levels of other immunoglobulin isotypes. Patients with selective IgA deficiency have a higher incidence of autoimmune diseases, allergies, and malignancies. They are also at risk for anaphylactic transfusion reactions due to the presence of anti-IgA antibodies.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of frequent headaches and blurry vision during the past 4 months. He has also had difficulties achieving an erection over the past few weeks. Physical examination shows a temporal visual field deficit bilaterally. An MRI of the brain shows an intrasellar mass. The mass is most likely derived from which of the following types of cells?

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of episodic headaches involving both temples for 5 months. The patient has been taking acetaminophen, but it has not provided relief. He has also had double vision. Ophthalmic examination shows impaired peripheral vision bilaterally. Contrast MRI of the head shows a 14 x 10 x 8-mm intrasellar mass. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of headache and bitemporal hemianopia, along with the finding of an intrasellar mass on MRI, are suggestive of a pituitary macroadenoma. These tumors often present with symptoms due to mass effect (eg, headache, visual field defects) and/or hypopituitarism. Hypopituitarism occurs when the adenoma's size exceeds 1 cm (macroadenoma), leading to compression of normal pituitary tissue and impaired hormone synthesis. The pituitary hormones are typically lost in the following sequence: growth hormone, luteinizing hormone/follicle-stimulating hormone (LH/FSH), thyroid-stimulating hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and prolactin. Therefore, the earliest and most common hormonal deficiency is growth hormone, followed by LH/FSH. LH/FSH deficiency in men leads to decreased libido and impotence due to decreased testosterone synthesis.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [C] > [D] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old male presents to the hospital complaining of frequent headaches and a decreased libido. During the physical exam, the patient also states that he has recently been experiencing vision problems. The patient is suffering from what type of adenoma?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of headaches, decreased libido, and vision problems are suggestive of a pituitary adenoma. The most common type of pituitary adenoma is a lactotroph adenoma, also known as a prolactinoma. These tumors produce excess prolactin, which can cause symptoms such as decreased libido and erectile dysfunction in men. The tumor can also compress the optic chiasm, leading to vision problems. Headaches are a common symptom of any type of pituitary adenoma due to the increased pressure in the sella turcica.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician for evaluation of 2 months of progressive clumsiness, falls, and increased urinary frequency. Physical examination shows bilateral temporal visual field loss. An MRI of the head shows a small calcified suprasellar mass. The patient undergoes surgery with complete removal of the mass. Pathological examination of the specimen shows a lobular tumor composed of cysts filled with oily, brownish-yellow fluid. This mass is most likely derived from which of the following structures?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of progressive clumsiness, falls, and increased urinary frequency are suggestive of a mass effect in the brain. The MRI findings of a small calcified suprasellar mass and the pathological findings of a lobular tumor composed of cysts filled with oily, brownish-yellow fluid are consistent with a craniopharyngioma. Craniopharyngiomas are benign tumors that are derived from remnants of Rathke pouch, an embryonic precursor of the anterior pituitary. They are the most common suprasellar tumor in children and can cause symptoms due to mass effect (eg, headache, visual field defects) or endocrine abnormalities (eg, growth retardation, delayed puberty).

So, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of episodic headaches for 5 months. The headaches involve both temples and are 4/10 in intensity. The patient has been taking acetaminophen, but the headaches did not subside. He has also had visual disturbances, including double vision. He has no nausea, temperature intolerance, or weight changes. The patient does not smoke. He drinks 2–3 beers on weekends. He appears pale. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure 125/80 mm Hg. Ophthalmologic examination shows impaired peripheral vision bilaterally. An MRI scan of the head with contrast shows a 16 × 11 × 9 mm intrasellar mass. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of headache and bitemporal hemianopia, along with the finding of an intrasellar mass on MRI, are suggestive of a pituitary macroadenoma. These are benign tumors >1 cm that arise from the adenohypophysis and are among the most common types of sellar masses. As they enlarge, pituitary macroadenomas can cause symptoms due to mass effect (eg, headache, visual field defects) and/or hypopituitarism. Hypopituitarism occurs when the tumor impinges on normal pituitary tissue, causing decreased production of one or more pituitary hormones. The sequence of hormone loss usually follows the pattern of GH, LH/FSH, TSH, and ACTH, although there is significant variability.

Loss of LH and FSH in men leads to decreased testosterone production, resulting in symptoms of hypogonadism (eg, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction). Women may develop oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea. In contrast, hyperprolactinemia due to stalk effect or a prolactinoma typically presents with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and sexual dysfunction in women, and sexual dysfunction alone in men.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of headaches and blurry vision for the past 6 months. He also reports frequent episodes of vomiting over the last month. His father has died of renal cell carcinoma at the age of 37 years. Examination shows 20/40 vision bilaterally. Fundoscopic examination shows bilateral optic disc swelling and growth of capillary vessels in the temporal peripheral retina. An MRI of the brain shows an infratentorial mass. The patient undergoes surgical resection of the mass. A photomicrograph of the resected specimen is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of headaches, blurry vision, and vomiting is suggestive of increased intracranial pressure due to a brain tumor. The finding of retinal capillary hemangioblastomas (ie, growth of capillary vessels in the temporal peripheral retina) in a patient with a family history of renal cell carcinoma is suggestive of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease. VHL is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by the development of various benign and malignant tumors. The most common tumors seen in VHL are hemangioblastomas of the central nervous system (especially the cerebellum) and retina, renal cell carcinomas, and pheochromocytomas.

Hemangioblastomas are highly vascular tumors that consist of stromal cells and abundant capillaries. They can produce erythropoietin, leading to secondary polycythemia.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely

question: A 34-year-old woman is assaulted and suffers a number of stab wounds to her abdomen. Bystanders call paramedics and she is subsequently taken to the nearest hospital. On arrival to the emergency department, her vitals are T: 36 deg C, HR: 110 bpm, BP: 100/60, RR: 12, SaO2: 99%. A FAST and abdominal CT are promptly obtained which are demonstrated in Figures A and B, respectively. Her chart demonstrates no other medical problems and vaccinations/boosters up to date. The patient is diagnosed with a Grade V splenic laceration and is immediately brought to the OR for emergent splenectomy. The splenectomy is successfully performed with removal of the damaged spleen (Figure C). Following the operation, the patient should receive which of the following vaccines: (I) H. influenzae (II) Tetanus (III) N. meningitidis (IV) S. pneumoniae (V) Hepatitis B

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old man presents to the primary care clinic in June for post-discharge follow-up. The patient was recently admitted to the hospital after a motor vehicle collision. At that time he arrived at the emergency department unconscious, hypotensive, and tachycardic. Abdominal CT revealed a hemoperitoneum due to a large splenic laceration; he was taken to the operating room for emergency splenectomy. Since that time he has recovered well without complications. Prior to the accident, he was up-to-date on all of his vaccinations. Which of the following vaccinations should be administered at this time?
few_shot.explanation:
The spleen plays a critical role in the immune response to encapsulated bacteria (eg, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis) by producing opsonizing antibodies and facilitating their clearance. Asplenic patients are at increased risk for rapidly progressive infections with these organisms, which can lead to sepsis and death. Therefore, all asplenic patients should receive the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13), the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23), the meningococcal vaccine, and the H influenzae type b vaccine. The PCV13 should be administered first, followed by the PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later. The meningococcal vaccine and H influenzae type b vaccine can be given at any time. If the patient has not yet received these vaccines at the time of splenectomy, they should be administered as soon as possible postoperatively.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 35 minutes after being involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which he was an unrestrained passenger. He was ambulatory at the accident scene, with stable vital signs and no major external injuries except abrasions to both upper extremities. On arrival, he is alert and oriented. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows ecchymosis over the upper abdomen, with tenderness to palpation over the left upper quadrant. There is no guarding or rigidity. Rectal examination is unremarkable. A CT scan of the abdomen with intravenous contrast shows a subcapsular splenic hematoma comprising 8% of the surface area, with no contrast extravasation and minimal blood in the peritoneal cavity. Which of the following is the next best step in management?

answer_choices.D: Coil embolization of short gastric vessels

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a splenic injury due to blunt abdominal trauma. The American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) has a grading system for splenic injuries based on CT findings. This patient's injury is AAST grade I (subcapsular hematoma of <10% of the surface area, capsular laceration <1 cm in depth), which is considered a minor injury. Hemodynamically stable patients with minor splenic injuries can be managed nonoperatively with close monitoring in the hospital, serial abdominal examinations, and possible serial imaging. This approach avoids the risks of surgery and preserves splenic immune function. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being assaulted. The paramedics report that the patient was found conscious and reported being kicked many times in the torso. She is alert and able to respond to questions. She denies any head trauma. She has a past medical history of endometriosis and a tubo-ovarian abscess that was removed surgically two years ago. Her only home medication is oral contraceptive pills. Her temperature is 98.5°F (36.9°C), blood pressure is 82/51 mmHg, pulse is 136/min, respirations are 10/min, and SpO2 is 94%. She has superficial lacerations to the face and severe bruising over her chest and abdomen. Her lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally and her abdomen is soft, distended, and diffusely tender to palpation. Her skin is cool and clammy. Her FAST exam reveals fluid in the perisplenic space.

Which of the following is the next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has signs of hypovolemic shock (eg, hypotension, tachycardia, cool and clammy skin) due to intra-abdominal hemorrhage from blunt abdominal trauma. The initial management of a trauma patient in shock should be to establish two large-bore IVs and begin aggressive fluid resuscitation with crystalloid solution (eg, normal saline, lactated Ringer solution). If the patient does not respond to fluid resuscitation, blood transfusion should be initiated. After initial resuscitation, the patient should be taken to the operating room for exploratory laparotomy to control the source of bleeding.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after falling down a flight of stairs. On arrival, she has shortness of breath, right-sided chest pain, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and right shoulder pain. She is otherwise healthy. She takes no medications. She appears pale. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 115/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 85/45 mm Hg. Examination shows several ecchymoses over the right chest. There is tenderness to palpation over the right chest wall and right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Bowel sounds are normal. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Neck veins are flat. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's right upper quadrant abdominal pain, right shoulder pain, and hypotension following a fall are suggestive of a liver laceration with intra-abdominal hemorrhage. The liver is the most frequently injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma due to its size and location. Hemorrhage can lead to hypovolemic shock, which is characterized by tachycardia, hypotension, and signs of decreased perfusion (eg, pallor, cool extremities, altered mental status). The right shoulder pain (referred pain) is due to diaphragmatic irritation, which is sensed by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5 nerve roots).

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department for a fever and abdominal pain. The patient states that his pain has been worsening over the past week in the setting of a fever. He has a past medical history of IV drug abuse and multiple admissions for septic shock. His temperature is 102°F (38.9°C), blood pressure is 94/54 mmHg, pulse is 133/min, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a murmur over the left upper sternal border. Abdominal exam reveals left upper quadrant tenderness. Laboratory values are ordered as seen below.

Hemoglobin: 15 g/dL
Hematocrit: 44%
Leukocyte count: 16,700/mm^3
Platelet count: 299,000/mm^3

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of IV drug abuse, multiple admissions for septic shock, and new murmur are suggestive of infective endocarditis (IE). IE can lead to septic emboli, which can cause metastatic infections such as a splenic abscess. Splenic abscesses often present with left upper quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and leukocytosis, as seen in this patient. Splenic abscess is a serious condition that requires prompt drainage and antibiotics.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: An otherwise healthy 50-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of increasingly frequent episodes of upper abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He has had a 3.2-kg (7-lb) weight loss during this time. Physical examination shows bilateral pitting pedal edema. An endoscopy shows prominent rugae in the gastric fundus. Biopsy shows parietal cell atrophy. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of epigastric pain and a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss. He feels full and bloated even after eating small portions of food. His hemoglobin concentration is 9.5 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 78 μm3. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy shows a 2-cm raised lesion with central ulceration on the lesser curvature of the stomach. Histologic examination of a gastric biopsy specimen from the lesion is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of early satiety, weight loss, and iron deficiency anemia is concerning for gastric adenocarcinoma. Gastric adenocarcinoma is the most common malignancy of the stomach and is often associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, tobacco use, and consumption of smoked foods, salted fish and meat, and pickled vegetables. The tumor can be exophytic (polypoid), flat, or excavated (ulcerated). Histologically, gastric adenocarcinoma is characterized by gland-forming cuboidal cells.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 21-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of severe abdominal pain, bloating, and episodic diarrhea. He has also had a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss during this time. Physical examination shows a mildly distended abdomen, hyperactive bowel sounds, and diffuse abdominal tenderness. A biopsy specimen of the colonic mucosa shows scattered areas of inflammation with fibrosis and noncaseating granulomas. Which of the following is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?

answer_choices.A: Increased activity of type 1 T helper cells
answer_choices.D: Accumulation of intracellular bacteria in macrophages

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's chronic abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, and weight loss, along with the finding of noncaseating granulomas on biopsy, are suggestive of Crohn disease (CD). CD is a type of inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus. It is characterized by transmural inflammation, which can lead to strictures, abscesses, and fistulas.

The pathogenesis of CD is thought to involve an inappropriate immune response to intestinal flora in genetically susceptible individuals. This immune response is characterized by increased activity of type 1 T helper (Th1) cells, which secrete proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. These cytokines recruit and activate macrophages, which form granulomas and lead to tissue damage.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [D] > [C] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 75-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of upper abdominal pain, nausea, and sensation of early satiety. He has also had a 9.4-kg (20.7-lb) weight loss over the past 4 months. He has osteoarthritis. He drinks two beers every night with dinner. His only medication is ibuprofen. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy shows an ulcerated mass in the lesser curvature of the stomach. A biopsy specimen obtained during endoscopy shows irregular-shaped tubules with intraluminal mucus and debris. Which of the following is the most likely predisposing factor for this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's upper abdominal pain, early satiety, and weight loss are concerning for gastric cancer. The biopsy findings of irregular-shaped tubules with intraluminal mucus and debris are consistent with intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, the most common type of gastric cancer. Intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with environmental factors such as Helicobacter pylori infection, tobacco smoking, and consumption of certain dietary substances. These include high intake of smoked foods, salted fish and meat, and pickled vegetables, which are high in nitrates and nitrites. Nitrates and nitrites are converted to carcinogenic N-nitroso compounds by bacteria in the stomach.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely

few_shot.question: An otherwise healthy 56-year-old man comes to the physician for a 2-year history of recurrent upper abdominal pain and fullness that worsens after meals. Urea breath test is positive. An endoscopy shows diffuse mucosal atrophy and patchy erythema, but no ulcer. A biopsy from which of the following areas is most likely to yield an accurate diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of postprandial abdominal pain and fullness, along with the positive urea breath test, are suggestive of Helicobacter pylori infection. H. pylori is a gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the stomach and causes chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, gastric adenocarcinoma, and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. The bacteria produce urease, which converts urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide. The ammonia neutralizes gastric acid, allowing the bacteria to survive in the acidic environment of the stomach. The carbon dioxide can be detected in the breath, forming the basis of the urea breath test.

H. pylori preferentially colonizes the gastric antrum, which is less acidic than the gastric fundus. Therefore, a biopsy from the gastric antrum is most likely to yield an accurate diagnosis.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [D] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old man comes to the physician because of an episode of bloody vomiting this morning and a 1-week history of burning upper abdominal pain. Two weeks ago, he sustained a head injury and was in a coma for 3 days. An endoscopy shows multiple, shallow hemorrhagic lesions predominantly in the gastric fundus and greater curvature. Biopsies show patchy loss of epithelium and an acute inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria that does not extend beyond the muscularis mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a recent head injury and coma, along with the endoscopic findings of multiple, shallow hemorrhagic lesions in the gastric fundus and greater curvature, are suggestive of stress-related mucosal disease (SRMD). SRMD is a form of erosive gastritis that is seen in critically ill patients. It is characterized by superficial mucosal erosions that can cause upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The pathogenesis of SRMD is multifactorial and includes reduced mucosal blood flow due to splanchnic vasoconstriction, impaired mucosal defense mechanisms, and hypersecretion of gastric acid. The condition is typically self-limited and resolves with correction of the underlying illness.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [B] > [A] > [C].

question: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician for evaluation of a learning disability. His teachers have reported hyperactivity during class, difficulties with social interaction, and poor scores on reading and writing assessments. Molecular analysis shows an increased number of CGG trinucleotide repeats. Which of the following findings are most likely to be seen on physical examination of this patient?

answer_choices.B: Long face and large everted ears
answer_choices.D: Thin upper lip and receding chin

few_shot.question: A 4-year-old boy presents to his pediatrician for severe developmental delay. On exam he is noted to have macroorchidism, hypertelorism, large protruding ears, a large jaw, and a long thin face. Suspicious of what the diagnosis may be, the pediatrician orders a PCR and DNA sequencing. The results reveal an expansion of 250 repeats of CGG. What is the diagnosis of the boy?
few_shot.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked disorder that is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and autism. It is caused by a trinucleotide repeat disorder (CGG) in the FMR1 gene. Normal individuals have fewer than 45 repeats, those with a "premutation" have 55-200 repeats, and those with over 200 repeats have "full mutation" fragile X syndrome. The gene is located on the long arm of the X chromosome, and the excess trinucleotide repeats cause hypermethylation and subsequent inactivation of the FMR1 gene. This gene is responsible for making a protein (FMRP) that plays a role in the development of synapses. 

The classic physical findings in fragile X syndrome include a long face with a large jaw, large protruding ears, and macroorchidism. Behavioral characteristics can include autism, ADHD, social anxiety, hand biting and/or flapping, and poor eye contact.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [C] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother for an annual check-up. The family recently moved from Nebraska and is hoping to establish care. The patient is home schooled and mom is concerned about her son’s development. He is only able to say 2 to 3 word sentences and has been “behind on his alphabet." He always seems to be disinterested and "just seems to be behind.” The patient is observed to be focused on playing with his cars during the interview. Physical examination demonstrate a well-nourished child with poor eye contact, a prominent jaw, a single palmar crease, and bilaterally enlarged testicles. What is the most likely mechanism of this patient’s findings?

answer_choices.C: Microdeletion of the short arm of chromosome 5
answer_choices.D: Microdeletion of the long arm of chromosome 7

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's developmental delay, poor eye contact, and stereotypic behavior (eg, playing with cars) suggest an autism spectrum disorder. The presence of a long face with a large jaw, large everted ears, and macroorchidism (postpubertal) is suggestive of fragile X syndrome, the most common inherited form of intellectual disability and the most common known genetic cause of autism. Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene, which leads to hypermethylation and a subsequent decrease in the gene product, FMRP. FMRP is involved in the development of synapses. 

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [D] > [C].

few_shot.question: A mother from rural Louisiana brings her 4-year-old son to a pediatrician. Her son is intellectually disabled, and she hopes that genetic testing will help determine the cause of her son's condition. She had previously been opposed to allowing physicians to treat her son, but his impulsive behavior and learning disabilities are making it difficult to manage his care on her own. On exam, the child has a long, thin face with a large jaw, protruding ears, and macroorchidism. The physician also hears a high-pitched holosystolic murmur at the apex of the heart that radiates to the axilla. Which of the following trinucleotide repeats is most likely affected in this individual?

answer_choices.C: CGG on the sex chromosome X

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's intellectual disability, long face, large jaw, large ears, and macroorchidism are characteristic of fragile X syndrome, the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion of CGG in the FMR1 gene. The gene product, FMRP, is an RNA-binding protein that regulates the translation of many dendritic mRNAs. In fragile X syndrome, the lack of FMRP leads to excess and dysregulated mRNA translation and abnormal synaptic development and plasticity. The syndrome is associated with connective tissue dysplasia (eg, mitral valve prolapse, as suggested by the murmur in this patient), and macroorchidism (postpubertal).

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [D] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because his parents are concerned that he has been unable to keep up with his classmates at school. He is at the 4th percentile for height and at the 15th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows dysmorphic facial features. Psychologic testing shows impaired intellectual and adaptive functions. Genetic analysis shows a deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7. Which of the following is the most likely additional finding in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's dysmorphic facial features, intellectual disability, and deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7 are consistent with Williams syndrome. This is a genetic disorder that is characterized by a distinctive, "elfin" facial appearance, along with a low nasal bridge, prominent lips, and wide mouth. Patients with this syndrome also have intellectual disability, unique personality characteristics (overfriendliness), and growth abnormalities. Cardiovascular abnormalities, especially supravalvular aortic stenosis, are common in these patients.

So, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 14-year-old boy presents as a new patient to your practice. While conducting your physical exam, you observe the findings depicted in Figures A and B. Which of the following additional findings would most likely be found in this patient?

answer_choices.B: A family history of seizures and mental retardation
answer_choices.D: A white tuft of scalp hair since birth

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's physical examination findings of multiple café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling are suggestive of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). NF1 is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary or inguinal freckling, neurofibromas, optic gliomas, and Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas). Therefore, the most likely additional finding in this patient would be iris hamartomas.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [D] > [B] > [A].

question:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician for evaluation of pallor and increasing lethargy for 2 days. One week ago, he experienced abdominal pain, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea that have since subsided. The patient's father states that they returned early from a 6-week roadtrip in Mexico because of these symptoms. His parents have been giving him oral rehydration solution. His immunizations are up-to-date. He appears pale. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 35/min, and blood pressure is 95/50 mm Hg. Examination shows scleral icterus. The abdomen is soft and nontender; there is no rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 94 μm3
Leukocyte count 18,000/mm3
Platelet count 45,000/mm3
Prothrombin time 12 sec
Partial thromboplastin time 34 sec
Serum
Urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL
Bilirubin
Total 2.5 mg/dL
Direct 0.1 mg/dL
Lactate dehydrogenase 1658 U/L
A blood smear shows schistocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

few_shot.question:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician for evaluation of pallor and increasing lethargy for 3 days. Six days ago, he experienced abdominal pain, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea that have since resolved. The family returned from a road trip to Mexico 4-weeks ago. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and scleral icterus. The abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 92 μm3
Leukocyte count 18,500/mm3
Platelet count 45,000/mm3
Prothrombin time 12 sec
Partial thromboplastin time 34 sec
Serum
Urea nitrogen 32 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL
Bilirubin
Total 2.0 mg/dL
Direct 0.1 mg/dL
Lactate dehydrogenase 1685 U/L
A peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's presentation?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recent history of bloody diarrhea, pallor, lethargy, and laboratory findings of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, elevated lactate dehydrogenase), thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury are consistent with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). HUS is most commonly caused by Shiga toxin-producing bacteria (eg, Escherichia coli O157:H7, Shigella), which are often contracted through contaminated food or water. Shiga toxin binds to and inhibits the 60S ribosomal subunit, halting protein synthesis and leading to cell death. Endothelial injury and cell death trigger platelet activation and aggregation, leading to formation of microthrombi. These microthrombi cause mechanical destruction of erythrocytes (ie, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia) and occlusion of the renal vasculature, leading to acute kidney injury.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question:
A 4-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of diarrhea and vomiting for 5 days. Vaccinations are up-to-date. She appears pale and irritable. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows petechiae on her trunk and extremities. Abdominal examination shows diffuse abdominal tenderness with hyperactive bowel sounds. The remainder of the exam shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 8 g/dL
Leukocyte count 17,000/mm3
Platelet count 49,000/mm3
Serum
Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL
Lactate dehydrogenase 300 U/L
Coagulation studies are normal. A peripheral blood smear is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of vomiting, diarrhea, pallor, petechiae, and anemia is suggestive of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). HUS is characterized by the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. It is most commonly seen in children and is typically preceded by a diarrheal illness. The most common cause of HUS is infection with Shiga toxin-producing bacteria, most commonly Escherichia coli O157:H7, which is often contracted through contaminated, undercooked beef or other contaminated foods.

The Shiga toxin produced by the bacteria binds to a host cell receptor, is internalized, and then inhibits the 60S ribosome, leading to cell death. Endothelial injury and cell death lead to exposure of the subendothelial space, platelet adhesion, and thrombus formation. This microthrombi formation and mechanical injury by fibrin strands results in shearing of red blood cells as they pass through partially occluded vessels, leading to intravascular hemolysis and schistocyte formation.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: An 8-year-old boy presents with a 7-day history of fever and abdominal pain for the past 4 days. Past medical history is significant for an exchange transfusion for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and recurrent attacks of pallor during the course of upper respiratory tract infections. His vital signs include: blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse 105/min, respiratory rate 40/min, and temperature 37.0℃ (98.6℉). On physical examination, the patient is ill-looking. Conjunctivae are pale and the sclera is icteric. The liver is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory findings show hemoglobin of 5.9 gm/dL, Hct of 20%, and haptoglobin of 28 gm/dL. A peripheral blood smear shows hypochromic anemia, polychromasia, anisocytosis, and occasional Heinz bodies. The reticulocyte count was 15%. A direct Coombs test was negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, recurrent episodes of pallor during infections, and current findings of anemia, jaundice, and reticulocytosis suggest a chronic hemolytic anemia. The presence of Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) on the peripheral smear is indicative of oxidative damage to the red blood cells (RBCs). This is seen in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, an X-linked disorder that is one of the most common causes of hemolytic anemia worldwide.

G6PD is an enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway that generates NADPH. NADPH is necessary to keep glutathione in its reduced form. Reduced glutathione protects RBCs from oxidative damage. In G6PD deficiency, RBCs are more susceptible to oxidative stress. Oxidative stress can be precipitated by infections, certain drugs (eg, sulfonamides, dapsone, primaquine, nitrofurantoin), and fava beans. The oxidative stress denatures hemoglobin, forming Heinz bodies. Heinz bodies damage the RBC membrane, leading to intravascular hemolysis or bite cells (RBCs with a "bite" taken out of the cell membrane) if the Heinz bodies are removed by splenic macrophages.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of progressive fatigue, abdominal pain, and loss of appetite over the past 3 days. He was treated in the emergency department once in the past year for swelling of his hands and feet. He was adopted as a baby from Sudan and his family history is unknown. He does not take any medication. He is lethargic. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 141/min, respirations are 25/min, and blood pressure is 68/40 mm Hg. Examination shows pale, dry mucous membranes and scleral icterus. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 93 fL
Reticulocyte count 11%
Serum
Lactate dehydrogenase 194 IU/L
Total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL
Direct bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL
Haptoglobin 21 mg/dL (N = 41–165)
Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigue, pallor, scleral icterus, and elevated reticulocyte count is suggestive of hemolytic anemia. The elevated lactate dehydrogenase level and low haptoglobin level are also consistent with hemolysis. The elevated indirect bilirubin level is due to increased breakdown of heme, a component of hemoglobin, into bilirubin. The patient's history of a prior episode of hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis) and adoption from Sudan, a region with a high prevalence of sickle cell disease (SCD), suggest that his hemolytic anemia is due to SCD. SCD is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a single amino acid substitution in the β-globin chain of hemoglobin, leading to the production of abnormal hemoglobin S (HbS). HbS polymerizes under conditions of low oxygen tension, causing red blood cells to become rigid and sickle-shaped. Sickled cells are prone to hemolysis and can occlude small blood vessels, leading to vaso-occlusive crises. Dactylitis, a common early manifestation of SCD, is a vaso-occlusive crisis occurring in the small bones of the hands and feet. Chronic hemolysis in SCD can lead to the development of functional asplenia by age 2 years and autosplenectomy (ie, fibrosis and shrinkage of the spleen) by adolescence or early adulthood. However, splenomegaly can occur due to sequestration of sickled cells in the spleen, especially in children younger than 4 years of age.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of colicky abdominal pain and vomiting for 1 day. He has a history of a sore throat 2 weeks ago. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, blood pressure is 90/55, and respirations are 28/min. Examination of the lower extremities shows non-blanching raised erythematous papules. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Bowel sounds are high-pitched. Both ankles are swollen and tender; range of motion is limited by pain. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL
Leukocyte count 9800/mm3
Platelet count 265,000/mm3
Serum
Glucose 78 mg/dL
Antinuclear antibodies negative
Urine
Glucose negative
Protein negative
Blood 2+
RBC 10-12/hpf with dysmorphic features
WBC 0-1/hpf
Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows a portion of the bowel with alternating echogenic and hypoechogenic bands in transverse view. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a recent upper respiratory tract infection, palpable purpura, arthralgias, abdominal pain, and hematuria is suggestive of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura). This is the most common form of systemic vasculitis in children. It is characterized by the tetrad of palpable purpura (often over the buttocks and lower extremities), arthritis/arthralgias, abdominal pain, and renal disease. The abdominal pain can be colicky, mimicking an acute abdomen, and may be associated with intussusception. The renal disease often manifests as hematuria and may progress to IgA nephropathy (Berger disease). The disease is caused by the deposition of IgA immune complexes in the skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys, leading to a leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

question: A 24-year-old man with chronic back pain comes to the physician to establish care after moving to Florida. He complains of anxiety, nausea, abdominal cramping, vomiting, and diarrhea for three days. He denies smoking, drinking alcohol, and using illicit drugs. He appears restless. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 150/86 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dilated pupils, diaphoresis, and piloerection. His abdominal exam shows diffuse mild tenderness. There is no rebound tenderness or guarding. His hemoglobin concentration is 14.5 g/dL, leukocyte count is 8,000/mm, and platelet count is 250,000/mm3; serum studies and urinalysis show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old homeless man presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and vomiting. He has a known history of intravenous drug use and has been admitted to the hospital several times before. On physical examination his temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 19/min, and pulse oximetry is 99% on room air. The patient is in obvious discomfort. There is increased salivation and lacrimation. Pupils are reactive to light and 5 mm bilaterally. Cardiopulmonary exam is unremarkable. There is diffuse abdominal tenderness to palpation with no rebound or guarding. Which of the following interventions would have prevented this patient’s current condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of intravenous drug use, abdominal pain, vomiting, and increased salivation and lacrimation are suggestive of opioid withdrawal. Opioid withdrawal is not life-threatening but can be very uncomfortable, leading to strong cravings and continued drug use. Buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist that is used for maintenance therapy in patients with opioid use disorder. It can prevent withdrawal symptoms and reduce cravings, without producing the euphoria and sedation caused by full opioid agonists. Therefore, it could have prevented this patient's current condition.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of abdominal pain, a runny nose, and chills for 6 hours. He has also had diarrhea and difficulty sleeping. He appears irritable. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows cool, damp skin with piloerection. The pupils are 7 mm in diameter and equal in size. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is tender to palpation. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ bilaterally. Withdrawal from which of the following substances is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of abdominal pain, diarrhea, piloerection ("goose bumps"), mydriasis, and hypertension are consistent with opioid withdrawal. Opioid withdrawal is characterized by symptoms that are opposite to the effects of opioid intoxication. For example, opioids cause miosis, decreased bowel sounds, and euphoria, while opioid withdrawal causes mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds, and dysphoria. Other symptoms of opioid withdrawal include lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning, insomnia, and piloerection ("goose bumps"), which can lead to the appearance of "cold turkey." Although opioid withdrawal can be extremely uncomfortable, it is not life-threatening.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question:
A 33-year-old man presents to the emergency department with back pain. He is currently intoxicated but states that he is having severe back pain and is requesting morphine and lorazepam. The patient has a past medical history of alcohol abuse, drug seeking behavior, and IV drug abuse and does not routinely see a physician. His temperature is 102°F (38.9°C), blood pressure is 127/68 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable for tenderness over the thoracic and lumbar spine. The pain is exacerbated with flexion of the spine. The patient’s laboratory values are notable for the findings below.

Hemoglobin: 12 g/dL
Hematocrit: 36%
Leukocyte count: 16,500/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 197,000/mm^3

Serum:
Na+: 139 mEq/L
Cl-: 100 mEq/L
K+: 4.3 mEq/L
HCO3-: 25 mEq/L
BUN: 20 mg/dL
Glucose: 99 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL
Ca2+: 10.2 mg/dL
CRP: 5.2 mg/L

Further imaging is currently pending. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's back pain, fever, and elevated white blood cell count are concerning for a spinal epidural abscess. Spinal epidural abscess is a neurosurgical emergency that can lead to permanent neurologic damage or death if not promptly recognized and treated. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, trauma, IV drug use, alcoholism, and immunosuppression. The classic triad of spinal pain, fever, and neurologic deficits is seen in fewer than half of patients at presentation. Back pain is the most common presenting symptom and is often severe and localized, with percussion tenderness over the affected area. Fever may be absent in up to 25% of patients. Neurologic deficits (eg, paralysis, radiculopathy, bowel/bladder incontinence) may not occur until later in the disease course. Laboratory studies often show leukocytosis and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein. MRI of the spine is the diagnostic modality of choice. Treatment involves emergent neurosurgical consultation for possible surgical decompression and IV antibiotics.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [C] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his girlfriend discovered him at home in a minimally responsive state. He has a history of drinking alcohol excessively and using illicit drugs. On arrival, he does not respond to commands but withdraws all extremities to pain. His pulse is 90/min, respirations are 8/min, and blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry while receiving bag-valve-mask ventilation shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. Examination shows cool, dry skin, with scattered track marks on his arms and legs. The pupils are pinpoint and react sluggishly to light. His serum blood glucose level is 80 mg/dL. The most appropriate next step in management is intravenous administration of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of drug use, pinpoint pupils, and depressed mental status are suggestive of opioid overdose. Opioids (eg, heroin, morphine, fentanyl) bind to mu receptors in the central nervous system, leading to analgesia, euphoria, and decreased respiratory drive. Opioid overdose can cause life-threatening respiratory depression, and patients may present with bradypnea or apnea, pinpoint pupils, and stupor or coma.

Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist that can rapidly reverse the effects of opioids. It should be administered intravenously, intramuscularly, or intranasally to any patient with suspected opioid overdose and respiratory depression (respiratory rate <12/min) or a Glasgow Coma Scale score <15. Naloxone has a short half-life, and patients with severe intoxication may require additional doses or a continuous infusion.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [D] > [C] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police for aggressive behavior. The patient is combative and shouts sexually aggressive remarks at the nursing staff. While obtaining the patient’s vitals, it is noted that he has markedly dilated pupils. His temperature is 98.2°F (36.8°C), pulse is 112/min, blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg, respirations are 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Urine toxicology is obtained and sent off. Physical exam is notable for an energetic patient with dilated pupils and increased sweating. The patient spends the night in the emergency department. In the morning the patient is withdrawn and has a notable depressed affect. He apologizes for his behavior the previous night and states that he is concerned about his problem and wants help. Which of the following is appropriate management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of aggression, combativeness, and sexual disinhibition is suggestive of intoxication with methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA), also known as "ecstasy." MDMA is a popular recreational drug that is chemically similar to both amphetamines and hallucinogens. It causes the release and reuptake inhibition of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. MDMA increases energy, empathy, and pleasure (from dopamine and norepinephrine release) and induces perceptual changes and emotional excitability (from serotonin release). MDMA also has sympathomimetic effects, which can lead to significantly increased heart rate and blood pressure, hyperthermia, and death. The day following MDMA use, users often experience a "crash" that includes symptoms of depression, irritability, and fatigue. This is due to the depletion of monoamine stores and temporary down-regulation of certain receptors.

The mainstay of treatment for MDMA use disorder is psychotherapy. Cognitive-behavioral interventions have been shown to be effective in reducing use. No pharmacologic therapies have been shown to be effective in treating MDMA use disorder.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [C] > [B] > [A].

question: A 62-year-old man presents with episodes of palpitations for the past 3 weeks. He says that he has episodes where he feels his heart is ‘racing and pounding’, lasting 1–2 hours on average. Initially, he says the episodes would happen 1–2 times per week but now happen almost every day. This last episode has been constant for the past 2 days. He denies any seizure, loss of consciousness, dizziness, chest pain, or similar symptoms in the past. His past medical history is significant for an ischemic stroke of the right anterior cerebral artery 1 month ago, status post intravenous (IV) tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) with still some residual neurologic impairment, and long-standing gastroesophageal reflux secondary to a hiatal hernia, managed medically. The patient reports a 15-pack-year smoking history, but no alcohol or recreational drug use. The vital signs include: temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, pulse 105/min, and respiratory rate 16/min. On physical examination, muscle strength in the lower extremities is 4/5 on the left and 5/5 on the right, along with sensory loss on the left, all of which is improved from his previous exam 3 weeks ago. There is a loss of the left half of the visual field bilaterally which is stable from the previous exam. Cardiac examination is significant for a new-onset irregular rate and rhythm. No rubs, thrills or murmurs.
