few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of right-sided weakness and subjective decreased sensation that started 30 minutes ago. The patient reports that his symptoms started to ease 5 minutes after onset and have now completely resolved. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. His current medications include lisinopril, metformin, and sitagliptin. He is 183 cm (6 ft 0 in) tall and weighs 105 kg (220 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m2. He appears well. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 150/88 mm Hg. Neurological examination shows no abnormalities. Cardiac examination shows regular rate and rhythm and a left-sided carotid bruit. Complete blood count, serum glucose, and electrolytes are within the reference ranges. An ECG shows sinus rhythm and left axis deviation. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows no abnormalities. Carotid doppler ultrasound shows 45% stenosis in the left carotid artery and 15% stenosis in the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden-onset, focal neurologic symptoms that completely resolved within 60 minutes are consistent with a transient ischemic attack (TIA). TIAs are often warning signs of an impending stroke, and patients with a TIA are at highest risk for stroke in the first 48 hours after the event. Therefore, rapid evaluation and intervention are necessary to prevent a subsequent stroke.

The ABCD2 score (Age, Blood pressure, Clinical features, Duration of symptoms, Diabetes) can be used to risk-stratify patients with a TIA. This patient's score is 5 (1 point each for age >60, blood pressure >140/90 mm Hg, unilateral weakness, and duration of symptoms >10 minutes; 0 points for absence of speech disturbance), which indicates a moderate risk of stroke in the next 2 days.

The most effective intervention to prevent stroke following a TIA is initiation of antiplatelet therapy (eg, aspirin, clopidogrel). Aspirin is typically used first-line, but clopidogrel is preferred in patients with aspirin allergy or in whom aspirin is contraindicated.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 70-year-old man presented to the emergency department complaining of left-sided weakness for the past 5 hours. He also has a history of type-II diabetes mellitus and hypertension. He takes an 81 mg aspirin, amlodipine, atorvastatin, and a vitamin supplement with calcium and vitamin D. A brain MRI reveals a small atrophic area of the left occipital lobe and a new acute infarct involving the territory of the right middle cerebral artery. Electrocardiogram (ECG) shows normal sinus rhythm. An echocardiogram reveals mild left ventricular hypertrophy with an ejection fraction of 55%. Doppler ultrasound of the carotid arteries reveals no significant narrowing. What is the next step in the management to prevent future risks of stroke?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a history of recurrent ischemic strokes despite taking aspirin. The most likely cause of his recurrent strokes is atherosclerosis, given his history of hypertension and diabetes. In patients with recurrent ischemic strokes despite taking aspirin, the addition of dipyridamole to aspirin has been shown to be beneficial. Dipyridamole is a platelet inhibitor and a vasodilator. It inhibits the uptake of adenosine into platelets, endothelial cells, and erythrocytes, which increases the concentration of adenosine in the blood. This leads to an increase in coronary vasodilation and inhibition of platelet aggregation.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 77-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of headache, nausea, and vomiting for 24 hours. His wife says that over the past 2 weeks, he has been more irritable and has had trouble remembering to do routine errands. Two weeks ago, he fell during a skiing accident but did not lose consciousness. He has coronary artery disease and hypertension. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 50 years. He has had 2 glasses of wine daily since his retirement 10 years ago. Current medications include atenolol, enalapril, furosemide, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He appears acutely ill. He is oriented to person but not to place or time. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 99/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. During the examination, he is uncooperative and unable to answer questions. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ on the left and 2+ on the right. Babinski's sign is present on the left. There is mild weakness of the left iliopsoas and hamstring muscles. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows a high-density, 15-mm crescentic collection across the right hemispheric convexity. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a fall, acute headache, and progressive neurologic symptoms (eg, irritability, memory problems, focal neurologic deficits) along with the imaging findings are consistent with a subdural hematoma (SDH). SDH is caused by tearing of the bridging veins that extend from the brain to the dural sinuses. It is most commonly seen in elderly patients, alcoholics, and patients with a history of falls or mild head trauma. The classic presentation is a fluctuating level of consciousness or new-onset seizures over the span of several days to weeks following head trauma. Focal neurologic deficits may also be seen, as in this patient. 

The management of SDH depends on the size of the hematoma, the presence of midline shift, and the patient's neurologic status. In general, symptomatic patients with a hematoma thickness >10 mm or a midline shift >5 mm on CT scan should undergo surgical evacuation regardless of the Glasgow Coma Scale score. This patient's SDH measures 15 mm and he has significant neurologic symptoms, so he should undergo surgical evacuation.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 77-year-old man presents to the emergency department complaining of feeling like “his heart was racing” for the last 8 days. He denies any chest pain, dizziness, or fainting but complains of fatigue, difficulty breathing with exertion, and swelling of his legs bilaterally for the last 2 weeks. He has had hypertension for the last 25 years. He has a long history of heavy alcohol consumption but denies smoking. His blood pressure is 145/70 mm Hg and the pulse is irregular at the rate of 110/min. On examination of his lower limbs, mild pitting edema is noted of his ankles bilaterally. On cardiac auscultation, heart sounds are irregular. Bibasilar crackles are heard with auscultation of the lungs. An ECG is ordered and the result is shown in the image. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a reduced ejection fraction of 32% and dilatation of all chambers of the heart without any obvious intracardiac thrombus. answer_choices.D: Catheter ablation for pulmonary vein isolation

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has atrial fibrillation (AF) with rapid ventricular response and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). AF is a common cause of heart failure and can be managed with either a rate control or rhythm control strategy. In patients with HFrEF, a rhythm control strategy is preferred because restoration and maintenance of sinus rhythm can improve cardiac function. This patient's symptoms of heart failure (eg, dyspnea on exertion, bilateral lower extremity edema) have been present for 2 weeks, and his AF has been present for 8 days. Therefore, he is still within the 48-hour window when cardioversion can be performed without the need for anticoagulation. However, given his heart failure symptoms, it is likely that his AF has been present for longer than he is aware, so he should be fully anticoagulated prior to cardioversion. The patient should be started on a direct oral anticoagulant (eg, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) or warfarin for at least 3 weeks prior to elective cardioversion. Anticoagulation should be continued for at least 4 weeks after successful cardioversion, but long-term anticoagulation is determined by the patient's stroke risk.

question: A 3466-g (7-lb, 10-oz) female newborn is delivered at 38 weeks' gestation to a 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1. Apgar scores are 7 and 8, at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The mother has a history of schizophrenia and was treated with lithium until 5 weeks' gestation, when she found out that she was pregnant. The mother was treated for alcohol abuse disorder 2 years ago. She has been sober for 14 months now. Examination shows that the child has micrognathia, a broad nasal bridge, a short philtrum, and small, low-set ears. Examination of the mouth shows a cleft palate. few_shot.question: A 2720-g (6-lb) female newborn is delivered at term to a 39-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2. Apgar scores are 6 and 7 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Examination in the delivery room shows micrognathia, prominent occiput with flattened nasal bridge, and pointy low-set ears. The eyes are upward slanting with small palpebral fissures. The fists are clenched with fingers tightly flexed. The index finger overlaps the third finger and the fifth finger overlaps the fourth. A 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the lower left sternal border. The nipples are widely spaced and the feet have prominent heels and convex, rounded soles. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn's findings of micrognathia, prominent occiput, low-set ears, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, and rocker-bottom feet are characteristic of trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome). Trisomy 18 is the second most common autosomal trisomy at the time of birth. It is associated with severe intellectual disability and malformations involving many organs. Most affected infants die within the first year of life. The most common abnormalities include intrauterine growth restriction, polyhydramnios, micrognathia, low-set ears, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, congenital heart disease (eg, ventricular septal defect), and renal defects. Maternal age is the primary risk factor.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 2200-g (4-lbs 13-oz) female newborn is delivered at term to a 37-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman. The newborn is at the 10th percentile for length, 14th percentile for weight, and 3rd percentile for head circumference. Examination shows “punched-out“ skin lesions on the scalp, cleft lip, and a small chin. There is a convex-shaped deformity of the plantar surface of the feet. Auscultation shows a holosystolic murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border. Some of her intestines protrude through the umbilicus, covered by a thin membranous sac. An MRI of the brain shows a single ventricle and a fusion of the basal ganglia. Which of the following additional findings is most likely to be seen in this patient?

This newborn has trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome), which is characterized by severe intellectual disability and multiple congenital anomalies. The most common findings include microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, microphthalmia, cleft lip/palate, postaxial polydactyly, cutis aplasia, congenital heart disease, and omphalocele. The prognosis is poor, with most infants dying within the first year of life.

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old gravida 3 para 1 is admitted to labor and delivery with uterine contractions. She is at 37 weeks gestation with no primary care provider or prenatal care. She gives birth to a boy after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with APGAR scores of 7 at 1 minute and 8 at 5 minutes. His weight is 2.2 kg (4.4 lb) and the length is 48 cm (1.6 ft). The infant has weak extremities and poor reflexes. The physical examination reveals microcephaly, palpebral fissures, thin lips, and a smooth philtrum. A systolic murmur is heard on auscultation. Identification of which of the following factors early in the pregnancy could prevent this condition?
few_shot.explanation:
The infant's physical examination findings (microcephaly, palpebral fissures, thin lips, smooth philtrum) and history of maternal alcohol consumption are consistent with fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS). FAS is the most severe form of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, a group of conditions that can occur in a person whose mother drank alcohol during pregnancy. FAS is characterized by growth retardation, facial abnormalities, and central nervous system dysfunction. The facial abnormalities include short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum, and a thin vermilion border of the upper lip. Central nervous system dysfunction can manifest as intellectual disability, learning disabilities, or behavioral problems. Early identification of maternal alcohol consumption and counseling to avoid alcohol during pregnancy can prevent FAS.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old woman (gravida 3 para 1) with no prenatal care delivers a boy at 37 weeks gestation. His Apgar score is 5 at 1 minute and 8 at 5 minutes. His weight is 2.1 kg (4.2 lb) and length is 47 cm (1 ft 7 in). The mother’s history is significant for chronic pyelonephritis, atrial fibrillation, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. She has a 5-pack-year smoking history and also reports alcohol consumption during pregnancy. Examination of the infant shows a short depressed nasal bridge, wide nose, brachydactyly, and a short neck. Ophthalmoscopy reveals bilateral cataracts. What is the most likely cause of the newborn’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn's physical findings (eg, low birth weight, short depressed nasal bridge, wide nose, brachydactyly, short neck, cataracts) are consistent with warfarin embryopathy, a rare disorder that occurs in infants exposed to warfarin in utero. Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist that readily crosses the placenta and can cause birth defects, especially when used in the first trimester. The most common features of warfarin embryopathy include nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses. Central nervous system abnormalities (eg, Dandy-Walker malformation, intellectual disability) and eye abnormalities (eg, microphthalmia) can also occur. Fetal warfarin exposure during the second and third trimesters can cause optic atrophy and fetal intracranial bleeding.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: One day after a 4700-g (10-lb 6-oz) male newborn is delivered to a 28-year-old primigravid woman, the newborn has bluish discoloration of the lips and fingernails. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 166/min, respirations are 63/min, and blood pressure is 68/44 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 81%. Examination shows central cyanosis. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard over the left lower sternal border. A single second heart sound is present. Supplemental oxygen does not improve cyanosis. An x-ray of the chest shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with a narrowed mediastinum. Further evaluation of the mother is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has transposition of the great arteries (TGA), the most common cause of cyanotic heart disease in the first 24 hours of life. TGA is characterized by the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle, resulting in two parallel circulations. The only communication between the systemic and pulmonary circulations is through a patent foramen ovale and/or patent ductus arteriosus. Clinical findings include profound cyanosis within the first day of life, a single second heart sound (S2), and a systolic ejection murmur due to increased flow across the pulmonary valve. Chest x-ray shows an "egg on a string" appearance, with an enlarged cardiac silhouette and a narrowed mediastinum.

Maternal diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for TGA. Hyperglycemia during the first trimester of pregnancy, when organogenesis occurs, can lead to various congenital malformations, including cardiac defects. Therefore, an elevated hemoglobin A1c, which reflects the average blood glucose level over the past 3 months, is the most likely finding in this patient's mother.

So, the answer is [D].

question:

His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg. Urine toxicology is positive for opiates and cocaine. Intravenous fluids and sodium nitroprusside drip are started. The patient is most likely to have which of the following?"

A 36-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his neighbor because of altered mental status. He was found 6 hours ago stumbling through his neighbor's bushes and yelling obscenities. The neighbor helped him home but found him again 1 hour ago slumped over on his driveway in a puddle of vomit. He is oriented to self but not to place or time. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.5°F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 122/80 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary exam shows no abnormalities. He is unable to cooperate for a neurological examination. Muscle spasms are seen in his arms and jaw. Serum laboratory studies show:
Na+ 140 mEq/L
K+ 5.5 mEq/L
Cl- 101 mEq/L
HCO3- 9 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL
Creatinine 2.3 mg/dL
Glucose 75 mg/dL
Calcium 7.2 mg/dL
Osmolality 320 mOsm/kg
Calculated serum osmolality is 294 mOsm/kg. Arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.25 and lactate level of 3.2 mmol/L (N=< 1 mmol/L). Examination of the urine shows oxalate crystals and no ketones. This patient is most likely experiencing toxicity from which of the following substances?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of altered mental status, anion gap metabolic acidosis, and acute kidney injury is suggestive of toxic alcohol ingestion. The absence of ketones in the urine helps differentiate between toxic alcohol ingestion and alcoholic ketoacidosis or diabetic ketoacidosis, both of which would be expected to cause ketonuria.

The most commonly ingested toxic alcohols are methanol (eg, windshield wiper fluid), ethylene glycol (eg, antifreeze), and isopropyl alcohol (eg, rubbing alcohol). Methanol and ethylene glycol are metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to toxic metabolites (formaldehyde/formic acid and glycolic acid/glyoxylic acid/oxalic acid, respectively), which cause an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis. Isopropyl alcohol is metabolized to acetone, which does not cause an anion gap metabolic acidosis but can cause an increased osmolal gap due to its osmolar contribution.

This patient's presentation is most consistent with ethylene glycol poisoning, which can cause acute kidney injury due to precipitation of calcium oxalate crystals in the renal tubules. These crystals can be seen on urine microscopy and are suggestive of ethylene glycol ingestion. Methanol toxicity, in contrast, can cause retinal damage leading to blindness.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
Two days after admission to the hospital, a 74-year-old man develops confusion and headache. He has also been vomiting over the past hour. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. He is lethargic and oriented only to person. Examination shows flushed skin. Fundoscopic examination shows bright red retinal veins. Serum studies show:
Na+ 138 mEq/L
K+ 3.5 mEq/L
Cl- 100 mEq/L
HCO3- 17 mEq/L
Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL
Urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL
Lactate 8.0 mEq/L (N = 0.5 - 2.2 mEq/L)
Glucose 75 mg/dL
Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows a pH of 7.13. This patient's current presentation is most likely due to treatment for which of the following conditions?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of confusion, headache, vomiting, and bright red retinal veins is suggestive of cerebral edema due to hyperperfusion syndrome. This condition can occur when there is a rapid decrease in blood pressure in a patient with chronic hypertension. The autoregulatory mechanisms of the cerebral vasculature are impaired in chronic hypertension, leading to an increase in the upper limit of autoregulation. If the blood pressure is rapidly lowered below this limit, as can occur with aggressive antihypertensive treatment, cerebral blood flow can become pressure passive, leading to cerebral hyperperfusion and cerebral edema.

The patient's arterial blood gas shows a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, which is likely due to lactic acidosis from the cerebral hyperperfusion. The other laboratory values are within normal limits.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department when he was found obtunded at the homeless shelter. The patient is currently not responsive and smells of alcohol. The patient has a past medical history of alcohol use, IV drug use, and hepatitis C. His temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 95/65 mmHg, pulse is 95/min, respirations are 13/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. The patient is started on IV fluids, and his pulse decreases to 70/min. On physical exam, the patient has an abdominal exam notable for distension and a positive fluid wave. The patient displays mild yellow discoloration of his skin. The patient has notable poor dentition and poor hygiene overall. A systolic murmur is heard along the left sternal border on cardiac exam. Pulmonary exam is notable for mild bibasilar crackles. Laboratory values are ordered, and return as below:

Hemoglobin: 10 g/dL
Hematocrit: 32%
Leukocyte count: 7,500 cells/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 227,000/mm^3

Serum:
Na+: 125 mEq/L
Cl-: 100 mEq/L
K+: 5.0 mEq/L
HCO3-: 24 mEq/L
BUN: 51 mg/dL
Glucose: 89 mg/dL
Creatinine: 2.2 mg/dL
Ca2+: 10.0 mg/dL
AST: 22 U/L
ALT: 19 U/L

Urine:
Color: Amber
Nitrites: Negative
Sodium: 12 mmol/24 hours
Red blood cells: 0/hpf

Over the next 24 hours, the patient produces very little urine. Which of the following best explains this patient’s renal findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a history of alcohol use and hepatitis C, and presents with jaundice, ascites, and hyponatremia, suggesting cirrhosis. The kidneys attempt to compensate for the decreased effective arterial blood volume seen in cirrhosis by avidly reabsorbing sodium in the proximal tubule, leading to a low fractional excretion of sodium (FENa). This can lead to oliguria and azotemia, as seen in this patient. The patient's urine sodium concentration is low (<20 mEq/L), suggesting that the kidneys are appropriately reabsorbing sodium in response to the decreased effective arterial blood volume. This is consistent with hepatorenal syndrome (HRS), a form of functional renal impairment seen in patients with advanced cirrhosis or acute liver failure.

HRS is thought to occur due to splanchnic arterial vasodilation, leading to decreased effective arterial blood volume and renal hypoperfusion. The renal hypoperfusion triggers the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, leading to sodium and water retention in an attempt to increase the intravascular volume. However, because the fundamental problem is arterial vasodilation and not volume depletion, the kidneys continue to sense a volume deficit, leading to continued sodium and water retention. This can result in dilutional hyponatremia, as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department with intense chest pain that radiates to his left arm and jaw. He also complains of feeling lightheaded. Upon arrival, his blood pressure is 104/60 mm Hg, pulse is 102/min, respiratory rate is 25/min, body temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), and oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. An electrocardiogram shows an ST-segment elevation in I, aVL, and V5-6. The patient is transferred to the cardiac interventional suite for a percutaneous coronary intervention. The patient is admitted to the hospital after successful revascularization. During his first night on the ICU floor his urinary output is 0.15 mL/kg/h. Urinalysis shows muddy brown casts. Which of the following outcomes specific to the patient’s condition would you expect to find?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with acute tubular necrosis (ATN), the most common cause of acute kidney injury in hospitalized patients. ATN is characterized by acute renal failure and muddy brown casts on urinalysis. The most common causes of ATN are ischemia (eg, from hypotension) and nephrotoxicity (eg, from aminoglycosides, radiocontrast dye). This patient's recent myocardial infarction and percutaneous coronary intervention with contrast dye exposure likely caused renal ischemia and nephrotoxicity, respectively, leading to ATN.

In ATN, the renal tubules become necrotic and slough off, leading to intraluminal obstruction and back leak of the glomerular filtrate. This results in a decrease in the BUN:Cr ratio to <15:1 (normal: 10:1 to 15:1) and a decrease in urine osmolality to <350 mOsm/kg H2O (normal: 500-800 mOsm/kg H2O). The decrease in urine osmolality is due to impaired urinary concentration ability.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

The neighbor helped him home, but found him again 1 hour later slumped over on his driveway in a puddle of vomit. He is oriented to self, but not to place or time. His vitals are as follows: temperature, 36.9°C (98.5°F); pulse, 82/min; respirations, 28/min; and blood pressure, 122/80 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination indicates no abnormalities. He is unable to cooperate for a neurological examination. Physical examination reveals muscle spasms involving his arms and jaw. Laboratory studies show:
Na+ 140 mEq/L
K+ 5.5 mEq/L
CI- 101 mEq/L
HCO3- 9 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL
Creatinine 2.3 mg/dL
Glucose 75 mg/dL
Calcium 7.2 mg/dL
Osmolality 320 mOsm/kg
The calculated serum osmolality is 294 mOsm/kg. The arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.25 and a lactate level of 3.2 mmol/L. Urine examination shows oxalate crystals and the absence of ketones. What is the most appropriate treatment indicated for this patient experiencing apparent substance toxicity?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with ethylene glycol poisoning. Ethylene glycol is a common component of antifreeze and is often ingested accidentally or in suicide attempts. It is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and is metabolized in the liver by alcohol dehydrogenase to glycoaldehyde, which is then further metabolized to glycolic acid, glyoxylic acid, and finally oxalic acid. These metabolites are responsible for the major toxic effects of ethylene glycol ingestion.

The patient's presentation of altered mental status, vomiting, and muscle spasms is consistent with the early, or neurologic, phase of ethylene glycol poisoning, which occurs within 12 hours of ingestion. This phase is due to the direct effects of ethylene glycol on the central nervous system.

The patient's laboratory findings of an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis, increased osmolal gap, and calcium oxalate crystals in the urine are consistent with the metabolic phase of ethylene glycol poisoning, which occurs 12-24 hours after ingestion. This phase is due to the metabolism of ethylene glycol to its toxic metabolites.

The treatment of ethylene glycol poisoning involves blocking its metabolism to its toxic metabolites. This can be accomplished with either ethanol or fomepizole, both of which inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase. Fomepizole is generally preferred because it has fewer side effects and is easier to administer.

question: A 2050-g (4.5-lb) female newborn and a 2850-g (6.3-lb) female newborn are delivered at 37 weeks' gestation to a 23-year-old, gravida 2, para 1 woman. The mother had no prenatal care. Examination of the smaller newborn shows a flattened nose and left-sided clubfoot. The hematocrit is 42% for the smaller newborn and 71% for the larger newborn. This pregnancy was most likely which of the following?

few_shot.question: A 2250-g (5.0-lb) male newborn and a 2900-g (6.4-lb) male newborn are delivered at 36 weeks' gestation to a 24-year-old, gravida 1, para 1 woman. The mother had no prenatal care. Examination of the smaller newborn shows low-set ears, retrognathia, and right-sided clubfoot. The hematocrit is 41% for the smaller newborn and 69% for the larger newborn. This pregnancy was most likely which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's pregnancy was most likely a monochorionic-diamniotic monozygotic twin gestation. Monochorionic twins share a single placenta, which can lead to vascular anastomoses between the twins. Twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) can occur when there is a net flow of blood from one twin (the "donor") to the other (the "recipient"). The donor twin becomes anemic and hypovolemic, which can lead to intrauterine growth restriction and oligohydramnios. The recipient twin becomes hypervolemic and polycythemic, which can lead to high-output heart failure and polyhydramnios. The smaller twin in this case is likely the donor twin, and the larger twin is likely the recipient twin.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 2200-g (4-lbs 13-oz) female newborn is delivered at term to a 37-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman. The newborn is at the 10th percentile for length, 14th percentile for weight, and 3rd percentile for head circumference. Examination shows “punched-out“ skin lesions on the scalp, cleft lip, and a small chin. There is a convex-shaped deformity of the plantar surface of the feet. Auscultation shows a holosystolic murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border. Some of her intestines protrude through the umbilicus, covered by a thin membranous sac. An MRI of the brain shows a single ventricle and a fusion of the basal ganglia. Which of the following additional findings is most likely to be seen in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome), which is characterized by severe intellectual disability and multiple congenital anomalies. The most common findings include microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, microphthalmia, cleft lip/palate, postaxial polydactyly, cutis aplasia, congenital heart disease, and omphalocele. The prognosis is poor, with most infants dying within the first year of life.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 40 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in active labor. Her first pregnancy and delivery were complicated by iron deficiency anemia and pregnancy-induced hypertension. She has had no routine prenatal care during this pregnancy but was diagnosed with oligohydramnios 4 weeks ago. The remainder of her medical history is not immediately available. A 2400-g (5.4-lb) female newborn is delivered vaginally. Examination of the newborn shows a short, mildly webbed neck and low-set ears. Ocular hypertelorism along with slanted palpebral fissures are noted. A cleft palate and hypoplasia of the nails and distal phalanges are present. There is increased coarse hair on the body and face. Which of the following best explains the clinical findings found in this newborn?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn's findings of growth retardation, craniofacial abnormalities (eg, ocular hypertelorism, slanted palpebral fissures, cleft palate), hypoplasia of the nails and distal phalanges, and hirsutism are consistent with fetal hydantoin syndrome, which is caused by in utero exposure to phenytoin. Phenytoin is used in the treatment of seizures, and it is associated with a distinct pattern of malformations when used during pregnancy. The risk of major malformations in infants exposed to phenytoin in utero is approximately 10%, compared with 2%-3% in the general population. The risk of malformations is highest with first-trimester exposure, but exposure later in pregnancy can also cause growth retardation and other abnormalities.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 2300-g (5.07-lb) male newborn is delivered at term to a 39-year-old woman. Examination shows a sloping forehead, a flat nasal bridge, increased interocular distance, low-set ears, a protruding tongue, a single palmar crease and an increased gap between the first and second toe. There are small white and brown spots in the periphery of both irises. The abdomen is distended. An x-ray of the abdomen shows two large air-filled spaces in the upper quadrant. This patient's condition is most likely associated with which of the following cardiac anomalies?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn's physical findings (eg, sloping forehead, flat nasal bridge, increased interocular distance, low-set ears, protruding tongue, single palmar crease, increased gap between the first and second toes, Brushfield spots in the iris) are consistent with Down syndrome (trisomy 21). The most common congenital heart disease in patients with Down syndrome is an atrioventricular septal defect (also known as endocardial cushion defect or atrioventricular canal defect), which accounts for approximately 45% of cases. This defect is characterized by a primum atrial septal defect, inlet ventricular septal defect, and a single common atrioventricular valve. Other cardiac anomalies seen in Down syndrome include ventricular septal defect (32%), secundum atrial septal defect (10%), and tetralogy of Fallot (6%).

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 2720-g (6-lb) female newborn is delivered at term to a 39-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2. Other findings can include rocker-bottom feet, microcephaly, and intellectual disability. Trisomy 18 is often associated with maternal age >35 years. Most affected infants die within the first year of life.

question: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after he sustained a stab wound to the left chest just below the clavicle. On arrival, he has rapid, shallow breathing and appears anxious. His pulse is 135/min, respirations are 30/min and shallow, and palpable systolic blood pressure is 80 mm Hg. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated. Infusion of 0.9% saline is begun. Five minutes later, his pulse is 133/min and blood pressure is 82/45 mm Hg. Examination shows no active external bleeding. There is a 2.5-cm single stab wound to the left chest at the 4th intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Cardiovascular examination shows muffled heart sounds and jugular venous distention. Breath sounds are normal. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.A: Tracheal deviation toward the right side
answer_choices.C: A drop in systolic blood pressure of 14 mmHg during inspiration
answer_choices.D:
Paradoxical motion of part of the chest with breathing

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 10 minutes after he sustained a stab wound to the left chest just below the clavicle. On arrival, he is hypotensive with rapid and shallow breathing and appears anxious and agitated. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated. Infusion of 0.9% saline is begun. Five minutes later, his pulse is 137/min and blood pressure is 84/47 mm Hg. Examination shows a 3-cm single stab wound to the left chest at the 4th intercostal space at the midclavicular line without active external bleeding. Cardiovascular examination shows muffled heart sounds and jugular venous distention. Breath sounds are normal bilaterally. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.A: A 15 mm Hg decrease in systolic blood pressure during inspiration
answer_choices.B: Lateral shift of the trachea toward the right side
answer_choices.C: Subcutaneous crepitus on palpation of the chest wall
answer_choices.D: Inward collapse of part of the chest with inspiration

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypotension, jugular venous distention, and muffled heart sounds following penetrating chest trauma is consistent with cardiac tamponade. Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening condition that occurs when fluid (eg, blood, pus, serum) accumulates in the pericardial sac and compresses the heart, leading to decreased cardiac output. The classic findings of cardiac tamponade are hypotension, jugular venous distention, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad). Pulsus paradoxus, defined as a >10 mm Hg decrease in systolic blood pressure during inspiration, is also commonly seen in cardiac tamponade. This is due to increased filling of the right heart during inspiration, which pushes the interventricular septum toward the left, decreasing left ventricular filling and stroke volume.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old male arrives in the emergency department with a stab wound over the precordial chest wall. The patient is in distress and is cold, sweaty, and pale. Initial physical examination is significant for muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins, and a 3 cm stab wound near the left sternal border. Breath sounds are present bilaterally without evidence of tracheal deviation. Which of the following additional findings would be expected on further evaluation?

answer_choices.B: Steadily decreasing heart rate to 60 beats per minute
answer_choices.C: 15 mmHg decrease in systolic blood pressure with inspiration
answer_choices.D: Decrease in central venous pressure by 5 mmHg with inspiration

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds following penetrating chest trauma is consistent with cardiac tamponade. Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening condition that occurs when fluid (eg, blood, effusion) in the pericardial sac compresses the heart and impairs cardiac filling. This leads to decreased cardiac output and can cause obstructive shock.

Pulsus paradoxus, an exaggeration (>10 mmHg) of the normal inspiratory decrease in systolic blood pressure, is a classic finding in cardiac tamponade. It occurs due to increased right ventricular filling and decreased left ventricular filling during inspiration. The increased right ventricular filling causes the interventricular septum to bulge leftward, which decreases left ventricular filling and cardiac output, leading to a drop in systolic blood pressure.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old soldier sustains a stab wound to his chest during a military attack in Mali. He is brought to the combat medic by his unit for a primary survey. The soldier reports shortness of breath. He is alert and oriented to time, place, and person. His pulse is 99/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 112/72 mm Hg. Examination shows a 2-cm wound at the left fourth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Bubbling of blood is seen with each respiration at the wound site. There is no jugular venous distention. There is hyperresonance to percussion and decreased breath sounds on the left side. The trachea is at the midline. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of a penetrating chest wound with hyperresonance to percussion and decreased breath sounds on the affected side is consistent with a traumatic open pneumothorax (sucking chest wound). This occurs when the chest wall defect is large enough (usually >2/3 the size of the trachea) to allow outside air to pass freely in and out of the thoracic cavity. This disrupts the negative intrathoracic pressure needed for lung expansion, causing the lung to collapse.

The initial management of an open pneumothorax involves covering the defect with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides. This creates a one-way flutter valve that allows air to exit the pleural space but not reenter. A completely occlusive dressing should be avoided as it can result in a tension pneumothorax. Definitive treatment involves tube thoracostomy.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after falling 7 feet onto a flat-top wooden post. On arrival, he is in severe pain and breathing rapidly. His pulse is 135/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg. There is an impact wound in the left fourth intercostal space at the midaxillary line. Auscultation shows tracheal deviation to the right and absent breath sounds over the left lung. There is dullness to percussion over the left chest. Neck veins are flat. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. Two large-bore intravenous catheters are placed and intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypotension, tachycardia, and decreased breath sounds following trauma is concerning for hemothorax. Hemothorax is the accumulation of blood in the pleural space, most commonly due to trauma. It can cause decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and contralateral tracheal deviation in cases of large volume hemothorax. The most common cause of hemothorax is injury to the intercostal arteries. Other sources can include the internal mammary artery, lung parenchyma, and heart. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 43-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 25 minutes after being involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which he was a restrained passenger. On arrival, he has shortness of breath and is in severe pain. His pulse is 130/min, respirations are 35/min, and blood pressure is 90/40 mm Hg. Examination shows superficial abrasions and diffuse crepitus at the left shoulder level. Cardiac examination shows tachycardia with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The upper part of the left chest wall moves inward during inspiration. Breath sounds are absent on the left. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated. Two large bore intravenous catheters are placed and infusion of 0.9% saline is begun. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of paradoxical chest wall movement (inward during inspiration) and absent breath sounds on the left is consistent with a flail chest. Flail chest is a life-threatening condition that occurs when a segment of the rib cage breaks due to trauma and becomes detached from the rest of the chest wall. This can occur when three or more adjacent ribs are broken in two or more places, resulting in the detached (flail) segment. The flail segment moves in the opposite direction to the rest of the chest wall (ie, inward during inspiration and outward during expiration). This is because the negative intrathoracic pressure generated by inspiration pulls the flail segment inward, and the positive pressure generated by expiration pushes it outward. This can cause severe pain and impair ventilation, leading to hypoventilation and hypoxia.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department for evaluation of hemoptysis. A chest X-ray reveals bilateral focal pulmonary consolidation. On further questioning, he admits having hematuria. Urinalysis shows RBC casts and 400 mL of urine is excreted in 24 hours. What is the most likely cause of hemoptysis and hematuria in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old male visits his primary care physician with complaints of hemoptysis and dysuria. Serum blood urea nitrogen and creatinine are elevated, blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg, and urinalysis shows hematuria and RBC casts. A 24-hour urine excretion yields 1 gm/day protein. A kidney biopsy is obtained, and immunofluorescence shows linear IgG staining in the glomeruli. Which of the following antibodies is likely pathogenic for this patient’s disease?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hemoptysis, hematuria, and renal failure is suggestive of Goodpasture syndrome, an autoimmune disease characterized by the production of anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies. These antibodies bind to the basement membrane in the glomeruli and alveoli, leading to a type II hypersensitivity reaction that causes damage to these structures. The linear IgG staining seen on immunofluorescence is a characteristic finding in Goodpasture syndrome and is due to the binding of these antibodies along the basement membrane.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with hematuria and hemoptysis that started in the morning. He notes that he has had frequent lung infections throughout his adult life, the most recent being 2 weeks ago. He also mentions that he has had hematuria twice before but never as severe as he is having currently. His medical history is otherwise non-significant, and his only medication is acetaminophen as needed. His blood pressure is 136/92 mm Hg, heart rate is 86/min, respiratory rate is 16/min, and temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). Chest radiography shows a resolving right middle lobe airspace opacity. His initial laboratory tests are notable for elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level. While in the examination room, the patient develops a spontaneous nosebleed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis, is a systemic vasculitis that affects small- and medium-sized vessels. It is characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and is strongly associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs). The classic triad of GPA includes upper airway, lung, and kidney disease. Upper airway involvement can manifest as sinusitis, otitis media, oral or nasal ulcers, or saddle-nose deformity due to septal perforation. Pulmonary involvement often presents as cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, or chest discomfort, and chest radiography may show nodular or cavitary infiltrates. Renal involvement typically presents as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with hematuria and red cell casts. This patient's history of recurrent lung infections, hemoptysis, and hematuria is suggestive of GPA.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old previously healthy man comes to his physician because of dyspnea and hemoptysis for the past week. Examination shows inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. His hemoglobin concentration is 14.2 g/dL, leukocyte count is 10,300/mm3, and platelet count is 205,000/mm3. Urine dipstick shows 2+ proteins. Urinalysis shows 80 RBC/hpf and 1–2 WBC/hpf. An x-ray of the chest shows pulmonary infiltrates. Further evaluation is most likely to show increased serum titers of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's hemoptysis, dyspnea, and pulmonary infiltrates, along with hematuria and proteinuria, are suggestive of Goodpasture syndrome (anti-glomerular basement membrane [anti-GBM] disease). This is an autoimmune disease caused by autoantibodies directed against the noncollagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, which is found in the basement membranes of the glomeruli and alveoli. The antibodies bind to the GBM, leading to inflammation and damage to the kidneys and lungs. The disease typically presents with a combination of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage, as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old male presents to clinic complaining of coughing up small amounts of blood daily for the past week. He denies smoking, sick contacts, or recent travel. Chest radiographs demonstrates interstitial pneumonia with patchy alveolar infiltrates suggestive of multiple bleeding sites. Urinalysis is positive for blood and protein. A positive result is returned for anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody (anti-GBM Ab). What is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Goodpasture disease is an autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies (anti-GBM Ab). These antibodies target the basement membranes of both the glomeruli in the kidneys and the alveoli in the lungs, leading to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage, respectively. The classic presentation is a young male with hemoptysis, hematuria, and renal failure. The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of anti-GBM Ab in the serum.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old male presents with several months of fatigue, malaise, dry cough, and occasional episodes of painless hematuria. He recalls having had a sore throat several days prior to the onset of these symptoms that resolved without antibiotics. Physical exam is remarkable for diffusely coarse breath sounds bilaterally. Urinalysis reveals 2+ protein, 2+ blood, and numerous red blood cell casts are visible under light microscopy. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigue, malaise, dry cough, and hematuria is suggestive of a systemic vasculitis. The presence of red blood cell casts on urinalysis is indicative of glomerulonephritis, which is a common manifestation of vasculitis. The most likely diagnosis in this case is microscopic polyangiitis, a small-vessel vasculitis that commonly affects the lungs and kidneys. It is associated with MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) antibodies.

The other options are less likely given the patient's presentation. Diffuse membranous glomerulopathy and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis are both causes of nephrotic syndrome, which typically presents with proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema. Transitional cell bladder carcinoma can cause painless hematuria, but would not explain the patient's other symptoms.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 65-year-old man presents with left-sided numbness, diplopia, and blurring of vision. The diplopia is more prominent on his left-side lateral gaze. He denies having fever, headache, ocular pain, lacrimation, changes in color vision, or limb weakness. He has a past medical history of type-2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and ischemic heart disease. In addition, he had an ischemic stroke 9 years ago, from which he recovered completely with physiotherapy and rehabilitation. He has a history of a 56-pack-year cigarette smoking habit. His medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, glimepiride, metformin, metoprolol, and ramipril. The mental status examination is unremarkable. His muscle strength is normal in all 4 limbs. His sensations are decreased on his left side, including his face. The examination of extraocular movements is shown in the image. A lesion in which of the following locations explains the findings during eye examination?

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of headache, blurring of vision, and numbness of the right leg for the past 2 hours. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications include enalapril and metformin. He is oriented only to person. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 99/min and blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg. Examination shows equal pupils that are reactive to light. Muscle strength is normal in all extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. Sensation to fine touch and position is decreased over the right lower extremity. The confrontation test shows loss of the nasal field in the left eye and the temporal field in the right eye with macular sparing. He is unable to read phrases shown to him but can write them when they are dictated to him. He has short-term memory deficits. Which of the following is the most likely cause for this patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.A: Infarct of the right posterior cerebral artery
answer_choices.B: Infarct of the right anterior cerebral artery
answer_choices.D: Infarct of the left posterior cerebral artery

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of acute onset headache, visual field defects, and right leg sensory loss are suggestive of a stroke. The visual field defects are consistent with a left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, which is characteristic of an infarct in the distribution of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). The PCA supplies the occipital lobe (responsible for vision) and parts of the temporal lobe (involved in memory). The sensory loss in the right leg is due to involvement of the thalamus, which is also supplied by the PCA. The PCA is a branch of the basilar artery, which is formed by the confluence of the vertebral arteries. The PCA gives off many branches, including the thalamoperforating arteries to the thalamus and the calcarine branch to the occipital lobe. The thalamus is responsible for sensory relay and the occipital lobe is responsible for vision. Therefore, occlusion of the left PCA would cause right-sided sensory loss and left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician due to worsening headache and double vision. His headache began several months ago, and he describes them as sharp and localized to the left side of the head. His double vision began one week prior to presentation. Medical history is significant for hypertension and type II diabetes mellitus, which is treated with lisinopril and metformin. He smokes a pack of cigarettes a day for the last 40 years. His temperature is 98.3°F (37°C), blood pressure is 148/84 mmHg, pulse is 60/min, and respirations are 14/min. On physical exam, a mild head turning towards the left is appreciated. Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light, with a more pronounced esotropia on left-lateral gaze. The rest of the neurologic exam is otherwise normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head and MR angiography shows a left-sided intracavernous carotid aneurysm. Which of the following nerves is most likely compressed by the aneurysm in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
The cavernous sinus is a dural venous sinus located on either side of the sella turcica. It contains the internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve (CN VI) within the sinus itself. The oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), and the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1 and V2) are located within the lateral wall of the sinus. The optic nerve (CN II) is not located within the cavernous sinus.

This patient's symptoms of headache and double vision are due to compression of the abducens nerve by a carotid aneurysm within the cavernous sinus. The abducens nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which abducts the eye. Compression of the abducens nerve results in unopposed action of the medial rectus muscle, leading to esotropia (ie, "cross-eyed") and diplopia that is most pronounced on attempted lateral gaze.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 74-year-old gentleman presents to his family practitioner with the complaint of an inability to open his left eye since this morning. He also complains of intermittent pain and numbness in his left arm that has been present for the last few days. He denies ocular pain, difficulty swallowing, fatigability, or diplopia. His symptoms remain constant without fluctuation. He has a history of diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia. Further history reveals that he has lost 5.4 kg (12 lb) of weight in the past 4 months. He is a chronic smoker with a 72 pack-year smoking history. His blood pressure is 142/76 mm Hg, the heart rate is 76/min, the respiratory rate is 12/min, the temperature is 36.8°C (98.4°F), and BMI is the 18.2 kg/m2. The patient is awake, alert, and oriented to person, place, and time. He has partial drooping of the left eyelid while the right eyelid appears normal. The left pupil is 1 mm and the right pupil is 3 mm in diameter. Extraocular muscle movements are normal. What additional clinical feature would most likely be present in this patient?

answer_choices.C: Tongue deviation to the left side

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis is consistent with Horner syndrome. Horner syndrome is caused by a disruption of the sympathetic nerve fibers anywhere along the oculosympathetic pathway. The oculosympathetic pathway begins in the hypothalamus and descends through the brainstem to synapse in the intermediolateral column of the spinal cord at the C8-T2 level (first-order neuron). The second-order neuron exits the spinal cord and travels over the apex of the lung to synapse in the superior cervical ganglion, which is located at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery. The third-order neuron then travels along the internal carotid artery and through the cavernous sinus to supply the eye and forehead.

This patient's history of significant weight loss and heavy smoking raises concern for a Pancoast tumor (superior sulcus tumor), which is a lung cancer that occurs at the lung apex and invades the local structures. Pancoast tumors can disrupt the second-order neuron as it passes over the lung apex, resulting in Horner syndrome. Other symptoms of Pancoast tumors can include shoulder pain and weakness and/or paresthesias of the upper extremities due to invasion of the brachial plexus.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department because of a sudden loss of vision in his left eye for 2 hours. He has no pain. He had a similar episode 1 month ago which lasted only seconds. He has no history of a headache or musculoskeletal pain. He has had ischemic heart disease for 8 years and hypertension and diabetes mellitus for 13 years. His medications include metoprolol, aspirin, insulin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes for 39 years. The vital signs include: blood pressure 145/98 mm Hg, pulse 86/min, respirations 16/min, and temperature 36.7°C (98.1°F). Physical examination of the left eye shows a loss of light perception. After illumination of the right eye and conceptual constriction of the pupils, illumination of the left eye shows pupillary dilation. A fundoscopy image is shown. Which of the following best explains these findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden, painless, monocular vision loss is most likely due to central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). CRAO is an ophthalmologic emergency that occurs when the central retinal artery, a branch of the ophthalmic artery, becomes occluded. This is typically due to an embolus from a carotid artery plaque or the heart. The retina becomes ischemic, leading to sudden, painless, monocular vision loss. The retina will appear pale with a characteristic "cherry-red spot" at the fovea, where the choroidal circulation maintains a small amount of blood flow. The optic disc may be normal initially but may become pale over time.

This patient's history of atherosclerotic risk factors (eg, smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia) and a prior episode of transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) suggest that his CRAO is likely due to an atheroembolic event.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old man with longstanding history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset numbness. On your neurological exam, you note that he has loss of sensation on the left side of his face, arm, and leg. His motor strength exam is normal, as are his cranial nerves. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of contralateral hemisensory loss with a normal motor exam is suggestive of a thalamic stroke. The thalamus is a relay station for sensory information from the body to the cerebral cortex. It is supplied by small penetrating arteries known as thalamoperforators, which arise from the posterior cerebral artery. Occlusion of these arteries can cause a thalamic (or thalamic lacunar) stroke, leading to contralateral hemisensory loss. Other symptoms can include contralateral hemiparesis, hemiataxia, and possibly a mild language disturbance if the dominant hemisphere is involved.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: An asymptomatic 65-year-old woman is found to have T-score of -2.6 SD on routine bone mineral density screening. She has a 10-year history of hypertension and an esophageal stricture due to severe gastroesophageal reflux disease. She was diagnosed with endometrial hyperplasia 20 years ago and treated with medroxyprogesterone. Menarche started at 11 years of age and her last menstrual period was 8 years ago. Her last mammography and PAP smear 6 months ago showed no abnormalities. Her mother died of breast cancer at the age of 45 years. The patient does not have any children. Current medications include lansoprazole and hydrochlorothiazide. Her blood pressure is 135/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Treatment is begun with a drug that prevents further bone resorption and reduces her risk of developing breast cancer. This drug puts her at an increased risk of which of the following adverse effects?

few_shot.question: A 58-year-old woman presents to the office after receiving a bone mineral density screening test result with a T score of -4.1 and a Z score of -3.8. She is diagnosed with osteoporosis. A review of her medical history reveals that she has taken estrogen-containing oral contraceptive pills from the age of 20 to 30. She suffered from heartburn from the age of 45 and took lansoprazole and ranitidine often for her symptoms. She also was on lithium for 2 years after being diagnosed with bipolar disorder at the age of 54. Last year she was diagnosed with congestive heart failure and was started on low dose hydrochlorothiazide. Which of her medications most likely contributed to the development of her osteoporosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as lansoprazole are commonly used for the treatment of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). PPIs decrease the production of gastric acid, which can lead to decreased absorption of calcium and other minerals necessary for bone health. This can lead to decreased bone mineral density and an increased risk of fractures. Therefore, the use of PPIs has been associated with an increased risk of osteoporosis.

The other medications listed do not have a significant effect on bone mineral density. Estrogen is actually protective against osteoporosis, and is sometimes used in the treatment of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women. Hydrochlorothiazide can cause hypercalcemia by decreasing calcium excretion, and lithium can cause hyperparathyroidism, leading to increased bone resorption and hypercalcemia, but these effects are not typically associated with a significant decrease in bone mineral density.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of constipation, loss of appetite, and increased urinary frequency for the past 8 weeks. She has a history of hypertension and underwent mastectomy for breast cancer 9 months ago. Her sister has hyperthyroidism and her mother died of complications from breast cancer at the age of 52 years. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Current medications include chlorthalidone. Her temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F), pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes. Abdominal examination shows mild, diffuse abdominal tenderness to palpation with decreased bowel sounds. Her serum creatinine concentration is 1.2 mg/dL and serum calcium concentration is 12 mg/dL. Serum parathyroid hormone levels are decreased. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of breast cancer, hypercalcemia, and low parathyroid hormone levels suggest the presence of metastatic bone disease with subsequent hypercalcemia of malignancy. The most common cancers that metastasize to bone are breast, lung, and prostate. Hypercalcemia of malignancy is most often due to the production of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) by cancer cells. PTHrP binds to the same receptor as parathyroid hormone and increases bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. Hypercalcemia can cause a variety of symptoms, including constipation, anorexia, polyuria, and altered mental status.

The initial treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy is aggressive intravenous hydration with normal saline, followed by calcitonin for patients with severe symptoms or markedly elevated calcium levels. However, the most effective long-term management is with bisphosphonates (eg, zoledronic acid, pamidronate), which inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Bisphosphonates are also used for the prevention of pathologic fractures in patients with known bony metastases.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old African American G1P0010 presents to her gynecologist for an annual visit. She has a medical history of hypertension, for which she takes hydrochlorothiazide. The patient’s mother had breast cancer at age 68, and her sister has endometriosis. At this visit, the patient’s temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 138/74 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 13/min. Her BMI is 32.4 kg/m^2. Pelvic exam reveals a nontender, 16-week sized uterus with an irregular contour. A transvaginal ultrasound is performed and demonstrates a submucosal leiomyoma. This patient is at most increased risk of which of the following complications?
few_shot.explanation:
Leiomyomas, or uterine fibroids, are benign smooth muscle tumors of the uterus. They are the most common pelvic tumors in women and are often asymptomatic. However, when symptoms do occur, they can include abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain or pressure, and reproductive dysfunction. The most common symptom is abnormal uterine bleeding, which is often prolonged and can lead to iron deficiency anemia. This is especially true for submucosal fibroids, which distort the endometrial cavity and can cause particularly heavy menstrual bleeding.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old woman presents to her physician for a regular checkup. She is a community-dwelling, retired teacher without any smoking history. She has arterial hypertension and takes hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg and valsartan 80 mg daily. She was recently discharged from the hospital after admission for an ulnar fracture she received after a fall from the second step of a ladder in her garden. A year ago, she had a clavicular fracture from tripping over some large rocks in her yard. She does not report lightheadedness or fainting. Her medical history is also significant for an appendectomy 11 years ago. She is in menopause. She mostly consumes vegetables and dairy products. Her height is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) and weight is 55 kg (123 lb). Her blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg without orthostatic changes, heart rate is 73/min and regular, respiratory rate is 14/min, and temperature is 36.6°C (97.9°F). Her lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac auscultation reveals S2 accentuation over the aorta. The abdomen is mildly distended on palpation; there are no identifiable masses. The neurological examination is unremarkable. Considering the history and presentation, which of the following medications most likely will be prescribed to this patient after additional investigations?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of multiple fractures from low-energy trauma (eg, falls from standing height) is concerning for osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is a common condition in postmenopausal women due to decreased estrogen levels. Estrogen deficiency leads to increased osteoclast activity and bone resorption. The diagnosis of osteoporosis can be confirmed with a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan, which measures bone mineral density.

The first-line treatment for osteoporosis is lifestyle modification (eg, weight-bearing exercise, smoking cessation) and optimization of calcium and vitamin D intake, followed by a bisphosphonate. Vitamin D increases the efficiency of intestinal calcium absorption and decreases urinary calcium excretion. The Endocrine Society recommends at least 600-800 IU/day of vitamin D in postmenopausal women. This patient's diet of mostly vegetables and dairy is likely deficient in vitamin D, which is found in fatty fish, cod liver oil, and fortified dairy products. Therefore, she should be started on supplemental vitamin D (cholecalciferol).

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [D] > [A] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and a 9-kg (20-lb) weight gain over the past 12 months. She also has irregular menstrual cycles and difficulty sleeping. Menses occur at irregular 35- to 50-day intervals and last 3–7 days. Menarche was at age of 13 years and her last menstrual period was 4 weeks ago. She has 1-year history of hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. She drinks a glass of wine daily. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 85 kg (187 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 125/86 mm Hg. Examination shows acne on the face and hair on the chin and around the umbilicus. The face has a rounded shape and is reddened. There are several smaller bruises on both forearms. This patient is most likely to have which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's weight gain, irregular menses, hypertension, and hirsutism are suggestive of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). However, her additional findings of facial plethora, easy bruising, and central obesity are suggestive of Cushing syndrome. Cushing syndrome is characterized by an excess of glucocorticoids, which can be due to endogenous overproduction (eg, pituitary or adrenal tumor) or exogenous administration (eg, for treatment of autoimmune or inflammatory disorders). Chronic glucocorticoid excess has multiple effects on bone, including decreased calcium absorption in the gut, increased urinary calcium excretion, and direct inhibition of osteoblast function. These effects result in a negative calcium balance and decreased bone formation, leading to an overall decrease in bone mineral density and an increased risk of fractures.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [D] > [A] > [C].

question:
A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of fever, chills, and generalized weakness. He has no cough. He was treated for a neck abscess 6 months ago. He takes no medications. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 10 years and drinks two to three beers daily. He has been using intravenous cocaine and heroin for 6 years. He appears ill. His temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows track marks on both cubital fossae. There are retinal hemorrhages with pale centers. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the lower left sternal border. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL
Leukocyte count 14,300/mm3
Platelet count 278,000/mm3
Serum
Glucose 96 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL
Total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL
AST 18 U/L
ALT 22 U/L
Transthoracic echocardiography shows multiple vegetations on the tricuspid valve and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Two sets of blood cultures are collected. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"

few_shot.question:
A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 6-day history of fever and chills. During this period, he has had generalized weakness, chest pain, and night sweats. He has a bicuspid aortic valve and recurrent migraine attacks. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 5 years. He does not drink alcohol. He has experimented with intravenous drugs in the past but has not used any illicit drugs in the last two months. Current medications include propranolol and a multivitamin. He appears ill. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 150/50 mm Hg. Diffuse crackles are heard. A grade 3/6 high-pitched, early diastolic, decrescendo murmur is best heard along the left sternal border. An S3 gallop is heard. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL
Leukocyte count 13,300/mm3
Platelet count 270,000/mm3
Serum
Glucose 92 mg/dL
Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
Total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL
AST 25 U/L
ALT 28 U/L
Three sets of blood cultures are sent to the laboratory. Transthoracic echocardiography confirms the diagnosis. In addition to antibiotic therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"

answer_choices.B: Mechanical valve replacement of the aortic valve
answer_choices.C: Porcine valve replacement of the aortic valve

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, chills, night sweats, and new murmur are concerning for infective endocarditis (IE). His history of bicuspid aortic valve and intravenous drug use are both risk factors for IE. The early diastolic, decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border is consistent with aortic regurgitation, which can occur due to valvular damage from IE. The S3 gallop and crackles on lung auscultation suggest heart failure due to aortic regurgitation.

In patients with IE complicated by heart failure, valve replacement surgery is indicated. Mechanical valves are more durable than bioprosthetic valves and are preferred in patients <65 years of age who can take lifelong anticoagulation. Bioprosthetic valves are typically used in patients who have a contraindication to anticoagulation, are >65 years of age, or have IE caused by resistant organisms (eg, fungal).

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old man presents to the emergency department for a persistent fever. The patient states he has felt unwell for the past week and has felt subjectively febrile. The patient has a past medical history of a suicide attempt and alcohol abuse. He is not currently taking any medications. The patient admits to using heroin and cocaine and drinking 5-8 alcoholic drinks per day. His temperature is 103°F (39.4°C), blood pressure is 92/59 mmHg, pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Cardiopulmonary exam is notable for a systolic murmur heard best along the left sternal border. Dermatologic exam reveals scarring in the antecubital fossa. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, hypotension, tachycardia, and systolic murmur are concerning for infective endocarditis (IE). The most common cause of IE is Staphylococcus aureus, especially in patients with a history of intravenous drug use. The diagnosis of IE is made by the modified Duke criteria, which include two major criteria (positive blood cultures and evidence of endocardial involvement on echocardiography) and five minor criteria (predisposition to IE, fever, vascular phenomena, immunologic phenomena, and microbiologic evidence). This patient meets two minor criteria (predisposition and fever) and possibly one major criterion (new murmur). The next best step in management is to obtain blood cultures prior to initiating antibiotic therapy. Blood cultures should be obtained from different sites and at different times to increase the yield of the cultures and to avoid potential contaminants.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 21-year-old man presents to a physician because of extreme fatigue, palpitations, fever, and weight loss. He developed these symptoms gradually over the past 3 months. His blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg, heart rate is 109/min, respiratory rate is 17/min, and temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). The patient is emaciated and pale. There are conjunctival hemorrhages and several bruises noted in the inner cubital area bilaterally. There are also a few lesions on the left foot. The cardiac examination reveals a holosystolic murmur best heard at the 4th intercostal space at the left sternal edge. Two blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus, and echocardiography shows a tricuspid valve aneurysm. Which of the following would most likely be revealed in a detailed history from this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, weight loss, and a new heart murmur is suggestive of infective endocarditis (IE). The presence of Staphylococcus aureus in the blood cultures and the tricuspid valve aneurysm on echocardiography confirm this diagnosis. The most common cause of right-sided IE is intravenous drug use, which can introduce bacteria directly into the bloodstream. The tricuspid valve is most commonly affected in these patients because it is the first valve encountered by the bacteria after they are injected. The presence of conjunctival hemorrhages and bruises in the inner cubital area bilaterally are also suggestive of intravenous drug use.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after losing consciousness upon rising from his chair at work. The patient has had progressive cough, shortness of breath, fever, and chills for 6 days but did not seek medical attention for these symptoms. He appears distressed, flushed, and diaphoretic. He is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 120 kg (265 lbs); BMI is 41.5 kg/m2. His temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse is 129/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 91/50 mm Hg when supine. Crackles and bronchial breath sounds are heard over the right posterior hemithorax. A 2/6 midsystolic blowing murmur is heard along the left upper sternal border. Examination shows diffuse diaphoresis, flushed extremities, and dullness to percussion over the right posterior hemithorax. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Multiple nurses and physicians have been unable to attain intravenous access. A large-bore central venous catheter is inserted into the right internal jugular vein by standard sterile procedure. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, cough, and shortness of breath, along with the physical examination findings of bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right posterior hemithorax, are suggestive of a right-sided pneumonia complicated by a parapneumonic effusion. The patient's hypotension, tachycardia, and altered mental status (eg, loss of consciousness) suggest septic shock due to pneumonia. The most appropriate next step in management is to obtain a chest x-ray to confirm the diagnosis of pneumonia and evaluate for complications (eg, effusion, empyema, abscess, necrotizing pneumonia). 

So, the answer is [D].
