few_shot.question:
A 56-year-old African-American man comes to the physician for intermittent episodes of dark urine and mild flank pain. The patient has had 3 episodes of frank reddish discoloration of his urine within 1 month. He has chronic headaches and back pain for which he has been taking aspirin and ibuprofen daily for 1 year. The patient has sickle cell trait. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 10 years. He appears well. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F). His pulse is 66/min, and his blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Physical exam shows mild, bilateral flank tenderness. Laboratory analysis shows a serum creatinine concentration of 2.4 mg/dL. Urine studies are shown below.
Urine
Blood 3+
Protein 2+
RBC > 10/hpf
WBC 3/hpf
Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's hematuria?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of sickle cell trait, chronic analgesic use, and smoking, along with the presence of hematuria and renal insufficiency, suggest renal papillary necrosis. This condition is characterized by coagulative necrosis of the renal medullary pyramids and papillae. It is most commonly associated with conditions that lead to renal ischemia or vascular insufficiency, such as analgesic nephropathy, sickle cell disease or trait, diabetes mellitus, urinary tract obstruction, and pyelonephritis. The renal papillae are particularly susceptible to ischemic injury due to their location at the end of the vascular supply of the kidney. Sludging of sickled red blood cells in the vasa recta can lead to vascular congestion and ischemia, particularly in the setting of hypoxia, acidosis, or hyperosmolality. Analgesic nephropathy is associated with chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis and papillary necrosis due to decreased prostaglandin synthesis and medullary ischemia. Patients with renal papillary necrosis often present with gross hematuria, flank pain, and passage of sloughed papillae in the urine.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old African American male presents to his primary care physician with complaints of persistent back pain and fatigue over 12 months. This patient's presentation of back pain, fatigue, hyperlipidemia, and renal failure is suggestive of multiple myeloma. The renal biopsy findings of eosinophilic, acellular material in the glomerular tuft and capillary walls that display apple green-colored birefringence in polarized light upon Congo red tissue staining are indicative of amyloidosis, which is a common complication of multiple myeloma. The amyloid deposits are derived from immunoglobulin light chains, which are produced in excess by the malignant plasma cells in multiple myeloma.

Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide, an albuterol inhaler, naproxen, and an aspirin-caffeine combination. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows conjunctival pallor. This patient's history of chronic lower back pain and use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as naproxen, along with the laboratory findings of chronic kidney disease (CKD), suggest analgesic nephropathy. Analgesic nephropathy is a type of CKD that results from the cumulative effects of taking large amounts of analgesics over many years. The most common analgesics implicated are NSAIDs and acetaminophen, either alone or in combination. The pathogenesis of analgesic nephropathy is not completely understood, but it is thought to involve inhibition of renal prostaglandin synthesis by NSAIDs. Prostaglandins are produced in the kidney and have a vasodilatory effect on the afferent arterioles. By inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, NSAIDs can cause unopposed vasoconstriction and decreased renal blood flow, leading to ischemic injury.

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old African-American male presents to his family physician after noticing red-tinged urine the week before, when he was suffering from a cold. The patient states that he had experienced that before. His father is with him and says that this happens to him on occasion as well. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of red-tinged urine during a cold, along with a similar history in his father, is suggestive of sickle cell trait. Sickle cell trait is a benign condition that affects approximately 8% of African Americans. It is caused by heterozygosity for the sickle hemoglobin (HbS) gene. Patients are usually asymptomatic and often unaware they have the condition. However, they can have microscopic or gross hematuria due to renal papillary necrosis. Sickling in the renal medulla can lead to microinfarctions and subsequent papillary necrosis. The renal medulla is particularly susceptible to sickling due to its relative hypoxia and hypertonicity, which promote HbS polymerization.

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old African-American man presents to his primary care provider with a history of fatigue and nausea that started about 6 months ago. Today his temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), the blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, and the pulse is 75/min. Physical examination reveals morbid obesity and 1+ pitting edema of both lower extremities. Urine dipstick reveals 2+ proteinuria. Urinalysis shows no abnormal findings. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigue, edema, and proteinuria is suggestive of nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by proteinuria (>3.5 g/24 hr), hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia. The most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in African Americans and Hispanics is focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). FSGS is also the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in patients with HIV, heroin addiction, and massive obesity. FSGS is a pattern of renal injury characterized by sclerosis (ie, scarring) in some glomeruli (focal) and only part of each glomerulus (segmental). The pathogenesis of primary FSGS is thought to involve injury to the podocytes, which are cells in the glomerulus that help to prevent proteins from being filtered into the urine. Secondary FSGS can occur due to any condition that increases the demand on the glomeruli, such as massive obesity, HIV infection, and heroin use.

question: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of colicky abdominal pain and diarrhea. He has bowel movements 10–12 times daily; the stool contains blood and mucus. few_shot.question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of persistent abdominal cramping, diarrhea, and rectal pain. During the past 2 weeks, she has had up to 4 small volumed, blood-tinged stools with mucus daily. She has also had intermittent fevers and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during this time. She traveled to Southeast Asia 3 months ago and received all appropriate vaccinations and medications beforehand. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 125/80 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft, and there is tenderness to palpation of the left lower quadrant with guarding but no rebound. Bowel sounds are normal. The stool is brown, and a test for occult blood is positive. Flexible sigmoidoscopy shows a granular, hyperemic, and friable rectal mucosa that bleeds easily on contact. Which of the following is this patient at greatest risk of developing?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal cramping, diarrhea, rectal pain, and bloody stools is suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The sigmoidoscopic findings of a granular, hyperemic, and friable rectal mucosa that bleeds easily on contact are consistent with ulcerative colitis (UC), a form of IBD that is limited to the colon and rectum. UC is a chronic, relapsing condition characterized by diffuse mucosal inflammation, which usually begins in the rectum and may extend proximally to involve part or all of the colon. The inflammation is limited to the mucosa and submucosa and is characterized by crypt abscesses and crypt distortion.

Patients with UC are at increased risk for colorectal cancer. The risk is related to the extent and duration of disease, with those having pancolitis for >8-10 years being at greatest risk. Other risk factors include a family history of sporadic colorectal cancer and concomitant primary sclerosing cholangitis. Patients with long-standing extensive UC should undergo surveillance colonoscopy every 1-2 years.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old man presents to clinic with a complaint of fatigue that has developed over the past 6 months. Crohn's disease is a type of inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus. It is characterized by transmural inflammation, which can lead to the development of fistulas, abscesses, and strictures.

Patients with Crohn's disease are at increased risk for the development of kidney stones. This is due to increased absorption of oxalate in the colon, which can lead to hyperoxaluria and the formation of calcium oxalate stones.

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician with intermittent bloody diarrhea over the past 2 months. He has occasional abdominal pain. His symptoms have not improved over this time. He has no history of a serious illness and takes no medications. His blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 75/min, respirations are 14/min, and temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F). Deep palpation of the abdomen shows mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Colonoscopy shows diffuse erythema with a sandpaper pattern involving the rectosigmoid and descending colon, with normal mucosa of the rest of the colon. Biopsy shows involvement of the mucosal and submucosal layers with distortion of crypt architecture and crypt abscess formation. This patient is most likely to develop which of the following hepatobiliary diseases?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and endoscopic findings of continuous colonic inflammation involving the rectum is consistent with ulcerative colitis (UC). UC is an idiopathic inflammatory bowel disease that is characterized by chronic, relapsing inflammation of the colonic mucosa. Patients with UC are at increased risk for primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), a chronic, progressive disease of the bile ducts characterized by inflammation, fibrosis, and strictures of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. PSC can lead to cholestasis, cirrhosis, and portal hypertension. Patients with PSC often present with fatigue, pruritus, or jaundice, but some patients are asymptomatic and are diagnosed based on abnormal liver function tests. The diagnosis of PSC is confirmed by cholangiography, which shows multifocal stricturing and segmental dilations of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts ("beaded" appearance). PSC is also a risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old male presents to the emergency room with weight loss, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea. He reports having intermittent bloody stools and crampy left lower quadrant abdominal pain over the past several days. He is otherwise healthy, does not smoke, and takes no medications. His family history is notable for colon cancer in his father. He subsequently undergoes a colonoscopy which demonstrates a hyperemic friable mucosa with inflammation extending continuously from the rectum proximally through the colon. A biopsy of the rectal mucosa is notable for crypt abscesses and pseudopolyps. This patient’s condition is most commonly associated with what other condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and continuous colonic inflammation on colonoscopy is consistent with ulcerative colitis (UC). UC is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that is characterized by continuous mucosal inflammation that starts in the rectum and extends proximally to involve part or all of the colon. The inflammation is limited to the mucosa and submucosa and does not involve the entire bowel wall, as seen in Crohn disease. The most common extraintestinal manifestation of UC is primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), which is a chronic, progressive disease characterized by inflammation, fibrosis, and stricturing of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. PSC can lead to cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease. Patients with PSC are also at increased risk for cholangiocarcinoma.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [D] > [A] > [C].

question: A 52-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia comes to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of substernal chest pain while sitting in a chair at home. He reports drinking 2 glasses of whiskey earlier that day, after a stressful day at work. Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide and atorvastatin. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 20 years. His pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 135/88 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows normal heart sounds. An ECG obtained on arrival at the emergency department shows ST-segment elevations in the anterior leads. 15 minutes later, the patient's chest pain has resolved and a repeat ECG shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient’s chest pain?

few_shot.question: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe chest pain and uneasiness. He says that symptoms onset acutely half an hour ago while he was watching television. He describes the pain as being 8/10 in intensity, sharp in character, localized to the center of the chest and retrosternal, and radiating to the back and shoulders. The patient denies any associated change in the pain with breathing or body position. He says he has associated nausea but denies any vomiting. He denies any recent history of fever, chills, or chronic cough. His past medical history is significant for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus for which he takes lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, simvastatin, and metformin. He reports a 30-pack-year smoking history and has 1–2 alcoholic drinks during the weekend. Family history is significant for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and an ST elevation myocardial infarction in his father and paternal uncle. His blood pressure is 220/110 mm Hg in the right arm and 180/100 mm Hg in the left arm. On physical examination, the patient is diaphoretic. Cardiac exam reveals a grade 2/6 diastolic decrescendo murmur loudest over the left sternal border. Remainder of the physical examination is normal. The chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. The electrocardiogram (ECG) reveals non-specific ST segment and T wave changes. Intravenous morphine and beta-blockers are started. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe, sharp, tearing chest pain radiating to the back, unequal blood pressures in the arms, and a widened mediastinum on chest radiograph is suggestive of aortic dissection. Aortic dissection is a life-threatening condition that occurs when blood enters the media of the aortic wall through a tear in the intima. This can lead to separation of the layers of the aortic wall, creating a false lumen. The most common risk factors for aortic dissection are hypertension and conditions associated with medial degeneration of the aorta (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, cocaine use). The pain of aortic dissection is typically described as abrupt in onset, severe, and tearing or ripping in character. It is often felt in the anterior chest, but can also be felt in the back or abdomen, depending on the location of the dissection. Physical examination may reveal a diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation, which is caused by dilation of the aortic root or dissection into the aortic valve leading to central valvular regurgitation. Other findings may include pulse or blood pressure differential between the extremities, focal neurologic deficits, or signs of congestive heart failure. The diagnosis is confirmed by imaging studies such as CT angiography, magnetic resonance angiography, or transesophageal echocardiography.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [C] > [D] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of chest pain. The pain occurs intermittently in 5-minute episodes. It is not conclusively brought on by exertion and sometimes occurs at rest. He has a history of hyperlipidemia and takes a high-dose statin daily. His father died of lung cancer at the age of 67 years and his mother has type 2 diabetes. He smokes a pack of cigarettes daily and does not drink alcohol. His temperature is 37°C (98.8°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 124/72 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. He has no chest wall tenderness and pain is not reproduced with palpation. While waiting for laboratory results, he has another episode of chest pain. During this event, an ECG shows ST elevations in leads II, III, and aVF that are > 1 mm. Thirty minutes later, a new ECG shows no abnormalities. Troponin I level is 0.008 ng/mL (normal value < 0.01 ng/mL). Cardiac angiography is performed and shows a 30% blockage of the proximal right circumflex artery and 10% blockage in the distal left circumflex artery. This patient's condition is most closely associated with which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's chest pain, which is not consistently brought on by exertion and sometimes occurs at rest, along with transient ST-segment elevations on ECG, is suggestive of Prinzmetal (variant) angina. This condition is caused by coronary artery vasospasm, which leads to transient ST-segment elevations on ECG (due to transmural ischemia). The pain of Prinzmetal angina is often severe and can occur at rest, often in the early morning. It is frequently associated with ST-segment elevations on ECG, which normalize when the patient is asymptomatic. Unlike typical angina, Prinzmetal angina is not usually due to atherosclerosis and may occur in the absence of coronary artery disease. The diagnosis is confirmed by coronary angiography, which can also provoke spasm and reproduce chest pain with accompanying ST-segment elevations.

Prinzmetal angina is associated with other vasospastic disorders such as Raynaud phenomenon and migraine headaches. It is also associated with tobacco use, which is a risk factor for coronary artery vasospasm.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [C] > [B] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of severe, migrating anterior chest pain, shortness of breath, and sweating at rest. He has hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Medications include atorvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, and metformin. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. He is in severe distress. His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Cardiac examination shows a grade 3/6, high-pitched, blowing, diastolic murmur heard best over the right sternal border. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Femoral pulses are decreased bilaterally. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia and left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe, migrating chest pain, diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation, and decreased femoral pulses is suggestive of aortic dissection. Aortic dissection is a life-threatening condition that occurs when blood enters the media of the aortic wall through a tear in the intima. This can lead to separation of the layers of the aortic wall, creating a true lumen and a false lumen. The false lumen can rupture, leading to hemorrhage, or it can compress the true lumen, leading to decreased blood flow to organs and tissues. This patient's decreased femoral pulses suggest that the dissection extends to the iliac arteries.

Risk factors for aortic dissection include hypertension, smoking, dyslipidemia, and diabetes, all of which are present in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 50-year-old man presents the emergency department for intense chest pain, profuse sweating, and shortness of breath. The onset of these symptoms was 3 hours ago. The chest pain began after a heated discussion with a colleague at the community college where he is employed. Upon arrival, he is found conscious and responsive; the vital signs include a blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, a heart rate at 90/min, a respiratory rate at 20/min, and a body temperature of 36.4°C (97.5°F). His medical history is significant for hypertension diagnosed 7 years ago, which is well-controlled with a calcium channel blocker. The initial electrocardiogram (ECG) shows ST-segment depression in multiple consecutive leads, an elevated cardiac troponin T level, and normal kidney function. Which of the following would you expect to find in this patient?

answer_choices.C: Incomplete occlusion of a coronary artery

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with an acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which includes unstable angina, non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The patient's symptoms (chest pain, diaphoresis, dyspnea), ECG findings (ST-segment depression), and elevated cardiac troponin T level are consistent with NSTEMI. NSTEMI is typically caused by a partially occluded coronary artery, which results in subendocardial ischemia and necrosis. The subendocardium is particularly susceptible to ischemia because it is farthest from the epicardial coronary arteries and is exposed to the highest wall tension. In contrast, STEMI is caused by a completely occluded coronary artery and results in transmural ischemia and necrosis.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [C] > [D] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 73-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute substernal chest pain that began a few hours ago. The pain is described as a “pressure” that radiates to his left arm. His past medical history is significant for hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He is on chlorthalidone for his hypertension and simvastatin for hyperlipidemia. He has a 30 pack-year history of smoking and drinks 1-2 beers on weekends. His EKG shows ST depressions in the anterior precordial leads and he is given the proper medications and sent for emergency revascularization. Seven days later, he develops dyspnea that worsens in the supine position. Bibasilar crackles are heard on pulmonary auscultation. Cardiac exam reveals a new 3/6 holosystolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border. What is the most likely etiology of this patient’s new symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with a papillary muscle rupture, a mechanical complication of myocardial infarction (MI). Papillary muscle rupture typically occurs 2-7 days after an MI and presents with acute-onset dyspnea and a new holosystolic murmur due to acute mitral regurgitation. The murmur is often best heard at the apex and radiates to the axilla, but in severe cases, it can be best heard at the left sternal border due to the large left-to-right pressure gradient across the mitral valve. Bibasilar crackles on pulmonary auscultation are indicative of pulmonary edema, which is a common finding in acute mitral regurgitation.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

question: A 75-year-old man presents to his physician with a 1-year history of dysphagia for solids. His more recent complaints include dysphagia for liquids as well. The patient states that he has no difficulty initiating swallowing but occasionally food is stuck in his throat. He does not complain of pain while swallowing but has noticed minor unintentional weight loss. The patient has no history of speech-related pain or nasal regurgitation. His family history is unremarkable. During the examination, the patient appears ill, malnourished, and slightly pale. He is not jaundiced nor cyanotic. Physical examination is unremarkable. A swallowing study reveals a small outpouching in the posterior neck (see image). Which nerve is most likely involved in this patient’s symptoms?

few_shot.question: A 47-year-old man presents to you with gradual loss of voice and difficulty swallowing for the past couple of months. The difficulty of swallowing is for both solid and liquid foods. His past medical history is insignificant except for occasional mild headaches. Physical exam also reveals loss of taste sensation on the posterior third of his tongue and palate, weakness in shrugging his shoulders, an absent gag reflex, and deviation of the uvula away from the midline. MRI scanning was suggested which revealed a meningioma that was compressing some cranial nerves leaving the skull. Which of the following openings in the skull transmit the affected cranial nerves?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of loss of voice, difficulty swallowing, loss of taste sensation on the posterior third of his tongue and palate, weakness in shrugging his shoulders, an absent gag reflex, and deviation of the uvula away from the midline are indicative of a lesion affecting cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. These nerves exit the skull via the jugular foramen.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensory innervation to the posterior third of the tongue and the pharynx, and also carries parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland. The vagus nerve (CN X) provides motor innervation to the muscles of the pharynx and larynx, and also carries parasympathetic fibers to the thoracic and abdominal viscera. The accessory nerve (CN XI) provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old man presents to his primary care provider with dysphagia. He notes that his symptoms began several weeks ago and have worsened over time. He now has trouble swallowing solids and liquids. He denies any other symptoms. He has no significant past medical history. Travel history reveals a recent trip to South America but no other travel outside the United States. His temperature is 100°F (37.8°C), blood pressure is 120/81 mmHg, pulse is 99/min, respirations are 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. HEENT exam is unremarkable. He has no palpable masses in his abdomen. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's dysphagia to both solids and liquids, lack of systemic symptoms, and recent travel to South America are suggestive of achalasia, a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the loss of peristalsis in the distal two-thirds of the esophagus and failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter. Achalasia can be idiopathic or secondary to diseases such as Chagas disease, malignancy, or neurodegenerative disorders.

The initial diagnostic test of choice for suspected achalasia is a barium swallow, which typically shows a dilated esophagus with an area of distal stenosis ("bird's beak" appearance). If the barium swallow is inconclusive, esophageal manometry can be performed, which is the gold standard for diagnosis.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [D] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with anxiety and trouble swallowing. He states that his symptoms have slowly been getting worse over the past year, and he now struggles to swallow liquids. He recently recovered from the flu. Review of systems is notable only for recent weight loss. The patient has a 33 pack-year smoking history and is a former alcoholic. Physical exam is notable for poor dental hygiene and foul breath. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking and alcohol use, poor dental hygiene, and weight loss are concerning for squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus. This is a common malignancy in patients with a history of smoking and alcohol use. It often presents with progressive dysphagia, first to solids and then to liquids, and weight loss. Other symptoms can include hoarseness, cough, and hematemesis. Poor dental hygiene is a risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus, as it can lead to chronic inflammation of the esophagus.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old man presents to the office with his wife complaining of difficulty in swallowing, which progressively worsened over the past month. He has difficulty in initiating swallowing and often has to drink water with solid foods. He has no problems swallowing liquids. His wife is concerned about her husband’s bad breath. Adding to his wife, the patient mentions a recent episode of vomiting where the vomit smelled ‘really bad’ and contained the food that he ate 2 days before. On examination, the patient’s blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse rate is 72/min, with normal bowel sounds, and no abdominal tenderness to palpation. A barium swallow radiograph is taken which reveals a localized collection of contrast material in the cervical region suggestive of an outpouching. Which of the following statements best describes the lesion seen on the radiograph?

answer_choices.B: Outpouching of all 3 layers of the esophageal mucosal tissue distal to the upper esophageal sphincter
answer_choices.C: Increased pressure above the upper esophageal sphincter resulting in a defect in the wall
answer_choices.D: Failure of neural crest migration into the Auerbach plexus

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of dysphagia, halitosis, and regurgitation of undigested food are suggestive of Zenker diverticulum. This is a false diverticulum that occurs in the posterior hypopharynx, just above the upper esophageal sphincter (cricopharyngeus muscle). It is caused by increased intraluminal pressure that results in herniation of the mucosa and submucosa through a weak point in the posterior hypopharynx known as Killian's triangle. This triangle is bordered superiorly by the inferior constrictor muscle and inferiorly by the cricopharyngeus muscle. The diverticulum can cause a variety of symptoms, including dysphagia, halitosis, regurgitation of undigested food, and aspiration.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old woman comes to the physician with dysphagia and halitosis for several months. She feels food sticking to her throat immediately after swallowing. Occasionally, she regurgitates undigested food hours after eating. She has no history of any serious illness and takes no medications. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination including the oral cavity, throat, and neck shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study at this time?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dysphagia to solids and liquids, halitosis, and regurgitation of undigested food are suggestive of Zenker diverticulum (ZD). ZD is a false diverticulum that occurs in the posterior hypopharynx, just above the upper esophageal sphincter. It is caused by increased intraluminal pressure that leads to herniation of the mucosa and submucosa through the Killian triangle, an area of muscular weakness between the cricopharyngeus and the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles. The diagnosis of ZD is confirmed by barium swallow with video fluoroscopy, which can show the diverticulum as well as evaluate the patient's swallowing mechanics.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [D] > [B] > [C].

question: A 15-year-old boy with poorly controlled asthma presents to the emergency room complaining of severe shortness of breath. His mother reports that he had trouble breathing soon after he started playing soccer with some friends and was unable to use his inhaler as it was empty. His family history is notable for emphysema in his paternal uncle and cirrhosis in his maternal grandfather. The child’s temperature is 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 130/90 mmHg, pulse is 130/min, respirations are 28/min, and oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. Physical examination demonstrates wheezing bilaterally in all lung fields. The child is started on supplemental oxygen and a nebulized bronchodilator. Which of the following is a downstream effect of this medication?

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy with asthma is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of shortness of breath and cough. Current medications are inhaled albuterol and beclomethasone. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F) and respirations are 24/min. Pulmonary examination shows bilateral expiratory wheezing. Serum studies show increased concentrations of interleukin-5. Which of the following is the most likely effect of the observed laboratory finding in this patient?

answer_choices.B: Differentiation of bone marrow stem cells
answer_choices.D: Suppression of MHC class II expression

few_shot.explanation:
Interleukin-5 (IL-5) is a cytokine produced by Th2 cells that plays a key role in the pathogenesis of asthma. It promotes the growth and differentiation of eosinophils in the bone marrow and their release into the circulation. In addition, IL-5 enhances the survival of eosinophils in the tissues by inhibiting apoptosis. Eosinophils are the primary effector cells in the inflammatory response seen in asthma. They release a variety of mediators that cause airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction, and airway remodeling.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old boy presents with shortness of breath after prolonged exposure to cold air during a recent hike with his friends. Past medical history is significant for asthma, untreated because he doesn't like using medications. The patient says he is a non-smoker and occasionally drinks alcohol. On physical examination, his temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse rate is 120/min, blood pressure is 114/76 mm Hg, and respiratory rate is 32/min. Auscultation of the chest reveals bilateral wheezing. Nebulized ipratropium bromide results in significant clinical improvement. Which of the following second messenger systems is affected by this drug?
few_shot.explanation:
Ipratropium bromide is a muscarinic antagonist that is used in the treatment of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It works by blocking the action of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors in the bronchial smooth muscle, leading to bronchodilation. The muscarinic receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor that is linked to the phosphoinositol second messenger system. When acetylcholine binds to the muscarinic receptor, it activates a G protein that in turn activates phospholipase C. This enzyme catalyzes the conversion of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG). IP3 causes the release of calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, leading to smooth muscle contraction, while DAG activates protein kinase C, which phosphorylates various proteins and also leads to smooth muscle contraction. By blocking the muscarinic receptor, ipratropium prevents these downstream effects and causes bronchodilation.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy with asthma is brought to the physician because of a 1-month history of worsening shortness of breath and cough. The mother reports that the shortness of breath usually occurs when he is exercising with his older brother. His only medication is an albuterol inhaler that is taken as needed. The physician considers adding zafirlukast to his drug regimen. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of action of this drug?
few_shot.explanation:
Zafirlukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist that is used for the prophylaxis and chronic treatment of asthma. Leukotrienes are inflammatory mediators that are released from mast cells, eosinophils, and basophils, and cause bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability leading to edema, and recruitment of inflammatory cells. By blocking the action of leukotrienes, zafirlukast can reduce these effects and help control the symptoms of asthma.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [D] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 19-year-old woman with a history of poorly controlled asthma presents to her pulmonologist for a follow-up visit. She was recently hospitalized for an asthma exacerbation. It is her third hospitalization in the past five years. She currently takes inhaled salmeterol and medium-dose inhaled budesonide. Her past medical history is also notable for psoriasis. She does not smoke and does not drink alcohol. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 110/65 mmHg, pulse is 75/min, and respirations are 20/min. Physical examination reveals bilateral wheezes that are loudest at the bases. The patient’s physician decides to start the patient on zileuton. Which of the following is the most immediate downstream effect of initiating zileuton?

answer_choices.D: Decreased signaling via the muscarinic receptor

few_shot.explanation:
Zileuton is a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor that blocks the conversion of arachidonic acid to leukotrienes. Leukotrienes are potent bronchoconstrictors and pro-inflammatory mediators that increase vascular permeability and mucus production in the airways. By blocking leukotriene synthesis, zileuton can decrease bronchoconstriction and inflammation in the airways.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his parents due to recurrent episodes of wheezing for the last 2 years. He uses a salbutamol inhaler for relief from wheezing, but his symptoms have recently worsened. He often coughs during the night, which awakens him from sleep almost every other day. He is not able to play football because he starts coughing after 10–15 minutes of play. His current physical examination is completely normal and auscultation of his chest does not reveal any abnormal breath sounds. His peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) is 75% of expected for his age, gender, and height. After a complete diagnostic evaluation, the pediatrician prescribes a low-dose inhaled fluticasone daily for at least 3 months. He also mentions that the boy may require continuing inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) therapy for a few years if symptoms recur after discontinuation of ICS. However, the parents are concerned about the side effects of corticosteroids. Which of the following corticosteroid-related adverse effects is most likely?
few_shot.explanation:
Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are the most effective long-term control therapy for persistent asthma. They reduce airway inflammation, bronchial hyperreactivity, and asthma symptoms, and improve lung function and quality of life. The most common local adverse effects of ICS are oropharyngeal candidiasis and dysphonia (hoarseness of voice). Dysphonia is thought to be due to myopathy of the vocal cord muscles and/or direct deposition of the drug on the vocal cords. It is usually reversible and can be minimized by using a spacer device and rinsing the mouth after inhalation.

Systemic adverse effects of ICS are rare and occur only at high doses. These include adrenal suppression, growth suppression, decreased bone mineral density, cataracts, and skin bruising. Adrenal suppression is usually clinically insignificant and does not require monitoring in children receiving low to moderate doses of ICS. Growth suppression is also usually minimal (approximately 1 cm) and is most apparent in the first year of therapy. Long-term studies have shown that final adult height is not affected by ICS use.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [D] > [B].

question:
A 65-year-old woman presents to a physician with painful ankles for 2 days. Her symptoms began 1 week ago with a severe fever (40℃ (104℉)) for 3 days. When the fever subsided, she developed a maculopapular rash over the trunk and extremities with painful wrists and fingers. She also reports abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and headaches. Last week she returned from a trip to Africa where she spent several weeks, mostly in rural areas. Her temperature is 37.5℃ (99.5℉); pulse is 75/min; respiratory rate is 13/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. A maculopapular rash is observed over the trunk and limbs. Both ankles are swollen and painful to active and passive motion. The abdomen is soft without organomegaly. Laboratory studies show the following:
Laboratory test
Hemoglobin 11.4 g/d
Mean corpuscular volume 90 µm3
Leukocyte count 4,500/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 70%
Lymphocytes 15%
Platelet count 250,000/mm3
Ring-form trophozoites are absent on the peripheral blood smear. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this patient’s illness?

few_shot.question: A 13-year-old boy is brought to a physician with severe fevers and headaches for 3 days. The pain is constant and mainly behind the eyes. He has myalgias, nausea, vomiting, and a rash for one day. Last week, during an academic winter break, he traveled on a tour with his family to several countries, including Brazil, Panama, and Peru. They spent many evenings outdoors without any protection against insect bites. There is no history of contact with pets, serious illness, or use of medications. The temperature is 40.0℃ (104.0℉); the pulse is 110/min; the respiratory rate is 18/min, and the blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. A maculopapular rash is seen over the trunk and extremities. Several tender lymph nodes are palpated in the neck on both sides. A peripheral blood smear shows no organisms. Which of the following is most likely responsible for this patient’s presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne viral illness that is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions, including Central and South America. The virus is transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, which bites during the day. The incubation period is 3-14 days. Symptoms include high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgias/arthralgias, nausea/vomiting, and a maculopapular rash. The rash typically appears 3-5 days after the onset of fever and spreads from the trunk to the extremities and face. Lymphadenopathy is also common. Severe disease can manifest as dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome, which can cause bleeding, thrombocytopenia, and hypotension. Diagnosis is usually clinical, but serologic testing can be performed. Treatment is supportive.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old man presents to the physician with fever and malaise for 4 days. He has headaches and joint pain. A pruritic rash appeared on the trunk yesterday. He had blood in his ejaculate twice. His hearing has become partially impaired. There is no history of serious illnesses or the use of medications. Ten days ago, he traveled to Brazil where he spent most of the time outdoors in the evenings. He did not use any control measures for mosquito bites. His temperature is 38.2℃ (100.8℉); the pulse is 88/min; the respiratory rate is 13/min, and the blood pressure is 125/60 mm Hg. Conjunctival suffusion is noted. A maculopapular rash is present over the trunk and proximal extremities without the involvement of the palms or soles. Several joints of the hands are tender to palpation. The abdomen is soft with no organomegaly. A peripheral blood smear shows no pathogenic organisms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Zika virus is a flavivirus transmitted by the Aedes mosquito. It is endemic in many parts of the world, including Brazil. The virus can also be transmitted sexually, from mother to child, and through blood transfusion. Most infected individuals are asymptomatic, but some may develop a mild, self-limited illness characterized by low-grade fever, malaise, conjunctivitis, and a pruritic maculopapular rash. Other symptoms can include headache, myalgia, and arthralgia, especially of the small joints of the hands and feet. Less commonly, patients may have genitourinary symptoms (eg, hematospermia, as in this patient) or gastrointestinal symptoms. Neurologic complications (eg, Guillain-Barré syndrome, meningoencephalitis) and congenital Zika syndrome can occur but are rare. Diagnosis is confirmed by reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction testing of serum or urine collected within 2 weeks of symptom onset.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 10-year-old girl presents to your office with a fever and rash. Her mother first noticed the rash 2 days ago after a camping trip. The rash began on her wrists and ankles and has now spread to her palms and the soles of her feet. This morning, she was feeling unwell and complaining of a headache. She had a fever of 102°F (39°C) prompting her mother to bring her to your office. She is otherwise healthy and does not take any medications. Her medical history is significant for a broken arm at age 8. On physical exam her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 22/min. You notice a petechial rash on the palms, soles, ankles, and wrists. Which of the following findings would confirm the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.A: Granulocytes with morulae in the cytoplasm
answer_choices.B: Cross-reactivity of serum with proteus antigens
answer_choices.C: Monocytes with morulae in the cytoplasm

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, headache, and rash that began on the wrists and ankles and spread to the palms and soles are suggestive of Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), a tick-borne illness caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. The rash of RMSF is classically described as maculopapular, but it can also be petechial as in this patient. RMSF is a serious illness that can be rapidly fatal; therefore, treatment with doxycycline should be initiated as soon as the diagnosis is suspected.

The diagnosis of RMSF is usually made clinically, but it can be confirmed by serologic testing. The most widely available and frequently used test is an indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) that detects R. rickettsii antibodies. However, this test is often negative in the first 7-10 days of illness. In the later stages of disease, the IFA can demonstrate a fourfold or greater rise in IgG-specific antibody titers. Cross-reactivity can occur with antigens from Proteus species, and this reaction forms the basis of the Weil-Felix test, which is neither sensitive nor specific for RMSF.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of an intermittent, diffuse abdominal pain. She has also had a nonpruritic rash on her legs and swelling of her ankles for 1 week. Two weeks ago, she had a sore throat, which was treated with oral amoxicillin. Examination of the lower extremities shows non-blanching, raised erythematous papules. The ankle joints are swollen and warm, and their range of motion is limited by pain. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 450,000/mm3. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of palpable purpura, arthralgias, and abdominal pain following an upper respiratory tract infection is suggestive of leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV), also known as hypersensitivity vasculitis. LCV is a small-vessel vasculitis that is often precipitated by infections, drugs, or malignancies. It is characterized by immune complex deposition in postcapillary venules, leading to endothelial swelling and subsequent extravasation of red blood cells. The most common symptom of LCV is palpable purpura, which is often distributed symmetrically over the lower extremities. Other symptoms include fever, myalgia, and arthralgia. Involvement of the small vessels of the GI tract can lead to abdominal pain and GI bleeding, as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

It presents with palpable purpura that does not blanch with pressure, most prominently on the legs and buttocks. Extracutaneous manifestations are seen in approximately half of patients and can include gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, abdominal pain, bloody stools due to vasculitis of the bowel wall), arthralgias, and renal disease (eg, hematuria, proteinuria). Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy of the skin lesions, which shows neutrophilic infiltration and fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels. Treatment involves discontinuation of the offending drug and administration of glucocorticoids in severe cases.

question: A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with severe knee, hip, and groin pain. The patient has a past medical history notable only for obesity and asthma. His temperature is 98°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 124/65 mmHg, pulse is 128/min, respirations are 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for an inability of the patient to bear weight on his left leg and limited range of motion of the left hip. Which of the following is the best management for this patient?

answer_choices.B: Immobilization of the hip in a Pavlik harness
answer_choices.D: Surgical pinning of the femoral head

few_shot.question: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 5-week history of pain in his left thigh. The mother reports that her son fell from a ladder while playing with friends about a month and a half ago. He had a runny nose 3 weeks ago. He has no history of serious illness. He has reached all developmental milestones for his age. His immunizations are up-to-date. His 7-year-old brother has asthma. He is at 60th percentile for height and 65th percentile for weight. He appears healthy. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a mild left-sided antalgic gait. The left groin is tender to palpation; abduction and internal rotation are limited by pain. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. His hemoglobin concentration is 13.3 g/dL, leukocyte count is 8,800/mm3, and platelet count is 230,000/mm3. An x-ray of the pelvis shows a left femoral epiphysis that is smaller than the right with widening of the medial joint space on the left. The femoral head shows little discernible damage. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.D: Limited weight bearing and physical therapy

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a recent fall, antalgic gait, and limited hip abduction and internal rotation, along with radiographic findings of a smaller left femoral epiphysis and widening of the medial joint space, are consistent with Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD). LCPD is a self-limited condition that results from idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head. It typically presents in children aged 4-10 years, with a male predominance. The disease is characterized by an insidious onset of hip or knee pain and an antalgic gait. On examination, patients often have limited hip abduction and internal rotation. Radiographs show a smaller femoral epiphysis on the affected side. The goal of treatment is to relieve pain and maintain range of motion of the hip joint. This is achieved by limiting weight bearing and through physical therapy. The disease process is self-limited, and the prognosis is generally good, although some patients may develop femoral head deformities that can lead to osteoarthritis later in life.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy presents to his primary care physician with hip pain that started this morning. The patient claims the pain is severe and is stopping him from skateboarding. The patient recently recovered from a upper respiratory infection that he caught from his siblings but has otherwise been healthy. The patient has a past medical history of obesity. His temperature is 98.1°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 100/55 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On physical exam, you note an obese boy in no acute distress. Cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Inspection of the hip reveals no abnormalities or swelling. The hip exhibits a normal range of motion and physical exam only elicits minor pain. The patient's gait appears normal and pain is elicited when the patient jumps or runs. Which of the following is the best next step in management for this patient's most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with transient synovitis, which is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children aged 3-10. Transient synovitis is a self-limited inflammatory condition that often occurs following a viral infection, as in this patient. Patients typically present with hip pain that may be referred to the thigh or knee, a limp, and decreased range of motion of the hip. Systemic symptoms such as fever and leukocytosis are usually absent. The diagnosis is clinical, and treatment involves rest and NSAIDs (eg, ibuprofen).

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy presents with right hip pain for the past 2 days. He reports gradual onset of pain and states it hurts to walk. He had a recent cold last week but is otherwise healthy. His temperature is 98.2°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 107/70 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, respiratory rate is 19/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals no swelling or warmth surrounding the joint. The patient is sitting with the right hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. Passive range of motion of the hip causes discomfort. The patient is able to ambulate but states it hurts. An initial radiograph of the hip is unremarkable. The patient's CRP is 0.10 mg/L. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with transient synovitis, which is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children aged 3-10 years. It is thought to be related to a recent viral infection or trauma. Patients typically present with hip pain and an antalgic gait, and prefer to hold the hip slightly flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. Systemic symptoms (eg, fever) are usually absent. Laboratory studies typically show a normal ESR and CRP, and radiographs are usually normal. Management is supportive, with NSAIDs for pain and rest.

few_shot.question:
A previously healthy 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever and pain in the left lower extremity. His mother says that he has refused to walk for the last two days and has had a poor appetite. He returned from a weekend camping trip about a month ago. His maternal cousin died of osteosarcoma at the age of 12. His immunizations are up-to-date. He is at the 80th percentile for height and 70th percentile for weight. He appears ill. His temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 115/min, respirations are 19/min, and blood pressure is 95/50 mm Hg. Examination of the left hip shows tenderness; range of motion is limited. Minimal attempts to rotate the hip cause severe discomfort. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 12 g/dL
Leukocyte count 19,800/mm3
Platelet count 254,000/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 55 mm/h
Serum
Glucose 80 mg/dL
CRP 15 mg/L
X-rays of the pelvis shows a widened acetabular space on the left side. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"

answer_choices.B: Synovial fluid drainage plus cefazolin therapy

few_shot.explanation:
This child has septic arthritis of the hip, which is a pediatric emergency. The most common pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S aureus (MRSA). Other pathogens include Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus) and Kingella kingae in children <4 years of age, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in sexually active adolescents. Septic arthritis typically presents with fever, refusal to bear weight, and a painful joint with decreased range of motion. The hip is the most commonly involved large joint in children. Laboratory studies often show leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein). Radiographs of the affected joint may show a widened joint space due to increased fluid, joint space narrowing from cartilage destruction, or periosteal elevation and soft tissue swelling.

Treatment of septic arthritis involves prompt IV antibiotics and surgical intervention. Empiric antibiotic therapy should include an agent with MRSA coverage (eg, vancomycin, clindamycin) and a third-generation cephalosporin (eg, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime) for additional streptococcal and gram-negative coverage. Surgical intervention is necessary to drain the purulent fluid, which can cause rapid and irreversible destruction of articular cartilage. The hip joint is unique in that it is not easily accessible to aspiration, and arthrotomy is often required for adequate drainage.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents for severe right hip pain that suddenly started about 2 hours ago. The parents are extremely anxious and feel overwhelmed because the boy has been hospitalized several times in the past for similar episodes of pain. The boy was born at 39 weeks of gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. He is up to date on all vaccinations and is meeting all developmental milestones. His only medication is hydroxyurea, which he has been receiving for 3 years. His blood pressure is 125/84 mm Hg, the respirations are 23/min, the pulse is 87/min, and the temperature is 36.7°C (98.0°F). On physical examination, the patient is in distress and has severe pain (8/10) elicited by gentle palpation of the right femoral head. Which of the following conditions has the same pathophysiology as the likely diagnosis for the patient described in this case?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent episodes of severe pain and hydroxyurea use suggest a diagnosis of sickle cell disease (SCD). The most common musculoskeletal manifestation of SCD is vaso-occlusive crisis, which is characterized by severe pain due to tissue ischemia and infarction. The femoral head is a common site of vaso-occlusive crisis and can lead to avascular necrosis (AVN) due to its tenuous blood supply. AVN, also known as osteonecrosis, is a disease characterized by death of cellular components of bone and marrow due to interruption of the subchondral blood supply. It is often idiopathic but can also be associated with corticosteroid use, alcoholism, SCD, and other conditions. AVN of the femoral head can lead to collapse of the articular surface and subsequent degenerative joint disease.

Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is a condition that also involves AVN of the femoral head. It typically occurs in children aged 4-10 and presents with a limp and hip or knee pain. The exact etiology is unknown, but it is thought to be due to idiopathic interruption of the blood supply to the femoral head.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 36-year-old man undergoes open reduction and internal fixation of a left femur fracture sustained after a motor vehicle collision. Three days after the surgery, he develops fever and redness around the surgical site. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F). Physical examination shows purulent discharge from the wound with erythema of the surrounding skin. Wound culture of the purulent discharge shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Treatment with oral dicloxacillin is initiated. Four days later, the patient continues to have high-grade fever, pain, and purulent discharge. Which of the following characteristics of the infecting organism best explains the failure to improve with antibiotic therapy?

answer_choices.A: Presence of an impenetrable outer membrane

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old man returns to the hospital 3 weeks after open reduction and internal fixation of left tibia and fibula fractures from a motor vehicle accident. The patient complains that his surgical site has been draining pus for a few days, and his visiting nurse told him to go to the emergency room after he had a fever this morning. On exam, his temperature is 103.0°F (39.4°C), blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg, pulse is 115/min, and respirations are 14/min. The ED physician further documents that the patient is also starting to develop a diffuse, macular rash. The patient is started on broad spectrum antibiotics, and Gram stain demonstrates purple cocci in clusters. Which of the following toxins is likely to be the cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, hypotension, and rash in the setting of a recent surgical site infection with Staphylococcus aureus are concerning for toxic shock syndrome (TSS). TSS is a toxin-mediated illness that can occur with S. aureus infection, and it is most commonly associated with the toxin known as toxic shock syndrome toxin 1 (TSST-1). TSST-1 is a superantigen that binds to major histocompatibility complex class II molecules and T-cell receptors, leading to polyclonal T-cell activation and massive cytokine release. This results in the clinical manifestations of TSS, which include fever, hypotension, and a diffuse, macular rash that can lead to desquamation, particularly on the palms and soles, 1-2 weeks after the onset of the illness.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: Four days after being admitted to the hospital for widespread second-degree burns over his arms and thorax, a 29-year-old man develops a fever and wound discharge. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). Examination shows a discolored burn eschar with edema and redness of the surrounding skin. The wounds have a sickly, sweet odor. A culture of the affected tissue grows an aerobic, gram-negative rod. The causal pathogen most likely produces which of the following substances?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, wound discharge, and discolored burn eschar with surrounding erythema are concerning for a burn wound infection. The most common pathogens in burn wound infections are Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The latter is suggested in this patient by the presence of a sweet, grape-like odor. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative rod that produces multiple virulence factors, including phospholipase C (also known as hemolysin). Phospholipase C degrades cell membranes, leading to tissue destruction and necrosis, and can also inhibit human leukocyte function.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: Six days after undergoing an elective hip replacement surgery, a 79-year-old man develops dysuria, flank pain, and fever. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F). Examination shows marked tenderness in the right costovertebral area. Treatment with an antibiotic is begun, but his symptoms do not improve. Further evaluation shows that the causal organism produces an enzyme that inactivates the antibiotic via phosphorylation. An agent from which of the following classes of antibiotics was most likely administered?
few_shot.explanation:
Aminoglycosides are bactericidal antibiotics that inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit. They are particularly effective against aerobic gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. However, resistance to aminoglycosides is common and can occur via several mechanisms, including production of enzymes that modify the antibiotic (eg, acetyltransferase, phosphotransferase, nucleotidyltransferase). These enzymes catalyze the transfer of specific chemical groups to the antibiotic, which inhibits its binding to the bacterial ribosome.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old woman with a history of multiple sclerosis and recurrent urinary tract infections comes to the emergency department because of flank pain and fever. Her temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). Examination shows left-sided costovertebral angle tenderness. She is admitted to the hospital and started on intravenous vancomycin. Three days later, her symptoms have not improved. Urine culture shows growth of Enterococcus faecalis. Which of the following best describes the most likely mechanism of antibiotic resistance in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of the peptidoglycan precursor units, thereby preventing their incorporation into the growing peptidoglycan chain. This leads to cell wall instability and lysis.

Resistance to vancomycin in Enterococcus species (eg, E faecalis, E faecium) is due to a modification in the structure of the peptidoglycan precursors. Specifically, the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus is replaced with D-alanyl-D-lactate. This substitution results in decreased binding of vancomycin to the peptidoglycan precursors, thereby reducing its effectiveness.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: Three days after admission to the hospital following a motor vehicle accident, a 45-year-old woman develops a fever. A central venous catheter was placed on the day of admission for treatment of severe hypotension. Her temperature is 39.2°C (102.5°F). Examination shows erythema surrounding the catheter insertion site at the right internal jugular vein. Blood cultures show gram-positive, catalase-positive cocci that have a low minimum inhibitory concentration when exposed to novobiocin. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) due to Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species. S epidermidis is a common skin commensal and is the most common cause of CLABSI. It is often resistant to methicillin due to the presence of the mecA gene, which codes for an altered penicillin-binding protein with decreased affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics. Therefore, empiric treatment of serious S epidermidis infections should include vancomycin, especially in patients with prosthetic devices or intravascular catheters.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 21-year-old female presents to the office after a health screening in which she was found to have high blood pressure. At the office, the blood pressure is 168/114 mm Hg. You have seen the patient in the past for amenorrhea and infertility issues, but she denies taking any medication at this time. On examination, the patient is short and normal weight but has a webbed neck. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the elevated blood pressure?

answer_choices.A: Central fusion of the inferior poles of the kidneys
answer_choices.C: Neuroendocrine tumor of the adrenal gland

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up visit for elevated blood pressure. Two weeks ago, her blood pressure was 154/78 mm Hg at a routine visit. Subsequent home blood pressure measurements at days 5, 10, and 14 have been: 156/76 mm Hg, 158/80 mm Hg, and 160/80 mm Hg. She has trouble falling asleep but otherwise feels well. She had a cold that resolved with over-the-counter medication 2 weeks ago. She has a history of primary hypothyroidism and a cyst in the right kidney, which was found incidentally 20 years ago. She takes levothyroxine. She is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 67 kg (148 lb); BMI is 21.3 kg/m2. Her pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 162/79 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies, including thyroid function studies, serum electrolytes, and serum creatinine, are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's blood pressure findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's blood pressure measurements are consistent with isolated systolic hypertension (ISH), defined as systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140 mm Hg and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) <90 mm Hg. ISH is the most common form of hypertension in individuals >60 years of age. It is due to decreased arterial compliance (ie, increased arterial stiffness) as a result of age-related arterial wall collagen deposition and loss of arterial elastin. Decreased arterial compliance leads to an increase in SBP due to the decreased ability of the large arteries to absorb the pressure wave generated by left ventricular ejection. The DBP decreases because the increased arterial stiffness leads to earlier reflected waves, which augment late systolic pressure but reduce diastolic pressure. The widened pulse pressure (ie, SBP - DBP) increases left ventricular workload and oxygen demand, leading to left ventricular hypertrophy and increasing the risk for myocardial ischemia and infarction.

Hence, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician for a prenatal visit at 14 weeks' gestation. She has had episodic headaches over the past month. At home, blood pressure measurements have ranged from 134/82 mm Hg to 148/94 mm Hg. Today, her blood pressure is 146/91 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 13-week gestation. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, serum ALT is 17 U/L, and platelet count is 320,000/mm3. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's blood pressure (BP) is >140/90 mm Hg prior to 20 weeks' gestation, which is diagnostic of chronic hypertension. Chronic hypertension is present in approximately 1%-5% of pregnancies and is associated with increased risk of superimposed preeclampsia, preterm delivery, and fetal growth restriction. Chronic hypertension can be diagnosed in a pregnant woman if hypertension was known to be present before pregnancy or if hypertension is diagnosed before 20 weeks' gestation. After 20 weeks' gestation, new-onset hypertension is diagnosed as gestational hypertension or preeclampsia.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of morning headaches. He also has fatigue and trouble concentrating on his daily tasks at work. He sleeps for 8 hours every night; his wife reports that he sometimes stops breathing for a few seconds while sleeping. His pulse is 71/min and blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 31.6 kg/m2 . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypertension?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's morning headaches, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating are suggestive of sleep apnea syndrome. Sleep apnea is characterized by recurrent episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to hypoxemia and hypercapnia. The hypoxemia stimulates the carotid and aortic bodies to increase sympathetic outflow, leading to systemic and pulmonary hypertension, as well as cardiac arrhythmias. The hypercapnia stimulates the respiratory centers in the medulla, leading to arousal and hyperventilation. This cycle repeats multiple times during the night, leading to nonrestorative sleep and excessive daytime sleepiness. Risk factors for sleep apnea include obesity, male sex, and age >40 years.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 32-year-old man presents with hypertension that has been difficult to control with medications. His symptoms include fatigue, frequent waking at night for voiding, and pins and needles in the legs. His symptoms started 2 years ago. Family history is positive for hypertension in his mother. His blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg in the right arm and 165/107 mm Hg in the left arm, pulse is 85/min, and temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F). Physical examination reveals global hyporeflexia and muscular weakness. Lab studies are shown:
Serum sodium 147 mEq/L
Serum creatinine 0.7 mg/dL
Serum potassium 2.3 mEq/L
Serum bicarbonate 34 mEq/L
Plasma renin activity low
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis are suggestive of primary aldosteronism. Primary aldosteronism is characterized by autonomous production of aldosterone, leading to increased sodium reabsorption and potassium and hydrogen ion excretion. This results in hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. The hypokalemia can cause muscle weakness and hyporeflexia, as seen in this patient. The low plasma renin activity is due to feedback inhibition from the high aldosterone levels.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician for an initial prenatal visit at 13 weeks' gestation. She has had episodic headaches over the past month. She has no history of serious illness. Her immunizations are up-to-date. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F) and pulse is 90/min. Repeated measurements show a blood pressure of 138/95 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 13-week gestation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis is within normal limits. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, serum ALT is 19 U/L, and platelet count is 210,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely condition in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's blood pressure is elevated (>140/90 mm Hg) before 20 weeks' gestation, which is diagnostic of chronic hypertension. Chronic hypertension is present in about 1-5% of pregnancies and is associated with increased risk of superimposed preeclampsia, preterm delivery, placental abruption, and fetal growth restriction. Chronic hypertension can be differentiated from gestational hypertension, which is diagnosed when hypertension first presents after 20 weeks' gestation in a previously normotensive woman.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [C] > [A] > [B].

question: A 20-year-old man comes to the physician because of worsening gait unsteadiness and bilateral hearing loss for 1 month. He has had intermittent tingling sensations on both cheeks over this time period. He has no history of serious medical illness and takes no medications. Audiometry shows bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Genetic evaluation shows a mutation of a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 22 that encodes merlin. This patient is at increased risk for which of the following conditions?

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of hearing loss and unsteadiness while standing and walking for the past 2 months. She needs support from a wall to prevent herself from falling. She has not had any recent injuries and has no history of serious illness. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows an unsteady gait. She sways when asked to stand upright with her feet together. She is unable to hear fingers rubbing next to her ears or repeat words whispered in her ears bilaterally. An MRI of the brain shows a 3-cm tumor in the right cerebellopontine angle and a 4.5-cm tumor in the left cerebellopontine angle. This patient is most likely to develop which of the following in the future?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's bilateral cerebellopontine angle tumors, hearing loss, and ataxia are suggestive of neurofibromatosis type II (NF2). NF2 is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by bilateral vestibular schwannomas, which typically present in young adulthood with symptoms of tinnitus, hearing loss, and imbalance. Other findings in NF2 can include multiple meningiomas, ependymomas, and schwannomas involving other cranial, spinal, and peripheral nerves.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of decreased hearing, dizziness, and ringing in his right ear for the past 6 months. Physical examination shows multiple soft, yellow plaques and papules on his arms, chest, and back. There is sensorineural hearing loss and weakness of facial muscles bilaterally. His gait is unsteady. An MRI of the brain shows a 3-cm mass near the right internal auditory meatus and a 2-cm mass at the left cerebellopontine angle. The abnormal cells in these masses are most likely derived from which of the following embryological structures?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's clinical presentation is consistent with neurofibromatosis type II (NF2), an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by bilateral vestibular schwannomas, multiple meningiomas, and juvenile posterior subcapsular lenticular opacities. The hallmark of NF2 is bilateral vestibular schwannomas, which often present with tinnitus, hearing loss, and imbalance. Schwannomas can also occur on other cranial nerves, spinal roots, and peripheral nerves. Meningiomas and ependymomas are also associated with NF2. 

Schwann cells, which are affected in NF2, are derived from the neural crest. The neural crest also gives rise to the cells of the dorsal root ganglia, melanocytes, and chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, among others.

Therefore, the answer is [C].
