Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department for complaints of crushing chest pain for 4 hours. He was shoveling snow outside when the pain started. It is rated 7/10 and radiates to his left arm. An electrocardiogram (ECG) demonstrates ST-segment elevation in leads V2-4. He subsequently undergoes percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and is discharged with aspirin, clopidogrel, carvedilol, atorvastatin, and lisinopril. Five days later, the patient is brought to the emergency department by his wife with complaints of dizziness. He reports lightheadedness and palpitations for the past 2 hours but otherwise feels fine. His temperature is 99.7°F (37.6°C), blood pressure is 95/55 mmHg, pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 17/min. A pulmonary artery catheter is performed and demonstrates an increase in oxygen concentration at the pulmonary artery. What finding would you expect in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Harsh, loud, holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of dizziness, lightheadedness, and palpitations is concerning for hypotension and tachycardia. His recent history of myocardial infarction (MI) and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), along with the finding of increased oxygen concentration in the pulmonary artery, suggests the development of a ventricular septal defect (VSD) as a mechanical complication of MI. This is a life-threatening condition that can lead to cardiogenic shock due to left-to-right shunting of blood. On examination, a new harsh, loud, holosystolic murmur would be heard at the lower left sternal border.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for crushing substernal chest pain at rest for the past 2 hours. The pain began gradually while he was having an argument with his wife and is now severe. He does not take any medications. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years. He is diaphoretic. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 21/min, and blood pressure is 115/65 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Cardiac examination shows an S4 gallop. The lungs are clear to auscultation. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

answer_choices.A: Occlusion of the left anterior descending artery
answer_choices.B: Thromboembolism to the right interlobar pulmonary artery
answer_choices.C: Occlusion of the left circumflex artery
answer_choices.D: Tear in the intimal lining of the aorta

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe, crushing substernal chest pain at rest, diaphoresis, and an S4 gallop is consistent with acute myocardial infarction (MI). The ECG shows ST-segment elevations in leads V1-V4, which are indicative of an anterior wall MI. The most common cause of MI is rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with subsequent thrombus formation, leading to occlusion of a coronary artery. The left anterior descending (LAD) artery is the most commonly occluded vessel in MI and supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, and the apex of the heart. Occlusion of the LAD artery can lead to an anterior wall MI, which would present with ST-segment elevations in the precordial leads V1-V4.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [C] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 50-year-old man presents the emergency department for intense chest pain, profuse sweating, and shortness of breath. The onset of these symptoms was 3 hours ago. The chest pain began after a heated discussion with a colleague at the community college where he is employed. Upon arrival, he is found conscious and responsive; the vital signs include a blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, a heart rate at 90/min, a respiratory rate at 20/min, and a body temperature of 36.4°C (97.5°F). His medical history is significant for hypertension diagnosed 7 years ago, which is well-controlled with a calcium channel blocker. The initial electrocardiogram (ECG) shows ST-segment depression in multiple consecutive leads, an elevated cardiac troponin T level, and normal kidney function. Which of the following would you expect to find in this patient?

answer_choices.C: Incomplete occlusion of a coronary artery

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with an acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which includes unstable angina, non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The patient's symptoms (chest pain, diaphoresis, dyspnea), ECG findings (ST-segment depression), and elevated cardiac troponin T level are consistent with NSTEMI. NSTEMI is typically caused by a partially occluded coronary artery, which results in subendocardial ischemia and necrosis. The subendocardium is particularly susceptible to ischemia because it is farthest from the epicardial coronary arteries and is exposed to the highest wall tension. In contrast, STEMI is caused by a completely occluded coronary artery and results in transmural ischemia and necrosis.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [C] > [D] > [A].

question:
A 59-year-old woman presents to her primary care provider complaining of diffuse bodily aches. She reports a 3-month history of gradually worsening pain in her shoulders and hips that is worse in her right hip. She has a history of hypertension and recurrent renal stones for which she takes lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. She was admitted to the hospital earlier in the year after falling in her front yard and sustaining a distal radius fracture and vertebral compression fracture. Her temperature is 98.5°F (36.9°C), blood pressure is 145/85 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, and respirations are 20/min. On exam, she is well-appearing with mild tenderness to palpation in her shoulders and hips. She has mild pain with hip flexion and shoulder abduction. She has full range of motion in her bilateral upper and lower extremities. Serum findings are notable for the following:

Serum:
Na+: 141 mEq/L
Cl-: 100 mEq/L
K+: 4.8 mEq/L
HCO3-: 22 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen: 17 mg/dL
Glucose: 110 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.12 mg/dL
Ca2+: 11.2 mg/dL
Phosphate: 2.3 mg/dL
Mg2+: 1.9 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase: 120 U/L

A radiograph of this patient’s right hip would most likely reveal which of the following?

answer_choices.A: Expansile lytic lesion with thin sclerotic margins
answer_choices.B: Medullary bone destruction with elevated periosteum from cortical bone
answer_choices.C: Poorly marginated lesion extending into adjacent soft tissue
answer_choices.D: Well-defined cystic lesion with peritrabecular fibrosis

few_shot.question: A 54-year-old female presents to her primary care physician with complaints of fatigue, constipation, and what the patient describes as "aching in her bones." Her medical history is significant for hypertension, well-controlled on lisinopril, and two prior kidney stones that both passed spontaneously without need for surgery. Vital signs are within normal limits, and physical exam is not significant for any notable findings. Preliminary lab work is ordered and reveals: calcium 11.6 mg/dL (normal range 8.5 - 10.9 mg/dL), phosphorus 2.1 mg/dL (normal range 2.4 - 4.1 mg/dL), and an elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) level. Which of the following findings would most likely be expected on radiographic evaluation of this patient's hands?

answer_choices.A: Joint space narrowing at the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints
answer_choices.B: Osteoid matrix accumulation around bony trabeculae
answer_choices.D: Dense bone filling the medullary cavity of the phalanges and metacarpals

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fatigue, constipation, and bone pain, along with her history of kidney stones and lab findings of hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and elevated PTH, are consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism. This condition is most commonly caused by a parathyroid adenoma, which leads to overproduction of PTH. The resulting hypercalcemia is due to increased bone resorption and increased renal calcium reabsorption. The hypophosphatemia is due to increased renal phosphate excretion, which is also stimulated by PTH.

Radiographic findings in primary hyperparathyroidism are due to the increased bone resorption and include subperiosteal resorption of the radial aspects of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers, which can lead to subperiosteal cortical thinning. Other findings can include a "salt-and-pepper" appearance of the skull due to loss of the lamina dura around the teeth, and brown tumors (localized collections of osteoclasts, hemorrhage, and fibrous tissue) in severe cases.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [B] > [D] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a constant, dull headache and generalized body pains for the past 8 months. She has also had difficulty hearing from her left side, which started a month after the onset of the headaches. Five months ago, she had surgery to correct a fracture of the right femur that occurred without a fall or any significant trauma. Five years ago, she underwent a total thyroidectomy for localized thyroid carcinoma. She takes levothyroxine and calcium supplements, which she started after menopause. Physical examination reveals a prominent forehead and irregular, tender skull surface. Bony tenderness is present over bilateral hip and knee joints, with decreased range of motion of the right hip joint and increased anterior curvature of both tibias. Laboratory studies show a highly elevated level of alkaline phosphatase, with vitamin D, calcium and PTH levels within normal limits. A plain x-ray of the head is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.A: Lytic lesions with no sclerotic margin
answer_choices.C: Periosteal trabeculations with radiolucent marrow hyperplasia

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of generalized bone pain, hearing loss, and pathologic fracture, along with the physical examination findings of an enlarged skull and bowed tibias, are suggestive of Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans). This is a common condition of abnormal bone remodeling that typically occurs in older adults. The disease is characterized by an initial phase of increased osteoclastic activity, leading to excessive bone resorption, followed by a disorganized and excessive bone formation by osteoblasts. The new bone that is formed is larger but weaker, and is prone to fractures and deformities. The skull, spine, pelvis, and long bones are most commonly affected. 

On x-ray, Paget disease appears as a mixed picture of radiolucent (dark) areas due to osteoclastic bone resorption and dense, sclerotic (white) areas due to osteoblastic bone formation. The bone trabeculae are thickened and disorganized, producing a mosaic pattern. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [D] > [C] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old woman comes to the physician because of lower back pain that began suddenly 2 weeks ago after getting up from her chair. She has hypertension, chronic bilateral knee pain, and a history of breast cancer 15 years ago that was treated with lumpectomy. Her mother has rheumatoid arthritis. Medications include hydrochlorothiazide and acetaminophen. She appears well. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows tenderness to palpation of the lower spine. Both knees are enlarged and swollen. Neurologic examination shows sensorineural hearing impairment of the left ear. Her gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) is 30 U/L (N: 0–30 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is 310 U/L, and serum calcium is 10.2 mg/dL. A spinal x-ray shows a fracture in the L4 vertebra. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of isolated elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), hearing loss, and bone pain is suggestive of Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans). Paget disease is a common condition that typically presents in older adults. It is characterized by disordered and excessive bone remodeling that results in bone that is larger but weaker and more chaotic in structure. The disease may be asymptomatic or present with bone pain, pathologic fractures, or neurologic complications (eg, hearing loss due to impingement of the cranial nerves at the skull base). The most common laboratory abnormality is isolated elevation of ALP, which is a marker of osteoblast activity. 

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department for right hip pain 1 hour after she fell while walking around in her house. She has been unable to stand or walk since the fall. She has hypertension and gout. Her sister died of multiple myeloma at the age of 55 years. Current medications include amlodipine and febuxostat. She does not smoke cigarettes. She drinks a glass of wine daily. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 101/min, and blood pressure is 128/86 mm Hg. Examination shows right groin tenderness. Range of motion of the right hip is limited by pain. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A complete blood count and serum creatinine concentration are within the reference range. An x-ray of the hip shows a linear fracture of the right femoral neck. She is scheduled for surgery. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's fracture?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's age, female sex, and low-energy mechanism of injury (fall from standing height) are suggestive of a fragility fracture due to osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is characterized by reduced bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, leading to enhanced bone fragility and a consequent increase in fracture risk. The most common sites of osteoporotic fractures are the vertebral bodies, distal radius (Colles fracture), and proximal femur (hip). Osteoporosis is especially common among postmenopausal women due to decreased estrogen levels. Estrogen deficiency accelerates bone loss by both increasing osteoclastic bone resorption and decreasing osteoblastic bone formation. The balance between the activities of osteoclasts and osteoblasts (coupling) is lost, with the rate of bone resorption exceeding the rate of bone formation. This imbalance is due to both increased osteoclast activity and reduced osteoblast activity, leading to a net loss of bone.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 46-year-old African American woman presents to her primary care doctor complaining of muscle aches and weakness. She reports a 3 month history of gradually worsening upper and lower extremity pain. She is having trouble keeping up with her children and feels tired for most of the day. A review of systems reveals mild constipation. Her past medical history is notable for hypertension, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and obesity. She takes lisinopril, metformin, and methotrexate. Her family history is notable for chronic lymphocytic leukemia in her mother and prostate cancer in her father. Her temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 145/95 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 17/min. On exam, she appears well and in no acute distress. Muscle strength is 4/5 in her upper and lower extremities bilaterally. Patellar and brachioradialis reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. answer_choices.A: Decreased PTH, decreased phosphate, and increased calcium
answer_choices.B: Decreased PTH, increased phosphate, and decreased calcium
answer_choices.C: Increased PTH, decreased phosphate, and increased calcium
answer_choices.D: Increased PTH, increased phosphate, and decreased calcium

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's muscle aches and weakness, constipation, and hypertension are suggestive of hypercalcemia. Hypercalcemia can be caused by a variety of conditions, including hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, granulomatous diseases, and medications such as thiazide diuretics and lithium. In this patient, the most likely cause of hypercalcemia is primary hyperparathyroidism, which is characterized by increased parathyroid hormone (PTH), decreased phosphate, and increased calcium.

question:
A 41-year-old G3P1 woman presents with a sudden onset throbbing headache, tinnitus, nausea, and left-sided weakness. Patient has no significant past medical history and takes no medications.  Her last two pregnancies ended with spontaneous abortions before the 10th week of gestation. No significant family history. Her vital signs include: blood pressure 130/90 mm Hg, pulse 58/min, respiratory rate 11/min, and temperature 36.8℃ (98.2℉). GCS is 14/15. Physical examination shows 3+ deep tendon reflexes and increased muscle tone in the left upper and lower extremities. Laboratory findings are significant for the following:
Platelet count 230,000/mm3

 A non-contrast CT of the head is performed and shown in the picture. Which of the following would be the next best diagnostic step in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 77-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of headache, nausea, and vomiting for 24 hours. His wife says that over the past 2 weeks, he has been more irritable and has had trouble remembering to do routine errands. Two weeks ago, he fell during a skiing accident but did not lose consciousness. He has coronary artery disease and hypertension. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 50 years. He has had 2 glasses of wine daily since his retirement 10 years ago. Current medications include atenolol, enalapril, furosemide, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He appears acutely ill. He is oriented to person but not to place or time. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 99/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. During the examination, he is uncooperative and unable to answer questions. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ on the left and 2+ on the right. Babinski's sign is present on the left. There is mild weakness of the left iliopsoas and hamstring muscles. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows a high-density, 15-mm crescentic collection across the right hemispheric convexity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a fall, acute headache, and progressive neurologic symptoms (eg, irritability, memory problems, focal neurologic deficits) along with the imaging findings are consistent with a subdural hematoma (SDH). SDH is caused by tearing of the bridging veins that extend from the brain to the dural sinuses. It is most commonly seen in elderly patients, alcoholics, and patients with a history of falls or mild head trauma. The classic presentation is a fluctuating level of consciousness or new-onset seizures over the span of several days to weeks following head trauma. Focal neurologic deficits may also be seen, as in this patient. 

The management of SDH depends on the size of the hematoma, the presence of midline shift, and the patient's neurologic status. In general, symptomatic patients with a hematoma thickness >10 mm or a midline shift >5 mm on CT scan should undergo surgical evacuation regardless of the Glasgow Coma Scale score. This patient's SDH measures 15 mm and he has significant neurologic symptoms, so he should undergo surgical evacuation.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman presents at 24 weeks gestation with complaints of blurred vision and headaches. Her symptoms have increased in frequency over the past several weeks. Her medical history is significant only for occasional tension headaches. She takes no medications besides an oral folic acid supplement. The vital signs are: blood pressure, 159/90 mm Hg; pulse, 89/min; and respiratory rate, 18/min. She is afebrile. She states that her husband, a nurse, took her blood pressure 2 days earlier and found it to be 154/96 mm Hg at the time. Previously, her blood pressures have always been < 120/80 mm Hg. What is the next best step to solidify the diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's new-onset hypertension and symptoms of headache and blurred vision are concerning for preeclampsia. Preeclampsia is a multisystem disorder characterized by new-onset hypertension and proteinuria after 20 weeks of gestation. Hypertension is defined as a blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart. Proteinuria is defined as urinary excretion of ≥300 mg protein in a 24-hour urine specimen. In the absence of proteinuria, preeclampsia can be diagnosed with new-onset hypertension and any of the following: thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function, pulmonary edema, or cerebral or visual symptoms. 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 72-year-old Caucasian female presents to the emergency department with complaints of a new-onset, right-sided throbbing headache which becomes markedly worse when eating. The daughter also reports that her mother has recently had difficulties with performing daily activities, such as climbing stairs or standing up. Past medical history is significant for a lower extremity deep vein thrombosis. The blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, the heart rate is 72/min, and the respiratory rate is 15/min. The physical examination is unremarkable except for the right visual field defect. Laboratory results are presented below:
Hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL
Hematocrit 37.7%
Leukocyte count 6,200/mm3
Mean corpuscular volume 82.2 μm3
Platelet count 200,000/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 75 mm/h
C-reactive protein 50 mg/dL
Which of the following medications would be most beneficial for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's new-onset headache, jaw claudication, and visual field defect, in combination with an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), are highly suggestive of giant cell arteritis (GCA). GCA is a granulomatous vasculitis that primarily involves the branches of the carotid artery, especially the temporal artery. It is the most common form of systemic vasculitis in adults aged >50 years. The disease is more common in women and in individuals of Northern European descent. The most feared complication of GCA is irreversible vision loss due to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Therefore, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone 40-60 mg/day) should be initiated immediately in all patients with suspected GCA, even before the diagnosis is confirmed with temporal artery biopsy. Glucocorticoids reduce inflammation in the arterial wall and decrease the risk of further visual loss. 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 34-year-old G3P2 is admitted to the hospital after being physically assaulted  by her husband. She developed severe vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. She is at 30 weeks gestation. Her previous pregnancies were uncomplicated, as has been the course of the current pregnancy. The vital signs are as follows: blood pressure, 80/50 mmHg; heart rate, 117/min and irregular; respiratory rate, 20/min; and temperature, 36.2℃ (97.1). The fetal heart rate is 103/min. On physical examination, the patient is pale and lethargic. Abdominal palpation reveals severe uterine tenderness and tetanic contractions. The perineum is grossly bloody. There are no vaginal or cervical lesions. There is active  heavy bleeding with blood clots passing through the cervix. An ultrasound shows a retroplacental hematoma with a volume of approximately 400 ml.
Laboratory workup shows the following findings:
Red blood cells count: 3.0 millions/mL
Hb%: 7.2 g/dL
Platelet count: 61,000/mm3
Prothrombin time: 310 seconds (control 20 seconds)
Partial prothrombin time: 420 seconds
Serum fibrinogen: 16 mg/dL
Elevated levels of which of the following laboratory markers is characteristic for this patient’s complication?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness, and tetanic contractions in the setting of trauma is suggestive of abruptio placentae, a premature separation of the placenta from the uterus. The most common cause of abruptio placentae is maternal hypertension; however, abdominal trauma (as in motor vehicle accidents or physical abuse) can also cause the placenta to shear away from the uterus. 

The elevated D-dimer level is consistent with the diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a systemic activation of the coagulation cascade that leads to widespread deposition of fibrin in the circulation. This can lead to microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and multiorgan system dysfunction. DIC is suggested by this patient's low platelet count, prolonged PT and PTT, and low fibrinogen level. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset severe headache, nausea, vomiting, and neck pain for the past 90 minutes. She describes her headache as a ‘thunderclap’, followed quickly by severe neck pain and stiffness, nausea and vomiting. She denies any loss of consciousness, seizure, or similar symptoms in the past. Her past medical history is significant for an episode 6 months ago where she suddenly had trouble putting weight on her right leg, which resolved within hours. The patient denies any history of smoking, alcohol or recreational drug use. On physical examination, the patient has significant nuchal rigidity. Her muscle strength in the lower extremities is 4/5 on the right and 5/5 on the left. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. A noncontrast CT scan of the head is normal. Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.C: Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging of the brain

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden-onset, severe headache, described as a "thunderclap," is concerning for a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). SAH is a type of stroke that occurs when there is bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. The most common cause of nontraumatic SAH is rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm. Other symptoms of SAH can include nausea, vomiting, meningismus (neck pain and stiffness), and loss of consciousness. Focal neurologic deficits may also be present due to increased intracranial pressure or aneurysm compression of adjacent structures.

The initial diagnostic test for suspected SAH is a noncontrast head CT, which has a high sensitivity for blood, especially within the first 6 hours of symptom onset. However, the sensitivity of head CT decreases substantially after 6 hours. If the CT scan is negative but clinical suspicion for SAH remains high, a lumbar puncture should be performed. The presence of xanthochromia (yellow-tinged, blood-contaminated cerebrospinal fluid) is diagnostic of SAH.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 24-year-old woman gravida 2, para 1 at 24 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a prenatal visit. She feels well. Her earlier pregnancy was uncomplicated. This is her 4th prenatal visit. She had an ultrasound scan 2 weeks ago that showed a live intrauterine pregnancy consistent with a 22-week gestation with no anomalies. She had a normal Pap smear 2 years ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 24-week gestation. Her blood group and type is B positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 36 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a prenatal visit. She feels well. Fetal movements are adequate. This is her 7th prenatal visit. She had an ultrasound scan performed 1 month ago that showed a live intrauterine pregnancy consistent with a 32-week gestation with no anomalies. She had a Pap smear performed 1 year ago, which was normal. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 36-week gestation. Her blood group and type is A negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends that all pregnant women be screened for group B streptococcus (GBS) colonization at 35-37 weeks' gestation. This is done by obtaining a vaginal and rectal swab for culture. GBS is a common cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis, and can also cause pneumonia. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for all women who are GBS positive to prevent transmission to the newborn.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 1, at 22 weeks gestation visits her physician for a prenatal visit. She feels well. Her current pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She has attended many prenatal appointments and followed the physician's advice about screening for diseases, laboratory testing, diet, and exercise. The patient’s previous pregnancies were complicated by preterm labor at 24 weeks gestation in one pregnancy and spontanious abortion at 22 weeks in the other. She takes a multivitamin with folate every day. At the physician’s office, her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), and blood pressure is 109/61 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation. Fetal heart sounds are normal. An ultrasound shows a short cervix, measured at 20 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a history of spontaneous preterm birth and a short cervix on transvaginal ultrasound, which are both risk factors for preterm birth. The most appropriate next step in management is placement of a cerclage, a stitch placed in the cervix to keep it closed. This is typically done between 12 and 24 weeks gestation and is removed around 37 weeks gestation. Cerclage is recommended in women with a history of spontaneous preterm birth and a short cervix (<25 mm) on transvaginal ultrasound.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:

She had an uncomplicated 1st pregnancy that ended in an uncomplicated vaginal delivery at the age of 28 years. Her elder sister has a child born with Down syndrome. The patient denies smoking and alcohol consumption. Her blood analysis reveals the following findings:
  Measured values

The patient's blood analysis reveals a high beta-hCG and low PAPP-A, which is suggestive of Down syndrome. Given that her elder sister has a child with Down syndrome, this patient is at a higher risk of having a child with Down syndrome. few_shot.question: A 25-year-old nulliparous woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to her physician accompanied by her husband for her first prenatal visit. She has no personal or family history of serious illness. Her vaccinations are up-to-date and she takes no medications. She has no history of recreational drug use and does not drink alcohol. Her vital signs are within normal limits. She is 167 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 24.3 kg/m2. She tested negative for HIV, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae 4 years ago. Which of the following tests should be done at this visit?

answer_choices.A: Culture for group B streptococci, hepatitis C serology, and PPD skin test
answer_choices.B: Serum TSH, CMV serology, and PCR for HSV-2
answer_choices.C: VDRL, Western blot for HIV, and serum HBsAg
answer_choices.D: ELISA for HIV, rapid plasma reagin test, and serum HBsAg

few_shot.explanation:
The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends that all pregnant women be screened for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B virus (HBV) at their first prenatal visit. HIV screening is important because antiretroviral therapy can reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission. Syphilis screening is important because it can cause stillbirth, neonatal death, or infant disorders such as deafness and neurologic impairment. HBV screening is important because it can lead to chronic infection of the newborn, which can be prevented by administration of the HBV vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin.

The USPSTF recommends the use of an enzyme immunoassay (EIA) to screen for HIV, followed by a Western blot or immunofluorescence assay for confirmation. For syphilis, the USPSTF recommends the use of a nontreponemal test (eg, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or rapid plasma reagin [RPR] test) for screening, followed by a treponemal test (eg, fluorescent treponemal antibody absorbed [FTA-ABS] or Treponema pallidum particle agglutination [TP-PA] assay) for confirmation. For HBV, the USPSTF recommends screening for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 23-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician at 36 weeks' gestation for her first prenatal visit. She confirmed the pregnancy with a home urine pregnancy kit a few months ago but has not yet followed up with a physician. She takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Serum
Glucose 88 mg/dL
Hepatitis B surface antigen negative
Hepatitis C antibody negative

HIV load 11,000 copies/mL (N < 1000 copies/mL)

answer_choices.A: Intrapartum zidovudine and vaginal delivery when labor occurs
answer_choices.B: Start cART and schedule cesarean delivery at 38 weeks' gestation
answer_choices.C: Start cART and prepare for vaginal delivery at 38 weeks' gestation

few_shot.explanation:
This patient is HIV positive and has a high viral load. The risk of vertical transmission of HIV is highest in patients with high viral loads. The goal of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in pregnancy is to reduce the maternal viral load to undetectable levels, thereby reducing the risk of vertical transmission. The current recommendation is to start combination ART (cART) as soon as an HIV diagnosis is made, regardless of CD4 count. In patients diagnosed late in pregnancy, as in this patient, cART should be started immediately. If the viral load is >1000 copies/mL near the time of delivery, a scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks' gestation is recommended to prevent vertical transmission during labor and delivery.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question:
A 9-month-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother for a routine health checkup. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. He is up to date on all vaccines and is meeting all developmental milestones. He was breastfed for the first 3 months and then switched to cow’s milk and about two months ago she started giving him fruits and vegetables. Family history is noncontributory. Today, his heart rate is 120/min, respiratory rate is 40/min, blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg, and temperature of 37.0°C (98.6°F). On examination, he has a heartbeat with a regular rate and rhythm and his lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Generally, the boy looks pale. His weight and height fall within the expected range. A complete blood count (CBC) shows the following:
Hemoglobin (Hb): 9.1 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV): 65 fL
Total iron binding capacity (TIBC): 550 μg/dL
Serum iron: 45 µg/dL
Serum lead: < 5 µg/dL
What is the best treatment for this patient?

few_shot.question:
A 5-month-old male presents to the pediatrician with his mother for a well visit. The patient was born at 35 weeks gestation to a 30-year-old gravida 2 via vaginal delivery. The pregnancy and labor were uncomplicated. The patient required no resuscitation after delivery and was discharged from the hospital on day two of life. His mother now reports that the patient has been exclusively breastfed since birth, and she says that feedings have been going well, and that the patient appears satisfied afterwards. The patient feeds for 30 minutes every two hours and urinates 8-10 times per day. The patient’s mother reports that she eats a varied diet that includes animal products, but she worries that the patient is not meeting his nutritional needs with breastmilk alone. The patient’s height and weight at birth were in the 15th and 20th percentile, respectively. His height and weight are now in the 20th and 25th percentile, respectively. His temperature is 98.1°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 58/46 mmHg, pulse is 128/min, and respirations are 34/min. On physical exam, the patient appears well-developed and well-nourished. He has mild conjunctival pallor.

Which of the following is the most appropriate guidance regarding this patient’s nutritional needs?

answer_choices.A: Add cow's milk to his diet
answer_choices.B: Add pureed foods to his diet
answer_choices.D: Supplement his diet with iron and vitamin D

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of exclusive breastfeeding and mild conjunctival pallor are concerning for iron deficiency anemia. Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency in children. Although human milk is the best source of nutrition for infants, it is low in iron. Full-term infants are born with iron stores that last for the first 4 months of life. After this time, breastfed infants require additional sources of iron. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that exclusively breastfed infants begin receiving 1 mg/kg/day of an oral iron supplement by age 4 months. Iron supplementation should continue until iron-rich complementary foods (eg, iron-fortified cereals, pureed meats) have been introduced.

In addition to iron, breastfed infants require vitamin D supplementation. Human milk contains only trace amounts of vitamin D. Therefore, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that all breastfed infants begin receiving 400 IU/day of oral vitamin D supplementation within the first few days of life.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
An 11-year-old boy presents to his pediatrician for a wellness checkup. The child is an immigrant, and this is his first visit. The patient is in the 99th percentile for height and 50th percentile for weight. The child is struggling in school, and basic cognitive testing suggests he is moderately mentally disabled. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 107/68 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Laboratory values are obtained and shown below.

Hemoglobin: 9 g/dL
Hematocrit: 30%
MCV: 110 fL
Leukocyte count: 5,500/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 192,000/mm^3

Serum:
Na+: 140 mEq/L
Cl-: 101 mEq/L
K+: 4.4 mEq/L
HCO3-: 24 mEq/L
BUN: 20 mg/dL
Glucose: 90 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.0 mg/dL
Ca2+: 10.0 mg/dL
AST: 12 U/L
ALT: 10 U/L

The patient is started on vitamin B9 and B12. Which of the following interventions could decrease the risk for cardiac complications the most in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's tall stature, intellectual disability, and macrocytic anemia are suggestive of homocystinuria, an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by deficiency of cystathionine beta-synthase. This enzyme normally converts homocysteine to cystathionine in the methionine salvage pathway. When this enzyme is deficient, homocysteine accumulates and is instead converted back to methionine. This leads to elevated levels of both methionine and homocysteine, which can be detected in the urine.

Patients with homocystinuria are at risk for both thrombotic and atherogenic complications, including myocardial infarction and stroke, due to the hypercoagulable state induced by homocysteine. Therefore, reducing homocysteine levels is a priority in these patients.

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is a cofactor for cystathionine beta-synthase, and supplementation can reduce homocysteine levels in some patients with homocystinuria. This can help to decrease the risk of cardiac complications.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 9-month-old male infant is brought to his pediatrician by his mother with lethargy and decreased oral intake for one day. His mother also mentions that he did not sleep well the previous night. A review of the medical record reveals several missed appointments and that the boy was born at 36 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. At the clinic, his temperature is 37.2ºC (99.0ºF), pulse rate is 140/minute, respirations are 44/minute, and blood pressure is 92/60 mm Hg. On physical exam the infant is awake but irritable and the rest of the physical is within normal limits for his age. On ophthalmologic examination, there are multiple retinal hemorrhages that extend to the periphery in both eyes. Which of the following investigations is most likely to be helpful in the management of the infant?
few_shot.explanation:
The presence of retinal hemorrhages in an infant, especially when they extend to the periphery, is highly suggestive of nonaccidental trauma (child abuse), specifically abusive head trauma (formerly known as shaken baby syndrome). This is a form of child abuse that occurs when a child is violently shaken, leading to acceleration-deceleration forces that cause shearing of the bridging veins and subdural hemorrhages. The violent shaking can also cause retinal hemorrhages. The most common presenting symptoms are nonspecific and include vomiting, poor feeding, seizures, and altered mental status, as seen in this patient.

The most appropriate next step in management is to obtain a noncontrast head CT to evaluate for subdural hematomas, cerebral edema, and other intracranial injuries. If abusive head trauma is confirmed, a skeletal survey should also be obtained to evaluate for additional signs of abuse, such as metaphyseal fractures (corner or bucket-handle fractures).

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician for generalized fatigue and multiple episodes of abdominal pain and vomiting for the past week. His last bowel movement was 4 days ago. He has been having behavioral problems at home for the past few weeks as well. He can walk up stairs with support and build a tower of 3 blocks. He cannot use a fork. He does not follow simple instructions and speaks in single words. His family emigrated from Bangladesh 6 months ago. He is at the 40th percentile for height and weight. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 115/min, and blood pressure is 84/45 mm Hg. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and gingival hyperpigmentation. His hemoglobin concentration is 10.1 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume is 68 μm3, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin is 24.5 pg/cell. The patient is most likely going to benefit from administration of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This child's symptoms of abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, and behavioral changes, along with the physical examination findings of pallor and gingival hyperpigmentation, are suggestive of lead poisoning. Lead poisoning is a common problem in children, especially those living in older homes with lead-based paint or those who have recently emigrated from countries with less strict regulations on lead. The child's microcytic anemia is also consistent with lead poisoning, as lead inhibits several enzymes in the heme synthesis pathway, leading to anemia.

The treatment for lead poisoning is chelation therapy, which involves the use of agents that bind to lead in the body and promote its excretion. Succimer and calcium disodium edetate are two such agents that are commonly used.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after losing consciousness. His mother states that he was running with other kids in the park when he suddenly fell down and became unresponsive for less than 1 minute. He has not had any immunizations due to their religious beliefs. The parents report that he plays with other children, but tires easily. He has had difficulty feeding, but there was no follow-up with a pediatrician. The heart rate was 120/min and the oxygen saturation was 91%. The height is in the 40th percentile and the weight is in the 50th percentile. On examination, the boy is crying with perioral cyanosis. The lung sounds are clear. S-1 is normal and there is a single S-2. A grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur is appreciated at the left upper sternal border. When the child squats, the murmur is intensified and the cyanosis improves. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.B: Morphine, oxygen, IV fluids, and beta blockers

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of squatting during play, perioral cyanosis, and single S2 on cardiac examination is suggestive of tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). TOF is the most common cause of cyanotic congenital heart disease beyond the neonatal period. It consists of a ventricular septal defect, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO), overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. The degree of RVOTO determines the severity of the disease. Patients with severe RVOTO have diminished pulmonary blood flow and present with early cyanosis (blue babies). Those with mild RVOTO may not have cyanosis at rest but can develop it during episodes of increased RVOTO (eg, crying, feeding, defecation). These "tet spells" are characterized by irritability, increased cyanosis, and possible syncope. They are thought to be due to infundibular spasm, which worsens the RVOTO and results in decreased pulmonary blood flow and increased right-to-left shunting across the ventricular septal defect.

Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance, which decreases right-to-left shunting and improves cyanosis. The murmur of TOF is due to RVOTO and not the ventricular septal defect; therefore, maneuvers that decrease right-to-left shunting (eg, squatting) increase the intensity of the murmur.

Treatment of a tet spell involves placing the child in the knee-chest position and administering oxygen. If the spell persists, morphine (to relieve infundibular spasm), IV fluids (to increase preload), and beta blockers (to decrease infundibular spasm) should be administered.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain. She states that she was walking up the stairs at work when she felt sudden and severe abdominal pain followed by nausea and vomiting. Her past medical history is non-contributory and she is not currently taking any medications. Her temperature is 99.7°F (37.6°C), blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable for an absence of abdominal tenderness, a left adnexal mass, and left adnexal tenderness. A transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates free fluid surrounding the ovary with edema and the presence of doppler flow. A urinary pregnancy test is negative. The patient's symptoms persisted after ibuprofen and acetaminophen. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for evaluation of lower abdominal pain. She endorses 6 hours of progressively worsening pain. She denies any significant past medical history and her physical examination is positive for non-specific, diffuse pelvic discomfort. She denies the possibility of pregnancy given her consistent use of condoms with her partner. The vital signs are: blood pressure, 111/68 mm Hg; pulse, 71/min; and respiratory rate, 15/min. She is afebrile. Which of the following is the next best step in her management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient presents with acute lower abdominal pain, which is concerning for an ectopic pregnancy. Ectopic pregnancy is a life-threatening condition that occurs when a fertilized egg implants outside of the uterus, most commonly in the fallopian tubes. Risk factors include prior ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery, history of sexually transmitted infections, and smoking. However, up to 50% of women with ectopic pregnancies have no identifiable risk factors. Therefore, all women of reproductive age presenting with abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding should receive a serum pregnancy test, regardless of reported contraceptive use. This is because no contraceptive method is 100% effective, and contraceptive failures can and do occur.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 25-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-hour history of sudden severe lower abdominal pain. The pain started shortly after having sexual intercourse. The pain is worse with movement and urination. The patient had several urinary tract infections as a child. She is sexually active with her boyfriend and uses condoms inconsistently. She cannot remember when her last menstrual period was. She appears uncomfortable and pale. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows a palpable, tender right adnexal mass. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dL and her hematocrit is 30%. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 5 x 3-cm right ovarian sac-like structure with surrounding echogenic fluid around the structure and the uterus. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden-onset, severe lower abdominal pain, adnexal mass, and hypotension are concerning for ovarian torsion. Ovarian torsion occurs when the ovary twists around its vascular pedicle, leading to venous obstruction, edema, and eventually arterial obstruction and infarction if not promptly treated. Risk factors include ovarian masses (eg, cysts, tumors) and ovarian hyperstimulation. The pain is typically sudden in onset, severe, and unilateral. Nausea and vomiting are common. On examination, an adnexal mass may be palpated. Ultrasonography often reveals an enlarged ovary with peripheral follicles and may show decreased or absent blood flow on Doppler. However, normal flow does not rule out the diagnosis as it may be present in early or intermittent torsion. Management of ovarian torsion involves prompt surgical intervention to untwist the ovary and preserve function. If the ovary is necrotic, oophorectomy is performed.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old woman with a history of asthma presents to the emergency room with persistent gnawing left lower quadrant abdominal pain. She first noticed the pain several hours ago and gets mild relief with ibuprofen. She has not traveled recently, tried any new foods or medications, or been exposed to sick contacts. She is sexually active with her boyfriend and admits that she has had multiple partners in the last year. Her temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure 77/45 mmHg, pulse is 121/min, and respirations are 14/min. On exam, she appears uncomfortable and diaphoretic. She has left lower quadrant tenderness to palpation, and her genitourinary exam is normal. Her urinalysis is negative and her pregnancy test is positive. Which of the following would be the appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal pain, hypotension, and tachycardia in the setting of a positive pregnancy test is concerning for a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Ectopic pregnancy occurs when the fertilized ovum implants outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube. Risk factors include prior ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery, history of sexually transmitted infections, and smoking. Patients typically present 6-8 weeks after their last menstrual period with abdominal pain and/or vaginal bleeding. However, presentation can be variable, and the classic triad of abdominal pain, delayed menses, and vaginal bleeding is seen in fewer than 50% of cases. If rupture occurs, patients can present with signs of hemodynamic instability secondary to intraperitoneal hemorrhage, as seen in this patient.

In a hemodynamically stable patient, the diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy can be confirmed with a transvaginal ultrasound. However, in a patient with suspected rupture and hemodynamic instability, as in this patient, an immediate surgical consult for exploratory laparoscopy or laparotomy is indicated.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her roommate with severe right lower quadrant pain for the last 8 hours. The pain is progressively getting worse and is associated with vomiting. When you ask the patient about her last menstrual period, she tells you that although she stopped keeping track of her cycle after undergoing surgical sterilization 1 year ago, she recalls bleeding yesterday. The physical examination reveals a hemodynamically stable patient with a pulse of 90/min, respiratory rate of 14/min, blood pressure of 125/70 mm Hg, and temperature of 37.0°C (98.6°F). The abdomen is tender to touch (more tender in the lower quadrants), and tenderness at McBurney's point is absent. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe right lower quadrant pain and vomiting is concerning for ectopic pregnancy. Although she has had a tubal ligation, this procedure is not 100% effective, and the failure rate is approximately 1%-2% over 10 years. Ectopic pregnancy is a leading cause of maternal mortality in the first trimester and should be considered in all women of reproductive age who present with abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding. The first step in the evaluation of possible ectopic pregnancy is a urine or serum pregnancy test. If the test is positive, a transvaginal ultrasound should be performed to visualize the location of the pregnancy.

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman with a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis and severe anemia of chronic disease presents to the emergency department for nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain that started this morning. She has been unable to tolerate oral intake during this time. Her blood pressure is 107/58 mmHg, pulse is 127/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for left lower quadrant abdominal pain upon palpation. A urine pregnancy test is positive, and a serum beta-hCG is 1,110 mIU/mL. A transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates no free fluid and is unable to identify an intrauterine pregnancy. The patient states that she intends to have children in the future. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is concerning for an ectopic pregnancy. The diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy is made by a combination of clinical symptoms, serial beta-hCG measurements, and ultrasound findings. In a normal pregnancy, the beta-hCG level doubles approximately every 48 hours. If the beta-hCG level is above the discriminatory zone (1500-2000 mIU/mL) and no intrauterine pregnancy is visualized on transvaginal ultrasound, an ectopic pregnancy is likely. However, if the beta-hCG level is below the discriminatory zone, as in this patient, the absence of an intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound does not definitively indicate an ectopic pregnancy. Instead, the pregnancy may be too early to visualize on ultrasound (ie, early gestational age), or it may be a failing intrauterine pregnancy. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is to repeat the beta-hCG level in 48 hours. If the beta-hCG level increases appropriately (doubles), an intrauterine pregnancy is likely, and a follow-up ultrasound may show a gestational sac. If the beta-hCG level plateaus or decreases, a failing intrauterine pregnancy or ectopic pregnancy is likely.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 49-year-old woman comes to the physician for a scheduled colposcopy. Two weeks ago, she had a routine Pap smear that showed atypical squamous cells. Colposcopy shows an area of white discoloration of the cervix with application of acetic acid solution. Biopsy of this area shows carcinoma-in-situ. few_shot.question: A 34-year-old G2P2 undergoes colposcopy due to high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia detected on a Pap smear. Her 2 previous Pap smears showed low-grade intraepithelial neoplasia. She has had 2 sexual partners in her life, and her husband has been her only sexual partner for the last 10 years. She had her sexual debut at 16 years of age. She had her first pregnancy at 26 years of age. She uses oral contraceptives for birth control. Her medical history is significant for right ovary resection due to a large follicular cyst and cocaine abuse for which she completed a rehabilitation program. Colposcopy reveals an acetowhite lesion with distorted vascularity at 4 o’clock. A directed biopsy shows the following on histologic evaluation. Which of the following factors present in this patient is a risk factor for the detected condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's biopsy shows cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), which is characterized by immature, disorganized cells in the cervical epithelium. CIN is a precursor to invasive cervical cancer and is caused by high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. HPV is a sexually transmitted infection, and the risk of acquiring HPV and developing CIN is increased with certain sexual behaviors, including early age of sexual debut (eg, <18 years of age). Other risk factors for CIN include multiple sexual partners, history of other sexually transmitted infections, and immunosuppression.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 39-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist for a routine visit. She has no complaints during this visit. She had an abnormal pap test 6 years ago that showed atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance. The sample was negative for human papillomavirus. On her follow-up Pap test 3 years later, there was no abnormality. The latest pap test results show atypical glandular cells with reactive changes in the cervical epithelium. The gynecologist decides to perform a colposcopy, and some changes are noted in this study of the cervical epithelium. The biopsy shows dysplastic changes in the epithelial cells. Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.C: Follow-up pap smear in one year

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's pap test results show atypical glandular cells, which is a high-risk finding. Atypical glandular cells can be a sign of adenocarcinoma in situ or invasive adenocarcinoma of the cervix or endometrium. The patient's colposcopy and biopsy results show dysplastic changes in the epithelial cells, which is concerning for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) or adenocarcinoma in situ. 

The next best step in the management of this patient is cold knife conization. This procedure involves the removal of a cone-shaped piece of tissue from the cervix, which includes the transformation zone where most cervical cancers arise. The tissue is then examined under a microscope to check for abnormal cells. Cold knife conization is preferred over loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) in this case because it provides a more intact specimen for histologic evaluation, which is important for determining the extent of disease and planning further treatment.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 34-year-old G3P2 undergoes colposcopy at 15 weeks gestation due to high-grade intraepithelial lesion detected on a Pap smear. She has no history of the gynecologic disease and had normal Pap smear results prior to the current pregnancy. The pelvic examination does not reveal any cervical lesions. Colposcopy shows a non-deformed cervix with a well-visualized transformation zone. Application of acetic acid reveals an area of acetowhite epithelium 2 cm in the largest diameter located at 6 o’clock with sharp irregular borders. A punch biopsy shows irregularly shaped tongues of pleomorphic squamous epithelium cells invading the stroma to a depth of 2 mm. Which of the following describes the proper management strategy for this patient?

answer_choices.B: Terminate the pregnancy and perform a radical hysterectomy

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) on Pap smear and a colposcopy showing an acetowhite lesion with sharp irregular borders. The punch biopsy shows invasion of the stroma by pleomorphic squamous epithelial cells, which is consistent with cervical cancer. The next step in management is to perform a diagnostic conization to determine the extent of the disease. This procedure involves removing a cone-shaped piece of tissue from the cervix and cervical canal. The tissue is then examined under a microscope to look for abnormal cells. If the cancer is found to be confined to the cervix, the patient can be managed conservatively with close observation until 34 weeks of gestation, at which time a cesarean hysterectomy can be performed. If the cancer has spread beyond the cervix, the patient may need to undergo a radical hysterectomy, which involves removal of the uterus, cervix, part of the vagina, and lymph nodes in the pelvis. This would require termination of the pregnancy.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old G2P2 presents to her gynecologist to discuss the results of her diagnostic tests. She has no  current complaints or concurrent diseases. She underwent a tubal ligation after her last pregnancy. Her last Pap smear showed a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion and a reflex HPV test was positive. answer_choices.D: Repeat cytology and HPV co-testing in 6 months

This patient's high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) on Pap smear and positive high-risk HPV test are concerning for high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN 2 or 3). However, her biopsy results show only CIN 1, which is a low-grade lesion. This discrepancy between the cytology and histology results is concerning and could be due to a sampling error during colposcopy and biopsy. Therefore, the next step in management should be a diagnostic excisional procedure (eg, loop electrosurgical excision procedure, cold knife conization) to evaluate for CIN 2 or 3 or invasive cancer.

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old post-menopausal woman comes to the physician because of intermittent, bloody post-coital vaginal discharge for the past month. She does not have pain with intercourse. Eleven years ago, she had LSIL on a routine Pap smear and testing for high-risk HPV strains was positive. Colposcopy showed CIN 1. She has not returned for follow-up Pap smears since then. She is sexually active with her husband only, and they do not use condoms. She has smoked half a pack of cigarettes per day for the past 25 years and does not drink alcohol. On speculum exam, a 1.4 cm, erythematous exophytic mass with ulceration is noted on the posterior wall of the upper third of the vagina. Which of the following is the most probable histopathology of this mass?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of high-risk HPV infection, smoking, and lack of follow-up Pap smears are all risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the vagina. SCC is the most common type of vaginal cancer, accounting for 85% of all primary vaginal malignancies. It is most common in postmenopausal women and typically presents with post-coital bleeding. On examination, SCC can appear as an exophytic mass, an ulcerative lesion, or a diffuse, infiltrative process.

question: A 68-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of worsening fatigue and weight loss. He is especially concerned about a recent episode in which he noticed a blurring of his vision and headache; he also notes that his “memory is not as good as it used to be,” which his wife confirms. Physical exam is notable only for pallor and general weakness. Laboratory studies reveal anemia as well as an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) reveals a sharp, narrow spike of monoclonal IgM; serum IgM concentration is 6.3 g/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?

answer_choices.A: IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS)

few_shot.question: A 78-year-old man presents to the emergency department because of confusion that started 2 hours ago. The patient’s daughter says that he has had blurred vision for several days. His right leg became weak 10 days ago, and he couldn’t walk for a few days before recovering. He was diagnosed with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance 2 years ago. His temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F), pulse is 75/min, respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 125/70 mm Hg. He also has gingival bleeding. Cervical lymphadenopathy is palpated on physical exam. Both the liver and spleen are palpated 5 cm below the costal margins. The serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation is shown. Urine electrophoresis shows no abnormalities. A skeletal survey shows no abnormalities. Which of the following best explains these findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's findings of hyperviscosity syndrome (eg, blurred vision, confusion), peripheral neuropathy, and serum protein electrophoresis with a monoclonal spike in the gamma region are suggestive of Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia (WM). WM is a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by bone marrow infiltration with lymphoplasmacytic cells and excessive production of IgM. The IgM protein is large and can lead to increased serum viscosity (hyperviscosity syndrome), which can cause neurologic symptoms (eg, confusion, visual disturbances, headache, dizziness), bleeding (eg, gingival bleeding), and less commonly, symptoms of peripheral neuropathy (eg, distal limb weakness). Hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy can also be seen in WM, unlike in multiple myeloma.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of headache and worsening vision. Ophthalmologic examination shows a visual acuity of 20/120 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left eye. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 14.2 g/dL and total serum calcium of 9.9 mg/dL. A photomicrograph of a peripheral blood smear is shown. Serum electrophoresis shows increased concentration of a pentameric immunoglobulin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of headache and vision changes, along with the finding of a pentameric immunoglobulin (IgM) on serum electrophoresis, are suggestive of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (WM). WM is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma characterized by bone marrow infiltration with lymphoplasmacytic cells, as well as IgM monoclonal gammopathy. The IgM protein can lead to hyperviscosity syndrome, which can cause a variety of neurologic and ophthalmologic symptoms. These can include headache, dizziness, tinnitus, blurred or double vision, epistaxis, and even stupor or coma in severe cases. Other findings in WM can include hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and cytopenias.

The peripheral blood smear in this patient shows a rouleaux formation, which is a common finding in conditions with high serum protein concentration such as WM. Rouleaux formation occurs when red blood cells stack together in a column ("stack of coins") due to the presence of abnormal proteins.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: An 80-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of a decreasing level of consciousness. He had blurred vision for several days. Two weeks ago, he had transient numbness in the right arm for 3 days. He was diagnosed with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance 2 years ago. He is not fully alert. His temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F), pulse is 75/min, respiratory rate is 13/min, and blood pressure is 125/70 mm Hg. He has gingival bleeding. Cervical lymphadenopathy is noted on palpation. Both the liver and spleen are palpated 6 cm below the costal margins. Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation is shown. Urine electrophoresis shows no abnormalities. A skeletal survey shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of blurred vision, altered mental status, and gingival bleeding, along with the physical examination findings of hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, are suggestive of hyperviscosity syndrome. This is a medical emergency that can occur in patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM), a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma that produces monoclonal IgM. The large size of the IgM molecule and its propensity to form autoantibodies can lead to hyperviscosity of the blood, which can cause a variety of symptoms, including those seen in this patient. The diagnosis of WM is supported by the serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, which shows a large monoclonal spike in the gamma region, indicating a high level of IgM.

The treatment of hyperviscosity syndrome involves plasmapheresis to remove the excess IgM from the blood. This can rapidly improve symptoms and prevent further complications. Other treatments for WM, such as chemotherapy, can be considered once the patient is stabilized.

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for a routine check-up. Physical examination demonstrates asymmetric peripheral neuropathy in her feet. The patient has no previous relevant history and denies any symptoms of diabetes. Routine blood work shows normal results, and she is referred to a hematologist. Subsequent serum protein electrophoresis demonstrates a slightly elevated gamma globulin level, and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance is diagnosed. Which of the following diseases is most likely to develop over the course of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is a premalignant plasma cell disorder characterized by the presence of a serum monoclonal protein (M protein) at a concentration <3 g/dL, <10% clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow, and the absence of end-organ damage (eg, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions). MGUS is usually an incidental finding on serum protein electrophoresis performed for unrelated reasons. The prevalence of MGUS increases with age, and it is found in over 3% of individuals >50 years of age. MGUS is associated with a small risk of progression to multiple myeloma or, less commonly, Waldenström macroglobulinemia or amyloidosis. Therefore, patients with MGUS should be followed with periodic serum protein electrophoresis to monitor for progression.

So, the answer is [B].

question:
A 78-year-old woman presents to the office for an annual health check-up with her family physician accompanied by her daughter. She has no complaints during this visit but her daughter states that she is having difficulty locating objects such as the television remote, car keys, and her purse. Her medical history is significant for Alzheimer’s dementia, coronary artery disease, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, congestive heart failure, osteoarthritis and centrilobular emphysema. The patient takes memantine, atorvastatin, metformin, levothyroxine, lisinopril, aspirin, albuterol, and ipratropium. The patient’s vitals are within normal limits today. Physical exam reveals an elderly female in no acute distress, oriented to person, place and year, but not to month or day of the week. She has a 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border along with an S3 gallop. There are mild crackles at the lung bases. The remainder of the exam is normal. A previous urine culture reports growth of > 100,000 CFU of Enterobacter. Urinalysis findings are offered below:
Leukocyte esterase  positive
WBCs 50-100 cell/HPF
Nitrites positive
RBCs 2 cell/HPF
Epithelial cells 2 cell/HPF
Urine pH 5.7
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

few_shot.question:
A 66-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of fever, chills, night sweats, and progressive shortness of breath for 1 week. She also reports generalized fatigue and nausea. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism. Current medications include metformin, sitagliptin, and levothyroxine. She appears ill. Her temperature is 38.7° (101.7°F), pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and small nontender hemorrhagic macules over her palms and soles. Crackles are heard at both lung bases. A grade 2/6 mid-diastolic murmur is heard best at the third left intercostal space and is accentuated by leaning forward. The spleen is palpated 1–2 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL
Leukocyte count 18,300/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/h
Urine
Protein 1+
Blood 2+
RBCs 20-30/hpf
WBCs 0-2/hpf
An echocardiography shows multiple vegetations on the aortic valve. Blood cultures grow S. gallolyticus. She is treated with ampicillin and gentamicin for 2 weeks and her symptoms resolve. A repeat echocardiography at 3 weeks shows mild aortic regurgitation with no vegetations. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"

answer_choices.D: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

few_shot.explanation:
Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis) bacteremia or endocarditis is strongly associated with colonic neoplasia (eg, colon cancer, adenomatous polyps). The exact mechanism of this association is not known, but it is hypothesized that the bacteria colonize the neoplastic colonic tissue and translocate into the bloodstream. Therefore, all patients with S. gallolyticus bacteremia or endocarditis should undergo colonoscopy to screen for colonic neoplasia.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department for evaluation of fever, chest pain, and a cough that has produced a moderate amount of greenish-yellow sputum for the past 2 days. During this period, she has had severe malaise, chills, and difficulty breathing. Her past medical history is significant for hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and type 2 diabetes, for which she takes lisinopril, atorvastatin, and metformin. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. Her vital signs show her temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 33/min, and blood pressure is 143/88 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Crackles are heard on auscultation of the right upper lobe. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 12,300/mm3, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/h, and urea nitrogen of 15 mg/dL. A chest X-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to manage this patient’s symptoms?

answer_choices.A: ICU admission and administration of ampicillin-sulbactam and levofloxacin
answer_choices.B: Inpatient treatment with azithromycin and ceftriaxone
answer_choices.C: Inpatient treatment with cefepime, azithromycin, and gentamicin
answer_choices.D: Inpatient treatment with cefepime, azithromycin, and gentamicin

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, cough productive of purulent sputum, and focal lung findings are consistent with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). The CURB-65 severity score (Confusion, Urea nitrogen >7 mmol/L [>20 mg/dL], Respiratory rate ≥30/min, low systolic [<90 mm Hg] or diastolic [≤60 mm Hg] Blood pressure, age ≥65 years) is used to determine the appropriate level of care for patients with CAP. This patient has 1 point for age ≥65 years, indicating that she can be treated as an inpatient. The recommended empiric treatment for inpatient, non-ICU treatment of CAP is a combination of a β-lactam (eg, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime) and a macrolide (eg, azithromycin) or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy (eg, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin). The β-lactam provides reliable coverage for Streptococcus pneumoniae, and the macrolide or fluoroquinolone covers atypical pathogens (eg, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Legionella species).

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 71-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of fatigue and a cough productive of a blood-tinged phlegm. Over the past month, he has had a 5.0-kg (11-lb) weight loss. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Eight months ago, he underwent a kidney transplantation. The patient does not smoke. His current medications include lisinopril, insulin, prednisone, and mycophenolate mofetil. His temperature is 38.9°C (102.1°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 152/92 mm Hg. Rhonchi are heard at the right lower lobe of the lung on auscultation. There is a small ulceration on the left forearm. An x-ray of the chest shows a right lung mass with lobar consolidation. Antibiotic therapy with levofloxacin is started. Three days later, the patient has a seizure and difficulty coordinating movements with his left hand. An MRI of the brain shows an intraparenchymal lesion with peripheral ring enhancement. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage yields weakly acid-fast, gram-positive bacteria with branching, filamentous shapes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of kidney transplantation, chronic immunosuppressive therapy, and the presence of a skin ulcer, lung mass, and brain abscess suggest disseminated infection with Nocardia. Nocardia is a weakly acid-fast, gram-positive bacterium found in soil worldwide. It is a common cause of infection in immunocompromised patients, especially those with defects in cell-mediated immunity (eg, organ transplant recipients, patients with HIV/AIDS). The organism typically gains entry through inhalation or direct inoculation through the skin, and can disseminate to any organ, most commonly the lungs, skin, and brain. Pulmonary nocardiosis can present with cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, and constitutional symptoms, and can resemble tuberculosis or lung cancer on imaging. Cutaneous nocardiosis can present with cellulitis, abscess, or ulceration. Central nervous system involvement can manifest with headache, altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits.

The treatment of choice for nocardiosis is sulfonamide antibiotics, such as trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX). Alternative regimens (eg, for sulfa-allergic patients) include amikacin, imipenem, or a third-generation cephalosporin (eg, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime).

So, the answer is [C].
