Six skin snip biopsies are taken from the pelvic girdle, buttocks, and thigh, and are then incubated in saline. After 24 hours, microscopic examination shows motile microfilariae. This patient's pruritic rash, subcutaneous nodules, and visual symptoms, along with the finding of microfilariae on skin snip biopsy, are suggestive of onchocerciasis (river blindness). Onchocerciasis is caused by the nematode Onchocerca volvulus and is transmitted through the bite of the blackfly (Simulium species). The disease is endemic in many parts of Africa, including Nigeria.

The adult worms live in subcutaneous nodules, where they produce microfilariae that migrate to the skin and eyes. The microfilariae cause intense pruritus and skin changes, including depigmentation (leopard skin) and loss of elasticity. Ocular involvement can lead to blindness.

Tinea corporis is often spread by direct skin-to-skin contact with an infected human or animal, or indirectly through contact with contaminated objects (eg, towels, clothing, bedding). few_shot.question: A 29-year-old man presents to his primary care provider after complaining of a rash on his penis. HPV types 6 and 11 are responsible for 90% of genital warts. The warts are usually asymptomatic, although they may cause itching, burning, or tenderness. They can be found on the penis, vulva, vagina, cervix, perineum, perianal skin, and within the anus. The warts are usually skin-colored, discrete, soft, and papular, and they may coalesce into a cauliflower-like mass.

Treatment of genital warts depends on the preferences of the patient and the provider, the size and location of the lesions, and the experience of the provider. Options include patient-applied treatments (eg, imiquimod, podofilox) and provider-administered treatments (eg, cryotherapy, trichloroacetic acid, surgical removal). Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen is a provider-administered treatment that is safe, well-tolerated, and does not require local anesthesia. It is the preferred treatment for small, external warts and can be used for vaginal and anal warts. It is not recommended for larger warts (>2 cm) or extensive warts because it can cause significant local irritation.

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old man presents to his primary care provider for a routine examination. His heart has a regular rate and rhythm, and his lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Weight loss and abstaining from alcohol are discussed. He is receptive to weight loss measures including a low-salt, high-vegetable diet, but he is uninterested in cutting back on alcohol consumption. Which of the following best describes his stage of overcoming addiction?
few_shot.explanation:
The stages of overcoming addiction are precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance, and relapse. In the precontemplation stage, the individual is not yet acknowledging that there is a problem behavior that needs to be changed. In the contemplation stage, the individual is acknowledging that there is a problem but is not yet ready or sure of wanting to make a change. In the preparation/determination stage, the individual is getting ready to change. In the action/willpower stage, the individual is changing his or her behavior. In the maintenance stage, the individual is maintaining the behavior change. In the relapse stage, the individual returns to old behaviors and abandons the new changes.

In this case, the patient is receptive to weight loss measures but is uninterested in cutting back on alcohol consumption. This suggests that he is in the precontemplation stage of overcoming addiction with respect to his alcohol use.

question: A previously healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of depressed mood and fatigue. During this time, she has had a 5-kg (11-lb) weight gain. few_shot.question: A previously healthy 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of fatigue and daytime sleepiness. He is diagnosed with major depressive disorder and treatment with paroxetine is begun. The patient is at greatest risk for which of the following adverse effects?
few_shot.explanation:
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) such as paroxetine are first-line treatment for major depressive disorder. SSRIs block the reuptake of serotonin into presynaptic neurons, thereby increasing the availability of serotonin within the synaptic cleft. SSRIs are generally well tolerated, but they can cause a number of adverse effects. The most common adverse effects are gastrointestinal (eg, nausea, diarrhea) and neurologic (eg, headache, insomnia). However, SSRIs can also cause sexual dysfunction, including decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, delayed ejaculation, and anorgasmia. These effects are seen in up to 30%-40% of patients taking SSRIs and can be a reason for discontinuation of the medication.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 72-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with altered mental status. 90 minutes ago, the patient was found by a neighbor unarousable on the couch with multiple empty bottles of medication on the floor next to her. few_shot.question: A 60-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of altered mental status for 2 hours. She and her husband were at the grocery store when she suddenly could not remember why she was there or how she got there. She has not had any head trauma. She has a history of depression and migraines. She does not smoke and drinks a glass of wine each night with dinner. She takes fluoxetine daily. She appears distressed and anxious. Her vital signs are within normal limits. She is fully alert and oriented to self and place but not to time. Every few minutes she asks how she got to the emergency department. She is able to follow commands and sustain attention. She recalls 3/3 objects immediately and recalls 0/3 objects at 5 minutes. The remainder of the neurological exam shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden onset of anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories) and repetitive questioning is characteristic of transient global amnesia (TGA). TGA is a syndrome of unknown etiology that is most common in patients aged 50-80. Patients with TGA present with sudden onset of memory loss, often with repetitive questioning, in the absence of other cognitive or neurologic deficits. The memory impairment in TGA involves an inability to form new memories (anterograde amnesia) and, in some cases, an inability to recall past memories (retrograde amnesia). Episodes of TGA are time-limited, typically lasting less than 24 hours, and patients usually have no memory of the episode. TGA is a diagnosis of exclusion, and patients with suspected TGA should undergo neuroimaging and other studies to rule out other causes of amnesia (eg, stroke, seizure).

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police officers because he was acting strangely in public. The patient’s vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a disheveled male who is oriented to person, but not time or place. Neurologic examination shows nystagmus and severe gait ataxia. A T1/T2 MRI is performed and demonstrates evidence of damage to the mammillary bodies. The patient is given the appropriate treatment for recovering most of his cognitive functions. However, significant short-term memory deficits persist. The mammillary bodies, which are part of the limbic system and play a role in memory, are often affected in WE. If left untreated, WE can progress to Korsakoff syndrome (KS), which is characterized by significant memory loss and confabulation (making up stories). Although treatment with thiamine can prevent progression of WE to KS, once KS has developed, memory loss is often irreversible, as in this patient. Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her son for an evaluation of cognitive decline. Her son reports that she has had increased difficulty finding her way back home for the last several months, despite having lived in the same city for 40 years. He also reports that his mother has been unable to recall the names of her relatives and been increasingly forgetting important family gatherings such as her grandchildren's birthdays over the last few years. The patient has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her current medications include enalapril and metformin. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. She is confused and oriented only to person and place. She recalls 2 out of 3 words immediately and 1 out of 3 after 5 minutes. Her gait and muscle strength are normal. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Further evaluation is most likely to reveal which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's progressive memory loss, disorientation, and inability to recall words are suggestive of Alzheimer disease (AD), the most common cause of dementia in the elderly. AD is a neurodegenerative disorder that typically presents with insidious onset and gradual progression of cognitive decline. The earliest and most prominent symptom is memory impairment, which often manifests as forgetfulness for recent events and difficulty learning and retaining new information. As the disease progresses, cognitive impairment extends to language, visuospatial skills, and executive function. Patients may also develop psychiatric symptoms such as depression, apathy, social withdrawal, delusions, agitation, and, less commonly, hallucinations.

Neuroimaging in AD typically shows diffuse cerebral atrophy most prominently affecting the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus. This is in contrast to frontotemporal dementia, which shows focal atrophy of the frontal and/or temporal lobes, and vascular dementia, which shows multiple infarcts or hemorrhages.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her husband because of multiple falls and difficulty maintaining balance while standing or walking over the past year. During this period, she has had blurred vision and diplopia. Her husband has had difficulty understanding her speech for the past 3 months. She has become withdrawn and now refuses to go to social gatherings. Examination shows a broad-based gait and dysarthria. The visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. There is conjugate limitation of both eyes while looking down. Muscle tone is increased in bilateral upper extremities. Bradykinesia is present. Mental status examination shows apathy. She responds to questions with 1–2 words after a delay of several seconds. Grasp reflex is present. An MRI of the brain is most likely to show which of the following?

answer_choices.D: Enlarged ventricles with mild cortical atrophy

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of falls, difficulty maintaining balance, and blurred vision/diplopia is suggestive of a neurodegenerative disorder. The presence of a broad-based gait, dysarthria, and bradykinesia suggests parkinsonism. The presence of vertical gaze palsy (conjugate limitation of both eyes while looking down) and cognitive impairment (apathy, delayed responses) is suggestive of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). PSP is a neurodegenerative disorder that is often misdiagnosed as Parkinson disease. However, it can be distinguished by early falls (within the first year of disease onset), supranuclear vertical gaze palsy, and prominent cognitive dysfunction. The cognitive impairment seen in PSP is characterized by apathy, slowed thought processes, and personality changes, which can be mistaken for depression. PSP is also associated with axial rigidity and dysarthria, which can lead to dysphagia and resultant aspiration pneumonia, a common cause of death in these patients. On neuroimaging, PSP is associated with midbrain atrophy (the "hummingbird" sign on sagittal MRI) with an intact pons.

So, the answer is [B].

The son reports that when he returned home from work earlier in the day, he found his mother minimally responsive. She regained consciousness soon after his arrival and did not recall the event. The son also reports that for the past two years, his mother has had trouble remembering names and addresses. She still goes shopping on her own and cooks regularly. Her past medical history is notable for major depressive disorder, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension. She takes clomipramine, glyburide, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide. She recently saw her primary care provider who adjusted some of her medication dosages. Her temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 135/75 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 18/min. On examination, she is easily distractible with disorganized speech. She does not recognize her son and thinks that her intravenous line is a rope. She says she feels fine and would like to go home. Brain imaging would likely reveal which of the following?

answer_choices.B: Focal atrophy of the frontal and temporal cortices

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with delirium, a syndrome characterized by acute onset of fluctuating consciousness, attention, and cognition. Delirium is common in hospitalized and elderly patients and is often due to a medical condition, substance, or medication. In this patient, the recent adjustment of her medications, particularly clomipramine, is the likely cause. Clomipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant that can cause anticholinergic side effects, including delirium, particularly in the elderly. Brain imaging in delirium is typically normal unless there is an underlying structural cause (eg, stroke, hemorrhage).

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 29-year-old G1P0 woman is giving birth at 38 weeks gestation to a  boy via vaginal delivery. As soon as the infant is clear of the vagina, a congenital malformation of the abdomen is observed. The infant is removed from the delivery room for further evaluation. Visual inspection shows loops of intestine protruding out of his abdomen on the right side. His APGAR scores are 7 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes. His heart rate is 125/min, and his respirations are 45/min. All reflexes appear normal. There are no other visible defects. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: Wrap the intestines in a sterile bowel bag
answer_choices.B: Transfer the newborn to the NICU
answer_choices.D: Transfer the newborn for immediate surgery

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old woman presents to the emergency department in active labor. She has had no prenatal care and is unsure of the gestational age. Labor progresses rapidly and spontaneous vaginal delivery of a baby boy occurs 3 hours after presentation. On initial exam, the child is 1.9 kg (4.2 lb) with a small head and jaw. A sac-like structure containing intestine, as can be seen in the picture, protrudes from the abdominal wall. What complication is closely associated with this presentation?

answer_choices.D: Twisting of the bowel around itself

few_shot.explanation:
This baby has gastroschisis, a congenital defect of the anterior abdominal wall that leads to herniation of abdominal contents directly into the amniotic cavity. It is not covered by a membrane, unlike omphalocele, which is covered by peritoneum and amnion. Gastroschisis is usually to the right of the umbilical cord and is associated with young maternal age. It is not associated with chromosomal anomalies or other congenital malformations, unlike omphalocele, which is associated with cardiac defects and chromosomal anomalies (eg, trisomies 13, 18, 21).

However, gastroschisis is associated with intestinal atresia due to vascular compromise of the herniated bowel. This can lead to bowel necrosis and perforation, which can cause peritonitis and sepsis. Therefore, gastroschisis is a surgical emergency and requires immediate surgical repair after birth.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 2-day-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of irritability and vomiting for two hours. During this period, he has vomited bilious fluid three times. He has not yet passed stool. The mother has breastfed the newborn every two hours. He has wet two diapers during the last two days. He was born at term and was delivered at home. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. The mother had no prenatal care during pregnancy. The patient currently weighs 3100 g (6 lb 13 oz) and is 50 cm (19.6 in) in length. The newborn appears restless. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.14°F), pulse is 166/min, respirations are 60/min, and blood pressure is 60/45 mm Hg. There is no redness or warmth around the umbilical cord stump. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Bowel sounds are sparse. The abdomen is distended. Digital rectal examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the abdomen with contrast shows dilated small bowel loops, a microcolon, a mixture of gas and meconium located in the right lower quadrant. A nasogastric tube is placed and fluid resuscitation is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has bilious vomiting, abdominal distention, and failure to pass meconium, which are concerning for intestinal obstruction. The abdominal x-ray findings of dilated small bowel loops, a microcolon, and a mixture of gas and meconium located in the right lower quadrant are suggestive of meconium ileus, which is often the presenting sign of cystic fibrosis (CF) in the newborn period. Meconium ileus occurs due to abnormally thick and sticky meconium obstructing the terminal ileum. 

The initial management of uncomplicated meconium ileus (ie, no signs of bowel perforation such as pneumoperitoneum or peritonitis) is nonoperative and involves rehydration, electrolyte repletion, and relief of the intestinal obstruction. Hyperosmolar contrast enema with a water-soluble agent (eg, Gastrografin) is both diagnostic and therapeutic. The contrast draws water into the bowel lumen, which can help loosen the thick meconium and relieve the obstruction. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 4700-g (10.3-lb) male newborn is delivered at 37 weeks' gestation to a 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1. Apgar scores are 7 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The newborn appears pale. Temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 180/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Examination in the delivery room shows midfacial hypoplasia, infraorbital creases, and a large tongue. The right side of the body is larger than the left. Abdominal examination shows that the abdominal viscera protrudes through the abdominal wall at the umbilicus; the viscera are covered by the amniotic membrane and the peritoneum. The liver is palpated 2–3 cm below the right costal margin. Fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 60 mg/dL. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows enlarged kidneys bilaterally. In addition to surgical closure of the abdominal wall, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS), an overgrowth syndrome characterized by macrosomia, macroglossia, and abdominal wall defects (eg, omphalocele, umbilical hernia). Other findings can include ear creases/pits, neonatal hypoglycemia, and hemihyperplasia. BWS is associated with mutations of imprinted genes on chromosome 11p15.5. These genes regulate growth, and their alteration leads to disordered growth affecting the entire body or segments of the body.

Children with BWS are at increased risk for developing embryonal tumors, most commonly Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma. The risk is greatest in the first 8 years of life. Therefore, these patients should undergo screening with serial abdominal ultrasonography every 3 months until age 4, and measurement of serum alpha-fetoprotein every 6 weeks until age 4 to screen for hepatoblastoma.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 3-week-old newborn is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of 4 episodes of vomiting that occurred that morning. The parents report that the vomit was yellowish-green with no blood in it. The patient was born at 38 weeks' gestation via vaginal delivery and has generally been healthy. He has passed normal stools each day. There is no family history of serious illness. He appears irritable and pale. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 146/min, and blood pressure is 90/55 mm Hg. Examination shows a soft, mildly distended abdomen with no masses or organomegaly. A nasogastric tube is inserted and intravenous fluid resuscitation is initiated. An x-ray shows no gas distal to the duodenum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's bilious vomiting and x-ray findings of no gas distal to the duodenum are concerning for a malrotation with midgut volvulus. This is a surgical emergency that can lead to bowel ischemia and necrosis if not promptly diagnosed and treated. The most appropriate next step in management is an upper gastrointestinal contrast series, which can confirm the diagnosis and help guide further management.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 2-week-old neonate in the intensive care unit presents as severely ill. His mother says he was a bit irritated earlier this week, and his condition deteriorated quickly. It is apparent that he is in constant pain. He could not be fed easily and vomited three times since yesterday alone. The physical examination is remarkable for a distended abdomen and diminished bowel sounds. The neonate is sent for an abdominal/chest X-ray, which shows substantial intraluminal gas affecting most of the bowel. The neonate was born at 32 weeks of gestation by a normal vaginal delivery. Which of the following is the best next step for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of feeding intolerance, abdominal distention, and bilious vomiting in the setting of pneumatosis intestinalis on imaging is concerning for necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). NEC is the most common gastrointestinal emergency in neonates, especially in premature infants. It is characterized by diffuse patchy necrosis of the intestinal mucosa, leading to inflammation and bacterial invasion. The exact etiology is unknown, but it is thought to be multifactorial, with contributing factors including intestinal ischemia, abnormal bacterial colonization, and an exaggerated inflammatory response. 

The mainstay of treatment for NEC is bowel rest (ie, cessation of feedings), nasogastric decompression, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and supportive care. However, patients with signs of advanced disease (eg, pneumoperitoneum due to bowel perforation, clinical deterioration despite medical therapy) require surgical intervention. 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after he was found undressing himself outside in 110°F weather. The patient refuses to answer any questions as he suspects that his care team is spying on him. The patient recently started college and has presented to the emergency department once before for polysubstance intoxication. The patient attempts to assault a nurse, is restrained, and given diphenhydramine and haloperidol. When the patient is able to be examined, he is somnolent and non-responsive. His temperature is 104°F (40°C), blood pressure is 147/98 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. He does not comply with any commands, and it is not possible to freely manipulate his extremities due to rigidity. His mucous membranes are dry. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old man presents to the emergency department acutely confused. The patient was found down at a local construction site by his coworkers. The patient has a past medical history of a seizure disorder and schizophrenia and is currently taking haloperidol. He had recent surgery 2 months ago to remove an inflamed appendix. His temperature is 105°F (40.6°C), blood pressure is 120/84 mmHg, pulse is 150/min, respirations are 19/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a confused man who cannot answer questions. His clothes are drenched in sweat. He is not making purposeful movements with his extremities although no focal neurological deficits are clearly apparent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Exertional heat stroke is a life-threatening condition characterized by hyperthermia (core body temperature >40°C [104°F]) and central nervous system dysfunction (eg, altered mental status, seizure) that occurs in the setting of strenuous physical activity, often in a hot environment. It is most common in young, otherwise healthy individuals, such as athletes, military recruits, and outdoor laborers. The pathogenesis involves failure of thermoregulation due to excessive heat generation and/or inadequate heat dissipation. The latter can occur due to dehydration, high humidity, or, as in this patient, use of antipsychotic medications, which can inhibit central thermoregulation and impair sweating. 

Heat exhaustion is a milder form of heat illness that can develop after several days of exposure to high temperatures and inadequate or unbalanced replacement of fluids. It is the body's response to an excessive loss of the water and salt contained in sweat. Those most prone to heat exhaustion are elderly people, people with high blood pressure, and people working or exercising in a hot environment.

Malignant hyperthermia is a potentially fatal reaction to certain medications used during general anesthesia. In susceptible individuals, these medications can induce a drastic and uncontrolled increase in skeletal muscle oxidative metabolism, which overwhelms the body's capacity to supply oxygen, remove carbon dioxide, and regulate body temperature, eventually leading to circulatory collapse and death if not treated quickly.

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening neurological disorder most often caused by an adverse reaction to neuroleptic or antipsychotic drugs. Symptoms include high fever, confusion, rigid muscles, variable blood pressure, sweating, and fast heart rate. Complications may include rhabdomyolysis or high blood potassium.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after he was found locked in a bathroom at a local gas station. The patient states that he was being followed. The patient is unable to reveal additional medical history due to his condition. The patient’s sister is contacted and states that he has trouble taking care of himself and has observed him maintaining a dialogue with what appears to be no one on several occasions. The patient’s temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), pulse is 90/min, blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg, respirations are 14/min, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and BMI is 22 kg/m^2. The patient is medicated and transferred to the inpatient psychiatric unit. The patient is kept there for three weeks and maintained on his medication regimen. Towards the end of his hospitalization, the patient is grooming himself properly, denies hearing voices, and no longer believes he is being followed. The patient’s temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), pulse is 80/min, blood pressure is 130/75 mmHg, respirations are 15/min, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and BMI is 24 kg/m^2. Which of the following medications was this patient most likely started on?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with schizophrenia, which is characterized by hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized speech and behavior. The patient's symptoms improved with treatment, but he also gained weight. This is a common side effect of atypical antipsychotics, which include olanzapine, clozapine, risperidone, quetiapine, ziprasidone, and aripiprazole. Of these, olanzapine and clozapine are most likely to cause significant weight gain. Therefore, the patient was most likely started on olanzapine.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his roommates for aggressive and unusual behavior. His roommates state that he has been under a lot of stress lately from his final exams and has been more reclusive. They state that this evening he was very irritable and was yelling at his computer prior to breaking it, followed by him spending several hours at the gym. His temperature is 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 137/98 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 23/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for an irritable young man. Cardiopulmonary exam is notable for tachycardia and bilateral clear breath sounds. Neurological exam reveals dilated pupils. The patient is notably diaphoretic and speaks very rapidly during the physical exam and is aggressive. He is given haloperidol, diphenhydramine, and diazepam for sedation and placed in soft restraints. His symptoms resolved over the next 10 hours in the emergency department. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of agitation, aggression, tachycardia, and diaphoresis is suggestive of a sympathomimetic toxidrome. Sympathomimetic agents include amphetamines, cocaine, and synthetic cathinones ("bath salts"). Amphetamines are often used by students as study aids due to their ability to increase wakefulness and concentration. They are available in many forms, including prescription medications for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (eg, lisdexamfetamine, mixed amphetamine salts) that are commonly sold and used illicitly. Amphetamines increase the release and inhibit the reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin in the brain. Symptoms of amphetamine intoxication include severe agitation, combativeness, psychosis, delirium, myoclonus, and, rarely, seizures. Increased sympathetic outflow may lead to significantly increased blood pressure and heart rate. Increased muscular activity can lead to hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis. The most important aspect of management is sedation, usually with a benzodiazepine.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old man is brought into the emergency department as he was wandering the streets naked with a sword. The patient had to be forcibly restrained by police and is currently combative. Upon calming the patient and obtaining further history, the patient states that he is being pursued and that he needs to kill them all. The patient is given intramuscular (IM) haloperidol and diphenhydramine, and is admitted into the psychiatric ward. The patient has a past medical history of schizophrenia, obesity, anxiety, recurrent pneumonia, and depression. The patient is started on his home medication and is discharged 5 days later with prescriptions for multiple psychiatric medications including mood stabilizers and antidepressants. One week later, the patient is found by police standing outside in freezing weather. He is brought to the emergency department with a rectal temperature of 93.2°F (34°C). Resuscitation is started in the emergency department. Which of the following medications most likely exacerbated this patient's current presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypothermia is most likely due to his antipsychotic medication, fluphenazine. Antipsychotic medications are known to cause hypothermia by blocking dopamine in the hypothalamus, which disrupts temperature regulation. This can be exacerbated by exposure to cold weather. Other side effects of antipsychotic medications include extrapyramidal symptoms, hyperprolactinemia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

The other options, lithium, fluoxetine, and valproic acid, are not typically associated with hypothermia.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by the police after a motor vehicle accident. He was reportedly speeding in a residential area and collided with a tree. He was later found by police naked in the street, screaming "shoot me so the devil will leave". A review of his medical record is unremarkable. At the hospital, he continues to act agitated and bizarre. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), the blood pressure is 140/86 mm Hg, and the heart rate is 90/min. The physical exam is notable for agitation, pacing around the room, occasionally yelling at the staff to help him "kill the devil". An ocular exam is significant for mild horizontal nystagmus. The patient appears to be drooling and has some difficulty with coordination. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
Phencyclidine (PCP) is a recreational drug that is commonly smoked, ingested orally, or inhaled. It is a dissociative anesthetic that acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist in the brain. PCP intoxication can cause a variety of symptoms, including severe agitation, combativeness, psychosis, delirium, hallucinations, and seizures. Physical exam findings can include nystagmus, ataxia, and, in severe cases, hypertensive crisis and trauma from violent behavior. The most distinguishing feature of PCP intoxication is the presence of violent behavior and agitation in combination with nystagmus.

So, the answer is [C].

question:
A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with confusion. The patient lives in a nursing home and has Alzheimer dementia at baseline. His nurse noticed that he was more confused than usual and was somnolent for the past 12 hours. The patient’s nurse also noticed that he was soiling his diapers more frequently with copious amounts of urine. The patient has lost 15 pounds since his last physician appointment 3 weeks ago. Laboratory values are ordered as seen below.

few_shot.question:
A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with altered mental status. The patient is non-verbal at baseline, but his caretakers at the nursing home noticed he was particularly somnolent recently. The patient has a past medical history of diabetes and Alzheimer dementia. His temperature is 99.7°F (37.6°C), blood pressure is 157/98 mmHg, pulse is 150/min, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Laboratory values are obtained and shown below.

Hemoglobin: 9 g/dL
Hematocrit: 33%
Leukocyte count: 8,500/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 197,000/mm^3

Serum:
Na+: 139 mEq/L
Cl-: 102 mEq/L
K+: 4.3 mEq/L
HCO3-: 25 mEq/L
BUN: 37 mg/dL
Glucose: 99 mg/dL
Creatinine: 2.4 mg/dL
Ca2+: 12.2 mg/dL

The patient has lost 20 pounds over the past month. His parathyroid hormone is within normal limits, and his urinary calcium is increased. Physical exam demonstrates discomfort when the patient's lower back and extremities are palpated. Which of the following is the most accurate diagnostic test for this patient's underlying diagnosis?

answer_choices.C: Urine, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid cultures

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, and bone pain (manifested as tenderness to palpation of the lower back and extremities) is suggestive of multiple myeloma (MM). MM is a malignancy of plasma cells that primarily occurs in older adults. The hypercalcemia is due to increased osteoclastic bone resorption, and the renal insufficiency can be caused by hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, amyloidosis, and/or nephrotoxic light chain proteins. The anemia is due to replacement of normal bone marrow elements by malignant plasma cells and, in some cases, suppression of normal plasma cell development by cytokines.

The most accurate diagnostic test for MM is bone marrow biopsy, which typically shows >10% clonal plasma cells. Other diagnostic criteria for MM include evidence of end-organ damage (eg, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) and the presence of a monoclonal protein (M protein) in the serum or urine.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 67-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her caretakers for a change in behavior. The patient lives in a nursing home and was noted to have abnormal behavior, urinary incontinence, and trouble walking. The patient has been admitted to the hospital before for what seems to be negligence from her caretakers. Laboratory values are ordered as seen below.

Serum:
Na+: 120 mEq/L
Cl-: 98 mEq/L
K+: 4.3 mEq/L
HCO3-: 25 mEq/L
BUN: 20 mg/dL
Glucose: 99 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL
Ca2+: 10.2 mg/dL

Urinalysis is notable for bacteruria without pyuria or nitrates. Physical exam is notable for a confused woman who is unable to answer questions appropriately. She states she has no pain or symptoms and is not sure why she is here. She thinks the year is 1982. Which of the following complications could be seen with treatment of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's confusion, urinary incontinence, and gait disturbance are suggestive of the classic triad of symptoms seen in normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH): dementia, urinary incontinence, and gait disturbance. NPH is a condition that typically affects elderly patients and is due to an idiopathic increase in the volume of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the ventricles of the brain. This leads to an increase in intracranial pressure, which can cause the symptoms seen in this patient.

The patient's hyponatremia is likely due to the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), which can be seen in NPH. This is due to an increase in the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the posterior pituitary, leading to increased water reabsorption in the kidneys and subsequent dilutional hyponatremia.

The treatment of hyponatremia involves fluid restriction and slow correction of the sodium level. Rapid correction of hyponatremia can lead to osmotic demyelination syndrome (also known as central pontine myelinolysis). This is a serious and potentially life-threatening complication that can cause neurologic symptoms such as dysarthria, dysphagia, and flaccid paralysis.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with confusion. The patient’s wife states that her husband has become more somnolent over the past several days and now is very confused. The patient has no complaints himself, but is answering questions inappropriately. The patient has a past medical history of diabetes and hypertension. His temperature is 98.3°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 127/85 mmHg, pulse is 138/min, respirations are 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a confused man with dry mucous membranes. Initial laboratory studies are ordered as seen below.

Serum:
Na+: 135 mEq/L
Cl-: 100 mEq/L
K+: 3.0 mEq/L
HCO3-: 23 mEq/L
BUN: 30 mg/dL
Glucose: 1,299 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.5 mg/dL
Ca2+: 10.2 mg/dL

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hyperglycemia, polyuria, and altered mental status is consistent with hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS). HHS is a life-threatening complication of diabetes mellitus type 2 that is often precipitated by an underlying illness (eg, infection, myocardial infarction). It is characterized by severe hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL), hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), and dehydration in the absence of significant ketoacidosis (bicarbonate >15 mEq/L). The absence of significant ketoacidosis is due to the presence of enough insulin to suppress lipolysis and subsequent ketogenesis.

The primary treatment for HHS is aggressive fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline to correct for the severe volume depletion that results from the osmotic diuresis. This can also help to lower the serum glucose. Insulin therapy should be started once aggressive fluid resuscitation has been initiated and any underlying precipitating cause (eg, infection) should be sought and treated. 

Hypokalemia is common in HHS and can be exacerbated by insulin therapy, which drives potassium intracellularly. Therefore, potassium replacement should be initiated with insulin therapy to prevent severe hypokalemia. However, insulin should not be delayed if potassium levels are not yet available.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
An 81-year-old man is brought in by his neighbor with altered mental status. The patient’s neighbor is unsure exactly how long he was alone, but estimates that it was at least 3 days. The neighbor says that the patient usually has his daughter at home to look after him but she had to go into the hospital recently. The patient is unable to provide any useful history. Past medical history is significant for long-standing hypercholesterolemia and hypertension, managed medically with rosuvastatin and hydrochlorothiazide, respectively. His vital signs include: blood pressure, 140/95 mm Hg; pulse, 106/min; temperature, 37.2°C (98.9°F); and respiratory rate, 19/min. On physical examination, the patient is confused and unable to respond to commands. His mucus membranes are dry and he has tenting of the skin. The remainder of the exam is unremarkable. Laboratory findings are significant for the following:
Sodium 141 mEq/L
Potassium 4.1 mEq/L
Chloride 111 mEq/L

BUN 40 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL
Glucose (fasting) 80 mg/dL
  Magnesium 1.9 mg/dL

24-hour urine collection
Urine Sodium 169 mEq/24 hr (ref: 100–260 mEq/24 hr)
Urine Creatinine 79.5 g/24 hr (ref: 1.0–1.6 g/24 hr)
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s acute renal failure?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of being alone for several days, dry mucous membranes, and skin tenting are suggestive of dehydration. His elevated BUN and creatinine are indicative of acute kidney injury (AKI), likely due to prerenal azotemia from volume depletion. Prerenal azotemia is the most common cause of AKI and is due to decreased renal perfusion. In this patient, decreased renal perfusion is likely due to dehydration. The BUN:creatinine ratio is often >20:1 in prerenal azotemia, as seen in this patient, due to increased proximal tubular reabsorption of urea in the setting of volume depletion.

So, the answer is [A].

A 64-year-old female with a history of end-stage renal disease presents to her primary care physician complaining of weakness. She reports a six-month history of progressive weakness accompanied by occasional dull aching pain in her arms, legs, and lower back. She has also started to increase her fiber intake because of occasional strained bowel movements. Her past medical history is notable for poorly controlled diabetes, major depressive disorder, and obesity. She takes insulin and sertraline. She has a twenty pack-year smoking history and drinks alcohol socially. Her temperature is 98.5°F (36.9°C), blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 16/min. Laboratory findings are shown below:

Serum:
Na+: 138 mEq/L
Cl-: 99 mEq/L

This patient's symptoms of weakness, bone pain, and constipation, along with her elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels, are suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. However, given her history of end-stage renal disease, the most likely diagnosis is secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease (CKD). CKD can cause decreased production of calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3) and decreased phosphate excretion, leading to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, respectively. The hypocalcemia stimulates PTH secretion, leading to secondary hyperparathyroidism. Over time, the parathyroid glands become hyperplastic and autonomously secrete PTH, leading to hypercalcemia.

The treatment of choice for secondary hyperparathyroidism due to CKD is calcimimetic agents, which activate the calcium-sensing receptor in the parathyroid gland and decrease PTH secretion.

question: A 2-year-old girl with recurrent urinary tract infections is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination. Renal ultrasound shows bilateral dilation of the renal pelvis. few_shot.question: A 34-year-old female presents to her primary care physician with complaints of fevers, nausea/vomiting, and severe left flank pain that has developed over the past several hours. answer_choices.B: Thickening of the capillaries and glomerular basement membrane
answer_choices.D: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with 'wire-looping' of capillaries

This condition is characterized by infection of the renal parenchyma and is most commonly caused by ascending infection from the lower urinary tract. few_shot.question: A 49-year-old female with a long history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus visits her primary care physician with 2+ non-pitting edema in her legs. The patient has a serum creatinine of 2.9 mg/dL and a blood urea nitrogen of 61 mg/dL. A 24-hour urine collection reveals 8.5 grams of protein. A renal biopsy is obtained. Which of the following histologic findings is most likely to be seen upon tissue analysis:

answer_choices.B: Nodular thickening of the glomerular basement membrane

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, peripheral edema) due to diabetic nephropathy. Diabetic nephropathy is the most common cause of end-stage renal disease in the United States. It is characterized by progressive proteinuria in patients with longstanding, often poorly controlled, diabetes mellitus. Early in the course of diabetic nephropathy, patients may have microalbuminuria (30-300 mg/day), which can progress to overt proteinuria (>300 mg/day) if not adequately treated. Other clinical features include hypertension and a progressive decline in renal function.

The earliest morphologic change seen in diabetic nephropathy is thickening of the glomerular basement membrane. As the disease progresses, mesangial expansion and nodular sclerosis (ie, Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules) develop. These nodules are pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy and represent accumulations of mesangial matrix material.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a sore throat, nonproductive cough, and bloody urine for 3 days. This is the most common cause of primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. It is characterized by deposition of IgA in the mesangium of the glomeruli, leading to an inflammatory response and subsequent hematuria. The disease is usually benign, but can slowly progress to end-stage renal disease over 20-30 years in 25%-30% of cases.

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man goes to the emergency room (ER) for an intense lower abdominal pain associated with inability to urinate. Physical examination shows tenderness of the lower abdomen bilaterally. Rectal examination reveals an enlarged, smooth, and symmetrical prostate. The ER team fails to pass a Foley catheter through the urethra, and the urology team decides to place a suprapubic catheter to drain the urine and relieve the patient’s symptoms. An ultrasound shows dilation of the collecting system in both kidneys. Laboratory studies show an elevated serum creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL for an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 50 ml/min/1.73 m2. However, his serum creatinine stays elevated at 1.5 mg/dL. What renal gross findings correlate with this patient’s condition?

This patient's presentation is consistent with acute urinary retention secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). BPH is a common condition in older men that can cause bladder outlet obstruction and subsequent urinary retention. If severe, this can lead to bilateral hydronephrosis and acute kidney injury (AKI) due to increased pressure in the urinary collecting system and renal tubules. Over time, this can cause tubulointerstitial inflammation and fibrosis, leading to a thin cortical rim on gross examination of the kidneys.

question: A 36-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the emergency department because of sudden-onset, severe right flank pain. Her temperature is 37.1°C (99.3°F). Abdominal examination shows tenderness in the right lower quadrant with guarding. Pelvic ultrasound shows a large simple cyst on the right ovary. Right ovarian artery flow is detectable on Doppler, but there is no flow detected in the right ovarian vein. Which of the following ligaments is most likely to have been involved?

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for 5 days of increasing pelvic pain. She says that the pain has been present for the last 2 months; however, it has become increasingly severe recently. She also says that the pain has been accompanied by unusually heavy menstrual periods in the last few months. Physical exam reveals a mass in the right adnexa, and ultrasonography reveals a 9 cm right ovarian mass. If this mass is surgically removed, which of the following structures must be diligently protected?
few_shot.explanation:
The ureter is at risk of injury during gynecologic surgery, especially during procedures involving the ovaries, uterine fundus, or uterosacral ligament. The ureter courses retroperitoneally and is crossed anteriorly by the uterine artery at the level of the internal cervical os ("water under the bridge"). It then runs in the base of the broad ligament, lateral to the uterus and medial to the ovarian vessels. The ureter is therefore at risk of injury during ligation of the ovarian vessels in oophorectomy or ligation of the uterine vessels in hysterectomy.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of increasing abdominal pain with associated nausea and vomiting. The symptoms began suddenly after having intercourse with her partner six hours ago. There is no associated fever, diarrhea, vaginal bleeding, or discharge. Menarche was at the age of 13 years and her last menstrual period was 4 weeks ago. She uses combination contraceptive pills. She had an appendectomy at the age of 12. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows severe right lower quadrant tenderness with associated rebound and guarding. Pelvic examination shows scant, clear vaginal discharge and right adnexal tenderness. There is no cervical wall motion tenderness. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10.5 g/dL, leukocyte count is 9,000/mm3, and platelet count is 250,000/mm3. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following imaging findings is most likely?

answer_choices.B: Decreased ovarian blood flow on doppler
answer_choices.D: Distended fallopian tube with incomplete septations

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden-onset, severe abdominal pain following intercourse is suggestive of ovarian torsion. Ovarian torsion occurs when the ovary twists around its vascular pedicle, leading to venous obstruction, edema, and hemorrhagic infarction. The torsion can also obstruct arterial blood flow, but this is a late finding. Risk factors include ovarian masses (eg, cysts, tumors) and ovarian hyperstimulation, which can cause the ovary to enlarge and increase the risk of torsion. However, torsion can also occur in women with normal-sized ovaries. The pain is typically sudden in onset, severe, and can be associated with nausea and vomiting due to the acute abdomen. There may be pelvic tenderness on examination, but findings can be nonspecific. Prompt diagnosis is important because irreversible ovarian damage can occur within hours. Transvaginal ultrasound with doppler may show decreased or absent blood flow to the ovary, although this finding is not always present. If torsion is suspected, the patient should be taken to the operating room for diagnostic laparoscopy and detorsion to prevent irreversible ovarian damage.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 21-year-old college student comes to the physician because of daytime fatigue for 2 months. He has problems getting to sleep at night and frequently falls asleep during class. When he wakes up at 8:30 a.m., he feels extremely drowsy, and he tries to overcome his fatigue by drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day. He naps at various times during the afternoon, often for more than an hour. He stopped watching videos on his smartphone at night because of suggestions from his peers. He states that he has tried over-the-counter melatonin pills and exercising at 8 p.m. without success. He has no history of serious illness. He does not smoke. He drinks three to five beers on weekends. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?

few_shot.question: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician with excessive daytime sleepiness over the past year. His parents are concerned with his below-average school performance over the last 3 months. He goes to bed around midnight and wakes up at 7 am on school days, but sleeps in late on weekends. He exercises regularly after school. He usually has a light snack an hour before bed. He does not snore or have awakenings during sleep. He has no history of a serious illness and takes no medications. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. He is up to date on all vaccines and is meeting all developmental milestones. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. There is no history of a similar problem in the family. His vital signs are within normal limits. His BMI is 22 kg/m2. Physical examination shows no abnormal findings. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation at this time?

answer_choices.C: Take a nap in the afternoon

This patient's excessive daytime sleepiness and decreased school performance are likely due to insufficient sleep. Adolescents require approximately 9 hours of sleep per night. This patient is getting only 7 hours of sleep on school nights, which is insufficient. This is a common problem in adolescents due to academic, social, and extracurricular demands, as well as a natural shift toward a later sleep phase. The most appropriate recommendation is to increase the amount of nighttime sleep. This can be achieved by setting a regular sleep schedule, creating a quiet sleep environment, and turning off electronic devices before bedtime.

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old high school student comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of insomnia. On school nights, he goes to bed around 11 p.m. but has had persistent problems falling asleep and instead studies at his desk until he feels sleepy around 2 a.m. He does not wake up in the middle of the night. He is worried that he does not get enough sleep. He has significant difficulties waking up on weekdays and has repeatedly been late to school. At school, he experiences daytime sleepiness and drinks 1–2 cups of coffee in the mornings. He tries to avoid daytime naps. On the weekends, he goes to bed around 2 a.m. and sleeps in until 10 a.m., after which he feels rested. He has no history of severe illness and does not take medication. Which of the following most likely explains this patient's sleep disorder?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's difficulty falling asleep at the desired bedtime, difficulty waking up in the morning, and daytime sleepiness are consistent with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder (DSWPD). DSWPD is a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder characterized by a delay in the timing of the major sleep period relative to the desired sleep and wake times. Patients with DSWPD have a delay in the timing of melatonin secretion, which is normally secreted a few hours before bedtime to promote sleep. As a result, these patients have difficulty falling asleep and waking up at socially acceptable times. However, when they are allowed to follow their preferred sleep schedule (eg, on weekends or during school vacations), they have normal sleep quality and duration. DSWPD is most common in adolescents and young adults and is often associated with excessive electronic media use at night, which can delay melatonin secretion.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old man presents to his primary care physician concerned about excessive sleepiness that has persisted his entire life. He notes that he has been having difficulty with his job as a waiter because he often falls asleep suddenly during the day. He also experiences a sensation of dreaming as he goes to sleep even though he still feels awake. He sleeps about 10 hours per day and still feels tired throughout the day. The patient has even reported driving into a tree once as he fell asleep while driving. The patient often stays up late at night working on the computer. Physical exam demonstrates an obese young man who appears tired. His oropharynx demonstrates high palatal ridges and good dental hygiene. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

answer_choices.C: Recommend scheduling regular naps and more time for sleep at night
answer_choices.D: Recommend to abstain from activities at night that expose the patient to blue light

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's excessive daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations are suggestive of narcolepsy. Narcolepsy is a chronic sleep disorder characterized by overwhelming daytime drowsiness and sudden attacks of sleep. It is caused by a deficiency in hypocretin (orexin), a neurotransmitter that regulates arousal, wakefulness, and appetite. The most effective treatment for narcolepsy is usually a combination of medications and lifestyle changes. Medications often include stimulants, such as modafinil, and inhibitors of dopamine reuptake, such as methylphenidate.

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old male presents to his primary care physician with a chief complaint of anxiety and fatigue. Otherwise, the patient has no significant past medical history and is not taking any medications. On physical exam you note a tired and anxious appearing young man. His neurological exam is within normal limits. The patient states that he fears he will fail his courses if he does not come up with a solution. Which of the following is the best initial step in management?

This patient is presenting with symptoms of insomnia. Insomnia is defined as difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or non-restorative sleep for at least 1 month. The first step in management of insomnia is to identify and treat any underlying causes. In this patient, the underlying cause is likely anxiety related to his final exams. The next step in management is to educate the patient on proper sleep hygiene. This includes maintaining a regular sleep schedule, avoiding daytime naps, avoiding caffeine and alcohol, and using the bed only for sleep and sex. If these measures fail, then pharmacologic therapy can be considered.

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old woman complains of difficulty falling asleep over the past 4 months. On detailed history taking, she says that she drinks her last cup of tea at 8:30 p.m. before retiring at 10:30 p.m. She then watches the time on her cell phone on and off for an hour before falling asleep. In the morning, she is tired and makes mistakes at work. Her husband has not noticed excessive snoring or abnormal breathing during sleep. Medical history is unremarkable. She has smoked 5–7 cigarettes daily for 7 years and denies excess alcohol consumption. Her physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the best initial step in the management of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's difficulty falling asleep, daytime fatigue, and normal physical examination are consistent with insomnia. Insomnia is a common disorder that can be due to poor sleep hygiene, medical or psychiatric illness, or certain medications. In this patient, poor sleep hygiene is suggested by her use of electronic devices (cell phone) in bed and consumption of caffeine (tea) close to bedtime. Electronic devices emit light that can suppress melatonin secretion and delay the onset of sleep. Caffeine is a stimulant that can also delay sleep onset and reduce total sleep time. The best initial step in management is to address these modifiable behaviors by recommending proper sleep hygiene. This includes:

- Maintaining a regular sleep schedule
- Ensuring that the sleep environment is dark, quiet, and cool
- Avoiding electronic devices in bed
- Avoiding caffeine and nicotine close to bedtime
- Regular exercise (but not close to bedtime)
- Avoiding daytime napping

question: A 45-year-old Caucasian male presents to a gastroenterologist complaining of heartburn and difficulty swallowing. He recalls that he has been told by his primary care physician that he suffers from gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The gastroenterologist decides to perform an upper endoscopy with biopsy. answer_choices.A: Presence of Paneth cells in the lower esophagus
answer_choices.C: A small region of red, velvet-like mucosa in the lower esophagus

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up evaluation of chronic, retrosternal chest pain. The pain is worse at night and after heavy meals. He has taken oral pantoprazole for several months without any relief of his symptoms. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy shows ulcerations in the distal esophagus and a proximally dislocated Z-line. A biopsy of the distal esophagus shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Which of the following microscopic findings underlie the same pathomechanism as the cellular changes seen in this patient?

answer_choices.C: Branching muscularis mucosa in the jejunum
answer_choices.D: Disorganized squamous epithelium in the endocervix

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's retrosternal chest pain, especially after meals and at night, is suggestive of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). His endoscopy findings of distal esophageal ulcerations and a proximally dislocated Z-line (ie, the junction between the squamous epithelium of the esophagus and the columnar epithelium of the stomach) are consistent with Barrett esophagus (BE), a complication of chronic GERD. BE is characterized by the replacement of the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus with metaplastic columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. This metaplasia is a protective response to chronic injury from acid reflux, as columnar epithelium is more resistant to acid-induced damage than squamous epithelium.

Squamous metaplasia of the bladder is a similar process that occurs in response to chronic irritation (eg, indwelling catheter, recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder stones). The normal transitional epithelium of the bladder is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium, which is more resistant to chronic injury.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-month history of recurrent retrosternal chest pain that often wakes her up at night. GERD occurs due to the reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, leading to inflammation and damage of the esophageal mucosa. This is often due to transient lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxations, a decrease in LES pressure, or anatomic disruption of the gastroesophageal junction (eg, hiatal hernia). The histologic findings of basal cell hyperplasia and papillary lengthening in the squamous epithelium, along with intraepithelial eosinophils and neutrophils, are characteristic of reflux esophagitis.

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old man comes to the physician because of intermittent retrosternal chest pain. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Endoscopy shows salmon pink mucosa extending 5 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsy specimens from the distal esophagus show nonciliated columnar epithelium with numerous goblet cells. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

This patient's endoscopy findings of salmon pink mucosa extending proximally from the gastroesophageal junction and biopsy findings of nonciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells are consistent with Barrett esophagus. Barrett esophagus is a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by metaplastic columnar epithelium. This metaplasia is thought to occur as an adaptation to the chronic acid exposure from GERD. Patients with Barrett esophagus are often asymptomatic but may also present with symptoms of GERD, such as heartburn, regurgitation, and chest pain.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: An esophageal biopsy sample from a 47-year-old male with chronic heartburn reveals intestinal metaplasia. Which of the following abnormal cell types is likely present in this patient’s esophagus:
few_shot.explanation:
The normal esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) can lead to Barrett esophagus, a condition in which the normal squamous epithelium of the esophagus is replaced by metaplastic columnar epithelium that resembles the lining of the stomach or intestines. This is a precancerous condition that can progress to esophageal adenocarcinoma. The presence of goblet cells is required to make the diagnosis of Barrett esophagus.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 34-year-old man with worsening refractory epigastric pain secondary to long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease presents for endoscopic evaluation. Past medical history is also significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus that was diagnosed 3 years ago, managed medically. Current medications are metformin, metoclopramide, and omeprazole. Which of the following best describes this patient’s most likely endoscopic findings?

answer_choices.B: Hypertrophy of the esophageal mucosa protruding into the lumen of the lower esophagus
answer_choices.D: A malignant proliferation of squamous cells

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and refractory symptoms despite proton pump inhibitor therapy are concerning for Barrett esophagus. Barrett esophagus is a complication of chronic GERD and is characterized by metaplasia of the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus to nonciliated, columnar, goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia). This change is thought to occur as a result of chronic inflammation and injury due to exposure of the esophageal mucosa to gastric acid. Barrett esophagus is associated with an increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 40-year-old man presents to the clinic with complaints of increased bilateral pain in his knees. The pain developed over time and now limits his mobility. He states that the pain is worse at the end of the day, though he does have some early-morning stiffness lasting about 20 minutes. He used to have some success with over-the-counter NSAIDs; however, they no longer help. The patient also has been taking metformin for the past 2 years and is severely obese, with a BMI of 41 kg/m2. Additionally, he states that he has felt increasingly tired during the day, often dozes off during work, and no longer feels refreshed when he wakes up in the morning. Upon examination, there is no tenderness on palpation or erythema; however, some crepitus is felt. He has no other complaints but has a family history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) on his mother’s side. Which of the following factors is the underlying cause of the patient’s pain, as well as the rest of his complaints?

few_shot.question: A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 9-month history of pain and stiffness in the right knee. He reports that the stiffness lasts approximately 10 minutes after waking up and that the pain is worse in the evening. There is no history of trauma. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 102 kg (225 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m2. Examination of the right knee shows tenderness in the anteromedial joint line and crepitus during knee movement. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 15 mm/h and a serum uric acid concentration of 6.9 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely finding on imaging of the right knee?

answer_choices.A: Osteophytes and narrowing of the joint-space
answer_choices.B: Marginal bony erosions and opacification of periarticular soft tissue
answer_choices.C: Loculated epiphyseal cyst with thinning of the overlying cortex
answer_choices.D: Bony ankylosis and bone proliferation at the entheses

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic knee pain that is worse in the evening and improves with rest, along with physical examination findings of crepitus and joint line tenderness, is suggestive of osteoarthritis (OA). OA is the most common joint disorder and is due to age-related degeneration of articular cartilage. Risk factors include age >40, female sex, obesity, and joint injury. Obesity is a strong risk factor for knee OA due to the increased mechanical load on weight-bearing joints.

Radiographic findings in OA include joint space narrowing (due to loss of articular cartilage), subchondral sclerosis (increased bone density due to increased bone turnover), subchondral cysts (from synovial fluid intrusion into subchondral bone), and osteophytes (bony outgrowths that represent attempts to repair the damaged joint).

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for pain when he walks. He states that the pain is the worst in his left great toe but is also present in his hips and knees. He says that his symptoms are worse with activity and tend to improve with rest. His symptoms have progressively worsened over the past several years. He has a past medical history of obesity, type II diabetes mellitus, smoking, and hypertension. He drinks roughly ten beers per day. His current medications include metformin, insulin, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide. The patient has a recent travel history to Bangkok where he admits to having unprotected sex. On physical exam, examination of the lower extremity results in pain. There is crepitus of the patient's hip when his thigh is flexed and extended. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of joint pain that is worse with activity and improves with rest, along with crepitus on physical exam, are suggestive of osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease that is characterized by the progressive loss of articular cartilage. It is the most common form of arthritis and is a leading cause of disability in the elderly. Risk factors for osteoarthritis include age, obesity, joint injury, and genetic predisposition. The disease typically affects the hands, knees, hips, and spine. 

Infectious arthritis is less likely in this patient because it typically presents with an acutely swollen, painful joint and systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. Gout is also less likely because it typically presents with an acutely swollen, painful joint, most commonly the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Pseudogout is less likely because it typically presents with an acutely swollen, painful joint, most commonly the knee.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of worsening severe pain, swelling, and stiffness in her right knee for the past 2 days. She recently started running 2 miles, 3 times a week in an attempt to lose weight. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and osteoporosis. Her mother has rheumatoid arthritis. She drinks one to two glasses of wine daily. She is sexually active with multiple partners and uses condoms inconsistently. Current medications include metformin and alendronate. She is 161 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 74 kg (163 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m2. Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 74/min, and blood pressure is 115/76 mm Hg. She appears to be in discomfort and has trouble putting weight on the affected knee. Physical examination shows a 2-cm, painless ulcer on the plantar surface of the right toe. The right knee is swollen and tender to palpation. Arthrocentesis of the right knee with synovial fluid analysis shows a cell count of 55,000 WBC/μL with 77% polymorphonuclear (PMN) cells. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's presenting condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute monoarticular arthritis with fever and a high synovial fluid white blood cell count with a predominance of polymorphonuclear cells is suggestive of septic arthritis. The most common pathogen in nongonococcal septic arthritis is Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus. Risk factors for septic arthritis include age >80, diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, recent joint surgery, and skin infection. This patient's diabetes and skin ulcer suggest that her septic arthritis is due to hematogenous spread of bacteria from her skin ulcer.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 48-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an increasingly painful swelling behind her right knee for the past 2 months. During this time, she has also had intermittent low-grade fever and she has been more fatigued than usual. She has not had any trauma to the knee. Over the past year, she has had occasional pain in her hands and wrists bilaterally. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She drinks 1–2 glasses of wine daily and occasionally more on weekends. Current medications include enalapril, metformin, and glimepiride. Her mother and older brother have osteoarthritis. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a 3-cm nontender mass in the right popliteal fossa that becomes prominent when the knee is extended. There is mild swelling and redness of her right knee joint. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of a popliteal mass (Baker cyst), low-grade fever, fatigue, and bilateral hand and wrist pain is suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a systemic, autoimmune inflammatory disorder that primarily affects the joints. The most commonly involved joints are the small joints of the hands and feet, although any joint can be affected. The arthritis is typically symmetric and is associated with morning stiffness lasting >30 minutes. Extra-articular manifestations of RA include rheumatoid nodules, vasculitis, and systemic symptoms such as low-grade fever, fatigue, and weight loss. 

A Baker cyst (also known as a popliteal cyst) is a distention of the gastrocnemio-semimembranosus bursa with synovial fluid. It is located in the popliteal fossa and is best visualized when the knee is extended and the calf muscle is relaxed. Baker cysts are associated with intra-articular pathology that causes increased synovial fluid production. In adults, the most common conditions associated with Baker cysts are RA and osteoarthritis.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 60-year-old man comes to the clinic with the complaint of knee pain for the past few weeks. The pain is located in the left knee, associated with morning stiffness for about an hour, and improves with activities throughout the day. He also has a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, peptic ulcer disease, and ischemic heart disease. He underwent angioplasty last year for a STEMI. The patient takes metformin, aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, ramipril, omeprazole, and bisoprolol. He used to smoke one pack of cigarettes a day for the last 45 years but stopped smoking for the past one year following his heart attack. He drinks alcohol socially. His father has Alzheimer’s disease and is in adult home care, and his mother died of breast cancer when she was 55. His temperature is 37.6°C (99.8°F), blood pressure is 132/65 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 14/min, and BMI is 22 kg/m2. On examination, his left knee is swollen, warm, tender to touch, and has decreased range of movement due to pain. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations are negative. Laboratory investigation is shown below:
Complete blood count:
Hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL
Leukocytes 14,000/mm3
Platelets 155,000/mm3
ESR     40 mm/hr
What is the best next step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a monoarticular arthritis, which is most likely due to osteoarthritis (OA) given his age and the presence of risk factors (eg, age, male sex). However, the presence of systemic symptoms (eg, fever) and an elevated ESR make septic arthritis a possibility that must be ruled out. Therefore, the next best step in the management of this patient is arthrocentesis for synovial fluid analysis. This is because septic arthritis is a medical emergency and delay in diagnosis and treatment can lead to irreversible joint destruction and significant morbidity.

So, the answer is [B].
