few_shot.question: A 26-year-old woman, G1P0, at 22 weeks of gestation presents to the clinic for a prenatal visit. Her recent pregnancy scan shows a single live intrauterine fetus with adequate fetal movements. Facial appearance shows the presence of a cleft lip. The rest of the fetal development is within normal limits. The fetal heart rate is 138/min. Her prenatal screening tests for maternal serum α-fetoprotein (MSAFP) concentration, pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A), and free β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) are within normal ranges respectively. Her past medical and surgical histories are negative. She is worried about the health of her baby. The baby is at increased risk for which of the following birth defects?
few_shot.explanation:
Cleft lip and palate are the most common craniofacial malformations. They can occur as isolated defects or as part of a syndrome. The most common syndromes associated with cleft lip and palate are van der Woude syndrome and velocardiofacial syndrome (also known as 22q11.2 deletion syndrome). However, the majority of cleft lip and palate cases are nonsyndromic. The etiology of nonsyndromic cleft lip and palate is multifactorial, with both genetic and environmental factors playing a role. The recurrence risk in siblings of an affected individual is approximately 2%-8%.

Cleft lip and palate can lead to feeding difficulties, recurrent otitis media, speech difficulties, and dental problems. In addition, neonates with cleft palate are at risk for respiratory difficulties due to nasal regurgitation and aspiration of feeds.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question:
A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of high-grade fever, myalgia, and generalized fatigue for 3 days. She returned from a vacation to northern Brazil 4 days ago. She took the appropriate medications and immunizations prior to her visit. There is no family history of serious illness. She appears ill. Her temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), pulse is 110/min and blood pressure is 94/54 mm Hg. Examination shows jaundice of the conjunctivae and skin. The abdomen is soft and nontender; the spleen is palpated 2 to 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL
Leukocyte count 4,650/mm3

Bilirubin

few_shot.question:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-week history of generalized fatigue and malaise. He was born at term and has been healthy since. His mother has a history of recurrent anemia. He appears pale. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F) and pulse is 97/min. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and jaundice. The abdomen is soft and nontender; the spleen is palpated 3–4 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 81.3 μm3
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 39% Hb/cell
Leukocyte count 7300/mm3
Platelet count 200,000/mm3
Red cell distribution width 19% (N = 13–15)
Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's pallor, jaundice, and splenomegaly in the setting of a normocytic anemia with increased red cell distribution width (RDW) suggest a hemolytic anemia. The presence of a family history of anemia raises suspicion for a hereditary cause. Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is the most common inherited cause of hemolytic anemia in individuals of Northern European descent. It is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by defects in proteins that link the plasma membrane to the underlying spectrin-actin cytoskeleton. This leads to loss of membrane surface area and formation of spherocytes, which are rigid and less able to traverse the spleen's sinusoids, leading to extravascular hemolysis.

The eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test is the diagnostic test of choice for HS. EMA binds to the red blood cell membrane proteins, and flow cytometry is used to measure fluorescence intensity. Because HS red blood cells have a deficiency of these proteins, EMA binding is decreased, resulting in lower fluorescence intensity.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 13-month-old girl is brought to the pediatric clinic by her mother due to progressive abdominal distension, poor feeding, and failure to thrive. The perinatal history was uneventful. The family emigrated from Sudan 8 years ago. The vital signs include: temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure 100/55 mm Hg, and pulse 99/min. The physical examination shows conjunctival pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, and parietal and frontal bossing of the skull. The laboratory test results are as follows:
Hemoglobin     8.7 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 62 μm3
Red cell distribution width 12.2% (normal value is 11.5–14.5%)
Reticulocyte count    2.1 %
Leucocyte count     10,200/mm3
Platelet count   392,000/mm3
The peripheral blood smear shows microcytic red cells, target cells, and many nucleated red cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and bony changes (frontal bossing) is suggestive of thalassemia major (Cooley anemia). Thalassemia major is an autosomal recessive disorder that results from defective synthesis of the beta-globin chain. It is most common in individuals of Mediterranean, African, and Southeast Asian descent. Patients are usually asymptomatic at birth due to the presence of fetal hemoglobin (alpha2gamma2). However, once the switch to adult hemoglobin (alpha2beta2) production occurs at around 6 months of age, patients develop severe anemia and symptoms of ineffective erythropoiesis (eg, bone marrow expansion, extramedullary hematopoiesis). The peripheral blood smear shows microcytosis, hypochromia, target cells, nucleated red cells, and basophilic stippling. 

Hence, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician for evaluation of pallor and increasing lethargy for 3 days. Six days ago, he experienced abdominal pain, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea that have since resolved. The family returned from a road trip to Mexico 4-weeks ago. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and scleral icterus. The abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 92 μm3
Leukocyte count 18,500/mm3
Platelet count 45,000/mm3
Prothrombin time 12 sec
Partial thromboplastin time 34 sec
Serum
Urea nitrogen 32 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL
Bilirubin
Total 2.0 mg/dL
Direct 0.1 mg/dL
Lactate dehydrogenase 1685 U/L
A peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's presentation?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recent history of bloody diarrhea, pallor, lethargy, and laboratory findings of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, elevated lactate dehydrogenase), thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury are consistent with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). HUS is most commonly caused by Shiga toxin-producing bacteria (eg, Escherichia coli O157:H7, Shigella), which are often contracted through contaminated food or water. Shiga toxin binds to and inhibits the 60S ribosomal subunit, halting protein synthesis and leading to cell death. Endothelial injury and cell death trigger platelet activation and aggregation, leading to formation of microthrombi. These microthrombi cause mechanical destruction of erythrocytes (ie, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia) and occlusion of the renal vasculature, leading to acute kidney injury.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of progressive fatigue, abdominal pain, and loss of appetite over the past 3 days. He was treated in the emergency department once in the past year for swelling of his hands and feet. He was adopted as a baby from Sudan and his family history is unknown. He does not take any medication. He is lethargic. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 141/min, respirations are 25/min, and blood pressure is 68/40 mm Hg. Examination shows pale, dry mucous membranes and scleral icterus. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 93 fL
Reticulocyte count 11%
Serum
Lactate dehydrogenase 194 IU/L
Total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL
Direct bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL
Haptoglobin 21 mg/dL (N = 41–165)
Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigue, pallor, scleral icterus, and elevated reticulocyte count is suggestive of hemolytic anemia. The elevated lactate dehydrogenase level and low haptoglobin level are also consistent with hemolysis. The elevated indirect bilirubin level is due to increased breakdown of heme, a component of hemoglobin, into bilirubin. The patient's history of a prior episode of hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis) and adoption from Sudan, a region with a high prevalence of sickle cell disease (SCD), suggest that his hemolytic anemia is due to SCD. SCD is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a single amino acid substitution in the β-globin chain of hemoglobin, leading to the production of abnormal hemoglobin S (HbS). HbS polymerizes under conditions of low oxygen tension, causing red blood cells to become rigid and sickle-shaped. Sickled cells are prone to hemolysis and can occlude small blood vessels, leading to vaso-occlusive crises. Dactylitis, a common early manifestation of SCD, is a vaso-occlusive crisis occurring in the small bones of the hands and feet. Chronic hemolysis in SCD can lead to the development of functional asplenia by age 2 years and autosplenectomy (ie, fibrosis and shrinkage of the spleen) by adolescence or early adulthood. However, splenomegaly can occur due to sequestration of sickled cells in the spleen, especially in children younger than 4 years of age.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: An 8-year-old boy presents with a 7-day history of fever and abdominal pain for the past 4 days. Past medical history is significant for an exchange transfusion for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and recurrent attacks of pallor during the course of upper respiratory tract infections. His vital signs include: blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse 105/min, respiratory rate 40/min, and temperature 37.0℃ (98.6℉). On physical examination, the patient is ill-looking. Conjunctivae are pale and the sclera is icteric. The liver is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory findings show hemoglobin of 5.9 gm/dL, Hct of 20%, and haptoglobin of 28 gm/dL. A peripheral blood smear shows hypochromic anemia, polychromasia, anisocytosis, and occasional Heinz bodies. The reticulocyte count was 15%. A direct Coombs test was negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, recurrent episodes of pallor during infections, and current findings of anemia, jaundice, and reticulocytosis suggest a chronic hemolytic anemia. The presence of Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) on the peripheral smear is indicative of oxidative damage to the red blood cells (RBCs). This is seen in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, an X-linked disorder that is one of the most common causes of hemolytic anemia worldwide.

G6PD is an enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway that generates NADPH. NADPH is necessary to keep glutathione in its reduced form. Reduced glutathione protects RBCs from oxidative damage. In G6PD deficiency, RBCs are more susceptible to oxidative stress. Oxidative stress can be precipitated by infections, certain drugs (eg, sulfonamides, dapsone, primaquine, nitrofurantoin), and fava beans. The oxidative stress denatures hemoglobin, forming Heinz bodies. Heinz bodies damage the RBC membrane, leading to intravascular hemolysis or bite cells (RBCs with a "bite" taken out of the cell membrane) if the Heinz bodies are removed by splenic macrophages.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A previously healthy 30-year-old woman comes to the physician for the evaluation of pain during sexual intercourse for 6 months. She also reports frequent episodes of crampy pelvic pain that starts one day before menses and lasts for 7 days. Her symptoms are not relieved with pain medication. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 days. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She is sexually active with her husband. She uses a combined oral contraceptive pill. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows rectovaginal tenderness. Cervical and urethral swabs are negative. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old female presents to her primary care provider with pelvic pain. She reports that for the last several years, she has had chronic pain that is worst just before her menstrual period. Over the past two months, she has also had worsening pain during intercourse. She denies dysuria, vaginal discharge, or vaginal pruritus. The patient has never been pregnant and previously used a copper intrauterine device (IUD) for contraception, but she had the IUD removed a year ago because it worsened her menorrhagia. She has now been using combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) for nearly a year. The patient reports improvement in her menorrhagia on the OCPs but denies any improvement in her pain. Her past medical history is otherwise unremarkable. Her temperature is 98.0°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 124/73 mmHg, pulse is 68/min, and respirations are 12/min. The patient has tenderness to palpation during vaginal exam with lateral displacement of the cervix. A pelvic ultrasound shows no abnormalities, and a urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the best next step in management to confirm the diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic pelvic pain that worsens with menses and intercourse is suggestive of endometriosis. Endometriosis is characterized by the presence of endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity. The most common sites of involvement are the ovaries, uterosacral ligaments, and the pouch of Douglas. The cyclic bleeding of these ectopic endometrial implants during menstruation leads to inflammation and fibrosis, causing chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, and dyspareunia. The pain is often most severe just before and during menses, as hormonal changes lead to hypertrophy and bleeding of the ectopic endometrial tissue. 

The diagnosis of endometriosis is suggested by the clinical history and physical examination, but definitive diagnosis requires direct visualization of endometrial implants on laparoscopy. Laparoscopy also allows for biopsy of suspicious lesions to confirm the diagnosis histologically.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old woman who has never been pregnant presents to the physician for a follow-up examination. She has had 5 months of deep pain during sexual intercourse and pelvic pain that intensified prior to her menses. The pain has not subsided despite taking oral contraceptives. She denies any vaginal discharge or foul smell. She is in a monogamous relationship with her husband of 2 years. She has no history of any serious illnesses. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows tenderness on deep palpation of the hypogastrium. A speculum examination of the vagina and cervix shows no abnormalities or discharge. Serum studies show a beta hCG of 6 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is most likely to establish a diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, and pelvic pain are suggestive of endometriosis. Endometriosis is a condition in which endometrial tissue is found outside the uterus, most commonly on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and tissue lining the pelvis. The endometrial tissue can cause pain, especially around the time of the patient's period. The pain can be severe and can also occur during sexual intercourse or during bowel movements or urination.

The diagnosis of endometriosis can be suggested by symptoms and physical findings, but the only way to definitively diagnose endometriosis is by visualizing the implants during surgery, most commonly laparoscopy. During laparoscopy, the surgeon can also obtain biopsies of the implants to confirm the diagnosis.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of pelvic discomfort and heavy menstrual bleeding. The pain is dull and pressure-like and occurs intermittently; the patient is asymptomatic between episodes. Menses occur at regular 30-day intervals and last 8 days with heavy flow. Her last menstrual period ended 5 days ago. She is sexually active and does not use contraception. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.8°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 106/68 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows white cervical mucus and a firm, irregularly-shaped uterus consistent in size with a 5-week gestation. A spot urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic discomfort, along with the finding of an enlarged, irregularly-shaped uterus on physical examination, are suggestive of uterine leiomyomas (fibroids). Leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle tumors that are often asymptomatic but can cause symptoms based on their size and location. For example, submucosal leiomyomas can cause heavy menstrual bleeding, and intramural or subserosal leiomyomas can cause bulk symptoms (eg, pelvic pressure, urinary frequency) due to compression of adjacent structures.

The initial diagnostic test of choice for suspected leiomyomas is pelvic ultrasound, which can show the size, number, and location of the fibroids. This information is important in guiding management. For example, a small, asymptomatic fibroid may simply be observed, whereas a large fibroid causing significant symptoms may require treatment with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist or surgery.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old woman comes to the physician because she is unable to conceive for 3 years. She and her partner are sexually active and do not use contraception. They were partially assessed for this complaint 6 months ago. Analysis of her husband's semen has shown normal sperm counts and hormonal assays for both partners were normal. Her menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 to 6 days. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She had a single episode of urinary tract infection 4 years ago and was treated with oral antibiotics. Vaginal examination shows no abnormalities. Bimanual examination shows a normal-sized uterus and no palpable adnexal masses. Rectal examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has primary infertility, defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse. The initial evaluation of an infertile couple includes a semen analysis, assessment of ovulation, and evaluation of the reproductive anatomy. This patient has regular menses and a midluteal progesterone level >3 ng/mL, which confirms ovulation. Her partner has a normal semen analysis. The next step in the evaluation of this couple is assessment of tubal patency and the uterine cavity. Hysterosalpingography is typically the initial test of choice to evaluate these structures. It involves the injection of radiopaque dye through the cervix, after which fluoroscopic images are obtained. Hysterosalpingography can detect tubal occlusion and abnormalities of the uterine cavity (eg, endometrial polyps, submucosal leiomyomas, intrauterine adhesions, congenital anomalies). If hysterosalpingography suggests tubal disease or an abnormal uterine cavity, further evaluation with hysteroscopy or laparoscopy may be necessary.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of left lower abdominal pain for 1 day. She describes the pain as 6 out of 10 in intensity. Over the past 5 months, she has had similar episodes of pain that occur once a month and last 1 to 2 days. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 to 6 days. Menarche was at the age of 13 years, and her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She has been sexually active with 1 male partner in the past and has used condoms inconsistently. She tested negative for sexually transmitted infections on her last visit 6 months ago. Abdominal and pelvic examination shows no abnormalities. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of recurrent, unilateral mid-cycle pain that lasts for a short duration are consistent with mittelschmerz, which is German for "middle pain." Mittelschmerz is thought to be caused by local peritoneal irritation due to follicular enlargement and/or rupture, and the subsequent release of follicular fluid and/or blood. It is a common cause of pelvic pain in young women and is a diagnosis of exclusion. No treatment is necessary for mittelschmerz, and patients can be reassured that it is a benign condition. NSAIDs can be used for symptomatic relief.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue, weight loss, and muscle aches during the past 2 months. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. Her only medication is a multivitamin. A metyrapone stimulation test is performed and the results rule out a diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency. Which of the following changes in laboratory findings are most likely to have been observed in this patient following the administration of the drug?

few_shot.question: A 41-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of fatigue, irregular menstrual cycles, and recurrent sinus infections. Examination shows hirsutism and hypopigmented linear striations on the abdomen. Serum studies show hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. A 24-hour urinary cortisol level is elevated. Serum ACTH is also elevated. High-dose dexamethasone does not suppress serum cortisol levels. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's clinical presentation is consistent with Cushing syndrome, which is characterized by central obesity, hirsutism, menstrual irregularities, and striae. The hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis are due to the mineralocorticoid effects of cortisol. The recurrent sinus infections are due to the immunosuppressive effects of cortisol.

The elevated ACTH level suggests that the Cushing syndrome is ACTH-dependent. The lack of suppression of cortisol levels with high-dose dexamethasone suggests that the source of ACTH is ectopic, rather than from a pituitary adenoma. The most common source of ectopic ACTH is small cell lung cancer.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of weight gain, generalized weakness, and irregular menstrual cycles for the past 16 months. She began having symptoms of insomnia and depression 10 months ago. More recently, she has been having difficulties rising from a chair. She has a 2-year history of hypertension. Current medications include citalopram and hydrochlorothiazide. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb). BMI is 36 kg/m2. Her pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 134/76 mm Hg. She appears tired and has a full, plethoric face and central obesity. Examination of the skin shows violaceous linear striations on her lower abdomen. Two midnight serum cortisol studies show measurements of 288 μg/L and 253 μg/L (N < 90); a 24-hour urinary cortisol measurement was 395 μg (N < 300). Upon follow-up laboratory examination, the patient's serum ACTH levels were also elevated at 136 pg/mL (N = 7–50). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

answer_choices.A: MRI of the head with contrast
answer_choices.B: Measure ACTH levels in inferior petrosal sinuses
answer_choices.D: CT scan of the abdomen with contrast

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's weight gain, central obesity, plethoric face, and abdominal striae are suggestive of Cushing syndrome. Her elevated midnight serum cortisol levels and 24-hour urinary cortisol confirm the diagnosis. The next step is to determine the cause of the hypercortisolism. The elevated ACTH level suggests that the hypercortisolism is ACTH-dependent (ie, due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma or an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor). The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test can help differentiate between these two causes. In this test, 2 mg of dexamethasone is given every 6 hours for 2 days. A >50% reduction in cortisol levels is consistent with Cushing disease (pituitary adenoma), whereas no reduction suggests an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor. If the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is consistent with Cushing disease, an MRI of the pituitary gland should be performed to visualize the adenoma. If the test suggests an ectopic source, a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis should be performed to localize the tumor.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 48-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with the complaints of persistent fatigue, dizziness, and weight loss for the past 3 months. She has hypothyroidism for 15 years and takes thyroxine replacement. Her blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg in a supine position and 65/40 mm Hg while sitting, temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F) and pulse is 75/min. On physical examination, there is a mild increase in thyroid size, with a rubbery consistency. Her skin shows diffuse hyperpigmentation, more pronounced in the oral mucosa and palmar creases. The morning serum cortisol test is found to be 3 µg/dL. Which of the following is the best next step in this case?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fatigue, weight loss, and hyperpigmentation are suggestive of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). The most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in developed countries is autoimmune adrenalitis, which may occur in isolation or as a component of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type II (APS II). APS II is characterized by primary adrenal insufficiency, autoimmune thyroid disease, and type 1 diabetes mellitus. This patient's history of hypothyroidism and the presence of a goiter suggest chronic autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis, which is associated with APS II.

The diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency is confirmed by a high-dose (250 µg) cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test. In this test, a baseline cortisol level is obtained, cosyntropin is administered, and then cortisol levels are measured at 30 and 60 minutes. A normal response is an increase in the serum cortisol level to >18-20 µg/dL. Patients with primary adrenal insufficiency will have a subnormal response due to adrenal atrophy or destruction and lack of reserve.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 53-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressive headache and fatigue for the past 2 months. One year ago, she was diagnosed with Cushing disease, which was ultimately treated with bilateral adrenalectomy. Current medications are hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Examination shows generalized hyperpigmentation of the skin and bitemporal visual field defects. Serum studies show an ACTH concentration of 1250 pg/mL (N = 20–100). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of Cushing disease treated with bilateral adrenalectomy, new bitemporal visual field defects, and elevated ACTH level suggest the presence of a pituitary macroadenoma (Nelson syndrome). Nelson syndrome is characterized by an enlarging pituitary adenoma and very high ACTH levels following bilateral adrenalectomy for refractory Cushing disease. The loss of cortisol negative feedback due to adrenalectomy leads to overgrowth of the existing ACTH-secreting tumor and hyperpigmentation due to high levels of ACTH (and its precursor, pro-opiomelanocortin, which has melanocyte-stimulating activity). The enlarging pituitary adenoma can cause mass effects, including visual field defects due to compression of the optic chiasm. The most appropriate next step in management is transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary adenoma. If surgery is contraindicated or if residual tumor remains postoperatively, radiotherapy is the treatment of choice.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her husband because of a gradual 20-kg (45-lb) weight loss and recurrent episodes of vomiting without diarrhea over the past 2 years. Her last menstrual period was 6 months ago. On physical examination, she appears fatigued and emaciated, and there is bilateral swelling of the retromandibular fossa. Laboratory studies show hypokalemia and a hemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of weight loss, vomiting, and amenorrhea is suggestive of anorexia nervosa. The bilateral swelling of the retromandibular fossa is due to parotid gland enlargement, which is a common finding in patients with eating disorders who induce vomiting. The hypokalemia is likely due to vomiting-induced losses, and the anemia is likely due to nutritional deficiencies.

Patients with anorexia nervosa often have multiple endocrine abnormalities. One of the most common is a decrease in the level of triiodothyronine (T3), the most active form of thyroid hormone. This is thought to be an adaptive response to the state of chronic starvation, as it decreases the basal metabolic rate and thus reduces caloric requirements. 

So, the answer is [C].

question: A male newborn born at 27 weeks' gestation is evaluated for rapid breathing and hypoxia shortly after birth. His mother had no prenatal care. Cardiopulmonary examination shows normal heart sounds, intercostal retractions, and nasal flaring. An x-ray of the chest shows low lung volumes, air bronchograms, and diffuse ground-glass opacities. He is started on nasal continuous positive airway pressure. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.A: Bilateral pleural effusions on lung ultrasound
answer_choices.B: Corkscrew-shaped organisms on umbilical cord culture
answer_choices.C: Hyaline membranes lining the alveoli on lung biopsy

few_shot.question: A 2350-g (5-lb 3-oz) male newborn delivered at 28 weeks’ gestation develops rapid breathing, grunting, and subcostal retractions 2 hours after delivery. The mother did not receive prenatal care. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 168/min, respirations are 88/min, and blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. Physical examination shows cyanosis and nasal flaring. Breath sounds are decreased bilaterally. An x-ray of the chest shows diffuse reticulonodular ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this patient's disease?
few_shot.explanation:
This premature infant has respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also known as hyaline membrane disease. RDS is characterized by poor lung compliance and atelectasis due to surfactant deficiency. Surfactant is a lipoprotein complex that reduces alveolar surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse at the end of expiration. It is synthesized by type II pneumocytes and stored in lamellar bodies within these cells. Surfactant production begins at approximately 24 weeks' gestation, but adequate amounts are not produced until 34-36 weeks' gestation. Therefore, premature infants are at risk for surfactant deficiency and RDS. The risk is inversely proportional to gestational age and birth weight. 

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 1-day-old male infant is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for dyspnea. He was born at 34 weeks gestation. Apgar scores were 6 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios. His mother is a healthy 33-year-old G1P1 woman who received adequate prenatal care. The nurse in the NICU noted increased oral secretions and intermittent desaturations. His temperature is 100.8°F (38.2°C), blood pressure is 100/55 mmHg, pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 28/min. On exam, the child appears to be in respiratory distress. Intercostal retractions are noted. Auscultation of the lungs reveals rales bilaterally. The patient’s abdomen is moderately distended. A chest radiograph is performed and demonstrates coiling of the nasogastric (NG) tube in the esophagus. This patient should be evaluated for which of the following conditions?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of polyhydramnios, respiratory distress, and inability to pass an NG tube into the stomach is suggestive of esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula (EA/TEF). EA/TEF is a congenital malformation in which the esophagus ends in a blind pouch (EA) and may connect with the trachea (TEF). The most common type of EA/TEF is proximal EA with distal TEF. This can lead to polyhydramnios due to impaired fetal swallowing and accumulation of amniotic fluid. After birth, infants with EA/TEF present with excessive oral secretions, choking, coughing, and cyanosis, especially with feeding due to aspiration. Pneumonia and pneumonitis can also occur due to gastric fluid refluxing through the TEF into the lungs.

EA/TEF is associated with the VACTERL association, which includes vertebral defects, anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheoesophageal fistula, renal anomalies, and limb abnormalities. Therefore, this patient should be evaluated for other anomalies in the VACTERL spectrum, including cardiac defects such as ventricular septal defect.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 3900-g (8-lb 11-oz ) male newborn is delivered at term to a 27-year-old woman. Immediately after delivery, he develops cyanosis and tachypnea. Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygen shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Examination shows decreased breath sounds in the left lung field. Despite appropriate treatment, the newborn dies. An x-ray of the chest performed prior to autopsy shows sharply demarcated fluid-filled densities in the left lung. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the x-ray findings?

answer_choices.A: Abnormal budding of the ventral foregut
answer_choices.B: Fistula between the esophagus and the trachea

few_shot.explanation:
This newborn's cyanosis, tachypnea, and decreased breath sounds in the left lung field are suggestive of a congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM), also known as congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation. This is a hamartomatous cystic lesion of the lung that is thought to result from abnormal budding of the tracheobronchial tree. The cysts are filled with fluid or mucus, which can cause compression of the normal lung tissue and mediastinal shift. This can lead to respiratory distress in the neonatal period. Chest x-ray typically shows multiple cysts of varying sizes.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 2500-g (5.5-lb) male newborn is delivered at 35 weeks' gestation to a 25-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1. The pregnancy was complicated by oligohydramnios. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 78%. Examination in the delivery room shows that the newborn's skin appears blue with weak cry and irregular breathing and gasping. The nose is flat with bilateral epicanthal folds. The ears are low-set with broad auricles. The lower jaw is abnormally displaced backwards. The right lower limb appears shorter than the left lower limb with displaced right great toe. Breath sounds are decreased bilaterally. Renal ultrasound shows bilateral dilatation of the renal pelvis and ureters. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the underlying cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has Potter sequence (Potter facies, pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities), which is caused by oligohydramnios. The most common cause of oligohydramnios is renal agenesis, but other causes include obstructive uropathies (eg, posterior urethral valves in males, ureteropelvic junction obstruction), and autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. In this patient, the presence of bilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureter suggests an obstructive uropathy. Voiding cystourethrogram is the diagnostic test of choice to evaluate for vesicoureteral reflux and posterior urethral valves, the most common cause of lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A newborn born at 33 weeks of gestation has a respiratory rate of 70/min and a heart rate of 148/min 2 hours after birth. He is grunting and has intercostal and subcostal retractions. He has peripheral cyanosis as well. An immediate chest radiograph is taken which shows a fine reticular granulation with ground glass appearance on both lungs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn's prematurity, respiratory distress, and characteristic chest x-ray findings are consistent with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also known as hyaline membrane disease. RDS is caused by surfactant deficiency due to lung immaturity. Surfactant is a lipoprotein complex that reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse at the end of expiration. Surfactant production begins at approximately 24 weeks of gestation and rapidly increases between 34 and 36 weeks. Therefore, RDS is most common in premature infants, especially those born before 28 weeks of gestation.

Clinical features of RDS include respiratory distress (eg, tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, cyanosis, intercostal retractions) that typically develops within minutes to a few hours after birth. Chest x-ray shows diffuse bilateral atelectasis causing a "ground-glass" appearance, air bronchograms, and low lung volumes.

So, the answer is [C].

question: A 45-year-old African-American woman comes to the physician after an episode of hemoptysis. Over the past 8 months, she has had a nonproductive cough, fatigue, and a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss. She drinks a glass of wine every night and does not smoke. She has a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis. She does not take any medications. She has never traveled out of the country. She works as an accountant. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 94/min, and blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg. Lungs are clear to auscultation. An x-ray of the chest shows a 2.5-cm nodule with irregular borders at the apex of the left lung with no mediastinal or hilar enlargement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.C: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old woman presents to her physician’s office with cough, increasing fatigue, and reports an alarming loss of 15 kg (33 lb) weight over the last 4 months. She says that she has observed this fatigue and cough to be present over the past year, but pushed it aside citing her age as a reason. The cough has been progressing and the weight loss is really worrying her. She also observed blood-tinged sputum twice over the last week. Past medical history is noncontributory. She does not smoke and does not use recreational drugs. She is relatively active and follows a healthy diet. Today, her vitals are normal. On examination, she appears frail and pale. At auscultation, her lung has a slight expiratory wheeze. A chest X-ray shows a coin-shaped lesion in the periphery of the middle lobe of the right lung. The nodule is biopsied by interventional radiology (see image). Which of the following types of cancer is most likely associated with this patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of cough, fatigue, weight loss, and hemoptysis, along with the chest X-ray findings of a peripheral lung nodule, are concerning for lung cancer. The biopsy image shows a glandular pattern of tumor cells, which is characteristic of adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Adenocarcinoma is more common in nonsmokers and women, and usually presents as a peripheral lung nodule. It is often associated with pleural involvement and may present with pleural effusion.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 71-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of worsening cough and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years. Physical examination shows wheezing over the right lung fields. Laboratory studies show a serum calcium concentration of 12.5 mg/dL. X-rays of the chest are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic cough, weight loss, smoking, and hypercalcemia, along with the chest x-ray findings, are suggestive of squamous cell lung carcinoma. This is a type of non-small cell lung cancer that is strongly associated with smoking. It often arises centrally in the lung and can cause symptoms due to local tumor effects (eg, cough, hemoptysis, postobstructive pneumonia) or paraneoplastic syndromes. The most common paraneoplastic syndrome associated with squamous cell lung carcinoma is hypercalcemia due to the production of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) by the tumor cells. PTHrP increases renal tubular calcium reabsorption and bone resorption, leading to hypercalcemia.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 70-year-old caucasian woman presents to her primary care provider complaining of a heavy cough with blood-tinged sputum. Her cough has bothered her for the last 2 weeks. Over the counter medications are no longer alleviating her symptoms. She also reports that she has unintentionally lost 6.8 kg (15 lb) in the last 5 months. Her past medical history is significant for peptic ulcer disease that was positive for H. pylori on biopsy and was treated with triple-drug therapy. She is a lifetime non-smoker and worked as a teacher before retiring at the age of 60. Today, her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg, pulse is 87/min, and pulse oximetry is 90% on room air. On physical exam, her heart has a regular rate and rhythm. Auscultation of the lungs revealed scattered crackles and wheezes. A CT scan of the lungs shows an irregular mass in the peripheral region of the inferior lobe of the right lung and a CT guided biopsy is positive for malignant tissue architecture and gland formation with a significant amount of mucus. Which of the following risk factors most likely predisposed this patient to her condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss in the setting of a peripheral lung mass on imaging is concerning for lung cancer. The biopsy results showing malignant tissue architecture and gland formation with a significant amount of mucus are consistent with adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Adenocarcinoma is more common in women and nonsmokers, and typically presents as a peripheral lung mass. The most significant risk factor for lung cancer is smoking, but given that this patient is a lifelong nonsmoker, her gender is the most likely predisposing factor.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old woman presents to her physician with a persistent and debilitating cough which began 3 weeks ago, and chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath for the past week. Past medical history is significant for breast carcinoma 10 years ago treated with mastectomy, chemotherapy and radiation, a hospitalization a month ago for pneumonia that was treated with antibiotics, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. Medications include chlorthalidone and metformin. She does not smoke but her husband has been smoking 3 packs a day for 30 years. Today her respiratory rate is 20/min and the blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Serum Na is 140 mmol/L, serum K is 3.8 mmol/L and serum Ca is 12.2 mg/dL. A chest X-ray (shown in image) is performed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of breast cancer, recent pneumonia, and persistent cough, chest pain, and shortness of breath are concerning for a new primary lung malignancy. The chest x-ray shows a hilar mass, which is a common finding in lung cancer. The hypercalcemia is also suggestive of malignancy, as hypercalcemia is a common paraneoplastic syndrome that can occur in patients with lung cancer. The most common type of lung cancer associated with hypercalcemia is squamous cell carcinoma, which is often centrally located and can present as a hilar mass. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis in this patient is squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic complaining of cough and unintentional weight loss over the past 3 months. He works as a computer engineer, and he informs you that he has been having to meet several deadlines recently and has been under significant stress. His medical history is significant for gout, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, diabetes mellitus type 2, and pulmonary histoplasmosis 10 years ago. He currently smokes 2 packs of cigarettes/day, drinks a 6-pack of beer/day, and he endorses a past history of cocaine use back in the early 2000s but currently denies any drug use. The vital signs include: temperature 36.7°C (98.0°F), blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg, heart rate 87/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. His physical examination shows minimal bibasilar rales, but otherwise clear lungs on auscultation, grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur, and a benign abdominal physical examination. However, on routine lab testing, you notice that his sodium is 127 mEq/L. His chest X-ray is shown in the picture. Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of significant tobacco use, cough, weight loss, and hyponatremia in the setting of a hilar mass on chest x-ray is suggestive of a lung malignancy, most likely small cell lung cancer (SCLC). SCLC is a neuroendocrine tumor that is almost always seen in smokers. It is highly malignant and tends to metastasize early, often presenting with hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, as seen in this patient. SCLC is also associated with several paraneoplastic syndromes, including the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), which is likely causing this patient's hyponatremia. SIADH is due to ectopic production of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) by the tumor, leading to excessive free water retention and subsequent hyponatremia.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 68-year-old man presents with difficulty breathing for the last 3 hours. Upon asking about other symptoms, he mentions that he had a cough for the last 4 months which he attributes to his smoking. He says he had frequent nasal stuffiness and headaches over the last 3 months, for which he takes over-the-counter cold medications and analgesics. Over the last 2 months, he often felt that his face was mildly swollen, especially in the morning hours, but he did not consider it to be anything serious. No significant past medical history. He reports a 20-pack-year smoking history. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.4°F), pulse is 96/min, blood pressure is 108/78 mm Hg, and the respiratory rate is 24/min. On physical examination, auscultation of the chest reveals rhonchi and crepitus over the right lung. The remainder of the exam is unremarkable. A chest radiograph reveals a mass in the middle lobe of the right lung. Which of the following clinical signs would most likely be present in this patient?

answer_choices.D: Sensory loss over the ulnar aspect of right forearm and right hand

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old man presents to the physician with difficulty in breathing for 3 hours. There is no history of chest pain, cough or palpitation. He is a chronic smoker and underwent elective cholecystectomy one month back. There is no history of chronic or recurrent cough, wheezing or breathlessness. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 108/min, blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg, and respirations are 25/min. His arterial oxygen saturation is 98% in room air as shown by pulse oximetry. After a detailed physical examination, the physician orders a plasma D-dimer level, which was elevated. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest shows a filling defect in a segmental pulmonary artery on the left side. Which of the following signs is most likely to have been observed by the physician during the physical examination of this patient’s chest?

answer_choices.B: Systolic murmur at the left sternal border

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recent surgery, tachycardia, and elevated D-dimer level, along with the CT findings, are suggestive of pulmonary embolism (PE). PE is a common and potentially fatal condition that can be difficult to diagnose due to its nonspecific clinical presentation. The most common symptoms of PE are dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and cough. Hemoptysis and syncope can also occur but are less common. On physical examination, tachypnea is the most common sign, but fever, tachycardia, and accentuation of the pulmonic component of the second heart sound can also be seen. Rales may be heard on lung auscultation, but the examination is often normal.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician for shortness of breath and chest discomfort that is becoming progressively worse. He has had increasing problems exerting himself for the past 5 years. He is now unable to walk more than 50 m on level terrain without stopping and mostly rests at home. He has smoked 1–2 packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. He appears distressed. His pulse is 85/min, blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, and respirations are 25/min. Physical examination shows a plethoric face and distended jugular veins. Bilateral wheezing is heard on auscultation of the lungs. There is yellow discoloration of the fingers on the right hand and 2+ lower extremity edema. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of heavy smoking, progressive exertional dyspnea, and wheezing is suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is characterized by chronic bronchitis (ie, cough and sputum production) and/or emphysema (ie, destruction of alveolar walls). Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as a cough with sputum production for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years. Emphysema is defined pathologically as abnormal, permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis. The most common cause of COPD is smoking.

Patients with severe COPD can develop pulmonary hypertension due to hypoxic vasoconstriction, destruction of the pulmonary vascular bed, and hyperinflation of the lungs with compression of the pulmonary vasculature. Pulmonary hypertension can lead to cor pulmonale (right ventricular hypertrophy and eventual failure due to pulmonary disease). Signs of cor pulmonale include exertional dyspnea, signs of right heart failure (eg, jugular venous distension, lower extremity edema), and loud P2 on cardiac examination.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department for shortness of breath. He was at home working on his car when he suddenly felt very short of breath, which failed to improve with rest. He states he was working with various chemicals and inhalants while trying to replace a broken piece in the engine. The patient was brought in by paramedics and is currently on 100% O2 via nasal cannula. The patient has a 52 pack-year smoking history and drinks 2 to 3 alcoholic drinks every night. He has a past medical history of asthma but admits to not having seen a physician since high school. His temperature is 98.2°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 157/108 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 29/min, and oxygen saturation is 77%. Physical exam demonstrates tachycardia with a systolic murmur heard best along the right upper sternal border. Breath sounds are diminished over the right upper lobe. Bilateral lower extremity pitting edema is noted. Which of the following best describes the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.A: Fe3+ hemoglobin in circulating red blood cells
answer_choices.B: Pulmonary edema secondary to decreased cardiac output

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of sudden-onset dyspnea, decreased breath sounds, and hypoxia in the setting of a significant smoking history is suggestive of a spontaneous pneumothorax. This condition is caused by rupture of an emphysematous bleb, which allows air to escape into the pleural space. The air compresses the lung, leading to decreased breath sounds and hypoxia. The tachycardia and systolic murmur heard best along the right upper sternal border are likely due to increased right-sided heart pressures from the decreased venous return caused by the pneumothorax.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old man comes to the physician for a 5-month history of progressive bilateral ankle swelling and shortness of breath on exertion. He can no longer walk up the stairs to his bedroom without taking a break. He also constantly feels tired during the day. His wife reports that he snores at night and that he sometimes chokes in his sleep. The patient has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. He has a history of hypertension treated with enalapril. His pulse is 72/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 145/95 mmHg. There is jugular venous distention. The lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The extremities are warm and well perfused. There is 2+ lower extremity edema bilaterally. ECG shows right axis deviation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of daytime fatigue, snoring, and choking during sleep are suggestive of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). OSA is characterized by recurrent episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to hypoxemia and hypercapnia. Chronic hypoxemia can lead to pulmonary vasoconstriction and, eventually, pulmonary hypertension. This can cause right-sided heart failure, also known as cor pulmonale, which is characterized by signs of right heart failure (eg, jugular venous distention, lower extremity edema) in the absence of left heart failure. The ECG finding of right axis deviation is also consistent with right ventricular hypertrophy due to pulmonary hypertension.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man presents to the physician for the evaluation of increasing dyspnea and swelling of the lower extremities over the past year. He has no cough. He also complains of frequent awakenings at night and excessive daytime sleepiness. He has no history of a serious illness. He takes no medications other than zolpidem before sleep. He is a 35-pack-year smoker. His blood pressure is 155/95 mm Hg. His BMI is 37 kg/m2. Oropharyngeal examination shows a small orifice and an enlarged tongue and uvula. The soft palate is low-lying. The examination of the nasal cavity shows no septal deviation or polyps. Symmetric pitting edema is seen below the knee, bilaterally. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Echocardiography shows a mildly dilated right ventricle and an elevated systolic pulmonary artery pressure with no abnormalities of the left heart. A ventilation-perfusion scan shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's obesity, snoring, frequent awakenings at night, and excessive daytime sleepiness are suggestive of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). OSA is characterized by repetitive episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to oxygen desaturation and frequent arousals. Risk factors for OSA include obesity, male sex, age >40, and craniofacial abnormalities (eg, retrognathia, macroglossia). Symptoms of OSA include snoring, nocturnal choking, restless sleep, frequent awakenings, and excessive daytime sleepiness. Nocturia may also be present due to increased atrial natriuretic peptide release in response to increased intra-atrial pressure from obstructive episodes.

OSA can lead to pulmonary hypertension due to hypoxic vasoconstriction, increased blood viscosity, and endothelial dysfunction. If left untreated, this can progress to cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure), manifesting as peripheral edema and elevated jugular venous pressure.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question:
A 23-year-old man presents to his primary care physician after bleeding from his gums while brushing his teeth for the past week. Although he has had gum bleeding in the past, it has never been this severe. He has no family history available as he was adopted. He does not have any significant past medical history. His physical exam is within normal limits. Screening lab work is ordered with the following values:
Platelet count 330,000/mm3
Bleeding time 6 mins
Prothrombin time 12 sec
Activated partial thromboplastin time 42 sec
Factor VIII activity decreased
Ristocetin cofactor assay decreased
He is subsequently referred to a hematologist for further work-up and treatment. Which of the following aspects of coagulation would most likely be affected?

few_shot.question:
An otherwise healthy 23-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of mild persistent bleeding from the site of a tooth extraction. He has no prior history of medical procedures or surgeries and no history of easy bruising. He appears well. Vital signs are within normal limits. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL
Platelets 200,000/mm3
Serum
Prothrombin time 25 seconds
Partial thromboplastin time (activated) 35 seconds
Deficiency of which of the following coagulation factors is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and normal activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) suggest a defect in the extrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade. The extrinsic pathway is initiated when tissue factor (factor III) is exposed to circulating factor VII, leading to the activation of factor VII. The PT measures the integrity of this pathway and is prolonged in deficiencies of factor VII, factor X, factor V, factor II (prothrombin), and factor I (fibrinogen). However, deficiencies in factors X, V, II, and I would also cause prolongation of the aPTT, which measures the integrity of the intrinsic pathway. Therefore, isolated prolongation of the PT is seen in factor VII deficiency.

So, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a recent history of easy bleeding. He experienced multiple episodes of epistaxis and bleeding gums over the past two days. He also had flu-like symptoms a week ago which resolved over the past few days. His past medical history is notable for well-controlled asthma. His temperature is 98.9°F (37°C). Physical examination is notable for a petechial rash. No splenomegaly is noted. A coagulation panel reveals an elevation in bleeding time with normal PT and PTT. The blood component that is most likely deficient in this patient contains granules of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recent viral illness, petechial rash, and mucocutaneous bleeding (eg, epistaxis, gingival bleeding) is suggestive of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). ITP is an acquired thrombocytopenia that occurs when antibodies form against platelets, leading to their premature destruction. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other causes of thrombocytopenia (eg, malignancy, medications, infection) should be ruled out. The peripheral blood smear typically shows isolated thrombocytopenia with normal erythrocytes and leukocytes.

Platelets are small, anucleate cell fragments that play a critical role in primary hemostasis. They contain three types of granules: alpha granules, dense granules, and lysosomes. Alpha granules are the most abundant and contain a variety of proteins, including platelet factor 4, beta-thromboglobulin, platelet-derived growth factor, and fibrinogen. They also contain von Willebrand factor (vWF), which is critical for platelet adhesion to the subendothelial collagen that becomes exposed following endothelial injury.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a hematoma after falling during gym class. He claims that he has a history of prolonged nosebleeds and bruising/bleeding after minor injuries. Physical exam is unrevealing other than the hematoma. Labs are obtained showing an increased bleeding time and an abnormal ristocetin cofactor assay. Coagulation assays reveal an increased partial thromboplastin time (PTT) and but a normal prothrombin time (PT). The patient is given desmopressin and is asked to avoid aspirin. Which of the following findings is most likely directly involved in the etiology of this patient's presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of prolonged nosebleeds and bruising/bleeding after minor injuries, along with the laboratory findings of increased bleeding time and abnormal ristocetin cofactor assay, are suggestive of von Willebrand disease (vWD). vWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and is caused by a deficiency or defect in von Willebrand factor (vWF), a plasma protein that promotes platelet adhesion and carries factor VIII. The ristocetin cofactor assay measures the activity of vWF; ristocetin, an antibiotic, induces binding of vWF to platelets, and a deficiency of vWF (as seen in vWD) results in decreased binding and an abnormal test. 

The PTT is prolonged in vWD because vWF carries and stabilizes factor VIII; deficiency of vWF, therefore, also causes a decrease in factor VIII, leading to a defect in the intrinsic coagulation pathway (which is measured by the PTT). The PT, which measures the extrinsic pathway, is normal.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question:
A 13-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician due to a 4-month history of heavy vaginal bleeding during menstrual periods. She endorses episodes of bleeding gums after brushing her teeth and experienced prolonged bleeding after tonsillectomy 6 years ago. Her mother states that she bled significantly during childbirth and that the girl’s older brother has similar symptoms including easy bruising. Vitals were stable and physical exam was not revealing. Laboratory studies show:

Platelet count: 72,000/mm^3
Bleeding time: 14 min
Prothrombin time: 12 secs (INR = 1)
Partial thromboplastin time: 40 secs

Blood smear demonstrates increased megakaryocytes and enlarged platelets. Platelets do not aggregate to ristocetin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet membrane glycoprotein (GP) Ib-IX-V complex. This complex is the receptor for von Willebrand factor (vWF), which mediates platelet adhesion to the subendothelial matrix. The lack of functional GP Ib-IX-V complex impairs the initial interaction of platelets with the subendothelial matrix at sites of vascular injury, resulting in a prolonged bleeding time. The lack of platelet adhesion also results in decreased platelet aggregation in response to ristocetin, which is used in the laboratory to induce platelet agglutination by causing vWF to bind the GP Ib-IX-V complex. 

Patients with Bernard-Soulier syndrome typically present with a lifelong history of mucocutaneous bleeding, including epistaxis, gingival bleeding, easy bruising, and menorrhagia. The peripheral blood smear shows giant platelets and a decreased platelet count (ie, thrombocytopenia). 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [C] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination after the removal of a tooth. During the procedure, he had prolonged bleeding that did not resolve with pressure and gauze packing and eventually required suture placement. His older brother had a similar episode a year ago, but his parents and two sisters have never had problems with prolonged bleeding. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Genetic analysis confirms an X-linked recessive disorder. Which of the following is most likely deficient in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of prolonged bleeding after a dental procedure and the X-linked recessive inheritance pattern suggest a diagnosis of hemophilia A, which is caused by a deficiency of factor VIII. Hemophilia A is the most common severe bleeding disorder and typically presents in males with a history of spontaneous bleeding or excessive bleeding after minor trauma or surgery. The most common sites of bleeding are the joints (eg, knees, elbows) and muscles. Intracranial hemorrhage can also occur and is the most common cause of death in these patients.

question: A 17-year-old female accidentally eats a granola bar manufactured on equipment that processes peanuts. She develops type I hypersensitivity-mediated histamine release, resulting in pruritic wheals on the skin. Which of the following layers of this patient's skin would demonstrate histologic changes on biopsy of her lesions?

few_shot.question: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of a rash on the elbows for several months. A biopsy of the affected area shows a thinned stratum granulosum as well as retained nuclei and spongiotic clusters of neutrophils in the stratum corneum. This patient's skin findings are most likely associated with which of the following conditions?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's skin biopsy findings are consistent with psoriasis, a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with overlying silvery scales. The histologic findings of psoriasis include parakeratosis (retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum), a diminished granular layer, and collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum (Munro microabscesses). Psoriasis is associated with several other conditions, including seronegative spondyloarthropathies (eg, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis), inflammatory bowel disease, and metabolic syndrome.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 46-year-old woman comes to her physician because of an itchy rash on her legs. She denies any recent trauma, insect bites, or travel. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the oral cavity shows white lace-like lines on the buccal mucosa. A photograph of the rash is shown. A biopsy specimen of the skin lesion is most likely to show which of the following?

answer_choices.A: Decreased thickness of the stratum granulosum
answer_choices.D: Deposition of antibodies around epidermal cells

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's pruritic, polygonal, purple papules and plaques on the extremities, along with the white reticulated patches on the oral mucosa (Wickham striae), are characteristic of lichen planus. Lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory disease that affects the skin and mucous membranes. The 5 P's of lichen planus are pruritic, polygonal, planar, purple papules and plaques.

Histologically, lichen planus is characterized by band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction, hypergranulosis, and irregular acanthosis. The inflammation can cause damage to the basal cell layer, leading to necrotic keratinocytes (Civatte bodies or apoptotic bodies) in the papillary dermis.

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of painful rash after spending several hours in the sun. Skin examination shows well-demarcated areas of erythema with some scaling on the face, chest, upper back, and arms. The affected areas are hot and sensitive to touch. The oral mucosa appears normal. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's skin findings?

answer_choices.A: Immune complex deposits at the dermoepidermal junction
answer_choices.B: Mast cell activation in the superficial dermis
answer_choices.C: Apoptosis of keratinocytes in the epidermis
answer_choices.D: T-cell-mediated inflammatory reaction in the dermis

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's skin findings are consistent with sunburn, which is caused by the ultraviolet (UV) radiation in sunlight. UV radiation causes DNA damage in the skin, leading to the formation of pyrimidine dimers. If the DNA damage is too severe to be repaired, the cell undergoes apoptosis, a form of programmed cell death. This is characterized by nuclear fragmentation, chromatin condensation, and cytoplasmic blebbing, but without loss of plasma membrane integrity or significant inflammation. The dead cells are then cleared by tissue phagocytes. In the skin, sunburn causes apoptosis of keratinocytes in the epidermis, leading to the characteristic findings of erythema, tenderness, and later, desquamation (peeling).

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 50-year-old female presents to her physician with vesicles and tense blisters across her chest, arms, and the back of her shoulders. Physical examination reveals that blistering is not present in her oral mucosa, and the epidermis does not separate upon light stroking of the skin. The patient most likely suffers from a hypersensitivity reaction located:

answer_choices.A: Linearly along the epidermal basement membrane
answer_choices.B: In granular deposits at the tips of dermal papillae
answer_choices.C: In fat cells beneath the skin

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's presentation is consistent with bullous pemphigoid, an autoimmune blistering disorder that typically affects elderly patients. Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense blisters that do not rupture easily, and the absence of mucosal involvement. The Nikolsky sign (separation of the epidermis upon light stroking of the skin) is negative in bullous pemphigoid, unlike in pemphigus vulgaris, another autoimmune blistering disorder. Bullous pemphigoid is caused by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180, BP230) that are located along the epidermal basement membrane. These autoantibodies trigger an inflammatory response that leads to subepidermal blister formation.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old woman presents with skin lesions on her elbows and forearms. She notes that they first started appearing 2 months ago and have not improved. She describes the lesions as painless and rarely itchy. She denies any similar symptoms in the past, and has no other significant past medical history. Review of systems is significant for recent joint pain, conjunctivitis, and corneal dryness. The patient is afebrile and vital signs are within normal limits. Non-tender, raised, inflamed, white-silver maculopapular lesions are present. Which of the following are the most likely histopathologic findings in this patient's skin biopsy?

answer_choices.C: Basal cell hyperplasia, proliferation of subepidermal vasculature, and keratinization

This patient's skin findings and symptoms are consistent with psoriasis, a chronic inflammatory skin disease. The most common form of psoriasis is plaque psoriasis, which is characterized by well-demarcated, raised, erythematous plaques with a silvery scale. The extensor surfaces (eg, elbows, knees) and scalp are most commonly affected. Nail changes (eg, pitting, onycholysis) are also common. Psoriasis is associated with several extracutaneous manifestations, including psoriatic arthritis, uveitis, and inflammatory bowel disease.

Histopathologic findings in psoriasis include parakeratosis (retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum), acanthosis (epidermal hyperplasia), and elongation of the rete ridges (epidermal downgrowths). There is also a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis.

question: A 29-year-old woman presents to her OB/GYN for a preconception visit. She wishes to become pregnant within the next several months. A thorough history reveals that the patient suffers from phenylketonuria (PKU). She recalls being instructed by prior physicians to follow a diet that avoids certain foods; however, she admits to not being complaint with these recommendations. Laboratory testing reveals a plasma phenylalanine level of 20.2 mg/dL (normal range <2 mg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient?

answer_choices.A: Improved PKU treatment will decrease the risks of spontaneous abortion and intrauterine fetal death
answer_choices.B: 3 months prior to conception, begin a restricted diet to lower phenylalanine levels to below 6 mg/dL
answer_choices.C: Begin a phenylalanine-restricted diet in your first trimester to reduce the risk of fetal morbidity
answer_choices.D: Your current phenylalanine levels do not pose a risk to any future pregnancy

few_shot.question: A 1-week-old male newborn is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination after the results of newborn screening showed an increased serum concentration of phenylalanine. Genetic analysis confirms a diagnosis of phenylketonuria. The physician counsels the patient's family on the recommended dietary restrictions, including avoidance of artificial sweeteners that contain aspartame. Aspartame is a molecule composed of aspartate and phenylalanine and its digestion can lead to hyperphenylalaninemia in patients with phenylketonuria. Which of the following enzymes is primarily responsible for the breakdown of aspartame?
few_shot.explanation:
Aspartame is a low-calorie artificial sweetener composed of two amino acids, aspartate and phenylalanine. It is used in a variety of foods and drinks as a sugar substitute. Aspartame is broken down in the small intestine by the enzyme dipeptidase, which cleaves the molecule into its constituent amino acids. These amino acids are then absorbed into the bloodstream. In patients with phenylketonuria, the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase is deficient, leading to an inability to metabolize phenylalanine into tyrosine. This can lead to a buildup of phenylalanine in the blood and brain, causing intellectual disability, seizures, and other serious health problems. Therefore, patients with phenylketonuria must avoid aspartame in their diet.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 32-year-old G6P1 woman presents to the obstetrician for a prenatal visit. She is 8 weeks pregnant. She has had 4 spontaneous abortions in the past, all during the first trimester. She tells you she is worried about having another miscarriage. She has been keeping to a strictly organic diet and takes a daily prenatal vitamin. She used to smoke a pack a day since she was 16 but quit after her first miscarriage. On a previous visit following fetal loss, the patient tested positive for VDRL and negative for FTA-ABS. Labs are drawn, as shown below:

Leukocyte count: 7,800/mm^3
Platelet count: 230,000/mm^3
Hemoglobin: 12.6 g/dL
Prothrombin time: 13 seconds
Activated partial thromboplastin time: 48 seconds
International normalized ratio: 1.2

Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent early pregnancy loss and positive VDRL with negative FTA-ABS test results is suggestive of antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). APS is an autoimmune disorder characterized by venous or arterial thrombosis, pregnancy morbidity (eg, recurrent early pregnancy loss, unexplained fetal death), and/or thrombocytopenia in the presence of persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies (eg, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I). The VDRL test, which detects anticardiolipin antibodies, can be falsely positive in APS. The FTA-ABS test is a specific treponemal test that is negative in this patient, ruling out syphilis.

The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) is prolonged in this patient, which is consistent with the presence of a lupus anticoagulant. Lupus anticoagulants and other antiphospholipid antibodies interfere with phospholipid-dependent steps in the coagulation cascade, leading to a prolonged aPTT. However, these antibodies paradoxically increase the risk of thrombosis.

The mainstay of treatment for APS in pregnancy is prophylactic-dose heparin (unfractionated or low molecular weight) plus low-dose aspirin. This regimen has been shown to significantly improve live birth rates in women with APS.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine physical examination. He feels well. He has no history of major medical illness and takes no medications. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and a standard electrolyte panel, are within normal limits. Urine dipstick is negative for glucose; a reducing substance test result of the urine is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate dietary recommendation for this patient?

answer_choices.D: Increase intake of ketogenic amino acids

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's urine is negative for glucose but positive for reducing substances, which suggests the presence of another reducing substance in the urine. The most common reducing substance found in urine is glucose, but others include galactose and fructose. This patient's presentation is consistent with essential fructosuria, a benign, autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of fructokinase. This enzyme is responsible for the phosphorylation of fructose to fructose-1-phosphate in the liver, the first step in fructose metabolism. In essential fructosuria, dietary fructose is not phosphorylated and instead spills into the urine. Because alternative pathways exist for fructose metabolism, there are no clinical consequences of this disorder. Therefore, no dietary changes are needed.

So, the answer is [B].
