If a patient does not respond to or cannot tolerate an SSRI, treatment alternatives include switching to another SSRI, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, or a drug from another class, such as bupropion or mirtazapine. Bupropion is a weak inhibitor of dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake. It is less likely to cause sexual side effects and can be used to augment sexual desire. Therefore, it would be the most appropriate choice for this patient.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [D] > [C] > [A].

question: A 36-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after being involved in a shooting. He sustained a gunshot wound in an altercation outside of a bar. On arrival, he is oriented to person but not to place or time. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 116/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 79/42 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Examination shows multiple abrasions over the arms and thorax. There is a 1-cm (0.4-in) entry wound with minimal bleeding on the right side of the chest in the 6th intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows diffuse mild tenderness to palpation with no guarding or rebound. A focused assessment with sonography shows no obvious free fluid in the pericardium; assessment of the abdomen is equivocal. An x-ray of the chest shows mild opacification of the right lower lobe. Two large-bore cannulas are inserted and intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun. The patient is intubated and mechanical ventilation is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after sustaining a gunshot wound to the abdomen. On arrival, he is awake and oriented to person, place, and time. He appears agitated. His pulse is 102/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. The pupils are equal and reactive to light. Abdominal examination shows an entrance wound in the right upper quadrant above the umbilicus. There is an exit wound on the right lower back next to the lumbar spine. Breath sounds are normal bilaterally. There is diffuse mild tenderness to palpation with no guarding or rebound. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. Intravenous fluid therapy is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a gunshot wound to the abdomen, which is a potentially life-threatening injury. The first step in management is to assess the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs), and to resuscitate as necessary. This patient is hemodynamically stable, so the next step is to determine the need for operative intervention. 

In general, patients with gunshot wounds to the abdomen should undergo exploratory laparotomy due to the high likelihood of intra-abdominal injury. However, in select patients who are hemodynamically stable and without signs of peritonitis, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis can be performed to determine the trajectory of the bullet and identify injuries that require surgical repair. 

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [D] > [C] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department with a gunshot wound to the abdomen. He complains of weakness and diffuse abdominal pain. Morphine is administered and IV fluids are started by paramedics at the scene. On admission, the patient’s blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg, heart rate is 103/min, respiratory rate is 17/min, the temperature is 36.2℃ (97.1℉), and oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. The patient is responsive but lethargic. The patient is diaphoretic and extremities are pale and cool. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac sounds are diminished. Abdominal examination shows a visible bullet entry wound in the left upper quadrant (LUQ) with no corresponding exit wound on the flanks or back. The abdomen is distended and diffusely tender with a rebound. Aspiration of the nasogastric tube reveals bloody contents. Rectal examination shows no blood. Stool guaiac is negative. Which of the following is the next best step in management?

answer_choices.B: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST)

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a gunshot wound to the abdomen with signs of hypovolemic shock (eg, hypotension, tachycardia, cool extremities, altered mental status) and peritonitis (eg, rebound tenderness). The nasogastric tube aspirate is bloody, suggesting hollow viscus injury. This patient requires immediate exploratory laparotomy to control hemorrhage and repair any injuries.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [D] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old male is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after sustaining a stab wound to the right chest. First-responders found the patient sitting on the curb smoking a cigarette, complaining of pain where he had been stabbed. On arrival, he is alert. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Examination shows several 1–2 cm lacerations and ecchymoses over the face and trunk. There is no neck crepitus. There is a pocket knife in the right fourth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line and blood oozing out of the wound. There is no bubbling of the blood at the wound. The lungs are clear to auscultation with equal breath sounds. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A chest x-ray shows the knife in situ extending into the right thorax. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a penetrating chest wound with a knife in situ. The knife should not be removed in the emergency department because it may be acting as a plug to control bleeding. The patient is hemodynamically stable and has no signs of tension pneumothorax (eg, hypotension, jugular venous distention, tracheal deviation) or cardiac tamponade (eg, hypotension, jugular venous distention, muffled heart sounds). Therefore, the next step in management is to obtain a CT scan of the chest to evaluate for injuries to the lung, heart, and great vessels. The patient should then be taken to the operating room for removal of the knife and repair of any injuries.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [B] > [A] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old soldier is brought to the emergency department of a military hospital 20 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle accident during a training exercise. He was an unrestrained passenger. On arrival, he has shortness of breath and chest pain. He appears pale and anxious. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg. He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and mucous membranes. There is bruising on the chest, extremities, and abdomen. The lungs are clear to auscultation. He has normal heart sounds and flat neck veins. The abdomen is flat, soft, and mildly tender. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. High-flow oxygen is applied, and intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun. An x-ray of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.B: CT scan of the chest with contrast

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is concerning for aortic injury, a life-threatening condition that requires immediate diagnosis and treatment. Aortic injury is most commonly caused by rapid deceleration injuries, such as motor vehicle accidents. The most common site of injury is the aortic isthmus, which is relatively fixed in position and therefore susceptible to shearing forces. Patients often present with chest pain and a widened mediastinum on chest x-ray, as seen in this patient. The most appropriate next step in management is a CT scan of the chest with contrast, which can confirm the diagnosis.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [D] > [C] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a car accident with pain in the middle of his chest and some shortness of breath. He has sustained injuries to his right arm and leg. He did not lose consciousness. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Examination shows several injuries to the upper extremities and chest. There are jugular venous pulsations 10 cm above the sternal angle. Heart sounds are faint on cardiac examination. The lungs are clear to auscultation. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypotension, tachycardia, and elevated jugular venous pressure following a motor vehicle collision is concerning for cardiac tamponade. Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening condition that occurs when fluid accumulates in the pericardial sac and compresses the heart, leading to decreased cardiac output. It is a common complication of penetrating chest trauma, but can also occur after blunt chest trauma. The ECG findings of low voltage QRS complexes and electrical alternans (ie, beat-to-beat alterations in QRS complex height) are characteristic of cardiac tamponade, but are not always present. The most appropriate next step in management is transthoracic echocardiography to confirm the diagnosis. If the diagnosis is confirmed, immediate pericardiocentesis is indicated to relieve the pressure on the heart.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [B] > [A] > [C].

question: A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden onset of slurred speech. The patient’s eldest daughter says that he couldn’t move his arm during the episode. Past medical history is significant for hypertension and a hemorrhagic stroke 6 years ago, which was treated surgically. After admission, the patient gets increasingly worse and loses consciousness. A noncontrast CT of the head shows a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). The patient is taken to the operating room, where the SAH evacuated, and the vessel is repaired. Postoperatively, the patient is unresponsive. Several days later, a repeat CT of the head shows an enlarging aneurysm in a different vessel in the brain. The patient’s daughter is asked to consent to a non-emergent, life-saving operation since the patient is in a comatose state. She does not consent to the operation even though the physician stresses it would be life-saving. Upon further discussion, the physician finds out that the patient was abusive and neglectful to his children, and the daughter wants “to live in peace.” The patient has no written advanced directive. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

answer_choices.A: Follow the daughter’s wishes to withhold the operation
answer_choices.B: Refer this case to the court
answer_choices.C: Contact another family member for consent
answer_choices.D: Report the daughter to the police

few_shot.question: A 76-year-old man is brought to the hospital after having a stroke. Head CT is done in the emergency department and shows intracranial hemorrhage. Upon arrival to the ED he is verbally non-responsive and withdraws only to pain. He does not open his eyes. He is transferred to the medical ICU for further management and intubated for airway protection. During his second day in the ICU, his blood pressure is measured as 91/54 mmHg and pulse is 120/min. He is given fluids and antibiotics, but he progresses to renal failure and his mental status deteriorates. The physicians in the ICU ask the patient’s family what his wishes are for end-of-life care. His wife tells the team that she is durable power of attorney for the patient and provides appropriate documentation. She mentions that he did not have a living will, but she believes that he would want care withdrawn in this situation, and therefore asks the team to withdraw care at this point. The patient’s daughter vehemently disagrees and believes it is in the best interest of her father, the patient, to continue all care. Based on this information, what is the best course of action for the physician team?

answer_choices.A: Listen to the patient’s wife’s wishes and withdraw care
answer_choices.B: Listen to the patient’s daughter’s wishes and continue all care
answer_choices.C: Compromise between the wife and daughter and withdraw the fluids and antibiotics but keep the patient intubated
answer_choices.D: Call other family members and consult them for their opinions

few_shot.explanation:
The patient’s wife is the durable power of attorney (DPOA) for the patient. This means that she has the legal authority to make medical decisions for the patient when he is unable to do so. The patient’s daughter does not have this legal authority. Therefore, the physician team should listen to the patient’s wife’s wishes and withdraw care.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old man with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department by his neighbor because of impaired consciousness and difficulty speaking for 1 hour. A diagnosis of acute ischemic stroke is made. Over the next three days after admission, the patient’s renal function slowly worsens and hemodialysis is considered. He is not alert and cannot communicate. The neighbor, who has been a close friend for many years, says that the patient has always emphasized he would refuse dialysis or any other life-prolonging measures. He also reports that the patient has no family besides his father, who he has not seen for many years. His wife died 2 years ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the physician?

answer_choices.A: Avoid dialysis in line with the patient's wishes
answer_choices.C: Try to contact the father for consent

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a life-threatening condition and is unable to make decisions about his medical care. In such situations, the physician should first determine if the patient has an advance directive or has appointed a health care proxy. If no such documents exist, the physician should seek a surrogate decision maker. The order of priority for decision makers is generally as follows: spouse, adult children, parents, adult siblings, other relatives. In this case, the patient's father is the only known relative and should be contacted to make medical decisions for the patient.

The neighbor, although a close friend, is not a legal surrogate decision maker. However, the neighbor's knowledge of the patient's wishes should be taken into account when making decisions about the patient's care.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency ward by her son for lethargy and generalized weakness. The patient speaks in short utterances and does not make eye contact with the provider or her son throughout the interview and examination. You elicit that the patient lives with her son and daughter-in-law, and she reports vague weakness for the last couple days. The emergency room provider notices 3-4 healing bruises on the patient's upper extremities; otherwise, examination is not revealing. Routine chemistries and blood counts are unremarkable; non-contrast head CT demonstrates normal age-related changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.B: Question the patient's son regarding the home situation
answer_choices.C: Ask the patient's son to leave the room
answer_choices.D: Call Adult Protective Services to report the patient's son

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is concerning for elder abuse, which is defined as intentional actions that cause harm or create a serious risk of harm to a vulnerable elder by a caregiver or other person in a trust relationship with the elder. Elder abuse can be physical, sexual, or emotional/psychological, and can also include neglect and financial exploitation. The patient's lethargy, poor eye contact, and reluctance to speak in the presence of her son are concerning for possible emotional abuse, and the multiple healing bruises on her extremities raise concern for possible physical abuse. The most appropriate next step in management is to interview the patient privately, without her son in the room. This will allow the patient to speak freely about her home situation and any potential abuse. If abuse is confirmed or highly suspected, Adult Protective Services should be contacted.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [B] > [D] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 35-year-old man and his 9-year-old son are brought to the emergency department following a high-speed motor vehicle collision. The father was the restrained driver. He is conscious. His pulse is 135/min and his blood pressure is 76/55 mm Hg. His hemoglobin concentration is 5.9 g/dL. His son sustained multiple body contusions and loss of consciousness. He remains unresponsive in the emergency department. A focused assessment of the boy with sonography is concerning for multiple organ lacerations and internal bleeding. The physician decides to move the man's son to the operating room for emergency surgical exploration. The father says that he and his son are Jehovah's witnesses and do not want blood transfusions. The physician calls the boy's biological mother who confirms this religious belief. She also asks the physician to wait for her arrival before any other medical decisions are undertaken. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the physician?

answer_choices.A: Consult hospital ethics committee for medical treatment of the son
answer_choices.B: Proceed to surgery on the son without transfusion
answer_choices.C: Seek a court order for medical treatment of the son
answer_choices.D: Transfuse packed red blood cells to the son but not to father

few_shot.explanation:
Jehovah's Witnesses are a religious group that often refuse blood transfusions due to their interpretation of biblical passages. However, the right to refuse medical treatment based on religious beliefs applies only to competent adults and mature minors. In the case of minors who lack decision-making capacity, parents generally have the authority to make medical decisions on their behalf. However, this authority is not absolute and can be overridden in life-threatening situations if the proposed intervention is likely to prevent significant harm or death. In such cases, medical professionals have a duty to provide life-saving treatment, even if it is against the wishes of the parents. Therefore, in this case, the physician should transfuse packed red blood cells to the son but not to the father.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [C] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being resuscitated in the field. Her husband is with her and recalls seeing pills beside her when he was in the bathroom. He reveals she has a past medical history of depression and was recently given a prescription for smoking cessation. On physical exam, you notice a right-sided scalp hematoma and a deep laceration to her tongue. She has a poor EEG waveform indicating limited to no cerebral blood flow and failed both her apnea test and reflexes. She is found to be in a persistent vegetative state, and the health care team starts to initiate the end of life discussion. The husband states that the patient had no advance directives other than to have told her husband she did not want to be kept alive with machines. The parents want all heroic measures to be taken. Which of the following is the most accurate statement with regards to this situation?

answer_choices.A: The patient’s husband may be appointed as her health care surrogate and may make end-of-life decisions on her behalf.
answer_choices.B: The patient’s parents may be appointed as her health care surrogate and may make end-of-life decisions on her behalf.
answer_choices.C: The patient’s adult daughter may be appointed as her health care surrogate and may make end-of-life decisions on her behalf.
answer_choices.D: The physician may be appointed as the patient’s health care surrogate and may make end-of-life decisions on her behalf.

few_shot.explanation:
In the absence of an advance directive, the spouse is the default surrogate decision maker. If the patient is unmarried, the surrogate decision maker is usually an adult child, a parent, or a sibling, in that order. The surrogate's role is to make decisions based on the patient's previously expressed wishes (substituted judgment) or, if these are unknown, to make decisions based on what a reasonable person would do in a similar situation (best interest standard). In this case, the patient's husband is the appropriate surrogate decision maker and can make decisions on her behalf.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [C] > [B] > [D].

question: A 55-year-old male presents to the emergency department with dyspnea and palpitations. He does not smoke cigarettes or consume alcohol, and past medical history is insignificant. Blood pressure is 115/75 mmHG and heart rate is 125/min. Heart rhythm is irregularly irregular. After initial treatment with IV digoxin the patient's heart rate drops to 85/min and remains irregular. Which of the following best explains the effect of digoxin in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of shortness of breath and palpitations for 3 hours. He has had similar episodes intermittently for 4 months. His pulse is 140/min and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. An ECG shows irregular narrow-complex tachycardia with no discernable P waves. Emergent electrical cardioversion is performed and the patient reverts to normal sinus rhythm. Pharmacotherapy with sotalol is begun. Which of the following is the most likely physiologic effect of this drug?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of irregularly irregular tachycardia without discernable P waves is consistent with atrial fibrillation (AF). AF is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with increased risk of stroke and heart failure. The management of AF involves rate control, rhythm control, and anticoagulation. Sotalol is a class III antiarrhythmic agent that is used for rhythm control in patients with AF. It works by blocking potassium channels, which prolongs repolarization and increases the refractory period. This can decrease AV nodal conduction and slow the ventricular rate in patients with AF. 

Hence, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [D] > [C] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old woman brought to the emergency department because of a 1-week history of palpitations and shortness of breath. She has congestive heart failure. Current medications include furosemide, lisinopril, and atenolol. Her pulse is 124/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows coarse crackles over the lower lung fields bilaterally. Treatment with digoxin is started. Five days later, an ECG shows prolongation of the PR interval. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the observed effect of this drug?

answer_choices.B: Inhibition of AV node L-type Ca2+ channels

few_shot.explanation:
Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside that is used in the treatment of heart failure and atrial fibrillation. It has a positive inotropic effect (increases the force of contraction) and a negative chronotropic effect (decreases heart rate). The positive inotropic effect is due to inhibition of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump, which leads to an increase in intracellular Na+ concentration. This in turn decreases the activity of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, leading to an increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration and thus increased contractility.

The negative chronotropic effect is due to an increase in vagal (parasympathetic) tone. Digoxin sensitizes the baroreceptors and increases the responsiveness of the vagal efferent nerves to the central nervous system. This leads to a decrease in the conduction velocity of electrical impulses through the AV node, and an increase in the refractory period. This is seen on ECG as a prolongation of the PR interval.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 59-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a complaint of palpitations for the last 30 minutes. He denies chest pain, breathlessness, and loss of consciousness. The medical history is negative for hypertension or ischemic heart disease. On physical examination, the temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), the pulse rate is 146/min and irregular, the blood pressure is 118/80 mm Hg, and the respiratory rate is 15/min. A 12-lead electrocardiogram reveals an absence of normal P waves and the presence of saw tooth-appearing waves. The physician treats him with a single intravenous infusion of ibutilide under continuous electrographic monitoring, which successfully converts the abnormal rhythm to sinus rhythm. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the therapeutic action of this drug in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Prolongation of action potential duration by blocking the rapid outward sodium current
answer_choices.B: Prolongation of cardiac depolarization by blocking the potassium channels and activating the slow inward sodium current
answer_choices.C: Slowing the rapid upstroke during phase 0 by blocking the calcium channels
answer_choices.D: Suppression of phase 4 upstroke in the myocardial fibers by slowly dissociating from sodium channels

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's irregularly irregular pulse and sawtooth pattern on EKG are consistent with atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality due to stroke and heart failure. The management of atrial fibrillation involves three main objectives: ventricular rate control, prevention of thromboembolism, and restoration of sinus rhythm.

Ibutilide is a class III antiarrhythmic drug that is used intravenously to convert atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter to normal sinus rhythm. It works by blocking the rapid component of the delayed rectifier potassium current, thereby prolonging repolarization and increasing the action potential duration. This results in a prolonged refractory period in atrial and ventricular myocardium, His-Purkinje system, and accessory pathways. Ibutilide also activates a slow, inward sodium current, which further prolongs the action potential duration.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [D] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of palpitations and dizziness. His pulse is 65/min and regular. An ECG is shown. A drug is administered that inhibits non-dihydropyridine calcium channels in the heart and his symptoms improve. The drug administered to the patient most likely has which of the following effects on the cardiac conduction system?

answer_choices.A: Prolongation of Purkinje fiber refractory period
answer_choices.B: Decrease in bundle of His refractory period
answer_choices.C: Decrease in ventricular myocardial action potential duration

few_shot.explanation:
The ECG shows a regular rhythm with narrow QRS complexes and no discernible P waves, consistent with junctional rhythm. The junctional (AV nodal) rhythm is an escape rhythm that occurs when the AV node, instead of the SA node, becomes the primary pacemaker of the heart. This usually occurs when there is a delay or block in the conduction of impulses from the atria to the ventricles (eg, due to increased vagal tone, medications, ischemia, structural heart disease). The AV node has an inherent firing rate of 40-60 beats/min, which is slower than the SA node's rate of 60-100 beats/min. Therefore, patients with a junctional rhythm may present with symptoms of decreased cardiac output such as fatigue, dizziness, or syncope.

Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, verapamil, diltiazem) slow conduction through the AV node by blocking the slow inward calcium current (phase 0) of nodal cells. This results in prolongation of the PR interval (prolonged AV node depolarization) and the refractory period (prolonged AV node repolarization). These agents are used to control the ventricular rate in conditions with rapid atrial rates (eg, atrial fibrillation or flutter) and to terminate certain types of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [C] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 70-year-old male immigrant from Asia is brought to the emergency room with complaints of palpitations and light-headedness for 1 hour. The patient was sitting in his chair watching television when he felt his heart racing and became dizzy. He was unable to stand up from his chair because of weakness and light-headedness. His past medical history is notable for mitral stenosis secondary to rheumatic fever as a child. On arrival to the emergency department, the patient's temperature is 99.7°F (37.6°C), blood pressure is 110/55 mmHg, pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 15/min. The patient appears comfortable but anxious. Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. The patient is started on dofetilide. Which of the following would be expected in this patient’s cardiac action potential as a result of this drug?
few_shot.explanation:
Dofetilide is a class III antiarrhythmic drug that works by blocking the rapid component of the delayed rectifier potassium current during phase 3 of the cardiac action potential. This delays repolarization and increases the action potential duration, which is seen on an EKG as an increase in the QT interval. This can be a dangerous side effect, as it can predispose to torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [C] > [B] > [A].

question: A 67-year-old man with peripheral neuropathy comes to the physician for a follow-up examination after the results of serum protein electrophoresis showed monoclonal gammopathy. A complete blood count, serum creatinine, and serum electrolyte concentrations are within the reference ranges. A bone marrow biopsy shows 6% monoclonal plasma cells. Further analysis shows that class I major histocompatibility molecules are downregulated in these monoclonal plasma cells. The proliferation of these monoclonal plasma cells is normally prevented by a class of immune cells that lyse abnormal cells without the need for opsonization, priming, or prior activation. Which of the following best describes this class of immune cells?

few_shot.question: A 78-year-old man presents to the emergency department because of confusion that started 2 hours ago. The patient’s daughter says that he has had blurred vision for several days. His right leg became weak 10 days ago, and he couldn’t walk for a few days before recovering. He was diagnosed with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance 2 years ago. His temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F), pulse is 75/min, respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 125/70 mm Hg. He also has gingival bleeding. Cervical lymphadenopathy is palpated on physical exam. Both the liver and spleen are palpated 5 cm below the costal margins. The serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation is shown. Urine electrophoresis shows no abnormalities. A skeletal survey shows no abnormalities. Which of the following best explains these findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's findings of hyperviscosity syndrome (eg, blurred vision, confusion), peripheral neuropathy, and serum protein electrophoresis with a monoclonal spike in the gamma region are suggestive of Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia (WM). WM is a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by bone marrow infiltration with lymphoplasmacytic cells and excessive production of IgM. The IgM protein is large and can lead to increased serum viscosity (hyperviscosity syndrome), which can cause neurologic symptoms (eg, confusion, visual disturbances, headache, dizziness), bleeding (eg, gingival bleeding), and less commonly, symptoms of peripheral neuropathy (eg, distal limb weakness). Hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy can also be seen in WM, unlike in multiple myeloma.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [C] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for a routine check-up. Physical examination demonstrates asymmetric peripheral neuropathy in her feet. The patient has no previous relevant history and denies any symptoms of diabetes. Routine blood work shows normal results, and she is referred to a hematologist. Subsequent serum protein electrophoresis demonstrates a slightly elevated gamma globulin level, and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance is diagnosed. Which of the following diseases is most likely to develop over the course of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is a premalignant plasma cell disorder characterized by the presence of a serum monoclonal protein (M protein) at a concentration <3 g/dL, <10% clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow, and the absence of end-organ damage (eg, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions). MGUS is usually an incidental finding on serum protein electrophoresis performed for unrelated reasons. The prevalence of MGUS increases with age, and it is found in over 3% of individuals >50 years of age. MGUS is associated with a small risk of progression to multiple myeloma or, less commonly, Waldenström macroglobulinemia or amyloidosis. Therefore, patients with MGUS should be followed with periodic serum protein electrophoresis to monitor for progression.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 68-year-old man, with a recent ischemic stroke due to a right middle cerebral artery thromboembolism, presents for evaluation. In addition to the abnormal neurologic findings, there are significant hepatosplenomegaly and multiple lymphadenopathies. Laboratory findings are significant for the following:
Hemoglobin  9.5 g/dL
Erythrocyte count 13,600/mm³
Platelet count 95,000/mm³
Urinalysis reveals the presence of Bence-Jones proteins. Bone marrow biopsy shows numerous small lymphocytes mixed with plasmacytoid dendritic cells and plasma cells, increased numbers of mast cells, and the presence of Russell bodies and Dutcher bodies in plasma cells. A diagnosis of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma is confirmed after further laboratory evaluation. Which of the following infectious agents would most likely be found in this patient, as well?
few_shot.explanation:
Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (LPL) is a rare, indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by small B lymphocytes, plasmacytoid lymphocytes, and plasma cells. The bone marrow, spleen, and lymph nodes are involved. It is associated with the production of monoclonal IgM (Waldenström macroglobulinemia) in most cases. Symptoms of hyperviscosity can occur (eg, blurry vision, Raynaud phenomenon, stroke). LPL has been associated with hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Other risk factors include a personal history of autoimmune conditions, immune-mediated conditions, and other cancers.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of worsening headaches and a rash for 2 weeks. His mother reports that the rash started on his abdomen and diffusely spread to other areas. Over the past 2 months, he has had recurrent episodes of otitis media. Examination shows a diffuse, erythematous, papular rash involving the groin, abdomen, chest, and back. His cervical lymph nodes are palpable bilaterally. An x-ray of the skull shows well-defined lytic lesions of the left occipital bone and the mastoid bone. Electron microscopy of a biopsy of the patient's posterior cervical lymph nodes shows polygonal cells with organelles shaped like tennis rackets. The cells stain positive for S-100. Clonal proliferation of which of the following types of cells is most likely seen on microscopy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent otitis media, rash, and lytic bone lesions are suggestive of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). LCH is a rare disorder characterized by clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells, which are dendritic cells normally found in the skin, lymph nodes, and bone marrow. Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting cells that play a role in cell-mediated immunity. In LCH, these cells proliferate and infiltrate various organ systems, leading to a variety of clinical manifestations. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, and patients often present with a rash that can be mistaken for eczema. Other common sites of involvement include the bone (causing lytic bone lesions and pathologic fractures), pituitary (causing diabetes insipidus), liver, spleen, and hematopoietic system. Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy of involved tissue, showing characteristic cells with convoluted, lobulated, or indented nuclei and abundant pink cytoplasm. Electron microscopy shows the presence of Birbeck granules, which are rod-shaped organelles with a linear central striation and a terminal expansion that resembles a tennis racket. The cells stain positive for S-100 and CD1a.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: An 80-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of a decreasing level of consciousness. He had blurred vision for several days. Two weeks ago, he had transient numbness in the right arm for 3 days. He was diagnosed with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance 2 years ago. He is not fully alert. His temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F), pulse is 75/min, respiratory rate is 13/min, and blood pressure is 125/70 mm Hg. He has gingival bleeding. Cervical lymphadenopathy is noted on palpation. Both the liver and spleen are palpated 6 cm below the costal margins. Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation is shown. Urine electrophoresis shows no abnormalities. A skeletal survey shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of blurred vision, altered mental status, and gingival bleeding, along with the physical examination findings of hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, are suggestive of hyperviscosity syndrome. This is a medical emergency that can occur in patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM), a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma that produces monoclonal IgM. The large size of the IgM molecule and its propensity to form autoantibodies can lead to hyperviscosity of the blood, which can cause a variety of symptoms, including those seen in this patient. The diagnosis of WM is supported by the serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, which shows a large monoclonal spike in the gamma region, indicating a high level of IgM.

The treatment of hyperviscosity syndrome involves plasmapheresis to remove the excess IgM from the blood. This can rapidly improve symptoms and prevent further complications. Other treatments for WM, such as chemotherapy, can be considered once the patient is stabilized.

So, the answer is [D].

question: A 31-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of acute onset neck pain and enlargement. Specifically, he reports that he has been experiencing pain and swelling of the anterior portion of his neck near the midline. Otherwise, he says that he has been getting tired easily and feels cold often. Physical exam reveals a painful diffusely enlarged thyroid gland with many small nodules. A biopsy is obtained showing diffuse cellular hyperplasia with areas of focal colloid hyperplasia. Given these findings, the patient is started on appropriate therapy, and the neck mass becomes smaller over time. Which of the following is most likely associated with the cause of this patient's symptoms?

few_shot.question:
A previously healthy 39-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a slowly enlarging, painless neck mass that she first noticed 3 months ago. During this period, she has also experienced intermittent palpitations, hair loss, and a weight loss of 4.5 kg (10 lb). There is no personal or family history of serious illness. She appears anxious and fidgety. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 101/min and irregular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a firm, nontender left anterior cervical nodule that moves with swallowing. Laboratory studies show:
TSH 0.4 μU/mL
T4 13.2 μg/dL
T3 196 ng/dL
Ultrasonography confirms the presence of a 3-cm solid left thyroid nodule. A thyroid 123I radionuclide scintigraphy scan shows increased uptake in a nodule in the left lobe of the thyroid gland with suppression of the remainder of the thyroid tissue. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's condition?"

answer_choices.A: Thyroid peroxidase autoantibody-mediated destruction of thyroid tissue
answer_choices.B: Gain-of-function mutations of the TSH receptor
answer_choices.D: Activation of oncogenes promoting cell division

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of weight loss, palpitations, and anxiety, along with her physical examination findings of a thyroid nodule and tachycardia, are suggestive of hyperthyroidism. The thyroid scan findings of a "hot" nodule with suppression of the remainder of the gland are consistent with a toxic adenoma (Plummer disease). Toxic adenomas are autonomously functioning thyroid nodules that produce thyroid hormone independent of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) stimulation. They are typically caused by gain-of-function mutations in the TSH receptor, which lead to constitutive activation of the receptor and subsequent increased synthesis and release of thyroid hormone.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician for a 1-week history of a painless swelling on the right side of his neck that he noticed while showering. He is 203 cm (6 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 85 kg (187 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m2. Physical examination shows long, thin fingers and an increased arm-length to body-height ratio. Examination of the neck shows a single 2-cm firm nodule. Ultrasonography of the neck shows a hypoechoic thyroid lesion with irregular margins. A core needle biopsy of the thyroid lesion shows sheets of polygonal cells surrounded by Congo red-stained amorphous tissue. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's tall stature, long, thin fingers, and increased arm-length to body-height ratio suggest Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene. The thyroid biopsy findings of polygonal cells surrounded by Congo red-stained amorphous tissue are consistent with medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), a neuroendocrine tumor that arises from the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland. MTC is associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by MTC, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism. MEN2 is caused by mutations in the RET proto-oncogene, which is also associated with Hirschsprung disease. The RET proto-oncogene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in cell growth and differentiation. 

The association between Marfan syndrome and MEN2 is not well established, but both conditions can occur in the same patient. In addition to MTC, patients with MEN2 are at risk for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism. They may also develop oral tumors, specifically neuromas, which are benign tumors of nerve tissue. These can occur on the tongue, buccal mucosa, and lips, and can cause a marfanoid body habitus.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 45-year old man comes to the physician because of a painless neck lump and a 2-month history of difficulty swallowing. He has a history of recurrent nephrolithiasis and episodic hypertension. Physical examination shows a 3 × 3-cm, nontender nodule at the level of the thyroid cartilage. A photomicrograph of a section of tissue obtained by core needle biopsy of the nodule is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The biopsy shows nests of cells in an amyloid stroma, which is characteristic of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). MTC arises from the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, which produce calcitonin. Calcitonin released by the tumor often leads to hypocalcemia, but this is usually asymptomatic as PTH can compensate. However, the increased calcitonin can lead to increased calcium phosphate product, leading to recurrent nephrolithiasis as seen in this patient.

MTC can occur sporadically or in a hereditary pattern as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2). Given this patient's episodic hypertension, he likely has MEN 2, which is associated with pheochromocytoma (causing episodic hypertension), MTC, and hyperparathyroidism.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of fever, anterior neck pain, and throat swelling. She has no history of serious illness. Her temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F) and pulse is 109/min. Physical examination shows diaphoresis and a fine tremor of the outstretched hands. The thyroid gland is enlarged, firm, and tender to palpation. Serum thyroid stimulating hormone level is 0.06 μU/mL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 65 mm/h. 123I scan shows an enlarged thyroid gland with diffusely decreased uptake. Histologic examination of a thyroid biopsy specimen is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.C: Lymphocytic infiltration with germinal follicle formation
answer_choices.D: Noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, anterior neck pain, and tender thyroid enlargement are suggestive of subacute thyroiditis, also known as de Quervain thyroiditis. This is a self-limited inflammatory disorder of the thyroid that is thought to be caused by a viral infection or postviral inflammatory process. It is often preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection and is more common in women.

Patients with subacute thyroiditis typically present with anterior neck pain that may radiate to the jaw or ears. On examination, the thyroid gland is usually enlarged and exquisitely tender. Patients may also have systemic symptoms such as fatigue, anorexia, and myalgia. Laboratory studies often show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level. Thyroid function tests may show a transient hyperthyroidism due to leakage of preformed thyroid hormone from the inflamed thyroid gland into the circulation. This is followed by a period of hypothyroidism as stores of thyroid hormone become depleted. Most patients eventually return to a euthyroid state.

Histologic examination of the thyroid gland in subacute thyroiditis shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. This is a nonspecific response to tissue injury and is not seen in other thyroid conditions.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man presents with a mass on his neck. He says that he first noticed the mass a few weeks ago while taking a shower. Since then, the mass has not increased in size. He denies any pain or difficulty in swallowing. Past medical history is unremarkable. Family history is significant for his father who had his thyroid removed when he was around his age but doesn’t know why. Review of systems is significant for occasional episodes of anxiety that include a pounding headache, racing heart, and sweating. His vital signs include: pulse 88/min, blood pressure 133/87 mm Hg, temperature 37.2°C (99.0°F), and respiratory rate 14/min. He is 183 cm (6 ft 2 in) tall with long extremities. On physical examination, the patient appears cachectic. There is a palpable 4 cm x 4 cm nodule present on the left lobe of the thyroid. Which of the following is the most likely thyroid pathology in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is suggestive of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B). MEN 2B is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytoma, and mucosal neuromas. MTC is a tumor of the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, which secrete calcitonin. It is the most common cause of death in MEN 2B and often presents as a thyroid nodule or mass. Pheochromocytoma can cause episodic hypertension and symptoms such as headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. Mucosal neuromas can cause a characteristic physical appearance, including thickened lips and bumpy tongue. Other features of MEN 2B include a marfanoid habitus (as seen in this patient) and intestinal ganglioneuromas, which can lead to constipation or diarrhea.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 56-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of sudden severe pain in his right great toe. Four months ago, he had an episode of severe joint pain involving his left knee that lasted several days and resolved with over-the-counter analgesics. He has a history of hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide and nephrolithiasis. Examination shows erythema, swelling, warmth, and tenderness of the right metatarsophalangeal joint; range of movement is limited by pain. His serum uric acid is 12 mg/dL. Arthrocentesis yields cloudy fluid with a leukocyte count of 18,500/mm3 (80% segmented neutrophils). Polarized light microscopy of the synovial fluid is shown. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the most appropriate long-term pharmacotherapy for this patient's condition?

answer_choices.A: Increased conversion of uric acid to allantoin

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency room for toe pain. He reports that his right great toe became acutely painful, red, and swollen approximately five hours prior. He has had one similar prior episode six months ago that resolved with indomethacin. His medical history is notable for obesity, hypertension, and alcohol abuse. He currently takes hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ). On physical examination, his right great toe is swollen, erythematous, and exquisitely tender to light touch. The patient is started on a new medication that decreases leukocyte migration and mitosis, and his pain eventually resolves; however, he develops nausea and vomiting as a result of therapy. Which of the following underlying mechanisms of action is characteristic of this patient’s new medication?

answer_choices.B: Prevents conversion of xanthine to uric acid
answer_choices.D: Metabolizes uric acid to water-soluble allantoin

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's acute onset of severe pain, swelling, and erythema of the great toe is consistent with gout. Gout is caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in the joints, leading to an inflammatory response. Risk factors for gout include obesity, alcohol abuse, and use of certain medications such as thiazide diuretics (eg, hydrochlorothiazide). 

Colchicine is a medication used for the treatment of acute gout flares. It works by inhibiting microtubule polymerization, which in turn inhibits leukocyte migration and phagocytosis, leading to decreased inflammation. However, colchicine can cause gastrointestinal side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 50-year-old man presents to the office with the complaint of pain in his left great toe. The pain started 2 days ago and has been progressively getting worse to the point that it is difficult to walk even a few steps. He adds that his left big toe is swollen and hot to the touch. He has never had similar symptoms in the past. He normally drinks 2–3 cans of beer every night but recently binge drank 3 nights ago. Physical examination is notable for an overweight gentleman (BMI of 35) in moderate pain, with an erythematous, swollen, and exquisitely tender left great toe. Laboratory results reveal a uric acid level of 9 mg/dL. A complete blood count shows:
Hemoglobin % 12 gm/dL
Hematocrit 45%
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 90 fL
Platelets 160,000/mm3
Leukocytes 8,000/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 65%
Lymphocytes 25%
Eosinophils 3%
Monocytes 7%
RBCs 5.6 million/mm3
Synovial fluid analysis shows:
Cell count 55,000 cells/mm3 (80% neutrophils)
Crystals negatively birefringent crystals present
Culture pending
Gram stain no organisms seen
Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the drug that will most likely be used in the long-term management of this patient?

answer_choices.A: Inhibits renal clearance of uric acid
answer_choices.D: Increases renal clearance of uric acid

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of an acutely painful, swollen, and erythematous joint, along with the finding of negatively birefringent crystals in the synovial fluid, is consistent with gout. Gout is caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in the joints due to hyperuricemia. The crystals trigger an inflammatory response, leading to the symptoms of gout.

The long-term management of gout involves the use of urate-lowering therapy to prevent recurrent attacks. Allopurinol is a first-line agent for this purpose. It is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that decreases the production of uric acid. Xanthine oxidase is an enzyme involved in the metabolism of purines, catalyzing the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. By inhibiting this enzyme, allopurinol reduces the production of uric acid, thereby lowering serum uric acid levels and preventing further attacks of gout.

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of severe pain and swelling of her left great toe. She has had similar episodes sporadically over the past 3 years. She drinks 6 beers daily. She does not smoke or use illicit drugs. She is allergic to hydrochlorothiazide and glipizide. Her current medications are amlodipine and metformin. Examination shows erythema, warmth, and tenderness of the left first metatarsophalangeal joint and a nodule over the right elbow. The most appropriate next step in treatment is the administration of a drug that has which of the following mechanisms of action?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's severe pain, swelling, and erythema of the first metatarsophalangeal joint are consistent with an acute gout attack. Gout is a disorder of purine metabolism that results in hyperuricemia and the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in tissues. Acute gout attacks are triggered by conditions that cause rapid changes in serum uric acid levels, such as alcohol consumption, starvation, surgery, or trauma. The first-line treatment for an acute gout attack is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), such as indomethacin or naproxen. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis by reversibly inhibiting the cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, which are responsible for the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins. Prostaglandins mediate inflammation and pain, so inhibiting their synthesis can help to relieve the symptoms of an acute gout attack.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 59-year-old man presents with intense, sharp pain in his toe for the past hour. He reports similar symptoms in the past and this is his 2nd visit to the emergency department this year with the same complaint. The patient is afebrile and the vital signs are within normal limits. On physical examination, there is significant erythema, swelling, warmth, and moderate pain on palpation of the right 1st toe. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable. A plain radiograph of the right foot reveals no abnormalities. Joint arthrocentesis of the inflamed toe reveals urate crystals. Laboratory studies show:
Serum glucose (random) 170 mg/dL
Sodium 140 mEq/L
Potassium 4.1 mEq/L
Chloride 100 mEq/L
Uric acid 7.2 mg/dL
Serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL

Cholesterol, total 170 mg/dL
HDL-cholesterol 43 mg/dL
LDL-cholesterol 73 mg/dL
Triglycerides 135 mg/dL
HDL: high-density lipoprotein; LDL: low-density lipoprotein
Ibuprofen is prescribed for the acute treatment of this patient's symptoms. He is also put on chronic therapy to prevent the recurrence of future attacks. Which of the following drugs is 1st-line for chronic therapy of gout?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent episodes of severe joint pain, swelling, and erythema are consistent with gout. Gout is a disorder of purine metabolism that results in the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in the joints and soft tissues. The 1st metatarsophalangeal joint is most commonly affected. The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals on joint fluid analysis.

The goal of chronic gout therapy is to prevent recurrent attacks and tophi formation. This is achieved by reducing serum uric acid levels to <6 mg/dL. Allopurinol, a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, is the 1st-line agent for chronic gout management. It reduces uric acid production and is effective in patients with overproduction or underexcretion of uric acid. Allopurinol is started once the acute attack has resolved and is often given along with colchicine or a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) to prevent an acute gout flare from the mobilization of stored uric acid.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old man presents to his physician with the complaint of a painful toe joint on his right foot. He states that the onset of pain came on suddenly, waking him up in the middle of the night. On physical exam, the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint of the big toe is swollen and erythematous. The physician obtains information regarding his past medical history and current medications. Which of the following medications would have the potential to exacerbate this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:

Gout is a disorder of purine metabolism that results in the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in the joints and soft tissues. It is often triggered by conditions that increase serum uric acid levels. Thiazide diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide, are a common cause of drug-induced hyperuricemia and gout. They decrease uric acid secretion in the proximal tubule, leading to increased serum uric acid levels.

question: A 65-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband after he found her with nausea, headache, and agitation 1 hour ago. When he left their lakeside cabin 6 hours before to go ice fishing and get more firewood, she did not have any symptoms. She has chronic migraines, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her medications include lisinopril and metformin, but she ran out of her anti-hypertensive medications over the weekend. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 21/min, and blood pressure is 154/92 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. She is confused and oriented only to person and place. She recalls only one of three objects after 5 minutes. Her gait is unsteady. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most effective intervention for this patient's current condition?

few_shot.question: A 63-year-old man is brought by his wife to the emergency department after he was found with nausea, headache, and agitation 1 hour ago. When the wife left their lakeside cabin earlier in the day to get more firewood, the patient did not have any symptoms. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Neurologic examination shows confusion and orientation only to person and place. He recalls only one of three objects after 5 minutes. His gait is unsteady. Which of the following is the most effective intervention for this patient's current condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's headache, nausea, and altered mental status after spending the day in a lakeside cabin with a wood-burning stove suggest carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. CO is a colorless, odorless gas produced by fuel-burning appliances. When inhaled, CO binds to hemoglobin with an affinity approximately 240 times that of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb). This reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and impairs oxygen release to the tissues, resulting in cellular hypoxia. The brain and heart are particularly sensitive to hypoxia, and the most common symptoms of CO poisoning are neurologic (eg, headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea/vomiting) and cardiac (eg, chest pain, dysrhythmias). Pulse oximetry is typically normal because it cannot differentiate between oxyhemoglobin and COHb.

The mainstay of treatment for CO poisoning is 100% normobaric oxygen, which accelerates the dissociation of CO from hemoglobin. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is recommended for patients with severe poisoning (eg, unconsciousness, neurologic signs, cardiovascular dysfunction, severe metabolic acidosis, COHb >25%). HBOT hastens clinical recovery and can prevent delayed neurologic sequelae by forcing oxygen into cells and displacing CO.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old woman presents to the emergency room with complaints of severe headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, and chest pain that have developed over the last several hours. Her past medical history is notable for diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Her temperature is 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 197/124 mm Hg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 19/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical examination is significant for papilledema. Urinalysis reveals gross hematuria and proteinuria. Which of the following is the next best step in management for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with hypertensive emergency, which is defined as severe hypertension (systolic blood pressure >180 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure >120 mm Hg) associated with evidence of acute end-organ damage. In this case, the patient has papilledema, which is indicative of hypertensive encephalopathy, and gross hematuria and proteinuria, which are indicative of hypertensive nephropathy. Hypertensive emergency is a medical emergency that requires immediate reduction in blood pressure to prevent or limit further end-organ damage. The goal is to reduce the mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% within minutes to 1 hour and then, if stable, to 160/100-110 mm Hg within the next 2-6 hours. Excessive falls in pressure can precipitate coronary, cerebral, or renal ischemia.

Intravenous (IV) antihypertensive agents are preferred for the initial management of hypertensive emergencies. IV beta blockers (eg, labetalol, esmolol) are often used as first-line agents. Esmolol is a cardioselective beta-1 adrenergic antagonist that decreases blood pressure by reducing systemic vascular resistance and has a rapid onset of action. It is an ideal agent for hypertensive emergencies because it is short-acting and easily titratable.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 44-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a severe headache and blurry vision for the past 3 hours. He has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. He has missed taking his medication for the past week as he was traveling. He is only oriented to time and person. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 92/min and regular, and blood pressure is 245/115 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Fundoscopy shows bilateral retinal hemorrhages and exudates. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. A complete blood count and serum concentrations of electrolytes, glucose, and creatinine are within the reference range. A CT scan of the brain shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's severe headache, blurry vision, altered mental status, and markedly elevated blood pressure are concerning for hypertensive emergency, specifically hypertensive encephalopathy. Hypertensive emergency is defined as severe hypertension (systolic blood pressure >180 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure >120 mm Hg) associated with evidence of acute end-organ damage. Hypertensive encephalopathy is a form of hypertensive emergency characterized by hypertension, altered mental status, and/or seizures. Neurologic examination is typically normal, but retinopathy (eg, flame-shaped hemorrhages, exudates, papilledema) is often present. Brain imaging is usually normal but may show cerebral edema. 

In hypertensive emergency, blood pressure should be reduced by no more than 25% within the first hour to avoid hypoperfusion of vital organs. Intravenous antihypertensive agents are preferred due to the ability to titrate to effect. Sodium nitroprusside is a direct arterial and venous vasodilator that is often used in hypertensive emergencies due to its rapid onset of action and easy titratability.

few_shot.question: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room by his mother for weakness, diaphoresis, and syncope. His mother says that he has never been diagnosed with any medical conditions but has been having “fainting spells” over the past month. Routine lab work reveals a glucose level of 25 mg/dL. The patient is promptly given glucagon and intravenous dextrose and admitted to the hospital for observation. The patient’s mother stays with him during his hospitalization. The patient is successfully watched overnight and his blood glucose levels normalize on his morning levels. The care team discusses a possible discharge during morning rounds. One hour later the nurse is called in for a repeat fainting episode. A c-peptide level is drawn and shown to be low. The patient appears ill, diaphoretic, and is barely arousable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this child?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent hypoglycemia, low C-peptide level, and the temporal relationship of his symptoms to his mother's presence are concerning for factitious disorder imposed on another (FDIA), also known as Munchausen syndrome by proxy. FDIA is a form of child abuse in which a caregiver, usually the mother, intentionally falsifies and/or induces a child's illness for attention or sympathy. The child is often subjected to unnecessary and potentially harmful medical care. In this case, the mother is likely administering insulin to the child, causing his hypoglycemia. The low C-peptide level supports exogenous insulin administration because C-peptide is released with endogenous insulin but not with exogenous insulin.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Fingerstick glucose at that time was 31 mg/dL and intramuscular glucagon was administered. The patient regained consciousness as she was being transported to the ambulance. Plasma glucose: 54 mg/dL
Plasma insulin: 29 pmol/L (normal < 19 pmol/L)
Plasma C-peptide: 272 pmol/L (normal < 200 pmol/L)
Plasma proinsulin: 8 pmol/L (normal < 5 pmol/L)
Plasma ß-hydroxybutyrate: 1.2 mmol/L (normal > 2.7 mmol/L after fasting)

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of sweating, tremulousness, and confusion are consistent with hypoglycemia. The Whipple triad is present: symptoms of hypoglycemia, documented low blood glucose, and resolution of symptoms after glucose administration. The patient's elevated insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin levels suggest endogenous hyperinsulinemia. The low ß-hydroxybutyrate level indicates that insulin is suppressing lipolysis and ketogenesis. The most likely cause of endogenous hyperinsulinemia in this patient is an insulinoma, a rare neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas. Insulinomas are typically small, solitary, and benign. They secrete insulin autonomously, causing hypoglycemia. Symptoms are often most pronounced after fasting or exercise, when insulin secretion should be suppressed. The diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide levels during a hypoglycemic episode.

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss are suggestive of new-onset diabetes mellitus. His presentation with vomiting, abdominal pain, and altered mental status is concerning for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a life-threatening complication of diabetes that typically occurs when insulin levels are insufficient to meet the body's basic metabolic requirements. DKA is characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. The most common precipitating factor is infection, but it may also be the initial presentation of diabetes, as in this patient.

Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, which results in an absolute insulin deficiency. The presence of anti-GAD antibodies in this patient is consistent with T1DM. GAD is an enzyme involved in the synthesis of gamma-aminobutyric acid in the brain and pancreatic beta cells. Anti-GAD antibodies are found in 70%-80% of patients with T1DM and can appear years before the onset of clinical symptoms.

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old man is brought in by ambulance to the ER, barely conscious, after feeling drowsy and falling to the floor during a presentation several hours ago. few_shot.question: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of fatigue and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss despite eating more than usual. The most common cause of hyperthyroidism is Graves' disease, an autoimmune disorder characterized by the presence of thyrotropin receptor autoantibodies (TRAb). These antibodies bind to and stimulate the thyrotropin receptor, leading to increased synthesis and release of thyroid hormone. The diffuse, non-tender swelling over the anterior neck is likely a goiter, which is a common finding in Graves' disease. The swelling of the eyelids and proptosis are due to Graves' ophthalmopathy, which is caused by inflammation and edema of the extraocular muscles due to TRAb.

few_shot.question: An otherwise healthy 47-year-old woman comes to the physician for the evaluation of a 4-month history of worsening fatigue and constipation. answer_choices.D: Activation of oncogenes promoting cell division

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of weight loss, palpitations, and anxiety, along with her physical examination findings of a thyroid nodule and tachycardia, are suggestive of hyperthyroidism. The thyroid scan findings of a "hot" nodule with suppression of the remainder of the gland are consistent with a toxic adenoma (Plummer disease). Toxic adenomas are autonomously functioning thyroid nodules that produce thyroid hormone independent of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) stimulation. They are typically caused by gain-of-function mutations in the TSH receptor, which lead to constitutive activation of the receptor and subsequent increased synthesis and release of thyroid hormone.

few_shot.question: A 48-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with complaints of persistent fatigue, dizziness, and weight loss for the past 3 months. She has a history of hypothyroidism and takes thyroxine replacement. Her blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg in a supine position and 65/40 mm Hg while sitting, temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), and pulse is 75/min. On physical examination, there is a mild increase in thyroid size, with a rubbery consistency. Her skin shows diffuse hyperpigmentation, more pronounced in the oral mucosa and palmar creases. Which of the following best represent the etiology of this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.A: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal gland
answer_choices.B: ↓ adrenocorticotropic hormone secretion from the pituitary gland
answer_choices.C: ↓ corticotropin-releasing hormone secretion from the hypothalamus
answer_choices.D: ↑ iron absorption and deposition in the body

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fatigue, dizziness, weight loss, and hyperpigmentation are suggestive of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). The most common cause of Addison's disease in developed countries is autoimmune destruction of the adrenal gland, often as part of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type II (APS II). APS II is characterized by the presence of autoimmune adrenal insufficiency and autoimmune thyroid disease (eg, Hashimoto thyroiditis, as suggested by this patient's hypothyroidism and enlarged thyroid gland), and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus. 

In primary adrenal insufficiency, the adrenal glands are unable to produce glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone). The lack of cortisol leads to increased adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) production via loss of negative feedback, and the high ACTH levels stimulate melanocytes, leading to hyperpigmentation. The lack of aldosterone impairs the kidney's ability to retain sodium and water, leading to volume depletion, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. This can cause postural hypotension, as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with fatigue, dry cough, and shortness of breath for 3 days. He reports a slight fever and has also had 3 episodes of watery diarrhea earlier that morning. Last week, he attended a business meeting at a hotel and notes some of his coworkers have also become sick. He has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He takes atorvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide, and lisinopril. He appears in mild distress. His temperature is 102.1°F (38.9°C), pulse is 56/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. Diffuse crackles are heard in the thorax. Examination shows a soft and nontender abdomen. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL
Leukocyte count 15,000/mm3
Platelet count 130,000/mm3
Serum
Na+ 129 mEq/L
Cl- 100 mEq/L
K+ 4.6 mEq/L
HCO3- 22 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL
An x-ray of the chest shows infiltrates in both lungs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fever, cough, and diarrhea, along with the history of recent travel and similar symptoms in his coworkers, are suggestive of Legionella pneumophila infection. Legionella is a gram-negative bacillus that is found in freshwater environments. It can colonize hot water tanks, hot tubs, and cooling towers, and is often associated with travel and cruise ships. Infection is caused by inhalation of aerosolized bacteria. The most common presentation is pneumonia, which can range from mild to severe. Gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, diarrhea, anorexia, abdominal pain) are also common. Hyponatremia is a common electrolyte abnormality seen in Legionella infection.

The diagnosis of Legionella infection is most often made by urinary antigen testing, which is both sensitive and specific for L pneumophila serogroup 1, the most common cause of human disease. The urinary antigen test can provide results within hours and can remain positive for days to weeks, allowing for retrospective diagnosis.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with altered mental status. The patient is non-verbal at baseline, but his caretakers at the nursing home noticed he was particularly somnolent recently. The patient has a past medical history of diabetes and Alzheimer dementia. His temperature is 99.7°F (37.6°C), blood pressure is 157/98 mmHg, pulse is 150/min, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Laboratory values are obtained and shown below.

Hemoglobin: 9 g/dL
Hematocrit: 33%
Leukocyte count: 8,500/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 197,000/mm^3

Serum:

Cl-: 102 mEq/L
K+: 4.3 mEq/L
HCO3-: 25 mEq/L
BUN: 37 mg/dL
Glucose: 99 mg/dL
Creatinine: 2.4 mg/dL
Ca2+: 12.2 mg/dL

The patient has lost 20 pounds over the past month. His parathyroid hormone is within normal limits, and his urinary calcium is increased. Physical exam demonstrates discomfort when the patient's lower back and extremities are palpated. Which of the following is the most accurate diagnostic test for this patient's underlying diagnosis?

answer_choices.C: Urine, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid cultures

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, and bone pain (manifested as tenderness to palpation of the lower back and extremities) is suggestive of multiple myeloma (MM). MM is a malignancy of plasma cells that primarily occurs in older adults. The hypercalcemia is due to increased osteoclastic bone resorption, and the renal insufficiency can be caused by hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, amyloidosis, and/or nephrotoxic light chain proteins. The anemia is due to replacement of normal bone marrow elements by malignant plasma cells and, in some cases, suppression of normal plasma cell development by cytokines.

The most accurate diagnostic test for MM is bone marrow biopsy, which typically shows >10% clonal plasma cells. Other diagnostic criteria for MM include evidence of end-organ damage (eg, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) and the presence of a monoclonal protein (M protein) in the serum or urine.

So, the answer is [A].
