few_shot.question:
A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with increased fatigue. He states that he has been feeling very tired lately but today lost consciousness while walking up the stairs. He report mild abdominal distension/discomfort, weight loss, a persistent cough, and multiple episodes of waking up drenched in sweat in the middle of the night. The patient does not see a primary care physician but admits to smoking 2 to 3 packs of cigarettes per day and drinking 1 to 3 alcoholic beverages per day. He recently traveled to Taiwan and Nicaragua. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 177/98 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On physical exam, you note a fatigued appearing elderly man who is well-groomed. Cardiopulmonary exam reveals mild expiratory wheezes. Abdominal exam is notable for a non-pulsatile mass in the left upper quadrant. Laboratory values are ordered as seen below.

Hemoglobin: 12 g/dL
Hematocrit: 36%
Leukocyte count: 105,500/mm^3
Platelet count: 197,000/mm^3

Serum:
Na+: 139 mEq/L
Cl-: 100 mEq/L
K+: 4.3 mEq/L
HCO3-: 25 mEq/L
BUN: 20 mg/dL
Glucose: 92 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.4 mg/dL
Ca2+: 10.2 mg/dL
Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score: 25 (range 20 - 100)
AST: 12 U/L
ALT: 17 U/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, and splenomegaly is concerning for a hematologic malignancy. The markedly elevated leukocyte count with a left shift (ie, increased immature cells) is consistent with a leukemia. The leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is used to help differentiate chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) from a leukemoid reaction (eg, due to infection, malignancy, severe hemorrhage or hemolysis). The LAP score reflects the activity of neutrophil alkaline phosphatase; mature neutrophils have more alkaline phosphatase than immature forms. Therefore, the LAP score is high in conditions associated with mature neutrophil proliferation (eg, leukemoid reaction) and low in conditions associated with proliferation of immature neutrophils (eg, CML). This patient's low LAP score is consistent with CML.

CML is a myeloproliferative disorder characterized by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, which results from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22. This translocation creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene, which codes for a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that promotes unregulated cell division and inhibits DNA repair and apoptosis. CML has 3 phases: chronic, accelerated, and blast crisis. Most patients are diagnosed in the chronic phase, which is often asymptomatic or associated with only mild symptoms (eg, fatigue, left upper quadrant fullness/discomfort). The accelerated phase is characterized by increasing symptoms, splenomegaly, and difficulty controlling the white blood cell count. Blast crisis resembles acute leukemia, with symptoms caused by bone marrow failure (eg, fever, bone pain, bleeding, infection) and extramedullary blast proliferation.

So, the answer is [C].

question: A 5-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician due to sore throat and fever. He was in his usual state of health until 3 days ago when he began to complain of a sore throat as well as general malaise. The patient's past medical history reveals recurrent upper respiratory infections but no skin or soft tissue infections. The child had cardiac surgery as an infant but has otherwise been healthy. On presentation, his temperature is 100°F (37.8 °C), blood pressure is 115/72 mmHg, pulse is 65/min, and respirations are 22/min. Physical exam shows white plaques on the tongue and mouth. A scraping of this material reveals a characteristic morphology after being treated with KOH. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a normal distribution of bands from this patient. answer_choices.A: Delayed separation of the umbilical cord

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician with a 2-day history of fever, chills, malaise, and a sore throat. He has otherwise been healthy and development is normal for his age. He takes no medications. His immunizations are up-to-date. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.4°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 121/71 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry shows an oxygen saturation of 100% on room air. Examination shows discrete 1–2-mm papulovesicular lesions on the posterior oropharynx and general erythema of the tonsils bilaterally. Which of the following conditions is most likely associated with the cause of this patient's findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, sore throat, and vesicular lesions on the posterior oropharynx are suggestive of herpangina, a disease caused by Coxsackie A virus. Coxsackie A virus is a member of the enterovirus family and is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. Herpangina is most common in children and typically occurs in the summer and early fall. Patients present with high fever, sore throat, and dysphagia. Oral lesions begin as small red macules that evolve into 1- to 2-mm vesicles with surrounding erythema, and then quickly ulcerate. The ulcers are usually located on the posterior oropharynx, including the tonsillar pillars, tonsils, uvula, and soft palate. Coxsackie A virus can also cause hand, foot, and mouth disease, which is characterized by oral ulcers and a vesicular rash on the hands and feet.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a sore throat and trouble breathing. His mother states that his symptoms started last night and have rapidly been worsening. The patient is typically healthy, has received all his childhood immunizations, and currently takes a daily multivitamin. His temperature is 103°F (39.4°C), blood pressure is 100/64 mmHg, pulse is 155/min, respirations are 29/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Physical exam is notable for an ill-appearing child who is drooling and is leaning forward to breathe. He does not answer questions and appears very uncomfortable. He will not comply with physical exam to open his mouth for inspection of the oropharynx. Which of the following is the most likely infectious etiology of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, sore throat, drooling, and stridor is consistent with epiglottitis. Epiglottitis is a life-threatening infection of the epiglottis and surrounding tissues that can cause airway obstruction. It is most commonly caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), but since the introduction of the Hib vaccine, the incidence of Hib epiglottitis has decreased dramatically. Other organisms that can cause epiglottitis include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Staphylococcus aureus.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy presents to his pediatrician accompanied by his mother for evaluation of a rash. The rash appeared a little over a week ago, and since that time the boy has felt tired. He is less interested in playing outside, preferring to remain indoors because his knees and stomach hurt. His past medical history is significant for an upper respiratory infection that resolved uneventfully without treatment 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 18/min. Physical exam shows scattered maroon macules and papules on the lower extremities. The abdomen is diffusely tender to palpation. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy or conjunctival injection. Which of the following will most likely be found in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of palpable purpura, arthralgia, and abdominal pain following an upper respiratory infection is suggestive of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura). This is the most common vasculitis of childhood and often presents following a recent infection. It is caused by the deposition of IgA immune complexes in the skin, gut, and glomeruli, leading to a leukocytoclastic vasculitis that affects small vessels. The classic tetrad of symptoms includes palpable purpura (often over the buttocks and lower extremities), arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal disease (hematuria and/or proteinuria). The abdominal pain can be severe and may be associated with intussusception.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 5-day history of fever, malaise, and joint pain. He had a sore throat 4 weeks ago that resolved without treatment. His temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F) and blood pressure is 84/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows several firm, painless nodules under the skin near his elbows and the dorsal aspect of both wrists. Cardiopulmonary examination shows bilateral basilar crackles and a blowing, holosystolic murmur heard best at the cardiac apex. Both knee joints are warm. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 129 mm/h. The immune response seen in this patient is most likely due to the presence of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, migratory polyarthritis, carditis, and subcutaneous nodules are suggestive of acute rheumatic fever (ARF), a delayed immune-mediated complication of group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis. The skin nodules seen in ARF are firm, painless, and measure 0.5-2 cm in diameter. They are typically located over bony prominences or extensor surfaces of joints. The carditis of ARF manifests as a new murmur, pericarditis, and/or congestive heart failure. The arthritis is migratory, involving large joints.

ARF is thought to result from molecular mimicry, in which structural components of GAS resemble molecules in human tissues. GAS M protein, a virulence factor that inhibits phagocytosis, shares antigenic epitopes with human tissues (eg, myocardium, synovium, brain). Antibodies formed against M protein can cross-react with human tissues, leading to inflammation and the clinical manifestations of ARF.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of fever for the past 3 days. They also state that he has been less active and has been refusing to eat. The patient has had two episodes of bilateral otitis media since birth. He was born at term and had severe respiratory distress and sepsis shortly after birth that was treated with antibiotics. Umbilical cord separation occurred at the age of 33 days. The patient appears pale. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 170/min, and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. He is at the 25th percentile for height and 15th percentile for weight. Examination shows a capillary refill time of 4 seconds. Oral examination shows white mucosal patches that bleed when they are scraped off. There is bilateral mucoid, nonpurulent ear discharge. Several scaly erythematous skin lesions are seen on the chest. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 38,700/mm3 with 90% neutrophils and a platelet count of 200,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent otitis media, and severe neonatal infection is suggestive of leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD). LAD is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by recurrent bacterial and fungal infections without pus formation, impaired wound healing, and delayed separation of the umbilical cord (>30 days). The most common type of LAD (type 1) is caused by a defect in the beta-2 integrin molecule (CD18) on phagocytes. This molecule is necessary for binding to adhesion molecules on endothelial cells and for migration out of blood vessels (diapedesis). As a result, patients with LAD have neutrophilia because neutrophils are unable to migrate from the vasculature into tissues. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 3-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-hour history of somnolence, poor feeding, and one episode of vomiting. He is exclusively breastfed. His serum glucose concentration is 88 mg/dL and his serum ammonia concentration is 850 μmol/L (N<90). Urinalysis shows an increased orotic acid to creatinine ratio. Urinary ketones are absent. This patient is most likely deficient in an enzyme that catalyzes which of the following reactions?

answer_choices.A: Ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate to citrulline
answer_choices.D: Glutamate and acetyl-coenzyme A to N-acetylglutamate

few_shot.question: A 4-day-old boy is brought to the physician because of somnolence, poor feeding, and vomiting after his first few breast feedings. He appears lethargic. His respiratory rate is 73/min. Serum ammonia is markedly increased. Genetic analysis shows deficiency in N-acetylglutamate synthase. The activity of which of the following enzymes is most likely directly affected by this genetic defect?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, tachypnea, and hyperammonemia suggest a urea cycle disorder. The urea cycle is a series of biochemical reactions in the liver that convert nitrogen, a waste product of protein metabolism, to urea for excretion in the urine. Deficiencies in any of the enzymes involved in the urea cycle can cause hyperammonemia.

N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS) deficiency is a rare cause of hyperammonemia that presents similarly to carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS1) deficiency. NAGS catalyzes the formation of N-acetylglutamate, which is an essential allosteric activator of CPS1, the first enzyme of the urea cycle. CPS1 catalyzes the reaction of bicarbonate, ammonia, and 2 ATP molecules to form carbamoyl phosphate. Therefore, a deficiency in NAGS impairs the activity of CPS1, leading to decreased synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate and subsequent hyperammonemia.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 2-week-old boy presents to the emergency department because of unusual irritability and lethargy. The patient is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit and minutes later develops metabolic encephalopathy. This progressed to a coma, followed by death before any laboratory tests are completed. The infant was born at home via vaginal delivery at 39 weeks' of gestation. His mother says that the symptoms started since the infant was 4-days-old, but since he only seemed ‘tired’, she decided not to seek medical attention. Further testing during autopsy shows hyperammonemia, low citrulline, and increased orotic acid. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of irritability, lethargy, and metabolic encephalopathy progressing to coma and death is suggestive of a urea cycle disorder. The urea cycle is responsible for the conversion of toxic ammonia to urea, which is then excreted in the urine. Defects in any of the enzymes involved in the urea cycle can lead to hyperammonemia, which can cause neurological symptoms due to the neurotoxic effects of ammonia.

The finding of low citrulline and increased orotic acid in this patient is indicative of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency. OTC is responsible for the conversion of ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate to citrulline in the urea cycle. Deficiency of this enzyme leads to an accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate, which is then converted to orotic acid, leading to increased levels of orotic acid in the blood and urine.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 25-day-old newborn is brought to the pediatrician for lethargy, poor muscle tone, and feeding difficulty with occasional regurgitation that recently turned into projectile vomiting. The child was born via vaginal delivery without complications. On examination, the vital signs include: pulse 130/min, respiratory rate 30/min, blood pressure 96/60 mm Hg, and temperature 36.5°C (97.7°F). The physical examination shows a broad nasal bridge, oral thrush, hepatosplenomegaly, and generalized hypotonia. Further tests of blood and urine samples help the pediatrician to diagnose the child with an enzyme deficiency. More extensive laboratory testing reveals normal levels of citrulline and hypoglycemia. There are also elevated levels of ketone bodies, glycine, and methylmalonic acid. Which of the following is the product of the reaction catalyzed by the deficient enzyme in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of lethargy, poor muscle tone, feeding difficulty, and vomiting, along with the physical findings of a broad nasal bridge, oral thrush, hepatosplenomegaly, and generalized hypotonia, are suggestive of a metabolic disorder. The laboratory findings of hypoglycemia, elevated levels of ketone bodies, glycine, and methylmalonic acid, and normal levels of citrulline, are consistent with a diagnosis of methylmalonic acidemia. This is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which catalyzes the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. This reaction is an important step in the breakdown of odd-chain fatty acids and certain amino acids. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 4-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of lethargy and vomiting since he woke up 1 hour ago. The mother says that he last breastfed the previous evening and slept through the night for the first time. His family recently immigrated from Bolivia. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.2°F). Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and enlarged, reddened tonsils. Serum studies show:

Ketones 0.2 mg/dL N = < 1 mg/dL
AST 40 U/L
ALT 60 U/L
Ammonia 80 μ/dL (N=15–45)
Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of lethargy, vomiting, and hypoglycemia after a period of fasting is suggestive of a disorder of fatty acid oxidation. Fatty acids are the major source of energy for the body during prolonged fasting. Inability to utilize fatty acids due to an enzymatic deficiency results in hypoketotic hypoglycemia. Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency is the most common disorder of fatty acid oxidation. It is an autosomal recessive disorder that typically presents between ages 3-24 months, often triggered by a minor illness or fasting. Symptoms include vomiting, lethargy, seizures, and possible progression to coma. Laboratory findings include hypoketotic hypoglycemia and increased liver transaminases. Treatment involves avoidance of fasting and aggressive glucose administration during times of illness.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to vomiting and weakness. He is attending a summer camp and was on a hike with the other kids and a camp counselor. His friends say that the boy skipped breakfast, and the counselor says he forgot to pack snacks for the kids during the hike. The child’s parents are contacted and report that the child has been completely healthy since birth. They also say there is an uncle who would have to eat regularly or he would have similar symptoms. At the hospital, his heart rate is 90/min, respiratory rate is 17/min, blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg, and temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). Physical examination reveals a visibly lethargic child with slight disorientation to time and place. Mild hepatosplenomegaly is observed but no signs of dehydration are noted. A blood sample is drawn, and fluids are started via an intravenous line.
Lab report
Serum glucose 44 mg/dL
Serum ketones absent
    Serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL
Blood urea nitrogen 32 mg/dL
    Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 425 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  372 U/L
    Hemoglobin (Hb%) 12.5 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 80 fl
Reticulocyte count 1%
Erythrocyte count 5.1 million/mm3
Which of the following is most likely deficient in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and elevated transaminases after fasting is suggestive of a glycogen storage disease (GSD). GSDs are a group of inherited disorders characterized by abnormal glycogen metabolism, leading to glycogen accumulation in various tissues. The specific subtype of GSD can often be determined based on the clinical presentation.

The most likely diagnosis in this patient is GSD type III (Cori disease), which is caused by a deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme (amylo-1,6-glucosidase). This enzyme has two main functions: 1) transfer of a trisaccharide unit from a branch to the main chain (transferase activity), and 2) cleavage of the α-1,6-linkage at the branch point, releasing free glucose (glucosidase activity). In Cori disease, both activities are deficient, leading to accumulation of short outer chains of glycogen (limit dextrin) in the cytosol.

Patients with Cori disease typically present in infancy or early childhood with hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and growth retardation. In contrast to GSD type I (von Gierke disease), lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia are typically absent because glucose-6-phosphatase is intact, allowing for shunting of glucose-6-phosphate into the glycolytic pathway. Additionally, these patients have normal lactate levels following meals. Although patients can have severe hypoglycemia, ketotic hypoglycemia is rare because the release of free glucose by the glucosidase activity of the debranching enzyme is not required for gluconeogenesis or ketogenesis.

So, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [C] > [B] > [D].

question: A 23-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal examination. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated and she gave birth to a healthy boy. Her blood group is A, Rh-negative. The father's blood group is B, Rh-positive. Administration of which of the following is most appropriate at this time?

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old G1P0 woman presents for her first prenatal visit. Past medical history reveals the patient is blood type O negative, and the father is type A positive. The patient refuses Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM), because it is derived from human plasma, and she says she doesn’t want to take the risk of contracting HIV. Which of the following is correct regarding the potential condition her baby may develop?

answer_choices.A: Rho(D) immune globulin is needed both before and immediately after delivery to protect this baby from developing the condition
answer_choices.B: She should receive Rho(D) immune globulin to prevent the development of Rh(D) alloimmunization
answer_choices.C: The Rho(D) immune globulin will also protect the baby against other Rh antigens aside from Rh(D)
answer_choices.D: The injection can be avoided because the risk of complications of this condition is minimal

few_shot.explanation:
Rh(D) alloimmunization is a condition that can occur in Rh(D)-negative mothers who are exposed to Rh(D)-positive fetal blood. This can occur during delivery, miscarriage, abortion, or trauma. The mother's immune system can then produce anti-Rh(D) antibodies, which can cross the placenta and cause hemolysis in an Rh(D)-positive fetus. This can lead to severe anemia, hydrops fetalis, and even death in the fetus or newborn. Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM) is a medication that can prevent the mother's immune system from becoming sensitized to the Rh(D) antigen, thereby preventing Rh(D) alloimmunization. It is typically given at 28 weeks gestation and within 72 hours after delivery of an Rh(D)-positive infant. It can also be given after a miscarriage, abortion, or trauma. However, it does not protect against other Rh antigens.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old G1P0 female at 32 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding. She has had minimal prenatal care to-date with only an initial visit with an obstetrician after a positive home pregnancy test. She describes minimal spotting that she noticed earlier today that has progressed to larger amounts of blood; she estimates 30 mL of blood loss. She denies any cramping, pain, or contractions, and she reports feeling continued movements of the baby. Ultrasound and fetal heart rate monitoring confirm the presence of a healthy fetus without any evidence of current or impending complications. The consulted obstetrician orders blood testing for Rh-status of both the mother as well as the father, who brought the patient to the hospital. Which of the following represents the best management strategy for this situation?

answer_choices.A: If mother is Rh-negative and father is Rh-positive then administer RhoGAM
answer_choices.B: If mother is Rh-positive and father is Rh-negative then administer RhoGAM
answer_choices.C: If mother is Rh-negative and father is Rh-positive, RhoGAM administration is not needed
answer_choices.D: After 28 weeks gestation, administration of RhoGAM will have no benefit

few_shot.explanation:
The Rh blood group system is a complex system of antigens that are expressed on the surface of red blood cells. The most important of these antigens is the D antigen, which is the most immunogenic of the Rh antigens. Individuals who express the D antigen are referred to as Rh-positive, while those who do not express the D antigen are referred to as Rh-negative.

Rh incompatibility can occur when an Rh-negative mother is exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood, either during delivery or due to fetomaternal hemorrhage during pregnancy. This can lead to the production of anti-D antibodies by the mother, which can cross the placenta and cause hemolytic disease of the newborn in subsequent pregnancies.

Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM) is a medication that can prevent the production of anti-D antibodies in Rh-negative mothers. It is typically given at 28 weeks gestation and within 72 hours after delivery if the baby is Rh-positive. It can also be given after any event that could potentially lead to fetomaternal hemorrhage, such as amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, abdominal trauma, or vaginal bleeding.

In this case, the patient is experiencing vaginal bleeding, which could potentially lead to fetomaternal hemorrhage. Therefore, if the mother is Rh-negative and the father is Rh-positive (meaning the baby could potentially be Rh-positive), RhoGAM should be administered to prevent the production of anti-D antibodies.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [C] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 38 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department in active labor. She received all of her prenatal care for this pregnancy. Pregnancy and delivery of her first child were uncomplicated. The patient's blood type is Rh-negative. Four hours after arrival, a healthy 3650-g (8-lb) female newborn is delivered. Delivery of the fetus is followed by placental retention and heavy vaginal bleeding. One hour later, the placenta is manually removed and the bleeding ceases. The mother's temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination shows blood on the vulva, the introitus, and on the medial aspect of each thigh. The neonate's blood type is Rh-positive. A single dose of anti-D immune globulin is administered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
The rosette test is a screening test used to detect fetomaternal hemorrhage (FMH) in Rh-negative mothers of Rh-positive infants. FMH can occur during pregnancy or at the time of delivery and can lead to maternal alloimmunization and hemolytic disease of the newborn in subsequent pregnancies. The rosette test is performed on maternal blood and is positive if FMH is >30 mL. If the rosette test is positive, the Kleihauer-Betke test is performed to quantify the volume of FMH and to determine the appropriate dose of anti-D immune globulin. 

In this patient, the retained placenta and heavy vaginal bleeding increase the risk of FMH. Therefore, the rosette test should be performed to screen for FMH.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [C] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old primigravid woman who recently immigrated to the United States presents to her gynecologist for the first time during the 28th week of her pregnancy. She hasn’t received any prenatal care or folic acid supplementation. The patient’s history reveals that she has received blood transfusions in the past due to “severe anemia.” Which of the following blood type situations would put the fetus at risk for hemolytic disease of the newborn?

answer_choices.A: Mother is O positive, father is B negative
answer_choices.B: Mother is A negative, father is B positive
answer_choices.C: Mother is AB negative, father is O negative
answer_choices.D: Mother is O positive, father is AB negative

few_shot.explanation:
Hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) is a condition that occurs when there is an incompatibility between the blood types of the mother and baby. This can lead to the mother's immune system attacking the baby's red blood cells, leading to hemolysis. The most common cause of HDN is Rh incompatibility, which occurs when the mother is Rh negative and the baby is Rh positive. This is because Rh negative individuals do not have the D antigen, and can produce anti-D antibodies if exposed to the D antigen, such as through a blood transfusion or during childbirth. In subsequent pregnancies, these antibodies can cross the placenta and cause hemolysis in an Rh positive fetus.

In this case, the mother is A negative and the father is B positive. This means that the baby could be Rh positive, which would put it at risk for HDN due to the mother's Rh negative status.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [D] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old woman presents to her new doctor at 27 weeks' gestation with her second pregnancy. Her blood type is B- and the father of the child is B+. Her first child had an Apgar score of 7 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes and has a B+ blood type. The fetus has a heart rate of 130/min and blood pressure of 100/58 mm Hg. There is a concern that the fetus may develop erythroblastosis fetalis (EF). Which of the following statements is true about erythroblastosis fetalis?

answer_choices.A: Can occur with an Rh-negative mother and Rh-positive father.
answer_choices.B: Rho(D) immune globulin should be administered during the first trimester.
answer_choices.C: The combination of an Rh-positive mother and an Rh-negative fetus will cause the condition.
answer_choices.D: In EF, IgM crosses the placenta and causes erythrocyte hemolysis in the fetus.

few_shot.explanation:
Erythroblastosis fetalis (EF) is a condition that occurs when the red blood cells of a fetus are attacked by antibodies produced by the mother's immune system. This can occur when the mother is Rh-negative and the father is Rh-positive, and the fetus inherits the Rh-positive blood type from the father. The mother's immune system can produce antibodies against the Rh antigen on the fetal red blood cells, leading to hemolysis and anemia in the fetus. This can cause a range of complications, including heart failure, hydrops fetalis, and death.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

question: An 18-year-old male is brought in by fire rescue. The patient was an unrestrained passenger in a motor vehicle crash and was ejected from the vehicle after collision. Upon arrival to the trauma bay, the patient has a Glasgow coma scale (GCS) of 6. He is rapidly intubated, and vitals are a temperature of 99.5°F (37.5°C), pulse of 130 bpm, and blood pressure of 83/64 mmHg. He is noted to have multiple ecchymoses over his body, as well as petechiae and purpura. He has a laceration over his clavicle that continues to bleed despite a pressure bandage. Radiographs of his lower extremity show multiple long bone fractures. Two large bore IV lines are placed, and the patient oozes from around the sites of venepuncture. Labs are notable for a WBC of 20,000/mm^3, Hb of 10.1g/dL, platelets of 48,000/mm^3, and prolongation of the PT and aPTT. This patient's presentation can best be explained by which of the following diagnoses?

few_shot.question: A 53-year-old man is brought in by EMS to the emergency room. He was an unrestrained driver in a motor vehicle crash. Upon arrival to the trauma bay, the patient's Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 13. He appears disoriented and is unable to follow commands. Vital signs are: temperature 98.9 F, heart rate 142 bpm, blood pressure 90/45 mmHg, respirations 20 per minute, shallow with breath sounds bilaterally and SpO2 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a midline trachea, prominent jugular venous distention, and distant heart sounds on cardiac auscultation. A large ecchymosis is found overlying the sternum. Which of the following best explains the underlying physiology of this patient's hypotension?

answer_choices.A: Hypovolemia due to hemorrhage resulting in decreased preload
answer_choices.B: Hypovolemia due to distributive shock and pooling of intravascular volume in capacitance vessels
answer_choices.C: Impaired left ventricular filling resulting in decreased left ventricular stroke volume
answer_choices.D: Increased peripheral vascular resistance, resulting in increased afterload

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with cardiac tamponade, a life-threatening condition that occurs when fluid accumulates in the pericardial sac and compresses the heart. This can occur due to trauma, malignancy, or other causes. The classic findings of cardiac tamponade are hypotension, jugular venous distention, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad). Other findings can include pulsus paradoxus and electrical alternans on EKG.

The underlying pathophysiology of cardiac tamponade involves impaired filling of the left ventricle due to the increased pressure in the pericardial sac. This leads to decreased stroke volume and cardiac output, resulting in hypotension.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question:
A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. The patient was found unconscious in his bedroom after a suicide attempt. The patient had cut his wrists using a kitchen knife. The patient is unresponsive and pale. His temperature is 96°F (35.6°C), blood pressure is 70/35 mmHg, pulse is 190/min, respirations are 19/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Pressure is applied to his bilateral wrist lacerations. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 7. A full trauma assessment is performed and reveals no other injuries. IV fluids are started as well as a rapid transfusion sequence. Norepinephrine is administered. Repeat vitals demonstrate that his blood pressure is 100/65 mmHg and pulse is 100/min. The patient is responsive and seems mildly confused. Resuscitation is continued and the patient's GCS improves to 15. Thirty minutes later, the patient's GCS is 11. His temperature is 103°F (39.4°C), blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 122/min, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. The patient complains of flank pain. Laboratory values are ordered and demonstrate the following:

Hemoglobin: 9 g/dL
Hematocrit: 27%
Leukocyte count: 10,500 cells/mm^3 with normal differential
Haptoglobin: 11 mg/dL
Platelet count: 198,000/mm^3

Serum:
Na+: 139 mEq/L
Cl-: 101 mEq/L
K+: 4.4 mEq/L
HCO3-: 23 mEq/L
BUN: 27 mg/dL
Glucose: 99 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.5 mg/dL
Ca2+: 10.0 mg/dL
Bilirubin: 3.2 mg/dL
AST: 22 U/L
ALT: 15 U/L

Which of the following describes the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with a transfusion reaction due to major blood group incompatibility. Major blood group incompatibility occurs when the recipient has preformed antibodies against the donor's red blood cell (RBC) antigens. This is most commonly due to ABO incompatibility, which can occur if a patient with blood type O (who has anti-A and anti-B antibodies) receives a transfusion of blood type A, B, or AB. This can cause an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, which is a medical emergency.

The symptoms of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction can include fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and flank pain due to hemoglobinuria. Laboratory findings can include anemia, hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and an increased indirect bilirubin level. The haptoglobin level can also be low due to its binding to free hemoglobin.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old male is brought in by fire rescue after being the restrained driver in a motor vehicle accident. There was a prolonged extraction. At the scene, the patient was GCS 13. The patient was boarded and transported. In the trauma bay, vitals are T 97.2 F, HR 132 bpm, BP 145/90 mmHG, RR 22 rpm, and O2 Sat 100%. ABCs are intact with a GCS of 15, and on secondary survey you note the following (Figure F). FAST exam is positive at Morrison's pouch. Abdominal exam shows exquisite tenderness to palpation with rebound and guarding. Which of the following radiographs is most likely to be present in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a positive FAST exam and a seatbelt sign on physical exam. The seatbelt sign is a physical exam finding that is associated with a high likelihood of intra-abdominal injury. The seatbelt sign is an ecchymosis that is seen in the distribution of a seatbelt. This is a result of the seatbelt holding the patient in place during a motor vehicle collision while the organs inside the body continue to move forward due to momentum. This can cause shearing forces that can result in injury to the organs and/or vasculature of the abdomen. The seatbelt sign is associated with a high likelihood of intra-abdominal injury, and in this case, the patient has a positive FAST exam and a peritoneal abdominal exam, which is an indication for emergent surgical exploration. The most likely radiograph to be seen in this patient is a Chance fracture, which is a horizontal fracture through the vertebral body and posterior elements (spinous process, lamina, pedicles). This is a result of the same forces that cause the seatbelt sign, and Chance fractures are associated with intra-abdominal injuries, especially hollow viscus injuries.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [C] > [D] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 46-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with a 3-day history of productive cough with purulent sputum and fever with chills. On the second day of admission, he develops bloody vomiting, altered mental status, and multiple red spots all over the body. He is oriented only to self. His temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg. Physical examination shows ecchymoses on both lower extremities. Crackles are heard at the right lung base. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 45,000/mm3, with a prothrombin time of 44 sec and partial thromboplastin time of 62 sec. D-dimer concentrations are elevated. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's ecchymoses?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, cough, and purulent sputum are suggestive of pneumonia. His hypotension, altered mental status, and signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) (eg, thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and PTT, elevated D-dimer, ecchymoses) suggest sepsis due to pneumonia. DIC is characterized by systemic activation of coagulation, leading to widespread deposition of fibrin in the circulation, which can disrupt blood flow and cause end-organ damage. The widespread thrombosis seen in DIC can paradoxically lead to bleeding due to consumption of platelets and coagulation factors.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [C] > [D] > [B].

few_shot.question:
A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 35 minutes after being involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. On arrival, he is alert, has mild chest pain, and minimal shortness of breath. He has one episode of vomiting in the hospital. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 23/min, and blood pressure is 90/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Examination shows multiple abrasions over his trunk and right upper extremity. There are coarse breath sounds over the right lung base. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs, rubs, or gallop. Infusion of 0.9% saline is begun. He subsequently develops increasing shortness of breath. Arterial blood gas analysis on 60% oxygen shows:
pH 7.36
pCO2 39 mm Hg
pO2 68 mm Hg
HCO3- 18 mEq/L
O2 saturation 81%
An x-ray of the chest shows patchy, irregular infiltrates over the right lung fields. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with a pulmonary contusion, which is a common injury following blunt chest trauma (eg, motor vehicle collision). Pulmonary contusions are characterized by pulmonary hemorrhage and edema, which can lead to ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxemia. This is reflected in the patient's arterial blood gas, which shows a decreased pO2 and O2 saturation. On imaging, pulmonary contusions appear as patchy, irregular infiltrates, typically in the lung adjacent to the site of injury.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [D] > [A] > [C].

question: A 68-year-old woman is referred to the outpatient psychiatry clinic from the medical clinic. The patient is being treated for urge incontinence but is being referred for psychiatric evaluation to help with some of her old avoidance behavior. For the 3 months that she had her urinary symptoms, she avoided places like long lines and long train rides. Even after being successfully treated for her urinary condition, she continues to show restricted social interaction. Which of the following is a true statement regarding the patient's condition?

answer_choices.A: She fears not being able to escape similar situations.
answer_choices.B: Her symptoms need to last for at least 1 month.
answer_choices.C: She requires only one fear or avoidance situation to meet criteria for this condition.
answer_choices.D: Patients may have accompanying social phobia.

few_shot.question: A 75-year-old woman presents to the physician with a complaint of a frequent need to void at nighttime, which has been disrupting her sleep. She notes embarrassingly that she is often unable to reach the bathroom in time, and experiences urinary leakage throughout the night as well as during the day. The patient undergoes urodynamic testing and a urinalysis is obtained which is normal. She is instructed by the physician to perform behavioral training to improve her bladder control. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis contributing to this patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
Urge incontinence is characterized by the sudden, intense urge to urinate, followed by an involuntary loss of urine. The need to urinate may be triggered by a sudden change in position or even by the sound of running water. The patient may need to urinate often, including throughout the night. Urge incontinence may be caused by a variety of conditions, including urinary tract infections, bladder irritants, bowel problems, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, stroke, injury, and nervous system damage associated with surgery. Treatment usually begins with behavioral strategies, such as bladder training, scheduled toilet trips, and fluid and diet management.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: An 11-year-old girl is brought to her primary care physician by her mother with complaints of constant lower abdominal pain and foul-smelling urine for the past 2 days. The patient has had several previous episodes of simple urinary tract infections in the past. Her vitals signs show mild tachycardia without fever. Physical examination reveals suprapubic tenderness without costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion. Urinalysis reveals positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite. Further questioning reveals that the patient does not use the school toilets and holds her urine all day until she gets home. When pressed further, she gets teary-eyed and starts to cry and complains that other girls will make fun of her if she uses the bathroom and will spread rumors to the teachers and her friends. She reports that though this has never happened in the past it concerns her a great deal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fear of using the school toilets due to concerns about embarrassment and humiliation is consistent with social anxiety disorder (SAD). SAD is characterized by an intense fear of humiliation or embarrassment in social or performance situations. Patients often fear that their actions will be scrutinized by others, leading to avoidance of the feared situations. In children, SAD may manifest as school refusal, as seen in this patient. SAD often begins in childhood or adolescence and, if left untreated, can lead to significant distress and impairment, including poor academic performance and low self-esteem. Treatment includes cognitive-behavioral therapy and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [C] > [D] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 63-year-old woman visits her family physician because she has been experiencing difficulty to get her urine stream started in the past 8 months with many occasions needing extra effort to pass the urine. She describes the stream as intermittent and slow, and comments that she needs to go to the restroom again immediately after urinating. Her personal medical history is negative for malignancies, and all of her cytologies have been reported as normal. The only medication she takes is an angiotensin receptor blocker to treat essential hypertension diagnosed 5 years ago. Physical examination is unremarkable except for herniation of the anterior wall of the vagina that goes beyond the hymen. Which of the following types of incontinence is affecting the patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of urinary hesitancy, slow stream, intermittency, and feeling of incomplete emptying are suggestive of overflow incontinence due to impaired detrusor contractility or bladder outlet obstruction. In women, the most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction is advanced pelvic organ prolapse, as in this patient. The prolapsed anterior vaginal wall (ie, cystocele) can cause a kink in the urethra, much like a kink in a garden hose, leading to urinary retention and subsequent overflow incontinence.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old woman comes to the physician for the evaluation of several episodes of urinary incontinence over the past several months. She reports that she was not able to get to the bathroom in time. During the past 6 months, her husband has noticed that she is starting to forget important appointments and family meetings. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin. The patient had smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years. Her vital signs are within normal limits. On mental status examination, she is confused and has short-term memory deficits. She walks slowly taking short, wide steps. Muscle strength is normal. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's urinary incontinence?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's forgetfulness, confusion, and gait disturbance are suggestive of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), a syndrome characterized by the triad of dementia, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence. NPH is caused by impaired reabsorption of cerebrospinal fluid, which leads to ventricular enlargement that is out of proportion to cortical atrophy. The gait disturbance seen in NPH is typically a magnetic, wide-based gait with short steps, turning en bloc, and a tendency to fall. The urinary incontinence seen in NPH is typically due to urgency and is often the earliest symptom of the triad. It is thought to be due to interruption of the cortical inhibition of the pontine micturition center, leading to an inability to suppress voiding.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [C] > [D] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old Caucasian female presents to her physician for episodes of urinary incontinence that began shortly after a breakup with her boyfriend. She claimed to be psychologically devastated when she found him sleeping with her brother and has had trouble caring for herself ever since. The patient states that the episodes came on suddenly and occur randomly. The patient denies any burning or pain upon urination. Upon obtaining further history, the patient also states that she has "stress spells" in which her vision becomes blurry or has blind spots. The patient also complains of frequent headaches. These symptoms have persisted for the past few years and she attributes them to arguments with her boyfriend. Embarrassed, the patient even admits to episodes of fecal incontinence which she also blames on her boyfriend's perpetual verbal and occasional physical abuse. The patient is teary and a physical exam is deferred until her mood improves. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head
answer_choices.B: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for symptoms of regression

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of urinary incontinence, visual disturbances, and headaches are concerning for multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is a chronic, immune-mediated disease that affects the central nervous system. It is characterized by inflammation, demyelination, and axonal loss. The disease is more common in women and typically presents in young adulthood (age 20-40). Symptoms depend on the location of lesions and often include motor, sensory, cerebellar, and/or autonomic dysfunction. Urinary incontinence can occur due to detrusor hyperreflexia or detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia. Visual disturbances can occur due to optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, or diplopia from brainstem involvement. Headaches are also common in MS, although the exact cause is unknown.

Given the high suspicion for MS in this patient, the most appropriate next step in management is to obtain an MRI of the brain and spinal cord, which typically shows multiple periventricular white matter lesions.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [D] > [C] > [B].

question:
A 55-year-old caucasian male is transferred to a tertiary care hospital from a small county hospital where he presented with jaundice and severe abdominal pain that radiates to the back. While in the county hospital, he did not develop fever, and his vital signs were stable for the 48 hours he spent at there. Initial laboratory tests are given below:
Total bilirubin 7 mg/dL
Direct bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL
AST 100
ALT 40
Alkaline phosphatase 480 IU/L
Glucose 160 mg/dL
The patient’s medical history is relevant for hypertension and diabetes mellitus. He admits to smoking cigarettes since his early teenage years. Moderate icterus is evident during physical examination, the abdomen is distended and dull to percussion, and there is periumbilical tenderness. Which of the following markers would you expect to be elevated in this patient?

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 48-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of progressively worsening jaundice, generalized itching, and epigastric discomfort. He also complains of nausea and loss of appetite. His stools have looked like clay for the past week. He has returned from a vacation in Thailand one week ago, where he got a new tattoo. He is sexually active with multiple partners and does not use protection. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows jaundice and scleral icterus. Superficial excoriations are seen on all limbs. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show a fasting glucose level of 198 mg/dL, total bilirubin concentration of 10.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin concentration of 9.8 mg/dl, and alkaline phosphatase activity of 450 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography shows dilation of the biliary and pancreatic ducts and a 3-cm hypoechoic solid mass with irregular margins in the head of the pancreas. An elevation of which of the following serum findings is most specific for this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of painless jaundice, pruritus, acholic stools, and weight loss, along with the finding of a pancreatic mass on imaging, is concerning for pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is the most common type of pancreatic cancer and typically arises within the head of the pancreas. Obstruction of the common bile duct by the tumor leads to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and subsequent clinical findings of dark urine, pale stools, and jaundice. Pruritus results from the deposition of bile salts in the skin. Weight loss is due to malabsorption (from obstruction of the pancreatic duct and decreased pancreatic enzyme secretion) and malignancy-associated anorexia/cachexia.

Cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9) is a tumor marker associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma. It can be used to monitor response to treatment and disease recurrence following treatment. However, it is not recommended for screening or diagnosis of pancreatic cancer because it can also be elevated in other conditions such as cholangiocarcinoma, gallstone disease, pancreatitis, and cirrhosis.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of malaise and abdominal pain. Six weeks ago, he had vomiting and watery diarrhea for 2 days that resolved without treatment. Twelve weeks ago, he underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for alcoholic cirrhosis. At the time of discharge, his total serum bilirubin concentration was 1.0 mg/dL. He stopped drinking alcohol one year ago. His current medications include daily tacrolimus, prednisone, valganciclovir, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. His temperature is 37.7°C (99.9°F), pulse is 95/min, and blood pressure is 150/80 mm Hg. He appears uncomfortable and has mild jaundice. Examination shows scleral icterus. The abdomen is soft and tender to deep palpation over the right upper quadrant, where there is a well-healed surgical scar. His leukocyte count is 2500/mm3, serum bilirubin concentration is 2.6 mg/dL, and serum tacrolimus concentration is within therapeutic range. Which of the following is the next appropriate step in diagnosis?

answer_choices.A: CT scan of the abdomen with contrast

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and leukopenia in the setting of recent liver transplantation is concerning for hepatic artery thrombosis (HAT). HAT is a serious vascular complication that occurs in 5%-10% of liver transplant recipients, typically within the first month post-transplant. Patients may present with fever, malaise, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Leukopenia may also be present due to sequestration and destruction of granulocytes in the necrotic liver. The most sensitive and specific test for HAT is Doppler ultrasound of the liver, which can assess hepatic artery patency and flow. If ultrasound findings are equivocal or if the diagnosis remains uncertain, further evaluation with CT angiography or hepatic angiography is indicated.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man with a history of biliary colic presents with one-day of intractable nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain radiating to the back. Temperature is 99.7 deg F (37.6 deg C), blood pressure is 102/78 mmHg, pulse is 112/min, and respirations are 22/min. On abdominal exam, he has involuntary guarding and tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant and epigastric regions. Laboratory studies show white blood cell count 18,200/uL, alkaline phosphatase 650 U/L, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL, amylase 500 U/L, and lipase 1160 U/L. Which of the patient's laboratory findings is associated with increased mortality?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe, constant abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and leukocytosis is consistent with acute pancreatitis. The most common causes of acute pancreatitis are gallstones and alcohol use. Gallstone pancreatitis is suggested in this patient by the presence of biliary colic symptoms and elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase levels, indicating biliary obstruction.

The Ranson criteria are used to predict the severity of acute pancreatitis on admission and at 48 hours. The presence of more criteria is associated with a higher risk of mortality. On admission, the Ranson criteria include age >55, white blood cell count >16,000/mm3, blood glucose >200 mg/dL, serum AST >250 U/L, and LDH >350 U/L. At 48 hours, the criteria include a hematocrit decrease >10%, blood urea nitrogen increase >5 mg/dL after IV fluid resuscitation, arterial PO2 <60 mmHg, serum calcium <8 mg/dL, base deficit >4 mEq/L, and estimated fluid sequestration >6 L.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 31-year-old man presents with jaundice, scleral icterus, dark urine, and pruritus. He also says that he has been experiencing abdominal pain shortly after eating. He says that symptoms started a week ago and have not improved. The patient denies any associated fever or recent weight-loss. He is afebrile and vital signs are within normal limits. On physical examination, the patient’s skin appears yellowish. Scleral icterus is present. Remainder of physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory findings are significant for:
Conjugated bilirubin 5.1 mg/dL
Total bilirubin 6.0 mg/dL
AST 24 U/L
ALT 22 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase 662 U/L
A contrast CT of the abdomen is unremarkable. An ultrasound of the right upper quadrant reveals a normal gallbladder, but the common bile duct is not visible. Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with obstructive jaundice, which is characterized by elevated conjugated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase levels. The most common causes of obstructive jaundice are choledocholithiasis and malignancy. However, this patient's imaging studies do not show any evidence of these conditions. Therefore, the next best step in management is endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), which can directly visualize the biliary tree and pancreatic duct, and can also be therapeutic if a stone or other cause of obstruction is found.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 62-year-old man presents with “yellowing” of the skin. He says he has been having intermittent upper abdominal pain, which is relieved by Tylenol. He also recalls that he has lost some weight over the past several months but can not quantify the amount. His past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus. He reports a 40-pack-year smoking history. The patient is afebrile and vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals mild jaundice and a palpable gallbladder. Laboratory findings are significant for the following:
Total bilirubin 13 mg/dL
Direct bilirubin: 10 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP): 560 IU/L
An ultrasound of the abdomen reveals a hypoechoic mass in the epigastric region. The patient is scheduled for a CT abdomen and pelvis with specific organ protocol for further evaluation. Which of the following best describes this patient’s most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.A: Caffeine consumption is an established risk factor for this condition.
answer_choices.B: The majority of cases occur in the body of the pancreas.
answer_choices.C: Patients with this condition often rapidly develop glucose intolerance and severe diabetes.
answer_choices.D: CA 19-9 is a marker for this condition.

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of painless jaundice, weight loss, and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) is concerning for pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic cancer is the fourth leading cause of cancer death in the United States. Risk factors include smoking, obesity, chronic pancreatitis, and diabetes. The majority of pancreatic cancers are adenocarcinomas that arise from the ductal epithelium. Most tumors occur in the head of the pancreas, leading to biliary obstruction and subsequent painless jaundice. Tumors in the body and tail of the pancreas typically present later with nonspecific symptoms such as weight loss and abdominal pain. The carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9) is a tumor marker that can be elevated in pancreatic cancer and is used to monitor response to treatment.

So, the answer is [D].

question: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room by his mother with confusion, abdominal pain, and vomiting for the previous day. The patient’s mother says he started complaining of pain in his abdomen after he got back from school yesterday and vomited 3 times during the night. This morning, he seemed confused so she rushed him to the ER. She has also noticed that he has been urinating frequently and drinking a lot of water recently, and he has lost 6 kg (13.2 lb) over the past 20 days. His vital signs include: blood pressure 100/50 mm Hg, heart rate 110/min, respiratory rate 27/min, and temperature 35.6°C (96.0°F). His BMI is 18 kg/m2. On physical examination, he is disoriented to time and place and is taking deep and labored breaths. There is diffuse tenderness to palpation in the abdomen with guarding. Laboratory tests are significant for a pH of 7.19 and a blood glucose level of 754 mg/dL. The doctor explains to his mother that her son has developed a life-threatening complication of a disease characterized by decreased levels of a hormone. Which of the following would you most likely expect to see in this patient?

answer_choices.B: Decreased activity of hormone sensitive lipase

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 14-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother because of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting for 6 hours. Over the past 6 weeks, she has also had increased frequency of urination, and she has been drinking more water than usual. She has lost 6 kg (13 lb) over the same time period despite having a good appetite. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 94/58 mm Hg. She appears lethargic. Physical examination shows deep and labored breathing and dry mucous membranes. The abdomen is soft, and there is diffuse tenderness to palpation with no guarding or rebound. Urine dipstick is positive for ketones and glucose. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and fatigue in association with glucosuria and ketonuria is consistent with new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus complicated by diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA is characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. It is typically precipitated by a stressor (eg, infection, trauma) in a patient with relative or absolute insulin deficiency.

Patients with DKA are usually hyperkalemic on presentation due to the extracellular shift of potassium caused by insulin deficiency, hypertonicity, and acidemia. However, total body potassium is decreased due to osmotic diuresis. Therefore, despite initial hyperkalemia, all patients with DKA have a substantial total body potassium deficit that will need to be replaced once serum levels normalize or decrease following insulin therapy.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A previously healthy 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room by his mother 5 hours after the onset of abdominal pain and nausea. Over the past 2 weeks, he has also had progressive abdominal pain and a 4-kg (8.8-lb) weight loss. The mother reports that her son has been drinking more water than usual during this period. Last week he wet his bed three times despite being completely toilet-trained since 3 years of age. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 35/min, and blood pressure is 95/55 mm Hg. He appears lethargic. Physical examination shows deep and labored breathing and dry mucous membranes. The abdomen is soft, and there is diffuse tenderness to palpation with no guarding or rebound. Serum laboratory studies show:
Na+ 133 mEq/L
K+ 5.9 mEq/L
Cl- 95 mEq/L
HCO3- 13 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen 25 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL
Urine dipstick is positive for ketones and glucose. Further evaluation is most likely to reveal which of the following?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and new-onset enuresis are suggestive of type 1 diabetes mellitus. His presentation with abdominal pain, tachypnea, and altered mental status is consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA is characterized by hyperglycemia, ketonemia, and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, as seen in this patient.

Patients with DKA typically have total body potassium depletion due to osmotic diuresis, vomiting, and a shift of potassium from the intracellular to the extracellular space in response to acidemia. Despite this total body potassium depletion, the serum potassium at presentation may be increased, normal, or decreased due to the extracellular shift. However, once insulin treatment is initiated, potassium will shift intracellularly, and the serum potassium concentration can decrease rapidly, leading to life-threatening arrhythmias. Therefore, all patients with DKA should receive potassium supplementation, unless hyperkalemia is severe or urine output is compromised.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with severe dyspnea, fatigue, and vomiting. His mother reports that he has been lethargic for the last several days with an increase in urine output. She thinks he may even be losing weight, despite eating and drinking more than normal for the last couple weeks. Laboratory results are notable for glucose of 440, potassium of 5.8, pH of 7.14 and HCO3 of 17. After administrating IV fluids and insulin, which of the following would you expect?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss in the setting of hyperglycemia are consistent with new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus. His nausea, vomiting, and Kussmaul respirations (ie, rapid, deep breathing) suggest concurrent diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a potentially life-threatening complication of diabetes. DKA is characterized by hyperglycemia, ketonemia, and an anion gap metabolic acidosis (low serum bicarbonate and arterial pH).

Insulin deficiency in DKA results in an osmotic diuresis that causes significant total body potassium depletion. However, acidemia and insulin deficiency promote a hyperkalemic state by driving potassium out of cells. Therefore, initial laboratory measurements may show normal or even increased serum potassium levels.

Insulin therapy and correction of acidemia shift potassium back into cells, rapidly decreasing serum potassium levels. In addition, the osmotic diuresis caused by hyperglycemia can result in significant urinary potassium losses. Therefore, patients with DKA are at risk for developing life-threatening hypokalemia with insulin therapy, despite initial hyperkalemia or normokalemia. To prevent hypokalemia, potassium replacement is initiated as soon as adequate urine flow is confirmed, even if serum potassium levels are initially within normal limits.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [D] > [A] > [C].

few_shot.question:
A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother due to frequent vomiting, abdominal pain, and weakness. Over the last 5 days, has been noted to have polydipsia and polyuria. Family history is irrelevant. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F), blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 110/min. Physical examination reveals no response to verbal commands, sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, and rapid deep respirations. Laboratory results are shown:
Random plasma glucose 420 mg/dL
Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate elevated
Fasting C-peptide undetectable
Antiglutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies positive
This patient's condition occurs as a result of which of the following?

answer_choices.B: Immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells
answer_choices.D: Defective synthesis or release of arginine vasopressin

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss are suggestive of new-onset diabetes mellitus. His presentation with vomiting, abdominal pain, and altered mental status is concerning for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a life-threatening complication of diabetes that typically occurs when insulin levels are insufficient to meet the body's basic metabolic requirements. DKA is characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. The most common precipitating factor is infection, but it may also be the initial presentation of diabetes, as in this patient.

Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, which results in an absolute insulin deficiency. The presence of anti-GAD antibodies in this patient is consistent with T1DM. GAD is an enzyme involved in the synthesis of gamma-aminobutyric acid in the brain and pancreatic beta cells. Anti-GAD antibodies are found in 70%-80% of patients with T1DM and can appear years before the onset of clinical symptoms.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old man presents to the emergency department with his family because of abdominal pain, excessive urination, and drowsiness since the day before. He has had type 1 diabetes mellitus for 2 years. He ran out of insulin 2 days ago. The vital signs at admission include: temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure 102/69 mm Hg, and pulse 121/min. On physical examination, he is lethargic and his breathing is rapid and deep. There is a mild generalized abdominal tenderness without rebound tenderness or guarding. His serum glucose is 480 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas of this patient will most likely show which of the following?

answer_choices.D: ↓ pH, ↓ bicarbonate and normal anion gap

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal pain, polyuria, and altered mental status in the setting of poor glycemic control is consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA is characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and an anion gap metabolic acidosis. The anion gap is calculated as follows: Anion gap = [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]). The normal anion gap is 8-12 mEq/L. In DKA, the anion gap is increased due to the accumulation of ketoacids (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate). The bicarbonate level is decreased as it is consumed to buffer the ketoacids. The pH is decreased (acidemia) due to the primary metabolic acidosis. The body compensates for the metabolic acidosis by increasing minute ventilation (hyperventilation), which decreases the pCO2 (respiratory alkalosis). This is often referred to as Kussmaul breathing and is described as rapid, deep, labored breathing.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [B] > [A].

question: A 16-year-old female presents to her physician’s office after noticing a round lump in her left breast 2 months ago. She reports that the lump seemed to enlarge and became tender just preceding her last 2 menses. It is otherwise painless, and the patient denies any discharge or skin changes. She has no past medical history but her grandmother, age 72, was just diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. The patient is an avid softball player at her high school and denies alcohol, smoking, or illicit drug use. On exam, the breasts appear symmetric and normal. A 3-cm round, mobile mass is palpated in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. There is slight tenderness to deep palpation of the mass. There is no axillary lymphadenopathy on either side. Which of the following is the most likely outcome of this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.A: This mass will decrease in size if the patient starts oral contraceptives
answer_choices.B: This mass slightly increases this patient’s risk of breast cancer in the future
answer_choices.C: This mass will most likely decrease in size or disappear over time
answer_choices.D: If this mass grows rapidly to greater than 5 cm, radiation and chemotherapy are indicated

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old nulligravid woman presents to her gynecologist after noticing a lump in her right breast while showering. She states that she first noticed the lump approximately 2 weeks ago, when the mass was slightly tender to touch. Since then, the lump has gotten slightly smaller and is now non-tender. The patient is otherwise healthy. She does not take oral contraceptives. Her last menses was approximately 2 weeks ago. There is no family history of cancer. On exam, the patient's temperature is 98.3°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 116/84 mmHg, pulse is 65/min, and respirations are 12/min. In her right breast, there is a small 1.5 cm mass that is mobile, well-circumscribed, and firm. Which of the following is most likely on histological examination of the mass?

answer_choices.A: Dilated glands with 2 cell layers present
answer_choices.B: Hypercellular stroma with overgrowth of fibrous and glandular tissues
answer_choices.C: Large, pleomorphic cells with associated central necrosis and microcalcifications
answer_choices.D: Terminal duct lobular units surrounded by dense stroma

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's age, the timing of the mass with her menstrual cycle, and the characteristics of the mass on physical examination are suggestive of fibrocystic changes of the breast. Fibrocystic changes are common in women of reproductive age and are often associated with the menstrual cycle. The most common symptoms are breast pain, tenderness, and lumpiness that often change with the menstrual cycle. The lumps are usually mobile and well-circumscribed. Fibrocystic changes are not associated with an increased risk of breast cancer.

Histologically, fibrocystic changes can be divided into nonproliferative and proliferative types. Nonproliferative changes include cyst formation, fibrosis, and apocrine metaplasia. Proliferative changes include epithelial hyperplasia and sclerosing adenosis. This patient's mass is most likely a fibroadenoma, which is a benign tumor composed of both glandular and stromal tissue. It is characterized by hypercellular stroma with overgrowth of fibrous and glandular tissues.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old woman recently noticed a mass in her left breast. The examination shows a 4-cm mass in the left upper quadrant. The mass is firm, mobile, and has well-defined margins. She complains of occasional tenderness. There is no lymphatic involvement. Mammography showed a dense lesion. What is the most likely cause?
few_shot.explanation:
Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor in women under 30 years of age. It is a well-circumscribed, mobile, firm mass that is often described as feeling like a marble. It is usually painless, but some women may experience tenderness. The mass may increase in size during pregnancy or with the menstrual cycle. Mammography often shows a dense, round, or oval mass with well-defined borders.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician 10 days after noticing a mass in her left breast while bathing. She is concerned that it is breast cancer because her sister was diagnosed with breast cancer 3 years ago at 61 years of age. Menopause occurred 6 months ago. She has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years. She took an oral contraceptive for 20 years. Current medications include hormone replacement therapy and a calcium supplement. Examination shows a 2.5-cm, palpable, hard, nontender, mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast; there is tethering of the skin over the lump. Examination of the right breast and axillae shows no abnormalities. Mammography shows an irregular mass with microcalcifications and oil cysts. A core biopsy shows foam cells and multinucleated giant cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's breast mass is most likely a fat necrosis. Fat necrosis is a benign, non-suppurative inflammatory process of adipose tissue. It is most commonly seen in obese, postmenopausal women and typically presents as a painless, hard lump that may be associated with skin or nipple retraction. Fat necrosis can occur following surgery, radiation, or trauma to the breast, but it may also occur spontaneously. Mammography often shows calcifications and oil cysts, which are pathognomonic for fat necrosis. Histologically, fat necrosis is characterized by lipid-filled macrophages (foam cells), multinucleated giant cells, and calcifications. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].
