This patient's history of smoking, chronic cough, and dyspnea, along with the presence of wheezing and obstructive findings on pulmonary function tests (eg, decreased FEV1:FVC ratio, increased total lung capacity due to air trapping), are consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The most effective intervention to slow the rate of decline in FEV1 in patients with COPD is smoking cessation. Smoking cessation also decreases the risk of death and improves quality of life in these patients.

question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother for worsening wheezing and shortness of breath over the past day. He has not had a fever, cough, vomiting, or diarrhea. He has asthma and eczema. He uses a glucocorticoid inhaler and an albuterol inhaler but has missed his medications for the past week while on vacation. He appears uncomfortable. His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 100/80. Expiratory and inspiratory wheezing is heard throughout both lung fields. There are moderate intercostal and subcostal retractions and a decreased inspiratory to expiratory ratio. Nebulized albuterol and ipratropium treatments and intravenous methylprednisolone are given in the emergency department for a presumed asthma exacerbation. One hour later, the child is limp and lethargic. Magnesium sulfate is administered. His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 150/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 100/70. few_shot.question: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents due to severe shortness of breath that started 20 minutes ago. She has a history of asthma and her current treatment regime includes a beta-agonist inhaler as well as a medium-dose corticosteroid inhaler. Her mother tells the physician that her daughter was playing outside with her friends when she suddenly started experiencing difficulty breathing and used her inhaler without improvement. On examination, she is struggling to breathe and with subcostal and intercostal retractions. She is leaning forward, and gasping for air and refuses to lie down on the examination table. Her blood pressure is 130/92 mm Hg, the respirations are 27/min, the pulse is 110/min and O2 saturation is 87%. There is prominent expiratory wheezes in all lung fields. The patient is put on a nonrebreather mask with 100% oxygen. An arterial blood gas is collected and sent for analysis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

This patient is experiencing a severe asthma exacerbation, as evidenced by her acute onset of dyspnea, hypoxemia, and refusal to lie flat. The first-line treatment for an acute asthma exacerbation is inhaled beta-2 agonists (eg, albuterol), which cause bronchodilation by relaxing airway smooth muscle. Inhaled beta-2 agonists are preferred over oral or intravenous forms due to their rapid onset of action and fewer systemic side effects.

few_shot.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of a cough and mild shortness of breath for the past 12 hours. He has not had fever. He has been to the emergency department 4 times during the past 6 months for treatment of asthma exacerbations. His 9-month-old sister was treated for bronchiolitis a week ago. His father has allergic rhinitis. Current medications include an albuterol inhaler and a formoterol-fluticasone inhaler. He appears in mild distress. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 101/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 86/60 mm Hg. Examination shows mild intercostal and subcostal retractions. Pulmonary examination shows decreased breath sounds and mild expiratory wheezing throughout the right lung field. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows hyperlucency of the right lung field with decreased pulmonary markings. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent "asthma" exacerbations, decreased breath sounds, and hyperlucency of the right lung field on chest x-ray are suggestive of foreign body aspiration. The most commonly aspirated objects are food items (eg, peanuts, popcorn, seeds), but small toy parts are also frequently implicated. The right mainstem bronchus is the most common site of foreign body aspiration due to its more vertical orientation. 

The diagnosis of foreign body aspiration is often delayed because the presentation can mimic common pediatric conditions such as asthma or pneumonia. The classic presentation of choking, coughing, or wheezing is seen in fewer than 50% of patients. The most common symptoms are cough (50%-75%), wheezing (10%-20%), and decreased breath sounds (10%-20%). Fever is usually absent unless pneumonia or lung abscess develops. Chest x-ray may show hyperinflation, atelectasis, or pneumonia, but up to 40% of radiographs are normal. 

Bronchoscopy is the diagnostic and therapeutic procedure of choice for foreign body aspiration. It allows for direct visualization and removal of the foreign object.

So, the answer is [A].

The most appropriate next step in management is endotracheal intubation to protect his airway and ensure adequate oxygenation and ventilation.

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department in the middle of the night because of difficulties breathing. Her parents say that the breathing noises have become progressively worse throughout the day and are mainly heard when she inhales. They say that a change in posture does not seem to have any effect on her breathing. For the last three days, she has also had a runny nose and a harsh cough. She has not had hemoptysis. The parents are worried she may have accidentally swallowed something while playing with her toys, since she tends to put small things in her mouth. Her immunizations are up-to-date. She appears lethargic, and high-pitched wheezing is heard at rest during inhalation. Her skin tone is normal. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 142/min, respirations are 33/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Examination shows supraclavicular and intercostal retractions. There is diminished air movement bilaterally. An x-ray of the neck and upper chest is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This child's symptoms of a harsh cough, high-pitched inspiratory stridor, and sternal retractions are consistent with croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), the most common cause of acute stridor in children. Croup is most often caused by parainfluenza virus and typically presents with several days of symptoms of upper respiratory tract infection (eg, rhinorrhea, congestion, cough), followed by the sudden onset of a barking (seal-like) cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness. Symptoms are often worse at night and can last up to one week. The x-ray shows subglottic narrowing (steeple sign), which is characteristic of croup.

Treatment of croup is based on the severity of symptoms. Mild croup (no stridor at rest, no retractions) can be managed with supportive care (eg, hydration, antipyretics). Moderate to severe croup (stridor at rest, retractions) is managed with a single dose of dexamethasone and nebulized epinephrine. Dexamethasone reduces airway inflammation and has been shown to improve symptoms, decrease rates of return visits and hospitalization, and increase the time to recurrence of symptoms. Nebulized epinephrine causes vasoconstriction and decreases airway edema, providing more rapid relief of symptoms. However, the effect is transient (up to 2 hours), and patients must be observed for recurrence of symptoms.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 32 weeks' gestation presents to the emergency department for clear vaginal discharge that started roughly 26 hours ago. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Her first child was born at term by vaginal delivery. She has no history of any serious illnesses. She does not drink alcohol or smoke cigarettes. Current medications include vitamin supplements. Her temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. Speculum examination demonstrates clear fluid at the cervical os. The fetal heart rate is reactive at 160/min with no decelerations. Tocometry shows uterine contractions. Nitrazine testing is positive. She is started on indomethacin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.C: Administer betamethasone, ampicillin, and proceed with cesarean section
answer_choices.D: Administer betamethasone, ampicillin, and proceed with induction of labor

few_shot.question: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department for sudden leakage of clear vaginal fluid. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Her first child was born at term by vaginal delivery. She has no history of serious illness. She does not drink alcohol or smoke cigarettes. Current medications include vitamin supplements. Her temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. Speculum examination demonstrates clear fluid in the cervical canal. The fetal heart rate is reactive at 160/min with no decelerations. Tocometry shows uterine contractions. Nitrazine testing is positive. She is started on indomethacin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: Administer betamethasone, ampicillin, and proceed with cesarean section
answer_choices.D: Administer betamethasone, ampicillin, and proceed with induction of labor

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), which is defined as rupture of membranes prior to the onset of labor and before 37 weeks' gestation. PPROM is associated with significant neonatal morbidity and mortality, primarily due to complications of prematurity and infection. Therefore, the main goals of management are to prolong the pregnancy to allow for fetal maturation and to prevent maternal and fetal infection.

The patient should be given betamethasone to promote fetal lung maturity and ampicillin to prevent infection. Indomethacin is also given to inhibit uterine contractions and prolong the pregnancy. Delivery is not indicated unless there is evidence of chorioamnionitis or fetal distress.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old primigravid woman at 36 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of worsening pelvic pain for 2 hours. Three days ago, she had a burning sensation with urination that resolved spontaneously. She has nausea and has vomited fluid twice on her way to the hospital. She appears ill. Her temperature is 39.7°C (103.5°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 33/min, and blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows diffuse tenderness. No contractions are felt. Speculum examination shows pooling of nonbloody, malodorous fluid in the vaginal vault. The cervix is not effaced or dilated. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 14 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 16,000/mm3, and a platelet count of 250,000/mm3. Fetal heart rate is 148/min and reactive with no decelerations. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: Administer intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin and perform C-section
answer_choices.C: Administer intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin and induce labor

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute-onset pelvic pain, fever, and malodorous vaginal discharge is concerning for chorioamnionitis, an infection of the amniotic fluid, placenta, and/or fetal membranes. Chorioamnionitis is most commonly due to ascending polymicrobial infection from the lower genital tract. Risk factors include prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labor, nulliparity, and internal fetal monitoring. The diagnosis is clinical and is based on the presence of maternal fever plus one or more of the following: maternal or fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, malodorous or purulent amniotic fluid, or maternal leukocytosis. 

Management of chorioamnionitis includes broad-spectrum antibiotics (eg, ampicillin and gentamicin) to cover polymicrobial flora and delivery of the fetus. In patients who are not in labor, induction of labor is the preferred method of delivery, regardless of gestational age. Cesarean delivery is reserved for the usual obstetric indications (eg, nonreassuring fetal status, cephalopelvic disproportion).

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 10 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department for vaginal bleeding, cramping lower abdominal pain, and dizziness. She also has had fevers, chills, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge for the past 2 days. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they use condoms inconsistently. Pregnancy and delivery of her first child were uncomplicated. She appears acutely ill. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 88/50 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows moderate tenderness to palpation over the lower quadrants. Pelvic examination shows a tender cervix that is dilated with clots and a solid bloody mass within the cervical canal. Her serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin concentration is 15,000 mIU/mL. Pelvic ultrasound shows an intrauterine gestational sac with absent fetal heart tones. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: Oral clindamycin followed by outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks
answer_choices.B: Intravenous clindamycin and gentamicin followed by suction and curettage
answer_choices.C: Intravenous clindamycin and gentamycin followed by close observation
answer_choices.D: Oral clindamycin followed by suction curettage

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, chills, abdominal pain, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge is consistent with septic abortion, a life-threatening condition that requires immediate intervention. Septic abortion is a serious complication of spontaneous or induced abortion and is most commonly caused by ascending infection from the lower genital tract. The most common pathogens are those associated with bacterial vaginosis (eg, Gardnerella vaginalis, Mobiluncus species, Bacteroides species, Peptostreptococcus species) and sexually transmitted infections (eg, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis). Patients typically present with signs of systemic toxicity (eg, fever, tachycardia, hypotension) and evidence of incomplete abortion (eg, open cervical os, products of conception in the cervical canal or vagina). 

Management of septic abortion involves prompt initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics (eg, clindamycin and gentamicin) to cover polymicrobial infection, followed by surgical evacuation of the uterus (eg, suction curettage) to remove the infected tissue. Delaying uterine evacuation can lead to progression of the infection and development of complications such as septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 26 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of frequent contractions. The contractions are 40 seconds each, occurring every 2 minutes, and increasing in intensity. Her first child was delivered by lower segment transverse cesarean section because of a nonreassuring fetal heart rate. Her current medications include folic acid and a multivitamin. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), heart rate is 88/min, and blood pressure is 126/76 mm Hg. Contractions are felt on the abdomen. There is clear fluid in the vulva and the introitus. The cervix is dilated to 5 cm, 70% effaced, and station of the head is -2. A fetal ultrasound shows polyhydramnios, a median cleft lip, and fused thalami. The corpus callosum, 3rd ventricle, and lateral ventricles are absent. The spine shows no abnormalities and there is a four chamber heart. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient is in active labor and has a history of a prior cesarean delivery. The decision to proceed with a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC) or to perform an elective repeat cesarean delivery (ERCD) should ideally be made after a discussion of the risks and benefits of both approaches. TOLAC is associated with risks of uterine rupture, need for emergent cesarean delivery, and, rarely, maternal and perinatal death. ERCD eliminates the risk of uterine rupture but is associated with increased risk of maternal hemorrhage, infection, and complications of abnormal placentation (eg, placenta previa, placenta accreta) in future pregnancies.

The patient's fetus has findings consistent with alobar holoprosencephaly (fused thalami, absent corpus callosum, 3rd ventricle, and lateral ventricles), which is associated with severe neurologic impairment and a high mortality rate. Given the poor prognosis, the risk of uterine rupture with TOLAC is outweighed by the potential benefits of avoiding surgical morbidity with ERCD, especially given the patient's future childbearing potential. Therefore, the most appropriate management is to allow for vaginal delivery.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 31 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital because her water broke one hour ago. Pregnancy has been complicated by iron deficiency anemia and hypothyroidism treated with iron supplements and L-thyroxine, respectively. The patient followed-up with her gynecologist on a regular basis throughout the pregnancy. Pregnancy and delivery of her first child were uncomplicated. Pulse is 90/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. The abdomen is nontender. She has had 8 contractions within the last hour. Pelvic examination shows cervical dilation of 3 cm. The fetal heart rate is 140/min with no decelerations. In addition to administration of dexamethasone and terbutaline, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient is in preterm labor, defined as regular contractions and cervical changes prior to 37 weeks' gestation. Management of preterm labor includes administration of corticosteroids (eg, betamethasone, dexamethasone) to accelerate fetal lung maturity and decrease the risk of intraventricular hemorrhage, necrotizing enterocolitis, and neonatal death. Tocolytics (eg, indomethacin, nifedipine, magnesium sulfate) can also be given to delay delivery by at least 48 hours, which allows time for the corticosteroids to take effect and for maternal transport to a tertiary care center if necessary. 

Magnesium sulfate is also used for fetal neuroprotection in patients at <32 weeks' gestation to reduce the risk of cerebral palsy. 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 36-year-old recent immigrant from India presents with a face similar to that seen in the image A. Examination of his face reveals skin that is thick and contains many lesions. few_shot.question: A 29-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of fatigue and loss of sensation in his lower legs. The patient notes no history of trauma or chronic disease but states that he spends a lot of time outside and often encounters wild animals. On examination, the patient has multiple dark lesions over the skin of his face and back, as well as a decreased sensation of fine touch and vibration bilaterally in the lower extremities. What is the morphology of the etiologic agent causing this patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's skin lesions, peripheral neuropathy, and exposure to wild animals are suggestive of leprosy (Hansen disease), which is caused by Mycobacterium leprae. M leprae is an acid-fast, intracellular bacillus that prefers cooler regions of the body, such as the skin and peripheral nerves. It is the only bacterium known to invade peripheral nerves, leading to the characteristic sensory loss seen in leprosy. The organism is thought to be transmitted via respiratory droplets, although some cases have been associated with handling armadillos, which are known to harbor the bacteria.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 34-year-old female visits her primary care physician because recently she has started to have painful, numb, and discolored toes. She is otherwise healthy and has no family history of similar conditions that she can recall. Occasionally during these episodes, her fingers and nose will also have similar symptoms. On examination, the patient's appearance is completely normal with warm and well perfused extremities. No evidence of discoloration is found. On closer questioning, she reveals that several months ago during the summer, she succumbed to a viral illness that caused her to feel fatigued and have a long bout of cold symptoms with sore throat and swollen lymph nodes. The bacterial species that is also associated with this patient's most likely condition has which of the following characteristics?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of painful, numb, and discolored toes, fingers, and nose are suggestive of Raynaud's phenomenon, a condition characterized by episodic vasospasm in response to cold or stress. The condition is often idiopathic (primary Raynaud's) but can also be secondary to a variety of conditions, including autoimmune diseases (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma), hematologic disorders, and infections. In this case, the patient's history of a recent viral illness with fatigue, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes suggests a possible infectious mononucleosis, which can be caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) or, less commonly, cytomegalovirus (CMV). Both of these are large, enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses that belong to the Herpesviridae family. They do not have a cell wall, which is a characteristic of bacteria, not viruses.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old man of Nepalese origin presents to a clinic complaining of skin rashes that have been troubling him for years. On examination, there are numerous poorly demarcated skin lesions present on all parts of the body. There is also evidence of significant facial thickening, eyebrow loss, and symmetrical sensory neuropathy in a ‘glove and stocking’ distribution. An examination of the hands reveals bilateral weakness. A skin biopsy is taken from one of the lesions, and the culture is positive for acid-fast bacilli. Which of the following pharmacological therapies is involved in the treatment of this condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's clinical presentation is consistent with leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease. Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an acid-fast bacillus that primarily affects the skin and peripheral nerves. It is characterized by skin lesions, thickening of peripheral nerves, and progressive debility. The disease is common in many countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America.

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends multidrug therapy for leprosy, which includes dapsone, rifampicin, and clofazimine. Dapsone is a bacteriostatic antimicrobial that is active against M. leprae. It inhibits bacterial synthesis of dihydrofolic acid by competing with para-aminobenzoic acid for the active site of dihydropteroate synthetase.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 48-year-old man comes to the physician because of a hypopigmented skin lesion on his finger. He first noticed it 4 weeks ago after cutting his finger with a knife while preparing food. He did not feel the cut. For the past week, he has also had fever, fatigue, and malaise. He has not traveled outside the country since he immigrated from India to join his family in the United States 2 years ago. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F). Physical examination shows a small, healing laceration on the dorsal aspect of the left index finger and an overlying well-defined, hypopigmented macule with raised borders. Sensation to pinprick and light touch is decreased over this area. Which of the following is the most likely causal pathogen of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's hypopigmented skin lesion with loss of sensation is suggestive of leprosy (Hansen disease), which is caused by Mycobacterium leprae. This organism prefers cooler areas of the body and has a predilection for skin and peripheral nerves. The disease is characterized by well-demarcated, hypopigmented, and anesthetic skin lesions. The lepromatous form of the disease can also present with symmetric neuropathy, whereas the tuberculoid form presents with asymmetric neuropathy. Leprosy is common in many parts of the world, including India, Africa, and South America. The disease is treated with dapsone and rifampin for tuberculoid leprosy, with the addition of clofazimine for lepromatous leprosy.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 58-year-old woman visits a physician because of fever, chills, dry cough, and a few enlarging masses on her cheeks and neck. Wart-like lesions are present on the nose as shown in the photograph. She reports that she visited the Mississippi area a few months before on a business trip. Her temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), the pulse is 80/min, and the blood pressure is 121/78 mm Hg. A fine needle aspirate of the lymph node is sent for pathological investigation. Culture growth shows white colonies on Sabouraud glucose agar (SGA). Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fever, chills, cough, and skin lesions, along with her history of travel to the Mississippi River Valley, are suggestive of blastomycosis, a systemic pyogranulomatous infection caused by the dimorphic fungus Blastomyces dermatitidis. The organism exists as a mold in the environment and converts to the yeast form in the body. It is found in moist soil and decomposing organic matter, and infection is acquired via inhalation of conidia. The infection can be asymptomatic or can present as an acute or chronic pneumonia. Dissemination to the skin, bone, genitourinary tract, and other organs can occur, especially in immunocompromised patients. Cutaneous lesions can be verrucous, ulcerative, or necrotic and are often mistaken for squamous cell carcinoma or basal cell carcinoma. Diagnosis is confirmed by visualization of the yeast on potassium hydroxide preparation, culture, or biopsy of sputum, skin, or other infected tissues. The yeast form is distinguished by broad-based budding.

question: A 55-year-old man presents with complaints of exertional dyspnea and dry cough. He reports using extra pillows at night to sleep and two nighttime awakenings to catch his breath in the last month. The patient lives in a homeless shelter and has not seen a doctor in the last 20 years. He has been drinking 5-8 drinks of alcohol per day for the last 20 years. Family history is non-significant, and the patient does not take any medications. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.9°F), blood pressure is 135/115 mm Hg, pulse is 85/min, and respiratory rate is 24/min. Physical examination reveals 2+ bilateral pitting edema. Chest auscultation reveals bibasilar crackles. Which of the following is associated with this patient’s condition?

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of a 2-month history of worsening fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. While he used to be able to walk 4–5 blocks at a time, he now has to pause every 2 blocks. He also reports waking up from having to urinate at least once every night for the past 5 months. Recently, he has started using 2 pillows to avoid waking up coughing with acute shortness of breath at night. He has a history of hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia. His medications include daily amlodipine and prazosin, but he reports having trouble adhering to his medication regimen. His pulse is 72/min, blood pressure is 145/90 mm Hg, and respiratory rate is 20/min. Physical examination shows 2+ bilateral pitting edema of the lower legs. Auscultation shows an S4 gallop and fine bibasilar rales. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following pathophysiologic changes in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Increased tone of efferent renal arterioles

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of hypertension, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral lower extremity edema is suggestive of congestive heart failure (CHF). CHF is a clinical syndrome that results from any structural or functional cardiac disorder that impairs the ability of the ventricle to fill with or eject blood. The most common cause of CHF is coronary artery disease, followed by hypertension, valvular heart disease, and dilated cardiomyopathy.

In CHF, decreased cardiac output leads to activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor, preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole, which increases filtration fraction and maintains glomerular filtration rate despite a decrease in renal perfusion. This is because efferent arteriolar constriction increases glomerular hydrostatic pressure, which opposes the decrease in renal blood flow. However, this comes at the cost of decreased sodium and water excretion, which can lead to volume overload and worsening heart failure.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old man presents with breathlessness for the past 3 months. His symptoms have been getting progressively worse during this time. He denies any history of cough, fever, or chest pain. He works at a local shipyard and is responsible for installing the plumbing aboard the vessels. His past medical history is significant for hypertension for which he takes metoprolol every day. He denies smoking and any illicit drug use. His pulse is 74/min, respiratory rate is 14/min, blood pressure is 130/76 mm Hg, and temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F). Physical examination is significant for fine bibasilar crackles at the end of inspiration without digital clubbing. Which of the following additional findings would most likely be present in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Decreased diffusion lung capacity of CO

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of working in a shipyard and his symptoms of progressive dyspnea and bibasilar inspiratory crackles are suggestive of asbestosis. Asbestosis is a form of pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of asbestos fibers. The fibers penetrate the distal airways and alveoli, and are then engulfed by macrophages. This leads to the release of fibrogenic cytokines and the development of diffuse pulmonary fibrosis. The fibrosis can cause a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function tests, with a decreased total lung capacity, functional residual capacity, and residual volume. The fibrosis can also impair gas exchange, leading to a decreased diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO).

Therefore, the answer is [A].

This patient's symptoms of orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and exertional dyspnea, along with physical examination findings of an S4 gallop, bibasilar rales, and lower extremity edema, are consistent with congestive heart failure (CHF). CHF is characterized by decreased cardiac output, which leads to activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Angiotensin II, a product of the RAAS, causes efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, which helps to maintain glomerular filtration rate despite a decrease in renal perfusion. few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of worsening shortness of breath and dry cough for 6 months. The patient's symptoms get worse when he walks more than about 150 yards. He also reports fatigue and difficulty swallowing solid foods. In cold weather, his fingers occasionally turn blue and become painful. He occasionally smokes cigarettes on weekends. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), and respirations are 22/min, pulse is 87/min, and blood pressure is 126/85 mm Hg. The skin over his trunk and arms is thickened and tightened. Fine inspiratory crackles are heard over bilateral lower lung fields on auscultation. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dyspnea, dry cough, and bibasilar crackles on lung auscultation, along with skin thickening and Raynaud phenomenon, are suggestive of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma). Scleroderma is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, including the lungs. Pulmonary involvement is common in scleroderma and can manifest as interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).

ILD is the most common pulmonary manifestation of scleroderma and is characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung parenchyma, leading to decreased lung compliance (increased elastance) and impaired gas exchange. The fibrosis seen in ILD primarily affects the lung interstitium, which is responsible for gas exchange. This leads to a decrease in the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO), which is a measure of the lungs' ability to transfer gas from inhaled air to the red blood cells in pulmonary capillaries.

few_shot.question:
A 58-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after 2 days of shortness breath, orthopnea, and lower limb edema. His past medical history is significant for hypertension and a myocardial infarction 3 years ago that required a coronary arterial bypass graft. He has not been able to take prescribed medicine in several months due to recent unemployment and issues with insurance. On admission, his blood pressure is 155/92 mmHg, heart rate is 102/min, respiratory rate is 24/min, and temperature is 36.4°C (97.5°F). On physical examination there are fine rales in both lungs, regular and rhythmic cardiac sounds with an S3 gallop and a grade II/VI holosystolic murmur. Initial laboratory tests are shown below:
Na+ 140 mEq/L
K+ 4.2 mEq/L
Cl- 105 mEq/L
BUN 20 mg/dL
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
The patient is stabilized and admitted to the hospital. The next day his blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg, heart rate is 110/min, respiratory rate is 18/min, and temperature is 36.4°C (97.5°F). This morning's laboratory tests are shown below:
Na+  135 mEq/L
K+ 3.2 mEq/L
Cl- 102 mEq/L
BUN 45 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.7 mg/dL
Which of the following best explains the changes seen in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of orthopnea, lower limb edema, and bibasilar rales is consistent with congestive heart failure (CHF). His history of hypertension and myocardial infarction are risk factors for CHF. The S3 gallop is a classic finding in CHF and is due to rapid filling of a noncompliant left ventricle during early diastole. The holosystolic murmur is likely secondary to functional mitral regurgitation due to left ventricular dilation and papillary muscle displacement.

The patient's initial blood pressure was elevated, likely due to increased systemic vascular resistance, a compensatory mechanism in CHF. The decrease in blood pressure and increase in heart rate on the second day are likely due to the initiation of medical therapy. The decrease in serum potassium and increase in BUN and creatinine are consistent with the use of loop diuretics, which are often used as first-line agents for acute CHF exacerbations. Loop diuretics inhibit the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, leading to decreased sodium and potassium reabsorption. This can result in a contraction alkalosis and hypokalemia. In addition, loop diuretics can increase BUN and creatinine by decreasing renal perfusion.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: An 11-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. He is growing along with the 75th percentile and meeting all milestones. Physical examination shows a poorly rugated scrotum. The palpation of the scrotum shows only 1 testicle. A 2nd testicle is palpated in the inguinal canal. The examination of the penis shows a normal urethral meatus. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 7-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. He was born at 36 weeks' gestation and has been healthy since. He is at the 60th percentile for length and weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. The abdomen is soft and nontender. The external genitalia appear normal. Examination shows a single palpable testicle in the right hemiscrotum. The scrotum is nontender and not enlarged. There is a palpable mass in the left inguinal canal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has an undescended testicle, also known as cryptorchidism. This is a common condition in which one or both of the testes fail to descend into the scrotum before birth. Most cases of cryptorchidism resolve spontaneously by 6 months of age. If the testis has not descended by this time, it is unlikely to do so, and surgical correction with orchiopexy is indicated. Orchiopexy should be performed between 6 and 18 months of age to preserve fertility and facilitate early detection of testicular cancer.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of vomiting and severe testicular pain for 3 hours. The boy has had 4–5 episodes of vomiting during this period. He has never had a similar episode in the past and takes no medications. His father died of testicular cancer at the age of 50. His immunizations are up-to-date. He appears anxious and uncomfortable. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities The abdomen is soft and nondistended. The left scrotum is firm, erythematous, and swollen. There is severe tenderness on palpation of the scrotum that persists on elevation of the testes. Stroking the inner side of the left thigh fails to elicit elevation of the scrotum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's severe testicular pain, vomiting, and abnormal physical examination findings (eg, firm, erythematous, swollen scrotum; absent cremasteric reflex) are concerning for testicular torsion. Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency that typically presents with the sudden onset of severe testicular pain often associated with nausea and vomiting. The most common physical examination finding is a high-riding testicle with an absent cremasteric reflex. The cremasteric reflex is elicited by lightly stroking the superior and medial part of the thigh, which normally causes the ipsilateral testicle to rise. This reflex is usually absent in testicular torsion.

The diagnosis of testicular torsion is primarily clinical, and surgical exploration should be performed immediately if torsion is suspected. Doppler ultrasonography can be used if the diagnosis is uncertain, but it should not delay surgical exploration. During surgical exploration, the testicle is detorsed and then bilaterally orchiopexied to prevent future torsion.

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because his parents are concerned about his early sexual development. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His brother was diagnosed with testicular cancer 5 years ago and underwent a radical orchiectomy. The patient is at the 85th percentile for height and 70th percentile for weight. Examination shows greasy facial skin. There is coarse axillary hair. Pubic hair development is at Tanner stage 3 and testicular development is at Tanner stage 2. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the wrist shows a bone age of 10 years. Basal serum luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are elevated. An MRI of the brain shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with central precocious puberty (CPP), which is defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls and age 9 in boys due to premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. The most common cause of CPP is idiopathic, but it can also be due to central nervous system abnormalities (eg, tumors, congenital anomalies, infections, trauma). This patient's bone age is advanced for his chronological age, and his luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone levels are elevated, which is consistent with CPP. The absence of central nervous system abnormalities on MRI makes idiopathic CPP the most likely diagnosis. 

The mainstay of treatment for CPP is gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist therapy (eg, leuprolide), which suppresses gonadotropin secretion and halts further sexual development. This therapy is typically continued until the age of normal puberty.

few_shot.question: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a right-sided scrotal swelling for the past 2 months. The swelling is intermittent and appears usually after the patient has been taken outdoors in a baby carrier, and disappears the next morning. The patient was born at term without complications and has been healthy. Examination shows a 3-cm, soft, nontender, and fluctuant right scrotal mass that is reducible and does not extend into the inguinal area. A light held behind the scrotum shines through. There are no bowel sounds in the mass. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.C: Ligation of the patent processus vaginalis

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history and physical examination findings are consistent with a communicating hydrocele. The processus vaginalis is an outpouching of the peritoneum that travels with the testis through the inguinal canal during its descent into the scrotum. Normally, the processus vaginalis obliterates by the time of birth, leaving the tunica vaginalis as a closed serous sac surrounding the testis. If the processus vaginalis remains patent, peritoneal fluid can travel from the abdominal cavity to the scrotum, leading to a hydrocele. A communicating hydrocele will change in size throughout the day as the fluid moves back and forth between the abdomen and the scrotum. In contrast, a noncommunicating hydrocele, which results from an imbalance of fluid production versus reabsorption within the tunica vaginalis, will not change in size.

Communicating hydroceles are common in infants and usually resolve spontaneously by age 1 year as the processus vaginalis obliterates. Therefore, the initial management is conservative with observation and reassurance. If the hydrocele persists beyond age 1 year or becomes significantly large or symptomatic, surgical repair is indicated.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: Ultrasonography of the scrotum shows a 2-cm hypoechoic, homogeneous testicular mass with sharp margins. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a single enlarged para-aortic lymph node. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's ultrasound findings are suggestive of a testicular tumor. The most common testicular tumors are germ cell tumors, which include seminomas and nonseminomas. The initial management of a testicular mass suspicious for malignancy is radical inguinal orchiectomy. This procedure allows for both definitive diagnosis and treatment. The spermatic cord is ligated as high as possible to prevent tumor seeding of the scrotum and to remove the lymphatic channels, which are the primary route of spread for testicular cancer.

Scrotal orchiectomy is contraindicated due to the risk of tumor seeding along the scrotal incision or within the scrotum. Similarly, open testicular biopsy is not recommended due to the risk of tumor seeding along the needle tract.

Systemic polychemotherapy is not the initial treatment for testicular cancer. It may be used as adjuvant therapy after orchiectomy in patients with advanced disease or poor prognostic features.

So, the answer is [C].

question: A 68-year-old female presents to her primary care physician with a 7-month history of fatigue and low back pain. Her pain is not improved by over the counter analgesics. Laboratory analysis is notable for a calcium level of 11.5 mg/dL, creatinine level of 2.0 mg/dL, and blood urea nitrogen level of 30 mg/dL. Large eosinophilic casts are seen on renal biopsy. Which of the following findings is most likely to be seen on peripheral blood smear?

answer_choices.B: Linear aggregations of red blood cells
answer_choices.D: Leukocytosis with abundant mature myeloid cells

few_shot.question:
A 75-year-old man presents to the physician with a complaint of persistent back pain. The patient states that the pain has been constant and occurs throughout the day. He says that he has also been experiencing greater fatigue when carrying out his daily activities. On review of systems, the patient notes that he lost more than 10 pounds in the past month despite maintaining his usual diet and exercising less often due to his fatigue. Physical exam is notable for a systolic murmur at the right sternal border, mild crackles at the bases of both lungs, and tenderness to palpation of his lumbar spine. Laboratory values are below:

Serum:
Na+: 141 mEq/L
Cl-: 101 mEq/L
K+: 4.2 mEq/L
HCO3-: 23 mEq/L
BUN: 20 mg/dL
Glucose: 101 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.6 mg/dL
Ca2+: 12.8 mg/dL

A peripheral blood smear is ordered for the patient’s work-up. Which of the following would be the most likely finding on peripheral blood smear?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of back pain, fatigue, weight loss, and hypercalcemia is concerning for multiple myeloma (MM). MM is a malignancy of plasma cells that primarily affects older adults. The most common presentation is bone pain with lytic lesions, usually in the axial skeleton (eg, back, skull). Other common findings include hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, and anemia. The hypercalcemia results from increased osteoclastic activity due to cytokines secreted by the neoplastic plasma cells. Renal insufficiency can be due to hypercalcemia, dehydration, and/or deposition of immunoglobulin light chains (Bence Jones proteins) in the renal tubules.

On peripheral blood smear, MM can cause rouleaux formation, which is the stacking of RBCs in a manner that resembles a stack of coins. This occurs due to increased serum protein, particularly fibrinogen and immunoglobulins, which cause the RBCs to stick together. The increased protein also leads to an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old woman comes to the physician because of lower back pain, generalized weakness, and weight loss that has occurred over the past 6 weeks. She also says that her urine has appeared foamy recently. Physical examination shows focal midline tenderness of the lumbar spine and conjunctival pallor. Her temperature is 100.5°F (38°C). A photomicrograph of a bone marrow biopsy specimen is shown. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of back pain, generalized weakness, weight loss, and foamy urine is suggestive of multiple myeloma (MM). MM is a malignancy of plasma cells that typically occurs in older adults. The bone marrow biopsy shows sheets of plasma cells, which are characterized by eccentric nuclei, clumped chromatin, and abundant, basophilic cytoplasm. 

In MM, the malignant plasma cells produce large amounts of monoclonal immunoglobulin (Ig), which can be detected in the serum (M spike on serum protein electrophoresis) and urine (Bence Jones proteins). The excess Ig light chains can precipitate in the distal tubules and collecting ducts, leading to renal tubular obstruction and damage. This can manifest as foamy urine due to proteinuria.

On peripheral blood smear, the excess Ig can cause erythrocytes to stick together in stacks, a phenomenon known as rouleaux formation. This gives the erythrocytes a "stacked-coin" appearance.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old man presents to your office with a chief complaint of constipation and many other perturbing minor medical concerns. He reports tiring easily, which he attributes to old age and years of persistent pain in his back and ribs. A complete blood count shows low hemoglobin and elevated serum creatinine. A peripheral blood smear shows stacks of red blood cells among other findings, and serum electropheresis reveals an abnormal concentration of protein resulting in a spike. Which of the following additional findings would you expect to see in this patient?

answer_choices.D: No additional findings - normal aging explains symptoms

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigue, back pain, anemia, and renal insufficiency, along with the finding of a monoclonal protein spike on serum electrophoresis, is suggestive of multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of plasma cells that primarily occurs in older adults. The most common presentation is related to hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, and bone pain (collectively referred to as CRAB symptoms). The bone pain is typically in the back or ribs and is due to osteolytic bone lesions or fractures from myeloma-induced bone disease. 

The monoclonal protein spike seen on serum electrophoresis is due to overproduction of a single class of immunoglobulin by the neoplastic plasma cells. Most commonly, the monoclonal protein is an intact immunoglobulin (usually IgG or IgA), but in some cases, it can be only free light chains (also known as Bence Jones proteins). These free light chains can be detected in the urine using a urine protein electrophoresis or a serum free light chain assay.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman seeks evaluation at a medical clinic with complaints of back pain and increased fatigue for 6 months. For the past week, the back pain has radiated to her legs and is stabbing in nature (7/10 in intensity). There are no associated paresthesias. Mean corpuscular volume 80 fL

A bone marrow biopsy shows increased plasma cells making up greater than 50% of the total cell population. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of back pain, anemia, renal insufficiency, hypercalcemia, and multiple osteolytic lesions on imaging is suggestive of multiple myeloma (MM). MM is a malignancy of plasma cells that produce a monoclonal immunoglobulin protein (M protein). The overproduction of this protein can lead to a hyperviscosity syndrome, renal damage, and suppression of normal immunoglobulin production, leading to an increased risk of infections. The malignant plasma cells can also cause bone destruction, leading to hypercalcemia and bone pain. The diagnosis of MM is confirmed by the presence of >10% clonal plasma cells on bone marrow biopsy and evidence of end-organ damage (eg, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) attributable to the plasma cell disorder.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of fatigue and bruises on her elbows. Examination shows a soft, nontender abdomen with no organomegaly. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 7 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 2,000/mm3, a platelet count of 40,000/mm3, and a reticulocyte count of 0.2%. The bone marrow is typically replaced by fat cells (adipocytes), which is the most likely finding on bone marrow biopsy in this patient.

Aplastic anemia can be caused by various factors, including drugs (eg, chloramphenicol, carbamazepine, NSAIDs, benzene, alkylating agents, antimetabolites), infections (eg, parvovirus B19, EBV, HIV, hepatitis C), autoimmune disease, and radiation. However, in many cases, no cause can be identified (idiopathic).

question: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents for an acute arm injury. The mother reports that they were walking in the park and the patient’s dad was swinging the patient in the air by her arms. The dad reports he then heard a click and the patient immediately began to cry. On examination, the patient is holding her right forearm in a pronated position and her elbow slightly flexed. Pain is localized to the lateral aspect of the elbow. She refuses to use the affected limb. She does allow passive flexion and extension with full range of motion but supination is limited and causes pain. Which of the following is the next step in management?

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room by his mother because of persistent crying and refusal to move his right arm. The episode began 30 minutes ago after the mother lifted him up by the arms. He appears distressed and is inconsolable. On examination, his right arm is held close to his body in a flexed and pronated position. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow) is a common injury in children younger than 5 years of age. It typically occurs when a longitudinal traction force is applied to the arm while the forearm is pronated and the elbow is extended. This can occur, for example, when an adult pulls a child up by the hand or wrist, or when a child is swung around by the arms during play. The annular ligament, which encircles the radial head and holds it in place, is lax in young children. This allows the radial head to slip out from under the annular ligament and become partially dislocated. The child typically refuses to use the affected arm and holds it in a flexed and pronated position. The injury is usually not associated with significant pain, swelling, or deformity. Treatment involves supination of the forearm followed by flexion of the elbow, which usually results in immediate relief of symptoms.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of right elbow swelling and pain 30 minutes after falling onto her outstretched right arm. She has been unable to move her right elbow since the fall. Physical examination shows bruising, swelling, and tenderness of the right elbow; range of motion is limited by pain. An x-ray of the right arm shows a supracondylar fracture of the humerus with anterior displacement of the proximal fragment. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
A supracondylar fracture of the humerus, especially with anterior displacement of the proximal fragment, is a common and serious injury in children. It can cause injury to the brachial artery, leading to compromised blood flow to the forearm and hand. Therefore, the most likely additional finding in this case would be an absent distal radial pulse due to this potential vascular compromise. This is a serious complication and requires immediate orthopedic consultation and likely surgical intervention to prevent long-term damage.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after falling from a trampoline and landing on his left arm. The boy's arm is reduced and placed into a splint pending surgical fixation. few_shot.explanation:
The patient's radiograph shows a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, a common fracture in children that results from a fall on an outstretched hand (eg, from monkey bars, a bicycle, or a trampoline). The distal fragment is often displaced posteriorly, which can cause injury to the brachial artery and/or median nerve. The median nerve innervates the majority of the flexor muscles of the forearm and intrinsic muscles of the hand. It is responsible for wrist flexion, forearm pronation, and flexion of the lateral fingers. Inability to flex the thumb would be indicative of a median nerve injury.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old child is brought to the emergency room by his parents in severe pain. They state that he fell on his outstretched right arm while playing with his friends. He is unable to move his right arm which is being supported by his left. On exam, his vitals are normal. His right extremity reveals normal pulses without swelling in any compartments, but there is crepitus above the elbow upon movement. The child is able to flex and extend his wrist, but this is limited by pain. The child has decreased sensation along his thumb and is unable to make the "OK" sign with his thumb and index finger. What is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The child's inability to make the "OK" sign with his thumb and index finger is indicative of a median nerve injury. The median nerve is responsible for flexion of the wrist and fingers, and opposition of the thumb. It also provides sensation to the palmar surface of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger. The median nerve is most commonly injured in supracondylar fractures of the humerus, which is the most common type of elbow fracture in children. This type of fracture typically occurs when a child falls onto an outstretched arm, causing the olecranon to drive the distal humerus proximally and posteriorly. This can cause injury to the brachial artery and median nerve, which are both closely associated with the distal humerus.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of arm pain following a fall that took place 5 hours ago. According to his mother, the boy was running in the yard when he fell and injured his right arm. The boy is crying and clutching his arm. During the past year, he has been brought in 4 other times for extremity pain following falls, all of which have been diagnosed as long bone fractures. He is at the 10th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 95/min, respirations are 21/min, and blood pressure is 97/68 mm Hg. His right forearm is diffusely erythematous. The patient withdraws and yells when his forearm is touched. His left arm has two small ecchymotic regions overlying the elbow and wrist. A photograph of his face is shown. An x-ray of the right forearm shows a transverse mid-ulnar fracture with diffusely decreased bone density. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of multiple fractures with minimal trauma, short stature, and blue sclerae is suggestive of osteogenesis imperfecta (OI). OI is a genetic disorder characterized by increased bone fragility and low bone mass. Most cases of OI are due to autosomal dominant mutations in the genes that encode the alpha-1 and alpha-2 chains of type I collagen (COL1A1 and COL1A2). Type I collagen is the most abundant collagen in the body and is a major component of the extracellular matrix of bone, skin, and tendons. Defects in type I collagen can therefore lead to bone fragility (leading to fractures), hyperextensible skin, and blue sclerae due to the underlying choroidal veins showing through the thin sclera. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 33-year-old man presents to the emergency department with altered mental status. He was at work as a construction worker when his coworkers found him down at the work site. The patient recently underwent anesthesia for an appendectomy several months ago. He also has a past medical history of schizophrenia well controlled with haloperidol and is currently taking phenytoin for epilepsy. He is also currently taking propranolol for anxiety and hyperthyroidism. His temperature is 106°F (41.1°C), blood pressure is 109/62 mmHg, pulse is 170/min, respirations are 23/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Physical exam is notable for an altered man with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 10. He has minimal muscle tone and is incoherent when answering questions. The patient is covered in sweat and dirt. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old man presents to the emergency department acutely confused. The patient was found down at a local construction site by his coworkers. The patient has a past medical history of a seizure disorder and schizophrenia and is currently taking haloperidol. He had recent surgery 2 months ago to remove an inflamed appendix. His temperature is 105°F (40.6°C), blood pressure is 120/84 mmHg, pulse is 150/min, respirations are 19/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a confused man who cannot answer questions. His clothes are drenched in sweat. He is not making purposeful movements with his extremities although no focal neurological deficits are clearly apparent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Exertional heat stroke is a life-threatening condition characterized by hyperthermia (core body temperature >40°C [104°F]) and central nervous system dysfunction (eg, altered mental status, seizure) that occurs in the setting of strenuous physical activity, often in a hot environment. It is most common in young, otherwise healthy individuals, such as athletes, military recruits, and outdoor laborers. The pathogenesis involves failure of thermoregulation due to excessive heat generation and/or inadequate heat dissipation. The latter can occur due to dehydration, high humidity, or, as in this patient, use of antipsychotic medications, which can inhibit central thermoregulation and impair sweating. 

Heat exhaustion is a milder form of heat illness that can develop after several days of exposure to high temperatures and inadequate or unbalanced replacement of fluids. It is the body's response to an excessive loss of the water and salt contained in sweat. Those most prone to heat exhaustion are elderly people, people with high blood pressure, and people working or exercising in a hot environment.

Malignant hyperthermia is a potentially fatal reaction to certain medications used during general anesthesia. In susceptible individuals, these medications can induce a drastic and uncontrolled increase in skeletal muscle oxidative metabolism, which overwhelms the body's capacity to supply oxygen, remove carbon dioxide, and regulate body temperature, eventually leading to circulatory collapse and death if not treated quickly.

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening neurological disorder most often caused by an adverse reaction to neuroleptic or antipsychotic drugs. Symptoms include high fever, confusion, rigid muscles, variable blood pressure, sweating, and fast heart rate. Complications may include rhabdomyolysis or high blood potassium.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 31-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of fever and increasing confusion for the past day. He has bipolar disorder with psychotic features and hypothyroidism. Current medications are lithium, haloperidol, and levothyroxine. He drinks one beer with dinner every night. His speech is confused and he is oriented to person only. His temperature is 40°C (104°F), pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 160/110 mm Hg. He appears acutely ill. Examination shows diaphoresis and muscle rigidity. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ bilaterally. There is minor rigidity of the neck with full range of motion. His lungs are clear to auscultation. The abdomen is soft and nontender. His leukocyte count is 15,100/mm3 and serum creatine kinase activity is 1100 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening condition that can occur after administration of antipsychotic drugs. It is characterized by fever, altered mental status, muscle rigidity, and autonomic dysfunction (eg, tachycardia, labile blood pressure, diaphoresis). Laboratory abnormalities include leukocytosis and elevated creatine kinase due to muscle breakdown. The most common offending agents are the typical antipsychotics (eg, haloperidol) and the atypical antipsychotic risperidone. NMS is thought to result from dopamine D2 receptor antagonism in the hypothalamus (leading to hyperthermia) and the nigrostriatal pathway (causing muscle rigidity). Treatment involves discontinuation of the antipsychotic medication and supportive care (eg, cooling blankets, volume resuscitation). Dantrolene or bromocriptine can be used in severe cases.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his roommates for aggressive and unusual behavior. His roommates state that he has been under a lot of stress lately from his final exams and has been more reclusive. They state that this evening he was very irritable and was yelling at his computer prior to breaking it, followed by him spending several hours at the gym. His temperature is 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 137/98 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 23/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for an irritable young man. Cardiopulmonary exam is notable for tachycardia and bilateral clear breath sounds. Neurological exam reveals dilated pupils. The patient is notably diaphoretic and speaks very rapidly during the physical exam and is aggressive. He is given haloperidol, diphenhydramine, and diazepam for sedation and placed in soft restraints. His symptoms resolved over the next 10 hours in the emergency department. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of agitation, aggression, tachycardia, and diaphoresis is suggestive of a sympathomimetic toxidrome. Sympathomimetic agents include amphetamines, cocaine, and synthetic cathinones ("bath salts"). Amphetamines are often used by students as study aids due to their ability to increase wakefulness and concentration. They are available in many forms, including prescription medications for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (eg, lisdexamfetamine, mixed amphetamine salts) that are commonly sold and used illicitly. Amphetamines increase the release and inhibit the reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin in the brain. Symptoms of amphetamine intoxication include severe agitation, combativeness, psychosis, delirium, myoclonus, and, rarely, seizures. Increased sympathetic outflow may lead to significantly increased blood pressure and heart rate. Increased muscular activity can lead to hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis. The most important aspect of management is sedation, usually with a benzodiazepine.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old man is brought to the emergency room because of fever and increasing confusion for the past 2 days. He has paranoid schizophrenia and hypertension. His current medications are chlorpromazine and amlodipine. He appears ill. He is not oriented to time, place, or person. His temperature is 40°C (104°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 29/min and blood pressure is 155/100 mm Hg. Examination shows diaphoresis. Muscle tone is increased bilaterally. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ bilaterally. Neurologic examination shows psychomotor agitation. His speech is incoherent. Lungs are clear to auscultation. His neck is supple. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Serum laboratory analysis shows a leukocyte count of 11,300/mm3 and serum creatine kinase concentration of 833 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, altered mental status, autonomic dysregulation (eg, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis), generalized muscle rigidity, and elevated serum creatine kinase level are suggestive of neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). NMS is a potentially life-threatening condition that can occur after administration of any antipsychotic medication. The exact pathophysiology is unknown, but it is thought to involve dopamine D2 receptor antagonism in the hypothalamus, leading to increased muscle rigidity and hyperthermia. 

Management of NMS involves discontinuation of the offending agent and supportive care (eg, cooling blankets, volume resuscitation). Dantrolene, a skeletal muscle relaxant, can be used to reduce muscle rigidity and hyperthermia. It acts by inhibiting calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle, thereby reducing intracellular calcium concentrations and muscle contraction.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old male presents with altered mental status. He was recently admitted to the hospital due to a tibial fracture suffered while playing soccer. His nurse states that he is difficult to arouse. His temperature is 98.6 deg F (37 deg C), blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, pulse is 60/min, and respirations are 6/min. Exam is notable for pinpoint pupils and significant lethargy. Which of the following describes the mechanism of action of the drug likely causing this patient's altered mental status?

answer_choices.A: Neuronal hyperpolarization due to potassium efflux
answer_choices.B: Neuronal hyperpolarization due to sodium influx
answer_choices.C: Neuronal depolarization due to sodium efflux
answer_choices.D: Neuronal hyperpolarization due to chloride influx

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's altered mental status, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils are suggestive of opioid toxicity. Opioids are commonly used for pain control in patients with fractures. They exert their effects by binding to opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta), which are G protein-coupled receptors that function via inhibition of adenylyl cyclase. This leads to decreased intracellular cAMP and inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels on presynaptic nerve terminals, which decreases the release of excitatory neurotransmitters. Opioid receptor activation also increases potassium efflux on postsynaptic membranes, leading to neuronal hyperpolarization and reduced neuronal firing.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 72-year-old anthropologist with long-standing hypertension visits your office for a routine exam. You notice an abnormality on his laboratory results caused by his regimen of captopril and triamterene. What abnormality did you most likely find?

few_shot.question: A 41-year-old African American man presents to his primary care physician a few months after being found to have a blood pressure of 152/95 mmHg. The patient denies any current symptoms, having any past medical history, or prior hospitalizations. He does not take any medications but takes one multivitamin daily. His blood pressures on three separate occasions have been 151/93 mmHg, 150/90 mmHg, and 155/97 mmHg. In today’s visit, his blood pressure is 149/91 mmHg despite exercise and dietary modifications. Physical examination is unremarkable. After extensive work-up he is started on appropriate monotherapy for his hypertension. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities may be found on follow-up testing?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has stage 1 hypertension (systolic blood pressure 130-139 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure 80-89 mmHg) and should be started on antihypertensive medication. The initial treatment of hypertension in black patients, including those with diabetes, should be with a thiazide-type diuretic or a calcium channel blocker. Thiazide diuretics decrease blood pressure by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, thereby promoting natriuresis and reducing plasma volume. Chronic use of thiazide diuretics can lead to hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and decreased glomerular filtration rate.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 64-year-old man presents to his primary care physician's office for a routine check-up. His past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation, and ischemic cardiomyopathy. On his last visit three months ago, he was found to have hyperkalemia, at which time lisinopril and spironolactone were removed from his medication regimen. Currently, his medications include coumadin, aspirin, metformin, glyburide, metoprolol, furosemide, and amlodipine. His T is 37 C (98.6 F), BP 154/92 mm Hg, HR 80/min, and RR 16/min. His physical exam is notable for elevated jugular venous pressure, an S3 heart sound, and 1+ pitting pedal edema. His repeat lab work at the current visit is as follows:

Sodium: 138 mEq/L, potassium: 5.7 mEq/L, chloride 112 mEq/L, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L, BUN 29 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.1 mg/dL.

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's acid-base and electrolyte abnormalities?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's laboratory results show a hyperchloremic, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, which is most consistent with renal tubular acidosis (RTA). The most likely type of RTA in this patient is type 4, or hyperkalemic RTA, which is suggested by his hyperkalemia. Type 4 RTA is caused by hypoaldosteronism or a resistance to the actions of aldosterone on the renal tubule. It is most commonly seen in patients with diabetic nephropathy, chronic tubulointerstitial disease, and those taking certain medications such as NSAIDs, calcineurin inhibitors, and potassium-sparing diuretics.

This patient's diabetes and hypertension put him at risk for chronic kidney disease, which can cause type 4 RTA. However, his relatively preserved glomerular filtration rate (GFR) makes this less likely. His medications, including furosemide and amlodipine, are not typically associated with RTA.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 66-year-old male presents to the outpatient cardiology clinic for evaluation of suspected primary hypertension. His blood pressure is elevated to 169/96 mm Hg, and his heart rate is 85/min. Physical examination reveals an overweight male with regular heart and lung sounds. Following repeated elevated blood pressure measurements, the diagnosis is made and the patient is started on hydrochlorothiazide. Of the following options, which is a side effect that one could experience from thiazide-like diuretics?
few_shot.explanation:
Thiazide diuretics are commonly used in the treatment of hypertension. They work by inhibiting the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, leading to increased sodium and chloride excretion. This leads to a decrease in extracellular fluid volume and cardiac output, which in turn decreases blood pressure.

However, thiazide diuretics can also cause several side effects. These include hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, and hyperuricemia. Hyperuricemia occurs because thiazides decrease uric acid secretion, leading to increased serum uric acid levels. This can precipitate gout in susceptible individuals.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old-man presents to the clinic for a 2-month follow-up. He is relatively healthy except for a 5-year history of hypertension. He is currently on lisinopril, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide. The patient has no concerns and denies headaches, weight changes, fever, chest pain, palpitations, vision changes, or abdominal pain. His temperature is 98.9°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 157/108 mmHg, pulse is 87/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Laboratory testing demonstrates elevated plasma aldosterone concentration and low renin concentration. What is the most likely explanation for this patient’s presentation?

answer_choices.C: Increased activity of the epithelial sodium channel at the kidney
answer_choices.D: Mutation of the Na-K-2C- cotransporter at the thick ascending limb

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis in the setting of elevated aldosterone and suppressed renin are suggestive of primary hyperaldosteronism. Primary hyperaldosteronism is most commonly due to an aldosterone-producing adenoma (APA) or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. APAs, also known as Conn syndrome, are usually solitary and unilateral. They cause increased aldosterone secretion, leading to volume expansion, hypertension, and suppression of plasma renin activity. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in principal cells of the cortical collecting duct, which enhances potassium secretion and hydrogen ion secretion, leading to hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, respectively.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 74-year-old man presents to the clinic for a routine health checkup. He has been hypertensive for the past 20 years, and he has had congestive heart failure for the past 2 years. He is currently on captopril and claims to be compliant with his medication. His most recent echocardiogram report shows that his ejection fraction has been decreasing, so the physician decides to add spironolactone to his drug regimen. Which of the following complications should be most closely monitored for in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that is used in the treatment of hypertension and heart failure. It works by antagonizing the effects of aldosterone in the distal tubules and collecting ducts of the nephron, leading to increased excretion of sodium and water and decreased excretion of potassium. This can lead to hyperkalemia, especially in patients with renal insufficiency or those taking other drugs that increase potassium levels, such as ACE inhibitors (eg, captopril). Therefore, the most important complication to monitor for in this patient is hyperkalemia.

So, the answer is [A].
