question: A 17-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. The patient was an unrestrained driver in a head-on collision. He has a past medical history of asthma, depression, and anxiety. He is not currently taking any medications. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 115/min, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. The patient's cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. The patient is breathing on his own and has strong distal pulses. Ultimately, the patient is discharged with follow up instructions after no significant fractures or injuries are found. The patient then presents 4 months later to his primary doctor with weakness. The patient's strength in his upper extremities is 1/5. He has reduced sensation in his upper extremities as well. The patient's lower extremities reveal 5/5 strength with intact sensation. A chest radiograph and basic labs are ordered. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. The patient is conscious and communicating with hospital personnel. He is in pain and covered in bruises and scrapes. The patient was the driver in a head-on motor vehicle collision. The patient's temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), pulse is 112/min, blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg, respirations are 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. A full trauma assessment is being performed and is notable for 0/5 strength in the right upper extremity for extension of the wrist. The patient is started on IV fluids and morphine, and radiography is ordered. The patient has bilateral breath sounds, a normal S1 and S2, and no signs of JVD. His blood pressure 30 minutes later is 122/70 mmHg. Which of the following fractures is most likely in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with a midshaft humerus fracture, which can cause injury to the radial nerve as it spirals around the humerus in the radial groove. The radial nerve provides motor innervation to the extensor muscles of the arm, which are responsible for extension at the elbow, wrist, and fingers, as well as sensory innervation to the posterior arm and forearm and the dorsal aspect of the lateral 3.5 fingers. Injury to the radial nerve can cause wrist drop, which is the inability to extend the wrist and fingers.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 74-year-old male is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after he fell from the top of the staircase at home. He reports pain in his neck as well as weakness of his upper extremities. He is alert and immobilized in a cervical collar. He has hypertension treated with hydrochlorthiazide. His pulse is 90/min and regular, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 140/70 mmHg. Examination shows bruising and midline cervical tenderness. Neurologic examination shows diminished strength and sensation to pain and temperature in the upper extremities, particularly in the hands. Upper extremity deep tendon reflexes are absent. Strength, sensation, and reflexes in the lower extremities are intact. Anal sensation and tone are present. Babinski's sign is absent bilaterally. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the cause of this patient's neurologic examination findings?

answer_choices.D: MRI of the cervical spine without contrast

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with central cord syndrome, a type of incomplete spinal cord injury that is most commonly seen in elderly patients with forced hyperextension injuries (eg, fall onto the face or back of the head). Patients with preexisting cervical spondylosis or stenosis are particularly susceptible. The syndrome is believed to result from damage to the central portion of the spinal cord, which is supplied by the central (sulcal) branch of the anterior spinal artery. The central cord contains the crossing fibers of the lateral corticospinal tract (which mediate motor function) and the axons transmitting pain and temperature sensation. The hands and upper extremities are predominantly affected because the axons innervating these areas are located in the center of the spinal cord. The lower extremities are spared because the axons innervating these areas are located more peripherally.

MRI of the cervical spine is the imaging modality of choice for patients with suspected spinal cord injury. It can detect cord compression, hemorrhage, edema, and transection, as well as preexisting degenerative changes (eg, spinal stenosis, herniated nucleus pulposus).

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with shortness of breath and chest pain, 35 minutes after he was involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He was the helmeted driver of a scooter hit by a truck. On arrival, he is alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale rating of 14. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 103/min, respirations are 33/min and blood pressure is 132/88 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Examination shows multiple abrasions over his abdomen and extremities. There is a 2.5-cm (1-in) laceration on the left side of the chest. There are decreased breath sounds over the left base. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is soft and there is tenderness to palpation over the left upper quadrant. Bowel sounds are normal. His hemoglobin concentration is 13.6 g/dL, leukocyte count is 9,110/mm3, and platelet count is 190,000/mm3. A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a high-speed motor vehicle collision, left-sided chest pain, and decreased breath sounds on the left side, along with the chest x-ray findings of an elevated left hemidiaphragm and nasogastric tube coiling in the chest, are suggestive of a traumatic diaphragmatic rupture. This is a surgical emergency that occurs most commonly due to blunt trauma from motor vehicle collisions. The sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure can cause a tear in the diaphragm, more commonly on the left side due to relative protection of the right hemidiaphragm by the liver. The initial tear can be small and may not cause symptoms until the defect enlarges over time, leading to herniation of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity. This can cause respiratory distress due to compression of the lung and/or visceral strangulation. Chest x-ray may show an elevated hemidiaphragm, nasogastric tube coiling in the chest, or visualization of intra-abdominal contents (eg, bowel, stomach) above the diaphragm.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 41-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after falling while mountain biking and hitting his head. Initially, he refused treatment, but an hour ago he began to develop a severe headache, nausea, and left leg weakness. He has no visual changes and is oriented to person, time, and place. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 68/min, respirations are 17/min and regular, and blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg. Examination shows a 5-cm bruise on the right side of his skull. The pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation. Muscle strength is 0/5 in his left knee and foot. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of head trauma, followed by a lucid interval and subsequent neurologic deterioration, is suggestive of an epidural hematoma. Epidural hematomas are often caused by rupture of the middle meningeal artery due to a temporal bone fracture. They can expand rapidly and cause a rapid increase in intracranial pressure (ICP), leading to herniation syndromes.

The most common type of herniation in epidural hematoma is subfalcine (cingulate) herniation, in which the cingulate gyrus is displaced under the falx cerebri. This can cause compression of the anterior cerebral artery, leading to infarction and the observed motor deficits.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which he was the unrestrained driver. After extrication, he had severe neck pain and was unable to move his arms and legs. On arrival, he is lethargic and cannot provide a history. Hospital records show that eight months ago, he underwent an open reduction and internal fixation of the right humerus. His neck is immobilized in a cervical collar. Intravenous fluids are being administered. His pulse is 64/min, respirations are 8/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 104/64 mm Hg. Examination shows multiple bruises over the chest, abdomen, and extremities. There is flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes in all extremities. Sensory examination shows decreased sensation below the shoulders. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is soft. There is swelling of the right ankle and right knee. Squeezing of the glans penis does not produce anal sphincter contraction. A focused assessment with sonography for trauma shows no abnormalities. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and loss of sensation below the shoulders following a high-speed motor vehicle collision is consistent with spinal shock, a form of neurogenic shock. Spinal shock is a temporary loss of all neurologic function, including motor, sensory, and reflex activity, below the level of a spinal cord injury. It is thought to be due to disruption of baseline sympathetic outflow, and it can last for days to weeks. 

The most appropriate next step in management is placement of a Foley catheter. This is because spinal shock can cause neurogenic bladder, leading to urinary retention. This can be complicated by urinary tract infections and renal damage if not managed promptly.

So, the answer is [A].

question:
A 62-year-old woman is evaluated because of a 3-day history of headache, nausea, and decreased urination. Laboratory studies show:
Serum

few_shot.question:
A 64-year-old female with a history of end-stage renal disease presents to her primary care physician complaining of weakness. She reports a six-month history of progressive weakness accompanied by occasional dull aching pain in her arms, legs, and lower back. She has also started to increase her fiber intake because of occasional strained bowel movements. Her past medical history is notable for poorly controlled diabetes, major depressive disorder, and obesity. She takes insulin and sertraline. She has a twenty pack-year smoking history and drinks alcohol socially. Her temperature is 98.5°F (36.9°C), blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 16/min. Laboratory findings are shown below:

Serum:
Na+: 138 mEq/L
Cl-: 99 mEq/L
K+: 3.9 mEq/L
HCO3-: 26 mEq/L
BUN: 20 mg/dL
Glucose: 140 mg/dL
Creatinine: 2.0 mg/dL
Parathyroid hormone: 720 µU/mL
Ca2+: 11.1 mg/dL
Phosphorus (inorganic): 4.8 mg/dl

A medication with which of the following mechanisms of action is most likely indicated to address this patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of weakness, bone pain, and constipation, along with her elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels, are suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. However, given her history of end-stage renal disease, the most likely diagnosis is secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease (CKD). CKD can cause decreased production of calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3) and decreased phosphate excretion, leading to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, respectively. The hypocalcemia stimulates PTH secretion, leading to secondary hyperparathyroidism. Over time, the parathyroid glands become hyperplastic and autonomously secrete PTH, leading to hypercalcemia.

The treatment of choice for secondary hyperparathyroidism due to CKD is calcimimetic agents, which activate the calcium-sensing receptor in the parathyroid gland and decrease PTH secretion.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 40-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of generalized weakness. He also reports increased urination and thirst. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease. His only medication is metformin. Serum studies show:

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of generalized weakness, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap is suggestive of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease). Primary adrenal insufficiency is most commonly due to autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands, but other causes include infections (eg, tuberculosis, HIV), hemorrhage, and metastatic cancer. In primary adrenal insufficiency, there is a deficiency of both glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone). 

Aldosterone deficiency results in impaired renal sodium reabsorption and potassium and hydrogen ion secretion, leading to hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. The increased potassium levels can cause generalized muscle weakness, and the metabolic acidosis can cause an increased anion gap and increased serum bicarbonate levels. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
Two days after admission to the hospital, a 74-year-old man develops confusion and headache. He has also been vomiting over the past hour. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. He is lethargic and oriented only to person. Examination shows flushed skin. Fundoscopic examination shows bright red retinal veins. Serum studies show:
Na+ 138 mEq/L
K+ 3.5 mEq/L
Cl- 100 mEq/L
HCO3- 17 mEq/L
Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL
Urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL
Lactate 8.0 mEq/L (N = 0.5 - 2.2 mEq/L)
Glucose 75 mg/dL
Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows a pH of 7.13. This patient's current presentation is most likely due to treatment for which of the following conditions?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of confusion, headache, vomiting, and bright red retinal veins is suggestive of cerebral edema due to hyperperfusion syndrome. This condition can occur when there is a rapid decrease in blood pressure in a patient with chronic hypertension. The autoregulatory mechanisms of the cerebral vasculature are impaired in chronic hypertension, leading to an increase in the upper limit of autoregulation. If the blood pressure is rapidly lowered below this limit, as can occur with aggressive antihypertensive treatment, cerebral blood flow can become pressure passive, leading to cerebral hyperperfusion and cerebral edema.

The patient's arterial blood gas shows a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, which is likely due to lactic acidosis from the cerebral hyperperfusion. The other laboratory values are within normal limits.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 32-year-old man presents with excessive urination. He reports that he urinates 10 times a day and wakes up multiple times a night to pee. He complains that this is affecting both his social life and his ability to concentrate at work. He states that he always has an “active bladder,” but his symptoms worsened when he started meeting with a physical trainer last month who told him he should increase his water intake to prevent dehydration. The patient has a history of migraines and bipolar I disorder. His medications include metoprolol, lithium, and naproxen as needed. A basic metabolic panel is performed, and the results are shown below:

Serum:
Na+: 149 mEq/L
Cl-: 102 mEq/L
K+: 3.4 mEq/L
HCO3-: 26 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen: 12 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.0 mg/dL
Glucose: 78 mg/dL
Ca2+: 9.5 mg/dL

A urinalysis is obtained, which reveals pale-colored urine with a specific gravity of 0.852 and a urine osmolarity of 135 mOsm/L. The patient undergoes a water deprivation test. The patient’s urine specific gravity increases to 0.897 and urine osmolarity is now 155 mOsm/L. The patient is given an antidiuretic hormone analogue. Urine osmolarity rises to 188 mOsm/L. Which of the following is the best initial management for the patient’s most likely condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of polyuria and polydipsia, along with a low urine osmolality and high serum osmolality, are suggestive of diabetes insipidus (DI). DI is a condition characterized by decreased responsiveness to or production of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), leading to excessive urination. The water deprivation test, which showed a minimal increase in urine osmolality, and the response to desmopressin (the ADH analogue), which showed a significant increase in urine osmolality, suggest that this patient has nephrogenic DI rather than central DI. Nephrogenic DI is caused by insensitivity of the kidneys to ADH, leading to an inability to concentrate urine.

The most common cause of nephrogenic DI is lithium, a mood stabilizer used in the treatment of bipolar disorder. Lithium can enter the cells of the collecting ducts in the kidneys via the epithelial sodium channel. Inside the cell, lithium inhibits glycogen synthase kinase type 3 beta, which results in increased intracellular concentrations of cyclic AMP and resistance to the action of ADH. The treatment for lithium-induced nephrogenic DI is discontinuation of lithium.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 44-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department for confusion and lethargy for the past 2 hours. Per the husband, the patient was behaving weirdly and forgot how to get to the bathroom at her house. She was also difficult to wake up from her nap. The husband denies any fever, weight loss, headaches, dizziness, chest pain, or gastrointestinal changes. He reports that she had frequent diarrhea over the past 3 days but attributed it to food poisoning. In the emergency room, the patient had a 1-minute episode of seizure activity. Following initial resuscitation and stabilization, laboratory studies were performed and the results are shown below.

Hemoglobin: 13 g/dL
Hematocrit: 38%
Leukocyte count: 7,600/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 170,000/mm^3

Serum:
Na+: 125 mEq/L
Cl-: 90 mEq/L
K+: 3.2 mEq/L
HCO3-: 20 mEq/L
BUN: 22 mg/dL
Glucose: 101 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.0 mg/dL
Thyroid-stimulating hormone: 3.2 µU/mL
Ca2+: 9.3 mg/dL
AST: 19 U/L
ALT: 22 U/L

What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

answer_choices.A: Increase the serum potassium with potassium solution
answer_choices.B: Increase the serum sodium slowly with hypertonic saline solution
answer_choices.C: Increase the serum sodium slowly with normal saline solution
answer_choices.D: Start patient on maintenance anti-epileptic medications

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's confusion, lethargy, and seizure activity in the setting of hyponatremia (serum sodium <135 mEq/L) are suggestive of severe symptomatic hyponatremia. The most common cause of euvolemic hyponatremia is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), which is characterized by excessive free water reabsorption in the renal collecting tubules due to pathologically elevated ADH levels. This patient's recent history of diarrhea may have stimulated ADH release as a physiologic response to volume depletion. Other common etiologies of SIADH include malignancy (eg, small cell lung cancer), pulmonary disease (eg, tuberculosis), CNS disorders (eg, stroke), and drugs (eg, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, carbamazepine).

The mainstay of therapy for severe symptomatic hyponatremia is hypertonic (3%) saline. This therapy promotes the rapid movement of water out of the brain cells, reducing cerebral edema. The goal is to increase the serum sodium by 4-6 mEq/L in the first 1-2 hours to a level not exceeding 10 mEq/L in the first 24 hours. Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia (>10-12 mEq/L in 24 hours) can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome, a potentially fatal disorder that can cause dysarthria, dysphagia, diplopia, and quadriparesis.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive pain and stiffness of the fingers of her right hand. The stiffness is worse at the end of the day. She recently retired after working for 28 years as a typist at a data entry firm. Physical examination shows swelling, joint-line tenderness, and decreased range of motion of the first metacarpophalangeal joint and the distal interphalangeal joints of the right hand. Discrete, hard, mildly tender nodules are palpated over the 2nd and 4th distal interphalangeal joints of the right hand. An x-ray of her right hand shows narrowing of the interphalangeal joint spaces with subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's condition?

answer_choices.A: Bacterial infection of the joint space
answer_choices.C: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal precipitation in the joints

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of progressive pain and stiffness of the fingers of her right hand that is worse at the end of the day. She works as a hair dresser and has to take frequent breaks to rest her hand. She has hypertension, for which she takes hydrochlorothiazide. Two weeks ago, she completed a course of oral antibiotics for a urinary tract infection. Her sister has systemic lupus erythematosus. She drinks one to two beers daily and occasionally more on weekends. Over the past 2 weeks, she has been taking ibuprofen as needed for the joint pain. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows swelling, joint-line tenderness, and decreased range of motion of the right first metacarpophalangeal joint as well as the 2nd and 4th distal interphalangeal joints of the right hand. Discrete, hard, mildly tender swellings are palpated over the 2nd and 4th distal interphalangeal joints of the right hand. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for these findings?

answer_choices.A: Bacterial infection of the joint space
answer_choices.D: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal precipitation in the joints

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of pain and stiffness in the distal interphalangeal (DIP) and first metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, along with the presence of bony enlargements (Heberden nodes) in the DIP joints, are suggestive of osteoarthritis (OA). OA is a degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive erosion of articular cartilage. It is the most common joint disease and typically affects the DIP joints, first carpometacarpal joint, knees, and hips. Risk factors for OA include age, female sex, obesity, joint injury, and certain occupations (eg, jobs requiring frequent kneeling/squatting or climbing). This patient's occupation as a hairdresser, which requires repetitive use of the hands, likely contributed to the development of OA in her hand.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old female presents to her primary care provider complaining of pain and stiffness in her hands and knees. She reports that the stiffness is worse in the morning and appears to get better throughout the day. She is otherwise healthy and denies any recent illness. She does not play sports. On examination, her metacarpal-phalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints are swollen and erythematous. Her distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints appear normal. She exhibits pain with both passive and active range of motion in her knees bilaterally. Serological analysis reveals high titers of anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies. Which of the following processes underlies this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.A: Precipitation of monosodium urate crystals in the intra-articular space
answer_choices.B: Post-infectious inflammation of the articular surfaces

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of joint pain and stiffness that is worse in the morning and improves throughout the day, along with the physical exam findings of swollen and erythematous MCP and PIP joints, are suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a systemic, inflammatory disorder that primarily affects the joints. It is characterized by a symmetric, erosive synovitis that often leads to progressive joint destruction, loss of function, and disability. The pathogenesis of RA involves synovial hypertrophy and the formation of a destructive granulation tissue (pannus) at the margins of the articular surfaces and at the bone-cartilage interface. The presence of anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies is highly specific for RA.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressive pain and stiffness in her hands and wrists for the past several months. Her hands are stiff in the morning; the stiffness improves as she starts her chores. Physical examination shows bilateral swelling and tenderness of the wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, and proximal interphalangeal joints. Her range of motion is limited by pain. Laboratory studies show an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate. This patient's condition is most likely associated with which of the following findings?

answer_choices.A: IgG antibodies with a TNF-α binding domain on the Fc region
answer_choices.B: HLA-DQ2 proteins on white blood cells
answer_choices.C: HLA-A3 proteins on white blood cells
answer_choices.D: IgM antibodies against the Fc region of IgG

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symmetric polyarthritis involving the small joints of the hands, associated with morning stiffness that improves with activity, is suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a systemic, inflammatory disorder that primarily involves the synovial joints. It is characterized by the presence of autoantibodies, including rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA). RF is an IgM antibody that targets the Fc portion of IgG. Immune complexes formed by RF and IgG activate the complement system, leading to a chronic, inflammatory state that results in synovial hypertrophy and progressive joint destruction.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the office complaining of bilateral joint pain and stiffness in her hand joints for the past 3 months. She reports increasing difficulty holding a coffee cup or pen due to stiffness, especially in the morning. Over-the-counter ibuprofen partially relieves her symptoms. Past medical history is significant for dysthymia and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Vital signs are normal except for a low-grade fever. On examination, there is mild swelling and tenderness in the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints and wrists. Nontender and non-pruritic nodules near the elbows are noted. Chest and abdominal examination are normal. X-rays of the hands reveal soft tissue swelling, joint space narrowing, and bony erosions. Her hematocrit is 32%, and her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 40 mm/hr. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of symmetric joint pain and stiffness, especially in the morning, along with the presence of rheumatoid nodules and radiographic findings of joint space narrowing and bony erosions, are consistent with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a systemic, autoimmune inflammatory disorder that primarily affects the synovial joints. Extra-articular manifestations can include rheumatoid nodules, vasculitis, and pulmonary disease (eg, pleuritis, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary nodules). 

Patients with RA are at increased risk for osteoporosis due to several factors. Chronic inflammation leads to increased production of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, interleukin-1, tumor necrosis factor-α), which stimulate osteoclast activity and inhibit osteoblast function, leading to increased bone resorption. In addition, patients with RA often have decreased mobility due to joint pain and stiffness, which can also contribute to bone loss. Glucocorticoids, which are often used in the treatment of RA, can further increase the risk of osteoporosis.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to her primary care provider complaining of a psoriatic flare that has worsened over the past 2 days. The patient states that her psoriasis is normally well-controlled. She also complains of some fatigue and states that she has recently developed pain and tenderness in the joints of her hands with the right hand being more tender than the left. Her hands are stiff in the morning, and sometimes her fingers swell up. She attributes these changes to her new job where she constantly uses her hands to manufacture cabinets. Physical exam reveals plaques with silvery scale on her elbows and knees. The distal joints of her right hand are mildly swollen and the nails on both hands appear pitted. What is the most likely pathogenesis of her joint pain?

answer_choices.A: Local invasive infection of the joint space
answer_choices.C: Deposition of crystals in the joint space
answer_choices.D: Release of TNF and activation of RANKL pathway

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's joint pain, stiffness, and swelling, along with her history of psoriasis, are suggestive of psoriatic arthritis. Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy that can occur in patients with psoriasis. It is characterized by asymmetric joint involvement, dactylitis (ie, "sausage digit"), and nail pitting. The pathogenesis of psoriatic arthritis is not completely understood, but it is thought to involve the release of TNF and activation of the RANKL pathway, leading to osteoclast activation and subsequent bone resorption. This is similar to the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question:
A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician because she has not had menstrual bleeding for the past 3 months. Menses had previously occurred at irregular 15–45 day intervals with moderate to heavy flow. Menarche was at the age of 14 years. She started having sexual intercourse with her boyfriend about 3 months ago. Six months ago she had a manic episode, which was treated with risperidone. Her mother has PCOS and her father has diabetes mellitus. She is very conscious of her weight and appearance. She is 171 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 79 kg (174 lb); BMI is 27.02 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 60/min, and blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Pelvic examination shows a normal vagina and cervix. Serum hormone studies show:
Prolactin 16 ng/mL
Thyroid-stimulating hormone 3.8 μU/mL
Follicle-stimulating hormone 6 mIU/mL
Luteinizing hormone 5.1 mIU/mL
Progesterone 0.8 ng/mL (follicular N <3; luteal N >3–5)
Testosterone 2.2 nmol/L (N <3.5)
A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?"

answer_choices.B: Congenital defect of the Mullerian ducts

few_shot.question:
A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because she has not had menstrual bleeding for the past 2 months. Menses had previously occurred at irregular 15–45 day intervals with moderate to heavy flow. Menarche was at the age of 14 years. Eight months ago, she was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and treatment with risperidone was begun. Her parents report that she is very conscious of her weight and appearance. She is 168 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 76 kg (168 lb); BMI is 26.9 kg/m2. Pelvic examination shows a normal vagina and cervix. Serum hormone studies show:
Prolactin 14 ng/mL
Follicle-stimulating hormone 5 mIU/mL
Luteinizing hormone 5.2 mIU/mL
Progesterone 0.9 ng/mL (follicular N <3; luteal N >3–5)
Testosterone 2.7 nmol/L (N <3.5)
A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's irregular menses, obesity, and normal androgen level are suggestive of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a disorder of androgen excess and ovulatory dysfunction. Although this patient's testosterone level is normal, the diagnosis of PCOS is clinical and does not require an elevated testosterone level. The Rotterdam criteria require any 2 of the following 3 findings: oligo-ovulation or anovulation, clinical or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. This patient has evidence of oligo-ovulation or anovulation (eg, irregular menses) and is at risk for clinical hyperandrogenism due to her obesity. Obesity is associated with insulin resistance, which can stimulate ovarian androgen production and lead to the development of hirsutism and acne.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of irregular menstrual bleeding. Menses have occurred at irregular 45- to 60-day intervals since menarche at the age of 13 years. Her last menstrual period was 5 weeks ago and lasted for 7 days with heavy flow and no cramping. She is not sexually active. She is 171 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 58 kg (128 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m2. Her temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a normal-appearing vagina and cervix. Bimanual examination shows a normal-sized uterus and no palpable adnexal masses. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's irregular menstrual bleeding is due to anovulation. Anovulation is common in the first 1-2 years after menarche and in women approaching menopause. This is because the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is often immature and may not regularly release an oocyte. Without the usual progesterone secretion from the corpus luteum after ovulation, the endometrium proliferates under the influence of estrogen. Eventually, the endometrium outgrows its blood supply and degenerates, leading to irregular, unpredictable, and often heavy and/or prolonged bleeding (menometrorrhagia). Anovulation is a diagnosis of exclusion in adolescents with abnormal uterine bleeding. Other potential causes (eg, pregnancy, anatomic lesions, bleeding disorders, infection) should be considered and ruled out as clinically indicated.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has not had her menstrual period for the past 4 months. During this period, she has had frequent headaches, difficulty sleeping, and increased sweating. She has not had any weight changes. Over the past year, menses occurred at irregular 30- to 45-day intervals with light flow. The patient underwent two successful cesarean sections at the ages of 28 and 32. She has two healthy children. She is sexually active with her husband and does not use condoms. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Estradiol 8 pg/mL (mid-follicular phase: N=27–123 pg/mL)
Follicle-stimulating hormone 200 mIU/mL
Luteinizing hormone 180 mIU/mL
Prolactin 16 ng/mL
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's amenorrhea, elevated follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), and low estradiol levels are suggestive of primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), also known as premature ovarian failure. POI is a disorder characterized by amenorrhea, hypoestrogenism, and elevated serum gonadotropin levels in women younger than 40. The most common cause is idiopathic, but other causes include chromosomal disorders (eg, Turner syndrome, fragile X syndrome), autoimmune disorders, and iatrogenic causes (eg, surgery, chemotherapy, radiation). The diagnosis is confirmed by two measurements of FSH >40 mIU/mL obtained at least 1 month apart.

Patients with POI may present with symptoms of estrogen deficiency (eg, hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbances, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia), infertility, and emotional distress (eg, difficulty concentrating, depression, anxiety). Long-term consequences include an increased risk of osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease due to chronic hypoestrogenism.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 14-year-old girl comes to the physician because of excessive flow and duration of her menses. Since menarche a year ago, menses have occurred at irregular intervals and lasted 8–9 days. Her last menstrual period was 5 weeks ago with passage of clots. She has no family or personal history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 20th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's irregular menses, heavy menstrual flow, and normal physical examination are suggestive of anovulatory cycles, which are common in the first 1-2 years after menarche. During this time, the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is often immature. As a result, pulsatile secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus may be inadequate, leading to irregular secretion of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) from the pituitary. This can result in irregular menses due to failure to ovulate (anovulation) and unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium. Unopposed estrogen can cause overgrowth and instability of the endometrium, leading to heavy, irregular menses. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for the evaluation of irregular menstrual bleeding. Menses have occurred at 60- to 90-day intervals since menarche at the age of 12 years. Her last menstrual period was 4 weeks ago. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they use condoms consistently. She reports that she currently has no desire to have children. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 85 kg (187 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m2. Examination shows scattered pustules on the forehead and oily skin. There is coarse hair on the chin and upper lip. Fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 190 mg/dL. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's irregular menses, obesity, and signs of hyperandrogenism (acne, hirsutism) are suggestive of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion and is characterized by chronic anovulation and hyperandrogenism. Chronic anovulation presents as oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, and hyperandrogenism presents as hirsutism, acne, or androgenic alopecia. PCOS is also associated with insulin resistance, which can lead to acanthosis nigricans, impaired glucose tolerance, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

The treatment of PCOS depends on the patient's primary concern. For patients with hirsutism, weight loss is the first-line treatment. If hirsutism persists despite weight loss, pharmacologic treatment with combined oral contraceptives (COCs) is the next step. COCs increase sex hormone-binding globulin, which decreases the amount of free testosterone, and also suppress luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion, which decreases ovarian androgen production. COCs also regulate menses, provide contraception, and improve acne.

Metformin is used in PCOS patients with impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes mellitus, or for those who cannot tolerate COCs or who have not responded to COCs and have persistent menstrual irregularity.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 23-year-old man presents with swelling of the left knee. He noticed the swelling a day ago while preparing for the college basketball game. He has had approximately 10 different sexual partners in the past 3 months. Synovial fluid tap shows a WBC count of 90,000 cells/mm3. What is the mechanism of action of the drug which is indicated for the treatment of this patient’s most likely condition?

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old man presents with intense pain in his left knee that started after returning from a camping trip 2 days ago, during which he consumed copious amounts of alcohol and red meat. He says he has had similar episodes in the past that resolved spontaneously usually over a period of about 10 days. His past medical history is significant for essential hypertension managed with hydrochlorothiazide 20 mg/day. The patient is afebrile, and his vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows edema, warmth, and erythema of the left knee, which is also severely tender to palpation; The range of motion at the left knee joint is limited. A joint arthrocentesis of the left knee is performed, and synovial fluid analysis reveals 20,000 neutrophils and the following image is seen under polarized light microscopy (see image). Which of the following is the best course of treatment for this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe joint pain, swelling, and erythema after a camping trip during which he consumed large amounts of alcohol and red meat is suggestive of gout. Gout is a form of inflammatory arthritis that develops in some people who have high levels of uric acid in the blood. The acid can form needle-like crystals in a joint and cause sudden, severe episodes of pain, tenderness, redness, warmth, and swelling. The synovial fluid analysis showing 20,000 neutrophils and the image of negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals further confirm the diagnosis of gout.

The first-line treatment for acute gouty arthritis is nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as indomethacin or naproxen. NSAIDs are effective at relieving pain and inflammation. If NSAIDs are contraindicated, a glucocorticoid (eg, prednisone) or colchicine can be used.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a swollen and painful right knee for the last 3 days. He has no history of joint disease. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows erythema and swelling of the right knee, with limited range of motion due to pain. Arthrocentesis of the right knee joint yields 7 mL of cloudy fluid with a leukocyte count of 29,000/mm3 (97% segmented neutrophils). Compensated polarized light microscopy of the aspirate is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's knee pain?
few_shot.explanation:
The image shows weakly positively birefringent, rhomboid-shaped crystals, which are indicative of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals. These are the pathognomonic finding in pseudogout, a condition that is caused by the deposition of these crystals in the joint space. This leads to an inflammatory response that causes the symptoms of joint pain and swelling.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old man with a history of gout and hypertension presents to his family physician with a complaint of increased left knee pain over the past 2 days. He also reports swelling and redness of the left knee and is unable to bear weight on that side. He denies any prior surgery or inciting trauma to the knee. His temperature is 97.0°F (36.1°C), blood pressure is 137/98 mm Hg, pulse is 80/min, respirations are 13/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical examination reveals a left knee that is erythematous, swollen, warm-to-touch, and extremely tender to palpation and with attempted flexion/extension movement. His left knee range of motion is markedly reduced compared to the contralateral side. Joint aspiration of the left knee is performed with synovial fluid analysis showing turbid fluid with a leukocyte count of 95,000/mm^3, 88% neutrophils, and a low glucose. Gram stain of the synovial fluid is negative. Results from synovial fluid culture are pending. Which of the following is the best treatment regimen for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute monoarticular arthritis with a warm, erythematous, and extremely tender joint is concerning for septic arthritis, a medical emergency that can lead to rapid joint destruction and irreversible loss of function. The most common causative organisms are Staphylococcus aureus (including methicillin-resistant S aureus [MRSA]) and Streptococcus species. In sexually active young adults, Neisseria gonorrhoeae should also be considered. In patients with prosthetic joints, coagulase-negative staphylococci (eg, Staphylococcus epidermidis) are common pathogens. Gram-negative bacilli (eg, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) are more often seen in older adults, immunocompromised patients, and individuals with a history of intravenous drug use.

Initial treatment of septic arthritis involves empiric antibiotics to cover the most likely pathogens based on the patient's risk factors. In this patient with no specific risk factors, empiric treatment should include vancomycin for MRSA and streptococci, and a third-generation cephalosporin (eg, ceftriaxone, ceftazidime) for gram-negative bacilli. Once culture results are available, antibiotics can be narrowed based on the specific pathogen and its susceptibilities.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of a swollen right knee. Over the past several weeks, he has had similar episodes affecting the right knee and sometimes also the left elbow, in which the swelling lasted an average of 5 days. He has a history of a rash that subsided 2 months ago. He lives in Connecticut with his wife and works as a landscaper. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a tender and warm right knee; range of motion is limited by pain. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. His hematocrit is 44%, leukocyte count is 10,300/mm3, and platelet count is 145,000/mm3. Serum electrolyte concentrations are within normal limits. Arthrocentesis is performed and the synovial fluid is cloudy. Gram stain is negative. Analysis of the synovial fluid shows a leukocyte count of 70,000/mm3 and 80% neutrophils. Serologic testing confirms the diagnosis. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a rash, followed by migratory arthritis, and his occupation as a landscaper in Connecticut are suggestive of Lyme disease, which is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. Lyme disease is transmitted by the Ixodes tick, which is endemic in the northeastern and upper midwestern United States. The disease has three stages: early localized, early disseminated, and late. Early localized disease presents with erythema migrans, a rash that begins as a red macule or papule at the site of the tick bite and then expands over days to weeks to form a large annular, erythematous lesion often with central clearing (a "bull's-eye" rash). Early disseminated disease can manifest with multiple smaller erythema migrans lesions, cranial nerve palsies (most commonly of the facial nerve, causing Bell's palsy), and/or cardiac involvement (eg, atrioventricular nodal block). Late disease can present with intermittent or persistent arthritis in one or a few large joints, especially the knee. Encephalopathy and peripheral neuropathy can also occur.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of swelling and pain in her left knee. She has had similar episodes of swollen joints over the past 3 weeks. Two months ago, she had a rash on her upper back that subsided after a few days. She lives in Pennsylvania and works as a forest ranger. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F). Physical examination shows a tender and warm left knee. Arthrocentesis of the knee joint yields cloudy fluid with a leukocyte count of 65,000/mm3 and 80% neutrophils. A Gram stain of synovial fluid does not show any organisms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

answer_choices.B: Infection with round bacteria in clusters
answer_choices.C: Postinfectious activation of innate lymphoid cells of the gut

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a rash, recurrent monoarticular arthritis, and exposure to ticks in a Lyme disease-endemic area is suggestive of Lyme disease. Lyme disease is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, which is transmitted by the Ixodes tick. The disease has three stages: early localized, early disseminated, and late. Early localized disease presents with erythema migrans, a skin lesion that appears 1 week after the tick bite as a red macule or papule and expands over days to weeks to form a large annular, erythematous, and sometimes central clearing "bull's eye" rash. Early disseminated disease, which occurs weeks to months after the tick bite, can manifest with neurologic abnormalities (eg, cranial nerve palsies, meningitis, radiculoneuritis), cardiac involvement (eg, atrioventricular nodal block), and/or migratory musculoskeletal discomfort. Late disease, which occurs months to years after the tick bite, is most commonly associated with intermittent swelling and pain of one or a few joints, especially the knees. Lyme arthritis is thought to result from an immune response to the spirochete. Synovial fluid analysis typically shows an inflammatory process with leukocyte counts usually in the 25,000-100,000/mm3 range, predominantly neutrophils. 

Hence, the answer is [D].

question: A 22-year-old man presents to the medical clinic after getting bit in the hand by a stray dog 2 days ago. The patient has no past medical history and takes no prescription medications. He does not drink alcohol or smoke cigarettes. The patient’s vitals are currently within normal limits. On examination, the physician notices 2 clean puncture wounds with localized cellulitis. Capillary refill is 2 seconds. Sensorimotor evaluation of the hand is without deficits. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment choice for this patient?

few_shot.question: A 19-year-old woman presents to the family medicine clinic after noticing swelling of her right index finger a few hours ago. She has no past medical history and takes no prescription medications. She takes ibuprofen occasionally, as needed. She says that she has smoked a few cigarettes a day for the last year. On further questioning, the patient says that she has a dog and a cat at home. Her blood pressure is 108/67 mm Hg, heart rate is 94/min, respiratory rate is 12/min, and temperature is 37.8°C (100.1°F). On physical examination, the physician notices 2 clean puncture wounds with localized erythema and induration on the dorsum of the right second digit. Capillary refill is 2 seconds. Sensory and motor function are intact bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment choice for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a cat bite and the presence of puncture wounds on her finger suggest a Pasteurella multocida infection. P. multocida is a small, gram-negative coccobacillus that is part of the normal oral flora of many animals, including cats and dogs. It is the most common cause of infection resulting from cat or dog bites. Infections typically present within 24 hours of the bite and manifest as cellulitis. P. multocida is sensitive to penicillins, cephalosporins, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones. However, because cat bites are often polymicrobial, amoxicillin-clavulanate is the treatment of choice because it also covers for anaerobes and Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents after he was bitten by a friend's cat while playing at their house. The patient reports moderate pain of the right hand and wrist but has full range of motion and strength. He is up to date on his vaccinations and is generally healthy. His vitals are unremarkable. Physical exam reveals a deep puncture wound that is actively bleeding. The wound is irrigated and a dressing is applied. Which of the following is appropriate management of this patient?

answer_choices.A: Ampicillin-sulbactam, surgical debridgment, and laceration closure

few_shot.explanation:
Cat bites are often deep puncture wounds that can easily inoculate bacteria into deep tissues. The most common pathogen in cat bites is Pasteurella multocida, a gram-negative coccobacillus that is part of the normal oral flora of many animals. Other potential pathogens include Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species, Moraxella, Neisseria, and anaerobes. 

The first-line treatment for cat bites is amoxicillin-clavulanate, which covers P multocida and the other potential pathogens. In patients allergic to penicillin, doxycycline or a combination of a fluoroquinolone and clindamycin can be used.

Wound closure is generally not recommended for cat bites due to the high risk of infection. The wound should be left open to heal by secondary intention. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 30 minutes after she was bitten by her neighbor's cat. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She received all recommended immunizations during childhood but has not received any since then. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows four puncture wounds on the thenar eminence of the right hand. There is mild swelling but no erythema. There is normal range of motion of her right thumb and wrist. The wound is cleaned with povidone iodine and irrigated with saline. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.D: Close the wound with cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive

few_shot.explanation:
Cat bites are often deep puncture wounds that can easily inoculate bacteria into deep tissues. The most common pathogen in cat bite wounds is Pasteurella multocida, a small, gram-negative coccobacillus that is part of the normal oral flora of many animals, including cats and dogs. P multocida can cause rapidly progressive cellulitis within 24 hours of the bite. Other potential pathogens in cat bite wounds include Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species, as well as anaerobes such as Fusobacterium and Bacteroides.

Because of the high risk of infection, prophylactic antibiotics are recommended for all cat bites, as well as for dog bites that are deep, on the hands or feet, or in patients who are immunocompromised. The antibiotics chosen should cover P multocida, as well as common skin flora. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the treatment of choice, as it covers all of these organisms. Doxycycline or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus a beta-lactam (eg, amoxicillin) can be used in patients allergic to amoxicillin-clavulanate.

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric emergency department after having an accident at school. According to his parents, he punched a student in the mouth, which caused a deep laceration to his hand. The child’s past medical history is unremarkable and all of his vaccines are current. A physical examination is significant for stable vital signs and lacerations over the 3rd and 4th metacarpophalangeal joints of his dominant hand. Which of the following antibiotic regimens is best for this type of injury?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a human bite wound, which is considered to be a polymicrobial infection. The oral flora of humans contains more than 100 different species of bacteria, including aerobic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus, as well as anaerobic organisms such as Fusobacterium, Prevotella, and Peptostreptococcus. Therefore, the antibiotic of choice for human bite wounds is amoxicillin-clavulanate, which covers both aerobic and anaerobic organisms.

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old man presents to the emergency department after he cut his hand while working on his car. The patient has a past medical history of antisocial personality disorder and has been incarcerated multiple times. His vitals are within normal limits. Physical exam is notable for a man covered in tattoos with many bruises over his face and torso. Inspection of the patient's right hand reveals 2 deep lacerations on the dorsal aspects of the second and third metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints. The patient is given a tetanus vaccination, and the wound is irrigated. Which of the following is appropriate management for this patient?

answer_choices.B: Closure of the wound with sutures
answer_choices.D: Surgical irrigation, debridement, and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a human bite wound, which is a common injury that can occur during a fight when a closed fist strikes an opponent's mouth (also known as a "fight bite"). The injury typically occurs over the dorsal aspect of the third MCP joint. These wounds are prone to infection due to direct inoculation of oral flora into the joint space or tendon sheath. The most common pathogens involved in human bite wound infections are Streptococcus and Eikenella species, as well as Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes. 

Human bite wounds over a joint space or tendon sheath should be treated with surgical irrigation and debridement due to the high risk of septic arthritis or pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis. Empiric antibiotic therapy should be initiated with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid to cover for the above-mentioned organisms. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 34-year-old patient is brought to the emergency room after a motor vehicle accident. An EKG shows sinus tachycardia and chest radiograph reveals an enlarged cardiac silhouette. While observing sinus tachycardia on the patient's telemetry, you note that the radial pulse cannot be palpated during inspiration. What should be the next step in management of this patient?

few_shot.question: An otherwise healthy 57-year-old man presents to the emergency department because of progressive shortness of breath and exercise intolerance for the past 5 days. He denies recent travel or illicit habits. His temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), the blood pressure is 88/57 mm Hg, and the pulse is 102/min. The radial pulse becomes so weak with inspiration. Physical examination reveals bilateral 1+ pedal edema. There is jugular venous distention at 13 cm and muffled heart sounds. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows reciprocal respiratory ventricular inflow and ventricular diastolic collapse. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of dyspnea, hypotension, jugular venous distention, and pulsus paradoxus (ie, decrease in systolic blood pressure >10 mm Hg during inspiration) is consistent with cardiac tamponade. This is a life-threatening condition that occurs when fluid in the pericardial sac compresses the heart and impairs diastolic filling. The most common cause of cardiac tamponade is malignancy, but it can also be due to other causes such as idiopathic pericarditis, uremia, and bacterial/viral infections.

Echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice and may show diastolic collapse of the right atrium and/or ventricle, a large pericardial effusion, and a dilated inferior vena cava. Doppler echocardiography may show increased respiratory variation in mitral and tricuspid inflow velocities.

The treatment of cardiac tamponade is pericardial drainage via pericardiocentesis or pericardial window to relieve the increased pericardial pressure.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old soldier is brought to the emergency department of a military hospital 20 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle accident during a training exercise. He was an unrestrained passenger. On arrival, he has shortness of breath and chest pain. He appears pale and anxious. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg. He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and mucous membranes. There is bruising on the chest, extremities, and abdomen. The lungs are clear to auscultation. He has normal heart sounds and flat neck veins. The abdomen is flat, soft, and mildly tender. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. High-flow oxygen is applied, and intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun. An x-ray of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.B: CT scan of the chest with contrast

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is concerning for aortic injury, a life-threatening condition that requires immediate diagnosis and treatment. Aortic injury is most commonly caused by rapid deceleration injuries, such as motor vehicle accidents. The most common site of injury is the aortic isthmus, which is relatively fixed in position and therefore susceptible to shearing forces. Patients often present with chest pain and a widened mediastinum on chest x-ray, as seen in this patient. The most appropriate next step in management is a CT scan of the chest with contrast, which can confirm the diagnosis.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 66-year-old female with hypertension and a recent history of acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) 6 days previous, treated with percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA), presents with sudden onset chest pain, shortness of breath, diaphoresis, and syncope. Vitals are temperature 37°C (98.6°F), blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg, pulse 125/min, respirations 12/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. On physical examination, the patient is pale and unresponsive. Cardiac exam reveals tachycardia and a pronounced holosystolic murmur loudest at the apex and radiates to the back. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with clear lung fields. ECG is significant for ST elevations in the precordial leads (V2-V4) and low-voltage QRS complexes. Emergency transthoracic echocardiography shows a left ventricular wall motion abnormality along with a significant pericardial effusion. The patient is intubated, and aggressive fluid resuscitation is initiated. What is the next best step in management?

answer_choices.C: Immediate transfer to the operating room

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of chest pain, hypotension, and a new holosystolic murmur following a recent myocardial infarction (MI) is concerning for ventricular free wall rupture, a mechanical complication of MI. This is a life-threatening condition that can lead to cardiac tamponade and electromechanical dissociation. The diagnosis is suggested by the presence of a new murmur (often described as holosystolic and loudest at the apex), and confirmed by echocardiography, which typically shows a pericardial effusion. The next step in management is immediate surgical repair.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a car accident with pain in the middle of his chest and some shortness of breath. He has sustained injuries to his right arm and leg. He did not lose consciousness. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Examination shows several injuries to the upper extremities and chest. There are jugular venous pulsations 10 cm above the sternal angle. Heart sounds are faint on cardiac examination. The lungs are clear to auscultation. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypotension, tachycardia, and elevated jugular venous pressure following a motor vehicle collision is concerning for cardiac tamponade. Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening condition that occurs when fluid accumulates in the pericardial sac and compresses the heart, leading to decreased cardiac output. It is a common complication of penetrating chest trauma, but can also occur after blunt chest trauma. The ECG findings of low voltage QRS complexes and electrical alternans (ie, beat-to-beat alterations in QRS complex height) are characteristic of cardiac tamponade, but are not always present. The most appropriate next step in management is transthoracic echocardiography to confirm the diagnosis. If the diagnosis is confirmed, immediate pericardiocentesis is indicated to relieve the pressure on the heart.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department for evaluation of intermittent chest pain over the past 6 months. His history reveals that he has had moderate exertional dyspnea and 2 episodes of syncope while working at his factory job. These episodes of syncope were witnessed by others and lasted roughly 30 seconds. The patient states that he did not have any seizure activity. His vital signs include: blood pressure 121/89 mm Hg, heart rate 89/min, temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), and respiratory rate 16/min. Physical examination reveals a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur in the right second intercostal area. An electrocardiogram is performed, which shows left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following is the best next step for this patient?

answer_choices.C: Computed tomography (CT) chest scan without contrast

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of exertional dyspnea, syncope, and a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur in the right second intercostal area is suggestive of aortic stenosis (AS). AS is the most common valvular heart disease in the elderly and is typically due to progressive calcification of a congenitally abnormal (bicuspid) or tricuspid aortic valve. The murmur of AS is harsh and systolic and is best heard at the right second intercostal space, radiating to the carotid arteries. The murmur increases with maneuvers that increase afterload (eg, handgrip) and decreases with maneuvers that decrease preload or afterload (eg, Valsalva, standing). 

The best initial test for suspected AS is transthoracic echocardiography, which can confirm the diagnosis and assess the severity of the stenosis. It can also evaluate left ventricular size and function, left ventricular hypertrophy, and other valvular abnormalities. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician for sleeping problems and the inability to concentrate for 3 months. She says she is worried because she and her husband have been trying to conceive for more than a year with no success. Conception by in vitro fertilization was attempted once 3 months ago but was unsuccessful. Analysis of her husband's semen has shown normal sperm counts and morphology. She has a 6-year-old daughter who was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. She has no history of severe illness and tries to stay healthy by going to the gym an hour per day. Her menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 to 6 days; her last menstrual period started 2 days ago. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's inability to conceive?

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician for evaluation of fertility. She has been unable to conceive for one year despite regular intercourse with her husband 1–2 times per week. Recent analysis of her husband's semen showed a normal sperm count. Two years ago, she had an episode of a febrile illness with lower abdominal pain, which resolved without treatment. Menarche was at age 12 and menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 4 to 5 days. Before her marriage, she was sexually active with 4 male partners and used a combined oral contraceptive pill with estrogen and progesterone consistently, as well as barrier protection inconsistently. One year ago, she stopped using the oral contraceptive pill in order to be able to conceive. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 84 kg (185 lb); BMI is 30.8 kg/m2. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's infertility?

answer_choices.B: Long-term use of the oral contraceptive pill

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a febrile illness with lower abdominal pain is suggestive of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which is often caused by sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. PID can lead to tubal scarring and obstruction, which can cause infertility. This is the most likely cause of this patient's infertility, given her history of multiple sexual partners and inconsistent barrier protection.

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common cause of infertility, but this patient's regular menstrual cycles make this diagnosis unlikely. Long-term use of the oral contraceptive pill does not cause infertility. Primary ovarian insufficiency is unlikely in a woman of this age with regular menstrual cycles.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for a checkup. She has been trying to get pregnant with her husband for the past 7 months but has been unsuccessful. The patient states that they have been having unprotected intercourse daily during this time frame. She states that she experiences her menses every 28 days. Her husband has 2 children from another marriage. Otherwise, the patient only complains of mild vaginal dryness during intercourse. The patient's past medical history is notable for seasonal allergies for which she takes loratadine and a chlamydial infection which was treated in college. On physical exam, you note a healthy woman. Cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and pelvic exam are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient is presenting with infertility, which is defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse. However, in women over the age of 35, infertility is diagnosed after 6 months of regular unprotected intercourse. This patient has regular menses, indicating that she is likely ovulating regularly. Her husband has 2 children from another marriage, indicating that he is likely fertile. The patient's history of chlamydial infection is concerning for tubal scarring, which can cause infertility. However, the patient's history of vaginal dryness is concerning for decreased cervical mucus, which can be seen in decreased ovarian reserve. Decreased ovarian reserve is a normal part of aging and is the most common cause of infertility in women over the age of 40. 

Hence, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician for evaluation of infertility. She has been unable to conceive for 14 months. One year ago, she stopped taking the oral contraceptive pill, which she had been taking since she was 17. Her husband's semen analysis was normal. Four years ago, she had an episode of a pelvic tenderness and vaginal discharge that resolved without treatment. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. Before her marriage, she was sexually active with 5 male partners and used condoms inconsistently. She is 169 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 31.6 kg/m2. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's infertility?

answer_choices.C: Adverse effect of oral contraceptive pill

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of pelvic pain and vaginal discharge suggests a prior episode of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which is often caused by sexually transmitted infections (eg, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae). PID can lead to tubal factor infertility due to loss of ciliary action and tubal occlusion from inflammation and fibrosis. The fallopian tubes are responsible for picking up the ovulated oocyte from the ovary and transporting the fertilized embryo to the uterus for implantation. Normal tubal function requires an intact, motile ciliary lining and a patent lumen. Disruption of these can lead to infertility or ectopic pregnancy.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old woman comes to the physician because she is unable to conceive for 3 years. She and her partner are sexually active and do not use contraception. They were partially assessed for this complaint 6 months ago. Analysis of her husband's semen has shown normal sperm counts and hormonal assays for both partners were normal. Her menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 to 6 days. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She had a single episode of urinary tract infection 4 years ago and was treated with oral antibiotics. Vaginal examination shows no abnormalities. Bimanual examination shows a normal-sized uterus and no palpable adnexal masses. Rectal examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has primary infertility, defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse. The initial evaluation of an infertile couple includes a semen analysis, assessment of ovulation, and evaluation of the reproductive anatomy. This patient has regular menses and a midluteal progesterone level >3 ng/mL, which confirms ovulation. Her partner has a normal semen analysis. The next step in the evaluation of this couple is assessment of tubal patency and the uterine cavity. Hysterosalpingography is typically the initial test of choice to evaluate these structures. It involves the injection of radiopaque dye through the cervix, after which fluoroscopic images are obtained. Hysterosalpingography can detect tubal occlusion and abnormalities of the uterine cavity (eg, endometrial polyps, submucosal leiomyomas, intrauterine adhesions, congenital anomalies). If hysterosalpingography suggests tubal disease or an abnormal uterine cavity, further evaluation with hysteroscopy or laparoscopy may be necessary.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has not had her menstrual period for the past 4 months. During this period, she has had frequent headaches, difficulty sleeping, and increased sweating. She has not had any weight changes. Over the past year, menses occurred at irregular 30- to 45-day intervals with light flow. The patient underwent two successful cesarean sections at the ages of 28 and 32. She has two healthy children. She is sexually active with her husband and does not use condoms. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Estradiol 8 pg/mL (mid-follicular phase: N=27–123 pg/mL)
Follicle-stimulating hormone 200 mIU/mL
Luteinizing hormone 180 mIU/mL
Prolactin 16 ng/mL
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's amenorrhea, elevated follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), and low estradiol levels are suggestive of primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), also known as premature ovarian failure. POI is a disorder characterized by amenorrhea, hypoestrogenism, and elevated serum gonadotropin levels in women younger than 40. The most common cause is idiopathic, but other causes include chromosomal disorders (eg, Turner syndrome, fragile X syndrome), autoimmune disorders, and iatrogenic causes (eg, surgery, chemotherapy, radiation). The diagnosis is confirmed by two measurements of FSH >40 mIU/mL obtained at least 1 month apart.

Patients with POI may present with symptoms of estrogen deficiency (eg, hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbances, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia), infertility, and emotional distress (eg, difficulty concentrating, depression, anxiety). Long-term consequences include an increased risk of osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease due to chronic hypoestrogenism.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 50-year-old man comes to the physician because of swelling of his legs for 2 months. Three months ago, he was diagnosed with hypertension and started on a new medication. His blood pressure is 145/95 mm Hg. Physical examination shows 2+ edema in both lower extremities. Laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. This patient was most likely treated with which of the following drugs?

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 45-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He has been having recurrent headaches, especially early in the morning, and sometimes feels dizzy. There is no family history of serious illness. The patient runs 5 miles 3 days a week. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. He is 177 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 72 kg (159 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies are within normal limits. Two weeks later, the patient's blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg in both arms. He is started on an antihypertensive medication. One month later, physical examination shows 2+ pretibial edema bilaterally. This patient was most likely treated with which of the following medications?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has hypertension and was started on an antihypertensive medication. His new finding of bilateral lower extremity edema suggests a side effect of a calcium channel blocker (CCB), most likely amlodipine. CCBs are often used as first-line therapy for hypertension, particularly in the elderly and in those with isolated systolic hypertension. Side effects of dihydropyridine CCBs (eg, amlodipine, nifedipine) include peripheral edema, flushing, headache, and dizziness. The edema occurs due to dilation of the precapillary arterioles with a resultant increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid extravasation into the interstitium. This type of edema is not responsive to diuretics but improves with elevation of the legs or use of a different class of antihypertensive medication.

Therefore, the answer is [D].
