few_shot.question: A 61-year-old man with Alzheimer disease is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after ingesting an unknown amount of his medications in a suicide attempt. He reports abdominal cramps, diarrhea, diaphoresis, and muscular weakness and spasms in his extremities. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 51/min, respirations are 12/min and labored, and blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. Physical examination shows excessive salivation and tearing, and small pupils bilaterally. Treatment with atropine is initiated. Shortly after, most of his symptoms have resolved, but he continues to have muscular spasms. Administration of which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of abdominal cramps, diarrhea, diaphoresis, muscular weakness and spasms, excessive salivation and tearing, and small pupils are consistent with cholinergic toxicity. This can occur due to ingestion of organophosphates, which are found in many insecticides and nerve gases, or certain medications such as those used to treat myasthenia gravis and Alzheimer disease. Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to an excess of acetylcholine and overstimulation of muscarinic and nicotinic receptors.

Treatment of organophosphate poisoning involves removal of contaminated clothing, decontamination of the skin if applicable, and administration of atropine and pralidoxime. Atropine is a competitive inhibitor of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, and is used to reverse the muscarinic symptoms of toxicity. Pralidoxime regenerates acetylcholinesterase if given before "aging" occurs, and is used to reverse both the muscarinic and nicotinic symptoms of toxicity. Therefore, in this patient who continues to have muscular spasms (a nicotinic symptom) despite atropine treatment, the next step in management is administration of pralidoxime.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [B] > [C] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a dry mouth and blurred vision for the past 30 minutes. Prior to this, he was on a road trip and started to feel nauseous, dizzy, and fatigued, so his friend gave him a drug that had helped in the past. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and dilated pupils. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Administration of which of the following drugs is most likely to cause a similar adverse reaction in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dry mouth, blurred vision, and dilated pupils are suggestive of anticholinergic toxicity. Anticholinergic agents competitively inhibit the muscarinic actions of acetylcholine at postganglionic parasympathetic neuroeffector sites. This results in decreased secretions (eg, dry mouth, decreased sweating), increased heart rate, decreased gastrointestinal motility, and mydriasis with cycloplegia (ie, paralysis of the ciliary muscle of the eye, leading to loss of accommodation).

Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic medication used to treat overactive bladder. It can cause the same symptoms as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [D] > [A] > [C].

question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his parents for a routine visit. Since his 18-month visit, the parents have become concerned that his speech does not seem to be developing appropriately. The parents report that the patient’s vocabulary is still limited to fewer than 10 words, and he is still only using single words to describe things. The parents say that his motor milestones do not seem to be affected, as the patient is very physically active and can run and kick a ball. At times the patient seems hyperactive and can be difficult to redirect. On exam, his temperature is 98.4°F (36.9°C), blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 14/min. The rest of the exam is unremarkable, except that the patient’s face appears to be abnormally long and narrow. The patient is further referred to a geneticist, as he is believed to have a trinucleotide repeat disorder. Which of the following is the most likely inheritance pattern of this disorder?

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents for a well-child visit. During his last well-child visit 9 months ago, the patient had not begun talking. The parents report that their son frequently avoids eye contact and has no friends at daycare. He was born at term and has been healthy except for an episode of otitis media 6 months ago, which was treated with amoxicillin. His immunizations are up-to-date. He is at the 95 percentile for height, 20 percentile for weight, and 95 percentile for head circumference. He appears shy. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 100/55 mm Hg. Examination shows elongated facial features and large ears. The patient does not speak. He does not follow instruction to build a stack of 2 blocks. Throughout the examination, he continually opens and closes his mother's purse and does not maintain eye contact. Which of the following findings is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

answer_choices.D: Three copies of the same chromosome

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's developmental delay, lack of eye contact, and repetitive behaviors are suggestive of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). ASD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impaired social communication and restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities. The etiology of ASD is multifactorial and includes genetic and environmental factors. The most common single-gene cause of ASD is Fragile X syndrome, which is characterized by an expansion of the CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. This leads to hypermethylation of the gene and decreased production of the FMR1 protein, which is important in synaptic plasticity and dendritic maturation.

Fragile X syndrome is also the most common inherited form of intellectual disability. Affected individuals may have a characteristic appearance with a long face, large ears, and macroorchidism (postpubertal). Connective tissue dysplasia can result in hyperextensible finger joints and soft, velvety skin. Mitral valve prolapse can also be seen.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [D] > [C].

few_shot.question: An 18-month-old boy is brought in by his parents for a routine check-up. The parents state that the patient still has not had any language development, and they are concerned about developmental delay. Of note, they have also noticed that the patient’s facial features have changed significantly in the last year. The patient also seems to have trouble visually focusing on objects or on the television. On exam, the patient's temperature is 98.2°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 108/72 mmHg, pulse is 86/min, and respirations are 14/min. Of interest, the patient has not increased much in length or weight in the past 3 months. He is now in the 25th percentile for weight but is in the 90th percentile for head circumference. The patient does not appear to have any gross or fine motor deficiencies. Of note, he has coarse facial features that were not previously noted, including a long face, prominent forehead, and protruding eyes. The patient has corneal clouding bilaterally. At rest, the patient keeps his mouth hanging open. After extensive workup, the patient is found to have 2 mutated copies of the IDUA gene, with no production of the protein iduronidase. Which of the following is the likely mutation found in this disease?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's coarse facial features, corneal clouding, and developmental delay are suggestive of Hurler syndrome, a type of mucopolysaccharidosis. Hurler syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-L-iduronidase, which is responsible for the degradation of the glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. Accumulation of these GAGs in various tissues leads to the clinical findings seen in Hurler syndrome.

The most common type of mutation in Hurler syndrome is a nonsense mutation, which introduces a premature stop codon into the DNA sequence. This leads to the production of a truncated, nonfunctional protein.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 9-month-old female infant is brought in by her mother to the pediatrician because she is concerned that her daughter is not growing normally. On physical exam, the head circumference is 95th percentile and the height is 5th percentile. The child has disproportionate growth such that both the upper and lower extremities show a rhizomelic pattern of shortening, but the axial skeleton appears to be normal. The child appears to have normal intelligence, but has delayed motor milestones; specifically, she is not able to roll or sit up by herself. Which of the following best describes the mode of inheritance for this disorder?
few_shot.explanation:
This child's physical findings are consistent with achondroplasia, the most common form of dwarfism. Achondroplasia is characterized by rhizomelic (proximal) shortening of the extremities, macrocephaly with frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, exaggerated lumbar lordosis, and normal trunk length. Intelligence is normal, but motor milestones may be delayed due to hypotonia and ligamentous laxity. The disorder is caused by a mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 (FGFR3) gene, which leads to abnormal cartilage formation. The FGFR3 gene is located on chromosome 4, and the mutation is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. However, 80% of cases result from spontaneous (de novo) mutations, with increased paternal age being a significant risk factor.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 3-year-old is brought in to the pediatrician's office for a routine checkup. Her parents report that they noticed some regression in their daughter’s behavior. She seemed to be progressing well during the first 18 months of her life. She had started saying words such as ‘I’, ‘you’ and ‘mama’ and she was linking words together. She also learned to follow simple instructions. However, over the past few months, they have noticed that she has been forgetting some of the things that she had previously learned and difficulty walking. On examination, the physician observes an apparently healthy girl who refuses to make eye contact and only slowly responds to her name. She is observed to wring her hands repeatedly in her lap. Which of the following genetic patterns of inheritance is responsible for this behavioral regression?
few_shot.explanation:
This girl's loss of purposeful hand skills, development of stereotypic hand movements (eg, hand-wringing), and loss of social engagement are characteristic of Rett syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder that occurs almost exclusively in girls. Rett syndrome is caused by a mutation in the MECP2 gene, which is located on the X chromosome. The disorder is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern. Most cases are sporadic and caused by new (de novo) mutations, with the disease occurring almost exclusively in females. Males with the disease-causing mutation often die in utero or shortly after birth.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her parents for a 1-year history of gradual loss of speech and motor skills. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated, and development was normal until the age of 3 years. Her parents say she used to run and speak in short sentences but now is only able to walk slowly and cannot form sentences. She avoids eye contact and constantly rubs her hands together. There are no dysmorphic facial features. Neurologic examination shows marked cognitive and communicative delay. She has a broad-based gait and is unable to hold or pick up toys on her own. Which of the following mutations is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

answer_choices.A: Microdeletion of methyl-CpG binding protein 2 on X-chromosome
answer_choices.B: CGG trinucleotide repeat in FMR1 gene on X-chromosome
answer_choices.C: CTG trinucleotide repeat in DMPK gene on chromosome 19
answer_choices.D: Partial deletion of long arm of chromosome 7

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's loss of purposeful hand skills, development of stereotypic hand movements (eg, hand-wringing), and loss of social engagement are characteristic of Rett syndrome, a disorder caused by a mutation in the MECP2 gene on the X chromosome. This gene codes for methyl-CpG-binding protein 2, a protein involved in DNA transcription and modification of chromatin structure. Rett syndrome is characterized by normal development for the first 6-18 months of life, followed by a period of regression with loss of purposeful hand skills and speech, development of stereotypic hand movements, and slowing of head growth. Other features include impaired social interaction (similar to autism), ataxia, and seizures.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

question: A previously healthy 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressive shortness of breath, fatigue, and chest pain during exercise for the last 6 months. She does not smoke. Her maternal uncle had similar symptoms. Cardiac examination shows wide splitting of S2. The second component of S2 is loud and best heard at the 2nd left intercostal space. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's cardiac findings?

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 2 episodes of loss of consciousness over the past week. She recovered immediately and was not confused following the episodes. During the past 5 months, she has also had increased shortness of breath and palpitations. She has been unable to carry out her daily activities. She also reports some chest tightness that resolves with rest. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She immigrated with her family from India 10 years ago. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 115/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention and pitting edema below the knees. Bilateral crackles are heard at the lung bases. Cardiac examination shows an accentuated and split S2. There is an opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic murmur in the fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation and right axis deviation. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of these findings?

answer_choices.A: Increased left ventricular end diastolic pressure

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and lower extremity edema is suggestive of congestive heart failure. The presence of an opening snap and diastolic murmur at the apex suggests mitral stenosis (MS), most likely due to rheumatic heart disease, which is common in developing countries. In MS, the mitral valve orifice is narrowed, impeding blood flow from the left atrium (LA) to the left ventricle (LV) during diastole. This leads to elevated LA pressures, particularly during exercise when the heart rate increases and the diastolic filling period shortens. The elevated LA pressure is transmitted to the pulmonary vasculature, causing pulmonary congestion and resultant dyspnea, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Atrial fibrillation, the most common arrhythmia in patients with MS, can develop due to chronic LA enlargement. This can lead to decreased cardiac output and/or tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy, both of which can cause or exacerbate heart failure symptoms. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [C] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of intermittent chest pain and dizziness on exertion for 6 months. Her pulse is 76/min and blood pressure is 125/82 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a grade 3/6, late-peaking, crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border. An echocardiogram confirms the diagnosis. Three months later, the patient returns to the physician with worsening shortness of breath for 2 weeks. An ECG is shown. Which of the following changes is most likely responsible for this patient's acute exacerbation of symptoms?

answer_choices.C: Decreased impulse conduction across the AV node

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of chest pain and dizziness on exertion, along with a late-peaking, crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border, are suggestive of aortic stenosis (AS). The ECG shows atrial fibrillation (AF), which is characterized by an irregularly irregular rhythm and the absence of discrete P waves. AF is common in patients with AS due to elevated left atrial pressure and left atrial enlargement. 

AF can lead to rapid clinical deterioration in patients with AS because loss of atrial contraction can result in decreased left ventricular preload and cardiac output. This is because the atria normally contribute to ventricular filling by contracting and pushing blood into the ventricles just prior to ventricular contraction (atrial kick). This is especially important in patients with AS, who have impaired ventricular filling due to a hypertrophied and stiff left ventricle. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [D] > [C] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 74-year-old man comes to the physician for a 6-month history of progressively worsening fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. He immigrated to the United States 35 years ago from India. His pulse is 89/min and blood pressure is 145/60 mm Hg. Crackles are heard at the lung bases. Cardiac examination shows a grade 3/6 early diastolic murmur loudest at the third left intercostal space. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's early diastolic murmur heard best at the left sternal border is consistent with aortic regurgitation (AR). AR can be caused by aortic root dilation (eg, hypertension, aortic dissection, syphilis, ankylosing spondylitis, Reiter syndrome) or valve leaflet abnormalities (eg, endocarditis, rheumatic heart disease, bicuspid aortic valve, myxomatous degeneration, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis). In developing countries, the most common cause of AR is rheumatic heart disease. However, in developed countries, the most common causes are aortic root dilation (eg, due to hypertension or age-related degeneration) and bicuspid aortic valve.

Patients with chronic severe AR may present with exertional dyspnea and fatigue due to left ventricular volume overload. On physical examination, the high stroke volume results in a wide pulse pressure (systolic blood pressure - diastolic blood pressure), manifesting as a water hammer (Corrigan) pulse, characterized by a rapid upstroke and subsequent collapse.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of worsening shortness of breath, lower extremity swelling, and a 3-kg (6.6-lb) weight gain. Crackles are heard on auscultation of the chest. Cardiac examination shows a dull, low-pitched early diastolic sound at the 5th left intercostal space that becomes louder in the left lateral decubitus position at end-expiration. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these auscultation findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of dyspnea, lower extremity edema, and weight gain is consistent with heart failure. The physical examination finding of a dull, low-pitched early diastolic sound at the 5th left intercostal space that becomes louder in the left lateral decubitus position at end-expiration is consistent with a third heart sound (S3). An S3 is a normal finding in children and young adults but is abnormal in individuals >40 years old. It is associated with increased left ventricular end-diastolic volume and pressure, as seen in heart failure. The S3 is thought to be produced by blood from the left atrium slamming into an already overdistended left ventricle during early diastole.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 77-year-old male presents to the emergency department because of shortness of breath and chest discomfort. The patient states his ability to withstand activity has steadily declined, and most recently he has been unable to climb more than one flight of stairs without having to stop to catch his breath. On physical exam, the patient has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard over the right sternal boarder, with radiation to his carotids. Which of the following additional findings are most likely in this patient?

answer_choices.A: A wide and fixed split S2
answer_choices.B: A constant, machine-like murmur heard between the scapulae
answer_choices.D: A diastolic murmur heard at the cardiac apex

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of exertional dyspnea and chest discomfort, along with the harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard over the right sternal border, are suggestive of aortic stenosis. Aortic stenosis can be caused by age-related calcification of the aortic valve, which is the most common cause in developed countries, or by rheumatic heart disease. It can also be caused by a congenital bicuspid aortic valve, which is the most common cause in patients younger than 70.

In severe aortic stenosis, the time required to open the stenotic aortic valve is prolonged, which can delay the onset of the S2 heart sound. This can lead to a paradoxical splitting of S2, in which the pulmonic valve closes before the aortic valve during expiration, and the delay in aortic valve closure is overcome by the normal delay in pulmonic valve closure during inspiration.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

question: A 29-year-old G1P0 female presents at 22 weeks gestation for her first prenatal care appointment. Physical exam demonstrates a uterine size greater than expected for her gestational age and taut, shiny skin with scattered striae on her abdomen. Ultrasound examination of the fetus reveals 2.5 L of amniotic fluid (normal 1.5-2.0 L) with an amniotic fluid index (AFI) of 34 (normal AFI 20-25). Which of the following fetal abnormalities or dysfunctions could have contributed to these abnormal ultrasound findings?

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 18 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a prenatal visit. Ultrasonography at a previous visit when she was at 12 weeks' gestation showed a hypoplastic nasal bone. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with an 18-week gestation. Maternal serum studies show low α-fetoprotein and free estriol concentrations, and increased inhibin A and β-hCG concentrations. Physical examination of the infant after delivery is most likely to show which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's prenatal ultrasound and maternal serum studies are suggestive of Down syndrome (trisomy 21). The ultrasound finding of a hypoplastic nasal bone is associated with Down syndrome. Maternal serum studies in the second trimester typically show low α-fetoprotein and free estriol concentrations, and increased inhibin A and β-hCG concentrations. Physical examination of the infant after delivery may show characteristic findings such as upslanting palpebral fissures, single transverse palmar crease (simian crease), and a flat facial profile.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [C] > [B] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a prenatal visit. Pregnancy and delivery of her first child were uncomplicated. She has type 1 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 110/86 mm Hg. Examination shows minimal bilateral edema below the knees. The uterus is consistent in size with a 29-week gestation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Transabdominal ultrasound shows an intrauterine pregnancy in longitudinal lie, normal fetal cardiac activity, an amniotic fluid index of 5 cm and calcifications of the placenta. This patient's child is at greatest risk of developing which of the following conditions?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's ultrasound findings of oligohydramnios (amniotic fluid index <5 cm) and placental calcifications are concerning for uteroplacental insufficiency. Uteroplacental insufficiency can occur due to maternal vascular disease (eg, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, lupus), placental abnormalities (eg, placental abruption, placenta previa), or fetal abnormalities (eg, intrauterine growth restriction, multiple gestations). In this patient, the most likely cause is maternal diabetes mellitus, which can lead to placental insufficiency due to accelerated vasculopathy.

Oligohydramnios is associated with fetal renal anomalies, as the kidneys contribute to amniotic fluid production via urine output. However, in the setting of uteroplacental insufficiency, the fetus attempts to conserve fluid by decreasing urine output, which can lead to oligohydramnios. This patient's fetus is at greatest risk for pulmonary hypoplasia due to oligohydramnios. Pulmonary hypoplasia is a condition characterized by incomplete development of the lungs, resulting in an abnormally low number or size of bronchopulmonary segments or alveoli. A normal amount of amniotic fluid is necessary to allow for fetal lung growth and development. Oligohydramnios can cause pulmonary hypoplasia by preventing normal movement and expansion of the fetal chest, which is necessary for lung development.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [B] > [A] > [C].

few_shot.question: A newborn girl is rushed to the neonatal ICU after an emergency cesarean section due to unstable vital signs after delivery. The pregnancy was complicated due to oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia. Gestation was at 38 weeks. APGAR scores were 6 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes respectively. The newborn’s temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), the blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg, the respiratory rate is 45/min, and the pulse is 140/min. Physical examination reveals irregularly contoured bilateral abdominal masses. Abdominal ultrasound reveals markedly enlarged echogenic kidneys (5 cm in the vertical dimension) with multiple cysts in the cortex and medulla. This patient is at highest risk of which of the following complications?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of bilateral renal masses, oligohydramnios, and pulmonary hypoplasia is consistent with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD). ARPKD is a congenital disorder characterized by the development of cysts in the collecting ducts and hepatic fibrosis. The hepatic fibrosis can lead to portal hypertension, which can present with splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and gastrointestinal bleeding. Therefore, this patient is at highest risk of developing portal hypertension.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [C] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 19-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 21 weeks’ gestation comes to the physician for a follow-up prenatal visit. At her previous appointment, her serum α-fetoprotein concentration was elevated. She had smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 3 years but quit at 6 weeks' gestation. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 21-week gestation. Ultrasonography shows fetal viscera suspended freely into the amniotic cavity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Gastroschisis is a congenital defect of the anterior abdominal wall that typically occurs to the right of the umbilical cord. It is characterized by herniation of the abdominal contents directly into the amniotic cavity. The herniated organs (usually small and large bowel, and sometimes stomach and liver) are not covered by a membrane. The exact cause of gastroschisis is unknown, but it is associated with young maternal age and possibly with maternal smoking and use of vasoconstrictive recreational drugs (eg, cocaine, amphetamines). 

In contrast, omphalocele is a midline defect of the abdominal wall that results in herniation of abdominal contents into the base of the umbilical cord. The herniated organs are covered by a sac composed of peritoneum and amnion. Omphalocele is associated with chromosomal abnormalities (eg, trisomy 13, trisomy 18, trisomy 21) and other congenital anomalies (eg, cardiac defects).

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 29-year-old primigravid woman at 18 weeks’ gestation comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. She works as a paralegal and lives with her husband. Her current pregnancy was unexpected, and she did not take any prenatal medications or supplements. Physical examination shows a uterus 2 inches above the umbilicus. The concentration of α-fetoprotein in the maternal serum and concentrations of both α-fetoprotein and acetylcholinesterase in the amniotic fluid are elevated. Ultrasonography of the uterus shows an increased amniotic fluid volume. The fetus most likely has which of the following conditions?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fetus has an elevated maternal serum α-fetoprotein (MSAFP) level, elevated amniotic fluid α-fetoprotein and acetylcholinesterase levels, and polyhydramnios. These findings are most consistent with anencephaly, a neural tube defect (NTD) characterized by the absence of the cranial vault and cerebral hemispheres. Anencephaly is the most common cause of elevated MSAFP. The absence of a fetal cranium allows α-fetoprotein produced by the fetal liver to leak directly into the amniotic fluid, which is then absorbed into the maternal circulation. Acetylcholinesterase is also elevated in the amniotic fluid due to the direct contact of the amniotic fluid with the exposed neural tissue. Polyhydramnios is common in anencephaly due to impaired swallowing by the fetus.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [C] > [A] > [B].

question: A previously healthy 29-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of burning with urination for several days. He has also had pain in the right ankle for 3 days and pain and swelling in the left knee for 1 day. Two weeks ago, he had several days of fever and bloody diarrhea, for which he was treated with antibiotics. Examination shows a small left knee effusion and bilateral conjunctival injection. Which of the following is the most likely additional finding in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Circular erythematous rash with central clearing
answer_choices.B: Pain on passive extension of the fingers
answer_choices.C: Palpable mass in the right lower quadrant
answer_choices.D: Tenderness at the insertion of the Achilles tendon

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of fever for the past few hours as well as pain and swelling in his right knee and left ankle. He denies any recent history of trauma or injury. The patient is otherwise a healthy, active young man. He recently recovered from a case of gastroenteritis which caused significant abdominal pain and bloody stool 4 weeks ago. He believes the infection was related to eating undercooked chicken while camping. His blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, his heart rate is 76/min, and his temperature is 36.9 ℃ (98.4 ℉). Physical examination reveals tenderness to palpation of his right knee and left ankle as well as erythematous conjunctiva. Which of the following features would be least likely to develop in patients with this condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recent gastroenteritis, asymmetric oligoarthritis, and conjunctivitis is suggestive of reactive arthritis (ReA), a type of spondyloarthritis. ReA is a sterile inflammatory arthritis that occurs 1-4 weeks after an extra-articular infection, most commonly genitourinary (eg, Chlamydia trachomatis) or enteric (eg, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia) infections. The classic triad of ReA includes urethritis, conjunctivitis, and arthritis, although not all components need to be present for diagnosis. Other findings may include circinate balanitis (painless, shallow ulcers on the glans penis), keratoderma blennorrhagica (hyperkeratotic skin lesions on the palms and soles), and oral ulcers. 

ReA, like other spondyloarthropathies, typically affects the axial skeleton and lower extremity joints. The distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints are typically spared, unlike in other forms of inflammatory arthritis such as psoriatic arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician for frequent and painful urination. He has also had progressive painful swelling of his right knee over the past week. He is sexually active with two female partners and uses condoms inconsistently. His mother has an autoimmune disease that involves a malar rash. Examination shows conjunctivitis bilaterally. The right knee is warm, erythematous, and tender to touch; range of motion is limited. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 62 mm/h. Urinalysis shows WBCs. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to reveal which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of urethritis, conjunctivitis, and arthritis is consistent with reactive arthritis (ReA), formerly known as Reiter syndrome. ReA is a type of spondyloarthritis that occurs one to four weeks after a gastrointestinal (eg, Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter, Clostridium difficile) or genitourinary (eg, Chlamydia trachomatis) infection. It is more common in men and is strongly associated with the HLA-B27 genotype. Other findings can include enthesitis (eg, Achilles tendonitis, plantar fasciitis), dactylitis, and sacroiliitis. Extra-articular manifestations include keratoderma blennorrhagica (hyperkeratotic skin lesions on the palms and soles) and circinate balanitis (painless, shallow ulcers on the glans penis). Treatment is with NSAIDs and physical therapy. Antibiotics are used if the inciting infection is still present.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old male presents to his primary care physician complaining of pain with urination and eye redness. He reports that he developed these symptoms approximately one week ago. He also has noticed left knee and right heel pain that started a few days ago. He denies any recent trauma. He had an episode of abdominal pain and diarrhea ten days ago that resolved. He has otherwise felt well. On exam, he walks with a limp and his conjunctivae are erythematous. Laboratory findings are notable for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP). Which of the following is most likely associated with this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of urethritis, conjunctivitis, and arthritis is consistent with reactive arthritis, a type of spondyloarthritis. Reactive arthritis is a sterile inflammatory arthritis that occurs 1-4 weeks after a gastrointestinal (eg, Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Yersinia) or genitourinary (eg, Chlamydia trachomatis) infection. The arthritis is typically asymmetric and oligoarticular, and it often involves the lower extremities. Enthesitis (inflammation at sites of tendon/ligament insertion) is also common and can cause heel pain (eg, Achilles tendinitis, plantar fasciitis). Extra-articular manifestations can include conjunctivitis and urethritis. The presence of urethritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis, and arthritis is known as the classic triad of reactive arthritis. However, the full triad is present in fewer than one third of patients. The diagnosis is clinical, and the most important initial step in management is symptomatic treatment with NSAIDs. The disease is strongly associated with the HLA-B27 haplotype.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 67-year-old man comes to the emergency department for the evaluation of two episodes of red urine since this morning. He has no pain with urination. He reports lower back pain and fever. Six months ago, he was diagnosed with osteoarthritis of the right knee that he manages with 1–2 tablets of ibuprofen per day. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 45 years. He does not drink alcohol. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 95/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows faint, diffuse maculopapular rash, and bilateral flank pain. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows:
Blood +3
Protein +1
RBC 10–12/hpf
RBC cast negative
Eosinophils numerous
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute kidney injury, fever, rash, and eosinophiluria is suggestive of acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). AIN is most commonly due to an allergic drug reaction, especially to antibiotics (eg, beta-lactams, sulfonamides) and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The patient's chronic NSAID use likely caused AIN in this case. Other manifestations of AIN can include arthralgias and, rarely, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Urinalysis typically shows white blood cells and white blood cell casts, although the latter are not always present. Eosinophiluria, detected by Hansel or Wright stain, is suggestive but not diagnostic of AIN. The diagnosis is confirmed by renal biopsy, which shows an interstitial infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and plasma cells, with sparing of the glomeruli and blood vessels. 

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old man presents with fever, malaise, and severe pain in his right wrist and left knee for the last 2 days. He describes the pain as 8/10 in intensity, sharp in character, and extending from his right wrist to his fingers. He denies any recent inciting trauma or similar symptoms in the past. His past medical history is unremarkable. He is sexually active with multiple partners and uses condoms inconsistently. The vital signs include blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse 100/min, and temperature 38.3°C (101.0°F). On physical examination, the right wrist and left knee joints are erythematous, warm, and extremely tender to palpation. Both joints have a significantly restricted range of motion. A petechial rash is noted on the right forearm. An arthrocentesis is performed on the left knee joint. Which of the following would be the most likely finding in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Arthrocentesis aspirate showing gram-positive cocci in clusters
answer_choices.B: Arthrocentesis aspirate showing minimal, purulent joint effusion with negative culture
answer_choices.D: Radiographs of right wrist and left knee showing osteopenia and joint space narrowing

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, malaise, and severe pain in multiple joints is suggestive of disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI). DGI is a complication of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection and typically occurs in sexually active individuals. It is more common in women, especially around the time of menstruation or during pregnancy, but can also occur in men. DGI is characterized by tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and migratory polyarthralgias or polyarthritis. The tenosynovitis usually involves the wrists, fingers, ankles, and toes, and is extremely painful. The dermatitis manifests as a petechial or pustular rash, often with necrotic centers. The polyarthralgias or polyarthritis can affect any joint, but more commonly involve the knees, wrists, ankles, and elbows.

Arthrocentesis in patients with DGI often shows a purulent joint effusion, but cultures of the synovial fluid are often negative. Blood cultures are also negative in about half of all cases. The diagnosis of DGI is usually made based on the characteristic clinical findings and a positive culture from the cervix, urethra, rectum, or pharynx.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 28-year-old woman presents following a suicide attempt 2 days ago. She says that her attempt was a result of a fight with her boyfriend and that she slit her wrists in an attempt to keep him from breaking up with her. In the past, she has had many turbulent relationships, both romantic and in her family life. Since she was admitted to the hospital, she has spit at several staff members and alternated between sobbing and anger. She has no significant past medical history. The patient denies any history of smoking, alcohol use, or recreational drug use. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 25 year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her boyfriend after she cut her forearms with a knife. She has had multiple visits to the emergency department in the past few months for self-inflicted wounds. She claims that her boyfriend is the worst person in the world. She and her boyfriend have broken up 20 times in the past 6 months. She says she cut herself not because she wants to kill herself; she feels alone and empty and wants her boyfriend to take care of her. Her boyfriend claims that she is prone to outbursts of physical aggression as well as mood swings. He says that these mood swings last a few hours and vary from states of exuberance and self-confidence to states of self-doubt and melancholy. On examination, the patient appears well-dressed and calm. She has normal speech, thought processes, and thought content. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of unstable relationships, self-mutilation, impulsivity, and mood instability is suggestive of borderline personality disorder (BPD). BPD is characterized by a pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affect, as well as marked impulsivity. Patients with BPD often have intense, unstable relationships and may alternate between extremes of idealization and devaluation. They may also have a chronic feeling of emptiness and engage in self-mutilating behavior. Mood instability in BPD is characterized by marked reactivity of mood (eg, intense episodic dysphoria, irritability, or anxiety usually lasting a few hours and only rarely more than a few days).

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency room after a suicidal gesture following a fight with his new girlfriend. Patients with BPD often have a chronic feeling of emptiness and may have inappropriate, intense anger or difficulty controlling anger. They may also have transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociative symptoms. The diagnosis of BPD is made clinically and does not require any specific laboratory or imaging studies.

few_shot.question: A 21-year-old female was brought to the emergency room after losing large amounts of blood from slicing her wrists longitudinally. Which of the following personality disorders does this female most likely have?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of intense, unstable relationships, fear of abandonment, self-mutilation, and chronic feelings of emptiness are suggestive of borderline personality disorder. They also often exhibit identity disturbance with markedly or persistently unstable self-image or sense of self. Impulsivity in at least two areas that are potentially self-damaging (eg, spending, sex, substance abuse, reckless driving, binge eating) is another common feature. Recurrent suicidal behavior, gestures, or threats, or self-mutilating behavior are often observed. These patients can also have affective instability due to a marked reactivity of mood (eg, intense episodic dysphoria, irritability, or anxiety usually lasting a few hours and only rarely more than a few days) and chronic feelings of emptiness. Inappropriate, intense anger or difficulty controlling anger and transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociative symptoms can also be seen.

few_shot.question: A 19-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of difficulty sleeping. She worries that the lack of sleep will ruin her career prospects as a model. Patients with this disorder are often excessively emotional and continually demand to be the center of attention. They may use physical appearance to draw attention to themselves and can be inappropriately sexually provocative or seductive. They are often uncomfortable in situations where they are not the center of attention, have rapidly shifting and shallow expression of emotions, and have a style of speech that is excessively impressionistic and lacking in detail. They may also show self-dramatization, theatricality, and exaggerated expression of emotion, and can be suggestible (ie, easily influenced by others or circumstances).

question: A 22-year-old woman with a history of asthma visits her physician for worsening shortness of breath. She states that she feels as though her “lungs are falling apart,” noting that her lung function has been steadily deteriorating. She further states that she has visited a number of other physicians who prescribed several different types of inhalers, but she feels that they have not helped her control her asthma exacerbations. She has experienced 4 episodes of pneumonia in the last 3 years and often suffers from “random” bouts of excessive coughing and wheezing. When asked if her coughing episodes produce sputum, she states, “Yes, the stuff is greenish with specks of red in it.” She also states that her coughing and wheezing episodes are associated with fever, malaise, and occasional expectoration of brown mucous plugs. The vital signs include: blood pressure 122/70 mm Hg, pulse 66/min, respiratory rate 26/min, and temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F). On physical exam, the patient appears frail-looking and in moderate respiratory distress. Auscultation reveals inspiratory crackles in the right lung base and coarse breath sounds in the bilateral upper lung lobes. Chest radiograph, as shown below, reveals atelectasis in the right lung base. There are also branched radiodensities that the radiologist notes as being “glove-finger shadows” (noted by the arrow in the image). Serum immunoglobulin E (IgE) levels are elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of intermittent cough productive of thick, yellow phlegm and increasing shortness of breath. She especially becomes short of breath while playing with her children. She has worked as a farmer for 18 years. She has asthma treated with a salbutamol inhaler. She has smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily for 12 years. Her pulse is 65/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg. Scattered wheezing and decreased breath sounds are heard throughout both lung fields. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is soft and nondistended; liver span in midclavicular line is 14 cm.Spirometry shows a FEV1:FVC ratio of 66% and a FEV1 of 50% of predicted. An x-ray of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, decreased breath sounds, and obstructive pattern on spirometry (FEV1:FVC <70%) are suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). However, her relatively young age and the presence of basilar-predominant changes on chest x-ray are atypical for COPD, which usually occurs in patients >40 years of age and causes apical-predominant disease. These findings instead suggest alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder that can cause panacinar emphysema in young patients, often with basilar predominance. AAT is a protease inhibitor that protects the lung against neutrophil elastase. In AAT deficiency, uninhibited neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar tissue, leading to panacinar emphysema. Patients with AAT deficiency are also at risk for developing liver disease due to accumulation of misfolded AAT protein within hepatocytes. This patient's enlarged liver span suggests that she may have associated liver disease.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, cough, and chest pain. Physical examination shows diffuse inspiratory crackles over the left lung field. An x-ray of the chest shows hilar lymphadenopathy and well-defined nodules with central calcifications. Urine studies show the presence of a polysaccharide antigen. A biopsy specimen of the lung shows cells with basophilic, crescent-shaped nuclei and pericellular halos located within macrophages. This patient's history is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, cough, and chest pain, along with the presence of hilar lymphadenopathy and well-defined nodules with central calcifications on chest x-ray, are suggestive of a fungal infection. The presence of cells with basophilic, crescent-shaped nuclei and pericellular halos located within macrophages on lung biopsy is characteristic of Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus that is found in soil and material contaminated with bird or bat droppings. Infection is acquired by inhalation of the microconidia, which transform into yeast in the lungs. The yeast can then disseminate to other organs, including the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. 

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of generalized fatigue and malaise. During this period, she has had a non-productive cough with a low-grade fever. Over the past 6 months, she has had a 13-kg (28.6-lb) weight loss and intermittent episodes of watery diarrhea. She has generalized anxiety disorder and hypothyroidism. She has a severe allergy to sulfa drugs. She is sexually active with 3 male partners and uses condoms inconsistently. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years and drinks 2–3 beers daily. She does not use illicit drugs. Current medications include paroxetine, levothyroxine, and an etonogestrel implant. She is 162.5 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 50.3 kg (110.2 lbs); BMI is 19 kg/m2. She appears pale. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.6°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 100/75 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Examination of the lungs shows bilateral crackles and rhonchi. She has white plaques on the lateral aspect of the tongue that cannot be scraped off. A chest x-ray shows symmetrical, diffuse interstitial infiltrates. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of weight loss, diarrhea, and oral thrush, along with her sexual history, suggest advanced HIV infection. The diffuse interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray and hypoxemia are most consistent with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), the most common opportunistic infection in patients with AIDS. PJP typically presents with fever, nonproductive cough, and dyspnea over weeks, often with little to no physical examination findings despite extensive disease on imaging. The preferred treatment for PJP is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX). However, this patient has a severe sulfa allergy, which is a contraindication to TMP-SMX use. Alternative regimens for PJP in patients with a sulfa allergy include intravenous pentamidine or oral atovaquone. Another option is clindamycin plus primaquine, which is preferred in this patient because it also covers other potential pathogens (eg, bacterial pneumonia) given her physical examination findings (eg, rhonchi, crackles).

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 20-year-old man comes to the physician because of recurrent episodes of shortness of breath and a nonproductive cough for the past 4 months. He has two episodes per week, which resolve spontaneously with rest. Twice a month, he wakes up at night with shortness of breath. His pulse is 73/min, respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Spirometry shows an FVC of 95%, an FEV1:FVC ratio of 0.85, and an FEV1 of 81% of predicted. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent episodes of shortness of breath and cough are suggestive of asthma. The diagnosis of asthma is supported by the presence of symptoms that vary over time and in intensity, and by the presence of normal lung function between episodes. The severity of asthma is classified based on the frequency of daytime symptoms, nighttime awakenings, interference with normal activity, short-acting β2-agonist use for symptom control, and lung function (FEV1 and FEV1:FVC ratio). This patient's symptoms (ie, daytime symptoms >2 days/week, nighttime awakenings >2 times/month) are consistent with moderate persistent asthma.

The goal of asthma therapy is to achieve good symptom control and to minimize future risk of exacerbations, fixed airflow limitation, and side effects. The Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) recommends that all patients with asthma, even those with the mildest form of the disease, receive a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) to reduce the risk of serious exacerbations and to control symptoms. For patients with moderate persistent asthma, GINA recommends the use of a combination of a low-dose ICS and a long-acting β2-agonist (LABA) as initial therapy. Therefore, this patient should be started on a combination inhaler containing budesonide (an ICS) and formoterol (a LABA).

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of cough and dyspnea. The cough is productive of small amounts of green phlegm. She has stage IV colon cancer and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Her medications include 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, a fluticasone-salmeterol inhaler, and a tiotropium bromide inhaler. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 107/min, respirations are 31/min, and blood pressure is 89/68 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 87%. Pulmonary examination shows diffuse crackles and rhonchi. An x-ray of the chest shows a left upper-lobe infiltrate of the lung. Two sets of blood cultures are obtained. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain shows gram-negative rods that are oxidase-positive. Two large bore cannulas are inserted and intravenous fluids are administered. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) as evidenced by her hypotension, tachypnea, and hypoxemia. The most common pathogens in CAP include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and atypical bacteria (eg, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Legionella species). However, this patient's gram stain shows gram-negative rods that are oxidase-positive, which is suggestive of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. P aeruginosa is not a common cause of CAP, but it should be suspected in patients with structural lung disease (eg, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis), COPD, or malignancy. 

The recommended treatment for severe CAP is a beta-lactam (eg, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime) plus a macrolide (eg, azithromycin) or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (eg, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin). However, if Pseudomonas is suspected, the regimen should be adjusted to include antipseudomonal coverage with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (eg, piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, imipenem, meropenem) and either ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin; if these agents are contraindicated or unavailable, an aminoglycoside can be added to the beta-lactam instead.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician with a 2-month history of difficulty concentrating at work. He is worried he may lose his job due to poor performance. He feels constantly tired but attributes his fatigue to waking up early most mornings and being unable to fall back asleep. His wife has noticed that he has been speaking more slowly than usual and his appetite has decreased. He used to enjoy dance classes with her but has not been as interested in this recently. He is a veteran who returned from a deployment to Afghanistan 2 years ago. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man is brought to the physician by his wife because of difficulty sleeping and poor appetite for the past 4 weeks. During this period, he also has had persistent sadness and difficulty concentrating on tasks, because of which he has been reprimanded at work for poor performance. Over the past 3 years, he has often had such phases, with a maximum symptom-free gap of one month between each of them. His behavior is causing a strain in his relationships with his wife and children. His mother died 4 months ago from breast cancer. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Mental status examination shows a depressed mood and constricted affect. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of depressed mood, difficulty sleeping, poor appetite, and difficulty concentrating, along with the duration of his symptoms, meet the criteria for a major depressive episode. However, the fact that he has had these symptoms for at least 2 years with no more than 2 months' remission at a time makes the diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder (PDD) (formerly dysthymia) more likely. PDD is a chronic form of depression that often has an early onset (eg, childhood, adolescence, young adulthood) and a protracted course, with few symptom-free intervals. Patients with PDD can also have episodes of major depression, known as "double depression." PDD causes significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of persistent sadness and difficulty concentrating for the past 6 weeks. During this period, he has also had difficulty sleeping. He adds that he has been “feeling down” most of the time since his girlfriend broke up with him 4 years ago. Since then, he has only had a few periods of time when he did not feel that way, but none of these lasted for more than a month. He reports having no problems with appetite, weight, or energy. He does not use illicit drugs or alcohol. Mental status examination shows a depressed mood and constricted affect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's 4-year history of depressed mood, with only brief periods of remission, is consistent with persistent depressive disorder (PDD), formerly known as dysthymia. PDD is a chronic form of depression that is characterized by a depressed mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years (1 year in children and adolescents). During periods of depressed mood, at least two of the following symptoms must be present: poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy or fatigue, low self-esteem, poor concentration or difficulty making decisions, and feelings of hopelessness. In addition, during the 2-year period (1 year in children and adolescents), any symptom-free intervals last no longer than 2 months. PDD often has an early onset (eg, childhood, adolescence, young adulthood) and a chronic course. Patients with PDD may also have superimposed periods of major depression, which is referred to as "double depression."

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old man who works as a resident in general surgery presents feeling "burned out" for the last 2 months. He says he has been working extremely long hours under stressful conditions, which makes him irritable, edgy, unfocused, and forgetful. He says he also has severe anxiety about how these symptoms are affecting his performance at work, making it difficult for him to sleep even when he has time off. The patient is referred for counseling and is prescribed some mild sleep aids. At follow-up a few months later, he says he is feeling much improved due to improved staffing at the hospital and a more manageable workload. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of irritability, difficulty concentrating, and insomnia developed in response to a specific stressor (ie, long work hours, stressful work conditions) and resolved when the stressor was removed. These findings are consistent with adjustment disorder, which is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor. Symptoms occur within 3 months of the onset of the stressor and typically resolve within 6 months after the stressor or its consequences have terminated. The stress-related disturbance causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. 

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 39-year-old woman comes to the physician for difficulty sleeping and poor concentration at work. She sleeps with the lights turned on and wakes up frequently during the night with palpitations and profuse sweating. Three weeks ago she was sexually assaulted in her car. Since the assault she has avoided using her car and only uses public transportation. She also has nightmares of her attacker. She has been sent home from work for yelling at her coworkers. She has Hashimoto thyroiditis. Current medications include levothyroxine. She has been treated for pelvic inflammatory disease in the past. She has tried alcohol and melatonin to help her sleep. Mental status examination shows a depressed mood and a negative affect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of difficulty sleeping, poor concentration, nightmares, and avoidance of her car following a traumatic event (sexual assault) are consistent with acute stress disorder (ASD). ASD is characterized by intrusion symptoms (eg, recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event; recurrent distressing dreams; dissociative reactions [flashbacks]; intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event), negative mood, dissociative symptoms, avoidance symptoms, and arousal symptoms (eg, sleep disturbance, irritability, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, difficulty concentrating). Symptoms occur 3 days to 1 month after exposure to the traumatic event. If symptoms persist for more than 1 month, the diagnosis is changed to posttraumatic stress disorder.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of difficulty sleeping. She is afraid of falling asleep and gets up earlier than desired. Four months ago, she was the driver in a car accident that resulted in the death of her unborn child. She has vivid nightmares of the event and reports that she frequently re-experiences the accident. She blames herself for the death of her child, has stopped working as an accountant, avoids driving in cars, and has withdrawn from her parents and close friends. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of re-experiencing a traumatic event, avoidance of reminders of the event, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal are consistent with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PTSD is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that can occur following exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence. Symptoms must be present for more than 1 month and cause significant distress or functional impairment. This patient's symptoms have been present for 4 months and have caused her to stop working and withdraw from her family and friends, indicating significant functional impairment.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 45-year-old man presents to the physician with complaints of increased urinary frequency and decreasing volumes for the past 2 months. He does not complain of any pain during urination. He is frustrated that he has to wake up 2 or 3 times per night to urinate even though he tried reducing the amount of water he consumes before bed and made some other dietary changes without any improvement. He has no family history of prostate disease. Physical examination is negative for any suprapubic mass or tenderness, and there is no costovertebral angle tenderness. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient?

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressively worsening urinary frequency. He feels the urge to urinate every hour or two, which restricts his daily activities and interferes with his sleep. He has no fever, hematuria, or burning pain on micturition. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications include metformin and amlodipine. He does not smoke and drinks 1 to 2 beers daily. His vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Digital rectal examination shows a nontender, firm, symmetrically enlarged prostate with no nodules. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of urinary frequency, nocturia, and urgency are suggestive of overactive bladder (OAB), a syndrome characterized by urgency, with or without urge incontinence, usually with frequency and nocturia. OAB can be due to involuntary detrusor contractions (detrusor overactivity) or, less commonly, to other conditions such as bladder outlet obstruction (eg, benign prostatic hyperplasia [BPH]).

The initial evaluation of suspected OAB includes a history, physical examination, and urinalysis. The history should focus on identifying factors that may contribute to urinary symptoms, such as medications (eg, diuretics), fluid intake, and comorbid conditions (eg, diabetes, neurologic disease). Physical examination should include an abdominal examination to assess for a distended bladder and a digital rectal examination to evaluate prostate size in men. Urinalysis is performed to rule out hematuria and urinary tract infection, which can mimic OAB symptoms.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 59-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of frequent urination. He has to urinate every 1–2 hours during the day and wakes up at least 2–3 times at night to urinate. He also reports that over the last 2 months, he has difficulty initiating micturition and the urinary stream is weak, with prolonged terminal dribbling. His pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 158/105 mm Hg. Rectal exam shows a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate without any tenderness or irregularities. Prostate-specific antigen is within the reference range and urinalysis shows no abnormalities. A postvoid ultrasound shows a residual bladder volume of 110 mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of urinary frequency, nocturia, difficulty initiating micturition, weak urinary stream, and postvoid dribbling are suggestive of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). BPH is a common condition in older men and is caused by proliferation of prostatic stromal and epithelial cells, leading to enlargement of the prostate. This can cause both static (due to increased size of the prostate) and dynamic (due to increased smooth muscle tone in the prostate and bladder neck) obstruction of the bladder outlet.

The first-line treatment for BPH is medical therapy with alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blockers (eg, terazosin, tamsulosin) or 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride, dutasteride). Alpha-1 blockers work by relaxing smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck, improving urine flow and reducing symptoms of BPH. They have a rapid onset of action (within days to weeks) and are particularly useful in patients with moderate to severe symptoms. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors work by blocking the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, leading to a decrease in prostate size. They have a slower onset of action (up to 6 months) and are more useful in patients with very large prostates and longer life expectancy.

Given this patient's moderate to severe symptoms, the most appropriate next step in management would be to start therapy with an alpha-1 blocker such as terazosin.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [C] > [D] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of nocturia and a weak urinary stream. These symptoms began 1 year ago, but have progressively worsened over the past 6 months. He now wakes up 3–5 times every night to urinate. He has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide and lisinopril. The patient has smoked a half-pack of cigarettes daily for the past 30 years. He appears well. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 77/min, and blood pressure is 128/77 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. His abdomen is soft and nontender. Digital rectal examination shows a diffusely enlarged prostate with a firm nodule in the right posterior lobe. Urinalysis is within normal limits. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level is 6.5 ng/mL (N = 0–4). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.B: Repeat PSA level in one year
answer_choices.D: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's nocturia, weak urinary stream, and diffusely enlarged prostate with a firm nodule are concerning for prostate cancer. Prostate cancer is the most common solid organ malignancy in men and the second leading cause of cancer death. Risk factors include age >60, African American race, and a family history of prostate cancer. The diagnosis is suggested by an elevated or rapidly rising prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level and/or an abnormal digital rectal examination (eg, nodularity, induration, asymmetry). However, these tests are not diagnostic, and the definitive diagnosis of prostate cancer requires a transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy of the prostate. Biopsy is typically performed in men with a PSA level >4.0 ng/mL or an abnormal digital rectal examination, as in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 97-year-old man visits the urology clinic 5 days after experiencing urinary retention at an emergency department visit. The patient has a history of hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, stroke, dyslipidemia, a past myocardial infarction, and severe osteoarthritis in his right hip. He is not compliant with his medications and his multiple comorbidities are poorly managed. In the hospital, the patient’s urinary retention was treated with Foley catheterization. At clinic, the patient’s serum-specific prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is 6.0 ng/mL (normal is < 4 ng/mL). Digital rectal examination (DRE) demonstrates a nontender prostate with several rock hard nodules. The patient's Foley is removed and he is able to urinate on his own. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a high PSA and an abnormal DRE, both of which are concerning for prostate cancer. However, the patient is 97 years old and has multiple comorbidities that are poorly managed. The patient is also noncompliant with his medications. Given the patient's advanced age and poor health, the risks and burdens of prostate cancer treatment (eg, surgery, radiation, hormonal therapy) would likely outweigh the benefits. In addition, this patient's life expectancy is likely less than 10 years. Even if left untreated, prostate cancer is unlikely to impact his survival given his comorbidities. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is reassurance and focusing on managing the patient's other health issues.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 62-year-old man presents to the physician because of difficulty initiating urination, terminal dribbling of urine, and bone pain for 3 months. He has no medical history of serious illness, and he currently takes no medications. His father had prostate cancer at age 58. His vital signs are within normal limits. The physical examination shows tenderness over the lower lumbar vertebrae and the right pelvis. The digital rectal exam (DRE) shows a prostate size equivalent to 2 finger pads with a hard nodule. The laboratory tests show the following results:
Serum
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) 15 ng/mL
Testosterone 350 ng/mL (N=270–1070 ng/mL)
The prostate biopsy confirms the presence of prostate cancer with aggressive histologic features. The MRI shows local extension of the tumor. The radionuclide bone scan shows multiple metastatic sites. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has advanced prostate cancer, as evidenced by the presence of a hard nodule on DRE, elevated PSA, aggressive histologic features on biopsy, and multiple metastatic sites on bone scan. The mainstay of treatment for advanced prostate cancer is androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). This is because prostate cancer cells are dependent on androgens for growth and survival. ADT can be achieved through surgical castration (bilateral orchiectomy) or medical castration with gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists or antagonists. Antiandrogens (eg, bicalutamide) can also be used to block the action of androgens at the receptor level. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question: A 28-year-old female comes to the physician’s office with a complaint of episodic chest pain. She describes the pain as squeezing and tightness in her chest. This pain has been happening every few days for 3 months. She says there is no association of the pain with food or exercise. She is able to climb up to her fourth floor apartment daily without issue. Her only past medical history is migraines for which she takes appropriate medication. Here temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 120/68 mmHg, pulse is 60/min, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. She has no known family history. The patient is not in pain on presentation and EKG in the office is normal. 24-hour ECG monitoring shows transient ST elevations during the episodes of pain that resolve completely. The mechanism of this patient’s chest pain is most similar to the mechanism behind which of the following?

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for chest pain and shortness of breath. She was at home making breakfast when her symptoms began. She describes the pain as sharp and located in her chest. She thought she was having a heart attack and began to feel short of breath shortly after. The patient is a college student and recently joined the soccer team. She has no significant past medical history except for a progesterone intrauterine device which she uses for contraception, and a cyst in her breast detected on ultrasound. Last week she returned on a trans-Atlantic flight from Russia. Her temperature is 98.4°F (36.9°C), blood pressure is 137/69 mmHg, pulse is 98/min, respirations are 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam reveals an anxious young woman. Cardiac and pulmonary exam are within normal limits. Deep inspiration and palpation of the chest wall elicits pain. Neurologic exam reveals a stable gait and cranial nerves II-XII are grossly intact. Which of the following best describes the most likely underlying etiology?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's pleuritic chest pain (ie, sharp, worse with inspiration) and reproducible pain with palpation of the chest wall are suggestive of costochondritis, an inflammation of the costochondral joints that is often idiopathic but can be associated with overuse or trauma. It is a common cause of chest pain in children and young adults. The pain is usually localized to the costochondral junctions 2-5 and may be unilateral or bilateral. Diagnosis is clinical, and treatment is with NSAIDs and reassurance.

So, the answer is [C].
