question: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department for the evaluation of persistent bleeding from his nose over the past hour. The bleeding started spontaneously. He has no history of a similar episode. He takes no medications. There is no history of abnormal bleeding in the family. His vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, he is pressing a gauze against his left nostril while hyperextending his head. The gauze is stained with blood and upon withdrawal of the gauze blood slowly drips out of his left nostrils. There is no bleeding from the right nostril. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?

answer_choices.C: Placement of an epinephrine gauze in the left nostril
answer_choices.D: Squeezing the nostrils manually for 10 minutes with the head elevated

few_shot.question: A 56-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of persistent nasal bleeding. The bleeding started spontaneously. The patient experienced a similar episode last year. Currently, she has hypertension and takes hydrochlorothiazide and losartan. She is anxious. Her blood pressure is 175/88 mm Hg. During the examination, the patient holds a blood-stained gauze against her right nostril. Upon removal of the gauze, blood slowly drips down from her right nostril. Examination of the left nostril reveals no abnormalities. Squeezing the nostrils for 20 minutes fails to control bleeding. Which of the following interventions is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.A: Anterior nasal packing with topical antibiotics
answer_choices.D: Silver nitrate cauterization of the bleeding vessel

few_shot.explanation:
Epistaxis is a common condition that can be caused by local trauma, inflammation, or systemic diseases. The most common site of bleeding is the anterior septum, also known as Kiesselbach's plexus. This area is highly vascular and is easily traumatized. Initial management of epistaxis involves direct pressure, usually by pinching the nostrils together. If this fails, as in this case, the next step is to use a topical vasoconstrictor such as oxymetazoline. This can help to decrease blood flow to the area and may allow better visualization for further interventions if needed.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old man is brought to the physician for the evaluation of severe nosebleeds and two episodes of bloody vomit over the past 40 minutes. He reports that he has had recurrent nosebleeds almost daily for the last 3 weeks. The nosebleeds last between 30 and 40 minutes. He appears pale. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 95/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination of the nose with a speculum does not show an anterior bleeding source. The upper body of this patient is elevated and his head is bent forward. Cold packs are applied and the nose is pinched at the nostrils for 5–10 minutes. Topical phenylephrine is administered. Despite all measures, the nosebleed continues. Anterior and posterior nasal packing is placed, but bleeding persists. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: Endoscopic ligation of the sphenopalatine artery
answer_choices.B: Endoscopic ligation of the anterior ethmoidal artery
answer_choices.C: Endoscopic ligation of the lesser palatine artery
answer_choices.D: Endoscopic ligation of the greater palatine artery

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent, severe nosebleeds (epistaxis) that are unresponsive to conservative measures (eg, pressure, vasoconstrictors, packing) are concerning for a posterior source of bleeding. The sphenopalatine artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, is the most common source of posterior epistaxis. When bleeding is refractory to conservative management, surgical ligation or embolization of the sphenopalatine artery may be required.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 3-week history of a foul-smelling discharge from the left nostril. There was one episode of blood-tinged fluid draining from the nostril during this period. She has been mouth-breathing in her sleep for the past 4 days. She was born at term. Her 1-year-old brother was treated for viral gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago. She is at 60th percentile for height and at 70th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 23/min, and blood pressure is 96/54 mm Hg. Examination shows mucopurulent discharge in the left nasal cavity. Oral and otoscopic examination is unremarkable. Endoscopic examination of the nose confirms the diagnosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
Unilateral nasal discharge in a child, especially if it is foul-smelling, should raise suspicion for a foreign body in the nose. This is particularly true if the child is in the preschool age group, as these children often insert small objects into their noses out of curiosity. The foreign body can cause local inflammation and secondary infection, leading to the production of purulent or bloody discharge. If the foreign body is not removed, a chronic inflammatory response may develop, leading to the formation of granulation tissue and, rarely, nasal septal perforation.

The diagnosis can usually be confirmed by anterior rhinoscopy or nasal endoscopy, which can reveal the foreign body. The treatment is removal of the foreign body, which usually leads to rapid resolution of the symptoms.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-month history of progressive difficulty breathing through his nose and a 2-week history of recurrent severe nosebleeds. When he holds the right nostril shut, he is unable to breathe nasally and his sense of smell is reduced. He has a 6-year history of asthma, which is well controlled with inhaled albuterol. Vital signs are within normal limits. Nasal inspection shows a pink, lobulated mass filling the left nasal cavity. The septum is deviated to the right side. The mass bleeds on touch. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

answer_choices.D: CT scan of head with contrast

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis, and nasal mass are concerning for a juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), a benign but locally aggressive tumor that occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males. JNAs are highly vascular and originate in the sphenopalatine foramen, located in the posterior nasal cavity. They can extend into the nasopharynx and sinuses and can also erode into the skull base and intracranial cavity. Although JNAs are histologically benign, they can cause significant morbidity due to their vascularity (causing epistaxis) and mass effect. 

The next step in the evaluation of a patient with a suspected JNA is imaging, typically with a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head, to determine the extent of the tumor and its blood supply. Biopsy is contraindicated due to the risk of severe hemorrhage.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his girlfriend for a nosebleed. Pinching the nose for the past hour has not stopped the bleeding. For the past several months, he has had recurring nosebleeds that resolved with pressure. He has no history of hypertension or trauma. He has asthma that is well controlled with an albuterol inhaler. He has intermittent tension headaches for which he takes aspirin. His temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 114/min, and blood pressure is 160/102 mm Hg. Physical examination shows active bleeding from both nostrils. Pupil size is 6 mm bilaterally in bright light. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The hemoglobin concentration is 13.5 g/dL, prothrombin time is 12 seconds, partial thromboplastin time is 35 seconds, and platelet count is 345,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of recurrent epistaxis, hypertension, and mydriasis (dilated pupils) are suggestive of cocaine use. Cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic that inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin in the central and peripheral nervous systems. This leads to increased sympathetic outflow, causing tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, and diaphoresis. Cocaine use can also cause significant vasoconstriction of the nasal mucosa, leading to ischemia and necrosis. This can result in chronic rhinitis, sinusitis, and recurrent epistaxis. Cocaine-induced rhabdomyolysis can also occur, leading to myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury.

So, the answer is [C].

question: A transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine heteroechoic mass with numerous anechoic spaces and no identifiable fetus or amniotic fluid. Both the ovaries are enlarged and have multiple thin-walled, septated cysts with clear content. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the ovarian findings?

few_shot.question: A 41-year-old nulliparous woman, at 15 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of an 8-hour history of light vaginal bleeding. She had a spontaneous abortion at 11 weeks' gestation 9 months ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. On pelvic examination, there is old blood in the vaginal vault and at the closed cervical os. There are bilateral adnexal masses. Serum β-hCG concentration is 122,000 mIU/ml. Results from dilation and curettage show hydropic chorionic villi and proliferation of cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts. There are no embryonic parts. Vaginal ultrasound shows that both ovaries are enlarged and have multiple thin-walled, septated cysts with clear content. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the ovarian findings?
few_shot.explanation:
Theca lutein cysts are the most common benign ovarian neoplasms associated with gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD). GTD is a spectrum of disorders characterized by abnormal proliferation of placental trophoblasts. The most common form of GTD is hydatidiform mole, which is characterized by hydropic swelling of chorionic villi and trophoblastic hyperplasia. Hydatidiform moles can be complete (as in this patient) or partial. Complete moles have no associated fetal tissue, and they usually have a 46,XX karyotype that is completely paternal in origin due to fertilization of an "empty" ovum.

Theca lutein cysts are usually bilateral and can become very large. They are caused by overstimulation of theca cells by high levels of β-hCG, which can also cause hyperthyroidism and hyperemesis gravidarum. The cysts are typically filled with clear, straw-colored fluid. Microscopically, they are lined by luteinized cells. The cysts usually regress spontaneously following resolution of the molar pregnancy.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of abnormal vaginal bleeding for the past 2 months. Apart from the past 2 months, she has had regular menstrual cycles. She had menarche at the age of 13. She has no personal or family history of any serious illnesses. She takes no medications. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormal findings. Laboratory studies show elevated serum beta-HCG and AFP levels. An abdominal ultrasound shows a predominantly solid mass in the left ovary. The right ovary and the uterus show no abnormal findings. Which of the following ovarian tumors best explains these findings?
few_shot.explanation:
Embryonal carcinoma is a malignant germ cell tumor that occurs in the ovaries and testes. It is composed of primitive, pluripotent cells that resemble embryonic cells and can differentiate into tissues from all three germ layers. Embryonal carcinoma is often part of a mixed germ cell tumor, but it can also occur in pure form. It is the most common malignant germ cell tumor in children and adolescents. It is associated with elevated serum levels of beta-HCG and AFP, which are both produced by the tumor cells. The tumor is typically large and solid, and it can be either unilateral or bilateral. It is highly malignant and can spread via the lymphatic and hematogenous routes.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old G2P0A2 woman comes to the office complaining of light vaginal spotting. She received a suction curettage 2 weeks ago for an empty gestational sac. Pathology reports showed hyperplastic and hydropic trophoblastic villi, but no fetal tissue. The patient denies fever, abdominal pain, dysuria, dyspareunia, or abnormal vaginal discharge. She has no chronic medical conditions. Her periods are normally regular and last 3-4 days. One year ago, she had an ectopic pregnancy that was treated with methotrexate. She has a history of chlamydia and gonorrhea that was treated 5 years ago with azithromycin and ceftriaxone. Her temperature is 98°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 125/71 mmHg, and pulse is 82/min. On examination, hair is present on the upper lip, chin, and forearms. A pelvic examination reveals a non-tender, 6-week-sized uterus and bilateral adnexal masses. There is scant dark blood in the vaginal vault on speculum exam. A quantitative beta-hCG is 101,005 mIU/mL. Two weeks ago, her beta-hCG was 63,200 mIU/mL. A pelvic ultrasound shows bilaterally enlarged ovaries with multiple thin-walled cysts between 2-3 cm in size. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s adnexal masses?
few_shot.explanation:
Theca lutein cysts are the most common benign ovarian neoplasm in pregnancy. They are usually bilateral and result from overstimulation of theca cells by human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). Theca lutein cysts are associated with conditions involving high levels of hCG, such as multiple gestations and molar pregnancies. This patient's history of a recent molar pregnancy, current high hCG level, and ultrasound findings of bilateral ovarian enlargement with multiple thin-walled cysts are consistent with theca lutein cysts. Theca lutein cysts usually regress spontaneously following evacuation of a molar pregnancy and normalization of hCG levels. However, they can cause complications such as ovarian torsion, rupture, and hemorrhage.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with gradual abdominal distension that has progressively increased over the past 3 months. The physical examination showed shifting dullness. A paracentesis showed malignant cells. An ultrasound shows an adnexal mass. Which is the most likely cause of this condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal distension, shifting dullness on physical examination, and malignant cells on paracentesis are suggestive of malignant ascites. The most common causes of malignant ascites are cancers of the ovary, breast, colon, stomach, and pancreas. In women, ovarian cancer is the most common cause of malignant ascites. The presence of an adnexal mass on ultrasound in this patient further supports the diagnosis of ovarian cancer.

Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma is a type of epithelial ovarian cancer that can present with abdominal distension due to the accumulation of mucin or ascitic fluid in the peritoneal cavity. It is often associated with pseudomyxoma peritonei, a condition characterized by copious mucinous ascites.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 49-year-old man presents with an 11-month history of progressive fatigue. On physical examination, mild splenomegaly is noted on abdominal percussion. Laboratory findings are significant for a leukocyte count of 16,700/mm3 and a low serum leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score. few_shot.question: A previously healthy 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of intermittent fever, easy fatiguability, and a 4.4-kg (9.7-lb) weight loss. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor. The spleen is palpated 5 cm below the left costal margin. A peripheral blood smear shows increased numbers of promyelocytes, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

This patient's presentation of fatigue, weight loss, and splenomegaly, along with a leukocytosis with a left shift (ie, increased immature granulocytes such as promyelocytes, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes), basophilia, and a decreased leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score, is suggestive of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). CML is a myeloproliferative disorder that results from the malignant transformation of a pluripotent stem cell. It is characterized by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, which results from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, leading to the formation of the BCR-ABL fusion gene. This gene codes for a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that promotes cell proliferation and inhibits DNA repair and apoptosis.

The LAP score is typically elevated in reactive conditions associated with a left shift (eg, infection, inflammation), but is low in CML. This is because the LAP score reflects the number of mature granulocytes, which are decreased in CML due to the shift toward immature forms.

This patient's peripheral blood smear shows small, mature lymphocytes and smudge cells, which are characteristic of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). CLL is a clonal disorder characterized by progressive accumulation of functionally incompetent lymphocytes, seen mostly in older adults. It is often discovered incidentally when a complete blood count with differential reveals lymphocytosis. The diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry, which shows a population of clonal B cells that co-express CD5 and CD19, as well as CD20 and CD23.

Patients with CLL are often asymptomatic at the time of diagnosis. Symptomatic patients may present with fatigue, lymphadenopathy, or symptoms related to cytopenias (eg, infection, bleeding). The Rai staging system is used to determine prognosis and guide management. Patients with low-risk disease (lymphocytosis only or lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy) are typically asymptomatic and do not require treatment. Instead, they can be managed with observation and routine follow-up. Treatment is reserved for patients with high-risk disease or those who become symptomatic (eg, anemia, thrombocytopenia, symptomatic lymphadenopathy, disease-related symptoms such as unintentional weight loss, fever, night sweats).

question: Six hours after birth, a newborn boy is evaluated for tachypnea. He was delivered at 41 weeks' gestation via Caesarian section and the amniotic fluid was meconium-stained. few_shot.question: One day after a 4700-g (10-lb 6-oz) male newborn is delivered to a 28-year-old primigravid woman, he has bluish discoloration of his lips and fingernails. Oxygen saturation on room air is 81%. Examination shows central cyanosis. A continuous machine-like murmur is heard over the left upper sternal border. A single S2 heart sound is present. Supplemental oxygen does not improve cyanosis. Echocardiography shows the pulmonary artery arising from the posterior left ventricle and aorta arising from the right ventricle with active blood flow between the right and left ventricles. Further evaluation of the mother is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has transposition of the great arteries (TGA), a cyanotic congenital heart disease characterized by the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle. This results in two parallel circulations (ie, systemic venous blood is pumped back into the systemic circulation without being oxygenated, and oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is pumped back into the pulmonary circulation). The presence of a murmur and the fact that the newborn is still alive suggest the presence of a shunt (eg, ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus) that allows for some degree of oxygenated blood to reach the systemic circulation.

TGA is strongly associated with maternal diabetes mellitus, which is also suggested by the history of a large for gestational age infant (birth weight >4000 g [8 lb 13 oz]). Maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia and resultant fetal hyperinsulinemia, which causes excessive growth. Maternal diabetes is also associated with other congenital anomalies, including caudal regression syndrome and small left colon syndrome.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: One day after a 4700-g (10-lb 6-oz) male newborn is delivered to a 28-year-old primigravid woman, the newborn has bluish discoloration of the lips and fingernails. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 166/min, respirations are 63/min, and blood pressure is 68/44 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 81%. Examination shows central cyanosis. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard over the left lower sternal border. A single second heart sound is present. Supplemental oxygen does not improve cyanosis. An x-ray of the chest shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with a narrowed mediastinum. Further evaluation of the mother is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has transposition of the great arteries (TGA), the most common cause of cyanotic heart disease in the first 24 hours of life. TGA is characterized by the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle, resulting in two parallel circulations. The only communication between the systemic and pulmonary circulations is through a patent foramen ovale and/or patent ductus arteriosus. Clinical findings include profound cyanosis within the first day of life, a single second heart sound (S2), and a systolic ejection murmur due to increased flow across the pulmonary valve. Chest x-ray shows an "egg on a string" appearance, with an enlarged cardiac silhouette and a narrowed mediastinum.

Maternal diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for TGA. Hyperglycemia during the first trimester of pregnancy, when organogenesis occurs, can lead to various congenital malformations, including cardiac defects. Therefore, an elevated hemoglobin A1c, which reflects the average blood glucose level over the past 3 months, is the most likely finding in this patient's mother.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: One day after doctors helped a 28-year-old primigravid woman deliver a 4700 g (10 lb 6 oz) boy, he has bluish discoloration of his lips and fingernails. Oxygen saturation on room air is 81%. Examination shows central cyanosis. A continuous machine-like murmur is heard over the left upper sternal border. A single S2 heart sound is present. Supplemental oxygen does not improve the cyanosis. Echocardiography shows the pulmonary artery arising from the posterior left ventricle and the aorta arising from the right ventricle with active blood flow between the right and left ventricles. Further evaluation of the mother is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This infant's echocardiogram findings of aorta arising from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle are consistent with transposition of the great arteries (TGA). TGA is the most common cause of cyanotic heart disease in the newborn period. It is characterized by ventriculoarterial discordance (ie, the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle) and atrioventricular concordance (ie, the morphologic right atrium is connected to the morphologic right ventricle and the morphologic left atrium is connected to the morphologic left ventricle). This results in two parallel circuits: a systemic circuit (right atrium to right ventricle to aorta to the body) and a pulmonary circuit (left atrium to left ventricle to pulmonary artery to the lungs). Mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood is necessary for survival and typically occurs at the atrial, ventricular, or ductal level. The continuous machine-like murmur in this patient is due to a patent ductus arteriosus, which is allowing for this necessary mixing of blood.

Maternal diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for TGA. Infants of diabetic mothers are also at risk for other congenital anomalies (eg, caudal regression syndrome, small left colon syndrome), as well as macrosomia, as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: One day after doctors helped a 28-year-old primigravid woman deliver a 4,700 g (10 lb 6 oz) boy, the newborn has bluish discoloration of the lips and fingernails. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), the pulse is 166/min, the respirations are 63/min, and the blood pressure is 68/44 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 81%. Examination shows central cyanosis. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard over the left lower sternal border. A single second heart sound is present. Supplemental oxygen does not improve cyanosis. An X-ray of the chest shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with a narrowed mediastinum. Which of the following cardiac defects would be associated with this newborn’s diagnosis?

answer_choices.B: Division of aorta and pulmonary artery

few_shot.explanation:
This newborn's central cyanosis, single second heart sound, and holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border are suggestive of a cyanotic congenital heart disease. The chest x-ray findings of an enlarged cardiac silhouette with a narrowed mediastinum ("egg on a string" appearance) are characteristic of transposition of the great arteries (TGA). TGA is the most common cause of cyanosis in the first 24 hours of life. It occurs due to failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral, causing the aorta to arise from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery to arise from the left ventricle. This leads to two parallel circulations (ie, systemic venous blood bypasses the lungs and is pumped into the aorta, and oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is pumped back into the pulmonary artery), which is incompatible with life unless a right-to-left shunt is present to allow for some degree of mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Such shunts can occur at the atrial level (eg, patent foramen ovale), ventricular level (eg, ventricular septal defect), or arterial level (eg, patent ductus arteriosus).

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 3-week-old male newborn is brought to the physician because his mother has noticed that he tires easily and sweats while feeding. During the past week, she has noticed that his lips and nails turn blue while crying. He was born at 35 weeks' gestation and weighed 2100 g (4 lb 10 oz); he currently weighs 2300 g (5 lb 1 oz). His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 168/min, respirations are 63/min, and blood pressure is 72/42 mm Hg. Examination shows a 3/6 systolic ejection murmur heard over the left upper sternal border. A single S2 is present. An echocardiography confirms the diagnosis. Which of the following factors is most responsible for this patient's cyanosis?

answer_choices.B: Degree of right ventricular outflow obstruction

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of poor weight gain, tiring easily with feeds, and cyanosis during crying is concerning for cyanotic congenital heart disease. The physical examination finding of a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and a single S2 is consistent with tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). TOF consists of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO), ventricular septal defect (VSD), overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. The degree of cyanosis in TOF is determined by the severity of the RVOTO. When the RVOTO is severe, right-to-left shunting across the VSD increases, leading to more desaturated blood entering the systemic circulation and causing cyanosis. This is why the patient's lips and nails turn blue when he cries; crying increases right-to-left shunting by increasing systemic vascular resistance.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of epigastric pain and multiple episodes of vomiting for 4 hours. Initially, the vomit was yellowish in color, but after the first couple of episodes it was streaked with blood. He had 2 episodes of vomiting that contained streaks of frank blood on the way to the hospital. He has been hospitalized twice in the past year for acute pancreatitis. He drinks 2 pints of vodka daily but had over 4 pints during the past 12 hours. He takes naproxen for his 'hangovers.' He appears uncomfortable. His temperature is 37°C (99.1°F), pulse is 105/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Examination shows dry mucous membranes and a tremor of his hands. The abdomen is soft and shows tenderness to palpation in the epigastric region; there is no organomegaly. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Rectal examination is unremarkable. His hemoglobin concentration is 11.3 g/dL and hematocrit concentration is 40%. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?

answer_choices.A: Transmural tear of the lower esophagus
answer_choices.C: Mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction
answer_choices.D: Neoplastic growth at the gastroesophageal junction

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of alcohol abuse, epigastric pain, and vomiting followed by hematemesis is suggestive of a Mallory-Weiss tear. Mallory-Weiss syndrome is characterized by longitudinal mucosal lacerations (not transmural tears) at the gastroesophageal junction or gastric cardia caused by forceful retching. Patients typically present with hematemesis, often following retching or vomiting precipitated by alcoholic binges or overeating. The bleeding is usually self-limited and stops spontaneously in over 90% of patients. Endoscopy is both diagnostic and potentially therapeutic in patients with Mallory-Weiss syndrome.

few_shot.question: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the past 25 years and drinks 24 oz of alcohol daily. He is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 48 kg (105 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m2. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows an epigastric mass. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent abdominal pain and vomiting, along with the presence of an epigastric mass, is suggestive of a pancreatic pseudocyst. Pancreatic pseudocysts are a common complication of both acute and chronic pancreatitis. They are typically round or oval, encapsulated fluid collections that are rich in pancreatic enzymes. They can cause a variety of symptoms, including abdominal pain, early satiety, and vomiting due to gastric outlet obstruction. This patient's history of heavy alcohol use and smoking, both of which are risk factors for pancreatitis, further supports this diagnosis.

few_shot.question: A 50-year-old Caucasian man is admitted to the ER with an 8-hour history of intense abdominal pain that radiates to the back, nausea, and multiple episodes of vomiting. Upon examination, he has significant epigastric tenderness, and hypoactive bowel sounds. The patient's abdominal CT findings of a well-circumscribed, homogeneous fluid collection are consistent with a pancreatic pseudocyst, a common complication of acute pancreatitis. Pancreatic pseudocysts are encapsulated fluid collections that develop over 4 weeks after an episode of acute pancreatitis. few_shot.question: A 54-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 5-hour history of diffuse, severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She reports that there is no blood or bile in the vomitus. Two weeks ago, she started having mild aching epigastric pain, which improved with eating. Since then, she has gained 1.4 kg (3 lb). She has a 2-year history of osteoarthritis of both knees, for which she takes ibuprofen. She drinks 1–2 glasses of wine daily. She is lying supine with her knees drawn up and avoids any movement. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows abdominal tenderness and guarding; bowel sounds are decreased. An x-ray of the chest is shown. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of NSAID use, alcohol consumption, and epigastric pain that improved with eating is suggestive of peptic ulcer disease (PUD). The abrupt onset of severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, along with the finding of peritoneal signs on examination, suggests a complication of PUD, such as perforation. Perforation is a surgical emergency and can lead to chemical and bacterial peritonitis. The chest x-ray shows free air under the diaphragm, which is indicative of perforation of a hollow viscus, such as the stomach or duodenum.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and vaginal discharge. She gave birth to a healthy baby boy three days prior to presentation. Since then, she has been feeling sick, and she is concerned that she has been getting worse over time. On presentation, her temperature is 100.7°F (38.1°C), blood pressure is 115/78 mmHg, pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 14/min. Physical exam reveals abdominal discomfort with uterine tenderness, and laboratory results show elevated white blood cell count with many plasma cells. The most likely cause of this patient's disorder has which of the following characteristics?

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old primigravid woman at 31 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of fever, myalgia, abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea for 3 days. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Her temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F). Physical examination shows diffuse abdominal pain. Blood cultures incubated at 4°C (39.2°F) grow a gram-positive, catalase-positive organism. The pathogen responsible for this patient's presentation was most likely transmitted via which of the following modes?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, myalgia, and gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea) is suggestive of listeriosis, an infection caused by Listeria monocytogenes. This is a gram-positive, catalase-positive rod that is facultatively intracellular and can grow at a wide range of temperatures, including refrigerator temperatures (0-4°C [32-39.2°F]). Listeria is typically transmitted through ingestion of contaminated food, especially unpasteurized dairy products (eg, soft cheeses), deli meats, and hot dogs. In pregnant women, Listeria can cross the placenta and cause chorioamnionitis, premature labor, or neonatal sepsis and meningitis. Therefore, pregnant women are advised to avoid high-risk foods and to heat deli meats and hot dogs until steaming hot to decrease the risk of Listeria infection.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old woman seeks evaluation at a local walk-in clinic for severe lower abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, and painful intercourse for the last couple of weeks. Her last day of menstruation was 1 week ago, and since then the pain has worsened. She is an out-of-town college student engaged in an open relationship with a fellow classmate and another partner from her hometown. Additional concerns include painful micturition and a low-grade fever for the same duration. The physical examination reveals a heart rate of 120/min, respiratory rate of 24/min, and temperature of 38.6°C (101.5°F). The pelvic examination shows an erythematous cervix with a mucopurulent exudate. The cervix bleeds when manipulated with a swab and is extremely tender with movement. Based on the clinical findings, which of the following agents is the most likely cause of her condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of lower abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, and painful intercourse is suggestive of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). PID is an infection of the upper genital tract (uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries) that can cause significant morbidity, including chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. It is often polymicrobial, but the most common pathogens are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. The patient's sexual history and physical examination findings of mucopurulent cervicitis and cervical motion tenderness are consistent with PID due to N. gonorrhoeae.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old gravida-1-para-1 (G1P1) presents to the emergency department with fever, malaise, nausea, and abdominal pain. She says her symptoms started 2 days ago with a fever and nausea, which have progressively worsened. 2 hours ago, she started having severe lower abdominal pain that is diffusely localized. Her past medical history is unremarkable. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. She has had 3 sexual partners in the past month and uses oral contraception. The vital signs include temperature 38.8°C (102.0°F) and blood pressure 120/75 mm Hg. On physical examination, the lower abdomen is severely tender to palpation with guarding. Uterine and adnexal tenderness is also elicited. A urine pregnancy test is negative. On speculum examination, the cervix is inflamed with positive cervical motion tenderness and the presence of a scant yellow-white purulent discharge. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an infection of the upper genital tract (endometrium, fallopian tubes, ovaries, pelvic peritoneum) that occurs when microorganisms ascend from the vagina or cervix. It is a polymicrobial infection that is often associated with sexually transmitted pathogens (eg, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae). Risk factors include multiple sexual partners, recent sexual encounter, and young age (<25 years). Clinical findings often include lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, and uterine or adnexal tenderness. Fever and/or abnormal cervical or vaginal mucopurulent discharge may also be present. PID can cause serious complications such as infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman with sickle cell disease and at 39-weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department in active labor. She has had multiple episodes of acute chest syndrome and has required several transfusions in the past. She has a prolonged vaginal delivery complicated by postpartum bleeding, and she receives a transfusion of 1 unit of packed red blood cells. One hour later, the patient experiences acute flank pain. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.6°F), pulse is 115/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 95/55 mm Hg. Foley catheter shows dark brown urine. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?

answer_choices.A: Serum antibodies against class I HLA antigens
answer_choices.D: Low levels of serum IgA immunoglobulins

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's acute flank pain, fever, and hemoglobinuria following transfusion are suggestive of a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR). DHTR is a common complication in patients with sickle cell disease who have been previously transfused. The reaction is due to an anamnestic response in which the recipient has been previously sensitized to donor red blood cell antigens (eg, from prior transfusion, pregnancy) and then re-exposed to these antigens through subsequent transfusions. The recipient forms antibodies against the foreign antigens, leading to extravascular hemolysis by the reticuloendothelial system (eg, spleen). This typically occurs 2-10 days after the transfusion, but can occur within hours in hyperhemolytic transfusion reactions. Patients present with symptoms of anemia and symptoms related to the underlying condition (eg, pain crisis in sickle cell disease). The direct antiglobulin test (Coombs test) is usually positive for IgG, and there is often a negative crossmatch.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with fever, rash, abdominal pain, and vaginal discharge for the past 3 days. She describes the pain as moderate, cramping in character, and diffusely localized to the suprapubic region. She says the rash is painless and does not itch. She also complains of associated generalized muscle aches and vomiting since last night. The patient denies any recent menstrual irregularities, dysuria, painful urination or similar symptoms in the past. Her past medical history is significant for chronic asthma, managed medically. There is no recent travel or sick contacts. Patient denies any smoking history, alcohol or recreational drug use. She has been sexually active for the past year with a single partner and has been using oral contraceptive pills. Her vital signs include: temperature 38.6°C (101.0°F), blood pressure 90/68 mm Hg, pulse 120/min, and respirations 20/min. Physical examination reveals a diffuse erythematous desquamating maculopapular rash over the lower abdomen and inner thighs. There is moderate tenderness to palpation of the suprapubic and lower right quadrants with no rebound or guarding. Abdomen is non-distended with no hepatosplenomegaly. Pelvic examination reveals a purulent vaginal discharge. Which of the following best describes the organism responsible for this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.A: Gram-positive cocci in clusters producing superantigens
answer_choices.B: Gram-positive bacilli in pairs producing superantigens
answer_choices.C: Gram-negative bacilli in chain producing an endotoxin
answer_choices.D: Gram-positive cocci in chain producing an exotoxin

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, rash, hypotension, and multiorgan involvement (eg, abdominal pain, vomiting) is suggestive of toxic shock syndrome (TSS). TSS is a toxin-mediated illness caused by the superantigens produced by Staphylococcus aureus (gram-positive cocci in clusters) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus, gram-positive cocci in chains). The superantigens produced by these bacteria can cross-link the major histocompatibility complex class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells with the T-cell receptor, leading to polyclonal T-cell activation. This results in a massive release of proinflammatory cytokines, causing the symptoms of TSS.

The most common cause of TSS is S. aureus, which is often associated with tampon use, skin infections, and surgical wounds. In this patient, the purulent vaginal discharge suggests that her TSS is associated with a vaginal infection, likely due to S. aureus.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 65-year-old woman schedules an appointment with her physician for evaluation of weight loss and weakness. The weakness is more noticeable when climbing stairs and combing hair. The weakness improves after brief exercise. She also has bladder incontinence for the past 4 weeks and was given an anticholinesterase agent with no improvement. What is the most likely cause of the symptoms?

answer_choices.D: Paraneoplastic syndrome from small cell carcinoma of the lung

few_shot.question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of double vision, difficulty climbing stairs, and weakness when trying to brush her hair. She reports that these symptoms are worse after she exercises and disappear after she rests for a few hours. Physical examination shows drooping of her right upper eyelid that worsens when the patient is asked to gaze at the ceiling for 2 minutes. There is diminished motor strength in the upper extremities. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fluctuating weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest, along with the physical examination findings of ptosis and proximal muscle weakness, are suggestive of myasthenia gravis (MG). MG is an autoimmune disorder caused by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction. These antibodies lead to a decrease in the number of available AChRs, impairing neuromuscular transmission and causing muscle weakness. The disease often presents with ocular symptoms (eg, ptosis, diplopia) but can progress to involve bulbar muscles (eg, dysarthria, dysphagia) and limb muscles, particularly those that are proximally located.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 71-year-old man with recently diagnosed small-cell lung cancer sees his physician because of increasing weakness over the past 3 months. He is unable to climb stairs or comb his hair. His weakness is worse after inactivity and improves with exercise. He is a former smoker with a 30-pack-year history. He is currently preparing for initiation of chemotherapy. His vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, ptosis of both eyelids is seen. Dry oral mucosa is notable. Significant weakness is detected in all four proximal extremities. The patellar and biceps reflexes are absent. Auscultation of the lungs reveals generalized wheezing and rhonchi. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for this patient’s weakness?

answer_choices.B: Autoantibody-impaired acetylcholine release from nerve terminals
answer_choices.C: Endomysial CD8+ T cell infiltration with vacuoles and inclusion bodies

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's proximal muscle weakness, ptosis, and dry mouth are suggestive of Lambert-Eaton syndrome (LES), a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with small-cell lung cancer. LES is caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels in the neuromuscular junction, which leads to impaired acetylcholine release from nerve terminals and subsequent muscle weakness. The weakness in LES is typically proximal and can involve the ocular muscles, leading to ptosis and diplopia. Autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth, impotence, and constipation can also occur due to impaired acetylcholine release in autonomic ganglia. Unlike myasthenia gravis, the weakness in LES often improves with repeated muscle use.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the physician because of 6 months of progressive weakness in her arms and legs. During this time, she has also had difficulty swallowing and holding her head up. Examination shows pooling of oral secretions. Muscle strength and tone are decreased in the upper extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ in the right upper and lower extremities, 3+ in the left upper extremity, and 4+ in the left lower extremity. Sensation to light touch, pinprick, and vibration are intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by both upper and lower motor neuron signs. Upper motor neuron signs include hyperreflexia and spasticity, while lower motor neuron signs include muscle weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations. The disease often begins focally and spreads contiguously. Bulbar symptoms (eg, dysarthria, dysphagia) are common and often accompanied by emotional lability. Sensory examination is typically normal. ALS is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other potential causes of the patient's symptoms (eg, cervical spondylosis, multifocal motor neuropathy) should be ruled out before making the diagnosis.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with weakness. She states that at the end of the day she feels so fatigued and weak that she can hardly care for herself. She currently feels this way. The patient has had multiple illnesses recently and has been traveling, hiking, and camping. Her temperature is 98.0°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 124/84 mmHg, pulse is 82/min, respirations are 12/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable for 2/5 strength of the upper extremities and 4/5 strength of the lower extremities. Visual exam is notable for mild diplopia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigable weakness that is worse at the end of the day and involves the ocular muscles is suggestive of myasthenia gravis (MG). MG is an autoimmune disorder caused by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction. These antibodies lead to degradation and loss of AChRs, impairing neuromuscular transmission and causing muscle weakness. The weakness in MG is often fatigable (ie, worsens with repetitive use) and classically improves with rest. Ocular symptoms (eg, ptosis, diplopia due to weakness of the extraocular muscles) are often the initial presentation and are seen in the majority of patients. However, the disease can also affect other muscle groups, leading to symptoms such as dysarthria, dysphagia, and limb weakness.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the clinic complaining of weakness that has progressively worsened over the past 2 weeks. She states that she has a hard time lifting both her arms but that they function normally. She notes no history of trauma or other deficits. On examination, that patient has 2/5 muscle strength on shoulder shrug and arm abduction bilaterally, but all other neurological exam findings are normal. You notice some skin changes and ask the patient about them. She states that she has had a rash around her eyes as well as on her lower face, going down to her neck and chest. She notes that the rashes started around the same time as the weakness began. Labs are drawn and a complete blood count and basic metabolic panel are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's proximal muscle weakness, Gottron's papules (flat-topped, violaceous papules over the knuckles), and heliotrope rash (blue-purple discoloration of the upper eyelids with edema) are characteristic of dermatomyositis. Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune disorder that affects skin and muscles. It is associated with malignancy (eg, ovarian, lung, colorectal, non-Hodgkin lymphoma) in adults, and patients should be screened accordingly. Diagnosis is suggested by clinical presentation and laboratory studies (eg, elevated muscle enzymes, positive antinuclear antibody, anti-Jo-1 antibody) and confirmed by muscle biopsy. Treatment involves glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive agents.

So, the answer is [C].

question: A 44-year-old man presents to the family medicine clinic for some small bumps on his left thigh. The lesions are non-pruritic and have been present for the last 3 weeks. He reports feeling fatigued and malaise for the past few months. The patient has no known medical problems and takes no medications. He smokes one pack of cigarettes per day and uses intravenous street drugs. His heart rate is 82/min, the respiratory rate is 14/min, the temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), and the blood pressure is 126/80 mm Hg. Auscultation of the heart is without murmurs. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Three 2-3 mm, dome-shaped, hardened papules are noted on the left thigh. Central umbilication can be observed in each papule. There is a non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy present. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 47-year-old man presents to the clinic for an evaluation of intense itching of his right thigh region for the past few days. He states some ‘red bumps’ just began to form. The patient mentions that he was recently at a business conference in Miami. He has a past medical history of hypertension, diabetes type 2, and hyperlipidemia. He takes enalapril, metformin, and atorvastatin. He does not smoke or drink. His vitals are within normal limits today. On physical examination, a linear line with 3 red papules is present along the medial aspect of his right thigh. Additionally, there are small rows of bumps on his left leg and right forearm. Excoriations are also apparent in the same region. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Bed bug bites are usually painless and often occur at night. They are typically found in a linear or clustered pattern on exposed skin surfaces. The bites are often associated with intense pruritus. The bugs are usually found in the seams of mattresses, box springs, and bed frames. They can also be found in other areas such as behind wallpaper, in the joints of furniture, and in the seams of upholstered furniture. Bed bugs are not known to transmit disease.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy presents to his pediatrician accompanied by his mother for evaluation of a rash. The rash appeared a little over a week ago, and since that time the boy has felt tired. He is less interested in playing outside, preferring to remain indoors because his knees and stomach hurt. His past medical history is significant for an upper respiratory infection that resolved uneventfully without treatment 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 18/min. Physical exam shows scattered maroon macules and papules on the lower extremities. The abdomen is diffusely tender to palpation. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy or conjunctival injection. Which of the following will most likely be found in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of palpable purpura, arthralgia, and abdominal pain following an upper respiratory infection is suggestive of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura). This is the most common vasculitis of childhood and often presents following a recent infection. It is caused by the deposition of IgA immune complexes in the skin, gut, and glomeruli, leading to a leukocytoclastic vasculitis that affects small vessels. The classic tetrad of symptoms includes palpable purpura (often over the buttocks and lower extremities), arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal disease (hematuria and/or proteinuria). The abdominal pain can be severe and may be associated with intussusception.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his host parents for evaluation of a progressively pruritic rash over his shoulders and buttocks for the past 6 months. He recently came to the United States from Nigeria to attend a year of high school. He reports that it has been increasingly difficult for him to read the whiteboard during classes. Physical examination shows symmetrically distributed papules 4–8 mm in diameter, excoriation marks, and patchy hyperpigmentation over his shoulders, waist, and buttocks. There is nontender inguinal lymphadenopathy and several firm, nontender subcutaneous nodules along the right iliac crest. Six skin snip biopsies are taken from the pelvic girdle, buttocks, and thigh, and are then incubated in saline. After 24 hours, microscopic examination shows motile microfilariae. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's pruritic rash, subcutaneous nodules, and visual symptoms, along with the finding of microfilariae on skin snip biopsy, are suggestive of onchocerciasis (river blindness). Onchocerciasis is caused by the nematode Onchocerca volvulus and is transmitted through the bite of the blackfly (Simulium species). The disease is endemic in many parts of Africa, including Nigeria.

The adult worms live in subcutaneous nodules, where they produce microfilariae that migrate to the skin and eyes. The microfilariae cause intense pruritus and skin changes, including depigmentation (leopard skin) and loss of elasticity. Ocular involvement can lead to blindness.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 7-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her parents for red papules over her left thigh and swelling in the right axilla for the past few days. Her parents say that she had a cat bite on her left thigh 2 weeks ago. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.4°F), pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 22/min. On her physical examination, hepatosplenomegaly is present with a healing area of erythema on her left hand. Her laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 12.9 gm/dL
Leukocyte count 9,300/mm3
Platelet count 167,000/mm3
ESR 12 mm/hr
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.D: Surgical excision of the lymph node

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a cat bite, regional lymphadenopathy, and systemic symptoms (eg, fever, hepatosplenomegaly) are suggestive of Bartonella henselae infection, also known as cat-scratch disease. This is a common cause of regional lymphadenopathy in children and is usually a benign, self-limited illness. However, in some cases, it can cause severe systemic disease, especially in immunocompromised patients. 

The treatment of choice for cat-scratch disease is azithromycin, which can be used alone or in combination with rifampin. Doxycycline is not typically used in children under 8 years of age due to the risk of tooth discoloration. Surgical excision of the lymph node is not usually necessary and is reserved for cases of suppuration or lack of response to antibiotic therapy.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old man presents with a 5-week history of multiple cutaneous ulcers on his left forearm and neck, which he first noticed after returning from a 2-month stay in rural Peru. He does not recall any trauma or arthropod bites. The lesions began as non-pruritic erythematous papules that became enlarged, ulcerated, and crusted. There is no history of fever or abdominal pain. He has been sexually active with a single partner since their marriage at 24 years of age. The physical examination reveals erythematous, crusted plaques with central ulceration and a raised border. There is no fluctuance, drainage, or sporotrichoid spread. A punch biopsy was performed, which revealed an ulcerated lesion with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Amastigotes within dermal macrophages are seen on Giemsa staining. What is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of travel to a rural area of Peru, the presence of erythematous, crusted plaques with central ulceration and a raised border, and the finding of amastigotes within dermal macrophages on Giemsa staining are consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis. This is a parasitic infection caused by the Leishmania species, which is transmitted by the bite of a sandfly. The disease is endemic in parts of Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and Central and South America. The cutaneous form of the disease is the most common and is characterized by skin ulcers that develop weeks to months after the sandfly bite. The ulcers are usually painless and can persist for months to years before healing with scarring. The diagnosis is confirmed by identifying the amastigote form of the parasite within macrophages on Giemsa staining.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 75-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her son because of a 2-day history of fever, headache, malaise, and dry cough. The patient lives with her son and his family and her son reports that other members of the family have had similar symptoms during the past week but that he has not had any symptoms. The result of a polymerase chain reaction test confirms that the woman is infected with a virus that has a helical capsid and a segmented genome. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the son being free of symptoms?

answer_choices.D: Homozygous mutation in the CCR5 gene

few_shot.question: An 82-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her daughter because of a 3-day history of a runny nose, headache, and cough. The patient's grandson recently had similar symptoms. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Testing of nasal secretions is performed to identify the viral strain. Electron microscopy shows a non-enveloped RNA virus with an icosahedral capsid. Binding to which of the following is responsible for the virulence of this virus?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of rhinorrhea, cough, and headache in the setting of a sick contact are suggestive of a common cold, most likely due to rhinovirus. Rhinovirus is a non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus that is part of the Picornaviridae family. It is the most common cause of the common cold, and is spread via respiratory droplets and fomites. Rhinovirus binds to intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) on respiratory epithelial cells, which is the first step in the viral replication cycle. ICAM-1 is a cell surface glycoprotein that is typically involved in leukocyte adhesion and migration.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [B] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician with chills, nausea, and diffuse muscle aches for 3 days. His niece had similar symptoms 2 weeks ago and H1N1 influenza strain was isolated from her respiratory secretions. He received his influenza vaccination 2 months ago. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F). A rapid influenza test is positive. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's infection despite vaccination?

answer_choices.A: Random point mutations within viral genome
answer_choices.B: Exchange of viral genes between chromosomes

few_shot.explanation:
Influenza viruses are RNA viruses that lack proofreading activity during replication. This leads to a high rate of random point mutations within the viral genome, a process known as antigenic drift. These mutations can lead to changes in the viral hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) antigens, which are the major targets of neutralizing antibodies. This can lead to evasion of the host immune response, including immunity acquired through vaccination. This is why the influenza vaccine must be updated annually to account for these changes.

So, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [C] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 49-year-old homeless man comes to the emergency department because of fatigue, cough, and worsening shortness of breath for 2 weeks. He was diagnosed with HIV-infection 25 years ago but has never had any symptoms. He has always refused to take antiretroviral medication. Pulmonary examination shows diffuse crackles over bilateral lower lung fields. An x-ray of the chest shows diffuse, symmetrical interstitial infiltrates. His serum level of beta-d-glucan is elevated. Further testing shows a heterozygous mutation that prevents entry of HIV into macrophages. Which of the following proteins is most likely affected by the mutation in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of untreated HIV infection, homelessness, and pulmonary symptoms, along with the finding of diffuse interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray, suggest Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). PJP is an opportunistic infection that occurs in patients with severe immunosuppression, such as those with untreated HIV/AIDS. The diagnosis is supported by the elevated serum level of beta-d-glucan, a component of the PJP cell wall.

The fact that this patient has survived for 25 years without antiretroviral therapy or opportunistic infections suggests that he may have a mutation in CCR5, a chemokine receptor on the surface of T cells and macrophages that is used by HIV to gain entry into these cells. CCR5 is the most common co-receptor that HIV uses to enter cells, along with the CD4 receptor. A 32-base pair deletion in the CCR5 gene (CCR5-delta32) results in a receptor that is not expressed on the cell surface, preventing HIV entry into the cell and conferring resistance to HIV infection. Homozygotes for this mutation are almost completely protected against HIV infection, while heterozygotes, like this patient, experience slower progression of disease.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 59-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of generalized fatigue, myalgia, and a pruritic skin rash for the past 5 months. As a child, he was involved in a motor vehicle accident and required several blood transfusions. Physical examination shows right upper abdominal tenderness, scleral icterus, and well-demarcated, purple, polygonal papules on the wrists bilaterally. Laboratory studies show an elevated replication rate of a hepatotropic virus. Further analysis shows high variability in the genetic sequence that encodes the glycosylated envelope proteins produced by this virus. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the variability in the genetic sequence of these proteins?

answer_choices.A: Viral RNA polymerase lacks proofreading ability
answer_choices.B: Incorporation of envelope proteins from a second virus
answer_choices.C: Integration of viral genes into host cell genome

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of blood transfusions, fatigue, myalgia, and pruritic skin rash are suggestive of chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. HCV is a single-stranded RNA virus that is transmitted primarily through blood and blood products. The virus is hepatotropic and can cause both acute and chronic hepatitis. Chronic HCV infection can lead to cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and extrahepatic manifestations such as mixed cryoglobulinemia (which can cause a palpable purpuric skin rash, arthralgias, and renal disease) and lichen planus (which can cause pruritic, purple, polygonal papules and plaques).

HCV is unique among the RNA viruses in that it demonstrates an extremely high replication rate, with up to one trillion virions produced daily. This, combined with a lack of proofreading ability by the HCV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, leads to a high mutation rate and significant heterogeneity in the HCV population within a single individual. This high genetic variability allows for rapid viral evolution and complicates vaccine development.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman who recently emigrated from Brazil comes to the physician because of fever, fatigue, decreased appetite, and mild abdominal discomfort. She has not seen a physician in several years and her immunization status is unknown. She drinks 2 alcoholic beverages on the weekends and does not use illicit drugs. She is sexually active with several male partners and uses condoms inconsistently. Her temperature is 38°C (99.8°F). Physical examination shows right upper quadrant tenderness and scleral icterus. Serology confirms acute infection with a virus that has partially double-stranded, circular DNA. Which of the following is most likely involved in the replication cycle of this virus?

answer_choices.B: Transcription of viral DNA to RNA in the cytoplasm
answer_choices.C: Reverse transcription of viral RNA to DNA
answer_choices.D: Adhesion of virus to host ICAM-1 receptor

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms, physical examination findings, and history of multiple sexual partners suggest acute hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. HBV is a partially double-stranded DNA virus that replicates via reverse transcription of an RNA intermediate. The viral polymerase transcribes the partially double-stranded DNA into a full-length, positive-sense RNA (ie, pregenomic RNA). This RNA is then reverse transcribed into negative-sense DNA, which serves as a template for the synthesis of positive-sense DNA. The resulting partially double-stranded DNA is packaged into new virions.

So, the answer is [C].

question: A 6-month-old boy presents to a pediatrician for the evaluation of recurrent bacterial infections. He has a history of a variety of bacterial infections since birth. Physical examination reveals light-colored skin with silver-colored hair. The pediatrician suspects an immunodeficiency disorder and decides to order several tests. Study of the boy’s neutrophils reveals that they contain large cytoplasmic vacuoles. Genetic studies show a mutation in the LYST gene. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 6-month-old baby boy presents to his pediatrician for the evaluation of recurrent bacterial infections. He is currently well but has already been hospitalized multiple times due to his bacterial infections. His blood pressure is 103/67 mm Hg and heart rate is 74/min. Physical examination reveals light-colored skin and silver hair. On examination of a peripheral blood smear, large cytoplasmic vacuoles containing microbes are found within the neutrophils. What diagnosis do these findings suggest?
few_shot.explanation:
Chediak-Higashi syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by partial oculocutaneous albinism (light-colored skin and silver hair), recurrent pyogenic infections, and peripheral neuropathy. The disease is caused by defects in lysosomal trafficking regulator gene (LYST), which leads to the formation of giant lysosomes within leukocytes. This impairs the degranulation of neutrophils, leading to recurrent bacterial infections. The presence of large cytoplasmic vacuoles containing microbes within the neutrophils on a peripheral blood smear is a characteristic finding in this condition.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: An 11-month-old boy is brought to the physician for the evaluation of recurrent otitis media since birth. The patient’s immunizations are up-to-date. He is at the 5th percentile for height and weight. Physical examination shows multiple petechiae and several eczematous lesions over the scalp and extremities. The remainder of the examination reveals no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 9,600/mm3 (61% neutrophils and 24% lymphocytes), a platelet count of 29,000/mm3, and an increased serum IgE concentration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by the clinical triad of thrombocytopenia, eczema, and immunodeficiency. The thrombocytopenia in WAS is due to both decreased platelet production and increased destruction. It manifests as petechiae, bruising, and bloody diarrhea in infancy. Eczema in WAS is due to immune dysregulation and is often the initial finding. The immunodeficiency in WAS is due to both cellular and humoral immune defects, leading to recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria (eg, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) and opportunistic pathogens. Laboratory findings include small platelets on peripheral smear, elevated IgA and IgE levels, and decreased to normal IgM and IgG levels. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician for the evaluation of recurrent skin lesions. The episodes of lesions started at the age of 3 months. He has also had several episodes of respiratory tract infections, enlarged lymph nodes, and recurrent fevers since birth. The boy attends daycare. The patient's immunizations are up-to-date. He is at the 5th percentile for length and 10th percentile for weight. He appears ill. Temperature is 38°C (100.4°F). Examination shows several raised, erythematous lesions of different sizes over the face, neck, groin, and extremities; some are purulent. Bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy are present. What is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.C: Impaired repair of double-strand DNA breaks
answer_choices.D: Impaired signaling to actin cytoskeleton reorganization

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent skin and pulmonary infections, lymphadenopathy, and failure to thrive are suggestive of chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). CGD is an immunodeficiency disorder characterized by a defect in the NADPH oxidase enzyme complex, which is responsible for the respiratory (oxidative) burst in phagocytes. The respiratory burst is a crucial step in the killing of certain microbes (eg, Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus) by producing toxic oxygen metabolites such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. Patients with CGD are susceptible to recurrent infections with these catalase-positive organisms, which produce catalase to break down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen before it can be converted into a bactericidal substance. The infections in CGD are often complicated by the formation of granulomas, which can obstruct the gastrointestinal or genitourinary tract.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 3-month-old boy presents to his pediatrician with persistent diarrhea, oral candidiasis, and signs and symptoms of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) pneumonia. He is very lean with weight in the 10th percentile. His blood pressure is 105/64 mm Hg and heart rate is 84/min. He is being evaluated for an immunodeficiency. Laboratory results for HIV are negative by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Which of the following is the most likely cause of this child’s presentation?

answer_choices.A: An X-linked inheritance of HLA genes
answer_choices.D: Grossly reduced levels of B cells

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of persistent diarrhea, oral candidiasis, and RSV pneumonia is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). SCID is a group of disorders characterized by defects in both T and B cell immunity. The most common form of SCID is X-linked and is due to mutations in the gene for the common gamma chain, a component of several interleukin receptors (eg, IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21). These interleukins are involved in the growth, proliferation, and differentiation of T and B cells. Therefore, defects in the common gamma chain can lead to a severe loss of both T and B cell function.

The other options listed, such as an X-linked inheritance of HLA genes, selective IgA deficiency, and grossly reduced levels of B cells, would not explain this patient's presentation.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with a history of recurrent bacterial infections, including several episodes of pneumococcal sepsis. His 2 maternal uncles died after having had similar complaints. Lab investigations reveal an undetectable level of all serum immunoglobulins. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent bacterial infections, low serum immunoglobulins, and family history of a similar condition in male relatives suggest X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia. Bruton agammaglobulinemia is a primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by low or absent B cells due to a mutation in the Bruton tyrosine kinase gene. This gene is necessary for B-cell maturation; therefore, patients with this condition have an absence of mature B cells and plasma cells, leading to a severe reduction in all types of immunoglobulins. Patients typically present with recurrent bacterial infections after 6 months of age, when the maternal IgG antibodies wane. The most common pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Staphylococcus aureus.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 47-year-old woman presents to a physician for evaluation of vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. Her symptoms began following a company picnic a few days ago. Initially, she was unable to tolerate any solids or liquids by mouth, but now has been able to drink sips of water. She had a mild headache, which was relieved with acetaminophen. The past medical history is unremarkable. She does not take any medications. The blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg and the heart rate is 60/min. On examination, the mucous membranes are dry and the eyes are slightly sunken. Where is most of the sodium reabsorbed in this patient’s kidneys?

answer_choices.B: Descending limb of loop of Henle
answer_choices.D: Ascending limb of loop of Henle

few_shot.question:
A 55-year-old woman presents to the emergency room with severe abdominal pain for the past 24 hours. She has also noticed blood in her urine. She does not have any significant past medical history. Family history is significant for her mother having cholecystitis status post cholecystectomy at age 45. Her vital signs include: temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse 103/min, respiratory rate 15/min, blood pressure 105/85 mm Hg. Physical examination is significant for a woman continuously moving on the exam table in an attempt to get comfortable. Laboratory findings are significant for the following:
Serum electrolytes
Na 138 mEq/L N: 135–145 mEq/L
K 4.0 mEq/L N: 3.5–5.0 mEq/L
Cl 102 mEq/L N: 98–108 mEq/L
CO2 27 mEq/L N: 22–32 mEq/L
Ca 9.2 mEq/dL N: 8.4–10.2 mEq/dL
PO4 3.5 mg/dL N: 3.0–4.5 mg/dL
A 24-hour urine collection is performed and reveals a urinary calcium of 345 mg/day (ref: < 300 mg/day in men; < 250 mg/day in women). A non-contrast CT of the abdomen is performed and is shown in the exhibit. The patient’s symptoms pass within the next 12 hours with hydration and acetaminophen for pain management. She is prescribed a medication to prevent subsequent episodes. At which of the following parts of the nephron does this medication most likely work?

answer_choices.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
answer_choices.D: Descending limb of the loop of Henle

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of severe abdominal pain and hematuria, along with the CT findings, are suggestive of nephrolithiasis. The most common type of kidney stone is composed of calcium oxalate, which is likely in this patient given her hypercalciuria. The first-line treatment for recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis is increased fluid intake to dilute the concentration of stone-forming solutes in the urine. If this fails, thiazide diuretics are the next step in management. Thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the early distal convoluted tubule, leading to increased sodium and water excretion. However, they also increase calcium reabsorption in the same segment, thereby reducing urinary calcium excretion and the risk of calcium stone formation.

So, the answer is [A].
