question:
A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a racing heart and lightheadedness for 3 hours. He has had similar episodes in the past, but the symptoms never lasted this long. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, headaches, and fevers. He had a myocardial infarction 4 years ago and currently takes captopril, metoprolol, and atorvastatin. His pulse is irregular and cardiac auscultation reveals an irregular heart rhythm. Laboratory reports show:
Serum glucose 88 mg/dL
Sodium 142 mEq/L
Potassium 3.9 mEq/L
Chloride 101 mEq/L
Serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
Blood urea nitrogen 10 mg/dL
Cholesterol, total 170 mg/dL
HDL-cholesterol 40 mg/dL
LDL-cholesterol 80 mg/dL
Triglycerides 170 mg/dL
Hematocrit 38%
Hemoglobin 13 g/dL
Leucocyte count 7,500/mm3
Platelet count 185,000 /mm3
Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) 30 seconds
Prothrombin time (PT) 12 seconds
Cardiac enzymes Negative
An ECG shows the absence of P-waves with an irregular RR complex. A few hours later, his symptoms subside and he is discharged with an additional anticoagulation drug. Which of the following mechanisms explains how this new medication will exert its effects?

answer_choices.C: Inhibition of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors

few_shot.question: A 66-year-old man with coronary artery disease and hypertension comes to the emergency department because of intermittent retrosternal chest pain, lightheadedness, and palpitations. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 39 years. His pulse is 140/min and irregularly irregular, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 108/60 mm Hg. An ECG shows an irregular, narrow-complex tachycardia with absent P waves. A drug with which of the following mechanisms of action is most likely to be effective in the long-term prevention of embolic stroke in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Binding and activation of antithrombin III
answer_choices.C: Interference with carboxylation of glutamate residues
answer_choices.D: Irreversible blockade of adenosine diphosphate receptors

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of an irregularly irregular, narrow-complex tachycardia without discernible P waves is consistent with atrial fibrillation (AF). AF is associated with a fivefold increased risk of stroke due to the formation of thrombi in the left atrial appendage. Anticoagulation is recommended for most patients with AF to prevent thromboembolic complications. Warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist, is commonly used for this purpose. Warfarin inhibits the vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of the clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as the anticoagulant proteins C and S. This carboxylation is necessary for these proteins to bind calcium and interact with the phospholipid surfaces of platelets, which is necessary for the coagulation cascade.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 71-year-old woman comes to the physician because of palpitations and shortness of breath that started 3 days ago. She has hypertension and congestive heart failure. Her pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows an irregularly irregular rhythm without any murmurs. An ECG shows a narrow-complex tachycardia without P waves. The patient is prescribed a prophylactic medication that can be reversed with idarucizumab. The expected beneficial effect of the prescribed drug is most likely due to which of the following effects?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves on ECG is consistent with atrial fibrillation (AF). AF is associated with a fivefold increased risk of stroke, and anticoagulation is recommended for most patients. Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor that is used for stroke prevention in nonvalvular AF. It works by directly inhibiting thrombin, thereby preventing the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin. Dabigatran is the only direct oral anticoagulant for which a specific reversal agent is available. Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds dabigatran and reverses its anticoagulant effect within minutes.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 5-month history of episodic palpitations, dizziness, and fatigue. His pulse is 134/min and irregularly irregular, and his blood pressure is 165/92 mm Hg. An ECG shows a narrow complex tachycardia with absent P waves. He is prescribed a drug that decreases the long-term risk of thromboembolic complications by inhibiting the extrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade. The expected beneficial effect of this drug is most likely due to which of the following actions?

answer_choices.A: Inhibit the absorption of vitamin K
answer_choices.D: Inhibit the reduction of vitamin K

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's irregularly irregular pulse and absence of P waves on ECG are consistent with atrial fibrillation (AF). AF is associated with a fivefold increased risk of stroke due to the formation of thrombi in the left atrium, particularly within the left atrial appendage. Anticoagulation is recommended for most patients with AF to decrease the risk of thromboembolic complications. Warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist, is commonly used for this purpose.

Vitamin K is a cofactor for the gamma-glutamyl carboxylase enzyme, which carboxylates and thereby activates clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. The reduced form of vitamin K is a necessary cofactor for this carboxylation. After it is oxidized, vitamin K is then reduced back to its active form by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase. Warfarin exerts its anticoagulant effect by inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase, thereby decreasing the regeneration of reduced vitamin K and subsequently the activation of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 54-year-old man with a history of hyperlipidemia presents to the emergency department complaining of left sided chest pain. He says the pain began 3 hours ago while he was cooking dinner in his kitchen. The pain radiates to his left arm and stomach. He also complains of feeling anxious and heart palpitations. Temperature is 98.7°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, pulse is 101/min, and respirations are 22/min. Inspection demonstrates a diffuse diaphoresis, and cardiac auscultation reveals an S4 gallop. Cardiac catheterization reveals occlusion of the left anterior descending artery, and a vascular stent is placed. The patient is discharged on aspirin, atorvastatin, and an antiplatelet medication. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the most likely prescribed antiplatelet medication?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with an acute myocardial infarction (MI) due to occlusion of the left anterior descending artery. The standard of care for patients with acute MI is dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor (eg, clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor) for at least 12 months following the event. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1, thereby preventing the formation of thromboxane A2, a potent platelet aggregator and vasoconstrictor. P2Y12 inhibitors prevent ADP-mediated platelet activation and aggregation by blocking the P2Y12 receptor. Clopidogrel and prasugrel are prodrugs that must be metabolized by the liver to an active form, which irreversibly binds the P2Y12 receptor. Ticagrelor is a directly acting reversible P2Y12 inhibitor.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 64-year-old man presents to his physician 6 months after experiencing a myocardial infarction. The patient currently denies any symptoms and is only in for a check up. The patient's past medical history is notable for diabetes (type II), obesity, hypertension and cyclothymia. His current medications are hydrocholorthiazide, metoprolol, metformin, insulin, fluoxetine, and fish oil. The patient returns 2 weeks later and presents his blood glucose diary to you demonstrating a mean blood glucose of 167 mg/dL. He is also complaining of flushing that occurs occasionally but otherwise is doing well. Which of the following is most likely to alleviate this patient's current symptom?

answer_choices.D: Decreased inhibition of HMG CoA reductase

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's low HDL and high LDL cholesterol levels indicate that he has dyslipidemia, a common finding in patients with diabetes mellitus. His physician likely started him on a statin (eg, atorvastatin, simvastatin) and niacin. Niacin is especially effective at raising HDL levels and is often used in patients with low HDL levels despite statin therapy. However, it commonly causes cutaneous flushing and pruritus due to prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation in the skin. Symptoms can be minimized by taking aspirin 30 minutes before niacin. question: A 76-year-old man is brought to his physician's office by his wife due to progressively worsening hearing loss. The patient reports that he noticed a decrease in his hearing approximately 10 years ago. His wife says that he watches television at an elevated volume and appears to have trouble understanding what is being said to him, especially when there is background noise. He states that he also experiences constant ear ringing and episodes of unsteadiness. On physical examination, the outer ears are normal and otoscopic findings are unremarkable. The patient is unable to repeat the sentence said to him on whisper testing. When a vibrating tuning fork is placed in the middle of the patient's forehead, it is heard equally on both ears. When the vibrating tuning fork is placed by the ear and then on the mastoid process, air conduction is greater than bone conduction. Which of the following structures is most likely impaired in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with progressively worsening hearing loss. He states that his trouble with hearing began approximately 7-8 years ago. He is able to hear when someone is speaking to him; however, he has difficulty with understanding what is being said, especially when there is background noise. In addition to his current symptoms, he reports a steady ringing in both ears, and at times experiences dizziness. Medical history is significant for three prior episodes of acute otitis media. Family history is notable for his father being diagnosed with cholesteatoma. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 138/88 mmHg, pulse is 14/min, and respirations are 13/min. On physical exam, when a tuning fork is placed in the middle of the patient's forehead, sound is appreciated equally on both ears. When a tuning fork is placed by the external auditory canal and subsequently on the mastoid process, air conduction is greater than bone conduction. Which of the following is most likely the cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of bilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness are suggestive of presbycusis, which is the most common cause of hearing loss in the elderly. Presbycusis is a sensorineural hearing loss that occurs gradually, often affecting both ears equally. It is characterized by degeneration of cochlear structures, including hair cells in the organ of Corti, stria vascularis, and cochlear neurons. Patients often complain of difficulty hearing in noisy environments and may also have tinnitus. The hearing loss is typically greater for high-frequency sounds. On physical exam, the Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction, and the Weber test shows no lateralization, both of which are normal findings.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old man comes to the physician with a 2-year history of progressive hearing loss. His hearing is worse in crowded rooms, and he has noticed that he has more difficulty understanding women than men. He has no history of serious illness and does not take any medications. A Rinne test shows air conduction is greater than bone conduction bilaterally. This condition is most likely associated with damage closest to which of the following structures?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's hearing loss is characterized by difficulty hearing high-frequency sounds (eg, women's and children's voices) and understanding speech in noisy environments. These findings, along with the normal Rinne test, are consistent with presbycusis, the most common type of sensorineural hearing loss. Presbycusis is caused by loss of hair cells in the cochlea, most commonly in the basal turn of the cochlea, which is responsible for hearing high-frequency sounds.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: An otherwise healthy 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of hearing loss. To test her hearing, the physician performs two tests. First, a vibrating tuning fork is held against the mastoid bone of the patient and then near her ear, to which the patient responds she hears the sound better on both sides when the tuning fork is held near her ear. Next, the physician holds the tuning fork against the bridge of her forehead, to which the patient responds she hears the sound better on the right side than the left. The patient's examination findings are most consistent with which of the following conditions?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's hearing loss is sensorineural, as evidenced by the Rinne test (air conduction > bone conduction). The Weber test (tuning fork on forehead) lateralizes to the right, indicating that the left ear is affected. The most likely cause of unilateral sensorineural hearing loss in an adult is an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma), a benign tumor of Schwann cells on the vestibular portion of the eighth cranial nerve. Acoustic neuromas are associated with neurofibromatosis type II but can also occur sporadically. Symptoms include unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and loss of balance. 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of tinnitus and progressive hearing loss in the left ear. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and Raynaud syndrome. Her current medications include metformin, nifedipine, and a multivitamin. She appears well. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A vibrating tuning fork is placed on the left mastoid process. Immediately after the patient does not hear a tone, the tuning fork is held over the left ear and she reports hearing the tuning fork again. The same test is repeated on the right side and shows the same pattern. The vibration tuning fork is then placed on the middle of the forehead and the patient hears the sound louder in the right ear. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's progressive unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus are concerning for an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Acoustic neuromas are benign tumors that arise from the Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve. They are slow-growing and typically present in middle-aged adults with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance. The hearing loss is often subtle and missed by the patient until it is detected on physical examination or audiometry. On examination, patients will have a positive Rinne test (air conduction > bone conduction) and Weber test lateralizes to the unaffected ear. The diagnosis is confirmed by MRI of the internal auditory canals.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 39-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of hearing loss. He reports difficulty hearing sounds like the beeping of the microwave or birds chirping, but can easily hear the pipe organ at church. He works as an aircraft marshaller. A Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. A Weber test does not lateralize. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

answer_choices.C: Destruction of the organ of Corti

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of occupational noise exposure and difficulty hearing high-frequency sounds (eg, microwave beeping, birds chirping) is suggestive of noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL). Chronic exposure to loud noise can lead to destruction of the hair cells in the organ of Corti, which are responsible for detecting sound waves and transmitting the signal to the cochlear nerve. The hair cells that detect high-frequency sounds are usually the first to be damaged because they are closest to the oval and round windows, where sound waves enter the cochlea. Over time, the hearing loss can progress to involve lower-frequency sounds as well. NIHL is a type of sensorineural hearing loss, which is characterized by symmetric hearing loss that does not lateralize on the Weber test and demonstrates normal (air conduction > bone conduction) results on the Rinne test.

So, the answer is [C].

question: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician with high-grade fever, headache, and muscle pain. A week ago, she returned from India, where she was working with an NGO to build houses in rural areas. The patient took one dose of chloroquine one week before her trip. She also took a further dose during her trip. She has no history of a serious illness. Her temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 112/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows jaundice. The abdomen is soft and nontender. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dL and a blood smear shows fragmented erythrocytes and occasional ring-shaped inclusion bodies within erythrocytes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of infection in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fever, chills, headache, and nausea over the past 3 days. Nine months ago, she returned from a vacation in Indonesia where she had experienced similar symptoms and episodic fever. She was treated with chloroquine and recovered uneventfully. Her temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), pulse is 97/min, and blood pressure is 123/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus. The abdomen is soft; bowel sounds are active. Neurologic examination is unremarkable. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dL. A photomicrograph of a peripheral blood smear is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the recurrence of symptoms in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of travel to Indonesia, episodic fever, and peripheral blood smear findings are consistent with malaria. Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species, which are transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito. The Plasmodium life cycle involves an exoerythrocytic cycle in the liver followed by an erythrocytic cycle in red blood cells. In the erythrocytic cycle, merozoites infect red blood cells, replicate, and cause cell lysis, leading to periodic fever, chills, and sweats. The peripheral blood smear shows red blood cells infected with Plasmodium species, with some cells containing multiple ring forms (as shown in the image).

P vivax and P ovale can form dormant hypnozoites in the liver that can reactivate months to years after the initial infection, causing a relapse of symptoms. This patient's recurrence of symptoms 9 months after her initial infection is most consistent with reactivation of dormant liver-stage parasites. Primaquine is used to kill hypnozoites and prevent relapse.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 46-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of headache, muscle pain, and recurrent fever spikes that occur without a noticeable rhythm. Two weeks ago, he returned from a 5-week-long world trip during which he climbed several mountains in India, Africa, and Appalachia. Chemoprophylaxis with chloroquine was initiated one week prior to the trip. Physical examination shows jaundice. The spleen is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. His hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dL. A photomicrograph of a peripheral blood smear is shown. Which of the following agents is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fever, headache, and myalgia, along with his recent travel history to India and Africa, are suggestive of malaria. The peripheral blood smear shows multiple ring forms within a single red blood cell, which is characteristic of Plasmodium falciparum. This species is the most virulent of the Plasmodium species and can cause severe disease, including cerebral malaria, severe anemia, and renal failure. Chloroquine is used for prophylaxis against P. falciparum, but resistance is common in many parts of the world, including India and Africa.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman who resides in an area endemic for chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum malaria presents to the physician with fatigue, malaise, and episodes of fever with chills over the last 5 days. She mentions that she has episodes of shivering and chills on alternate days that last for approximately 2 hours, followed by high-grade fevers; then she has profuse sweating and her body temperature returns to normal. She also mentions that she is currently in her 7th week of pregnancy. The physical examination reveals the presence of mild splenomegaly. A peripheral blood smear confirms the diagnosis of P. falciparum infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate anti-malarial treatment for the woman?
few_shot.explanation:
Pregnant women are at increased risk for severe malaria and malaria-related death. In addition, malaria infection during pregnancy can cause maternal anemia and low birth weight, a leading cause of infant mortality. Therefore, prompt and effective treatment of malaria in pregnancy is essential.

In areas with chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum, the World Health Organization recommends artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) as first-line treatment for uncomplicated malaria. However, ACT is not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy due to limited safety data. Instead, quinine plus clindamycin is recommended for the full 7-day treatment course. Quinine monotherapy is not recommended due to an increased risk of treatment failure.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 31-year-old woman presents to your office with one week of recurrent fevers. The highest temperature she recorded was 101°F (38.3°C). She recently returned from a trip to Nigeria to visit family and recalls a painful bite on her right forearm at that time. Her medical history is significant for two malarial infections as a child. She is not taking any medications. On physical examination, her temperature is 102.2°F (39°C), blood pressure is 122/80 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, respirations are 18/min, and pulse oximetry is 99% on room air. She has bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and a visible, enlarged, mobile posterior cervical node. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. She has an erythematous induration on her right forearm. The most likely cause of this patient's symptoms can be treated with which of the following medications?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recent travel to Africa, recurrent fevers, and erythematous induration at the site of a painful bite suggest African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness). This disease is caused by the protozoan parasites Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense (East Africa) or T. brucei gambiense (West Africa), which are transmitted by the tsetse fly. The painful chancre at the site of the tsetse fly bite is a characteristic feature of T. b. rhodesiense infection. The disease progresses from a hemolymphatic stage with nonspecific symptoms (eg, fever, lymphadenopathy, pruritus) to a meningoencephalitic stage with neurologic findings (eg, somnolence, abnormal behavior, motor weakness).

The treatment of African trypanosomiasis depends on the infecting species and the disease stage. For the hemolymphatic stage of T. b. rhodesiense infection, suramin is the treatment of choice. For the meningoencephalitic stage, melarsoprol, an arsenical compound, is used.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 26-year-old woman seeks evaluation at an urgent care clinic with complaints of fever and generalized muscle and joint pain for the past 3 days. She also complains of nausea, but denies vomiting. She does not mention any past similar episodes. Her past medical history is unremarkable, but she returned to the United States 1 week ago after spending 2 weeks in southeast Asia doing charity work. She received all the recommended vaccines prior to traveling. The temperature is 40.0°C (104.0°F), the respirations are 15/min, the pulse is 107/min, and the blood pressure is 98/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mild gingival bleeding and a petechial rash over the trunk. Laboratory studies show the following:
Laboratory test
Leukocyte count 4,000/mm³
Platelet count 100,000/mm³
Partial thromboplastin time (activated)  45 seconds
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, myalgias, arthralgias, rash, and thrombocytopenia after returning from Southeast Asia is suggestive of dengue fever. Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne illness caused by the dengue virus, a flavivirus. It is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions around the world, including Southeast Asia. The disease is characterized by high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgias, arthralgias, and a characteristic rash that is often described as "islands of white in a sea of red." Thrombocytopenia is common and can lead to bleeding complications, such as the gingival bleeding seen in this patient.

The other options listed (Ebola virus, leptospirosis, and yellow fever) can also cause similar symptoms, but are less likely given this patient's specific presentation and travel history.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question:

Her complete metabolic panel is otherwise within normal limits. Imaging studies show subperiosteal resorption and osteoporosis. Scintigraphy reveals the most common pathologic condition associated with the patient’s diagnosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 76-year-old woman presents to the office with a generalized weakness for the past month. She has a past medical history significant for uncontrolled hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus.  Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure is 135/82 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, respiratory rate is 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam shows no remarkable findings. Her last recorded glomerular filtration rate was 30 mL/min. A radiograph of the patient’s hand is given. Which of the following lab findings is most likely to be found in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Increased PTH, decreased calcium, increased phosphate
answer_choices.B: Increased PTH, decreased calcium, decreased phosphate
answer_choices.C: Increased PTH, increased calcium, increased phosphate
answer_choices.D: Normal PTH, increased calcium, normal phosphate

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's hand radiograph shows subperiosteal bone resorption, which is a classic finding in secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease (CKD). In CKD, the kidneys lose their ability to excrete phosphate and to convert vitamin D to its active form (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3). This leads to hyperphosphatemia and decreased calcium absorption from the gut, resulting in hypocalcemia. The hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia stimulate the parathyroid glands to secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), leading to secondary hyperparathyroidism. The increased PTH levels cause excessive bone resorption in an attempt to increase serum calcium levels, leading to the radiographic findings seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: At a routine exam, a 68-year-old woman is discovered to have a serum calcium level of 11.5 mg/dL. Follow-up laboratory tests show a high parathyroid hormone with low phosphorus and mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase. 24-hour urine calcium level is elevated. Review of symptoms includes complaints of fatigue, constipation, and diffuse bone pain for which she takes vitamin D. Past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus for 25 years and essential hypertension for 15 years. The patient has a history of kidney stones. Family history is irrelevant. Which of the following radiologic findings is consistent with the patient's condition?

answer_choices.A: Subperiosteal bone resorption on hand X-ray
answer_choices.B: Osteopenia, osteolytic lesions and pathological fractures
answer_choices.C: Lytic changes in early stage and sclerotic picture in later stage
answer_choices.D: Fibronodular opacities in upper lobes of the lung with or without cavitation

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's elevated serum calcium, elevated parathyroid hormone, and elevated 24-hour urine calcium are consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism. This condition is most commonly caused by a parathyroid adenoma, but can also be due to parathyroid hyperplasia or, rarely, parathyroid carcinoma. The most common presentation is asymptomatic hypercalcemia, but symptoms can also include fatigue, constipation, and bone pain, as seen in this patient. 

Radiologic findings in primary hyperparathyroidism include subperiosteal bone resorption, most commonly seen in the radial aspects of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers. Other findings can include a "salt-and-pepper" appearance of the skull due to loss of the lamina dura around the teeth, and brown tumors (localized collections of osteoclasts, hemorrhage, and fibrous tissue) that can cause pathologic fractures.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician for a pre-employment examination. Her current medications include an oral contraceptive and a daily multivitamin. Physical examination is unremarkable. Serum studies show calcium of 11.8 mg/dL, phosphorus of 2.3 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone level of 615 pg/mL. A 24-hour urine collection shows a low urinary calcium level. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s laboratory findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) level are suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism, which is most commonly due to a parathyroid adenoma. However, the low urinary calcium level is inconsistent with this diagnosis, as primary hyperparathyroidism typically causes hypercalciuria due to increased bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. 

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder characterized by hypercalcemia, relative hypocalciuria, and normal to mildly elevated PTH. It is caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the gene that codes for the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in the parathyroid glands and kidneys. The CaSR plays a crucial role in maintaining calcium homeostasis by regulating PTH secretion and urinary calcium excretion. In the parathyroid glands, a decrease in extracellular calcium levels is sensed by the CaSR, leading to increased PTH secretion. In the kidneys, activation of the CaSR in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle and distal convoluted tubule inhibits tubular reabsorption of calcium, leading to increased urinary calcium excretion. 

In FHH, the defective CaSR has a decreased sensitivity to extracellular calcium, leading to increased PTH secretion and renal calcium reabsorption, which results in hypercalcemia and hypocalciuria, respectively. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 43-year-old man presents to his primary care provider with concerns about general weakness and decreased concentration over the past several months. He reports constipation and unintentional weight loss of about 9.1 kg (20 lb). The past medical symptoms are noncontributory. He works as a bank manager and occasionally drinks alcohol but does not smoke tobacco. Today, the vital signs include blood pressure 145/90 mm Hg, heart rate 60/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and temperature 36.6°C (97.9°F). On physical examination, the patient looks fatigued. His heart has a regular rate and rhythm, and his lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Laboratory studies show:
Calcium 14.5 mg/dL  
Phosphate 2.2 mg/dL  
Parathyroid hormone (PTH)  18 pg/mL  
Parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) 4 pmol/L Normal value: < 2 pmol/L
Calcitriol 46 pg/mL Normal value: 25–65 pg/mL
T3 120 ng/mL  
T4 10.2 mcg/dL  
Taking into account the clinical and laboratory findings, what is the most likely cause of this patient’s hypercalcemia?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of fatigue, constipation, and weight loss, along with the laboratory findings of hypercalcemia and elevated parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP), are suggestive of malignancy. PTHrP is structurally similar to parathyroid hormone (PTH) and can bind to the same receptor, leading to increased renal tubular reabsorption of calcium, decreased renal phosphate reabsorption, and increased bone resorption of calcium. This can result in hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia, as seen in this patient. The most common malignancies associated with elevated PTHrP are squamous cell carcinomas of the lung, head, and neck, and renal cell carcinoma.

The other options (chronic kidney disease, hyperparathyroidism, and hypervitaminosis D) can also cause hypercalcemia, but they would not explain this patient's other findings.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

She drinks 4-5 glasses of wine per week and does not smoke. Her temperature is 99.2°F (37.3°C), blood pressure is 125/65 mmHg, pulse is 78/min, and respirations are 18/min. On exam, she is well-appearing and in no acute distress. A complete blood count is within normal limits. Additional workup is shown below:

Serum:

Cl-: 99 mEq/L
K+: 3.9 mEq/L
HCO3-: 23 mEq/L
BUN: 18 mg/dL
Glucose: 110 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL
Ca2+: 11.1 mg/dL
Parathyroid hormone: 700 pg/mL

Urine:
Na+: 100 mEq/L/24h
Ca2+: 100 mg/24h
Osmolality: 400 mOsmol/kg H2O

Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

answer_choices.C: Loss-of-function mutation in the calcium-sensing receptor

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's hypercalcemia and elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) level are suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism, which is most commonly due to a parathyroid adenoma. However, the low urine calcium level is inconsistent with this diagnosis, as PTH increases distal renal tubular calcium reabsorption and leads to hypercalciuria. Instead, this patient's findings suggest familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH), a generally benign condition characterized by hypercalcemia, normal to mildly elevated PTH, and low urinary calcium excretion. FHH is caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the gene encoding the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in the parathyroid glands and kidneys. The CaSR is responsible for maintaining calcium homeostasis by regulating PTH secretion and renal calcium reabsorption. Inactivation of the CaSR increases the "set point" at which the serum calcium level suppresses PTH release, leading to mild elevations in serum calcium and PTH. In the kidneys, the decreased CaSR function impairs urinary calcium excretion, leading to hypocalciuria. FHH is typically asymptomatic, and patients have a normal life expectancy. The diagnosis should be suspected in patients with mild hypercalcemia and a family history of hypercalcemia. However, as in this patient, FHH can also be seen in adopted individuals with no known family history.

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with eye dryness and a foreign body sensation in the eyes. On physical examination, the oral cavity shows mucosal ulceration and atrophy. few_shot.question: A 48-year-old female presents to your office with a 1-year history of dry eyes and difficulty swallowing. She complains of blinking frequently and of eye strain while using her computer at work. She also reports stiffness in her knees and lower back. Past medical history is unremarkable and she does not take medications. She denies cigarette or alcohol use. Family history is notable for Hashimoto's thyroiditis in her mother. Physical exam shows dry oral mucosa and enlargement of the parotid glands. Which of the following serologies is likely to be positive in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dry eyes and dry mouth are suggestive of Sjögren's syndrome, a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands. This leads to the classic sicca symptoms of dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia). Other symptoms can include parotid gland enlargement, nonerosive arthritis, Raynaud's phenomenon, and renal tubular acidosis. Sjögren's syndrome can occur alone (primary) or in association with another autoimmune disease (secondary). The most common autoantibodies in Sjögren's syndrome are anti-SS-A (Ro) and anti-SS-B (La), with anti-SS-A being more common.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 47-year-old woman presents to her physician for difficulty swallowing. She states that she intentionally delayed seeing a physician for this issue. This is due to an antigen-driven B-cell proliferation.

A previously healthy 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of a recurring rash that typically occurs on exposure to the sun and affects only the face. She also has noticed several nonpainful ulcers on the roof of her mouth. She is sexually active with one male partner and they use condoms inconsistently. Her mother has end-stage renal disease. This patient's malar rash, oral ulcers, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and positive antinuclear and anti-Smith antibodies are consistent with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The presence of proteinuria and urinary white blood cells (WBCs) suggests lupus nephritis, which is a common and serious complication of SLE. Lupus nephritis is a major determinant of the prognosis of SLE and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Therefore, it is important to diagnose and treat this condition promptly.

The diagnosis of lupus nephritis is made by renal biopsy, which can also help determine the severity of the disease and guide treatment. The presence of urinary WBCs in this patient suggests active inflammation in the kidneys, which would be an indication for immunosuppressive therapy.

question: A 74-year-old woman is brought to her primary care doctor by her adult son. The son says she has been very difficult at home and is "losing it". He seems very frustrated about her diminishing ability to take care of herself the way she used to and no longer thinks he can trust her watching his children. At her last visit you noted mild cognitive impairment. Today, she appears withdrawn and hesitates to make eye-contact with you. She lets her son do most of the talking. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

answer_choices.A: Discuss with the son the challenges of having a parent with dementia
answer_choices.C: Assess the patient's risk for depression
answer_choices.D: Ask the son to step out so you can speak with the patient alone

few_shot.question: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency ward by her son for lethargy and generalized weakness. The patient speaks in short utterances and does not make eye contact with the provider or her son throughout the interview and examination. You elicit that the patient lives with her son and daughter-in-law, and she reports vague weakness for the last couple days. The emergency room provider notices 3-4 healing bruises on the patient's upper extremities; otherwise, examination is not revealing. Routine chemistries and blood counts are unremarkable; non-contrast head CT demonstrates normal age-related changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.B: Question the patient's son regarding the home situation
answer_choices.C: Ask the patient's son to leave the room
answer_choices.D: Call Adult Protective Services to report the patient's son

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is concerning for elder abuse, which is defined as intentional actions that cause harm or create a serious risk of harm to a vulnerable elder by a caregiver or other person in a trust relationship with the elder. Elder abuse can be physical, sexual, or emotional/psychological, and can also include neglect and financial exploitation. The patient's lethargy, poor eye contact, and reluctance to speak in the presence of her son are concerning for possible emotional abuse, and the multiple healing bruises on her extremities raise concern for possible physical abuse. The most appropriate next step in management is to interview the patient privately, without her son in the room. This will allow the patient to speak freely about her home situation and any potential abuse. If abuse is confirmed or highly suspected, Adult Protective Services should be contacted.

few_shot.question: A 76-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her daughter for evaluation of progressive cognitive decline and a 1-year history of incontinence. She was diagnosed with dementia, Alzheimer type, 5 years ago. The daughter has noticed that in the past 2 years, her mother has had increasing word-finding difficulties and forgetfulness. She was previously independent but now lives with her daughter and requires assistance with all activities of daily living. Over the past year, she has had decreased appetite, poor oral intake, and sometimes regurgitates her food. During this time, she has had a 12-kg (26-lb) weight loss. She was treated twice for aspiration pneumonia and now her diet mainly consists of pureed food. She has no advance directives and her daughter says that when her mother was independent the patient mentioned that she would not want any resuscitation or life-sustaining measures if the need arose. The daughter wants to continue taking care of her mother but is concerned about her ability to do so. The patient has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Current medications include amlodipine and atorvastatin. Vital signs are within normal limits. She appears malnourished but is well-groomed. The patient is oriented to self and recognizes her daughter by name, but she is unaware of the place or year. Mini-Mental State Examination score is 17/30. Physical and neurologic examinations show no other abnormalities. A complete blood count and serum concentrations of creatinine, urea nitrogen, TSH, and vitamin B12 levels are within the reference range. Her serum albumin is 3 g/dL. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.C: Evaluation for alternative methods of feeding

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has advanced Alzheimer disease (AD) with significant cognitive impairment, functional decline, and weight loss. She has had recurrent aspiration pneumonia and now requires a pureed diet. The weight loss and low serum albumin level suggest protein-calorie malnutrition, which is common in advanced dementia due to anorexia, decreased oral intake, and dysphagia. The patient's daughter is her caregiver and is finding it increasingly difficult to care for her mother at home. Given the patient's advanced disease and the burden of care on the family, referral to home hospice is appropriate.

Hospice care focuses on providing comfort and support to patients with a life expectancy of <6 months. It is often underutilized in patients with nonmalignant terminal illnesses such as advanced dementia. Patients with advanced AD are eligible for hospice care if they meet criteria such as a score of <6 on the Functional Assessment Staging scale (eg, loss of ambulation, incontinence, inability to dress independently) and have had at least one of the following complications in the past year: aspiration pneumonia, pyelonephritis, septicemia, multiple stage 3-4 decubitus ulcers, or recurrent fever. This patient meets criteria for hospice care because she has a Functional Assessment Staging score of 7 (loss of speech, ambulation, and ability to sit up independently) and has had recurrent aspiration pneumonia.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 75-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with her son because she is convinced that people are stealing from her. Physical examination is unremarkable and the patient is oriented to person, time, and place. A mini-mental status examination (MMSE) is performed and she has difficulty recalling words after 5 minutes and also has problems with serial subtraction. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's forgetfulness, difficulty with serial subtraction, and difficulty recalling words after 5 minutes on the MMSE are suggestive of dementia. Dementia is a chronic, progressive decline in cognitive function that affects memory, language, visuospatial skills, and executive function. It is often associated with behavioral changes such as apathy, depression, and psychosis. The most common cause of dementia is Alzheimer's disease, which is characterized by insidious onset and gradual progression of memory loss and cognitive decline.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: An 82-year-old woman comes to the physician because of difficulty sleeping and increasing fatigue. Over the past 3 months she has been waking up early and having trouble falling asleep at night. During this period, she has had a decreased appetite and a 3.2-kg (7-lb) weight loss. Since the death of her husband one year ago, she has been living with her son and his wife. She is worried and feels guilty because she does not want to impose on them. She has stopped going to meetings at the senior center because she does not enjoy them anymore and also because she feels uncomfortable asking her son to give her a ride, especially since her son has had a great deal of stress lately. She is 155 cm (5 ft 1 in) tall and weighs 51 kg (110 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, she is tired and has a flattened affect. Cognition is intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

answer_choices.B: Recommend relocation to a nursing home

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of early morning awakening, anhedonia, weight loss, fatigue, feelings of guilt, and decreased concentration are consistent with major depressive disorder (MDD). MDD is common in elderly patients and can be associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Elderly patients with depression have a higher rate of suicide compared with younger adults. Therefore, all patients diagnosed with MDD should be screened for suicide risk by directly asking about suicidal ideation, intent, and plan. This is especially important in elderly patients, who have the highest suicide completion rate of any age group.

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old woman presents to her primary care doctor with her son who reports that his mother is not acting like herself. She has gotten lost while driving several times in the past 2 months and appears to be talking to herself frequently. Of note, the patient’s husband died from a stroke 4 months ago. The patient reports feeling sad and guilty for causing so much trouble for her son. Her appetite has decreased since her husband died. On examination, she is oriented to person, place, and time. She is inattentive, and her speech is disorganized. She shakes her hand throughout the exam without realizing it. Her gait is slow and appears unstable. This patient’s condition would most likely benefit from which of the following medications?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of cognitive impairment, hallucinations, and motor symptoms (eg, tremor, bradykinesia, gait instability) are suggestive of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). DLB is the third most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer disease and vascular dementia. It is characterized by fluctuating cognitive impairment, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism. Patients with DLB may also have features of autonomic dysfunction (eg, orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence) and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (eg, dream enactment, talking/yelling during sleep).

The cognitive impairment in DLB is thought to be due to disruption of neurotransmission in multiple neuronal systems, including the cholinergic system. Cholinesterase inhibitors (eg, rivastigmine, donepezil) are considered first-line treatment for DLB as they can improve cognition and reduce hallucinations.

question:
A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents for the evaluation of fatigue for several weeks. The parents report that their son quit doing sports at school because of low energy. The patient's academic performance has declined recently. He spends most of his time in the basement playing video games and eating bowls of cereal. He has no history of serious illness. His mother has Hashimoto's thyroiditis and his father has major depressive disorder. The patient does not smoke or drink alcohol. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows conjunctival pallor, inflammation and fissuring of the corners of the mouth, and concavity of the finger nails. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in treatment?"

few_shot.question:
An 8-year-old male presents to his pediatrician for a follow-up appointment for persistent fatigue. His mother reports that the patient’s teacher called her yesterday to tell her that her son has been sitting out of recess every day for the past week. The patient first developed symptoms of fatigue and weakness several years ago and has returned to the physician with similar episodes once or twice a year. These episodes seem to sometimes be triggered by viral illnesses, but others have no identifiable trigger. The patient has been on daily folate supplementation with some improvement and requires red blood cell transfusions several times a year. He has an allergy to sulfa drugs, and last month he was treated with amoxicillin for an ear infection. His paternal grandfather was recently diagnosed with multiple myeloma, but his parents deny any other family history of hematologic conditions. Her temperature is 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 103/76 mmHg, pulse is 95/min, and respirations are 14/min. On physical exam, the patient is tired-appearing with conjunctival pallor. Laboratory tests performed during this visit reveal the following:

Leukocyte count: 9,7000/mm^3
Hemoglobin: 8.4 g/dL
Hematocrit: 27%
Mean corpuscular volume: 97 µm^3
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC): 40% Hb/cell
Platelet count: 338,000/mm^3
Reticulocyte index (RI): 4.2%


What is the next step in management?

answer_choices.D: Vaccinations followed by splenectomy and penicillin for one year

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic hemolytic anemia with intermittent episodes of severe anemia, triggered by infections or exposure to oxidative stress (eg, sulfa drugs), is suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis (HS). HS is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by a deficiency or dysfunction of the proteins that link the red blood cell (RBC) membrane skeleton to the lipid bilayer (eg, ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.2, spectrin). This leads to loss of membrane surface area and the formation of small, round RBCs (spherocytes) that are rigid and less able to traverse the spleen's sinusoids. As a result, these cells become trapped and destroyed, leading to extravascular hemolysis.

The diagnosis of HS is suggested by evidence of hemolysis (eg, anemia, reticulocytosis, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia) and the presence of spherocytes on a peripheral blood smear. The definitive diagnosis is established by an abnormal eosin-5'-maleimide binding test, which measures the decreased levels of membrane proteins.

The treatment of HS depends on the severity of the disease. Mild cases can be managed conservatively with folic acid supplementation. However, in moderate to severe cases, or in patients with frequent, severe crises, splenectomy is the treatment of choice. Splenectomy should be delayed until age >5 years, if possible, to decrease the risk of postsplenectomy sepsis. Vaccination against encapsulated organisms (eg, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis) should be given prior to surgery, and prophylactic penicillin should be administered for 1 year postsplenectomy.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of fatigue. She has not had any change in weight. She had infectious mononucleosis 4 weeks ago. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 days with moderate flow. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. Her mother has Hashimoto thyroiditis. Examination shows pale conjunctivae, inflammation of the corners of the mouth, and brittle nails. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 74 μm3
Platelet count 280,000/mm3
Leukocyte count 6,000/mm3
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating this patient's illness?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fatigue, pallor, angular cheilitis, and brittle nails are suggestive of iron deficiency anemia (IDA). IDA is the most common cause of anemia worldwide and is particularly common in women of childbearing age due to menstrual blood loss. Other risk factors include pregnancy, multiparity, and low socioeconomic status. The diagnosis of IDA is supported by the presence of microcytic anemia (mean corpuscular volume <80 μm3) on complete blood count. The next step in management is to confirm the diagnosis by checking serum ferritin levels. Ferritin is an intracellular protein that stores iron; serum levels are the most specific test for IDA. In the early stages of IDA, ferritin may be normal as it is an acute phase reactant and can be falsely elevated in the setting of inflammation or infection. However, ferritin usually falls once iron stores are depleted.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician for the evaluation of fatigue since he returned from visiting family in South Africa one week ago. The day after he returned, he had fever, chills, and diffuse joint pain for 3 days. His symptoms improved with acetaminophen. He was born at term and has been healthy. His immunizations are up-to-date. His temperature is 37.6°C (99.68°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Examination shows conjunctival pallor. Red cell distribution width 14% (N = 13%–15%)

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recent travel to Africa, fever, chills, and joint pain suggest a diagnosis of malaria. The peripheral smear shows erythrocytes with a darkly stained center and peripheral rim, separated by a pale ring, which is consistent with Plasmodium infection. Malaria can cause a normocytic anemia due to hemolysis of infected erythrocytes. However, this patient's microcytic anemia and elevated hemoglobin A2 level suggest a concurrent diagnosis of beta-thalassemia trait (ie, beta-thalassemia minor). Beta-thalassemia trait is a common, generally asymptomatic condition that is characterized by mild microcytic, hypochromic anemia with an elevated red cell distribution width and hemoglobin A2 level >3.5%. The anemia in beta-thalassemia trait is due to decreased production of the beta-globin chains of hemoglobin, leading to an imbalance in the ratio of alpha-globin to beta-globin chains. This imbalance results in precipitation of the excess alpha-globin chains, leading to premature destruction of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow and peripheral destruction of erythrocytes. No treatment is necessary for beta-thalassemia trait, and patients should be reassured that they will have a normal life expectancy.

question: A 48-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for sudden onset of difficulty breathing 6 hours ago. For the past several months, he has had shortness of breath on exertion and while lying down on the bed, frequent headaches, and swelling of his feet. He does not take any medications despite being diagnosed with hypertension 10 years ago. His pulse is 90/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 150/110 mm Hg, and temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). Physical examination shows an overweight male in acute distress with audible wheezes. Crackles are heard bilaterally and are loudest at the lung bases. Which of the following findings on cardiac auscultation will most likely be present in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 74-year-old man comes to the physician for a 6-month history of progressively worsening fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. He immigrated to the United States 35 years ago from India. His pulse is 89/min and blood pressure is 145/60 mm Hg. Crackles are heard at the lung bases. Cardiac examination shows a grade 3/6 early diastolic murmur loudest at the third left intercostal space. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's early diastolic murmur heard best at the left sternal border is consistent with aortic regurgitation (AR). AR can be caused by aortic root dilation (eg, hypertension, aortic dissection, syphilis, ankylosing spondylitis, Reiter syndrome) or valve leaflet abnormalities (eg, endocarditis, rheumatic heart disease, bicuspid aortic valve, myxomatous degeneration, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis). In developing countries, the most common cause of AR is rheumatic heart disease. However, in developed countries, the most common causes are aortic root dilation (eg, due to hypertension or age-related degeneration) and bicuspid aortic valve.

Patients with chronic severe AR may present with exertional dyspnea and fatigue due to left ventricular volume overload. On physical examination, the high stroke volume results in a wide pulse pressure (systolic blood pressure - diastolic blood pressure), manifesting as a water hammer (Corrigan) pulse, characterized by a rapid upstroke and subsequent collapse.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old man presents to the emergency department with progressive dyspnea for the last 3 weeks. He complains of shortness of breath while lying flat and reports nighttime awakenings due to shortness of breath for the same duration. The patient has been a smoker for the last 30 years. Past medical history is significant for myocardial infarction 7 months ago. Current medications include metoprolol, aspirin, and rosuvastatin, but the patient is noncompliant with his medications. His temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), the blood pressure is 150/115 mm Hg, the pulse is 110/min, and the respiratory rate is 24/min. Oxygen saturation on room air is 88%. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral crackles and an S3 gallop. On physical examination, the cardiac apex is palpated in left 6th intercostal space. Bilateral pitting edema is present, and the patient is in moderate distress. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of the patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and bilateral crackles on lung auscultation is consistent with acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF). ADHF is a common and potentially serious cause of acute respiratory distress. The condition is characterized by the sudden or gradual onset of heart failure symptoms, which typically include dyspnea at rest or with exertion, orthopnea, and lower extremity edema. Physical examination may reveal pulmonary rales, an S3 gallop, and elevated jugular venous pressure. The most common precipitating factors for ADHF include ischemia, uncontrolled hypertension, medication noncompliance, and arrhythmias.

The initial management of ADHF involves measures to relieve congestion (preload reduction) and improve cardiac output. Intravenous loop diuretics (eg, furosemide) are the most effective agents for preload reduction and are typically the first-line treatment for patients with volume overload. Diuretics decrease blood volume, reducing ventricular filling pressures and alleviating pulmonary and systemic congestion.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician for shortness of breath and chest discomfort that is becoming progressively worse. He has had increasing problems exerting himself for the past 5 years. He is now unable to walk more than 50 m on level terrain without stopping and mostly rests at home. He has smoked 1–2 packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. He appears distressed. His pulse is 85/min, blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, and respirations are 25/min. Physical examination shows a plethoric face and distended jugular veins. Bilateral wheezing is heard on auscultation of the lungs. There is yellow discoloration of the fingers on the right hand and 2+ lower extremity edema. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of heavy smoking, progressive exertional dyspnea, and wheezing is suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is characterized by chronic bronchitis (ie, cough and sputum production) and/or emphysema (ie, destruction of alveolar walls). Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as a cough with sputum production for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years. Emphysema is defined pathologically as abnormal, permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis. The most common cause of COPD is smoking.

Patients with severe COPD can develop pulmonary hypertension due to hypoxic vasoconstriction, destruction of the pulmonary vascular bed, and hyperinflation of the lungs with compression of the pulmonary vasculature. Pulmonary hypertension can lead to cor pulmonale (right ventricular hypertrophy and eventual failure due to pulmonary disease). Signs of cor pulmonale include exertional dyspnea, signs of right heart failure (eg, jugular venous distension, lower extremity edema), and loud P2 on cardiac examination.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old man presents with breathlessness for the past 3 months. His symptoms have been getting progressively worse during this time. He denies any history of cough, fever, or chest pain. He works at a local shipyard and is responsible for installing the plumbing aboard the vessels. His past medical history is significant for hypertension for which he takes metoprolol every day. He denies smoking and any illicit drug use. His pulse is 74/min, respiratory rate is 14/min, blood pressure is 130/76 mm Hg, and temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F). Physical examination is significant for fine bibasilar crackles at the end of inspiration without digital clubbing. Which of the following additional findings would most likely be present in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Decreased diffusion lung capacity of CO

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of working in a shipyard and his symptoms of progressive dyspnea and bibasilar inspiratory crackles are suggestive of asbestosis. Asbestosis is a form of pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of asbestos fibers. The fibers penetrate the distal airways and alveoli, and are then engulfed by macrophages. This leads to the release of fibrogenic cytokines and the development of diffuse pulmonary fibrosis. The fibrosis can cause a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function tests, with a decreased total lung capacity, functional residual capacity, and residual volume. The fibrosis can also impair gas exchange, leading to a decreased diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO).

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 66-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of shortness of breath. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F) and pulse is 105/min. When the blood pressure cuff is inflated to 140 mm Hg, the patient's pulse is audible and regular. However, upon inspiration, the pulse disappears and does not reappear until expiration. Only when the blood pressure cuff is inflated to 125 mm Hg is the pulse audible throughout the entire respiratory cycle. Which of the following underlying conditions is most likely responsible for this patient's physical examination findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's physical examination findings are consistent with pulsus paradoxus, which is an exaggeration (>10 mm Hg) of the normal inspiratory decrease in systemic blood pressure. Pulsus paradoxus is not related to the pulse rate or rhythm; rather, it is due to changes in intrathoracic pressure that are transmitted to the systemic arterial tree. It is most commonly associated with conditions that involve marked changes in intrathoracic pressure (eg, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) or that impede diastolic filling (eg, cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis). In this patient, the most likely cause of his pulsus paradoxus is asthma.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A young infant is brought to an immunologist because of recurrent infections, which have not resolved despite appropriate medical treatment. On reviewing her medical history, the immunologist notes that the child has had frequent disseminated mycobacterial infections. He suspects a possible immunodeficiency. What is the most likely cause of this patient's immunodeficiency?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's recurrent mycobacterial infections suggest a defect in interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) signaling. IFN-γ is a cytokine that is produced by natural killer (NK) cells and T cells. It plays a critical role in the immune response against intracellular pathogens, such as mycobacteria, by activating macrophages to kill phagocytosed organisms. Defects in IFN-γ signaling can be due to mutations in the genes encoding IFN-γ or its receptor, leading to impaired macrophage activation and recurrent infections with intracellular pathogens.

few_shot.question: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for a 6-week history of fatigue, fever, and recurrent epistaxis. She has a history of duodenal atresia and an atrioventricular septal defect. She is at the 5th percentile for height and 30th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Her hands are short and broad and there is a space between the first and second toes bilaterally. The spleen tip is palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin. Bone marrow aspirate shows leukocytosis with 50% lymphoblasts. Which of the following best explains this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of duodenal atresia, atrioventricular septal defect, short stature, and characteristic physical findings (broad hands, gap between first and second toes) suggest Down syndrome (trisomy 21). The most common cause of Down syndrome is meiotic nondisjunction, which results in an extra copy of chromosome 21. This usually occurs during maternal meiosis I and is associated with advanced maternal age.

Children with Down syndrome are at increased risk for developing acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This patient's fatigue, fever, recurrent epistaxis, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, along with the finding of lymphoblasts on bone marrow aspirate, are consistent with a diagnosis of ALL.

few_shot.question: A 6-month-old girl presents with recurring skin infections. Past medical history is significant for 3 episodes of acute otitis media since birth. The patient was born at 39 weeks via an uncomplicated, spontaneous transvaginal delivery, but there was delayed umbilical cord separation. She has met all developmental milestones. On physical examination, the skin around her mouth is inflamed and red. Which of the following is most likely responsible for this child’s clinical presentation?

answer_choices.C: Absence of CD18 molecule on the surface of leukocytes

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of delayed umbilical cord separation and recurrent skin and ear infections is suggestive of leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD). LAD is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by recurrent bacterial and fungal infections and impaired wound healing. It is caused by a defect in the CD18 molecule, a beta-integrin protein found on the surface of leukocytes. This molecule is necessary for the formation of integrins, which are essential for leukocyte adhesion and migration. Without integrins, leukocytes are unable to adhere to the vascular endothelium and are therefore unable to migrate to sites of infection or inflammation.

few_shot.question: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever, fast breathing, and difficulty feeding for 2 days. His mother reports that he has had recurrent pneumonia and has been hospitalized for severe dehydration secondary to acute gastroenteritis caused by rotavirus infection three times in the past 4 months. He is at the 3rd percentile for both height and weight. Examination shows a generalized, erythematous, scaly rash and white patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa that bleed when scraped. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates and an absent thymic shadow. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent infections, failure to thrive, and dermatitis is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). SCID is a group of disorders characterized by defects in both T- and B-cell immunity. The most common form of SCID is X-linked SCID, which is due to a mutation in the gene for the IL-2 receptor gamma chain. This chain is shared by several other interleukin receptors (eg, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21), and its absence leads to a severe impairment in both cellular and humoral immunity. 

Affected infants typically present in the first few months of life with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, and severe, recurrent infections with a variety of pathogens, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, and opportunistic organisms. The most common viral infections are caused by respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza, and rotavirus. The most common fungal infections are due to Candida species, which can cause oral thrush, as seen in this patient. 

The diagnosis of SCID is suggested by lymphopenia, markedly reduced T-cell receptor excision circles, and absence of the thymic shadow on chest x-ray.

few_shot.question: A 1-year-old girl is brought to the physician for follow-up examination 1 week after admission to the hospital for bacterial pneumonia. few_shot.question: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with anxiety and trouble swallowing. Zenker diverticulum is a false diverticulum that occurs in the posterior hypopharynx, just above the upper esophageal sphincter. It is caused by dysfunction of the cricopharyngeus muscle, which leads to increased intraluminal pressure and subsequent herniation of the mucosa and submucosa through the Killian triangle, an area of muscular weakness between the cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus muscles. The diverticulum can fill with food and secretions, which may be regurgitated. The diverticulum can also become large enough to be palpated as a neck mass.

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man is referred to a gastroenterologist because of difficulty swallowing for the past 5 months.
