answer_choices.B: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's dysphagia to both solids and liquids, history of immigration from South America, and barium swallow study showing a dilated esophagus with an area of distal stenosis ("bird's beak" sign) are suggestive of achalasia. Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the loss of esophageal peristalsis and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). It is most commonly idiopathic but can also be caused by Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis), a parasitic infection endemic to Central and South America. Chagas disease is caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, which is transmitted through the feces of the reduviid (kissing) bug. The disease can manifest either as an acute illness with fever and malaise or as a chronic illness with cardiac and/or gastrointestinal involvement. In the esophagus, T cruzi infection can cause inflammation and destruction of the myenteric plexus, leading to loss of peristalsis and LES dysfunction.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [C] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 48-year-old man from Argentina presents to your office complaining of difficulty swallowing for the past few months. He is accompanied by his wife who adds that his breath has started to smell horrible. The patient says that he feels uncomfortable no matter what he eats or drinks. He also has lost 5 kg (11 lb) in the last 2 months. The patient is afebrile, and his vital signs are within normal limits. Physical exam is unremarkable. A barium swallow study along with esophageal manometry is performed and the results are shown in the image below. Manometry shows very high pressure at the lower esophageal sphincter. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's dysphagia, weight loss, and halitosis are suggestive of achalasia, a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the loss of peristalsis in the distal two-thirds of the esophagus (caused by loss of the myenteric plexus) and failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). The barium swallow study shows the classic "bird's beak" appearance of the esophagus seen in achalasia. The most common cause of achalasia is idiopathic, but it can also be caused by Chagas disease, a condition caused by infection with Trypanosoma cruzi. This is suggested by the patient's country of origin (Argentina), as Chagas disease is endemic in Central and South America.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old African American male presents to his primary care physician complaining of difficulty swallowing that was initially limited to solids but has now progressed to liquids. Biopsy of the esophagus reveals dysplastic cells, but does not show evidence of glands or increased mucin. Which of the following patient behaviors most contributed to his condition?

answer_choices.D: Radiation exposure in the past 6 months

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's dysphagia and biopsy findings are suggestive of squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus. Risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus include smoking, alcohol use, and certain dietary factors (eg, consumption of hot beverages, low fruit and vegetable intake). In contrast, adenocarcinoma of the esophagus is associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease, obesity, and Barrett esophagus.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

question: A 27-year-old female presents to her physician with a palpable thyroid nodule. Iodine uptake testing shows that the nodule has decreased iodine uptake compared with the rest of the thyroid gland. A fine-needle aspiration is performed and the physician calls telling the patient that she has a neoplasm of the thyroid. Which of the following diagnoses is the most likely?

few_shot.question: A 43-year-old female presents to her primary care physician complaining of a gradually enlarging neck mass. She reports that she first developed a firm nodular midline mass on the anterior aspect of her neck two months ago. She is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. A fine-needle aspiration is performed and a histological sample of the specimen is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The histological sample shows a papillary structure with a fibrovascular core and nuclear changes such as nuclear clearing, grooves, and pseudoinclusions. These findings are characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), the most common type of thyroid cancer. PTC often presents as a painless, firm, solitary thyroid nodule. It is more common in women and in individuals with a history of head or neck irradiation. PTC generally has a good prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate of over 90%.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 45-year old man comes to the physician because of a painless neck lump and a 2-month history of difficulty swallowing. He has a history of recurrent nephrolithiasis and episodic hypertension. Physical examination shows a 3 × 3-cm, nontender nodule at the level of the thyroid cartilage. A photomicrograph of a section of tissue obtained by core needle biopsy of the nodule is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The biopsy shows nests of cells in an amyloid stroma, which is characteristic of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). MTC arises from the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, which produce calcitonin. Calcitonin released by the tumor often leads to hypocalcemia, but this is usually asymptomatic as PTH can compensate. However, the increased calcitonin can lead to increased calcium phosphate product, leading to recurrent nephrolithiasis as seen in this patient.

MTC can occur sporadically or in a hereditary pattern as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2). Given this patient's episodic hypertension, he likely has MEN 2, which is associated with pheochromocytoma (causing episodic hypertension), MTC, and hyperparathyroidism.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 75-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of involuntary weight loss and a painless lump on her neck. Physical examination shows a firm, irregular swelling on the right side of the neck. Ultrasonography of the thyroid gland shows a 2-cm nodule with irregular margins and microcalcifications in the right thyroid lobe. A biopsy of the thyroid nodule is performed. Which of the following changes would be most consistent with anaplasia?

answer_choices.A: Negative staining of tumor cells for thyroglobulin
answer_choices.B: Reduced number of functional thyroid cells
answer_choices.C: Disorganized proliferation of mature thyroid cells
answer_choices.D: Increased expression of thyroid transcription factor-1

few_shot.explanation:
Anaplasia refers to the loss of cellular differentiation and orientation that is characteristic of malignancy. Anaplastic cells often have a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, pleomorphic nuclei, and numerous mitotic figures. They also lose the ability to perform their normal specialized functions. In the case of thyroid cells, this would mean that they lose the ability to produce thyroglobulin, which is necessary for the production of thyroid hormone. Therefore, the most likely finding in this case would be negative staining of tumor cells for thyroglobulin.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man presents with a mass on his neck. He says that he first noticed the mass a few weeks ago while taking a shower. Since then, the mass has not increased in size. He denies any pain or difficulty in swallowing. Past medical history is unremarkable. Family history is significant for his father who had his thyroid removed when he was around his age but doesn’t know why. Review of systems is significant for occasional episodes of anxiety that include a pounding headache, racing heart, and sweating. His vital signs include: pulse 88/min, blood pressure 133/87 mm Hg, temperature 37.2°C (99.0°F), and respiratory rate 14/min. He is 183 cm (6 ft 2 in) tall with long extremities. On physical examination, the patient appears cachectic. There is a palpable 4 cm x 4 cm nodule present on the left lobe of the thyroid. Which of the following is the most likely thyroid pathology in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is suggestive of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B). MEN 2B is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytoma, and mucosal neuromas. MTC is a tumor of the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, which secrete calcitonin. It is the most common cause of death in MEN 2B and often presents as a thyroid nodule or mass. Pheochromocytoma can cause episodic hypertension and symptoms such as headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. Mucosal neuromas can cause a characteristic physical appearance, including thickened lips and bumpy tongue. Other features of MEN 2B include a marfanoid habitus (as seen in this patient) and intestinal ganglioneuromas, which can lead to constipation or diarrhea.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [B] > [C] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old woman residing at an iodine-deficient endemic area presents to the physician with a painless and gradually progressive anterior neck mass. She has occasional dysphagia, but has no history of prior head and neck irradiation. The examination shows a mass that moves with deglutition, suggesting a thyroid mass. An ultrasound of the neck reveals a 3 cm x 3 cm (1.2 in x 1.2 in) mass in the right thyroid lobe with punctate microcalcifications, hypoechogenicity, irregular margins, and enhanced vascularity. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Her serum TSH is 3.3 mU/L, serum T3 is 2.2 nmol/L, and serum T4 is 111 nmol/L. An FNAC of the nodule shows abundant follicular cells suspicious of follicular neoplasm. A right lobectomy with isthmectomy is performed. Which of the following histopathological finding is diagnostic?

answer_choices.B: Well-differentiated follicular cells without vascular invasion
answer_choices.C: Follicular cells that lack nuclear atypia, with capsular and vascular invasion

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's ultrasound findings (punctate microcalcifications, hypoechogenicity, irregular margins, and enhanced vascularity) are suspicious for malignancy. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is the most accurate test for evaluating thyroid nodules, but it cannot distinguish between follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma because both have similar cytologic features. Therefore, a diagnostic lobectomy is performed when FNAC shows features of follicular neoplasm. The presence of capsular and/or vascular invasion on histopathology is diagnostic of follicular carcinoma. 

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

question: A 43-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her brother for severe chest pain. The patient recently lost her husband in a car accident and is still extremely shocked by the event. On physical examination, her blood pressure is 105/67 mm Hg, the heart rate is 96/min and regular, breathing rate is 23/min, and the pulse oximetry is 96%. An S3 heart sound and rales in the lower right and left lung lobes are heard. A 12-lead ECG shows no significant findings. Echocardiography shows an enlarged left ventricle and left atrium. The patient is stabilized and informed about the diagnosis and possible treatment options. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 2 episodes of loss of consciousness over the past week. She recovered immediately and was not confused following the episodes. During the past 5 months, she has also had increased shortness of breath and palpitations. She has been unable to carry out her daily activities. She also reports some chest tightness that resolves with rest. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She immigrated with her family from India 10 years ago. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 115/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention and pitting edema below the knees. Bilateral crackles are heard at the lung bases. Cardiac examination shows an accentuated and split S2. There is an opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic murmur in the fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation and right axis deviation. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of these findings?

answer_choices.A: Increased left ventricular end diastolic pressure

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and lower extremity edema is suggestive of congestive heart failure. The presence of an opening snap and diastolic murmur at the apex suggests mitral stenosis (MS), most likely due to rheumatic heart disease, which is common in developing countries. In MS, the mitral valve orifice is narrowed, impeding blood flow from the left atrium (LA) to the left ventricle (LV) during diastole. This leads to elevated LA pressures, particularly during exercise when the heart rate increases and the diastolic filling period shortens. The elevated LA pressure is transmitted to the pulmonary vasculature, causing pulmonary congestion and resultant dyspnea, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Atrial fibrillation, the most common arrhythmia in patients with MS, can develop due to chronic LA enlargement. This can lead to decreased cardiac output and/or tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy, both of which can cause or exacerbate heart failure symptoms. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [C] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 54-year-old woman presents to the emergency ward with a chief complaint of chest pain. The pain is sharp and present in the anterior part of the chest. There is no radiation of the pain; however, the intensity is decreased while sitting and leaning forward. There is no associated shortness of breath. Vital signs are the following: blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg; pulse rate is 82/min, rhythmic, and regular. Lungs are clear on auscultation and cardiovascular examination demonstrates scratchy and squeaking sounds at the left sternal border and a 'knock' heard on auscultation. Kussmaul sign is positive and ECG shows new widespread ST segment elevation and PR depression in leads II, III and aVF. The most likely cause for these findings in this patient is?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of chest pain that is relieved by sitting up and leaning forward, a pericardial friction rub, and diffuse ST-segment elevations on ECG is suggestive of acute pericarditis. The most common cause of acute pericarditis is idiopathic, but it can also be due to infections (eg, viral), systemic inflammatory conditions (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus), malignancy, uremia, or following myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery (Dressler syndrome).

The presence of a pericardial knock on examination and Kussmaul sign (ie, increase in jugular venous pressure during inspiration) suggest that this patient has developed constrictive pericarditis, a serious potential complication of acute pericarditis. Constrictive pericarditis occurs when the pericardium becomes thickened, fibrotic, and adherent to the heart, which restricts diastolic filling. The pericardial knock is an early diastolic sound that occurs slightly earlier than the third heart sound. It is due to the sudden cessation of ventricular filling in early to mid-diastole as a result of the noncompliant pericardium.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [C] > [D] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 49-year-old woman is brought in to the emergency department by ambulance after developing crushing chest pain and palpitations. Past medical history is significant for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity. She takes chlorthalidone, lisinopril, atorvastatin, metformin, and an oral contraceptive every day. She works as a lawyer and her job is stressful. She drinks wine with dinner every night and smokes 10 cigarettes a day. Emergency personnel stabilized her and administered oxygen while on the way to the hospital. Upon arrival, the vital signs include: blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, heart rate 120/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and temperature 37.7°C (99.9°F). On physical exam, she is an obese woman in acute distress. She is diaphoretic and has difficulty catching her breath. A bedside electrocardiogram (ECG) is performed which reveals ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The ECG findings of ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF are indicative of an inferior wall myocardial infarction (MI). The inferior wall of the heart is typically supplied by the right coronary artery (RCA) in 85% of individuals, and the left circumflex artery in the remaining 15%. The RCA also supplies the right ventricle in most individuals, and therefore, right ventricular infarction often accompanies inferior wall MI. 

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [D] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 75-year-old woman presents to the emergency department because of a brief loss of consciousness, slurred speech, and facial numbness. Family members report that she complained about feeling chest pain and shortness of breath while on her morning walk. Medical history is noncontributory. Physical examination shows decreased pupil reactivity to light and hemiplegic gait. Her pulse is 120/min, respirations are 26/min, temperature is 36.7°C (98.0°F), and blood pressure is 160/80 mm Hg. On heart auscultation, S1 is loud, widely split, and there is a diastolic murmur. Transthoracic echocardiography in a 4-chamber apical view revealed a large oval-shaped and sessile left atrial mass. Which of the following is the most likely complication of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of chest pain, shortness of breath, and neurologic symptoms (eg, loss of consciousness, slurred speech, facial numbness) is concerning for a cardioembolic stroke. The most common source of cardioembolic stroke is atrial fibrillation; however, this patient's echocardiogram shows a left atrial mass, which is concerning for a myxoma. Atrial myxomas are the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults. They are typically located in the left atrium and are attached to the interatrial septum by a stalk. Symptoms can be due to obstruction of blood flow across the mitral valve (eg, exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, pulmonary edema, sudden death), embolization of tumor fragments (eg, stroke), or constitutional symptoms (eg, fever, weight loss) caused by interleukin-6 production by the tumor. On physical examination, myxomas can cause a tumor "plop" early in diastole, which can be mistaken for the opening snap of mitral stenosis. 

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for crushing substernal chest pain at rest for the past 2 hours. The pain began gradually while he was having an argument with his wife and is now severe. He does not take any medications. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years. He is diaphoretic. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 21/min, and blood pressure is 115/65 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Cardiac examination shows an S4 gallop. The lungs are clear to auscultation. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

answer_choices.A: Occlusion of the left anterior descending artery
answer_choices.B: Thromboembolism to the right interlobar pulmonary artery
answer_choices.C: Occlusion of the left circumflex artery
answer_choices.D: Tear in the intimal lining of the aorta

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe, crushing substernal chest pain at rest, diaphoresis, and an S4 gallop is consistent with acute myocardial infarction (MI). The ECG shows ST-segment elevations in leads V1-V4, which are indicative of an anterior wall MI. The most common cause of MI is rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with subsequent thrombus formation, leading to occlusion of a coronary artery. The left anterior descending (LAD) artery is the most commonly occluded vessel in MI and supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, and the apex of the heart. Occlusion of the LAD artery can lead to an anterior wall MI, which would present with ST-segment elevations in the precordial leads V1-V4.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [C] > [B] > [D].

question: A 54-year-old male makes an appointment with his primary care physician due to chronic fatigue that has left him unable to hike or do other physically demanding activities with his friends. He has well-controlled hypertension and diabetes but has otherwise been healthy. He does not smoke but drinks socially with his friends. Physical exam reveals enlarged nodules that are not tender to palpation. A biopsy is obtained showing a characteristic change in chromosome 18. The regulation of which of the following proteins will be most abnormal in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old male presents to his primary care physician for a regularly scheduled check-up. Physical examination reveals nontender cervical lymphadenopathy. A biopsy of the lymph node reveals aggregates of follicular architecture, and cytogenic analysis shows a t(14;18) translocation. The protein most likely responsible for the patient’s condition does which of the following:

answer_choices.A: Regulates passage through the cell cycle
answer_choices.D: Regulates cell growth through signal transduction

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's presentation is consistent with follicular lymphoma, a non-Hodgkin lymphoma that is characterized by painless lymphadenopathy and a "waxing and waning" course. Follicular lymphoma is associated with the t(14;18) translocation, which results in overexpression of the BCL2 gene. BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that prevents the release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria, thereby inhibiting apoptosis. Overexpression of BCL2 leads to prolonged cell survival and an accumulation of neoplastic cells, which is a key feature of follicular lymphoma.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of blood in the urine and fatigue. He also has had a 5.0-kg (11-lb) weight loss during the past month. Physical examination shows pallor and cachexia. A nontender right flank mass is palpated. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows a 5-cm right upper pole renal mass and several pulmonary lesions. A biopsy specimen of an affected area of the lung is obtained. A photomicrograph of the biopsy specimen is shown. Molecular evaluation of the specimen is most likely to show which of the following genetic changes?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's presentation of hematuria, flank mass, and pulmonary lesions is suggestive of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with metastasis to the lungs. The photomicrograph shows clear cells, which is characteristic of clear cell RCC, the most common type of RCC. Clear cell RCC is associated with von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by the development of various benign and malignant tumors. In VHL disease, there is a deletion of the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3. The VHL protein is involved in the degradation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), a transcription factor that induces the expression of various genes involved in cell proliferation and angiogenesis (eg, vascular endothelial growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor). Loss of the VHL protein leads to accumulation of HIF and overexpression of these genes, promoting tumorigenesis.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of a painless lump on her neck. Examination shows a hard nodule on the left side of her neck. A fine-needle aspiration biopsy shows well-differentiated cuboidal cells arranged spherically around colloid. She undergoes thyroidectomy. Histopathological examination of the surgical specimen shows invasion of the thyroid capsule and blood vessels. Which of the following cellular events is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?

answer_choices.A: Activation mutation in the BRAF gene

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's thyroid nodule, which is hard and has evidence of capsular and vascular invasion, is concerning for malignancy. The presence of well-differentiated cuboidal cells arranged spherically around colloid is characteristic of follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC). FTC is the second most common type of thyroid cancer and is more common in women and in areas of iodine deficiency. FTC is unique among thyroid carcinomas in that hematogenous spread is more common than lymphatic spread, with the lung and bone being the most common sites of distant metastases.

The most common genetic alteration found in FTC is a PAX8-PPAR gamma rearrangement, which is a result of a chromosomal translocation. This rearrangement is found in about one-third of FTCs and leads to the formation of a fusion protein that acts as an overactive transcription factor, promoting cell growth.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressive fatigue and dyspnea on exertion for 3 months. During this time, he has also had increased straining during defecation and a 10-kg (22-lb) weight loss. He has no personal or family history of serious medical illness. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor. Laboratory studies show microcytic anemia. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Colonoscopy shows an exophytic mass in the ascending colon. Pathologic examination of the mass shows a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma. A gain-of-function mutation in which of the following genes is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, and conjunctival pallor is consistent with anemia, likely due to chronic gastrointestinal bleeding from colorectal cancer (CRC). The most common cause of CRC is sporadic adenocarcinoma, which accounts for approximately 70% of cases. Sporadic CRC typically arises from tubular adenomas via the adenoma-carcinoma sequence. This sequence is characterized by the stepwise accumulation of genetic mutations, including:

1. APC gene mutation: This is an early and initiating event in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence. APC is a tumor suppressor gene that inhibits the Wnt signaling pathway. Loss-of-function mutations in APC lead to increased cellular proliferation and the formation of a small adenomatous polyp (<5 mm).

2. KRAS gene mutation: This is an oncogene that encodes a G protein involved in intracellular signaling. Gain-of-function mutations in KRAS lead to unregulated cellular proliferation and the progression of a small adenomatous polyp to a larger adenoma.

3. TP53 and/or DCC gene mutation: These are late events in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence. TP53 is a tumor suppressor gene that regulates the cell cycle and induces apoptosis. DCC is a tumor suppressor gene that inhibits cellular proliferation. Loss-of-function mutations in TP53 and/or DCC lead to progression of a large adenoma to carcinoma.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [C] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive fatigue and abdominal pain. Physical examination shows pale mucous membranes and splenomegaly. Hemoglobin concentration is 9.1 g/dL and leukocyte count is 3,400/mm3. Peripheral blood smear shows nucleated red blood cells and teardrop poikilocytosis. A Janus kinase 2 gene mutation is present. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigue, pallor, and splenomegaly, along with the presence of nucleated red blood cells and teardrop cells on peripheral smear, is suggestive of a myeloproliferative disorder. The presence of a Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) gene mutation further supports this diagnosis. JAK2 is a tyrosine kinase that mediates cell growth, differentiation, and survival via downstream signaling pathways. Mutations in JAK2 are present in the majority of patients with polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis.

Primary myelofibrosis is a clonal stem cell disorder characterized by splenomegaly, extramedullary hematopoiesis, and bone marrow fibrosis. The bone marrow fibrosis is due to the proliferation of nonclonal fibroblasts in response to increased levels of inflammatory cytokines (eg, platelet-derived growth factor, transforming growth factor-β) released by the clonal myeloid cells. This results in extensive collagen deposition and osteosclerosis in the bone marrow, leading to ineffective hematopoiesis. The nucleated red blood cells and teardrop cells seen on the peripheral smear are a result of extramedullary hematopoiesis, which occurs primarily in the spleen and liver.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [C] > [D] > [A].

question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. Over the past 8 months, his mother reports difficulty understanding the boy's speech. On occasion during this period, she has noticed that he does not respond when called by name and cannot follow 1-step instructions. He has a history of recurrent ear infections treated with antibiotics since birth. He is at the 60th percentile for length and 50th percentile for weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. His speech is quiet and difficult to understand. Otoscopic examination shows retracted tympanic membranes bilaterally that are immobile on pneumatic otoscopy. Nasopharyngoscopy shows mild adenoid hypertrophy. Pure tone audiometry shows a conductive hearing loss of 26 dB on the right side and 28 dB on the left side. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to a pediatrician with a history of repeated episodes of right-ear symptoms, including irritability, fever, ear pain, and pulling at the ear, for the last 2 years. Each episode has been treated with an appropriate antibiotic for the recommended duration of time as prescribed by the pediatrician. The boy had experienced 3 episodes during his 3rd year of life and 5 episodes during the last year; the last episode occurred 2 months ago. There is no history of recurrent rhinosinusitis or nasal obstruction. On physical examination, vital signs are stable. Otoscopic examination of the right ear reveals a white tympanic membrane with decreased mobility. There is no erythema or bulging of the tympanic membrane. Which of the following interventions is most likely to be considered for further management of this child?

answer_choices.A: Antibiotic prophylaxis with subtherapeutic dose of sulfonamide
answer_choices.C: Myringotomy without insertion of a tympanostomy tube
answer_choices.D: Myringotomy with insertion of a tympanostomy tube

few_shot.explanation:
This child has a history of recurrent acute otitis media (AOM) and otitis media with effusion (OME). AOM is characterized by the rapid onset of symptoms such as otalgia, fever, and irritability, along with signs of middle ear inflammation and effusion (MEE) on otoscopy. OME is characterized by the presence of MEE without signs or symptoms of acute inflammation. The MEE in OME is often an effusion that persists for weeks to months following an episode of AOM. The effusion can cause hearing loss in the affected ear(s), which can lead to delays in speech and language development.

The American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians recommend tympanostomy tube insertion for children with recurrent AOM who have unilateral or bilateral OME at the time of assessment for tube candidacy. Recurrent AOM is defined as 3 episodes in 6 months or 4 episodes in 1 year with 1 episode in the preceding 6 months. The child in this vignette meets these criteria.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of fever and left ear pain for the past 3 days. He has a history of atopic dermatitis, and his mother is concerned that his symptoms may be caused by him itching at night. She says that he has not been having many flare-ups lately; the latest flare-up subsided in time for his second birthday party, which he celebrated at a swimming pool 1 week ago. Six months ago, he had an episode of urticaria following antibiotic treatment for pharyngitis. He takes no medications. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 25/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Otoscopy shows an opaque, bulging tympanic membrane. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, otalgia, and bulging tympanic membrane are consistent with acute otitis media (AOM). AOM is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. The patient's recent swimming pool exposure may have predisposed him to AOM by allowing water to enter the middle ear through the eustachian tube, creating a moist environment conducive to bacterial growth. 

First-line treatment for AOM is high-dose amoxicillin. However, this patient has a history of urticaria following antibiotic treatment, which is concerning for a type I hypersensitivity reaction. In patients with a history of type I hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin antibiotics, azithromycin is an appropriate alternative.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Coalescent mastoiditis occurs when infection spreads from the middle ear to the mastoid air cells, causing destruction of the bony septa. This condition is most common in children <2 years of age and typically follows a recent episode of AOM. The diagnosis is clinical, but a CT scan of the temporal bone is often performed to confirm the diagnosis and to evaluate for other complications (eg, subperiosteal abscess, venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess). Treatment involves parenteral antibiotics and often myringotomy with or without tympanostomy tube placement. Mastoidectomy is reserved for patients who do not respond to these measures.

few_shot.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever, fatigue, and productive cough for 2 days. He had similar symptoms 6 months ago, when he was diagnosed with pneumonia. Three weeks ago, he was diagnosed with otitis media for the sixth time since his birth and was treated with amoxicillin. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 84/40 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. Examination shows purulent discharge in the left ear canal and hypoplastic tonsils without exudate. Coarse crackles are heard over the right lung field on auscultation. An x-ray of the chest shows a right middle lobe consolidation. Flow cytometry shows absent B cells and normal T cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.C: Recombinant human granulocyte-colony stimulating factor administration

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent bacterial infections (eg, pneumonia, otitis media) and absent B cells on flow cytometry is suggestive of X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia. This condition is characterized by low levels of all immunoglobulin isotypes due to a mutation in the Bruton tyrosine kinase gene. This gene is necessary for B-cell maturation, and a mutation leads to an arrest in development at the pre-B-cell stage in the bone marrow. As a result, the number of mature B cells and plasma cells is markedly decreased, leading to a decrease in immunoglobulin production. Patients typically present with recurrent bacterial infections after 6 months of age, when the maternal IgG antibodies wane. The most common pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Staphylococcus aureus. The treatment of choice is regular administration of intravenous immunoglobulin to provide passive immunity.

So, the answer is [B].

question:
A 70-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department for the evaluation of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting for 1 day. Computed tomography shows a small bowel perforation. The patient is prepared for emergent exploratory laparotomy. She is sedated with midazolam, induced with propofol, intubated, and maintained on nitrous oxide and isoflurane for the duration of the surgery. A single perforation in the terminal ileum is diagnosed intraoperatively and successfully repaired. The patient is transferred to the intensive care unit. The ventilator is set at an FiO2 of 50%, tidal volume of 1000 mL, respiratory rate of 12/min, and positive end-expiratory pressure of 2.5 cm H2O. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 111/50 mm Hg. She is responsive to painful stimuli. Lung examination shows bilateral rales. Abdominal examination shows a distended abdomen and intact abdominal surgical incisions. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Arterial blood gas analysis shows:
pH 7.44
pO2 54 mm Hg
pCO2 31 mm Hg
HCO3- 22 mm Hg
Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient?"

few_shot.question:
A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department, 30 minutes after being involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He is obtunded on arrival. He is intubated and mechanical ventilation is begun. The ventilator is set at a FiO2 of 60%, tidal volume of 440 mL, and positive end-expiratory pressure of 4 cm H2O. On the third day of intubation, his temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 91/min, and blood pressure is 103/60 mm Hg. There are decreased breath sounds over the left lung base. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is soft and not distended. Arterial blood gas analysis shows:
pH 7.49
pCO2 29 mm Hg
pO2 73 mm Hg
HCO3- 20 mEq/L
O2 saturation 89%
Monitoring shows a sudden increase in the plateau airway pressure. An x-ray of the chest shows deepening of the costophrenic angle on the left side. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's acute respiratory distress, decreased breath sounds, and chest x-ray findings are consistent with a pneumothorax. The most likely cause is barotrauma from mechanical ventilation. Barotrauma is a well-known complication of mechanical ventilation and can manifest as pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, or pneumatocele. It is caused by alveolar rupture due to high airway pressures, leading to dissection of air along bronchovascular sheaths and subsequent rupture into the pleural space or mediastinum. The risk of barotrauma is increased by high tidal volumes, high peak airway pressures, and preexisting lung disease.

The most appropriate next step in management is insertion of a chest tube to evacuate the air and re-expand the lung.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 76-year-old female is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive in her room at her nursing facility. Past medical history is significant for Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, and diabetes. Surgical history is notable for an open cholecystectomy at age 38 and multiple cesarean sections. On arrival, she is non-responsive but breathing by herself, and her vital signs are T 102.9 F, HR 123 bpm, BP 95/64, RR 26/min, and SaO2 97% on 6L nasal cannula. On physical exam the patient has marked abdominal distension and is tympanic to percussion. Laboratory studies are notable for a lactic acidosis. An upright abdominal radiograph and CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast are shown in Figures A and B respectively. She is started on IV fluids and a nasogastric tube is placed to suction which returns green bilious fluid. Repeat vitals 1 hour later are T 101F, HR 140 bpm, BP 75/44, RR 30/min, and SaO2 is 100% on the ventilator after she is intubated for airway concerns. What is the next best step in management?

answer_choices.D: Sigmoidoscopy, attempted derotation and rectal tube placement

few_shot.explanation:
This patient presents with a markedly distended abdomen, lactic acidosis, and a history of multiple abdominal surgeries. The upright abdominal radiograph shows a markedly dilated loop of bowel with air-fluid levels, and the CT scan shows a "whirl sign" of the mesentery. These findings are consistent with a small bowel obstruction (SBO) due to adhesions from her prior surgeries. The whirl sign is a specific sign for bowel volvulus, which is a twisting of a loop of bowel around its mesenteric attachment site. This can lead to bowel obstruction, ischemia, and necrosis. The presence of lactic acidosis and hemodynamic instability in this patient suggests bowel ischemia and necrosis, which is a surgical emergency. Therefore, the next best step in management is immediate laparotomy and surgical management.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 14-year-old male presents to the emergency department with altered mental status. His friends who accompanied him said that he complained of abdominal pain while camping. They denied his consumption of anything unusual from the wilderness, or any vomiting or diarrhea. His temperature is 100.5°F (38.1°C), blood pressure is 95/55 mmHg, pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 30/min. His pupils are equal and reactive to light bilaterally. The remainder of the physical exam is unremarkable. His basic metabolic panel is displayed below:

Serum:
Na+: 116 mEq/L
Cl-: 70 mEq/L
K+: 4.0 mEq/L
HCO3-: 2 mEq/L
BUN: 50 mg/dL
Glucose: 1010 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.2 mg/dL

While the remainder of his labs are pending, the patient becomes bradypneic and is intubated. His ventilator is adjusted to volume control assist-control with a respiratory rate (RR) of 14/min, tidal volume (Vt) of 350 mL, positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 5 cm H2O, and fractional inspired oxygen (FiO2) of 40%. His height is 5 feet 5 inches. Intravenous fluids and additional medical therapy are administered. An arterial blood gas obtained after 30 minutes on these settings shows the following:

pH: 7.05
pCO2 :40 mmHg
pO2: 150 mmHg
SaO2: 98%

What is the best next step in management?

answer_choices.B: Increase respiratory rate and tidal volume
answer_choices.D: Increase tidal volume and positive end-expiratory pressure

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal pain, polyuria, polydipsia, and altered mental status in the setting of hyperglycemia and an anion gap metabolic acidosis is consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA is a medical emergency that requires immediate treatment with intravenous fluids, insulin, and correction of electrolyte disturbances. In addition, patients with DKA often have a primary respiratory compensation (hyperventilation or Kussmaul breathing) in response to the severe metabolic acidosis. If the patient becomes fatigued and is unable to maintain this compensatory hyperventilation, as in this patient, endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation may be required.

The goal of mechanical ventilation in DKA is to mimic the patient's compensatory hyperventilation to "blow off" carbon dioxide and correct the acidemia. This is achieved by increasing the alveolar minute ventilation (ie, the product of the respiratory rate [RR] and tidal volume [Vt]). Both RR and Vt contribute to minute ventilation, but Vt is the more efficient of the two. This is because a portion of each breath is wasted in the anatomic dead space of the conducting airways and does not participate in gas exchange. Therefore, increasing Vt is a more effective way of increasing minute ventilation than increasing RR. However, Vt should not be increased to the point of overdistention (ie, Vt >6-8 mL/kg of ideal body weight), as this can cause barotrauma. Therefore, in this patient with persistent acidemia (pH 7.05) despite mechanical ventilation, both RR and Vt should be increased, but Vt should not exceed 6-8 mL/kg of ideal body weight.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 63-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of severe abdominal pain and vomiting for the past 3 hours. She is alert and oriented. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), the pulse is 134/min, and the blood pressure is 90/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is rigid and diffusely tender. Guarding and rebound tenderness is present. The rectal examination shows a collapsed rectum. Infusion of 0.9% saline is begun, and a CT of the abdomen shows intestinal perforation. The surgeon discusses with the patient the need for emergent exploratory laparotomy and she agrees to the surgery. Written informed consent is obtained. While in the holding area awaiting emergent transport to the operating room, she calls for the surgeon and informs him that she no longer wants the surgery. He explains to her the risks of not performing the surgery and she indicates that she understands, but is adamant about not proceeding with surgery. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.C: Continue with the emergency life-saving surgery
answer_choices.D: Wait until the patient is unconscious, then proceed with surgery

few_shot.explanation:
Informed consent is a process that involves a discussion between the physician and the patient about the nature of the patient's illness, the proposed treatment and its potential benefits and risks, and the alternatives to the proposed treatment. The patient must have the capacity to understand the information and make a decision. The patient also has the right to refuse treatment, even if the treatment is life-saving. In this case, the patient has the capacity to make decisions and has been informed of the risks of not undergoing surgery. Therefore, the physician must respect her autonomy and cancel the surgery.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a headache. She has had episodic headaches like this in the past and states that her headache today is severe, worse when laying down, and not responding to ibuprofen. She also reports a transient episode of vision loss and current blurry vision. She states she has a ringing in her ears as well. The patient has a past medical history of headaches, obesity, polycystic ovarian syndrome, and constipation. Her temperature is 98.7°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 149/92 mmHg, pulse is 83/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is not remarkable and an initial head CT is within normal limits. Which of the following is the best next step in management for the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with blurred vision and ringing in her ears. She says she has a 6-month history of recurrent worsening bilateral pulsatile headaches that she manages with ibuprofen, which does very little to relieve the pain. For the past week, she says she has vomited nearly every morning and missed work due to the pain in her head. She first noticed vision problems 3 months ago that has occurred several times since then. Past medical history is significant for uncomplicated urinary tract infection for which she has just finished a course of antibiotics. She has a history of a mild urticarial reaction when she takes penicillin. Her vital signs include: blood pressure 115/74 mm Hg, pulse 75/min, and respiratory rate 16/min. Her body mass index (BMI) is 36 kg/m2. Physical examination is significant for bilateral peripheral visual field loss with preservation of visual acuity. Fundoscopic examination reveals blurring of the disc margins with vessel tortuosity. The remainder of her physical examination is unremarkable. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain is normal. Lumbar puncture (LP) is remarkable for a markedly elevated opening pressure. Which of the following is the next best step in the treatment of her condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of chronic headaches, transient visual obscurations, and pulsatile tinnitus, along with her physical examination findings of bilateral papilledema and a normal neurologic examination, are consistent with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), also known as pseudotumor cerebri. IIH is a condition of unknown etiology characterized by increased intracranial pressure. It most commonly affects obese women of childbearing age. The diagnosis is confirmed by normal neuroimaging and an elevated opening pressure on LP with normal cerebrospinal fluid constituents. The most serious complication of IIH is permanent visual loss due to chronic papilledema. Therefore, all patients diagnosed with IIH should have formal visual field testing at the time of diagnosis and close follow-up with an ophthalmologist. 

The first-line treatment for IIH is weight loss and acetazolamide. Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that decreases the production of cerebrospinal fluid. It can also help with weight loss. Topiramate is an alternative first-line agent that can also help with weight loss. Furosemide can be added to acetazolamide or topiramate if necessary. 

Surgical treatments (eg, optic nerve sheath fenestration, ventriculoperitoneal shunting) are reserved for patients with progressive visual loss despite maximum medical therapy.

Hence, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 66-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a throbbing headache. She states that the pain is worse when eating and is localized over the right side of her head. Review of systems is only notable for some blurry vision in the right eye which is slightly worse currently. The patient's past medical history is notable only for chronic pain in her muscles and joints for which she has been taking ibuprofen. Her temperature is 99.1°F (37.3°C), blood pressure is 144/89 mmHg, pulse is 87/min, respirations are 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical examination is significant for tenderness to palpation over the right temporal region. Which of the following is the best initial step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's headache, jaw claudication, and vision changes in the setting of elevated inflammatory markers are concerning for giant cell arteritis (GCA). GCA is a granulomatous vasculitis that affects medium- and large-sized arteries, most commonly the branches of the external carotid artery. The most feared complication of GCA is irreversible vision loss due to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Therefore, patients with suspected GCA should be treated empirically with high-dose glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 40-60 mg/day or equivalent) to prevent vision loss. Temporal artery biopsy should be performed to confirm the diagnosis, but it should not delay treatment.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question:
A 52-year-old woman is accompanied by her husband to the emergency department with a severe occipital headache that started suddenly an hour ago. She is drowsy but able to answer the physician’s questions. She describes it as the worst headache she has ever had, 9/10 in intensity. The husband says it was initially localized to the occiput but has now spread all over her head and she also complained of a generalized heaviness. She took an ibuprofen without experiencing any relief. She also complains of blurry vision and nausea and had 1 episode of vomiting. She denies a recent history of fever, chills, numbness, or seizures. Her past medical history is significant for hypertension controlled with lisinopril and metoprolol. On examination, she is drowsy but oriented. Papilledema is seen on ophthalmoscopy. Neck flexion is difficult and painful. The rest of the exam is unremarkable. Her blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg, heart rate is 100/min, and temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). The ECG, cardiac enzymes, and laboratory studies are normal. Lumbar puncture results are as follows:
Opening pressure 210 mm H2O
RBC 50/mm3, numbers steady over 4 test tubes
Cell count 5/mm3
Glucose 40 mg/dL
Proteins 100 mg/dL
The patient is admitted to the ICU for further management. Which of the following is the most likely pathophysiology based on her history and CSF findings?

answer_choices.D: Rupture of the communicating branches of the cerebral arteries

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden onset of severe headache, described as the "worst headache of her life," is characteristic of a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). SAH is most commonly due to rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm. The blood in the subarachnoid space increases intracranial pressure, which can cause a decrease in the level of consciousness, as seen in this patient. The blood can also cause meningeal irritation, resulting in symptoms such as neck stiffness and photophobia. On fundoscopic examination, retinal or subhyaloid hemorrhages may be seen. The diagnosis of SAH is confirmed by a lumbar puncture, which typically shows a bloody or xanthochromic (yellow-tinged) cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with an increased opening pressure. The CSF red blood cell (RBC) count does not decrease from the first to the last tube, as it would in a traumatic lumbar puncture. The CSF is usually also characterized by a slight increase in protein and a normal or slightly decreased glucose level.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of frontal throbbing headaches for 3 weeks. Yesterday, the patient had blurry vision in both eyes and a brief episode of double vision. She has been taking ibuprofen with only mild improvement of her symptoms. She has polycystic ovarian syndrome, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and facial acne. She has not had any trauma, weakness, or changes in sensation. Her current medications include metformin and vitamin A. She is 158 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 89 kg (196 lbs); BMI is 36 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows decreased peripheral vision. Fundoscopic examination of both eyes is shown. MRI of the brain shows an empty sella. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's headache, blurry vision, and diplopia are concerning for increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Funduscopic examination reveals bilateral optic disc swelling (papilledema), which is a hallmark of increased ICP. The most common cause of increased ICP in a young, obese woman is idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), also known as pseudotumor cerebri. IIH is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other causes of increased ICP (eg, mass lesion, venous sinus thrombosis) should be ruled out first. Brain imaging (eg, MRI) is performed to exclude a mass lesion or venous sinus thrombosis. If imaging is negative, lumbar puncture is performed to measure the opening pressure and analyze the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). In IIH, the opening pressure is elevated, but the CSF composition is normal. Lumbar puncture can also be therapeutic, as removal of a large volume of CSF can decrease the pressure and improve symptoms.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with a severe headache and neck pain for the past 60 minutes. She says the headache was severe and onset suddenly like a ‘thunderclap’. She reports associated nausea, vomiting, neck pain, and stiffness. She denies any recent head trauma, loss of consciousness, visual disturbances, or focal neurologic deficits. Her past medical history is significant for hypertension, managed with hydrochlorothiazide. She denies any history of smoking, alcohol use, or recreational drug use. The vital signs include: temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure 165/95 mm Hg, pulse 92/min, and respiratory rate 15/min. On physical examination, there is mild nuchal rigidity noted with limited flexion at the neck. An ophthalmic examination of the retina shows mild papilledema. A noncontrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the head is performed and shown in the exhibit (see image). Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of a sudden-onset, severe headache, described as the "worst headache of her life," is concerning for a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). SAH is most commonly due to rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm. The classic presentation is a sudden, severe headache that reaches maximum intensity instantaneously (thunderclap headache). Associated symptoms often include nausea, vomiting, meningismus (nuchal rigidity, photophobia, headache), and loss of consciousness. The diagnosis of SAH is suggested by noncontrast computed tomography (CT) of the head, which is the initial diagnostic test. However, CT may be falsely negative, especially if performed >6 hours after symptom onset. Therefore, a negative CT in patients with a high clinical suspicion for SAH should be followed by a lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia.

However, before performing a lumbar puncture, it is important to first evaluate for increased intracranial pressure (ICP) due to concerns of brain herniation with lumbar puncture. This patient's papilledema suggests increased ICP. Therefore, the next step in management is to lower her blood pressure to decrease ICP and the risk of further bleeding. Labetalol is a combined alpha/beta-adrenergic antagonist that can be used to lower blood pressure in the setting of a hypertensive emergency.

So, the answer is [D].

He had a known history of vascular disease including hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus. He did not take any medications for these conditions. An autopsy is performed to identify the cause of death. Although it is determined that the patient suffered from a massive cerebrovascular accident as the cause of death, an incidental finding of a tumor arising from the spinal cord meninges is noted. The tumor significantly compresses the left anterolateral lower thoracic spinal cord. The right side of the spinal cord and the posterior spinal cord appear normal. Which of the following would most likely be impaired due to this lesion?

answer_choices.A: Pain sensation from the right side of the body
answer_choices.B: Proprioceptive sensation from the left side of the body
answer_choices.C: Temperature sensation from the left side of the body
answer_choices.D: Vibratory sensation from the right side of the body

few_shot.explanation:
The anterolateral system (also known as the spinothalamic tract) carries pain and temperature sensation from the body. It decussates (crosses the midline) at the level of the spinal cord where the sensory neuron enters. Therefore, a lesion of the anterolateral system will cause contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation.

The dorsal columns carry vibration, proprioception, and fine touch sensation from the body. They decussate in the medulla. Therefore, a lesion of the dorsal columns will cause ipsilateral loss of these sensations.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [C] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 35-year-old man who suffered a motor vehicle accident 3 months ago presents to the office for a neurological evaluation. He has no significant past medical history and takes no current medications. He has a family history of coronary artery disease in his father and Alzheimer’s disease in his mother. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg, the pulse is 85/min, the temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), and the respiratory rate is 20/min. Neurological examination is suggestive of a lesion in the anterior spinal artery that affects the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, which is later confirmed with angiography. Which of the following exam findings would have suggested this diagnosis?

answer_choices.A: Negative plantar extensor response in his lower limbs
answer_choices.C: Flaccid paralysis on the right side
answer_choices.D: Loss of vibratory sense below the level of the lesion

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms are consistent with anterior cord syndrome, which is characterized by loss of motor function and pain and temperature sensation below the level of the lesion due to damage to the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts, respectively. However, the dorsal columns are spared, so vibration and proprioception are preserved. The anterior cord syndrome is most often due to anterior spinal artery infarction.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [D] > [A] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency room following a stab wound to the back. He was in a bar when he got into an argument with another man who proceeded to stab him slightly right of the midline of his back. He is otherwise healthy and does not take any medications. He has one previous admission to the hospital for a stab wound to the leg from another bar fight 2 years ago. His temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 115/80 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, and pulse oximetry is 99% on room air. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams are unremarkable; however, he has an abnormal neurologic exam. If this wound entered his spinal cord but did not cross the midline, which of the following would most likely be seen in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion
answer_choices.B: Contralateral loss of tactile, vibration, and proprioception below the lesion
answer_choices.C: Contralateral spasticity below the level of the lesion
answer_choices.D: Ipsilateral flaccid paralysis at the level of the lesion

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with a Brown-Séquard syndrome, a type of incomplete spinal cord syndrome that results from hemisection of the spinal cord. This can occur due to penetrating trauma (eg, gunshot or stab wounds), disc herniation, or spinal cord tumors. The syndrome is characterized by the following findings:

- Ipsilateral loss of motor function and proprioception (due to damage to the corticospinal and dorsal column tracts, respectively) below the level of the lesion
- Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (due to damage to the spinothalamic tract) below the level of the lesion
- Ipsilateral loss of all sensation at the level of the lesion (due to damage to the dorsal root ganglion)
- Ipsilateral flaccid paralysis at the level of the lesion (due to damage to the ventral horn)

Therefore, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [C] > [B] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old man is rushed to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. The patient states that he feels weakness and numbness in both of his legs. He also reports pain in his lower back. His airway, breathing, and circulation is intact, and he is conversational. Neurologic exam is significant for bilateral lower extremity flaccid paralysis and impaired pain and temperature sensation up to T10-T11 with normal vibration sense. A computerized tomography scan of the spine is performed which shows a vertebral burst fracture of the vertebral body at the level of T11. Which of the following findings is most likely present in this patient?

answer_choices.C: Hyperreflexia at the level of the lesion

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with anterior cord syndrome, which is characterized by loss of motor function and pain and temperature sensation below the level of the lesion, with preservation of proprioception and vibration sense. This is because the anterior cord syndrome affects the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, which includes the corticospinal tract (motor function) and the spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature sensation). The posterior one-third of the spinal cord, which carries the dorsal columns (proprioception, vibration, and fine touch), is spared. Therefore, the patient would have preserved fine touch.

So, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of increasing weakness of his arms and legs over the past year. He has also had difficulty speaking for the past 5 months. He underwent a partial gastrectomy for gastric cancer 10 years ago. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Examination shows dysarthria. There is mild atrophy and twitching of the tongue. Muscle strength is decreased in all extremities. Muscle tone is decreased in the right lower extremity and increased in the other extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in the right lower extremity and 4+ in the other extremities. Plantar reflex shows an extensor response on the left. Sensation is intact in all extremities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's clinical presentation is consistent with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a degenerative disorder of upper and lower motor neurons. ALS typically presents in the fifth to sixth decade with asymmetric limb weakness, often starting in the hands. As the disease progresses, patients develop muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and eventual bulbar symptoms (eg, dysarthria, dysphagia). Upper motor neuron signs (eg, hyperreflexia, spasticity, Babinski sign) are also present, except in the atrophic limb, where lower motor neuron signs predominate (eg, hyporeflexia, flaccidity).

Riluzole, a glutamate antagonist, is the only medication shown to modestly increase survival in ALS. It is believed to decrease excitotoxicity to motor neurons.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

question: A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with complaints of fever with chills and pain in her knee and ankle joints for the past 2 days. She also complains of headaches and difficulty moving her neck. Further questioning reveals that she had a tick bite on her arm while gardening a few days ago. Past medical history is noncontributory. She takes a multivitamin with iron and folate every day and has been receiving regular prenatal care and the pregnancy is progressing normally. On examination, an erythematous rash is seen on her right arm, as shown in the accompanying photograph. Her obstetric examination is normal. Ultrasound of the fetus is reassuring with a normal heartbeat and no gross abnormalities. A specimen is collected to test for Lyme disease. What is the next best step for this patient?

few_shot.question: A 48-year-old woman presented to the hospital with a headache, intermittent fevers and chills, generalized arthralgias, excessive thirst, increased fluid intake, and a progressive rash that developed on her back. Three days before seeking evaluation at the hospital, she noticed a small, slightly raised lesion appearing like a spider or insect bite on her back, which she considered to be a scab covering the affected region. The patient's fever reached 39.4°C (102.9°F) 2 days before coming to the hospital, with an intensifying burning sensation on the affected site. When a family member examined the bite, it was noticed that the bump had transformed into a circular rash. The patient took over-the-counter ibuprofen for intense pain so she could sleep through the night. The day before her hospital visit, the patient felt exhausted but managed to complete a normal workday. On the day of the hospital visit, she awoke feeling very ill, with shooting joint pains, high fevers, and excessive thirst, which led to her to seek medical attention. On physical examination, her temperature was 40.1°C (104.2°F), and there was a large circular red rash with a bulls-eye appearance (17 × 19 cm in diameter) on her back. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Her past medical and surgical histories were not significant apart from a history of anaphylaxis when taking a tetracycline. She recalled a walk in the woods 3 weeks before this exam but denied finding a tick or any other ectoparasite on her body. She denied any nutritional or inhalational allergies, although she emphasized that she is allergic to tetracyclines. Based on her symptoms, medical history, and physical examination findings, the attending physician decides to institute antimicrobial therapy immediately. Which antimicrobial drug did the physician prescribe?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of a tick bite, fever, headache, arthralgias, and a large erythema migrans rash are consistent with early disseminated Lyme disease. Lyme disease is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, which is transmitted through the bite of an infected Ixodes tick. The disease is endemic in the northeastern and upper midwestern United States, where Ixodes ticks are prevalent.

Early localized Lyme disease presents with erythema migrans, a skin lesion that begins as a red macule or papule at the site of the tick bite and then expands over days to weeks to form a large, annular, erythematous lesion that often clears centrally. The lesion is often associated with systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, headache, and regional lymphadenopathy. Early disseminated Lyme disease, which occurs days to weeks after the tick bite, is characterized by multiple erythema migrans lesions, fever, and other symptoms such as migratory musculoskeletal pain.

The treatment of choice for Lyme disease is doxycycline. However, in patients who are allergic to doxycycline, such as this patient, amoxicillin or cefuroxime can be used as alternatives.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the physician with complaints of fever with rigors, headache, malaise, muscle pains, nausea, vomiting, and decreased appetite for the past 3 days. He informs the physician that he had been backpacking on the Appalachian Trail in the woods of Georgia in the month of June, 2 weeks ago, and had been bitten by a tick there. His temperature is 39.0°C (102.3°F), pulse is 94/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 126/82 mm Hg. His physical exam does not reveal any significant abnormality except for mild splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:
Total white blood cell count 3,700/mm3 (3.7 x 109/L)
Differential count  
Neutrophils 85%
Lymphocytes 12%
Monocytes 2%
Eosinophils 1%
Basophils 0%
Platelet count 88,000/mm3 (95 x 109/L)
Serum alanine aminotransferase 140 IU/L
Serum aspartate aminotransferase 80 IU/L
Microscopic examination of a peripheral blood smear stained with Wright-Giemsa stain shows the presence of morulae in the cytoplasm of leukocytes. In addition to drugs for symptomatic relief, what is the most appropriate initial step in the treatment of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of tick bite, fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, and leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and transaminitis is suggestive of human granulocytic anaplasmosis (HGA). HGA is caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum, a gram-negative bacterium transmitted by the Ixodes scapularis tick, which also transmits Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease) and Babesia microti (babesiosis). HGA is most common in the upper Midwest and Northeastern United States, but it can also occur in Northern California and the Southeast. The presence of morulae (mulberry-shaped aggregates of Anaplasma organisms) within granulocytes on peripheral blood smear confirms the diagnosis.

Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for both adults and children with HGA, regardless of the severity of illness. It is also the preferred treatment for other tick-borne illnesses, including Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and ehrlichiosis. Therefore, empiric treatment with doxycycline is recommended in any patient with a febrile illness who has been exposed to ticks, even before the results of diagnostic tests are available.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 10 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a rash on her upper arm that appeared 3 days ago. She has also had headaches and muscle aches for 1 day. She went on a camping trip in Maine 10 days ago. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F). A photograph of her rash is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of camping in Maine, fever, headache, myalgias, and erythema migrans rash are suggestive of early localized Lyme disease. Lyme disease is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, which is transmitted through the bite of an Ixodes tick. The characteristic rash of Lyme disease, erythema migrans, is an erythematous, annular lesion that expands over days to weeks, often with central clearing (target lesion). It usually appears 1-2 weeks following a tick bite. Other symptoms of early localized Lyme disease include fever, malaise, headache, and myalgias.

Early Lyme disease should be treated with doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime. Doxycycline is relatively contraindicated in pregnant women due to the risk of permanent tooth discoloration in the developing fetus. Therefore, amoxicillin is the treatment of choice in this patient.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [B] > [C] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a headache, fevers with chills, rigors, and generalized joint pain for the past week. She also complains of a progressive rash on her left arm. She says that a few days ago she noticed a small, slightly raised lesion resembling an insect bite mark, which had a burning sensation. The medical and surgical histories are unremarkable. She recalls walking in the woods 2 weeks prior to the onset of symptoms, but does not recall finding a tick on her body. On examination, the temperature is 40.2°C (104.4°F). A circular red rash measuring 10 cm x 5 cm in diameter is noted on the left arm, as shown in the accompanying image. The remainder of her physical examination is unremarkable. The tick causing her disease is also responsible for the transmission of which of the following pathogens?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of walking in the woods, the presence of a circular rash, and the systemic symptoms of fever, headache, and joint pain are suggestive of Lyme disease, which is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. The rash, known as erythema migrans, is a characteristic feature of Lyme disease and typically begins as a small red papule at the site of the tick bite. The papule then expands over days to weeks to form a large, annular, erythematous lesion that often clears centrally, resulting in a "bull's-eye" appearance. The rash is usually accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, headache, and regional lymphadenopathy.

Lyme disease is transmitted by the Ixodes tick, which can also transmit other pathogens such as Anaplasma phagocytophilum (which causes human granulocytic anaplasmosis) and Babesia microti (which causes babesiosis). Babesiosis is a malaria-like illness characterized by fever, fatigue, and hemolytic anemia.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old woman presented to the clinic for her first prenatal appointment with fatigue and pain in the perineum for the past 8 days. The past medical history is benign and she claimed to have only had unprotected intercourse with her husband. She had a documented allergic reaction to amoxicillin 2 years ago. The vaginal speculum exam revealed a clean, ulcerated genital lesion, which was tender and non-exudative. No lymphadenopathy was detected. A rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test revealed a titer of 1:64 and the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA- abs) test was positive. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.A: Penicillin desensitization, then intramuscular benzathine penicillin, G 2.4 million units
answer_choices.B: Oral tetracycline, 500 mg 4 times daily x 1 week
answer_choices.C: Doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily x 14 days

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's genital ulcer and positive syphilis serologies are consistent with primary syphilis. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends benzathine penicillin G for the treatment of syphilis in pregnancy, regardless of the stage of syphilis or the patient's penicillin allergy status. This is because penicillin is the only antibiotic proven to prevent congenital syphilis. Penicillin allergic patients should undergo penicillin desensitization followed by treatment with penicillin. 

Therefore, the answer is [A].
