His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 86/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Auscultation of the right side of the neck shows a bruit. There is a right-sided reducible inguinal hernia. Neurological examination shows no abnormalities. A complete blood count and serum concentrations of electrolytes, creatinine, and glucose are within the reference ranges. An electrocardiogram shows signs of mild left ventricular hypertrophy. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of right-sided weakness and subjective decreased sensation that started 30 minutes ago. The patient reports that his symptoms started to ease 5 minutes after onset and have now completely resolved. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. His current medications include lisinopril, metformin, and sitagliptin. He is 183 cm (6 ft 0 in) tall and weighs 105 kg (220 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m2. He appears well. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 150/88 mm Hg. Neurological examination shows no abnormalities. Cardiac examination shows regular rate and rhythm and a left-sided carotid bruit. Complete blood count, serum glucose, and electrolytes are within the reference ranges. An ECG shows sinus rhythm and left axis deviation. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows no abnormalities. Carotid doppler ultrasound shows 45% stenosis in the left carotid artery and 15% stenosis in the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden-onset, focal neurologic symptoms that completely resolved within 60 minutes are consistent with a transient ischemic attack (TIA). TIAs are often warning signs of an impending stroke, and patients with a TIA are at highest risk for stroke in the first 48 hours after the event. Therefore, rapid evaluation and intervention are necessary to prevent a subsequent stroke.

The ABCD2 score (Age, Blood pressure, Clinical features, Duration of symptoms, Diabetes) can be used to risk-stratify patients with a TIA. This patient's score is 5 (1 point each for age >60, blood pressure >140/90 mm Hg, unilateral weakness, and duration of symptoms >10 minutes; 0 points for absence of speech disturbance), which indicates a moderate risk of stroke in the next 2 days.

The most effective intervention to prevent stroke following a TIA is initiation of antiplatelet therapy (eg, aspirin, clopidogrel). Aspirin is typically used first-line, but clopidogrel is preferred in patients with aspirin allergy or in whom aspirin is contraindicated.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 71-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He feels well. He goes for a 30-minute walk three times a week and does not experience any shortness of breath or chest or leg pain on exertion. He has not had any weakness, numbness, or vision disturbance. He has diabetes that is well controlled with insulin injections. He had smoked one pack of cigarettes every day for 40 years but quit 5 years ago. He appears healthy and well nourished. His temperature is 36.3°C (97.3°F), pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 136/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows normal heart sounds. There are systolic bruits over the neck bilaterally. LDL cholesterol 154 mg/dL

Glucose 102 mg/dL
Duplex ultrasonography of the carotid arteries shows a 85% stenosis on the left and a 55% stenosis on the right side. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis. The decision to perform carotid endarterectomy (CEA) in patients with asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis is based on the degree of stenosis and the patient's comorbid conditions. The Asymptomatic Carotid Atherosclerosis Study showed that for patients with asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis of 60% or more, CEA decreased the 5-year risk of ipsilateral stroke from 11% to 5.1%. Therefore, CEA is recommended for patients with 60% to 99% stenosis who have a life expectancy of at least 5 years and who undergo surgery at centers with surgical complication rates (ie, perioperative stroke or death) of less than 3%. This patient has an 85% stenosis on the left side and is otherwise healthy, so he would benefit from a left CEA.

few_shot.question: A 59-year-old man presents to the emergency department with right-sided weakness and an inability to speak for the past 2 hours. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min and irregular, temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), and respiratory rate is 18/min. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden onset of right-sided weakness and aphasia is suggestive of an acute ischemic stroke. His irregular pulse and history of noncompliance with medications suggest that he may have atrial fibrillation (AF), a common cause of cardioembolic stroke. AF is often asymptomatic and may be first detected when a patient presents with an embolic event such as a stroke or transient ischemic attack. An ECG should be performed emergently in all patients with suspected stroke to evaluate for AF and other cardiac conditions that may require specific management.

few_shot.question: A 71-year-old man comes to the physician for a health maintenance examination. Aside from occasional lower back pain in the last couple of years, he feels well. He had a right-sided myocardial infarction 4 years ago. Currently, he has no shortness of breath and has no anginal symptoms. He has a 30 pack-year history of smoking but stopped smoking 10 years ago and does not drink alcohol. His pulse is 59/min, and his blood pressure is 135/75 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals 1+ lower extremity edema. Cardiac and pulmonary auscultation show no abnormalities. There is no lymphadenopathy. His laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 13.2 g/dL and serum protein of 10.1 g/dL. ECG shows known Q wave abnormalities unchanged since the last ECG one year ago. A serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's findings of lower extremity edema, a history of heart disease, and an elevated total protein level with a monoclonal spike on serum protein electrophoresis suggest multiple myeloma (MM) with associated amyloidosis. MM is a plasma cell dyscrasia characterized by overproduction of monoclonal immunoglobulins, which can lead to renal disease, hypercalcemia, anemia, and lytic bone lesions. In some patients, the overproduced immunoglobulins form amyloid fibrils that deposit in various organs, leading to a condition known as primary (AL) amyloidosis. The heart is a common site of amyloid deposition, and cardiac involvement can manifest as restrictive cardiomyopathy with associated heart failure, as suggested by this patient's lower extremity edema.

The next step in the evaluation of this patient is a whole-body CT scan to look for lytic bone lesions, which are characteristic of MM. If lytic lesions are found, a bone marrow biopsy should be performed to confirm the diagnosis. If the CT scan is negative, a bone marrow biopsy should still be performed given the patient's other findings suggestive of MM.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department for a loss of vision. He was outside gardening when he suddenly lost vision in his right eye. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 140/95 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 12/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Cardiac exam is notable for a systolic murmur along the right sternal border that radiates to the carotids. Pulmonary exam reveals mild bibasilar crackles. Neurological exam reveals cranial nerves II-XII as grossly intact with 5/5 strength and normal sensation in the upper and lower extremities. The patient has a negative Romberg's maneuver, and his gait is stable. A CT scan of the head demonstrates mild cerebral atrophy but no other findings. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden, painless, monocular vision loss that spontaneously resolved is consistent with amaurosis fugax, a form of transient ischemic attack (TIA) caused by retinal ischemia. The most common cause of amaurosis fugax is embolism to the retinal artery, most often from a carotid artery plaque. This patient's systolic murmur along the right sternal border that radiates to the carotids is consistent with aortic stenosis, which is a risk factor for embolic stroke. Therefore, the next best step in management is to perform an ultrasound of the neck to evaluate for carotid artery stenosis.

question: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for a well-child examination. The mother reports that she had her first menstrual period 1 week ago. few_shot.question: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother for an annual well-exam. She is relatively healthy with an unremarkable birth history. She reports no specific concerns except for the fact that her friends “already got their periods and I still haven’t gotten mine.” Her mom reports that she also had her menarche late and told her not to worry. When alone, the patient denies any pain, fevers, weight changes, vaginal discharge, or psychosocial stressors. Physical examination demonstrates a healthy female with a Tanner 4 stage of development of breast, genitalia, and pubic hair. What findings would you expect in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Coarse hair across pubis and medial thigh

few_shot.explanation:
Tanner staging is a method of assessing the degree of sexual maturation in children. It is based on the development of secondary sexual characteristics, including breast development in girls and genital development in boys. The Tanner stages are as follows:

- Stage 1: Prepubertal (no sexual development)
- Stage 2: Breast budding in girls (small area of surrounding glandular tissue) and testicular enlargement in boys
- Stage 3: Enlargement of breast and areola with no separation of their contours in girls and further enlargement of penis and testes in boys
- Stage 4: Projection of areola and papilla to form a secondary mound in girls and further enlargement of penis and testes in boys
- Stage 5: Mature stage (adult); projection of papilla only in girls and adult genitalia in boys

This patient is at Tanner stage 4, which is characterized by the projection of the areola and papilla to form a secondary mound in girls. Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: An 11-year-old girl presents to the pediatrician with her mother, who is concerned about her sexual development. She mentions that she herself experienced the onset of menses at the age of 10.5 years, while her daughter has still not had a menstrual period. However, she is otherwise a healthy girl with no significant medical problems since birth. On physical examination, her vital signs are stable. Evaluation of breast and pubic hair are Tanner stage 2. He reassures the mother that her daughter’s sexual development is within the normal range for girls and there is nothing to worry about at present. Which is a sign of Tanner stage 2?
few_shot.explanation:
Tanner stage 2 is characterized by thelarche, or the onset of breast development. This is usually the first sign of puberty in girls and typically occurs between the ages of 8 and 13. The breast bud is palpable and the areola begins to enlarge. This is followed by pubarche, or the development of pubic hair, which is a sign of adrenarche. The pubic hair is initially fine and straight, and becomes coarser and curlier as puberty progresses.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 14-year-old girl presents to the pediatrician because she has not experienced the onset of menstruation. Her mother reports that her pubic hair developed at the age of 9 years. Her mother also informs that she has been experiencing recurrent serous otitis media since early childhood. The temperature is 36.8°C (98.4°F), pulse is 88/min, blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg, and respiratory rate is 14/min. The physical examination shows hypoplastic nails, along with short 4th and 5th metacarpals, and cubitus valgus bilaterally. In addition, the examination of her chest shows lack of breast development with widely spaced nipples. The auscultation of the chest reveals normal heart sounds with no murmur noted. The examination of the head and neck region shows a high arched palate, dental malocclusion, and a low hairline. Which of the following signs is most likely to be present on examination of her skin?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's lack of breast development, primary amenorrhea, and widely spaced nipples are suggestive of Turner syndrome (45,XO), a condition that occurs due to complete or partial absence of one of the two X chromosomes normally present in females. Other findings in Turner syndrome can include short stature, webbed neck, and low hairline. In addition, Turner syndrome is associated with an increased number of benign nevi. few_shot.question: A 9-year-old healthy female presents to her pediatrician for a healthy child visit. She is doing well in school and has good relationships with her teachers, friends, and family. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 85/min, and respirations are 16/min. On examination, a minimal amount of pubic hair is noted. Her breasts and papillae are slightly elevated with enlargement of the areolas. Which of the following is the most likely Tanner stage of development in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
The Tanner stages of sexual development are used to assess the onset and progression of puberty. The stages are as follows:

- Stage 1: Prepubertal (no sexual development)
- Stage 2: Breast budding (elevation of breast and papilla, enlargement of areola diameter) and sparse growth of long, slightly pigmented, downy straight pubic hair, primarily along the labia
- Stage 3: Further enlargement and elevation of breast and areola, with no separation of their contours; increased quantity and pigmentation of pubic hair
- Stage 4: Projection of areola and papilla to form a secondary mound above the level of the breast; adult-type hair quality, extending across the pubis but sparing the medial thighs
- Stage 5: Mature stage (projection of papilla only, due to recession of the areola to the general contour of the breast; adult quantity and quality of hair, with spread to the medial thighs)

This patient's physical examination findings are consistent with Tanner stage 2 of sexual development.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother for amenorrhea. The patient has never had a menstrual cycle and is worried as all her friends “have started to go through puberty.” She has been otherwise healthy with an uncomplicated birth history. “I told her not to worry since I also got my period late,” her mother reported during the encounter. Physical examination demonstrates Tanner stage 2 breasts, genital, and pubic hair. Temperature is 98.7 °F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 156/100mmHg, pulse is 92/min, and respirations are 12/min. What laboratory abnormalities would you expect to find in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's hypertension, hypokalemia, and delayed puberty are suggestive of 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, a rare form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. 17α-hydroxylase is necessary for the synthesis of cortisol and sex steroids (androgens and estrogens). Therefore, deficiency of this enzyme results in decreased synthesis of these hormones. This leads to increased adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion due to lack of negative feedback by cortisol, resulting in overproduction of adrenal mineralocorticoids (due to shunting of precursors) and causing hypertension and hypokalemia. Decreased sex steroid synthesis results in delayed puberty and primary amenorrhea in females and ambiguous genitalia in males. Because androstenedione is a sex steroid, its levels would be low in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

The treatment of acute mania involves mood stabilizers (eg, lithium, valproate, carbamazepine) and/or atypical antipsychotics (eg, olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine). few_shot.question: A 13-month-old boy with sickle cell anemia is brought to the emergency department because of continuous crying and severe left-hand swelling. The temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min. The physical examination reveals swelling and tenderness to palpation of the left hand. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of severe pain and swelling of the left hand is consistent with a vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC), also known as a pain crisis, which is the most common clinical manifestation of sickle cell disease (SCD). VOCs are caused by the occlusion of the microvasculature by sickled red blood cells, leading to tissue ischemia and infarction. The bones are commonly affected, and the resultant bone infarcts can cause severe pain. The best initial step in management is to provide analgesia, usually with opioids such as morphine or hydromorphone, as the pain can be severe. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can also be used, but are usually not sufficient as monotherapy for moderate to severe pain.

Leukocyte count 17,000/mm3
Platelet count 200,000/mm3

This patient's fever, cough, and tachypnea in the setting of sickle cell disease (SCD) are concerning for pneumonia, which can lead to sepsis and acute chest syndrome. The patient's altered mental status, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension are consistent with septic shock. The most common pathogens causing pneumonia in patients with SCD are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, similar to the general pediatric population. However, patients with SCD are at increased risk for invasive pneumococcal disease due to their impaired splenic function (autosplenectomy), which results in decreased clearance of encapsulated organisms.

The 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) covers more serotypes than the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13), but it is not consistently immunogenic in children <2 years of age. Therefore, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommends that children with SCD receive PCV13 as part of the routine childhood vaccination series (at 2, 4, 6, and 12-15 months of age) and receive PPSV23 at age 2 years, with a booster dose 5 years later. This patient's presentation could have been prevented by adherence to these vaccination guidelines.

few_shot.question: A 33-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden onset right hand and right leg weakness. The patient was at home cleaning when his symptoms began. He also complains of diffuse and severe pain throughout his entire body which he states he has experienced before. The patient is an immigrant from South America, and his medical history is not known. His temperature is 98.9°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 128/67 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. CT of the head demonstrates no bleeding. Physical exam is notable for 2/5 strength in the patient's right arm and right leg. Which of the following is the best management in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of sudden-onset right-sided weakness and severe pain is concerning for an ischemic stroke. The patient's history of severe pain crises and his origin from South America suggest sickle cell disease (SCD), a common cause of stroke in young patients. SCD is an autosomal recessive disorder most commonly seen in individuals of African and Mediterranean descent. It is characterized by a single amino acid substitution in the beta-globin chain, leading to the production of hemoglobin S (HbS). HbS polymerizes under deoxygenated conditions, causing red blood cells to assume a sickle shape. Sickled cells are rigid and can cause vaso-occlusion, leading to tissue ischemia and infarction. 

The brain is one of the organs most commonly affected by sickling. The primary mechanism of stroke in SCD is thought to be occlusion of the distal internal carotid and proximal middle cerebral arteries by sickled cells. This can lead to large-artery stroke, as seen in this patient. 

The treatment of an acute ischemic stroke in a patient with SCD is emergent exchange transfusion. This can be performed via simple transfusion (remove unit of patient's blood and replace with unit of donor blood) or via apheresis (remove patient's blood, separate RBCs, and replace RBCs with donor blood). The goal is to decrease the proportion of HbS in the patient's blood, reducing the sickling of RBCs and thereby improving blood flow to the brain.

So, the answer is [B].

A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of recurrent nose bleeds that occur with light trauma or at random times during the day. A peripheral blood smear detects tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?"

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia is suggestive of a myeloproliferative disorder. The presence of tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase activity on peripheral blood smear is diagnostic of hairy cell leukemia (HCL). HCL is a chronic B-cell malignancy characterized by splenomegaly, pancytopenia, and lymphocytes with cytoplasmic projections ("hairy cells") on peripheral blood smear. Hairy cells are characteristically positive for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase.

The treatment of choice for HCL is a purine analog, such as cladribine or pentostatin. These agents are toxic to both dividing and resting lymphocytes, making them particularly effective in treating low-grade lymphoid malignancies such as HCL. The most common side effect is myelosuppression, which can lead to serious and even fatal infections. Therefore, patients should be monitored closely during treatment.

TTP is a medical emergency, and plasma exchange therapy should be initiated immediately. Plasma exchange therapy removes the ultra-large vWF multimers and supplies functional ADAMTS13 protease.

few_shot.question: A 57-year-old woman presents to her physician for a checkup. The past medical history is significant for diabetes mellitus type 2, and a history of myocardial infarction. The current medications are aspirin, lisinopril, metoprolol, atorvastatin, and metformin. The patient’s HbA1c is 7.9%, and her fasting blood glucose is 8.9 mmol/L (160 mg/dL). answer_choices.B: It does not decrease cardiovascular outcomes.
answer_choices.C: There is a high risk of hypoglycemia in patients who use this medication.
answer_choices.D: This medication should not be combined with insulin.

few_shot.explanation:
Exenatide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist that is used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes. It works by increasing insulin secretion, decreasing glucagon secretion, and slowing gastric emptying. It is usually well-tolerated, but common side effects include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. It can be used in combination with other oral hypoglycemic agents, including metformin, as well as with insulin. The risk of hypoglycemia is low when used as monotherapy, but it can increase when combined with other agents such as sulfonylureas or insulin.

However, unlike some other GLP-1 receptor agonists (eg, liraglutide, semaglutide), exenatide has not been shown to decrease cardiovascular outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes. Therefore, it may not be the best choice for this patient, who has a history of myocardial infarction.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man with chronic obstructive lung disease, depression, and type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician with fever, chills, dyspnea, and a productive cough for 5 days. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F) and respirations are 30/min. An x-ray of the chest shows a right lower lobe infiltrate, and sputum culture grows bacteria that are sensitive to fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Pharmacotherapy with oral moxifloxacin is initiated. Three days later, the patient continues to have symptoms despite being compliant with the antibiotic. Serum moxifloxacin levels are undetectable. few_shot.explanation:
Fluoroquinolones are a class of antibiotics that are commonly used to treat a variety of infections, including community-acquired pneumonia. They work by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, which are necessary for DNA replication, transcription, and repair. However, their absorption can be significantly decreased by multivalent cations, such as aluminum, magnesium, calcium, and iron. These cations can bind to the fluoroquinolone in the gastrointestinal tract and prevent its absorption. Therefore, fluoroquinolones should not be taken with antacids, sucralfate, or multivitamin and mineral supplements, as these can all contain multivalent cations. In this patient, the concurrent ingestion of a multivitamin likely decreased the absorption of the moxifloxacin, leading to the lack of response to therapy.

She smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years, but quit 5 years ago. Current medications include simvastatin, captopril, and metformin. This patient has community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) as evidenced by her acute onset of fever, cough with purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, and a new infiltrate on chest x-ray. The most common pathogens in CAP are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and atypical pathogens (eg, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Legionella species). The choice between inpatient and outpatient treatment, as well as the choice of antibiotics, depends on the severity of illness and the presence of certain risk factors.

The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) and CURB-65 are validated prediction rules used to assess CAP severity and need for hospitalization. The PSI is a complicated prediction rule that uses 20 variables to stratify patients into 5 risk classes. The CURB-65 is a simpler prediction rule that uses 5 variables, each assigned 1 point: Confusion, Urea nitrogen >20 mg/dL, Respiratory rate ≥30/min, low Blood pressure (systolic <90 mm Hg or diastolic ≤60 mm Hg), and age ≥65 years. Patients with CURB-65 scores ≥2, like this patient, should be admitted to the hospital.

The recommended treatment for inpatient, non-ICU treatment of CAP is a respiratory fluoroquinolone (eg, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) or a combination of a β-lactam (eg, cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, ampicillin) plus a macrolide (eg, azithromycin, clarithromycin). The β-lactam provides reliable coverage against S pneumoniae and H influenzae, and the macrolide covers atypical pathogens.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 51-year-old man presents to his physician’s office with a persistent fever that started a week ago. He says that his temperature ranges between 37.8–39.1°C (100–102.5°F). His oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. On examination, he has decreased breath sounds in his right lung field with the presence of soft inspiratory crackles. He is sent to the laboratory for sputum analysis and chest imaging. Based on his history and physical examination, which of the following would be the next best step in the management of this patient?

The most common pathogens involved in aspiration pneumonia and lung abscess are anaerobic bacteria from the oral flora, including Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, and Bacteroides species. The most effective antibiotics against these organisms are clindamycin and amoxicillin-clavulanate. Clindamycin is often preferred due to its excellent oral bioavailability and its ability to inhibit protein synthesis in bacteria, which reduces the production of harmful bacterial enzymes and toxins.

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 12-week history of persistent cough. The cough is nonproductive and worse at night. She otherwise feels well. Her FEV1 is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's chronic cough, which is worse at night, and her history of seasonal rhinorrhea are suggestive of postnasal drip syndrome (also known as upper airway cough syndrome). This is a common cause of chronic cough and is often due to allergic or nonallergic rhinitis or sinusitis. Patients may report symptoms of rhinitis (eg, sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, postnasal drip), but some patients may have "silent" postnasal drip with cough as the only manifestation. Treatment involves use of a first-generation antihistamine (eg, diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine) for allergic causes or an intranasal corticosteroid for nonallergic causes.

question: A 66-year-old woman presents with urinary incontinence, difficulty urinating, incomplete voiding, and dull pain in the suprapubic region. She reports that she has not urinated for the past 2 days and that the urine leakage occurs during both day and night and is not associated with physical exertion. On gynecologic examination, the cervix was normally positioned, mobile, and without any visible lesions. Bulging of the posterior vaginal wall was noted. The adnexa were not palpable. few_shot.question: A 55-year-old woman seeks evaluation of difficult and incomplete voiding and spontaneous urine leakage that occurs continuously during the day and night. The symptoms are not associated with physical exertion. She denies any urethral or vaginal discharge. She is menopausal and does not take hormone replacement therapy. At 33 years of age, she had a right salpingectomy as treatment for an ectopic pregnancy. She has a 2-year history of a major depressive disorder and takes amitriptyline (100 mg before the bedtime). She was also diagnosed 5 years ago with arterial hypertension, which is controlled with enalapril (20 mg daily) and metoprolol (50 mg daily). The weight is 71 kg (156.5 lb) and the height is 155 cm (5 ft). The vital signs are as follows: blood pressure 135/80 mm Hg, heart rate 67/min, respiratory rate 13/min, and temperature 36.4℃ (97.5℉). The physical examination is significant for a palpable urinary bladder. The neurologic examination is within normal limits. The gynecologic examination shows grade 1 uterine prolapse. Which of the following is the most probable cause of the patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has overflow incontinence, which is characterized by continuous leakage of urine without a sensation of bladder fullness or an urge to void. It is caused by impaired detrusor contractility or bladder outlet obstruction. The most common cause of impaired detrusor contractility is a medication effect. Many medications can cause urinary retention by blocking the muscarinic cholinergic receptors on the detrusor muscle of the bladder, inhibiting bladder contraction. Examples include tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline), first-generation antihistamines, antiparkinsonian drugs, and antipsychotic medications. In this patient, the most likely cause of overflow incontinence is the amitriptyline she is taking for depression.

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of progressively worsening urinary incontinence. Her only medication is insulin. Physical examination shows a palpable suprapubic mass. Urinalysis is unremarkable. Urodynamic studies show an increased post-void residual volume. Which of the following interventions is most likely to benefit this patient?

This patient's symptoms of urinary incontinence, sensation of a full bladder even after voiding, and a palpable suprapubic mass are suggestive of overflow incontinence. Overflow incontinence is characterized by chronic urinary retention and an overdistended bladder, which leads to frequent overflow of urine. It is often seen in patients with diabetes mellitus due to autonomic neuropathy, which can cause impaired bladder sensation and detrusor muscle contractility. The most effective treatment for overflow incontinence is intermittent catheterization, which helps to drain the bladder and prevent overdistention.

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old woman was admitted to the surgical service after an uncomplicated appendectomy. She underwent surgery yesterday and had an uneventful postoperative course. You ask the nurse to perform a bladder scan, which reveals 450cc. What is the next appropriate step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has urinary retention, which is a common complication after surgery. It is often due to the use of anesthetics and analgesics, which can inhibit the micturition reflex. The patient's inability to void and the suprapubic pain are indicative of an overdistended bladder. The bladder scan confirms this, as a volume of 450cc is well above the normal post-void residual volume of <50cc.

The next step in management is catheterization, which will relieve the patient's discomfort and prevent further bladder distention. This is usually followed by a trial of voiding after removal of the catheter.

few_shot.question: A 49-year-old woman comes to the office complaining of 2 weeks of urinary incontinence. She says she first noticed some light, urinary dribbling that would increase with sneezing or coughing. This dribble soon worsened, soaking through a pad every 3 hours. She denies any fevers, chills, abdominal pain, hematuria, dysuria, abnormal vaginal discharge, or increased urinary frequency. The patient had a bilateral tubal ligation 3 weeks ago. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. Her menses are regular and last 5 days. She has had 3 pregnancies that each resulted in uncomplicated, term vaginal deliveries. Her last pregnancy was 2 years ago. The patient has hypothyroidism and takes daily levothyroxine. She denies tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use. She has no history of sexually transmitted diseases. She is sexually active with her husband of 25 years. Her BMI is 26 kg/m^2. On physical examination, the abdomen is soft, nondistended, and nontender without palpable masses or hepatosplenomegaly. Rectal tone is normal. The uterus is anteverted, mobile, and nontender. There are no adnexal masses. Urine is seen pooling in the vaginal vault. Urinalysis is unremarkable. Which of the following is next best step in diagnosis?

answer_choices.B: Methylene blue instillation into the bladder

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recent bilateral tubal ligation and continuous urinary incontiness that is not associated with increased intra-abdominal pressure (eg, coughing, sneezing) is suggestive of a vesicovaginal fistula (VVF). VVF is an abnormal communication between the bladder and vagina that results in continuous urinary incontiness. The most common cause of VVF in developed countries is surgical trauma, most often from procedures involving the female genital tract (eg, hysterectomy, cesarean section, tubal ligation). Other causes include radiation therapy, malignancy, and prolonged labor.

The diagnosis of VVF is usually made by directly visualizing leakage of urine from the vagina during a pelvic examination. If the diagnosis is uncertain, the next step is to instill methylene blue dye into the bladder via a urinary catheter. If a fistula is present, blue-tinged urine will be seen in the vagina.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 63-year-old woman presents to her primary care doctor with increased urinary frequency. She has noticed that over the past 6 months, she has had to urinate more often than usual. Several times per day, she develops a rapid-onset need to urinate and has occasionally been unable to reach the restroom. These symptoms have caused her a lot of distress and impacted her work as a grocery store clerk. She has tried pelvic floor exercises, decreasing her caffeine consumption, and has intentionally lost 20 pounds in an effort to alleviate her symptoms. She denies urinary hesitancy or hematuria. Her past medical history is notable for rheumatoid arthritis for which she takes methotrexate. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her temperature is 98.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 124/68 mmHg, pulse is 89/min, and respirations are 19/min. She is well-appearing and in no acute distress. Which of the following interventions would be most appropriate in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of urinary urgency and frequency are consistent with overactive bladder (OAB), a common condition that affects up to 30% of men and 40% of women in the United States. OAB is a clinical diagnosis defined as urinary urgency, usually accompanied by frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency urinary incontinence, in the absence of urinary tract infection or other obvious pathology. It is caused by detrusor overactivity, which can be due to myogenic or neurogenic dysfunction. 

First-line treatment for OAB includes lifestyle modifications such as bladder training, pelvic floor muscle exercises, and fluid management. If these interventions are not successful, as in this patient, second-line treatment includes antimuscarinic agents such as oxybutynin or beta-3 adrenergic agonists such as mirabegron. 

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with painless vaginal bleeding of sudden onset approx. 1 hour ago. The woman informs the doctor that, currently, she is in the 13th week of pregnancy. She also mentions that she was diagnosed with hyperemesis gravidarum during the 6th week of pregnancy. On physical examination, her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse rate is 110/min, blood pressure is 108/76 mm Hg, and respiratory rate is 20/min. A general examination reveals pallor. Examination of the abdomen suggests that the enlargement of the uterus is greater than expected at 13 weeks of gestation. An ultrasonogram shows the absence of a fetus and the presence of an intrauterine mass with multiple cystic spaces that resembles a bunch of grapes. The patient is admitted to the hospital and her uterine contents are surgically removed. The atypical tissue is sent for genetic analysis, which of the following karyotypes is most likely to be found?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of painless vaginal bleeding, an enlarged uterus, and an ultrasound showing a "bunch of grapes" is consistent with a complete hydatidiform mole. Complete moles are abnormal pregnancies characterized by hydropic swelling of placental villi and trophoblastic hyperplasia. They may present with vaginal bleeding, an enlarged uterus, hyperemesis gravidarum due to markedly elevated β-hCG levels, or preeclampsia. On ultrasound, a complete mole appears as a central heterogeneous mass with multiple small cystic spaces, giving a "snowstorm" or "bunch of grapes" appearance.

Complete moles are usually diploid and result from fertilization of an "empty" ovum (containing no maternal DNA) by a single sperm that then duplicates its DNA (46, XX) or, less commonly, by two sperm (46, XX or 46, XY). Because the genetic material is entirely of paternal origin, complete moles are androgenetic.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old G1P0 Caucasian woman in her 12th week of pregnancy presents to her obstetrician with vaginal bleeding. She also reports 3 episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis. Her family history is notable for ovarian cancer in her mother and endometrial cancer in her maternal grandmother. On examination, her uterus is at 16 weeks in size and she has mild tenderness to palpation on her right suprapubic region. A transvaginal ultrasound in this patient would most likely reveal which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with a molar pregnancy. Molar pregnancies are a type of gestational trophoblastic disease that result from abnormal fertilization. They are characterized by abnormal proliferation of trophoblastic tissue and villi, leading to the formation of a mass of vesicles (grape-like clusters) in the uterus. This mass can be seen on ultrasound as an intrauterine cystic mass, often described as having a "snowstorm" or "honeycomb" appearance. 

Risk factors for molar pregnancy include extremes of reproductive age (<20 or >35 years), prior molar pregnancy, and a history of miscarriage. 

This patient's symptoms of vaginal bleeding and an enlarged uterus are classic for molar pregnancy. The nausea and vomiting are likely due to the markedly elevated levels of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) seen in this condition.

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old, gravida 2, nulliparous woman, at 14 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 6-hour history of light vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal discomfort. This patient's presentation of vaginal bleeding, an enlarged uterus, and elevated β-hCG concentration is suggestive of a molar pregnancy. Molar pregnancies are a type of gestational trophoblastic disease and are characterized by abnormal proliferation of trophoblastic tissue. They can be complete (46, XX and entirely paternal in origin) or partial (69, XXY, XXX, or XYY and usually due to fertilization of a single egg by 2 sperm). Complete moles have a higher potential for malignant transformation into choriocarcinoma.

Transvaginal ultrasound is the most appropriate next step in management to confirm the diagnosis. It would show a uterus filled with a complex, echogenic mass with multiple small cystic spaces (representing swollen, edematous villi) described as a "snowstorm" or "cluster of grapes" appearance. Theca-lutein cysts (due to overstimulation of the ovaries by high levels of β-hCG) can also be seen and may be responsible for the bilateral adnexal masses found on examination.

There are scattered red, nonblanching pinpoints spots on his trunk and extremities. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 8.0 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 80,000/mm3, and a platelet count of 104,000/mm3. Genetic analysis of a bone marrow aspirate shows leukemic cells with a balanced translocation between the long arms of chromosome 15 and 17. These cells are most likely to stain positive for which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's presentation of fatigue, pallor, and bleeding is suggestive of acute leukemia. The presence of a balanced translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17 is characteristic of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). APL is associated with the PML/RARA fusion gene, which leads to the accumulation of abnormal promyelocytes.

Myeloperoxidase is a lysosomal enzyme present in the primary granules of myeloid cells, including promyelocytes. It catalyzes the formation of hypochlorous acid from hydrogen peroxide and chloride anion during the respiratory burst to kill phagocytosed organisms. Myeloperoxidase can be detected by cytochemical staining and is used along with flow cytometry to diagnose AML.

So, the answer is [A].

A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever and easy bruising for 3 days. He has had fatigue for 2 weeks. He has no past medical history, and takes no medications. Excessive bleeding from intravenous lines was reported by the nurse. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. The temperature is 38.2°C (102.6°F), pulse is 105/min, respiration rate is 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. On physical examination, he has multiple purpura on the lower extremities and several ecchymoses on the lower back and buttocks. Petechiae are noticed on the soft palate. Cervical painless lymphadenopathy is detected on both sides. The examination of the lungs, heart, and abdomen shows no other abnormalities. The laboratory test results are as follows:
Hemoglobin 8 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 90 μm3
Leukocyte count 18,000/mm3
Platelet count 10,000/mm3
Partial thromboplastin time (activated) 60 seconds
Prothrombin time 25 seconds (INR: 2.2)
Fibrin split products Positive
Lactate dehydrogenase, serum 1,000 U/L
A Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear is shown by the image. Intravenous fluids, blood products, and antibiotics are given to the patient. Based on the most likely diagnosis, which of the following is the best therapy for this patient at this time?

answer_choices.C: Rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP)

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, fatigue, and cervical lymphadenopathy, along with the presence of Auer rods on peripheral blood smear, is suggestive of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). APL is a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia that is characterized by a specific chromosomal translocation, t(15;17), which results in the fusion of the retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARα) gene on chromosome 17 and the promyelocytic leukemia (PML) gene on chromosome 15. This fusion gene product disrupts normal myeloid differentiation and promotes proliferation of immature myeloid cells (ie, promyelocytes).

APL is associated with a high risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which is suggested in this patient by the presence of thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and aPTT, and positive fibrin split products. Therefore, APL is considered a medical emergency and requires prompt treatment.

The treatment of choice for APL is all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), which binds to the altered retinoic acid receptor and allows the promyelocytes to differentiate into mature neutrophils. This leads to rapid resolution of the coagulopathy seen in APL. ATRA is typically combined with an anthracycline (eg, daunorubicin, idarubicin) for induction therapy.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A healthy 29-year-old woman comes to the doctor because of recurrent episodes of bleeding from the nose and gums during the past week. Examination shows punctate, nonblanching, reddish macules over the neck, chest, and lower extremities. Her leukocyte count is 8,600/mm3, hemoglobin concentration is 12.9 g/dL, and platelet count is 26,500/mm3. A peripheral blood smear shows a reduced number of platelets with normal morphology. Evaluation of a bone marrow biopsy in this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's spontaneous bleeding, petechiae, and thrombocytopenia are suggestive of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). ITP is an acquired disorder characterized by immune-mediated destruction of platelets, leading to isolated thrombocytopenia in an otherwise healthy individual. The pathogenesis involves the production of autoantibodies (usually IgG) against platelet antigens. These autoantibodies bind to platelets, leading to their premature destruction by the reticuloendothelial system, primarily in the spleen. The bone marrow responds to the peripheral destruction of platelets by increasing the production of platelets, leading to megakaryocyte hyperplasia.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

CML is characterized by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, which results from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, creating the BCR-ABL fusion gene. This gene codes for a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives unregulated cell division. Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that specifically targets the BCR-ABL fusion protein and is the treatment of choice for CML.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [B] > [C] > [A].

question: A previously healthy 60-year-old man comes to his physician because of progressively worsening shortness of breath for the past 2 months. He does not experience shortness of breath at rest. He also occasionally has a dry cough. He has not had fever, chills, or night sweats. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for the past 40 years. He drinks a beer daily and occasionally more on weekends. He does not use illicit drugs. He is 183 cm (6 ft 0 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145 lbs); BMI is 19.7 kg/m2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 94/min, respirations are 21/min, and blood pressure is 136/88 mm Hg. Lung auscultation reveals a prolonged expiratory phase and end-expiratory wheezing. Spirometry shows an FEV1:FVC ratio of 62%, an FEV1 of 60% of predicted, and a total lung capacity of 125% of predicted. The diffusion capacity of the lung (DLCO) is decreased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 64-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a dry cough and progressively worsening shortness of breath for the past 2 months. She has not had fever, chills, or night sweats. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 45 years. She appears thin. Examination of the lung shows a prolonged expiratory phase and end-expiratory wheezing. Spirometry shows decreased FEV1:FVC ratio (< 70% predicted), decreased FEV1, and a total lung capacity of 125% of predicted. The diffusion capacity of the lung (DLCO) is decreased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, physical examination findings, and spirometry results are consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is characterized by persistent airflow limitation that is not fully reversible. The airflow limitation is usually progressive and associated with an abnormal inflammatory response of the lungs to noxious particles or gases, such as those found in cigarette smoke. The two major forms of COPD are chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Chronic bronchitis is defined as a chronic productive cough for 3 months in each of 2 successive years in a patient in whom other causes of chronic cough have been excluded. Emphysema is defined as abnormal permanent enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls and without obvious fibrosis. The spirometry results in this patient are consistent with obstructive lung disease, and the decreased DLCO is consistent with emphysema.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department for evaluation of a 2-year history of increasing shortness of breath. He also has an occasional nonproductive cough. The symptoms get worse with exertion. The medical history is significant for hypertension and he takes chlorthalidone. He is a smoker with a 40-pack-year smoking history. On physical examination, the patient is afebrile; the vital signs include: blood pressure 125/78 mm Hg, pulse 90/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. The body mass index (BMI) is 31 kg/m2. The oxygen saturation is 94% at rest on room air. A pulmonary examination reveals decreased breath sounds bilaterally, but is otherwise normal with no wheezes or crackles. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable. A chest radiograph shows hyperinflation of both lungs with mildly increased lung markings, but no focal findings. Based on this clinical presentation, which of the following is most likely?

answer_choices.D: FEV1/FVC of 80% with an FEV1 of 82%

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic dyspnea, cough, and significant smoking history, along with physical examination findings of decreased breath sounds and chest radiograph findings of hyperinflation, are suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is characterized by persistent airflow limitation that is usually progressive and associated with an enhanced chronic inflammatory response in the airways and the lung to noxious particles or gases. The airflow limitation is caused by a mixture of small airway disease (obstructive bronchiolitis) and parenchymal destruction (emphysema), the relative contributions of which vary from person to person. Chronic inflammation causes structural changes and narrowing of the small airways. Destruction of the lung parenchyma leads to the loss of alveolar attachments to the small airways and decreases lung elastic recoil; in turn, these changes diminish the ability of the airways to remain open during expiration. 

Spirometry is required to make the diagnosis in this clinical context; the presence of a postbronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70 confirms the presence of persistent airflow limitation and thus of COPD. 

Therefore, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [D] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question:
A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of progressive shortness of breath, mild chest pain on exertion, and a cough for 2 days. One week ago, he had a low-grade fever and nasal congestion. He has hypertension but does not adhere to his medication regimen. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years and drinks 3–4 beers daily. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 29/min, and blood pressure is 145/86 mm Hg. He is in moderate respiratory distress while sitting. Pulmonary examination shows reduced breath sounds bilaterally. There is scattered wheezing over all lung fields. There is inward displacement of his abdomen during inspiration. Arterial blood gas analysis shows:
pH 7.29
PCO2 63 mm Hg
PO2 71 mm Hg
HCO3- 29 mEq/L
O2 saturation 89%
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?"

answer_choices.C: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
answer_choices.D: Acute decompensatation of congestive heart failure

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, chronic cough, and dyspnea, along with physical examination findings of decreased breath sounds and wheezing, are suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The arterial blood gas findings of a low pH, high PCO2, and relatively normal bicarbonate level are indicative of acute respiratory acidosis, which is likely due to an acute exacerbation of his COPD. Acute exacerbations of COPD are most commonly caused by respiratory tract infections and are characterized by increased dyspnea, sputum production, and/or sputum purulence. This patient's recent history of a low-grade fever and nasal congestion suggests a recent viral upper respiratory tract infection, which could have precipitated his COPD exacerbation.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [A] > [D] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old man presents to the physician with a cough which he has had for the last 5 years. He also mentions that he has been feeling breathless when playing any active sport for the last 1 year. He is a manager in a corporate company and has been a regular smoker for 10 years. He has visited multiple physicians and undergone multiple diagnostic evaluations, without permanent benefit. On physical examination his temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), the heart rate is 88/min, the blood pressure is 122/80 mm Hg, and the respiratory rate is 20/min. Inspection suggests a barrel chest and auscultation reveals the presence of bilateral end-expiratory wheezing and scattered rhonchi. He undergoes a detailed diagnostic evaluation which includes a complete blood count, chest radiogram, arterial blood gas analysis, and pulmonary function tests, all of which confirm a diagnosis of chronic obstructive lung disease. After analyzing all the clinical information and diagnostic workup, the physician differentiates between emphysema and chronic bronchitis based on a single clue. Which of the following is the most likely clue that helped the physician in making the differential diagnosis?

answer_choices.A: History of long-term exposure to cigarette smoke
answer_choices.C: Presence of chronic respiratory acidosis in arterial blood gas analysis
answer_choices.D: Decreased diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO)

few_shot.explanation:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a common, preventable, and treatable disease characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities. It is usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases, the most common being cigarette smoke. COPD includes two main conditions - emphysema and chronic bronchitis. Emphysema is characterized by destruction of the alveolar walls leading to permanently enlarged air spaces, while chronic bronchitis is characterized by chronic productive cough for 3 months in each of 2 successive years in a patient in whom other causes of chronic cough have been excluded. 

While both conditions can coexist in the same patient, they can be differentiated based on certain clinical features and diagnostic findings. For example, patients with emphysema are usually thin and have decreased breath sounds on auscultation, while those with chronic bronchitis are usually overweight and have wheezing and rhonchi on auscultation. However, the most reliable way to differentiate between the two conditions is by measuring the diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO). DLCO is decreased in emphysema due to destruction of the alveolar walls, but is normal or increased in chronic bronchitis due to normal alveolar walls and increased pulmonary blood volume.

So, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [B] > [C] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough over the past 6 months. She has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the past 40 years. Chest auscultation shows scattered expiratory wheezes in both lung fields. Spirometry shows an FEV1:FVC ratio of 65% and an FEV1 of 70% of predicted. Her diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is 42% of predicted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, chronic dyspnea, and dry cough, along with the physical examination finding of wheezing and the spirometry results showing an obstructive pattern (FEV1:FVC <70% and FEV1 <80% of predicted), are suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is a disease of the airways characterized by chronic bronchitis and/or emphysema. Chronic bronchitis is defined as a chronic productive cough for 3 months in each of 2 successive years in a patient in whom other causes of chronic cough have been excluded. Emphysema is defined as abnormal permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls and without obvious fibrosis. The most common cause of COPD is smoking.

The decreased DLCO in this patient suggests emphysema as the primary pathology. In emphysema, destruction of the alveolar walls leads to decreased surface area for gas exchange, resulting in decreased DLCO. In contrast, patients with chronic bronchitis as the primary pathology usually have a normal DLCO.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [C] > [D] > [A].

question: An 81-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his son to be evaluated for memory issues. The patient’s son says he has difficulty remembering recent events and names. He says the patient’s symptoms have progressively worsened over the last several years but became acutely worse just recently. Also, yesterday, the patient complained that he could not see out of his right eye, but today he can. When asked about these concerns, the patient seems to have no insight into the problem and reports feeling well. His medical history is significant for diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypertension. He had a left basal ganglia hemorrhage 12 years ago and a right middle cerebral artery infarction 4 years ago. Current medications are amlodipine, aspirin, clopidogrel, metformin, sitagliptin, and valsartan. He lives with his son and can feed himself and change his clothes. There is no history of urinary or fecal incontinence. His vitals include: blood pressure 137/82 mm Hg, pulse 78/min, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F). On physical examination, the patient is alert and oriented. He is unable to perform simple arithmetic calculations and the mini-mental status exam is inconclusive. He can write his name and comprehend written instructions. Muscle strength is 4/5 on the right side. The tone is also slightly reduced on the right side with exaggerated reflexes. His gait is hemiparetic. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old man is brought to the physician by his wife for forgetfulness, confusion, and mood changes for the past 4 months. His symptoms started with misplacing items such as his wallet and keys around the house. Two months ago, he became unable to manage their finances as it became too difficult for him. Last week, he became lost while returning home from the grocery store. His wife reports that he shows “no emotion” and that he is seemingly not concerned by his recent symptoms. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease. Current medications include aspirin, metoprolol, lisinopril, metformin, and rosuvastatin. His pulse is 56/min and blood pressure is 158/76 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows loss of sensation on his right leg and an unsteady gait. When asked to stand with his eyes closed and palms facing upward, his right arm rotates inward. An MRI of the brain shows multiple deep white matter lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's cognitive impairment, gait instability, and asymmetric neurologic findings (eg, right-sided sensory loss, pronator drift) suggest a vascular etiology. Vascular dementia is the second most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer disease. It is caused by chronic ischemia, often due to uncontrolled hypertension, leading to damage in the brain. This is often seen as multiple infarcts or white matter lesions on neuroimaging. Patients often have a history of stroke or transient ischemic attack, although this is not always the case. The cognitive impairment in vascular dementia is often in a stepwise, fluctuating pattern, with plateaus and sudden declines corresponding to acute ischemic events. This is in contrast to the slow, steady decline seen in Alzheimer disease.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 66-year-old man is brought into the emergency department by his daughter for a change in behavior. Yesterday the patient seemed more confused than usual and was asking the same questions repetitively. His symptoms have not improved over the past 24 hours, thus the decision to bring him in today. Last year, the patient was almost completely independent but he then suffered a "series of falls," after which his ability to care for himself declined. After this episode he was no longer able to cook for himself or pay his bills but otherwise had been fine up until this episode. The patient has a past medical history of myocardial infarction, hypertension, depression, diabetes mellitus type II, constipation, diverticulitis, and peripheral neuropathy. His current medications include metformin, insulin, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, sodium docusate, atorvastatin, metoprolol, fluoxetine, and gabapentin. On exam you note a confused man who is poorly kept. He has bruises over his legs and his gait seems unstable. He is alert to person and place, and answers some questions inappropriately. The patient's pulse is 90/minute and his blood pressure is 170/100 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of multiple falls, hypertension, and myocardial infarction, along with his stepwise decline in cognitive function, is suggestive of vascular dementia. Vascular dementia is the second most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer's disease. It is caused by ischemic or hemorrhagic damage to the brain, leading to cognitive decline. The cognitive decline in vascular dementia is typically stepwise, with patients experiencing a sudden decline in function after a cerebrovascular event, followed by a period of stability. This is in contrast to Alzheimer's disease, in which cognitive decline is gradual and progressive. Other features that suggest vascular dementia over other causes of dementia include early executive dysfunction and late memory impairment.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old man is brought into clinic by his daughter for increasing confusion. The daughter states that over the past 2 weeks, she has noticed that the patient “seems to stare off into space.” She reports he has multiple episodes a day during which he will walk into a room and forget why. She is also worried about his balance. She endorses that he has had several falls, the worst being 3 weeks ago when he tripped on the sidewalk getting the mail. The patient denies loss of consciousness, pre-syncope, chest pain, palpitations, urinary incontinence, or bowel incontinence. He complains of headache but denies dizziness. He reports nausea and a few episodes of non-bloody emesis but denies abdominal pain, constipation, or diarrhea. The patient’s medical history is significant for atrial fibrillation, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. He takes aspirin, warfarin, insulin, lisinopril, simvastatin, and ibuprofen. He drinks a half glass of whisky after dinner every night and smokes a cigar on the weekends. On physical examination, he is oriented to name and place but not to date. He is unable to spell "world" backward. When asked to remember 3 words, he recalls only 2. There are no motor or sensory deficits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of falls, headache, nausea, vomiting, and progressive confusion is concerning for a subdural hematoma. Subdural hematomas are caused by tearing of the bridging veins that connect the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses. They are most commonly seen in elderly patients, alcoholics, and patients with a history of falls or head trauma. Risk factors include conditions that cause brain atrophy (eg, dementia, alcoholism), which stretch and make the bridging veins more susceptible to rupture. Anticoagulation, as in this patient, is also a risk factor. Subdural hematomas can present acutely, subacutely, or chronically, with the presentation depending on the size and rate of accumulation of the hematoma. Acute hematomas present with severe headache, focal neurologic deficits, and decreased level of consciousness. Chronic hematomas may present with nonspecific symptoms such as headache, mild confusion, and imbalance. The diagnosis is confirmed by neuroimaging (noncontrast head CT).

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old man is brought to clinic by his daughter for poor memory. She states that over the past two years his memory has been slowly declining though he has been able to take care of himself, pay his own rent, and manage his finances. However, two months ago she noticed a sharp decline in his cognitive functioning as well as his gait. Then one month ago, she noticed a similar decline in his functioning again that came on suddenly. The patient has a past medical history of diabetes mellitus type II, hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, metformin, and glipizide. His blood pressure is 165/95 mmHg, pulse is 82/minute, he is afebrile, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Cardiac exam reveals a crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard in the left upper sternal border that radiates to the carotids. Abdominal exam is benign, and neurologic exam reveals an unsteady gait. Which of the following findings is associated with the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of hypertension, diabetes, and obesity, along with his stepwise decline in cognitive function, is suggestive of vascular dementia. This is the second most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer's disease. It is caused by multiple lacunar infarcts, which are small infarcts in the deeper parts of the brain (basal ganglia, thalamus, white matter) and in the brain stem. These infarcts are often clinically silent, but over time lead to significant brain damage. The stepwise decline in cognitive function is a key feature that distinguishes vascular dementia from most other forms of dementia.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question:
A 68-year-old man seeks evaluation by a physician with complaints of worsening forgetfulness and confusion for 1 year. According to his wife, he has always been in good health and is generally very happy; however, he has started to forget important things. He recently had his driving license revoked because of multiple tickets, but he cannot recall having done anything wrong. This morning, he neglected to put on his socks and was quite agitated when she pointed this out to him. He denies having a depressed mood, sleep problems, or loss of interest. He occasionally has a glass of wine with dinner and has never smoked or used recreational drugs. His medical history and family medical history are unremarkable. His pulse is 68/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. Except for a mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score of 20/30, the remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Imaging studies, including a chest X-ray and CT of the brain, reveal no pathologic findings. An electrocardiogram (ECG) is also normal. Laboratory testing showed the following:
Serum glucose (fasting) 76 mg/dL
Serum electrolytes:  
Sodium 140 mEq/L
Potassium 4.1 mEq/L
Chloride 100 mEq/L
Serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
Blood urea nitrogen 11 mg/dL
Cholesterol, total: 180 mg/dL
HDL-cholesterol 45 mg/dL
LDL-cholesterol 75 mg/dL
Triglycerides 135 mg/dL
Hemoglobin (Hb%) 16 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  85 fL
Reticulocyte count 0.9%
Erythrocyte count 5 million/mm³
Thyroid-stimulating hormone 3.5 µU/mL
Urinalysis 
Glucose Negative
Ketones Negative
Leucocytes Negative
Nitrite Negative
RBCs Negative
Casts Negative
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's forgetfulness, confusion, and agitation, along with a low MMSE score, are suggestive of dementia. The most common cause of dementia is Alzheimer's disease, which is characterized by an insidious onset and gradual progression of impairment in memory and at least one other cognitive domain (eg, executive function, visuospatial ability, language). Early in the disease, patients often have difficulty with recent memory and executive function, which can manifest as repetitive questioning, frequently misplacing items, and difficulty managing finances. As the disease progresses, patients develop worsening amnesia, aphasia, and agnosia (inability to interpret sensations). Behavioral changes such as agitation, aggression, wandering, and psychosis can also occur. The diagnosis is clinical, and neuroimaging is typically performed to rule out other causes of dementia (eg, brain tumor, normal pressure hydrocephalus, vascular dementia). In this patient, the insidious onset, gradual progression, and lack of focal neurologic deficits are most suggestive of Alzheimer's disease.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician because of episodic pelvic pain radiating to her back and thighs for 4 months. The pain occurs a few hours before her menstrual period and lasts for 2 days. She has been taking ibuprofen, which has provided some relief. Menses have occurred at regular 28-day intervals since menarche at the age of 12 years and last for 5 to 6 days. She is sexually active with two male partners and uses condoms inconsistently. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.A: Endometrial sloughing and uterine contractions mediated by prostaglandin
answer_choices.B: Ascending infection of the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, or surrounding tissue
answer_choices.D: Hormone-sensitive smooth muscle tumor of the myometrium

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist for painful menses. Her menses are regular, occurring every 28 days and lasting approximately 4 days. Menarche was at age 12. Over the past 6 months, she has started to develop aching pelvic pain during the first 2 days of her menstrual period. Ibuprofen provides moderate relief of her symptoms. She denies nausea, vomiting, dyschezia, dyspareunia, irregular menses, or menses that are heavier than usual. Her past medical history is notable for chlamydia 4 years ago that was treated appropriately. She currently takes no medications. She works as a copywriter and does not smoke or drink. She has been in a monogamous relationship with her boyfriend for the past 3 years. They use condoms intermittently. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 111/69 mmHg, pulse is 92/min, and respirations are 18/min. Pelvic examination demonstrates a normal appearing vagina with no adnexal or cervical motion tenderness. The uterus is flexible and anteverted. Which of the following is the underlying cause of this patient's pain?

answer_choices.A: Endometrial gland invasion into the uterine myometrium

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's regular menses, normal pelvic examination, and absence of other symptoms (eg, dyspareunia, dyschezia, heavy menses) suggest primary dysmenorrhea, which is caused by increased endometrial production of prostaglandins. Prostaglandins are released from the endometrium at the onset of menses when progesterone levels fall, leading to increased myometrial tone and uterine contractions. This results in the crampy lower abdominal pain that is characteristic of primary dysmenorrhea. The pain typically begins at or shortly after the onset of menses and lasts 8-72 hours. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are first-line treatment for primary dysmenorrhea. NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase, thereby decreasing the production of prostaglandins.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has been unable to conceive for 2 years. The patient also reports monthly episodes of pelvic and back pain accompanied by painful diarrhea for 6 years. She takes naproxen for the pain, which has provided some relief. Menses have occurred at regular 28-day intervals since menarche at the age of 11 years and last for 7 days. She is sexually active with her husband and does not use contraception. Pelvic and rectal examination shows no abnormalities. A hysterosalpingogram is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.A: Endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity
answer_choices.B: Smooth muscle tumor arising from the myometrium

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility is suggestive of endometriosis, which is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. The most common sites of involvement are the ovaries, uterosacral ligaments, and the pouch of Douglas. The cyclic bleeding of these ectopic endometrial implants during menstruation can cause fibrosis and adhesions, leading to chronic pelvic pain. The implants can also involve the bowel, causing painful defecation. The definitive diagnosis of endometriosis requires laparoscopy, but the clinical history is often suggestive.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician because of episodic lower abdominal pain for 5 months. The pain starts to occur a few hours before her menses and lasts for 2–3 days. Ibuprofen helped reduce the pain in the first months but has no effect now. She has missed a couple of days at school because of severe pain. Menarche was at the age of 14 years, and menses occur at regular 29-day intervals. She is sexually active with one male partner and uses condoms inconsistently. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Physical and pelvic examination show no abnormalities. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's cyclical lower abdominal pain that begins a few hours before menses and lasts for 2-3 days is consistent with primary dysmenorrhea. Primary dysmenorrhea is caused by increased endometrial production of prostaglandins, leading to increased uterine tone and strong, painful uterine contractions. It is a common cause of pelvic pain in adolescents and typically begins within years of menarche, after the establishment of regular ovulatory cycles. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are first-line treatment for primary dysmenorrhea because they inhibit prostaglandin synthesis. However, if symptoms persist despite NSAID therapy, combined oral contraceptives are the next step in management. Combined oral contraceptives work by suppressing ovulation and decreasing menstrual flow, thereby reducing the amount of endometrial tissue that produces prostaglandins.

Therefore, the answer is [C].
