few_shot.question: A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presents to her gynecologist complaining of recurrent menstrual pain. She reports a 4-month history of pelvic pain that occurs during her periods. It is more severe than her typical menstrual cramps and sometimes occurs when she is not on her period. She also complains of pain during intercourse. Her periods occur every 28-30 days. Her past medical history is notable for kyphoscoliosis requiring spinal fusion and severe acne rosacea. She takes trans-tretinoin and has a copper intra-uterine device. Her family history is notable for ovarian cancer in her mother and endometrial cancer in her paternal grandmother. Her temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 120/85 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 16/min. On exam, she appears healthy and is in no acute distress. A bimanual examination demonstrates a normal sized uterus and a tender right adnexal mass. Her intrauterine device is well-positioned. What is the underlying cause of this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.B: Chronic inflammation of the uterine endometrium
answer_choices.C: Endometrial glands and stroma within the peritoneal cavity
answer_choices.D: Endometrial glands and stroma within the uterine myometrium

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and pelvic pain are suggestive of endometriosis, which is characterized by the presence of endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity. The most common sites of involvement are the ovaries, uterosacral ligaments, and the pouch of Douglas. The disease is common in women of reproductive age and is a major cause of infertility. The pathogenesis of endometriosis is not completely understood, but retrograde menstruation is the most widely accepted theory. This theory proposes that viable endometrial cells are refluxed through the fallopian tubes during menstruation and implant on peritoneal surfaces. Other theories include coelomic metaplasia (metaplasia of the coelomic epithelium that lines the abdominopelvic cavity and female reproductive tract) and lymphatic dissemination.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [D] > [B] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 43-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of increased flow and duration of her menses. Menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals and lasted 5 days with normal flow. They now last 8–9 days and the flow is heavy with the passage of clots. During this period, she has also had lower abdominal pain that begins 2–3 days prior to onset of her menses and lasts for 2 days after the end of her menses. She has three children. Her mother died of endometrial cancer at the age of 61 years. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 86/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a uniformly enlarged, boggy uterus consistent in size with an 8-week gestation that is tender on palpation. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?

answer_choices.B: Endometrial tissue within the uterine wall

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia, and a uniformly enlarged uterus are suggestive of adenomyosis. Adenomyosis is a benign condition characterized by the presence of ectopic endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, with adjacent myometrial hypertrophy. It is most common in multiparous women aged 40–50. The pathogenesis is not well understood, but it is thought to result from invagination of the endometrial basalis layer into the myometrium, with a possible role of local hyperestrogenism. The ectopic endometrial tissue within the myometrium responds to normal hormonal changes during the menstrual cycle, leading to cyclic bleeding within the myometrium. This causes myometrial hypertrophy and hyperplasia, resulting in a diffusely enlarged uterus. The most common symptoms are dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia, which are thought to result from the increased menstrual bleeding and uterine distention. On examination, the uterus is often described as "boggy" or globular and may be tender.

question: A 16-year-old male presents to his pediatrician with complaints of malaise, fatigue, sore throat, and fever over the last several days. His vital signs are as follows: T 39.1 C, HR 82, BP 122/76, RR 14, and SpO2 99%. Physical examination is significant for splenomegaly, tonsillar exudate, and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy. The tonsils are not notably enlarged. Laboratory work-up shows an elevated lymphocyte count, atypical lymphocytes on a peripheral blood smear, and a positive heterophile antibody screen. few_shot.question: A 16-year-old boy comes to the physician with a 4-day history of sore throat and mild fever. He is on the varsity soccer team at his high school, but has been unable to go to practice for the last few days because he has been very tired and is easily exhausted. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His mother has type 2 diabetes mellitus. He appears weak and lethargic. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 116/78 mm Hg. Examination shows enlarged, erythematous, and exudative tonsils; posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is present. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. His hemoglobin concentration is 14.5 g/dL and leukocyte count is 11,200/mm3 with 48% lymphocytes. A heterophile antibody test is positive. In addition to supportive therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.A: Write a medical note that excuses from soccer events

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sore throat, fever, malaise, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and positive heterophile antibody test are consistent with infectious mononucleosis (IM) due to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). IM is a self-limited illness that typically resolves within 4 weeks, although malaise and fatigue can persist for several months. Treatment is supportive and includes rest, hydration, and analgesics for fever and sore throat.

Patients with IM are at risk for splenic rupture, which can occur spontaneously but is often associated with trauma. Splenic rupture typically presents with a sudden onset of severe left upper quadrant abdominal pain that can radiate to the left shoulder (Kehr sign). Hypotension and tachycardia may also be present due to intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Therefore, patients with IM should avoid contact sports and heavy lifting for at least 3-4 weeks, and until there is no palpable splenomegaly.

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a fever and a sore throat. He has had these symptoms for the past 2 weeks and has felt progressively more fatigued. His temperature is 102°F (38.9°C), blood pressure is 120/68 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. This patient's fever, sore throat, fatigue, tonsillar exudates, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly are suggestive of infectious mononucleosis (IM). The most appropriate next step in management is to confirm the diagnosis with a heterophile antibody (Monospot) test, which has high sensitivity and specificity for IM in this age group.

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician for evaluation of a sore throat. The sore throat began 4 days ago and has progressively worsened. Associated symptoms include subjective fever, pain with swallowing, cough, and fatigue. The patient denies any cough or rhinorrhea. Vital signs are as follows: T 38.6 C, HR 88, BP 115/67, RR 14, and SpO2 99%. Physical examination is significant for purulent tonsillar exudate; no cervical lymphadenopathy is noted. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is concerning for streptococcal pharyngitis (group A Streptococcus). The Centor criteria can be used to estimate the pretest probability of streptococcal pharyngitis in patients with a sore throat. The criteria include fever, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, absence of cough, and age <15 years. Each criterion is worth 1 point, and patients with a score of 4 have a 51%-53% likelihood of streptococcal pharyngitis. This patient has a score of 4, and therefore, the next best step in management is to perform a rapid antigen detection test (RADT) to confirm the diagnosis. If the RADT is negative, a throat culture should be performed to definitively rule out streptococcal pharyngitis. If the RADT is positive, the patient should be treated with antibiotics to prevent complications such as rheumatic fever.

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy comes to the physician because of a generalized rash for 3 days. Over the past 5 days, he has also had a high fever and a sore throat. His 16-year-old sister was treated for infectious mononucleosis 2 weeks ago. He returned from a summer camp a week ago. His immunizations are up-to-date. Three years ago, he required intubation after an allergic reaction to dicloxacillin. The patient appears ill. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). Examination shows circumferential oral pallor. Cervical lymphadenopathy is present. There is tonsillar erythema and exudate. A confluent, blanching, punctate erythematous rash with a rough texture is spread over his trunk and extremities. His hemoglobin concentration is 13.3 g/dL, leukocyte count is 12,000/mm3, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 43 mm/h. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy, and rash is consistent with group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis. GAS pharyngitis is most common in children age 5-15 and often occurs in the winter and spring. The rash of GAS infection (scarlet fever) is characterized by numerous erythematous papules that feel like sandpaper. The rash typically starts on the neck and chest and then becomes generalized; it spares the perioral area, causing circumoral pallor. The tonsils are usually erythematous and may have exudates. Strawberry tongue (prominent red papillae on a bright red tongue) may also be present. 

The treatment of choice for GAS pharyngitis is penicillin or amoxicillin. However, this patient has a history of a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a penicillin antibiotic (dicloxacillin). Therefore, he should not receive a beta-lactam antibiotic due to the risk of cross-reactivity. Instead, he should receive a macrolide antibiotic such as azithromycin.

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old girl presents with a sore throat. The patient says symptoms onset acutely 3 days ago and have progressively worsened. She denies any history of cough, nasal congestion or rhinorrhea. No significant past medical history or current medications. The vital signs include: temperature 37.7°C (99.9°F), blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, pulse 74/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination is significant for anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. There is edema of the oropharynx and tonsillar swelling but no tonsillar exudate. Which of the following is the next best step in management?

answer_choices.B: Ultrasound of the anterior cervical lymph nodes

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute onset sore throat, tonsillar swelling, and anterior cervical lymphadenopathy is suggestive of acute pharyngitis. The most common cause of acute pharyngitis is viral infection, but group A Streptococcus (GAS) is the most common bacterial cause. GAS pharyngitis is more common in children and adolescents and typically presents with sore throat, fever, headache, and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Tonsillar exudate and petechiae may be present but are not required for diagnosis. The absence of cough, rhinorrhea, and oral ulcers makes viral pharyngitis less likely.

The Centor criteria (fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, absence of cough, age <15) can be used to estimate the pretest probability of GAS pharyngitis. Patients with a Centor score of 2 or 3, like this patient, should undergo rapid antigen detection testing (RADT). If the RADT is negative, a throat culture should be performed to definitively rule out GAS pharyngitis, as the RADT has high specificity but only moderate sensitivity. Patients with a Centor score of 4 can be empirically treated with antibiotics, but some clinicians may still choose to confirm the diagnosis with RADT or throat culture.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 47-year-old man with a history of HIV1 infection presents to his HIV clinic to discuss his antiretroviral medications. He is interested in including maraviroc in his maintenance regimen after seeing advertisements about the medication. On exam, his temperature is 98.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 116/74 mmHg, pulse is 64/min, and respirations are 12/min. His viral load is undetectable on his current regimen, and his blood count, electrolytes, and liver function tests have all been within normal limits. In order to consider maraviroc for therapy, a tropism assay needs to be performed. Which of the following receptors is affected by the use of maraviroc?

few_shot.question: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Ten months ago, he was diagnosed with HIV infection and appropriate antiretroviral therapy was initiated. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show increased viral load despite ongoing treatment. His pharmacotherapy is switched to a new combination drug regimen including an agent that binds to glycoprotein 41. The expected effect of this drug is most likely due to inhibition of which of the following?

answer_choices.B: Viral docking and attachment to host cells
answer_choices.D: Viral fusion and entry into host cells

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's new antiretroviral regimen includes an agent that binds to glycoprotein 41 (gp41), a transmembrane protein on the HIV envelope. This class of drugs, known as fusion inhibitors, prevents the virus from entering host cells. The only drug in this class that is currently available is enfuvirtide.

Fusion of the HIV envelope with the host cell membrane is mediated by gp41 and another envelope protein, gp120. The process begins when gp120 binds to the host cell CD4 receptor, inducing a conformational change in gp120 that allows it to bind to a chemokine receptor (either CCR5 or CXCR4) on the host cell. This, in turn, induces a conformational change in gp41 that enables it to insert into the host cell membrane and promote fusion of the viral and cell membranes. Fusion inhibitors bind to gp41 and prevent the conformational change necessary for fusion, thereby blocking viral entry into the cell.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 49-year-old homeless man comes to the emergency department because of fatigue, cough, and worsening shortness of breath for 2 weeks. He was diagnosed with HIV-infection 25 years ago but has never had any symptoms. He has always refused to take antiretroviral medication. Pulmonary examination shows diffuse crackles over bilateral lower lung fields. An x-ray of the chest shows diffuse, symmetrical interstitial infiltrates. His serum level of beta-d-glucan is elevated. Further testing shows a heterozygous mutation that prevents entry of HIV into macrophages. Which of the following proteins is most likely affected by the mutation in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of untreated HIV infection, homelessness, and pulmonary symptoms, along with the finding of diffuse interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray, suggest Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). PJP is an opportunistic infection that occurs in patients with severe immunosuppression, such as those with untreated HIV/AIDS. The diagnosis is supported by the elevated serum level of beta-d-glucan, a component of the PJP cell wall.

The fact that this patient has survived for 25 years without antiretroviral therapy or opportunistic infections suggests that he may have a mutation in CCR5, a chemokine receptor on the surface of T cells and macrophages that is used by HIV to gain entry into these cells. CCR5 is the most common co-receptor that HIV uses to enter cells, along with the CD4 receptor. A 32-base pair deletion in the CCR5 gene (CCR5-delta32) results in a receptor that is not expressed on the cell surface, preventing HIV entry into the cell and conferring resistance to HIV infection. Homozygotes for this mutation are almost completely protected against HIV infection, while heterozygotes, like this patient, experience slower progression of disease.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 44-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Eight months ago, he was diagnosed with HIV infection and combined antiretroviral treatment was begun. He feels well. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. Current medications include lamivudine, zidovudine, atazanavir, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 102 μm3
Leukocyte count 2,600/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 38%
Lymphocytes 54%
Platelet count 150,000/mm3
Serum
Folate normal
Lactate 6.0 mEq/L (N = 0.5–2.2)
Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows:
pH 7.34
pCO2 55 mm Hg
pO2 99 mmHg
HCO3- 14 mEq/L
The drug most likely responsible for this patient's current laboratory findings belongs to which of the following classes of drugs?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's anemia, neutropenia, and elevated lactate level are suggestive of bone marrow suppression and lactic acidosis, both of which are toxicities associated with the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) class of antiretroviral drugs. NRTIs, which include agents such as zidovudine, lamivudine, and abacavir, cause DNA chain termination by acting as faulty substrates for the viral reverse transcriptase enzyme. 

Zidovudine, in particular, has been associated with significant bone marrow suppression, manifesting as anemia, neutropenia, or both. Additionally, NRTIs can cause a potentially life-threatening lactic acidosis, usually associated with hepatic steatosis. This is due to NRTIs' ability to inhibit human DNA polymerase gamma, the enzyme responsible for replication of mitochondrial DNA. This leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and decreased oxidative metabolism, resulting in overproduction and underutilization of lactate.

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old sexually active male presents to an internal medicine physician for a routine health check up after having several unprotected sexual encounters. Which of the following medications prescribed acts on the gp41 subunit of the HIV envelope glycoprotein?

Enfuvirtide is an HIV fusion inhibitor that acts on the gp41 subunit of the HIV envelope glycoprotein. It is used in combination with other antiretroviral agents for the treatment of HIV-1 infection. It is usually reserved for patients with multidrug-resistant HIV or intolerance to other regimens due to its inconvenient administration (subcutaneous injection) and high cost.

few_shot.question: A physician scientist is looking for a more efficient way to treat HIV. Patients infected with HIV mount a humoral immune response by producing antibodies against the HIV envelope proteins. These antibodies are the same antibodies detected by the ELISA and western blot assays used to diagnose the disease. The physician scientist is trying to generate a new, more potent antibody against the same HIV envelope proteins targeted by the natural humoral immune response. Of the following proteins, which is the most likely target of the antibody he is designing?
few_shot.explanation:
The envelope of HIV is composed of a lipid bilayer derived from the host cell membrane, studded with viral envelope proteins. The envelope proteins are responsible for the initial attachment of the virus to the host cell, and are the primary target of the humoral immune response. The envelope proteins are composed of two noncovalently associated subunits: gp120 and gp41. The gp120 protein is responsible for the initial attachment of the virus to the host cell by binding to the CD4 receptor. After gp120 binds to CD4, a conformational change occurs that allows gp120 to bind to a chemokine receptor (either CCR5 or CXCR4). This second binding event triggers a second conformational change that allows gp41 to mediate fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane. Because gp120 is the protein that mediates the initial attachment of the virus to the host cell, it is the most likely target of the antibody being designed by the physician scientist.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A obstetrician is working in a developing country to help promote maternal health and fetal well being. While there, he delivers a baby who he suspects has congenital hypothyroidism, most likely caused by inadequate maternal iodine intake. Which of the following signs and symptoms would NOT be expected to be observed in this child?

few_shot.question: A 3-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after his mother found him to be extremely lethargic. He was born at home with no prenatal care and has no documented medical history. On presentation, he is found to have shorter stature and increased weight compared to normal infants as well as coarse facial features. Physical exam reveals a large protruding tongue and an umbilical hernia. The patient otherwise appears normal. Laboratory tests confirm the diagnosis, and the patient is started on appropriate treatment. The physician counsels the parents that despite initiation of treatment, the boy may have lasting mental retardation. Which of the following is most likely associated with the cause of this patient's disorder?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's coarse facial features, large protruding tongue, umbilical hernia, and developmental delay are suggestive of congenital hypothyroidism. The most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism worldwide is iodine deficiency, but in the United States and other developed countries, most cases are due to thyroid dysgenesis (eg, agenesis, ectopy, hypoplasia). Other causes include inherited defects in thyroid hormone biosynthesis and maternal ingestion of antithyroid drugs.

Newborns are typically asymptomatic due to transplacental passage of maternal thyroid hormone. Symptoms usually begin after the first few months of life, when the infant's own thyroid hormone production becomes critical for growth and development. If left untreated, congenital hypothyroidism can lead to severe mental retardation and growth failure (cretinism).

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 1-month-old male newborn is brought to the physician because of poor feeding, a hoarse cry, and lethargy for 1 week. The boy was born in Mozambique, from where he and his parents emigrated 2 weeks ago. He is at the 95th percentile for head circumference, 50th percentile for length, and 70th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows scleral icterus, an enlarged tongue, and generalized hypotonia. The abdomen is distended and there is a reducible, soft protruding mass at the umbilicus. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's poor feeding, lethargy, hoarse cry, and hypotonia are suggestive of hypothyroidism. The presence of an enlarged tongue (macroglossia) and umbilical hernia are also consistent with this diagnosis. The most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism is thyroid dysgenesis (eg, thyroid agenesis, ectopic thyroid gland, or thyroid hypoplasia). In iodine-sufficient parts of the world, thyroid dysgenesis accounts for 85% of congenital hypothyroidism cases. In iodine-deficient parts of the world, maternal iodine deficiency is the most common cause. This patient is from Mozambique, a country with a high prevalence of iodine deficiency. However, the presence of an enlarged head circumference (macrocephaly) is not typically seen in iodine deficiency and suggests that thyroid dysgenesis is the more likely etiology in this patient.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 26-day-old newborn is brought to the physician because of poor feeding and lethargy for 2 weeks. During this period, he has had a raspy cry. The child was delivered at term at home and has not yet been evaluated by a physician. He is at the 90th percentile for head circumference, 50th percentile for length, and 60th percentile for weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows scleral icterus and an enlarged tongue. The abdomen is distended and there is a reducible, soft protruding mass at the umbilicus. Muscle tone is decreased in all extremities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has findings consistent with congenital hypothyroidism (CH), which is most commonly caused by thyroid dysgenesis (eg, thyroid agenesis, ectopic thyroid gland). CH is characterized by poor feeding, lethargy, macroglossia, a hoarse cry, constipation, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, and a large posterior fontanelle. An umbilical hernia may also be present. If not treated promptly, CH can lead to severe intellectual disability and growth retardation (cretinism).

few_shot.question: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 40 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in active labor. Her first pregnancy and delivery were complicated by iron deficiency anemia and pregnancy-induced hypertension. She has had no routine prenatal care during this pregnancy but was diagnosed with oligohydramnios 4 weeks ago. The remainder of her medical history is not immediately available. A 2400-g (5.4-lb) female newborn is delivered vaginally. Examination of the newborn shows a short, mildly webbed neck and low-set ears. Ocular hypertelorism along with slanted palpebral fissures are noted. A cleft palate and hypoplasia of the nails and distal phalanges are present. There is increased coarse hair on the body and face. Which of the following best explains the clinical findings found in this newborn?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn's findings of growth retardation, craniofacial abnormalities (eg, ocular hypertelorism, slanted palpebral fissures, cleft palate), hypoplasia of the nails and distal phalanges, and hirsutism are consistent with fetal hydantoin syndrome, which is caused by in utero exposure to phenytoin. Phenytoin is used in the treatment of seizures, and it is associated with a distinct pattern of malformations when used during pregnancy. The risk of major malformations in infants exposed to phenytoin in utero is approximately 10%, compared with 2%-3% in the general population. The risk of malformations is highest with first-trimester exposure, but exposure later in pregnancy can also cause growth retardation and other abnormalities.

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old woman delivers a girl by normal vaginal delivery, Apgar scores are 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes respectively. The newborn’s vitals are normal. On examination, the attending pediatrician finds a circular skin defect that measures 0.5 cm in diameter. The defect is hairless and extends into the dermis. The delivery was atraumatic and there were no surgical instruments in the area. The pediatric team believes this is a congenital defect. The remaining examination is normal. The mother gives past history of having constant diarrhea for 3 months about 2 years ago, weight loss of 5 kg (11 lb) in 3 months, palpitations, and sensitivity to heat. She visited a community hospital and was prescribed a medication for this problem. She did not visit the hospital for any of her routine check-ups and continued taking her medications. Which drug can predispose the newborn to this condition?
few_shot.explanation:
The newborn has a congenital skin defect, which is most likely aplasia cutis congenita (ACC). ACC is a rare condition characterized by localized or widespread areas of absent skin, typically presenting as solitary defects on the scalp vertex. The defects are usually round or oval, well-demarcated, and can vary in size. The base of the defect can be a thin, transparent membrane (epithelial or subepithelial tissue) or it can be deep, extending to the skull or dura. The hair surrounding the defect is often twisted in a clockwise direction, forming a hair collar sign. The exact cause of ACC is unknown, but it has been associated with methimazole use during pregnancy. Methimazole is an antithyroid drug used to treat hyperthyroidism. It is associated with a specific embryopathy that includes ACC, choanal or esophageal atresia, and minor anomalies (eg, dysmorphic facies, hypoplastic digits). Propylthiouracil, another antithyroid drug, is not associated with ACC and is therefore the preferred antithyroid drug for symptomatic control in the first trimester of pregnancy.

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of severe acne vulgaris over her face, upper back, arms, and buttocks. This medication decreases the patient's risk developing of which of the following conditions?

few_shot.question: An otherwise healthy 18-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of severe acne vulgaris over her face, upper back, and arms. Treatment with oral antibiotics and topical combination therapy with benzoyl peroxide and retinoid has not completely resolved her symptoms. Examination shows oily skin with numerous comedones, pustules, and scarring over the face and upper back. Long-term therapy is started with combined oral contraceptives. This medication significantly reduces the risk of developing which of the following conditions?
few_shot.explanation:
Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) are used for contraception and to treat a variety of gynecologic conditions (eg, dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia, polycystic ovary syndrome). COCs are also used to treat severe acne vulgaris that is unresponsive to other treatments, as in this patient. COCs decrease the production of ovarian androgens and increase sex hormone-binding globulin, which binds free testosterone in the circulation, thereby reducing sebum production.

COCs have several noncontraceptive health benefits. They decrease the risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer, benign breast disease, pelvic inflammatory disease, and iron deficiency anemia. The risk reduction for endometrial and ovarian cancer persists for many years after discontinuation of COCs.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old woman makes an appointment with a dermatologist for treatment of acne. As a result, she feels uncomfortable in public and feels as though everyone is looking at the pimples on her face. She cleans her face several times a day with face wash and avoids using make-up. She has tried many face creams and scar removal creams to help improve the condition of her skin, but nothing has worked. On examination, she has pustular acne on her cheeks and forehead. The physician prescribes an antibiotic along with isotretinoin. Which of the following drugs would you recommend in conjunction with isotretinoin?
few_shot.explanation:
Isotretinoin is a retinoid that is used to treat severe acne. It works by reducing the size and output of sebaceous glands and by making the cells that are sloughed off into the sebaceous glands less sticky, thereby reducing the risk of pore clogging and preventing the formation of new pimples. However, isotretinoin is a known teratogen and can cause severe birth defects. Therefore, it is recommended that women of childbearing age who are prescribed isotretinoin also use two forms of contraception, one of which is typically an oral contraceptive.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician for evaluation of severe acne on her face, chest, and back for the past 2 years. She has no itching or scaling. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they use condoms inconsistently. She does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. few_shot.explanation:

Isotretinoin works by decreasing the size and secretions of the sebaceous glands, inhibiting sebocyte differentiation and proliferation, and inhibiting androgen production. However, isotretinoin is teratogenic and can cause severe birth defects. Therefore, it is important to confirm that the patient is not pregnant before starting therapy. question:

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever and disorientation. Examination shows jaundice, palmar erythema, spider nevi on his chest, dilated veins on the anterior abdominal wall, and 2+ edema of the lower extremities. The abdomen is soft and diffusely tender; there is shifting dullness to percussion. His albumin is 1.4 g/dL, bilirubin is 5 mg/dL, and prothrombin time is 31 seconds (INR = 3.3). Hepatitis serology is negative. A CT scan of the abdomen is shown. Which of the following processes is the most likely explanation for these findings?

answer_choices.B: Ground-glass hepatocytes with cytotoxic T cells
answer_choices.D: Misfolded protein aggregates in hepatocellular endoplasmic reticulum

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of heavy alcohol use, physical examination findings (eg, jaundice, palmar erythema, spider nevi, caput medusae, ascites, peripheral edema), and laboratory results (eg, hypoalbuminemia, hyperbilirubinemia, coagulopathy) are consistent with cirrhosis and its complications. The CT scan shows a nodular liver contour, which is characteristic of cirrhosis. Cirrhosis is characterized histologically by the presence of regenerative nodules of hepatocytes surrounded by dense fibrotic bands. This disrupts the normal liver architecture, leading to hepatocellular dysfunction and increased intrahepatic vascular resistance.

few_shot.question:
A 54-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of abdominal distension for the past 3 weeks. He also complains of generalized abdominal discomfort associated with nausea and decreased appetite. He was discharged from the hospital 3 months ago after an inguinal hernia repair with no reported complications. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, congestive heart failure, and untreated hepatitis C. His current medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, lisinopril, and metformin. His father has a history of alcoholic liver disease. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years but quit 5 years ago. He drinks 3–4 beers daily. He appears cachectic. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a distended abdomen and shifting dullness. There is no abdominal tenderness or palpable masses. There is a well-healed surgical scar in the right lower quadrant. Examination of the heart and lung shows no abnormalities. He has 1+ bilateral lower extremity nonpitting edema. Diagnostic paracentesis is performed. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 10 g/dL
Leukocyte count 14,000/mm3
Platelet count 152,000/mm3
Serum

Albumin 3.5 g/dL

Peritoneal fluid analysis
Color Cloudy

Albumin 2.6 g/dL

Peritoneal fluid Gram stain is negative. Culture and cytology results are pending. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal distension, shifting dullness, and a cloudy peritoneal fluid with a lymphocytic predominance is suggestive of chylous ascites. Chylous ascites is characterized by the accumulation of lymph in the peritoneal cavity, which gives the fluid a milky appearance. The fluid is rich in triglycerides, which is confirmed by the markedly elevated triglyceride level in this patient's peritoneal fluid. The most common causes of chylous ascites are malignancies (eg, lymphoma), liver cirrhosis, and infections (eg, tuberculosis, filariasis). In developed countries, the most common cause is malignancy, particularly lymphoma, which can obstruct the lymphatic system and cause leakage of lymph into the peritoneal cavity.

few_shot.question:
A 48-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of a 3-day history of increasing confusion and lethargy. He complains of decreased urine output and abdominal pain for the past month. Two months ago, he was hospitalized for pyelonephritis and treated with ceftriaxone. He has a history of chronic hepatitis C. He does not take any medications. He appears pale and irritable. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. On mental status examination, he is oriented to person but not to time or place. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and jaundice. There is 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities. The abdomen is distended with a positive fluid wave. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL
Leukocyte count 4300/mm3
Platelet count 89,000/mm3
Prothrombin time 19 sec
Serum
Urea nitrogen 71 mg/dL
Glucose 99 mg/dL
Creatinine 3.5 mg/dL
ALT 137 mg/dL
AST 154 mg/dL
Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. The FeNa is < 1%. Ultrasound of the kidneys is unremarkable. Intravenous fluids are administered for 36 hours but do not improve urine output. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the kidney dysfunction in this patient?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic hepatitis C, jaundice, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, and ascites is suggestive of cirrhosis. The kidney dysfunction (elevated blood urea nitrogen and creatinine) in the setting of cirrhosis is most likely due to hepatorenal syndrome (HRS). HRS is a functional renal impairment with hallmark findings of low urine sodium (<10 mEq/L) and bland urine sediment. It is caused by renal vasoconstriction resulting from splanchnic arterial vasodilation, which leads to decreased renal perfusion. The splanchnic arterial vasodilation is due to increased nitric oxide production in the setting of advanced liver disease. HRS typically occurs in patients with advanced cirrhosis and ascites, often after a precipitating event such as gastrointestinal bleeding, infection (eg, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), or diuretic use. The renal vasoconstriction in HRS is a component of a systemic response to try to maintain perfusion pressure in the setting of the vasodilatory state. Unfortunately, the renal vasoconstriction can become severe enough to cause renal hypoperfusion and acute kidney injury. 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 49-year-old man presents to the emergency department with abdominal discomfort, fever, and decreased urination. He has a history of liver cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C infection. His blood pressure is 90/70 mm Hg, pulse is 75/min, and temperature 38°C (100.4°F). On physical examination he is jaundiced, and he has tense ascites with generalized abdominal tenderness. There is pitting edema to the level of his upper thighs. Which of the following excludes the diagnosis of hepatorenal syndrome in this patient?

answer_choices.D: Presence of 30 red cells/high powered field in the urine

few_shot.explanation:
Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a functional renal failure that occurs in patients with advanced liver disease. It is characterized by renal vasoconstriction leading to decreased glomerular filtration rate. The diagnosis of HRS is one of exclusion and requires the presence of advanced liver disease with ascites, low glomerular filtration rate (creatinine >1.5 mg/dL), absence of shock, no current or recent treatment with nephrotoxic drugs, and absence of parenchymal kidney disease (no proteinuria, no hematuria, and normal renal ultrasound). The presence of 30 red cells/high powered field in the urine of this patient suggests intrinsic renal disease and excludes the diagnosis of HRS.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

Past medical history is unremarkable. He reports heavy alcohol consumption for the past several years but says he quit recently. ALD encompasses a spectrum of conditions associated with chronic alcohol use, including hepatic steatosis, alcoholic hepatitis, and alcoholic cirrhosis. The patient's AST:ALT ratio >2 is also suggestive of ALD. The thrombocytopenia is likely due to splenic sequestration secondary to portal hypertension, which is a complication of cirrhosis. The patient's iron studies are normal, making hemochromatosis unlikely. Chronic viral hepatitis typically presents with a more indolent course and would not explain the patient's gynecomastia. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is unlikely in the setting of heavy alcohol use.

question: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician for intermittent stabbing face pain. The pain typically occurs in waves of several individual episodes lasting about one second. It is bilateral, but rarely occurs on both sides simultaneously. Touching her face or brushing her teeth can trigger an attack. Four months ago, she had an episode of weakness in her right arm that lasted for about a week. Family history is notable for migrainous headaches in her mother and brother. Vital signs are within normal limits. There is decreased sensation in the V2 and V3 distribution of her face bilaterally. Muscle strength is 3/5 in the left upper extremity and 5/5 in the right upper extremity. There is spasticity of the lower extremities with sustained clonus. Further evaluation is most likely going to reveal which of the following findings?

answer_choices.B: Erythematous papules in the V2/V3 nerve distribution

few_shot.question: A 43-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic in significant pain. She reports a sharp, stabbing electric-like pain on the right side of her face. The pain started suddenly 2 weeks ago. The pain is so excruciating that she can no longer laugh, speak, or eat her meals as these activities cause episodes of pain. She had to miss work last week as a result. Her attacks last about 3 minutes and go away when she goes to sleep. She typically has 2–3 attacks per day now. The vital signs include: blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg, heart rate 79/min, and respiratory rate 14/min. A neurological examination shows no loss of crude touch, tactile touch, or pain sensations on the left side of the face. The pupillary light and accommodation reflexes are normal. There is no drooping of her mouth, ptosis, or anhidrosis noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is a chronic pain condition that affects the trigeminal nerve, which carries sensation from your face to your brain. If you have TN, even mild stimulation of your face — such as from brushing your teeth or putting on makeup — may trigger a jolt of excruciating pain. The pain is often described as a sudden, severe, sharp, shooting, or electric shock-like pain, typically on one side of the jaw or cheek. The attacks of pain may be repeated one after the other. They may come and go throughout the day and last for days, weeks, or months at a time, and then disappear for months or years. The pain is usually triggered by normal daily activities such as eating, talking, shaving, and brushing teeth. Wind, even a slight breeze or air conditioning, can trigger the pain. The pain is so severe that people with TN avoid daily activities such as eating and talking that trigger the pain. 

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with headaches. She says the headaches started about a month ago, and although initially, they were intermittent, over the past 2 weeks, they have progressively worsened. She describes the pain as severe, worse on the left than the right, and relieved somewhat by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The headaches are usually associated with nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. She denies any changes in vision, seizures, similar past symptoms, or focal neurologic deficits. Past medical history is significant for a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, status post-clipping 10 years ago. Her vital signs include: blood pressure 135/90 mm Hg, temperature 36.7°C (98.0°F), pulse 80/min, and respiratory rate 14/min. Her body mass index (BMI) is 36 kg/m2. On physical examination, the patient is alert and oriented. Her pupils are 3 mm on the right and mid-dilated on the left with subtle left-sided ptosis. Ophthalmic examination reveals a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.4 on the right and 0.5 on the left. The remainder of her cranial nerves are intact. She has 5/5 strength and 2+ reflexes in her upper extremities bilaterally and her left leg; her right leg has 3/5 strength with 1+ reflexes at the knee and ankle. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following findings in this patient most strongly suggests a further diagnostic workup?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's headache, nausea, vomiting, and photophobia are suggestive of migraines. However, the presence of right-sided weakness is concerning for a secondary cause of her headache, such as a mass lesion. Although her posterior communicating artery aneurysm was clipped 10 years ago, the presence of a subtle left-sided ptosis and a mid-dilated left pupil are suggestive of a partial third nerve palsy, which could be due to an unruptured aneurysm. Therefore, this patient should undergo further diagnostic workup with neuroimaging to evaluate for a mass lesion or aneurysm.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old girl presents with episodes of sharp pain in her left upper limb. She says her symptoms gradually onset a few months ago and have progressively worsened. She describes her pain as severe and feeling like “someone stabbing me in my arm and then the pain moves down to my hand”. She says the pain is worse after physical activity and improves with rest. She also says she has some vision problems in her left eye. The patient is afebrile, and her vital signs are within normal limits. On physical examination, there are no visible deformities in the shoulders or upper extremities. Palpation of her left upper limb reveals tenderness mainly near her neck. Mild left-sided ptosis is present. There is anisocoria of her left pupil which measures 1 mm smaller than the right. The right upper limb is normal. A plain radiograph and an MRI are ordered (shown in the image). Which of the following focal neurologic deficits would most likely be seen on the left hand of this patient?

answer_choices.C: Numbness over her left index finger
answer_choices.D: Numbness over her left little finger

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS), a condition characterized by compression of the neurovascular structures that exit the thoracic outlet (ie, the area between the base of the neck and the axilla). The most common type of TOS is neurogenic TOS, which is caused by compression of the brachial plexus. This can lead to pain, paresthesias, and muscle weakness in the affected limb. The pain is often exacerbated by physical activity and improves with rest.

The brachial plexus is divided into roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and branches. The lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1) is most commonly affected in neurogenic TOS. This can cause numbness and tingling in the medial forearm and hand, including the fourth and fifth digits, as well as intrinsic hand muscle weakness and atrophy.

In this patient, the presence of left-sided ptosis and miosis (ie, Horner syndrome) suggests that she has a Pancoast tumor, which is a form of lung cancer that occurs at the lung apex and can cause TOS.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old female presents to her primary care physician complaining of headaches in her left temple and scalp area, neck stiffness, occasional blurred vision, and pain in her jaw when chewing. The appropriate medical therapy is initiated, and a subsequent biopsy of the temporal artery reveals arteritis. Five months later, the patient returns to her physician with a complaint of weakness, leading to difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, and combing her hair. The patient states that this weakness has worsened gradually over the last 2 months. She reports that her headaches, jaw pain, and visual disturbances have resolved. Physical examination is significant for 4/5 strength for both hip flexion/extension as well as shoulder flexion/extension/abduction. Initial laboratory work-up reveals ESR and creatine kinase levels within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient's current presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's proximal muscle weakness, normal ESR, and normal creatine kinase level in the setting of temporal arteritis suggest a drug-induced myopathy secondary to glucocorticoid use. Glucocorticoids are the treatment of choice for both temporal arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica. Glucocorticoid-induced myopathy is the most common drug-induced myopathy. It presents with insidious and symmetric proximal muscle weakness. Serum creatine kinase level is typically normal, and muscle biopsy reveals type II muscle fiber atrophy. The absence of pain and normal inflammatory markers can help distinguish it from polymyositis and polymyalgia rheumatica.

Hence, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 34-year-old G3P3 woman with a history of migraines presents with several weeks of headaches. The headaches are unlike her usual migraines and are worse in the morning. This morning she had an episode of emesis prompting her to seek medical care. She also has some right sided weakness which she believes is related to a new exercise routine. Her mother is a breast cancer survivor. Her medications include oral contraceptives and ibuprofen as needed, which has not helped her current headaches. She drinks 2-3 alcoholic drinks on the weekends and does not smoke. Physical examination is remarkable for bilateral papilledema. Motor exam is notable for upper and lower extremity strength 4/5 on the right and 5/5 on the left. Magnetic resonance venography demonstrates absent flow in the left venous sinuses. Which of the following predisposed this patient to her current condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's headache, nausea, vomiting, and papilledema are concerning for increased intracranial pressure. The finding of absent flow in the left venous sinuses on magnetic resonance venography confirms the diagnosis of cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT). CVT is a rare form of venous thromboembolism that often presents with nonspecific symptoms such as headache, nausea, vomiting, and visual disturbances. Focal neurologic deficits and seizures can also occur. The most common risk factors for CVT are those associated with a hypercoagulable state, including oral contraceptive use, pregnancy, puerperium, malignancy, and inherited thrombophilias. This patient's use of oral contraceptives likely predisposed her to CVT.

So, the answer is [D].

question: On routine screening, a 62-year-old man is found to have positive fecal occult blood tests. He is asymptomatic, but his father died of large intestinal cancer. Abdominal and rectal exams are normal. A colonoscopy subsequently reveals a polyp in the descending colon but no other abnormalities. Excisional biopsy of the polyp shows 75% tubular architecture. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 35-year-old woman comes to the physician for a 3-week history of alternating constipation and diarrhea with blood in her stool. She has not had any fevers or weight loss. Her father died of gastric cancer at 50 years of age. Physical examination shows blue-gray macules on the lips and palms of both hands. Colonoscopy shows multiple polyps throughout the small bowel and colon with one ulcerated polyp at the level of the sigmoid colon. Multiple biopsy specimens are collected. These polyps are most likely to be characterized as which of the following histological subtypes?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of multiple polyps throughout the small bowel and colon, blue-gray macules on the lips and palms, and a family history of gastric cancer is suggestive of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS). PJS is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by hamartomatous polyps in the GI tract and hyperpigmented macules on the lips, oral mucosa, and digits. The polyps can cause abdominal pain, bleeding, and obstruction. Patients with PJS are also at an increased risk for various cancers, including colorectal, gastric, small bowel, pancreatic, breast, and ovarian cancers.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He has a strong family history of colon cancer. A screening colonoscopy shows a 4 mm polyp in the upper sigmoid colon. Which of the following findings on biopsy is associated with the lowest potential for malignant transformation into colorectal carcinoma?

answer_choices.C: Finger-like projections with a fibrovascular core
answer_choices.D: Hyperplastic epithelium at the base of crypts

few_shot.explanation:
Colorectal polyps are classified as non-neoplastic or neoplastic based on their histologic features. Non-neoplastic polyps include hyperplastic polyps, hamartomatous polyps, and inflammatory polyps. Neoplastic polyps include adenomas (tubular, tubulovillous, and villous) and serrated polyps.

Hyperplastic polyps are the most common type of polyp in the colon. They are typically small (<5 mm) and are most often found in the rectosigmoid region. Histologically, they are characterized by a simple tubular architecture with elongated, straight crypts and an increased number of goblet cells. The cells appear hyperplastic (ie, increased in number) but lack nuclear atypia. The risk of malignant transformation of hyperplastic polyps is extremely low.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 19-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2 day history of blood-speckled stools and a protruding rectal mass. He has no abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, or fever. His mother has inflammatory bowel disease. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows multiple, small, hyperpigmented maculae on the lips, buccal mucosa, palms, and soles. The abdomen is soft with no organomegaly. Rectal examination shows a 4-cm pedunculated polyp with superficial excoriations on the mucosa. A colonoscopy shows 14 polyps. A biopsy shows hamartomatous mucosal polyps. This patient's diagnosis is most likely associated with which of the following conditions?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's multiple hamartomatous polyps, hyperpigmented macules on the lips and oral mucosa, and family history of gastrointestinal disease are suggestive of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS). PJS is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. The polyps can cause abdominal pain, obstruction, and intussusception. The mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation can involve the lips, oral mucosa, and the skin of the hands and feet. 

Patients with PJS have an increased risk of developing malignancies, particularly gastrointestinal cancers (eg, colorectal, stomach, small bowel, pancreatic), as well as breast and gynecologic cancers (eg, ovarian, cervical). 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician for a scheduled colonoscopy. She was diagnosed with familial adenomatous polyposis at the age of 13 years. Last year, her flexible sigmoidoscopy showed 12 adenomatous polyps (< 6 mm) that were removed endoscopically. Her father and her paternal grandmother were diagnosed with colon cancer at the age of 37 and 39 years, respectively. The patient appears nervous but otherwise well. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. A complete blood count and serum concentrations of electrolytes, urea nitrogen, and creatinine are within the reference range. A colonoscopy shows hundreds of diffuse 4–9 mm adenomatous polyps covering the colon and > 30 rectal adenomas. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by the development of hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps in the colon. The polyps begin to appear after puberty, and if left untreated, there is nearly a 100% chance that they will progress to colorectal cancer by the age of 40 years. Therefore, the mainstay of treatment for FAP is prophylactic colectomy. The timing of surgery is usually determined by the number, size, and histology of polyps, as well as the patient's family history of colorectal cancer. In general, earlier colectomy is recommended for patients with large or rapidly increasing polyp burden, high-grade dysplasia on biopsy, or a family history of early-onset colorectal cancer. This patient has a significant family history of early-onset colorectal cancer and a large polyp burden, so she should undergo proctocolectomy with ileoanal anastomosis.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and increased straining during defecation for 3 months. During this time, he has lost 5 kg (12 lb) despite no change in appetite. He has a family history of colon cancer in his maternal uncle and maternal grandfather. His mother died of ovarian cancer at the age of 46. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor. His hemoglobin concentration is 11.2 g/dL, hematocrit is 34%, and mean corpuscular volume is 76 μm3. Colonoscopy shows an exophytic mass in the ascending colon. Pathologic examination of the resected mass shows a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Genetic analysis shows a mutation in the MSH2 gene. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's family history of colon and ovarian cancer, along with the finding of a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon, is suggestive of Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer). This is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by early-onset colorectal cancer and an increased risk of extracolonic cancers, including endometrial, ovarian, gastric, small bowel, hepatobiliary tract, renal pelvis, and ureteral cancers. The cancers seen in Lynch syndrome are often poorly differentiated and have a characteristic microscopic appearance, including a mucinous/signet-ring cell differentiation or a medullary growth pattern, marked tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and Crohn-like lymphocytic reactions. 

Lynch syndrome is caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes, including MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2. The MSH2 mutation seen in this patient is one of the most commonly mutated genes in Lynch syndrome.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 21-year-old man comes to the emergency room with swelling and severe pain in his left lower leg that started 2 hours ago. He has no history of serious illness or trauma. His father has a history of pulmonary embolism. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily since he started college 3 years ago. He appears very distressed. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 92 kg (203 lb); BMI is 30.7 kg/m2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 94/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a tender and mildly swollen left lower leg; dorsiflexion of the left foot causes severe pain in the calf. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 184,000/mm3, a prothrombin time of 11 seconds, an activated partial thromboplastin time of 26 seconds, and positive fibrin split products. Ultrasonography of the left leg shows incompressibility of the popliteal vein with a hyperechoic mass and absent blood flow. The patient is administered a 5000 IU intravenous bolus of unfractionated heparin followed by a constant infusion. Six hours later, the activated partial thromboplastin time is 30 seconds. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

few_shot.question: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of pain and swelling of her left leg over the past 24 hours. The pain is worse while walking and improves when resting. Seven months ago, she was diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism and was started on warfarin. Anticoagulant therapy was discontinued 1 month ago. Her sister has systemic lupus erythematosus. The patient does not smoke. She currently takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 123/72 mm Hg. On physical examination, the left calf is diffusely erythematous, swollen, and tender. Dorsal flexion of the left foot elicits pain. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. On duplex ultrasonography, the left popliteal vein is not compressible. Laboratory studies show an elevated serum concentration of D-dimer and insensitivity to activated protein C. Further examination is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) at a young age, along with her laboratory findings, suggest a hypercoagulable state. The most common inherited thrombophilia is factor V Leiden, which is caused by a point mutation in the factor V gene. This mutation results in a factor V molecule that is resistant to inactivation by activated protein C (APC), leading to a hypercoagulable state. The APC resistance assay, which tests for the prolongation of the activated partial thromboplastin time in the presence of APC, is the most common screening test for factor V Leiden. A positive test (ie, no prolongation of aPTT with the addition of APC) is diagnostic for factor V Leiden.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [A] > [D] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 21-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of right leg pain. The pain is worse while walking and improves when resting. Eight months ago, she was diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism and was started on warfarin. Anticoagulant therapy was discontinued two months ago. Her mother had systemic lupus erythematosus. On examination, her right calf is diffusely erythematous, swollen, and tender. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. On duplex ultrasonography, the right popliteal vein is not compressible. Laboratory studies show an elevated serum level of D-dimer and insensitivity to activated protein C. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) at a young age, along with her insensitivity to activated protein C, is suggestive of factor V Leiden mutation. This is the most common inherited hypercoagulable state among whites. The mutation renders factor V resistant to inactivation by activated protein C, leading to a hypercoagulable state. The diagnosis is confirmed by DNA analysis or by the activated protein C resistance assay, which shows insensitivity of the patient's plasma to activated protein C.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question:
A 61-year-old man presents to the emergency room with a painful, swollen left leg. He states that his symptoms began that morning after a long flight from Australia. He denies shortness of breath, chest pain, or cough. On review of systems, he notes that he has been constipated recently and had several episodes of bright red blood per rectum. He has not noticed any weight loss, fevers, or night sweats. He has a past medical history of a deep vein thrombosis 4 years ago during a hospitalization for community acquired pneumonia and was treated with warfarin for 3 months afterward. He also has chronic hepatitis C from previous intravenous drug use. The patient has a 30 pack-year smoking history and has never had a colonoscopy. His father is 84-years-old and has chronic kidney disease from diabetes, and his mother passed away from a massive pulmonary embolus when pregnant with his younger sister. In the emergency room, his temperature is 98.7°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 142/85 mm/Hg, pulse is 79/min, and respirations are 14/min. On exam, he is in no acute distress. His left calf is larger in caliber than the right calf which is red and tender to palpation. Dorsiflexion of the foot worsens the pain. His abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended without hepatomegaly. The remainder of the physical exam is unremarkable. Labs are shown below:

Hemoglobin: 13.0 g/dL
Leukocyte count: 6,000/mm^3
Platelets: 160,000/mm^3

Aspartate aminotransferase: 15 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase: 19 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase: 81 IU/L
Hepatitis C antibody: reactive
Hepatitis C titer: 0 copies/mL

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.B: Loss of antithrombin III in urine
answer_choices.C: Resistance of factor V to inactivation by protein C

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a history of recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) in the setting of transient risk factors (eg, hospitalization, long travel). The most common inherited risk factor for VTE is factor V Leiden, which is due to a mutation that causes resistance of factor V to inactivation by activated protein C. This leads to a hypercoagulable state and an increased risk of VTE. The mutation is most common in whites of European descent. 

The other options, protein C deficiency and antithrombin III deficiency, are less common inherited hypercoagulable states. Protein C deficiency is associated with an increased risk of VTE and warfarin-induced skin necrosis. Antithrombin III deficiency is associated with an increased risk of VTE and resistance to heparin therapy. 

Malignancy is a common cause of acquired hypercoagulability, but this patient has no signs or symptoms of cancer. 

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of worsening right lower leg pain. He states that he believes his right leg is swollen when compared to his left leg. Past medical history is significant for generalized anxiety disorder, managed effectively with psychotherapy. He smokes a pack of cigarettes daily but denies alcohol and illicit drug use. His father died of a pulmonary embolism at the age of 43. His vital signs include: temperature 36.7°C (98.0°F), blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg, heart rate 74/min, respiratory rate 14/min. On physical examination, the right lower leg is warmer than the left, and dorsiflexion of the right foot produces pain. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for this patient’s presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of right lower leg pain and swelling, warmth, and a positive Homan's sign (pain with dorsiflexion of the foot) is suggestive of a deep venous thrombosis (DVT). His risk factors for DVT include smoking and a family history of venous thromboembolism (VTE). The most common inherited risk factor for VTE is factor V Leiden, an autosomal dominant disorder that is present in approximately 5% of the Caucasian population. Factor V Leiden is a mutated form of human factor V that causes an increase in blood clotting (hypercoagulability). It is associated with a mildly increased risk of DVT, but the risk greatly increases with concomitant exposure to acquired risk factors (eg, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, surgery, malignancy).

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician for evaluation of worsening pain, swelling, and erythema in her left leg for the past 4 hours. She returned from a trip to Taiwan to celebrate her sister's wedding 2 days ago. She has no history of serious illness. She is sexually active with one male partner and uses a combined oral contraceptive pill (OCP). She does not smoke, drink, or use illicit drugs. Her only other medication is a multivitamin. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 67/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Examination shows swelling in her left calf and pain behind her left knee when she is asked to dorsiflex her left foot. Laboratory results show elevated D-dimers. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's clinical presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's clinical presentation is consistent with deep venous thrombosis (DVT). DVT is a common condition that can lead to significant morbidity and mortality. Risk factors for DVT include recent surgery, malignancy, pregnancy, prolonged immobilization, and use of combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs). OCPs increase the risk of DVT by increasing the levels of procoagulant factors (eg, factors II, VII, VIII, X) and decreasing the levels of natural anticoagulants (eg, protein S, antithrombin). Therefore, the most likely cause of this patient's DVT is decreased protein S due to her use of OCPs.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

question: A 64-year-old man comes to the physician with a 1-week history of sore mouth. He says that swallowing is not painful. He has had asthma for more than 20 years. His only medication is a high-dose combination salmeterol/fluticasone inhaler. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 74/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 125/65 mm Hg. A photograph of his oral mucosa is shown. Indirect mirror examination of the posterior oropharynx, larynx, and hypopharynx shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of pain in his mouth and throat and difficulty swallowing. He has a history of COPD, for which he takes theophylline and inhaled budesonide-formoterol. Physical examination shows white patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa that can be scraped off easily. Appropriate pharmacotherapy is initiated. One week later, he returns because of nausea, palpitations, and anxiety. His pulse is 110/min and regular. Physical examination shows a tremor in both hands. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of white patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa that can be scraped off easily is consistent with oral candidiasis. This is a common opportunistic infection in patients with COPD who use inhaled corticosteroids, which can cause local immunosuppression. The first-line treatment for oral candidiasis is a topical antifungal medication (eg, clotrimazole troches, nystatin oral suspension). However, for moderate to severe infection, oral fluconazole is often used.

Fluconazole is a potent inhibitor of the cytochrome P450 system, and can increase the levels of many drugs, including theophylline. Theophylline toxicity can present with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, insomnia, and sinus tachycardia. Severe cases can cause seizures and life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 19-year-old woman comes to the physician because of worsening pain with swallowing for 3 days and a dry sensation in the mouth over the past week. She has a history of asthma controlled with inhaled fluticasone and albuterol. Physical examination shows white plaques on the dorsal surface of the tongue and buccal mucosa that bleed when scraped off. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of oral discomfort and white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa that bleed when scraped off are consistent with oral candidiasis (thrush). Oral candidiasis is an opportunistic infection caused by Candida species, most commonly Candida albicans. It is often seen in patients with immunosuppression (eg, HIV, malignancy, corticosteroid use) or those using inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) for asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. ICS can disrupt the normal oral flora and cause local immunosuppression, allowing Candida to proliferate. To decrease the risk of oral candidiasis, patients using ICS should rinse their mouths with water or brush their teeth after each use. 

Oral candidiasis is treated with topical antifungal agents such as nystatin oral suspension or clotrimazole troches. Patients should be instructed to swish the medication in the mouth and then swallow to also treat possible esophageal involvement. Systemic therapy with fluconazole is used for patients with severe or refractory disease or those who cannot tolerate oral medications.

So, the answer is [B].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [B] > [C] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old man presents with soreness and dryness of the oral mucosa for the past 3 weeks. No significant past medical history. The patient reports that he has had multiple bisexual partners over the last year and only occasionally uses condoms. He denies any alcohol use or history of smoking. The patient is afebrile and his vital signs are within normal limits. On physical examination, there is a lesion noted in the oral cavity, which is shown in the exhibit. Which of the following is the next best step in the treatment of this patient?

answer_choices.A: Change the patient’s toothbrush and improve oral hygiene

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of multiple sexual partners and the presence of a white, non-scrapable lesion on the lateral tongue are suggestive of oral hairy leukoplakia (OHL). OHL is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and is commonly seen in immunocompromised patients, especially those with HIV. The lesion is usually asymptomatic and does not require treatment unless it interferes with swallowing or is cosmetically unacceptable. In such cases, antiviral therapy with acyclovir, valacyclovir, or ganciclovir can be used. However, the most important next step in management is to confirm the diagnosis of HIV and initiate antiretroviral therapy, which can lead to resolution of the OHL.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [D] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-day history of fever, headache, earache, and sore throat that is worse when swallowing. He has not had a runny nose or cough. He had a similar problem 1 year ago for which he was prescribed amoxicillin, but after developing a skin rash and facial swelling he was switched to a different medication. His immunizations are up-to-date. He is at the 75th percentile for height and the 50th percentile for weight. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 136/min, and respirations are 28/min. Examination of the oral cavity reveals a coated tongue, red uvula, and enlarged right tonsil covered by a whitish membrane. The deep cervical lymph nodes are enlarged and tender. A throat swab is taken for culture. What is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, sore throat, and unilateral tonsillar enlargement with exudate are suggestive of peritonsillar abscess (PTA). PTA is a complication of acute tonsillitis and is most commonly seen in adolescents and young adults. It is often polymicrobial, with a mixture of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. Group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae are the most common aerobes, and Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, and Fusobacterium are the most common anaerobes.

Patients with PTA should be treated with antibiotics that cover both aerobes and anaerobes. Clindamycin or amoxicillin/clavulanate are often used. However, this patient has a history of a severe allergic reaction (skin rash and facial swelling) to amoxicillin, a penicillin derivative. Therefore, he should not receive beta-lactam antibiotics, including penicillins and cephalosporins. Instead, he should receive a combination of metronidazole for anaerobic coverage and a macrolide (eg, erythromycin, azithromycin) for aerobic coverage.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question:
A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of progressive pain while swallowing. She has the feeling that food gets stuck in her throat and is harder to swallow than usual. She has a history of high-grade cervical dysplasia which was treated with conization 12 years ago. Four months ago, she was diagnosed with Graves' disease and started on antithyroid therapy. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. She has had 8 lifetime sexual partners and uses condoms inconsistently. Her father died of stomach cancer. She has never smoked and drinks one glass of wine daily. She uses cocaine occasionally. Her current medications include methimazole and a vitamin supplement. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 75/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg. Examination of the oral cavity shows several white plaques that can be scraped off easily. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL
Leukocyte count 12,200/mm3
Platelet count 290,000/mm3
Prothrombin time 12 seconds
Partial thromboplastin time (activated) 38 seconds
Serum
pH 7.33
Na+ 135 mEq/L
Cl- 104 mEq/L
K+ 4.9 mEq/L
HCO3- 24 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen 13 mg/dL
Glucose 110 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL
HIV test positive
In addition to starting antiretroviral therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's oral examination findings of white plaques that can be scraped off easily are consistent with oral candidiasis (thrush), a common opportunistic infection in patients with HIV. Oral candidiasis is typically caused by Candida albicans and usually presents with white plaques or spots on the buccal mucosa, tongue, or oropharynx. Patients may be asymptomatic or complain of discomfort, altered taste, or difficulty swallowing. Diagnosis is usually made clinically, but can be confirmed by KOH preparation, which shows budding yeast and pseudohyphae.

Topical therapy with nystatin oral suspension or clotrimazole oral troches is usually effective for mild cases of thrush. However, this patient has odynophagia, which suggests the presence of esophageal candidiasis. Esophageal candidiasis should be suspected in any patient with oral thrush and either dysphagia or odynophagia. Endoscopy is the diagnostic procedure of choice, but empiric treatment is often started if the suspicion is high, as in this patient. Systemic antifungal therapy with fluconazole is the treatment of choice.

Therefore, the answer is [D].
