few_shot.question: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician for the evaluation of right knee pain for 1 week. The pain began after the patient twisted her knee during basketball practice. At the time of the injury, she felt a popping sensation and her knee became swollen over the next few hours. The pain is exacerbated by walking up or down stairs and worsens throughout the day. She also reports occasional locking of the knee. She has been taking acetaminophen during the past week, but the pain is worse today. Her mother has rheumatoid arthritis. The patient is 155 cm (4 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 75 kg (165 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows effusion of the right knee; range of motion is limited by pain. There is medial joint line tenderness. Knee extension with rotation results in an audible snap. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following?

answer_choices.A: Hyperintense line in the meniscus on MRI
answer_choices.B: Trabecular loss in the proximal femur on x-ray
answer_choices.C: Erosions and synovial hyperplasia on MRI

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of a twisting injury, immediate swelling, and mechanical symptoms (eg, locking, popping) suggest a meniscal tear. The menisci are fibrocartilaginous structures that provide shock absorption and joint stability. They are commonly injured by twisting motions that occur when the foot is planted and the knee is flexed. Meniscal tears are more common in obese individuals due to increased joint stress. On examination, patients may have joint line tenderness and a positive McMurray test (eg, palpable or audible snap during knee extension with rotation). MRI is the most sensitive and specific imaging modality for meniscal tears and typically shows a hyperintense line in the meniscus.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy presents to the pediatric emergency department for knee pain. The child fell while riding his skateboard yesterday. He claims that ever since then he has had swelling and knee pain that is severe. His parents state that he has trouble walking due to the pain. The child has a past medical history of seasonal allergies and asthma. His current medications include loratadine, albuterol, and fluticasone. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 95/48 mmHg, pulse is 110/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On physical exam, you note a young boy laying on the stretcher in pain. Cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Inspection of the patient's left knee reveals an erythamatous knee that is tender and warm to the touch. Passive movement of the knee elicits pain. The patient refuses to walk so you are unable to assess his gait. Which of the following is the best initial step in management?

answer_choices.D: Supportive therapy and further physical exam

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is concerning for septic arthritis. Septic arthritis is a medical emergency that can lead to rapid joint destruction and irreversible loss of function. It is most commonly caused by hematogenous spread of bacteria, but can also occur due to direct inoculation (eg, trauma, surgery) or contiguous spread from adjacent osteomyelitis. The most common pathogen in children with septic arthritis is Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus. Patients typically present with an acutely painful, swollen, warm joint. Fever may or may not be present. The knee is the most commonly affected joint.

The most important initial step in management is arthrocentesis. Synovial fluid analysis typically shows a white blood cell count >50,000/mm3 with >75% neutrophils. Gram stain and culture of the synovial fluid should be performed to identify the causative organism. Blood cultures should also be obtained. 

So, the answer is [B].

question: A 70-year-old woman with no significant medical history begins to experience memory loss and personality changes. Over the next few months, her symptoms become more severe, as she experiences rapid mental deterioration. She also starts to have sudden, jerking movements in response to being startled and gait disturbances. Eventually, she lapses into a coma and dies eight months after the onset of symptoms. What process likely caused this woman's illness?

answer_choices.A: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
answer_choices.B: Autoimmune inflammation and demyelination of the peripheral nervous system.
answer_choices.C: Conversion of a protein from an a-helix to a ß-pleated form, which resists degradation.
answer_choices.D: Frontotemporal atrophy and the accumulation of intracellular, aggregated tau protein.

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of worsening mental status over the past month. Her husband reports that she was initially experiencing lapses in memory but has recently started having difficulties performing activities of daily living. She appears withdrawn and avoids eye contact. Examination shows diffuse involuntary muscle jerking that can be provoked by loud noises. A cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows elevated concentration of 14-3-3 protein. Four months later, the patient dies. Pathologic examination of the brain on autopsy is most likely to show which of the following findings?

answer_choices.A: Marked atrophy of caudate and putamen

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and elevated cerebrospinal fluid 14-3-3 protein concentration are suggestive of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). CJD is a prion disease characterized by the accumulation of an abnormal isoform of the prion protein in the central nervous system. This leads to rapidly progressive neurodegeneration and a clinical syndrome of dementia, ataxia, and myoclonus. The disease is invariably fatal, usually within 1 year of symptom onset.

On gross examination, the brain in CJD often appears normal or may show mild atrophy. Microscopic examination, however, reveals diffuse spongiform degeneration, which is characterized by numerous, small, vacuole-like spaces in the neuropil that impart a "spongy" appearance to the tissue. Neuronal loss and reactive astrocytosis are also seen.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old woman is brought to your office by her husband. The husband says that she had been acting strange lately. She has been forgetful, and she sometimes becomes angered for no reason, which is highly unusual for her. She has also been having random, uncontrollable movements, which are also new. On examination, she appears withdrawn and flat. On further questioning, she reveals that her father died at age 45 from a movement disorder. Which of the following is the pathological hallmark of the patient's condition?

answer_choices.B: Loss of neurons in the caudate nucleus and putamen

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of forgetfulness, personality changes, and random, uncontrollable movements are suggestive of Huntington's disease. This is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by progressive motor, cognitive, and psychiatric disturbances. The motor disturbances often begin with subtle changes in coordination and progress to random, uncontrollable, jerking movements (chorea). The cognitive disturbances often begin with forgetfulness and progress to dementia. The psychiatric disturbances often begin with personality changes, such as irritability, and progress to depression, apathy, and social withdrawal.

The pathological hallmark of Huntington's disease is loss of neurons in the caudate nucleus and putamen, with relative sparing of the nucleus accumbens. This leads to atrophy of the caudate nucleus, which can be seen on imaging studies.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man with no significant medical history begins to have memory loss and personality changes. Rapidly, over the next few months his symptoms increase in severity. He experiences a rapid mental deterioration associated with sudden, jerking movements, particularly in response to being startled. He has gait disturbances as well. Eventually, he lapses into a coma and dies approximately ten months after the onset of symptoms. Which of the following would most likely be seen on autopsy of the brain in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and ataxia are suggestive of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a prion disease. Prion diseases are caused by the accumulation of an abnormal isoform of the prion protein (PrPSc) in the CNS. This accumulation leads to neuronal loss and reactive gliosis, which manifest as spongiform changes (intracellular vacuoles) on histologic examination. The spongiform changes are most prominent in the cerebral and cerebellar cortices.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 63-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her husband for the evaluation of progressive memory loss for the past 5 months. During the last 2 weeks, she has also had problems getting dressed and finding her way back home from the grocery store. She has had several episodes of jerky, repetitive, twitching movements that resolved spontaneously. She used to work as a teacher but quit her job due to her memory loss. The patient has hypertension. There is no family history of serious illness. Her only medication is hydrochlorothiazide. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 65/min, and blood pressure is 125/80 mmHg. She is oriented only to person and place. She follows commands and speaks fluently, but sometimes cannot recall objects. She is unable to read and seems to have difficulty recognizing objects. Cranial nerves II-XII are intact. Examination shows full muscle strength. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. Babinski sign is absent. Sensation to pinprick and light touch is normal. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and visual-spatial deficits are suggestive of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a prion disease caused by the accumulation of abnormal isoforms of the prion protein in the CNS. Prions are infectious proteins that can induce abnormal folding of normal cellular prion proteins in the brain, leading to neuronal death and the clinical manifestations of the disease. CJD typically presents in the sixth decade of life with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and neurologic signs such as ataxia, visual or cerebellar signs, pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs, or akinetic mutism. The disease progresses rapidly over weeks to months, often leading to severe disability and death within 1 year of onset.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old woman presented to a clinic because of dementia, hemiparesis, ataxia, aphasia, and dysarthria that developed over the last 5 days. She had a 15-year history of intravenous drug abuse and was treated for fever, cough, and shortness of breath before the onset of neurological symptoms. Her MRI shows multiple white matter lesions, as seen in the picture. Over the course of 2 weeks, the patient's condition worsens. Despite aggressive treatment, she lapses into a coma and dies. At autopsy, histologic examination of her brain tissue reveals gigantic, deformed astrocytes and oligodendrocytes with abnormal nuclei. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this woman's neurological symptoms?

answer_choices.C: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of intravenous drug abuse, rapid neurologic decline, and MRI findings of multiple white matter lesions are suggestive of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). PML is a demyelinating disease of the central nervous system caused by reactivation of the JC virus, a double-stranded circular DNA virus. The JC virus is a member of the Polyomaviridae family and is very common, with up to 86% of adults having antibodies to the virus. In most people, the virus remains latent in the kidneys and B lymphocytes and does not cause any symptoms. However, in immunocompromised individuals (eg, those with HIV/AIDS, hematologic malignancies, or organ transplants, or those receiving chronic immunosuppressive therapy), the virus can reactivate and infect oligodendrocytes, leading to widespread demyelination and the clinical syndrome of PML.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A 7-day-old infant boy presents to an emergency department due to poor feeding. His parents are recent immigrants to the United States. He was born in a traditional home birth and has never seen a medical provider. Mom had no prenatal care, has no medical issues, and is unvaccinated. The baby had been breastfeeding well until 24 hours ago when mom noticed he started having trouble latching. In the last 12 hours, he has completely refused to feed. He has had a decreased number of wet diapers and has stooled twice in the last 24 hours. His temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), pulse is 180/min, respirations are 52/min, and blood pressure is 70/50 mmHg. On exam, the infant has increased tone, a clenched jaw, no head lag, and clenched hands. Initial screening bloodwork is normal. What is the most likely organism causing this infant's presentation?

few_shot.question:
A 3100-g (6.9-lb) male newborn is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of fever and irritability. The newborn was delivered at home 15 hours ago. He was born at 39 weeks' gestation. The mother's last prenatal visit was at the beginning of the first trimester. She received all standard immunizations upon immigrating from Mexico two years ago. Seven weeks ago, she experienced an episode of painful, itching genital vesicles, which resolved spontaneously. Four hours before going into labor she noticed a gush of blood-tinged fluid from her vagina. The newborn is ill-appearing and lethargic. His temperature is 39.9°C (103.8°F), pulse is 170/min, respirations are 60/min, and blood pressure is 70/45 mm Hg. His skin is mildly icteric. Expiratory grunting is heard on auscultation. Skin turgor and muscle tone are decreased. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 15 g/dL
Leukocyte count 33,800/mm3
Platelet count 100,000/mm3
Serum glucose 55 mg/dL
Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?"
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has signs of early-onset neonatal sepsis (EOS), which presents within 72 hours of birth and is most commonly due to vertical transmission of maternal genital tract flora. Risk factors for EOS include maternal group B Streptococcus (GBS) colonization, preterm birth (<37 weeks' gestation), prolonged rupture of membranes (>18 hours), and maternal intrapartum fever. The most common pathogens causing EOS are GBS and Escherichia coli. 

This newborn's mother has several risk factors for EOS, including prolonged rupture of membranes and lack of prenatal care (which would have included GBS screening and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis if indicated). The newborn's clinical presentation of fever, lethargy, poor perfusion (tachycardia, hypotension), and respiratory distress (tachypnea, grunting) is concerning for EOS, most likely due to GBS. 

Hence, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 10-day-old infant is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of episodes of weakness and spasms for the past 12 hours. His mother states that he has also had difficulty feeding and a weak suck. He has not had fever, cough, diarrhea, or vomiting. He was born at 39 weeks' gestation via uncomplicated vaginal delivery at home. Pregnancy was uncomplicated. The mother refused antenatal vaccines out of concern they would cause side effects. She is worried his symptoms may be from some raw honey his older sister maybe inadvertently fed him 5 days ago. He appears irritable. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F). Examination shows generalized muscle stiffness and twitches. His fontanelles are soft and flat. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
few_shot.explanation:
This infant's symptoms of generalized muscle stiffness and twitches, difficulty feeding, and weak suck are suggestive of botulism. Botulism is a rare, life-threatening paralytic illness caused by neurotoxins produced by Clostridium botulinum. The most common form of botulism in infants is infant botulism, which occurs in infants aged <12 months. It is caused by ingestion of C botulinum spores, which are found in soil and dust worldwide. The spores germinate in the infant's intestine and produce botulinum toxin, which blocks the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing a descending flaccid paralysis. The most common sources of C botulinum spores are honey and corn syrup, and these products should not be given to children aged <12 months.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 24-hour-old newborn presents to the emergency department after a home birth because of fever, irritability alternating with lethargy, and poor feeding. The patient’s mother says symptoms acutely onset 12 hours ago and have not improved. No significant past medical history. His mother did not receive any prenatal care, and she had rupture of membranes 20 hours prior to delivery. His vital signs include: heart rate 150/min, respiratory rate 65/min, temperature 39.0°C (102.2°F), and blood pressure 60/40 mm Hg. On physical examination, the patient has delayed capillary refill. Laboratory studies show a pleocytosis and a low glucose level in the patient’s cerebrospinal fluid. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism for this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, irritability, lethargy, and poor feeding are concerning for neonatal sepsis, a systemic infection occurring in infants <28 days old. The most common cause of neonatal sepsis is group B Streptococcus (GBS), which is part of the normal vaginal flora in 15%-40% of women. Maternal GBS colonization is the principal risk factor for early-onset GBS sepsis (age <7 days), and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for colonized women to prevent vertical transmission during delivery. This patient's mother did not receive prenatal care and, therefore, was not screened or treated for GBS.

Early-onset GBS sepsis presents with nonspecific signs of systemic infection (eg, temperature instability, respiratory distress, lethargy, poor feeding, irritability) and can progress rapidly to septic shock. Meningitis is also common in early-onset disease, and lumbar puncture often reveals a CSF pleocytosis and low glucose level.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 6-day-old newborn is brought to the emergency department by his mother due to a high fever that started last night. His mother says that he was born via an uneventful vaginal delivery at home at 38 weeks gestation and was doing fine up until yesterday when he became disinterested in breastfeeding and spit up several times. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), pulse is 155/min, respirations are 45/min, and O2 sats are 92% on room air. He is lethargic and minimally responsive to stimuli. While on his back, his head is quickly lifted towards his chest which causes his legs to flex. The mother had only a few prenatal care visits and none at the end of the pregnancy. What is the most likely source of this patients infection?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, lethargy, poor feeding, and abnormal neurologic signs (eg, positive Brudzinski sign) are concerning for neonatal meningitis. The most common pathogens of neonatal meningitis are group B Streptococcus (GBS), Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes. GBS is the most common cause of meningitis in the first week of life (early-onset disease). Transmission of GBS is vertical, occurring during passage through the birth canal. Risk factors for early-onset GBS disease include maternal GBS colonization, preterm labor, prolonged rupture of membranes, and intrapartum fever. 

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 6-month-old girl has a weak cry, poor suck, ptosis, and constipation. Her condition began 2 days ago with a single episode of abundant watery stool and elevated temperature. The child was born at term to a healthy 26-year-old mother with an uneventful antenatal course and puerperium. The infant was exclusively breastfed till 5 months of age, after which she began receiving grated potatoes, pumpkin, carrots, and apples, in addition to the breastfeeding. She does not receive any fluids other than breast milk. The last new food item to be introduced was homemade honey that her mother added several times to grated sour apples as a sweetener 2 weeks before the onset of symptoms. The vital signs are as follows: blood pressure 70/40 mm Hg, heart rate 98/min, respiratory rate 29/min, and temperature 36.4°C (98.2°F). On physical examination, she is lethargic and has poor head control. A neurologic examination reveals ptosis and facial muscle weakness, widespread hypotonia, and symmetrically decreased upper and lower extremity reflexes. Which of the following options is a part of the pathogenesis underlying the patient’s condition?

answer_choices.A: Hypocalcemia due to a decrease in breast milk consumption
answer_choices.B: Hyperkalemia due to increased dietary intake
answer_choices.C: Vegetative form of Clostridium botulinum spores in the patient's colon
answer_choices.D: Development of antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of ptosis, facial muscle weakness, and hypotonia are suggestive of botulism. Botulism is a rare, life-threatening paralytic illness caused by neurotoxins produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum. The spores of these bacteria are found in soil and dust. If the spores are ingested, they can germinate in the intestines and produce the toxin. The toxin binds to the presynaptic membrane of the neuromuscular junction and prevents the release of acetylcholine, causing a flaccid paralysis. In infants, the most common source of the spores is honey or corn syrup, which is why these foods should not be given to children less than 12 months old.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [D] > [A] > [B].

question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents because he ‘hasn’t been himself lately’ and reportedly gets tired very easily from his swimming classes in comparison to the other kids. He also ‘can’t catch his breath’ at times. The mother also reports that he seems to be slightly shorter than other children his age. His temperature is 36.6°C (97.9°F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, and respiratory rate is 14/min. On auscultation, a localized harsh pansystolic murmur is heard over the left sternal border at the level of the 2nd–3rd intercostal space. The murmur becomes louder when the patient is asked to squat. An echocardiogram is performed. Which of the structures below gives rise to the defective structure that is causing this patient’s symptoms?

few_shot.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of increasing shortness of breath for 2 days. He is at 30th percentile for height and at 25th percentile for weight. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 144/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 80/44 mm Hg. Bilateral crackles are heard at the lung bases. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard over the left lower sternal border. A grade 2/6 mid-diastolic murmur is heard best in the left fourth intercostal space. Without treatment, this patient is at risk of developing which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, a mid-diastolic murmur at the apex, and signs of heart failure (eg, tachycardia, tachypnea, crackles) are suggestive of a large ventricular septal defect (VSD). VSD is the most common congenital heart defect and is often associated with other cardiac anomalies. Small defects may be asymptomatic and close spontaneously, whereas large defects can cause heart failure and poor weight gain due to the development of pulmonary hypertension from the left-to-right shunt. Over time, the increased pulmonary pressures can lead to reversal of the shunt (Eisenmenger syndrome) with ensuing late cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythemia.

So, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [B] > [D] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of recurrent nosebleeds and fatigue for the past 2 months. He also frequently complains his head hurts. The patient has met all motoric milestones for his age but does not like to run because his legs start to hurt if he does. He is at the 40th percentile for both height and weight. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure in the right arm is 130/85 mm Hg. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard in the left paravertebral region. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of hypertension, headache, fatigue, and claudication in a young child is concerning for coarctation of the aorta (CoA). CoA is a congenital narrowing of the aorta, typically located distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery at the level of the ductus arteriosus (juxtaductal). The narrowing results in increased afterload, which can lead to left ventricular hypertrophy. In addition, collateral circulation may develop over time to bypass the obstruction, leading to characteristic findings such as intercostal artery dilation and rib notching on chest x-ray.

However, rib notching is not typically seen in children because it takes years to develop. Instead, children with CoA may present with heart failure in infancy or, if the narrowing is not severe, may be asymptomatic until later in life. Older children may present with hypertension, headache, lower extremity claudication, cold lower extremities, or a systolic murmur heard posteriorly. The gold standard for diagnosis is angiography, but echocardiography is often used instead because it is less invasive.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his mother for an initial visit. He recently immigrated from Cambodia. Through an interpreter, the patient reports 6 months of mild exertional dyspnea. He denies chest pain or palpitations. His medical history is unremarkable and he has never had any surgeries. His family history is significant for hypertension and diabetes. His father died of tuberculosis. The patient’s vaccination history is unknown. His temperature is 98°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 113/71 mmHg, and pulse is 82/min. His BMI is 24 kg/m^2. Physical examination shows a well-nourished, cooperative boy without any grossly dysmorphic features. Cardiac auscultation reveals a grade II systolic ejection murmur along the left upper sternal border and a mid-diastolic rumble along the left sternal border. S1 is normal and the splitting of S2 does not change with inspiration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's physical examination findings of a systolic ejection murmur along the left upper sternal border and a mid-diastolic rumble along the left sternal border are suggestive of an atrial septal defect (ASD). ASDs are congenital heart defects that cause a left-to-right shunt. The systolic ejection murmur is due to increased flow across the pulmonic valve, and the mid-diastolic rumble is due to increased flow across the tricuspid valve. The splitting of S2 does not change with inspiration (fixed splitting) because the left-to-right shunt causes increased flow through the right ventricle, which delays closure of the pulmonic valve throughout the respiratory cycle.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [B] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 3-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of poor weight gain. She also reports a dusky blue discoloration to his skin during feedings and when crying. On examination, there is a harsh, systolic murmur heard over the left upper sternal border. An x-ray of the chest is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

answer_choices.B: Narrowing of the distal aortic arch
answer_choices.D: Anatomic reversal of aorta and pulmonary artery

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's cyanosis during feeding and crying, harsh systolic murmur, and boot-shaped heart on chest x-ray are suggestive of tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). TOF is the most common cause of cyanotic congenital heart disease beyond the neonatal period. It consists of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO), ventricular septal defect (VSD), overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. The degree of RVOTO determines the severity of the disease. In mild RVOTO, blood preferentially flows from the right ventricle (RV) to the pulmonary artery, and the VSD functions as a left-to-right shunt. These patients are acyanotic ("pink Tets"). In severe RVOTO, blood flow is directed from the RV to the aorta through the VSD, resulting in a right-to-left shunt and cyanosis. The cyanosis is exacerbated during episodes of increased RVOTO, which can be caused by any maneuver that decreases systemic vascular resistance (eg, crying, feeding, defecation) or increases RV contractility (eg, fever, anxiety). These episodes are known as "Tet spells" and can cause profound cyanosis.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [D] > [B] > [A].

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought by his parents to his pediatrician due to progressive fatigue and shortness of breath while playing sports. He is otherwise healthy with no known medical disorders and no other symptoms. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. He is up to date on all vaccines and is meeting all developmental milestones. On physical examination, his temperature is 36.9ºC (98.4ºF), pulse rate is 90/min, blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg, and respiratory rate is 18/min. Pulses in all four extremities are equal and normally palpated; there is no radio-femoral delay. The pediatrician suspects a congenital heart disease after auscultation of the heart. Which of the following congenital heart diseases is most likely to present with the clinical features listed above?

answer_choices.D: Double-outlet right ventricle with subaortic ventricular septal defect

few_shot.explanation:
Atrial septal defect (ASD) is a common congenital heart disease that often presents later in childhood or even in adulthood. It is characterized by a defect in the interatrial septum that allows for left-to-right shunting of blood. This shunting is usually well tolerated in childhood, but over time can lead to right heart volume overload, right atrial and ventricular enlargement, and increased pulmonary blood flow. This can cause symptoms such as fatigue and shortness of breath, especially during exercise. On physical examination, a fixed split S2 is often heard due to delayed closure of the pulmonic valve.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

question: A 75-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 3-day history of a productive cough and shortness of breath. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F) and respirations are 32/min. Crackles are heard over the right upper and the entire left lung fields. Sputum culture confirms infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae. Despite appropriate therapy, the patient dies. A photomicrograph of a section of the lung obtained during the autopsy is shown. Which of the following mediators is most likely responsible for the presence of the cell-type indicated by the arrow?

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever, malaise, cough, and shortness of breath for 2 months. He has had a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss during the same period. He works at a flour mill and does not smoke cigarettes. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F) and pulse oximetry shows 95% on room air. Diffuse fine crackles are heard over both lung fields. A chest x-ray shows patchy reticulonodular infiltrates in the mid and apical lung fields bilaterally. A photomicrograph of a lung biopsy specimen is shown. Which of the following cytokines have the greatest involvement in the pathogenesis of the lesion indicated by the arrow?

answer_choices.A: Tumor necrosis factor alpha and interleukin-4
answer_choices.D: Transforming growth factor beta and interleukin-12

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of occupational exposure to flour dust, chronic cough, and weight loss, along with the chest x-ray findings, suggest hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP). HP is an immune-mediated interstitial lung disease that occurs in response to repeated inhalation of organic dusts. The photomicrograph shows a noncaseating granuloma, which is a common finding in HP.

The pathogenesis of HP involves both the innate and adaptive immune responses. In the innate immune response, exposure to the inciting antigen (eg, thermophilic bacteria in moldy hay, avian proteins in bird droppings, isocyanates in spray paints) leads to activation of alveolar macrophages and secretion of proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha and interleukin-1. These cytokines recruit and activate inflammatory cells, leading to acute inflammation, fever, and dyspnea within hours of a heavy exposure.

In the adaptive immune response, which is responsible for the chronic symptoms of HP, antigen presenting cells activate CD4+ T-helper cells in the regional lymph nodes. These cells differentiate into effector T cells and, in response to interleukin-12, secrete interferon gamma and interleukin-2. Interferon gamma activates macrophages, leading to granuloma formation, and interleukin-2 promotes T-cell proliferation.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [A] > [D] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old male with a history of COPD presents to the emergency department with dyspnea, productive cough, and a fever of 40.0°C (104.0°F) for the past 2 days. His respiratory rate is 20/min, blood pressure is 125/85 mm Hg, and heart rate is 95/min. A chest X-ray is obtained and shows a right lower lobe infiltrate. Sputum cultures are pending and he is started on antibiotics. The patient has not received any vaccinations in the last 20 years. The physician discusses with him the importance of getting a vaccine that can produce immunity via which of the following mechanisms?

answer_choices.D: No need to vaccinate, as the patient has already had a pneumonia vaccine

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's fever, productive cough, and infiltrate on chest X-ray are consistent with pneumonia. Given his age and history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, he is at increased risk for invasive pneumococcal disease. The 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) is recommended for all adults >65 years of age and for younger persons with certain chronic illnesses. PPSV23 contains pneumococcal capsular polysaccharides that induce a T cell-independent B cell (ie, humoral) immune response. However, this type of response is not as robust as a T cell-dependent response; it wanes over time and does not elicit an anamnestic (memory) response on subsequent exposure to the antigen.

The 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) contains pneumococcal polysaccharides that are conjugated to a carrier protein. The carrier protein helps to convert the T cell-independent response into a T cell-dependent response, which is more robust, persists longer, and elicits an anamnestic response. Therefore, the PCV13 vaccine is also recommended for adults >65 years of age and should be administered first, followed by PPSV23.

So, the answer is [A].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [A] > [D] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 40-year-old man presents to the office complaining of chills, fever, and productive cough for the past 24 hours. He has a history of smoking since he was 18 years old. His vitals are: heart rate of 85/min, respiratory rate of 20/min, temperature 39.0°C (102.2°F), blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg. On physical examination, there is dullness on percussion on the upper right lobe, as well as bronchial breath sounds and egophony. The plain radiograph reveals an increase in density with an alveolar pattern in the upper right lobe. Which one is the most common etiologic agent of the suspected disease?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute onset fever, productive cough, and physical examination findings of consolidation (eg, dullness to percussion, bronchial breath sounds, egophony) are consistent with lobar pneumonia. The most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia in adults is Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus). Pneumococcal pneumonia classically presents as an acute illness with cough, fever, and pleuritic chest pain. Patients often have rigors and appear ill. The cough is typically productive with purulent sputum that may be blood-tinged or rust-colored. Physical examination reveals signs of lobar consolidation, including increased fremitus, egophony, and dullness to percussion. Chest x-ray shows lobar consolidation.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

Answer: [A] > [C] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 64-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain, and a productive cough with bloody sputum for the past several days. He has metastatic pancreatic cancer and is currently undergoing polychemotherapy. His temperature is 38.3°C (101°F). Pulmonary examination shows scattered inspiratory crackles in all lung fields. A CT scan of the chest shows multiple nodules, cavities, and patchy areas of consolidation. A photomicrograph of a specimen obtained on pulmonary biopsy is shown. Which of the following is the most likely causal pathogen?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of malignancy and chemotherapy, along with his symptoms of fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain, and hemoptysis, are suggestive of an invasive fungal infection. The CT scan findings of multiple nodules, cavities, and patchy areas of consolidation are also consistent with this diagnosis. The photomicrograph shows septate hyphae with acute angle branching, which is characteristic of Aspergillus species. Aspergillus fumigatus is the most common species to cause invasive aspergillosis.

Patients with prolonged neutropenia (eg, due to hematologic malignancies, chemotherapy) and those receiving chronic glucocorticoid therapy are at highest risk for invasive aspergillosis. The disease often manifests with fever and respiratory symptoms, including cough, dyspnea, and pleuritic chest pain. Hemoptysis may also occur due to invasion of the fungus into blood vessels with subsequent necrosis and cavitation.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [A] > [C] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old man with recurrent pneumonia comes to the physician for a follow-up examination one week after hospitalization for pneumonia. He feels well but still has a productive cough. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 5 years. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F) and respirations are 20/min. Cardiopulmonary examination shows coarse crackles at the right lung base. Microscopic examination of a biopsy specimen of the right lower lung parenchyma shows proliferation of clustered, cuboidal, foamy-appearing cells. These cells are responsible for which of the following functions?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's recurrent pneumonia and biopsy findings of clustered, cuboidal, foamy-appearing cells are consistent with alveolar proteinosis. This is a rare condition characterized by the accumulation of surfactant within alveoli. Surfactant is a lipoprotein complex that is synthesized and secreted by type II pneumocytes. It is composed of phospholipids (80%), neutral lipids (10%), and proteins (10%). The major phospholipid in surfactant is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC), also known as lecithin. Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A healthy 19-year-old man presents to his primary care provider complaining of painless “blisters” in his mouth. He reports that he noticed a white film on his tongue and the sides of his mouth 2 days ago while brushing his teeth. The film was easily brushed off. He also complains of a bitter metallic taste in his mouth but otherwise denies pain, burning, dysphagia, or hoarseness. He is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. He is a competitive swimmer and has had 8 sexual partners in the past year. He intermittently uses barrier protection. On exam, he is well-appearing and in no acute distress. His oral examination demonstrates patches of white pseudomembranes that can be wiped away to reveal erythematous mucosa. A medication with which of the following mechanisms of action is most appropriate in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 19-year-old woman comes to the physician because of worsening pain with swallowing for 3 days and a dry sensation in the mouth over the past week. She has a history of asthma controlled with inhaled fluticasone and albuterol. Physical examination shows white plaques on the dorsal surface of the tongue and buccal mucosa that bleed when scraped off. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of oral discomfort and white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa that bleed when scraped off are consistent with oral candidiasis (thrush). Oral candidiasis is an opportunistic infection caused by Candida species, most commonly Candida albicans. It is often seen in patients with immunosuppression (eg, HIV, malignancy, corticosteroid use) or those using inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) for asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. ICS can disrupt the normal oral flora and cause local immunosuppression, allowing Candida to proliferate. To decrease the risk of oral candidiasis, patients using ICS should rinse their mouths with water or brush their teeth after each use. 

Oral candidiasis is treated with topical antifungal agents such as nystatin oral suspension or clotrimazole troches. Patients should be instructed to swish the medication in the mouth and then swallow to also treat possible esophageal involvement. Systemic therapy with fluconazole is used for patients with severe or refractory disease or those who cannot tolerate oral medications.

So, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [C] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of pain in his mouth and throat and difficulty swallowing. He has a history of COPD, for which he takes theophylline and inhaled budesonide-formoterol. Physical examination shows white patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa that can be scraped off easily. Appropriate pharmacotherapy is initiated. One week later, he returns because of nausea, palpitations, and anxiety. His pulse is 110/min and regular. Physical examination shows a tremor in both hands. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of white patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa that can be scraped off easily is consistent with oral candidiasis. This is a common opportunistic infection in patients with COPD who use inhaled corticosteroids, which can cause local immunosuppression. The first-line treatment for oral candidiasis is a topical antifungal medication (eg, clotrimazole troches, nystatin oral suspension). However, for moderate to severe infection, oral fluconazole is often used.

Fluconazole is a potent inhibitor of the cytochrome P450 system, and can increase the levels of many drugs, including theophylline. Theophylline toxicity can present with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, insomnia, and sinus tachycardia. Severe cases can cause seizures and life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 16-year-old boy presents to his pediatrician because he has noticed white plaques forming on his tongue over the last 5 days. He recently returned from a boy scout trip where he traveled across the country and hiked through the woods. His past medical history is significant for asthma for which he uses an inhaler as needed. He says that during the trip he felt short of breath several times and had to use the inhaler. He also says that several of his friends appeared to get sick on the same trip and were coughing a lot. He has not experienced any other symptoms since returning from the trip. On presentation, he is found to have white plaques on the tongue that can be scraped off. Which of the following is a characteristic of the most likely cause of this patient's disease?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's white plaques on the tongue that can be scraped off are consistent with oral thrush, which is caused by Candida species. Candida is a yeast that is part of the normal human microbiota, but it can cause disease when the immune system is compromised or when the normal microbiota is disrupted. In this case, the patient's recent use of an inhaler for his asthma likely contained corticosteroids, which can cause local immunosuppression and predispose to oral thrush.

Candida is a yeast, and one of its defining characteristics is the ability to form germ tubes. Germ tubes are short outpouchings of the cell that go on to form true hyphae. They can be observed when Candida is incubated in serum at 37°C (98.6°F) and are an important part of the laboratory identification of Candida species.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old man presents with soreness and dryness of the oral mucosa for the past 3 weeks. No significant past medical history. The patient reports that he has had multiple bisexual partners over the last year and only occasionally uses condoms. He denies any alcohol use or history of smoking. The patient is afebrile and his vital signs are within normal limits. On physical examination, there is a lesion noted in the oral cavity, which is shown in the exhibit. Which of the following is the next best step in the treatment of this patient?

answer_choices.A: Change the patient’s toothbrush and improve oral hygiene

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of multiple sexual partners and the presence of a white, non-scrapable lesion on the lateral tongue are suggestive of oral hairy leukoplakia (OHL). OHL is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and is commonly seen in immunocompromised patients, especially those with HIV. The lesion is usually asymptomatic and does not require treatment unless it interferes with swallowing or is cosmetically unacceptable. In such cases, antiviral therapy with acyclovir, valacyclovir, or ganciclovir can be used. However, the most important next step in management is to confirm the diagnosis of HIV and initiate antiretroviral therapy, which can lead to resolution of the OHL.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of white lesions in his mouth for 4 days. He also has intense pain while chewing food. He was diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma around 8 months ago. He is undergoing chemotherapy and is currently on his fourth cycle. He was treated for herpes labialis 4 months ago with acyclovir. He has smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years. He appears healthy. Vital signs are within normal limits. Cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy is present. Oral examination shows white plaques on his tongue and buccal mucosa that bleed when scraped off. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's oral examination findings of white plaques that bleed when scraped off are consistent with oral candidiasis (thrush). Candida is a normal commensal organism in the oral cavity, but overgrowth can occur in certain conditions, such as immunosuppression (eg, HIV, chemotherapy), diabetes mellitus, use of inhaled corticosteroids, and antibiotic use. The diagnosis of oral candidiasis is usually made clinically, and treatment with topical antifungal agents (eg, nystatin, clotrimazole) is usually effective. Systemic therapy with fluconazole is used for severe or refractory cases.

So, the answer is [B].

question:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to a pediatrician by his parents for evaluation of frequent bed wetting during the night. A detailed history reveals that there has been no history of urinary incontinence during the day since the boy was 4 years of age, but that he has never been dry at night continuously for 1 week. There is no history of urinary tract infections, urgency, frequency, or hesitancy. On physical examination, the boy’s vital signs are stable. His neurologic and abdominal examinations are completely normal. His laboratory investigations are as follows:
Urine-specific gravity (first-morning sample) 1.035
Urine red blood cells Absent
Urine pus cells Absent
Urine culture Negative
Which of the following is the next step in the management of this patient?

answer_choices.A: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine
answer_choices.B: Reassuring the parents and use of an enuresis alarm

few_shot.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents for bedwetting. He went 3 months without wetting the bed but then started again 6 weeks ago. He has been wetting the bed about 1–2 times per week. He has not had daytime urinary incontinence or dysuria. His teachers report that he is attentive in preschool and plays well with his peers. He is able to name 5 colors, follow three-step commands, and recite his address. He can do a somersault, use scissors, and copy a square. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This child has primary nocturnal enuresis, defined as bedwetting in a child aged >5 years who has never achieved nighttime dryness for a period of >6 months. However, this child is only 4 years old. Most children achieve nighttime urinary continence by age 5 years, but 15%–20% of 5-year-olds and 10% of 6-year-olds continue to have episodes of nocturnal enuresis. Therefore, bedwetting in a 4-year-old is developmentally appropriate and does not require further evaluation or treatment. The child should not be punished for bedwetting. Instead, the parents should be reassured that their child is likely to achieve nighttime dryness as he gets older.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 6-year-old boy presents to the clinic because of monosymptomatic enuresis for the past month. Urinalysis, detailed patient history, and fluid intake, stool, and voiding diary from a previous visit all show no abnormalities. The parent and child are referred for education and behavioral therapy. Enuresis decreases but persists. Both the patient and his mother express concern and want this issue to resolve as soon as possible. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
The first-line treatment for primary nocturnal enuresis is behavioral therapy, which includes nighttime fluid restriction, avoidance of caffeine, regular voiding during the day, and positive reinforcement. If these measures are not successful, the next step is to use an enuresis alarm. This is a moisture-sensitive device that wakes the child at the onset of urination. The alarm helps condition the child to associate a full bladder with the need to awaken and void. Enuresis alarms have the highest cure rate and the lowest relapse rate of all treatments for enuresis.

Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a synthetic analog of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) that works by decreasing nocturnal urine production. It is typically used for sleepovers or camp, but is less effective for long-term management because of a high relapse rate after discontinuation.

Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic medication used to treat overactive bladder, a condition this patient does not have.

So, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question:
A 13-month-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician by her stepfather for irritability. He states that his daughter was crying through the night last night, but she didn’t want to eat and was inconsolable. This morning, she felt warm. The father also notes that she had dark, strong smelling urine on the last diaper change. The patient’s temperature is 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 100/72 mmHg, pulse is 128/min, and respirations are 31/min with an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. A urinalysis is obtained by catheterization, with results shown below:

Urine:
Protein: Negative
Glucose: Negative
White blood cell (WBC) count: 25/hpf
Bacteria: Many
Leukocyte esterase: Positive
Nitrites: Positive

In addition to antibiotics, which of the following should be part of the management of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a urinary tract infection (UTI), as evidenced by her irritability, fever, and malodorous urine, as well as pyuria and bacteriuria on urinalysis. UTIs are common in children and can lead to significant morbidity (eg, renal scarring, hypertension, end-stage renal disease) if not promptly diagnosed and treated. Therefore, it is important to obtain a urine culture to identify the causative organism and determine its antibiotic susceptibility pattern. The patient should also be started on empiric antibiotic therapy, typically with a third-generation cephalosporin (eg, ceftriaxone) or amoxicillin-clavulanate.

In addition to antibiotics, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends renal and bladder ultrasonography for all children aged 2 to 24 months following a first febrile UTI. This is performed to identify any anatomic abnormalities (eg, vesicoureteral reflux [VUR], ureteropelvic junction obstruction, multicystic dysplastic kidney) that may predispose the child to UTIs or renal damage.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for recurrent bedwetting. The child has an intellectual disability; thus, the mother is providing most of the history. She states that the child constantly drinks fluids and has a difficult time making it to the bathroom as often as he needs. Therefore, he sometimes wets himself during the day and at night. She has tried bedwetting alarms with no success. Review of systems is negative. His past medical history is unremarkable expect for moderate growth retardation. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 80/54 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 20/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Routine laboratory tests and a 24 hour urine test are shown below.

Serum:
Na+: 138 mEq/L
Cl-: 90 mEq/L
K+: 2.5 mEq/L
HCO3-: 35 mEq/L 
BUN: 9 mg/dL 
Glucose: 98 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.0 mg/dL
Thyroid-stimulating hormone: 1.2 µU/mL
Ca2+: 9.1 mg/dL
AST: 13 U/L
ALT: 10 U/L
pH: 7.49

Urine:
Epithelial cells: 5 cells
Glucose: Negative
WBC: 0/hpf
Bacterial: None
Protein: 60 mg/24h (Normal: < 150 mg/24h)
Calcium: 370 mg/24h (Normal: 100-300 mg/24h)
Osmolality 1600 mOsmol/kg H2O (Normal: 50-1400 mOsmol/kg H2O)

What is the most likely explanation for this patient’s findings?

answer_choices.A: Defect of NaCl reabsorption at the distal collecting tube
answer_choices.B: Defect of Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter at the thick ascending loop of Henle
answer_choices.C: Generalized reabsorptive defect in the proximal collecting tube

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's polyuria, polydipsia, and nocturnal enuresis are suggestive of diabetes insipidus (DI). DI is characterized by the inability to concentrate urine due to a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) (central DI) or renal resistance to ADH (nephrogenic DI). Central DI is often due to hypothalamic or posterior pituitary pathology (eg, trauma, tumor, inflammation), whereas nephrogenic DI is usually due to an inherited mutation or is acquired secondary to hypercalcemia, lithium, or demeclocycline.

The urine osmolality in DI is usually <300 mOsm/kg H2O, but this patient's urine osmolality is 1600 mOsm/kg H2O, which is inappropriately high given his low serum osmolality. This suggests impaired urinary dilution rather than concentration. The patient also has hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Taken together, these findings are suggestive of a diagnosis of Bartter syndrome, a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by impaired salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. This leads to a urinary concentration defect with polyuria, polydipsia, and a propensity for dehydration. Chronic volume depletion due to salt wasting results in increased renin, aldosterone, and angiotensin II levels, leading to potassium wasting and metabolic alkalosis. Patients may also have hypercalciuria due to impaired calcium reabsorption.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of irritability and poor feeding that began 2 days ago. His mother reports that he has been crying more than usual during this period. He refused to eat his breakfast that morning and has not taken in any food or water since that time. He has not vomited. When changing the boy's diapers this morning, the mother noticed his urine had a strong smell and pink color. He has not passed urine since then. He was born at term and has been healthy. He appears ill. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 116/min, and blood pressure is 98/54 mm Hg. The boy cries when the lower abdomen is palpated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's irritability, poor feeding, and strong-smelling, pink urine are concerning for a urinary tract infection (UTI). UTIs are common in children and can present with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, vomiting, poor feeding, irritability, or jaundice. Hematuria and foul-smelling urine can also be seen. UTIs are more common in uncircumcised boys and in girls due to the shorter length of the urethra. In children, UTIs can lead to renal scarring, which can cause hypertension and end-stage renal disease later in life.

The gold standard for diagnosing UTIs is urine culture. In children who are not toilet trained, the best way to obtain a urine sample for culture is via transurethral catheterization or suprapubic aspiration. Clean catch urine samples are often contaminated in these patients.

So, the answer is [C].

question: A 24-year-old man is brought in to the emergency department by his parents who found him in his room barely responsive and with slurring speech. The patients’ parents say that a bottle of oxycodone was found at his bedside and was missing 15 pills. On physical examination, the patient appears drowsy and lethargic and is minimally responsive to stimuli. His respiratory rate is 8/min and shallow, blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg, and pulse is 60/min. On physical examination, miosis is present, and the pupils appear pinpoint. The patient is given a drug to improve his symptoms. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the drug that was most likely administered?

answer_choices.A: μ, κ, and ẟ receptor antagonist
answer_choices.C: к receptor agonist and μ receptor antagonist
answer_choices.D: μ receptor partial agonist and к receptor agonist

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman was found lying unconscious on the side of the street by her friend. He immediately called the ambulance who were close to this neighborhood. On initial examination, she appears barely able to breathe. Her pupils are pinpoint. The needles she likely used were found on site but the drug she injected was unknown. The first responders were quick to administer a drug which is effectively used in these situations and her symptoms slowly began to reverse. She was taken to the nearest emergency department for further workup. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the drug administered by the first responders?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's presentation of unconsciousness, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils is suggestive of opioid overdose. The drug of choice in this situation is naloxone, a competitive antagonist at opioid receptors, with the highest affinity for the mu receptor. Naloxone can reverse the effects of opioid toxicity, including respiratory depression, sedation, and hypotension. It is often administered intranasally or intramuscularly by first responders when opioid overdose is suspected.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after he was found half dressed and incoherent in the middle of the road. In the emergency department he states that he has not slept for 36 hours and that he has incredible ideas that will make him a billionaire within a few months. He also states that secret agents from Russia are pursuing him and that he heard one of them speaking through the hospital intercom. His past medical history is significant only for a broken arm at age 13. On presentation, his temperature is 102.2°F (39°C), blood pressure is 139/88 mmHg, pulse is 112/min, and respirations are 17/min. Physical exam reveals pupillary dilation and psychomotor agitation. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of psychomotor agitation, insomnia, grandiosity, and auditory hallucinations is suggestive of a manic episode. His pupillary dilation, tachycardia, and hyperthermia suggest a sympathomimetic syndrome, which can be seen in intoxication with cocaine, amphetamines, or other stimulants. These agents cause an increase in the release of biogenic amines (eg, norepinephrine, dopamine, serotonin) in the brain, leading to the observed symptoms.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his girlfriend discovered him at home in a minimally responsive state. He has a history of drinking alcohol excessively and using illicit drugs. On arrival, he does not respond to commands but withdraws all extremities to pain. His pulse is 90/min, respirations are 8/min, and blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry while receiving bag-valve-mask ventilation shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. Examination shows cool, dry skin, with scattered track marks on his arms and legs. The pupils are pinpoint and react sluggishly to light. His serum blood glucose level is 80 mg/dL. The most appropriate next step in management is intravenous administration of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of drug use, pinpoint pupils, and depressed mental status are suggestive of opioid overdose. Opioids (eg, heroin, morphine, fentanyl) bind to mu receptors in the central nervous system, leading to analgesia, euphoria, and decreased respiratory drive. Opioid overdose can cause life-threatening respiratory depression, and patients may present with bradypnea or apnea, pinpoint pupils, and stupor or coma.

Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist that can rapidly reverse the effects of opioids. It should be administered intravenously, intramuscularly, or intranasally to any patient with suspected opioid overdose and respiratory depression (respiratory rate <12/min) or a Glasgow Coma Scale score <15. Naloxone has a short half-life, and patients with severe intoxication may require additional doses or a continuous infusion.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 20-year-old man is found lying unconscious on the floor of his room by his roommate. The paramedics arrive at the site and find him unresponsive with cold, clammy extremities and constricted, non-reactive pupils. He smells of alcohol and his vital signs show the following: blood pressure 110/80 mm Hg, pulse 100/min, and respiratory rate 8/min. Intravenous access is established and dextrose is administered. The roommate suggests the possibility of drug abuse by the patient. He says he has seen the patient sniff a powdery substance, and he sees the patient inject himself often but has never confronted him about it. After the initial assessment, the patient is given medication and, within 5–10 minutes of administration, the patient regains consciousness and his breathing improves. He is alert and cooperative within the next few minutes. Which of the following drugs was given to this patient to help alleviate his symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's presentation of unconsciousness, respiratory depression, and constricted pupils is suggestive of opioid overdose. Opioids are a class of drugs that include the illegal drug heroin, synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, and pain relievers available legally by prescription, such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, morphine, and many others. Opioid overdose can be fatal if not treated promptly. The drug of choice for the treatment of opioid overdose is naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist that rapidly reverses the effects of opioids. Naloxone can be given intravenously, intramuscularly, or intranasally. It has a rapid onset of action (within 2 minutes if given intravenously) and a short half-life (30–81 minutes), so patients who have taken long-acting or high doses of opioids may require repeated administration or continuous infusion.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A middle-aged homeless man is found lying unresponsive on the streets by the police and is rushed to the emergency department. His vital signs include: blood pressure 110/80 mm Hg, pulse rate 100/min, and respirations 10/min and shallow. On physical examination, his extremities are cold and clammy. Pupils are constricted and non-reactive. His blood glucose is 55 mg/dL. IV access is established immediately with the administration of dextrose and naloxone. In half an hour, the patient is fully conscious, alert and responsive. He denies any medical illnesses, hospitalizations, or surgeries in the past. Physical examination reveals injection track marks along both arms. He admits to the use of cocaine and heroin. He smokes cigarettes and consumes alcohol. His vital signs are now stable. A urine sample is sent for toxicology screening. Which of the following was the most likely cause of this patient’s respiratory depression?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of unresponsiveness, respiratory depression, and constricted pupils is consistent with opioid intoxication. Opioids (eg, heroin, morphine, fentanyl) bind to mu-opioid receptors in the central nervous system, leading to analgesia, euphoria, and decreased respiratory drive. Opioid intoxication can cause life-threatening respiratory depression and is a common cause of drug overdose death. Naloxone is an opioid receptor antagonist that can rapidly reverse the effects of opioid toxicity.

Hypoglycemia can cause altered mental status, but it would not cause respiratory depression or constricted pupils. Alcohol intoxication can cause altered mental status and respiratory depression, but it would not cause constricted pupils. Hallucinogens (eg, LSD, psilocybin) can cause hallucinations and other perceptual disturbances, but they do not typically cause respiratory depression or constricted pupils.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 60-year-old female presents to her gynecologist with vaginal bleeding. She underwent menopause ten years prior. She has a past medical history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus. On physical examination, her uterus is uniformly enlarged. Ultrasound reveals a thickened endometrial stripe and tissue biopsy reveals neoplastic endometrial cells. A workup for metastatic disease is negative and the gynecologist recommends a laparoscopic hysterectomy. During the procedure, the surgeon ligates multiple vessels in order to remove the entire uterus. In the immediate postoperative period, the patient develops left-sided flank pain and oliguria. Serum creatinine is found to be 1.4 mg/dl whereas it was 1.0 mg/dl prior to the operation. Renal ultrasound is normal. Urinalysis is notable for hematuria. Ligation of which of the following vessels most likely contributed to this patient’s condition?

few_shot.question: A 48-year-old woman presents with a 15-year history of long, painful menses that is only partially relieved with oral contraceptives. She desires definitive treatment. She denies weight loss or post-coital bleeding, and her husband has been her only sexual partner. She does not have a history of smoking, alcohol or illicit drug use, or sexually transmitted diseases. She sees her gynecologist annually. She takes no medications. An abdominal ultrasound shows a non-gravid uterus with hyperechoic islands and an irregular endometrial-myometrial junction, consistent with adenomyosis. A supracervical hysterectomy and left salpingo-oophorectomy are performed without incident. Later that day, the patient’s vitals are stable: temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), heart rate 98/min, respiratory rate 15/min, blood pressure 100/75 mm Hg, breathing 100% oxygen on room air. The patient is not in acute distress with a Foley catheter in place. The physical exam is unremarkable. However, she has only excreted a minimal amount of urine output in the past several hours after surgery. Only 10cc or urine is produced over the next 12 hours. A bladder scan shows minimal residual urine. CBC, CMP, and urinalysis are ordered, and renal ultrasound is shown in the picture. What are the likely cause of this patient’s anuria and ultrasound finding?

answer_choices.A: Iatrogenic injury near the suspensory ligaments
answer_choices.B: Prerenal azotemia secondary to excessive hemorrhage
answer_choices.C: Acute tubular necrosis secondary to hypovolemia

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's anuria and ultrasound findings are suggestive of bilateral ureteral obstruction. The ureters are retroperitoneal structures that course from the renal pelvis, over the common iliac vessels, and along the lateral pelvic wall to reach the bladder. They are susceptible to injury at 3 sites: the pelvic brim, as they cross anterior to the sacroiliac joint; at the infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament, as they course under the ovarian vessels; and at the uterine artery in the cardinal ligament, as they pass medial to and under the uterine artery ("water under the bridge"). The latter 2 sites are particularly vulnerable during hysterectomy and oophorectomy, as they are in close proximity to the surgical field. Ureteral injury can lead to urinary extravasation and resultant urinoma, as seen in this patient. 

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 60-year-old post-menopausal female presents to her gynecologist with vaginal bleeding. Her last period was over 10 years ago. Dilation and curettage reveals endometrial carcinoma so she is scheduled to undergo a total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. During surgery, the gynecologist visualizes paired fibrous structures arising from the cervix and attaching to the lateral pelvic walls at the level of the ischial spines. Which of the following vessels is found within each of the paired visualized structure?
few_shot.explanation:
The paired fibrous structures visualized by the gynecologist are the uterosacral ligaments. These ligaments are part of the cardinal ligament complex, which also includes the cardinal ligaments and the pubocervical ligaments. The uterosacral ligaments extend from the cervix to the sacrum, while the cardinal ligaments extend from the cervix to the lateral pelvic walls. The uterine arteries are found within the cardinal ligaments.

The uterine arteries are branches of the internal iliac arteries and are the primary blood supply to the uterus. They course within the cardinal ligament and give off several branches to supply the uterus, cervix, and superior part of the vagina. The uterine arteries also anastomose with the ovarian arteries along the lateral aspect of the uterus.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old nulliparous woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of heavy, prolonged bleeding with menstruation, dyspareunia, and cyclical abdominal pain. Menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals and lasted 4 days with normal flow. Pelvic examination shows an asymmetrically enlarged, nodular uterus consistent in size with a 10-week gestation. A urine pregnancy test is negative. A photomicrograph of a section of an endometrial biopsy specimen is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), dyspareunia, and cyclical abdominal pain, along with the finding of an asymmetrically enlarged, nodular uterus, are suggestive of leiomyoma (uterine fibroids). Leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle tumors that are often multiple and can vary in size. They are the most common indication for hysterectomy in the United States. Leiomyomas are estrogen-dependent and occur most commonly in women aged 30-50. They are more common in African American women.

The photomicrograph shows a well-circumscribed nodule composed of interlacing bundles of smooth muscle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. This is consistent with a leiomyoma.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of intermittent bleeding from her vagina. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Pelvic ultrasound shows a thickened endometrial stripe and a left adnexal mass. Endometrial biopsy shows a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma. Laboratory studies show increased levels of inhibin B. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's postmenopausal vaginal bleeding, thickened endometrial stripe, and well-differentiated endometrial adenocarcinoma are suggestive of an estrogen-secreting tumor. The most likely source of the estrogen is the left adnexal mass. Granulosa cell tumors are estrogen-secreting ovarian neoplasms that can cause endometrial hyperplasia and/or carcinoma due to unopposed estrogen stimulation. These tumors can occur at any age but are most common in postmenopausal women. They are often solid and may be large, with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. Microscopically, granulosa cell tumors are characterized by Call-Exner bodies, which are small gland-like structures filled with eosinophilic fluid. In addition to estrogen, granulosa cell tumors secrete inhibin, a peptide hormone that suppresses FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 58-year-old woman presents to the physician’s office with vaginal bleeding. The bleeding started as a spotting and has increased and has become persistent over the last month. The patient is G3P1 with a history of polycystic ovary syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She completed menopause 4 years ago. She took cyclic estrogen-progesterone replacement therapy for 1 year at the beginning of menopause. Her weight is 89 kg (196 lb), height 157 cm (5 ft 2 in). Her vital signs are as follows: blood pressure 135/70 mm Hg, heart rate 78/min, respiratory rate 12/min, and temperature 36.7℃ (98.1℉). Physical examination is unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound reveals an endometrium of 6 mm thickness. Speculum examination shows a cervix without focal lesions with bloody discharge from the non-dilated external os. On pelvic examination, the uterus is slightly enlarged, movable, and non-tender. Adnexa is non-palpable. What is the next appropriate step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has postmenopausal bleeding (PMB), which is defined as any bleeding that occurs 12 months or more after the last menstrual period. PMB is a common problem, occurring in up to 10% of postmenopausal women. The most common cause of PMB is atrophy of the endometrium or vagina due to decreased estrogen levels. However, PMB can also be a sign of endometrial cancer or atypical endometrial hyperplasia, a precursor to cancer. Therefore, all women with PMB should undergo evaluation to exclude endometrial cancer or hyperplasia.

The initial evaluation of PMB includes a transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness. An endometrial thickness ≤4 mm significantly decreases the likelihood of endometrial cancer in a patient with PMB. However, if the endometrial thickness is >4 mm, as in this patient, or if it cannot be adequately measured, an endometrial biopsy should be performed. Endometrial biopsy is an office-based procedure that involves dilating the cervix and passing a small suction catheter into the uterus to obtain a sample of the endometrium. It is the most cost-effective method for evaluating women with PMB and has a sensitivity of approximately 90% for diagnosing endometrial cancer.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

question:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of facial swelling that started 5 days ago. Two weeks ago, he had a sore throat that resolved spontaneously. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 107/min, and blood pressure is 94/67 mm Hg. Examination shows pitting edema of the upper and lower extremities as well as periorbital edema. The abdomen is mildly distended. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL
Serum
Albumin 2.1 g/dL
Total cholesterol 270 mg/dL
Triglycerides 175 mg/dL
Urine
Blood negative
Glucose negative
Protein 4+
Leukocyte esterase negative
A renal biopsy of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?"
