Answer: [C] > [D] > [B] > [A].

question:
A 65-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of repeated falls, postural dizziness, progressive fatigue, generalized weakness and a 13.6 kg (30 lb) weight loss. He is a vegetarian. The patient’s family says that he had been high functioning but has had significant behavioral changes over the past year. The patient denies any smoking history, alcohol consumption, or illicit drug use. No significant family history. His vital signs include: blood pressure 90/50 mm Hg without postural changes, pulse 92/min, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 37.0℃ (98.6℉). Physical examination reveals a poorly groomed, disheveled, thin man. He is irritable, paranoid, and delusional but denies any hallucinations. An unstable, wide-based ataxic gait is noted. Laboratory results are significant for the following:
Hb 6.1 g/dL
MCV 109 fL
Platelets 90,0000/mm3
Total count 3,000/mm3
Reticulocyte count 0.8%
A peripheral blood smear demonstrates hypersegmented neutrophils. Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?

few_shot.question:
A 65-year-old man presented to the hospital with a history of repeated falls, postural dizziness, progressive fatigue, generalized weakness, and a 13.6 kg (30 lb) weight loss over a duration of 6 months. He is a vegetarian. His family members complain of significant behavioral changes over the past year. The patient denies smoking, alcohol consumption, or illicit drug use. There is no significant family history of any illness. Initial examination reveals a pale, thin built man. He is irritable, paranoid, delusional, but denies any hallucinations. The blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg, heart rate is 92/min, respiratory rate is 16/min, and the temperature is 36.1℃ (97℉). He has an unstable, wide-based ataxic gait. The anti-intrinsic factor antibodies test is positive. The laboratory test results are as follows:
Hb 6.1gm/dL
MCV 99 fL
Platelets 900,000/mm3
Total WBC count 3,000/mm3
Reticulocyte 0.8%
The peripheral blood smear is shown in the image below. What is the most likely cause of his condition?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of fatigue, weakness, weight loss, and behavioral changes, along with the presence of anti-intrinsic factor antibodies and the peripheral blood smear findings of hypersegmented neutrophils and macrocytic anemia, are suggestive of pernicious anemia. Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disease that results in vitamin B12 deficiency due to the destruction of gastric parietal cells, which produce intrinsic factor. Intrinsic factor is necessary for the absorption of vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum. Vitamin B12 is necessary for DNA synthesis, and a deficiency can lead to ineffective erythropoiesis and intramedullary hemolysis, which can cause a decrease in hemoglobin and hematocrit. The decrease in DNA synthesis also affects the maturation of the nucleus in hematopoietic cells, which can cause hypersegmented neutrophils (as seen in the peripheral blood smear). Vitamin B12 is also necessary for the maintenance of the myelin sheath in neurons. A deficiency can lead to the demyelination of neurons, especially in the dorsal and lateral spinal columns, which can cause a wide-based ataxic gait, paresthesia, weakness, and loss of proprioception and vibratory sense.

So, the answer is [C].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [C] > [B] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question:
A 47-year-old man comes to the physician for gradual onset of fatigue for the last 4 months. He also reports shortness of breath and difficulty concentrating. His friends have told him that he appears pale. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the last 20 years. He does not drink alcohol. His vital signs are within normal limits. Neurological examination shows reduced sensation to light touch and pinprick in the toes bilaterally. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 108 μm3
Leukocyte count 4,200/mm3
Serum
Thyroid-stimulating hormone 2.6 μU/mL
Iron 67 μg/dL
Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) 51 ng/L (N = 170–900)
Folic acid 13 ng/mL (N = 5.4–18)
An oral dose of radiolabeled vitamin B12 is administered, followed by an intramuscular injection of nonradioactive vitamin B12. A 24-hour urine sample is collected and urine vitamin B12 levels are unchanged. The procedure is repeated with the addition of oral intrinsic factor, and 24-hour urine vitamin B12 levels increase. The patient is at increased risk for which of the following?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fatigue, pallor, and macrocytic anemia with low vitamin B12 levels are suggestive of vitamin B12 deficiency. The finding of decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the toes is consistent with peripheral neuropathy, which is seen in vitamin B12 deficiency but not in folate deficiency. The Schilling test results are consistent with pernicious anemia, the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency. Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to intrinsic factor deficiency and vitamin B12 malabsorption. Pernicious anemia is associated with an increased risk of gastric carcinoma, especially gastric carcinoid tumors. This is thought to be due to the chronic atrophic gastritis and subsequent intestinal metaplasia that occur in pernicious anemia.

So, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question:
A 64-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a fall. The patient states that he has felt abnormally clumsy lately and has noticed himself tripping and bumping into things. He states he otherwise is healthy but admits to having unprotected sex with multiple people recently. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 127/68 mm Hg, pulse is 100/min, respiratory rate is 24/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Laboratory values are ordered as seen below.

Hemoglobin: 9 g/dL
Hematocrit: 30%
Mean corpuscular volume: 110 fL
Leukocyte count: 6,500/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 197,000/mm^3
AST: 15 U/L
ALT: 22 U/L
GGT: 10 U/L

Physical exam is notable for a broad-based and unstable gait. Which of the following conditions is the most likely etiology of this patient's presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's macrocytic anemia and neurologic symptoms (eg, gait instability) suggest vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency. Cobalamin is a cofactor for methionine synthase, which converts homocysteine to methionine, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Deficiency impairs these reactions, leading to elevated levels of homocysteine and methylmalonic acid. Homocysteine is thought to be neurotoxic and may contribute to the neurologic symptoms seen in cobalamin deficiency.

Cobalamin is found in animal products, and deficiency can occur due to inadequate intake (eg, vegetarian diet), malabsorption, or lack of intrinsic factor due to pernicious anemia or gastric surgery. The most common cause of cobalamin deficiency in developed countries is food-cobalamin malabsorption syndrome, which is often due to atrophic gastritis or long-term use of medications that suppress gastric acid (eg, proton pump inhibitors, H2 blockers). Atrophic gastritis can be caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or can be an autoimmune disorder. It is associated with advancing age and can be asymptomatic or cause vague dyspeptic symptoms.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A previously healthy 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of a 2-day history of poor balance and difficulty walking. He has fallen multiple times and is unable to walk up the stairs unassisted. He has also had difficulty tying his shoes and dressing himself. His family adheres to a vegetarian diet. He has not yet received any routine childhood vaccinations. His mother has a history of anxiety. He is at the 70th percentile for height and 30th percentile for weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Physical examination shows a broad-based, staggering gait. He has difficulty touching his nose and cannot perform rapidly-alternating palm movements. Strength is 5/5 in the upper and lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ bilaterally. Skin examination shows several faint hyperpigmented macules on the chest. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's ataxia, dysmetria, and dysdiadochokinesia (inability to perform rapidly alternating movements) suggest cerebellar dysfunction. The most common cause of acute cerebellar ataxia in children is postinfectious cerebellitis, which typically occurs 2-3 weeks following a viral infection or vaccination. Varicella zoster virus is the most common cause, but other viruses (eg, coxsackievirus, Epstein-Barr virus, influenza) and bacterial infections (eg, Mycoplasma pneumoniae) can also be responsible. Patients typically present with acute onset of truncal ataxia and gait instability, often with associated nausea and vomiting due to increased intracranial pressure. Although the patient's history is not classic for a preceding varicella infection (eg, no mention of a vesicular rash), the presence of hyperpigmented macules suggests recent resolution of cutaneous lesions. The absence of varicella vaccination in this patient increases the likelihood of this diagnosis.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question:
A 36-year-old woman gravida 5, para 4 was admitted at 31 weeks of gestation with worsening fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion for the past month. She also has nausea and loss of appetite. No significant past medical history. The patient denies any smoking history, alcohol or illicit drug use. Her vital signs include: blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, pulse 120/min, respiratory rate 22/min and temperature 35.1℃ (97.0℉). A complete blood count reveals a macrocytosis with severe pancytopenia, as follows:
Hb 7.2 g/dL
RBC 3.6 million/uL
WBC 4,400/mm3
Neutrophils 40%
Lymphocytes 20%
Platelets 15,000/mm3
MCV 104 fL
Reticulocytes 0.9%
Serum ferritin and vitamin B12 levels were within normal limits. There was an elevated homocysteine level and a normal methylmalonic acid level. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's macrocytic anemia, elevated homocysteine level, and normal methylmalonic acid level are suggestive of folate deficiency. Folate is a water-soluble vitamin that is necessary for the synthesis of purines and pyrimidines, which are the building blocks of DNA. Folate deficiency can lead to megaloblastic anemia, which is characterized by macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral blood smear. In addition to anemia, folate deficiency can also cause leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, as seen in this patient.

Folate deficiency can be caused by inadequate dietary intake, malabsorption, increased requirements (eg, pregnancy), or medications (eg, methotrexate, phenytoin). In this patient, the most likely cause of folate deficiency is increased requirements due to her pregnancy.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of sudden-onset right-sided body numbness for 1 hour. He reports that he has a 15-year history of hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. He is alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Neurological examination shows decreased sensation to light pinprick and temperature on the right side of the face and body. Motor strength is 5/5 and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. Perfusion of which of the following structures of the brain is most likely impaired in this patient?

answer_choices.A: Posterior limb of the internal capsule

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of increasing weakness of his right arm and leg that began when he woke up that morning. He did not notice any weakness when he went to bed the night before. He has hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide and atorvastatin. He is alert and oriented to person, time, place. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 91/min, and blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg. Examination shows drooping of the right side of the face. Muscle strength is decreased in the right upper and lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ on the right side. Sensation is intact. His speech is normal in rate and rhythm. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An infarction of which of the following sites is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.A: Posterior limb of the left internal capsule

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of contralateral hemiparesis and hyperreflexia without involvement of the cranial nerves or sensory deficits suggest a lesion in the primary motor cortex or the corticospinal tract. The most common site of such lesions is the posterior limb of the internal capsule, which contains both ascending (sensory) and descending (motor) fibers. The motor fibers are somatotopically arranged, with the arm and face lateral to the leg. Therefore, a small lesion (lacunar infarct) in the posterior limb of the internal capsule can cause contralateral pure motor hemiparesis, as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of headache, blurring of vision, and numbness of the right leg for the past 2 hours. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications include enalapril and metformin. He is oriented only to person. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 99/min and blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg. Examination shows equal pupils that are reactive to light. Muscle strength is normal in all extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. Sensation to fine touch and position is decreased over the right lower extremity. The confrontation test shows loss of the nasal field in the left eye and the temporal field in the right eye with macular sparing. He is unable to read phrases shown to him but can write them when they are dictated to him. He has short-term memory deficits. Which of the following is the most likely cause for this patient's symptoms?

answer_choices.A: Infarct of the right posterior cerebral artery
answer_choices.B: Infarct of the right anterior cerebral artery
answer_choices.D: Infarct of the left posterior cerebral artery

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of acute onset headache, visual field defects, and right leg sensory loss are suggestive of a stroke. The visual field defects are consistent with a left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, which is characteristic of an infarct in the distribution of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). The PCA supplies the occipital lobe (responsible for vision) and parts of the temporal lobe (involved in memory). The sensory loss in the right leg is due to involvement of the thalamus, which is also supplied by the PCA. The PCA is a branch of the basilar artery, which is formed by the confluence of the vertebral arteries. The PCA gives off many branches, including the thalamoperforating arteries to the thalamus and the calcarine branch to the occipital lobe. The thalamus is responsible for sensory relay and the occipital lobe is responsible for vision. Therefore, occlusion of the left PCA would cause right-sided sensory loss and left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

So, the answer is [D].

## List all options from most likely to least likely
Answer: [D] > [A] > [B] > [C].

few_shot.question: A 54-year-old man is referred to a tertiary care hospital with a history of 5 months of progressive difficulty in walking and left leg numbness. He first noticed mild gait unsteadiness and later developed gradual right leg weakness. His left leg developed progressive numbness and tingling. His blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg, the heart rate is 72/min, and the temperature is 36.7°C (98.2°F). On physical examination, he is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Cranial nerves are intact. Muscle strength is 5/5 in both upper extremities and left lower extremity, but 3/5 in the right leg with increased tone. The plantar reflex is extensor on the right. Pinprick sensation is decreased on the left side below the umbilicus. Vibration and joint position senses are decreased in the right foot and leg. All sensations are normal in the upper extremities. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing are normal. This patient’s lesion is most likely located in which of the following parts of the nervous system?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's clinical presentation is consistent with Brown-Séquard syndrome, which is characterized by a hemisection of the spinal cord. This syndrome is usually caused by penetrating trauma, but can also be due to a spinal cord tumor or multiple sclerosis. The classic presentation includes ipsilateral motor dysfunction and loss of proprioception and vibration sense, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation. This is due to the fact that motor fibers and the dorsal columns carrying proprioception and vibration sensation cross within the brainstem, whereas the spinothalamic tract carrying pain and temperature sensation crosses within the spinal cord at the level of entry. Therefore, a hemisection of the spinal cord will affect the ipsilateral corticospinal tract and dorsal columns, and the contralateral spinothalamic tract.

In this patient, the right leg weakness and increased tone with an extensor plantar reflex indicate upper motor neuron dysfunction from a right-sided corticospinal tract lesion. The decreased vibration and joint position senses in the right leg localize to a lesion in the right dorsal columns. The decreased pinprick sensation on the left side of the body below the umbilicus indicates a lesion of the right spinothalamic tract.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

Answer: [C] > [A] > [B] > [D].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old man with longstanding history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset numbness. On your neurological exam, you note that he has loss of sensation on the left side of his face, arm, and leg. His motor strength exam is normal, as are his cranial nerves. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of contralateral hemisensory loss with a normal motor exam is suggestive of a thalamic stroke. The thalamus is a relay station for sensory information from the body to the cerebral cortex. It is supplied by small penetrating arteries known as thalamoperforators, which arise from the posterior cerebral artery. Occlusion of these arteries can cause a thalamic (or thalamic lacunar) stroke, leading to contralateral hemisensory loss. Other symptoms can include contralateral hemiparesis, hemiataxia, and possibly a mild language disturbance if the dominant hemisphere is involved.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension and coronary artery disease is brought to the emergency department after the sudden onset of right-sided weakness. Her pulse is 83/min and blood pressure is 156/90 mm Hg. Neurological examination shows right-sided facial drooping and complete paralysis of the right upper and lower extremities. Tongue position is normal and she is able to swallow liquids without difficulty. Knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes are exaggerated on the right. Sensation to vibration, position, and light touch is normal bilaterally. She is oriented to person, place, and time, and is able to speak normally. Occlusion of which of the following vessels is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of right-sided hemiplegia and facial drooping with sparing of sensation and higher cognitive function are consistent with a lacunar stroke. Lacunar strokes are small infarcts that occur in the deep brain structures (eg, basal ganglia, internal capsule) and are most commonly due to occlusion of the small, deep penetrating arteries such as the lenticulostriate arteries. These arteries are branches of the middle cerebral artery and supply the internal capsule, which contains the corticospinal tracts. Occlusion of these arteries can cause pure motor hemiparesis, a type of lacunar syndrome.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 67-year-old man with transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of ringing sensation in his ear. few_shot.question: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of headaches and back pain. Examination shows mild sensorineural hearing loss. Serum concentration of alkaline phosphatase is increased. An x-ray of the skull is shown. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient is a drug that has which of the following mechanisms of action?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of bone pain, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and the x-ray findings of thickened calvarium with a "cotton-wool" appearance are suggestive of Paget disease of bone. This is a localized disorder of bone remodeling caused by increased osteoclastic bone resorption followed by increased osteoblastic bone formation. The newly formed bone is disorganized and has reduced mechanical strength, leading to bone pain, deformities, and fractures. The most appropriate treatment for Paget disease is bisphosphonates, which are taken up by osteoclasts and induce osteoclast apoptosis, thereby decreasing bone resorption.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old male with a past medical history of diabetes type II, obesity, and hyperlipidemia presents to the general medical clinic with bilateral hearing loss. He also reports new onset vertigo and ataxia. The symptoms started a day after undergoing an uncomplicated cholecystectomy. If a drug given prophylactically just prior to surgery has caused this patient’s symptoms, what is the mechanism of action of the drug?

answer_choices.A: Inhibition of the formation of the translation initiation complex
answer_choices.D: Formation of free radical toxic metabolites that damage DNA

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's symptoms of bilateral hearing loss, vertigo, and ataxia are suggestive of ototoxicity, which can be caused by aminoglycoside antibiotics. Aminoglycosides (eg, gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) are often used for prophylaxis in gastrointestinal or genitourinary procedures due to their activity against gram-negative organisms. They work by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit and inhibiting the formation of the translation initiation complex, thereby inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. Ototoxicity is a well-known side effect of aminoglycosides and can manifest as cochlear damage (eg, hearing loss, tinnitus) or vestibular damage (eg, vertigo, ataxia). 

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 62-year-old male presents to his primary care physician complaining of a chronic cough. He reports a six-month history of progressively worsening cough and occasional hemoptysis. He has lost ten pounds over the same time frame. His medical history is notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus. He has a 50-pack-year smoking history. A chest radiograph reveals a coin-like central cavitary lesion. Tissue biopsy demonstrates findings consistent with squamous cell carcinoma. The patient is referred to a pulmonologist who starts the patient on a chemotherapeutic drug. However, after several weeks on the drug, the patient develops sensorineural hearing loss. Which of the following mechanisms of action is consistent with the most likely medication prescribed in this case?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss, along with a 50-pack-year smoking history and a central cavitary lesion on chest radiograph, is concerning for lung cancer. The biopsy results confirm squamous cell carcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). NSCLC is often treated with platinum-based chemotherapeutic agents such as cisplatin. Cisplatin works by forming intrastrand and interstrand DNA crosslinks, which inhibit DNA replication and transcription. However, cisplatin has several side effects, including nephrotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and ototoxicity, which can manifest as sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old male with a 60 pack-year smoking history presents to his oncologist for ongoing management of his recently diagnosed small cell lung cancer. His oncologist discusses several options and decides to start the chemotherapeutic medication, etoposide. The patient is warned that one side effect of this drug is myelosuppression so he should be vigilant for development of any infectious symptoms. The beneficial effect of this drug in treating cancer is most likely due to which of the following effects?
few_shot.explanation:
Etoposide is a chemotherapeutic agent that is used to treat a variety of malignancies, including small cell lung cancer, testicular cancer, and Hodgkin lymphoma. It works by inhibiting topoisomerase II, which is an enzyme that is responsible for relaxing supercoils in DNA. This allows the DNA to be unwound and separated, which is necessary for processes such as replication and transcription. By inhibiting topoisomerase II, etoposide prevents DNA unwinding and separation, thereby inhibiting DNA replication and cell division.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 74-year-old female with a history of lung adenocarcinoma status post lobectomy, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, congestive heart failure, and diabetic nephropathy presents to clinic complaining of hearing loss. Over the last week, she has noticed that she has had difficulty hearing the telephone or the television. When sitting in a quiet room, she also has noticed a high-pitched ringing in her ears. She denies any vertigo or disequilibrium. Further review reveals ongoing dyspnea on exertion and worsening cough productive of whitish sputum for the last month. The patient was recently discharged from the hospital for a congestive heart failure exacerbation. She lives alone and keeps track of all her medications, but admits that sometimes she gets confused. She has a 20 pack-year tobacco history. Her home medications include aspirin, lisinopril, furosemide, short-acting insulin, and a long-acting ß-agonist inhaler. Two weeks ago she completed a course of salvage chemotherapy with docetaxel and cisplastin. Her tympanic membranes are clear and intact with no signs of trauma or impaction. Auditory testing reveals bilateral hearing impairment to a whispered voice. The Weber test is non-lateralizing. Rinne test is unrevealing.

Hemoglobin: 11.8 g/dL
Leukocyte count: 9,400/mm^3
Platelet count: 450,000/mm^3

Serum (Present visit):
Na+: 134 mEq/L
K+: 3.8 mEq/L
Cl-: 95 mEq/L
HCO3-: 30 mEq/L
BUN: 45 mg/dL

Serum (1 month ago):

On follow up visit two weeks later, the patient's hearing has significantly improved. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her initial hearing loss?

This patient's hearing loss is most likely due to furosemide. Loop diuretics, such as furosemide, can cause reversible hearing loss and tinnitus. This is due to inhibition of the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the stria vascularis of the cochlea, which leads to a decrease in the endocochlear potential and subsequent inhibition of hair cell depolarization. This effect is usually reversible once the medication is discontinued.

Cisplatin can also cause hearing loss, but this is usually irreversible and associated with high-frequency hearing loss. Aspirin can cause tinnitus, but this is usually associated with salicylate toxicity and would also be accompanied by symptoms such as tachypnea, tinnitus, and altered mental status. question: A 3-day-old boy is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for seizures. He was born to a 33-year-old woman at 31 weeks gestation via cesarean section. His birth weight was 1400 grams. Vital signs are significant for systemic hypotension, bradycardia, and hypoventilation. On physical exam, the patient has an altered level of consciousness with decreased spontaneous and elicited movements. The patient is hypotonic on motor testing, has bulging anterior fontanelle, and appears cyanotic. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 16-day-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department because of fever and poor feeding for 2 days. He became very fussy the previous evening and cried for most of the night. He was born at 36 weeks' gestation and weighed 2430 g (5 lb 3 oz). The pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. The mother does not recall any sick contacts at home. He currently weighs 2776 g (6 lb 2 oz). He appears irritable. His temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 180/min, and blood pressure is 82/51 mm Hg. Examination shows scleral icterus. He becomes more agitated when picked up. There is full range of motion of his neck and extremities. The anterior fontanelle feels soft and flat. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Blood cultures are drawn and fluid resuscitation is initiated. A urinalysis obtained by catheterization shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This newborn has fever, irritability, and poor feeding, which are concerning for neonatal sepsis. Neonates with sepsis often present with nonspecific signs and symptoms, including temperature instability, apnea, lethargy, poor feeding, and irritability. The most common pathogens in the first month of life are group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes. 

In neonates with suspected sepsis, a full sepsis evaluation should be performed, including blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cultures. CSF is obtained by lumbar puncture. Empiric antibiotic therapy with ampicillin and gentamicin or cefotaxime should be initiated while awaiting culture results. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 3-month-old infant is brought to her pediatrician for a well-child visit. The infant was born to a 22-year-old mother via a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks of gestation in her home. She moved to the United States approximately 3 weeks ago from a small village. She reports that her infant had 2 episodes of non-bloody and non-bilious vomiting. The infant's medical history includes eczema and 2 seizure episodes that resolved with benzodiazepines in the emergency department. Physical examination is notable for a musty body odor, eczema, and a fair skin complexion. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This infant's vomiting, seizures, fair skin complexion, eczema, and musty body odor are suggestive of phenylketonuria (PKU). PKU is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. This leads to an accumulation of phenylalanine in the blood and urine. The excess phenylalanine and its metabolites are toxic to the brain and can cause intellectual disability, seizures, and other neurologic problems. The musty body odor is due to phenylacetic acid, a metabolite of phenylalanine.

The best next step in management is dietary restriction of phenylalanine. This involves a diet low in phenylalanine and high in tyrosine. If started early in life, this diet can prevent the neurologic complications of PKU.

So, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 21-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department in a state of confusion. He also had one seizure approx. 45 minutes ago. He was complaining of fever and headache for the past 3 days. There was no history of nausea, vomiting, head trauma, sore throat, skin rash, or abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals: blood pressure 102/78 mm Hg, heart rate 122/min, and temperature 38.4°C (101.2°F). The patient is awake but confused and disoriented. He is sensitive to light and loud noises. Heart rate is elevated with a normal rhythm. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The fundus examination is benign. Brudzinski’s sign is positive. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's fever, headache, and altered mental status, along with the positive Brudzinski's sign (neck flexion causing involuntary flexion of the knee and hip), are concerning for meningitis. However, before performing a lumbar puncture (LP), it is important to evaluate for signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) or a space-occupying lesion, as these conditions would make LP unsafe due to the risk of brain herniation. This patient's confusion, seizure, and bradycardia (relative to his elevated body temperature) are concerning for increased ICP. Therefore, the next best step in management is to perform a CT scan of the brain to evaluate for a space-occupying lesion or cerebral edema. If the CT scan is normal, then an LP should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of meningitis.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 9-month-old male infant is brought to his pediatrician by his mother with lethargy and decreased oral intake for one day. His mother also mentions that he did not sleep well the previous night. A review of the medical record reveals several missed appointments and that the boy was born at 36 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. At the clinic, his temperature is 37.2ºC (99.0ºF), pulse rate is 140/minute, respirations are 44/minute, and blood pressure is 92/60 mm Hg. On physical exam the infant is awake but irritable and the rest of the physical is within normal limits for his age. On ophthalmologic examination, there are multiple retinal hemorrhages that extend to the periphery in both eyes. Which of the following investigations is most likely to be helpful in the management of the infant?
few_shot.explanation:
The presence of retinal hemorrhages in an infant, especially when they extend to the periphery, is highly suggestive of nonaccidental trauma (child abuse), specifically abusive head trauma (formerly known as shaken baby syndrome). This is a form of child abuse that occurs when a child is violently shaken, leading to acceleration-deceleration forces that cause shearing of the bridging veins and subdural hemorrhages. The violent shaking can also cause retinal hemorrhages. The most common presenting symptoms are nonspecific and include vomiting, poor feeding, seizures, and altered mental status, as seen in this patient.

The most appropriate next step in management is to obtain a noncontrast head CT to evaluate for subdural hematomas, cerebral edema, and other intracranial injuries. If abusive head trauma is confirmed, a skeletal survey should also be obtained to evaluate for additional signs of abuse, such as metaphyseal fractures (corner or bucket-handle fractures).

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: Three days after delivery, a 1100-g (2-lb 7-oz) newborn has a tonic seizure that lasts for 25 seconds. She has become increasingly lethargic over the past 18 hours. She was born at 31 weeks' gestation. Antenatal period was complicated by chorioamnionitis. Apgar scores were 3 and 6 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. She appears ill. Her pulse is 123/min, respirations are 50/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 60/30 mm Hg. Examination shows a tense anterior fontanelle. The pupils are equal and react sluggishly to light. Examination shows slow, conjugate back and forth movements of the eyes. Muscle tone is decreased in all extremities. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This premature infant with a history of chorioamnionitis, low Apgar scores, and lethargy has signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) (eg, tense anterior fontanelle, sluggish pupillary light reflexes, decreased muscle tone). The slow, conjugate, back-and-forth movements of the eyes (ie, "sunset" sign) are also indicative of increased ICP. The most likely diagnosis is intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), a common complication of prematurity. IVH is due to rupture of the germinal matrix, a highly vascularized area in the subventricular zone where neuronal and glial cells migrate out during brain development. The germinal matrix is prominent until approximately 32 weeks' gestation, after which it regresses. Risk factors for IVH include low birth weight, prematurity, birth asphyxia, and rapid postnatal volume expansion. IVH typically occurs within the first 72 hours of life and presents with abrupt onset of anemia, thrombocytopenia, and/or declining hematocrit; bulging fontanelle; and seizures. 

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 62-year-old man presents with bright red blood in his stool which occurred 2 times this week. He denies fever, weight loss, pain, pruritus or urinary symptoms. Past medical history is significant for gastroesophageal reflux disease, and recent appendicitis, status post laparoscopic appendectomy complicated by delirium tremens. His vitals are a temperature of 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, pulse of 78/min, and respiratory rate of 12/min. Physical examination reveals a distended abdomen with shifting dullness on percussion. In addition, multiple purple spider web-like lesions are present on the chest and arms, which blanch when pressure is applied. Fecal occult blood test is negative. On anoscopy, a non-tender, dilated vascular protrusion is noted superior to the pectinate line. Which of the following is most likely true about this patient’s current symptoms?

answer_choices.A: This patient has peptic ulcer disease.
answer_choices.B: The vascular protrusion drains into the superior rectal vein.
answer_choices.C: The vascular protrusion drains into the inferior rectal vein.
answer_choices.D: Fecal leukocytes and a stool culture are required for diagnosis.

few_shot.question: A 70-year-old man presents with severe abdominal pain over the last 24 hours. He describes the pain as severe and associated with diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. He says he has had a history of postprandial abdominal pain over the last several months. The patient denies any fever, chills, recent antibiotic use. Past medical history is significant for peripheral arterial disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus. The patient reports a 20 pack-year smoking history. His vital signs include blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 100/min, respiratory 22/min, temperature 38.0°C (100.5°F), and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. On physical examination, the patient is ill-appearing. His abdomen is severely tender to palpation and distended with no rebound or guarding. Pain is disproportionate to the exam findings. Rectal examination demonstrates bright red-colored stool. Abdominal X-ray is unremarkable. Stool culture was negative for C. difficile. A contrast-enhanced CT scan reveals segmental colitis involving the distal transverse colon. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of peripheral arterial disease, diabetes, and smoking, along with his symptoms of postprandial abdominal pain (intestinal angina) and acute-onset severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings, are suggestive of acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI). AMI most commonly occurs due to embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery. However, in patients with a history of atherosclerosis, AMI can also occur due to acute thrombosis of a mesenteric artery. This is especially likely in patients with a history of intestinal angina, which is typically due to chronic mesenteric ischemia from gradual, progressive stenosis of the mesenteric vessels by atherosclerosis. These patients classically present with fear of eating due to postprandial abdominal pain, leading to significant weight loss.

The other options, hypokalemia, bacterial infection, and upper GI bleeding, are less likely in this patient given his history and presentation.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man presents to his primary care provider after noticing increasing fatigue over the past several weeks. He now becomes short of breath after going up 1 flight of stairs. He was previously healthy and has not seen a doctor for several years. He denies any fever or changes to his bowel movements. On exam, his temperature is 98.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 116/76 mmHg, pulse is 74/min, and respirations are 14/min. On basic labs, his hemoglobin is found to be 9.6 g/dL and MCV is 75 fL. Fecal blood testing is positive for occult blood. Imaging is notable for a mass in the cecum that is partially obstructing the lumen, as well as several small lesions in the liver. Which of the following structures is most at risk for involvement in this patient’s disease?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fatigue, shortness of breath, and microcytic anemia is concerning for iron deficiency anemia due to chronic blood loss. The positive fecal occult blood test and imaging findings of a cecal mass and liver lesions are concerning for colorectal cancer with hepatic metastases. The liver is the most common site of metastasis for colorectal cancer due to the venous drainage of the colon. The cecum is drained by the superior mesenteric vein, which drains into the portal vein and then into the liver. Therefore, the superior mesenteric vein is the most likely structure to be involved in this patient's disease.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressive abdominal distension and swelling of his legs for 4 months. He has a history of ulcerative colitis. Physical examination shows jaundice. Abdominal examination shows shifting dullness and dilated veins in the periumbilical region. This patient's abdominal findings are most likely caused by increased blood flow in which of the following vessels?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of ulcerative colitis, progressive abdominal distension, and lower extremity swelling are suggestive of cirrhosis. The most common cause of cirrhosis is alcohol abuse, but other causes include viral hepatitis, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune hepatitis. Patients with inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis, are also at increased risk for primary sclerosing cholangitis, which can lead to cirrhosis.

Cirrhosis can lead to portal hypertension, which can cause the formation of portosystemic venous shunts. One of the most common types of portosystemic shunts is the formation of esophageal varices due to shunting of blood from the left gastric vein to the azygos vein via the esophageal veins. Another common type of shunt is a caput medusae, which is caused by the shunting of blood from the paraumbilical veins to the small epigastric veins of the anterior abdominal wall. This can cause visible dilation of the veins around the umbilicus, leading to the classic "caput medusae" appearance.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of bright red blood in his stool for 5 days. He has had no pain during defecation and no abdominal pain. One year ago, he was diagnosed with cirrhosis after being admitted to the emergency department for upper gastrointestinal bleeding. He has since cut down on his drinking and consumes around 5 bottles of beer daily. Examination shows scleral icterus and mild ankle swelling. Palpation of the abdomen shows a fluid wave and shifting dullness. Anoscopy shows enlarged bluish vessels above the dentate line. Which of the following is the most likely source of bleeding in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of cirrhosis, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, and physical examination findings of scleral icterus, ascites, and ankle swelling are suggestive of portal hypertension. The most likely source of this patient's bleeding is the superior rectal vein, which is part of the portal venous system. The superior rectal vein drains the upper part of the rectum and is a continuation of the inferior mesenteric vein, which is a tributary of the portal vein. In portal hypertension, the superior rectal vein can become engorged, leading to the formation of internal hemorrhoids. These are typically located above the dentate line and can cause painless rectal bleeding, as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 79-year-old man with aortic stenosis comes to the emergency room because of worsening fatigue for 5 months. During this time, he has also had intermittent bright red blood mixed in with his stool. He has not had any abdominal pain or weight loss. Physical examination shows pale conjunctivae and a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur best heard at the second right intercostal space. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 8 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 71 μm3. Colonoscopy shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's bleeding?

answer_choices.A: Thrombus in the superior mesenteric artery
answer_choices.B: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the mesenteric arteries

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of aortic stenosis, iron deficiency anemia, and negative colonoscopy is suggestive of Heyde syndrome. Heyde syndrome is characterized by the triad of aortic stenosis, gastrointestinal bleeding, and anemia. The gastrointestinal bleeding is typically due to angiodysplasia of the colon, which is characterized by dilated, tortuous submucosal blood vessels. Angiodysplasia is a common cause of lower gastrointestinal bleeding in older adults, and is often difficult to visualize on endoscopy due to its small size and patchy distribution.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

question: A 58-year-old male is hospitalized after sustaining multiple fractures in a severe automobile accident. Soon after hospitalization, he develops respiratory distress with crackles present bilaterally on physical examination. The patient does not respond to mechanical ventilation and 100% oxygen and quickly dies due to respiratory insufficiency. Autopsy reveals heavy, red lungs and histology is shown in Image A. Which of the following is most likely to have been present in this patient shortly before death:

few_shot.question:
A 58-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for severe abdominal pain and confusion. He has a history of alcohol use disorder, with several previous admissions for intoxication. Twelve hours after admission, he has worsening shortness of breath. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on mask ventilation shows an oxygen saturation of 85%. The patient is intubated and mechanically ventilated with an FiO2 of 40%. Physical examination shows diffuse lung crackles, marked epigastric tenderness, and a periumbilical hematoma. Cardiac examination is normal with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. There is no jugular venous distension. Arterial blood gas analysis shows:
pH 7.29
PO2 60 mm Hg
PCO2 40 mm Hg
HCO3- 15 mmol/L
An x-ray of the chest shows bilateral opacities in the lower lung fields. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's respiratory symptoms?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's severe abdominal pain, periumbilical hematoma, and epigastric tenderness suggest acute pancreatitis, likely due to alcohol use disorder. Acute pancreatitis can cause acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), a form of diffuse alveolar damage that presents with acute onset of hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 <300) and bilateral pulmonary opacities on imaging. The diagnosis of ARDS requires that these findings not be fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. This patient's normal cardiac examination and absence of jugular venous distension argue against a cardiogenic etiology for his pulmonary findings.

ARDS is a common complication of severe acute pancreatitis and is associated with substantial mortality. The exact mechanism is unclear but likely involves the release of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor, interleukins), oxygen-derived free radicals, and pancreatic enzymes into the systemic circulation, causing increased alveolar-capillary membrane permeability and diffuse alveolar damage.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 94-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after she was found unresponsive and febrile at her home. Her son reports that she had an acute episode of coughing while having breakfast the day before. Six days after admission, the patient develops progressive tachypnea and a gradual decrease in oxygen saturation, despite ventilation with supplemental oxygen. Physical examination shows coarse bilateral breath sounds. An x-ray of the chest shows opacities in all lung fields. Despite appropriate care, the patient dies two days later. A photomicrograph of a specimen of the lung obtained at autopsy is shown. This patient's pulmonary condition is most likely associated with which of the following pathophysiologic changes?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's history of coughing while eating, fever, and bilateral lung opacities on chest x-ray are suggestive of aspiration pneumonia. The photomicrograph shows neutrophilic infiltration and destruction of the alveolar walls, consistent with pneumonia. Aspiration pneumonia can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which is characterized by diffuse alveolar damage and severe hypoxemia. The hypoxemia in ARDS is due to intrapulmonary shunting, which is the perfusion of non-ventilated alveoli. This is because the alveoli are filled with proteinaceous debris, neutrophils, and red blood cells, which impairs gas exchange. Therefore, the pathophysiologic change most likely associated with this patient's pulmonary condition is an increased pulmonary shunt fraction.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department complaining of difficulty in breathing for the past 2 days. He has had recurrent episodes of bacterial pneumonia in the right lower lobe during the last 6 months. His last episode of pneumonia started 7 days ago for which he is being treated with antibiotics. He has a 35-pack-year smoking history. Past medical history is significant for hypertension for which he takes lisinopril. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion in the right lung base. Chest X-ray reveals a large right-sided pleural effusion, and chest CT scan shows a large mass near the hilum of the right lung. Cytologic examination of pleural fluid shows evidence of malignancy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe, a large hilar mass, and malignant pleural effusion are suggestive of bronchogenic carcinoma. The most common types of bronchogenic carcinoma are adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma, and small cell carcinoma. Of these, small cell carcinoma is the most aggressive and is often widely disseminated at the time of diagnosis. It is strongly associated with smoking and often presents with paraneoplastic syndromes. 

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 3900-g (8-lb 11-oz ) male newborn is delivered at term to a 27-year-old woman. Immediately after delivery, he develops cyanosis and tachypnea. Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygen shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Examination shows decreased breath sounds in the left lung field. Despite appropriate treatment, the newborn dies. An x-ray of the chest performed prior to autopsy shows sharply demarcated fluid-filled densities in the left lung. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the x-ray findings?

answer_choices.A: Abnormal budding of the ventral foregut
answer_choices.B: Fistula between the esophagus and the trachea

few_shot.explanation:
This newborn's cyanosis, tachypnea, and decreased breath sounds in the left lung field are suggestive of a congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM), also known as congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation. This is a hamartomatous cystic lesion of the lung that is thought to result from abnormal budding of the tracheobronchial tree. The cysts are filled with fluid or mucus, which can cause compression of the normal lung tissue and mediastinal shift. This can lead to respiratory distress in the neonatal period. Chest x-ray typically shows multiple cysts of varying sizes.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 63-year-old man presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden-onset severe dyspnea and right-sided chest pain. The patient has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, peptic ulcer disease, and hyperthyroidism. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years, drinks socially, and does not take illicit drugs. The blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, the pulse is 98/min and regular, and the respiratory rate is 20/min. Pulse oximetry shows 90% on room air. On physical examination, he is in mild respiratory distress. Tactile fremitus and breath sounds are decreased on the right, with hyperresonance on percussion. The trachea is midline and no heart murmurs are heard. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's current condition?

answer_choices.A: Compression of a main bronchus due to neoplasia
answer_choices.B: Formation of an intimal flap in the aorta
answer_choices.D: Rupture of an apical alveolar bleb

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's sudden-onset dyspnea, unilateral chest pain, and physical examination findings of decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion are suggestive of a spontaneous pneumothorax. This condition occurs when air accumulates in the pleural space, leading to lung collapse. It is termed "spontaneous" when it occurs in the absence of trauma or iatrogenic cause. Spontaneous pneumothorax is further classified as primary (absence of underlying lung disease) or secondary (in the setting of underlying lung disease). This patient's history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) makes secondary spontaneous pneumothorax the most likely diagnosis.

The most common cause of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax is rupture of an apical subpleural bleb or bulla. Patients with COPD are at increased risk for developing these abnormal air-filled spaces in the lung due to the destructive changes associated with the disease. The apical location of blebs and bullae is thought to be due to the increased negative intrapleural pressure in the lung apices, which causes increased distension and rupture of these structures.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to your office with complaints of wheezing and dyspnea. Laboratory work reveals eosinophilia and positive skin tests for allergens. Which of the following types of drugs would be an effective treatment in this patient?

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy with asthma is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of shortness of breath and cough. Current medications are inhaled albuterol and beclomethasone. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F) and respirations are 24/min. Pulmonary examination shows bilateral expiratory wheezing. Serum studies show increased concentrations of interleukin-5. Which of the following is the most likely effect of the observed laboratory finding in this patient?

answer_choices.B: Differentiation of bone marrow stem cells

few_shot.question: A 7-year-old boy with asthma is brought to the physician because of a 1-month history of worsening shortness of breath and cough. The mother reports that the shortness of breath usually occurs when he is exercising with his older brother. His only medication is an albuterol inhaler that is taken as needed. The physician considers adding zafirlukast to his drug regimen. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of action of this drug?
few_shot.explanation:
Zafirlukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist that is used for the prophylaxis and chronic treatment of asthma. Leukotrienes are inflammatory mediators that are released from mast cells, eosinophils, and basophils, and cause bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability leading to edema, and recruitment of inflammatory cells. By blocking the action of leukotrienes, zafirlukast can reduce these effects and help control the symptoms of asthma.

few_shot.question: A new drug is designed to treat asthma by inhibiting bronchoconstriction. Experimental assays show that treated animals had markedly reduced acetylcholine binding to muscarinic receptors relative to untreated controls. The drug is most similar to which of the following:
few_shot.explanation:
The drug described in the question is an anticholinergic agent, which works by blocking the action of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors. This prevents bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion, both of which are beneficial in the treatment of asthma.

Ipratropium is an example of an anticholinergic drug that is used in the treatment of asthma and COPD. It is a quaternary ammonium compound that acts mainly on M3 muscarinic receptors located in the bronchi. It is usually administered by inhalation.

The other options listed do not have this mechanism of action. Cromolyn is a mast cell stabilizer, zafirlukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist, and prednisone is a corticosteroid.

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the office with allergic rhinitis. He reports symptoms of sneezing, nasal congestion, itching, and postnasal drainage every September at the start of the school year. He has a family history of childhood asthma and eczema. He has not tried any medications for his allergies. Which of the following medications is the most appropriate next step to manage the patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
Allergic rhinitis is a common condition characterized by paroxysms of sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal pruritus, and nasal congestion. It is often associated with postnasal drainage, cough, irritability, and fatigue. Allergic rhinitis is triggered by allergens such as pollens, molds, dust mites, and animal dander. The allergens cross-link IgE antibodies on mast cells and basophils, triggering the release of preformed mediators (eg, histamine) and the synthesis of new mediators (eg, leukotrienes, cytokines). These mediators cause vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, mucous gland secretion, and recruitment of inflammatory cells, leading to the symptoms of allergic rhinitis.

Intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective treatment for allergic rhinitis. They cover all symptoms of allergic rhinitis, including nasal congestion. They block the late-phase reaction to allergen exposure and inhibit cytokine production, reducing inflammation and symptoms. They are most effective when used regularly, rather than as needed, and full efficacy may take up to 2 weeks.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of episodic shortness of breath. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. few_shot.explanation:
This patient's episodic shortness of breath, elevated serum IgE levels, and positive methacholine challenge test are suggestive of asthma. The presence of eosinophilic, hexagonal, double-pointed crystals (Charcot-Leyden crystals) in the sputum is indicative of eosinophilic inflammation, which is a characteristic feature of asthma. Charcot-Leyden crystals are formed from the breakdown of eosinophils and are often seen in asthma and other eosinophilic lung diseases.

The most common triggers of asthma symptoms include allergens (eg, dust mites, animal dander, cockroaches, mold, and pollen), irritants (eg, tobacco smoke, wood smoke, strong odors), exercise, cold air, and certain medications (eg, aspirin, beta-blockers). However, given the chronicity of this patient's symptoms and the presence of eosinophilic inflammation, an allergic trigger such as dust mites is most likely.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

This patient's irregular menses, elevated luteinizing hormone, and elevated testosterone level are suggestive of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a disorder of androgen excess and ovulatory dysfunction. The diagnosis is made clinically and requires the presence of at least two of the following three criteria: (1) oligo- or anovulation, (2) clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism, and (3) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. The ovaries are typically enlarged and contain multiple small peripheral follicles.

This patient's elevated fasting glucose and insulin levels suggest insulin resistance, which is a common feature of PCOS. Insulin resistance leads to compensatory hyperinsulinemia, which stimulates ovarian androgen production and inhibits sex hormone-binding globulin synthesis in the liver, leading to an increase in free testosterone levels.

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician for evaluation of irregular periods. Menarche was at the age of 12 years. She is not sexually active. She drinks 3 alcoholic drinks on weekends and does not smoke. She takes metformin and sertraline. She appears well. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 118/75 mm Hg. BMI is 31.5 kg/m2. Physical exam shows severe cystic acne on her face and back. There are dark, velvet-like patches on the armpits and neck. Pelvic examination is normal. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following would help determine the cause of this patient's menstrual irregularities?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's obesity, irregular menses, and signs of hyperandrogenism (acne, acanthosis nigricans) are suggestive of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other causes of menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism must be ruled out before making the diagnosis. These include thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, and nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia. However, the most likely cause of this patient's amenorrhea is anovulation due to PCOS. 

The progesterone withdrawal test can be used to evaluate for anovulation. In this test, a woman is given a course of progesterone. If bleeding occurs after progesterone is stopped, this indicates that the patient is producing estrogen and the amenorrhea is due to anovulation. If no bleeding occurs, this suggests that the patient is not producing estrogen and further evaluation is needed.

few_shot.question: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for the evaluation of irregular menstrual bleeding. Menses have occurred at 60- to 90-day intervals since menarche at the age of 12 years. Her last menstrual period was 4 weeks ago. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they use condoms consistently. She reports that she currently has no desire to have children. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 85 kg (187 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m2. Examination shows scattered pustules on the forehead and oily skin. There is coarse hair on the chin and upper lip. Fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 190 mg/dL. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's irregular menses, obesity, and signs of hyperandrogenism (acne, hirsutism) are suggestive of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion and is characterized by chronic anovulation and hyperandrogenism. Chronic anovulation presents as oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, and hyperandrogenism presents as hirsutism, acne, or androgenic alopecia. PCOS is also associated with insulin resistance, which can lead to acanthosis nigricans, impaired glucose tolerance, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

The treatment of PCOS depends on the patient's primary concern. For patients with hirsutism, weight loss is the first-line treatment. If hirsutism persists despite weight loss, pharmacologic treatment with combined oral contraceptives (COCs) is the next step. COCs increase sex hormone-binding globulin, which decreases the amount of free testosterone, and also suppress luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion, which decreases ovarian androgen production. COCs also regulate menses, provide contraception, and improve acne.

Metformin is used in PCOS patients with impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes mellitus, or for those who cannot tolerate COCs or who have not responded to COCs and have persistent menstrual irregularity.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

The diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency should be confirmed with a cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test. In this test, serum cortisol is measured before and 60 minutes after IV cosyntropin administration. A normal response is an increase in serum cortisol to >18-20 μg/dL. few_shot.question: A 55-year-old female with a history of poorly controlled hyperlipidemia and obesity presents to her primary care physician for a follow-up visit. She reports that she feels well and has no complaints. She currently takes atorvastatin. Her temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 135/80 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 16/min. Her BMI is 31 kg/m2. Her total cholesterol is 290 mg/dl, triglycerides are 120 mg/dl, and LDL cholesterol is 215 mg/dl. Her physician considers starting her on a medication that forces the liver to consume cholesterol to make more bile salts. Which of the following adverse effects is this patient at highest risk of developing following initiation of the medication?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's physician is considering starting her on a bile acid sequestrant, such as cholestyramine, colestipol, or colesevelam. These medications bind bile acids in the gut, preventing their reabsorption and enterohepatic recycling. This forces the liver to consume cholesterol to make more bile salts, thereby reducing serum cholesterol levels. However, bile acid sequestrants can also bind other substances in the gut, including fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and drugs (eg, digoxin, warfarin, thiazides), leading to malabsorption and decreased bioavailability, respectively. Therefore, the most likely adverse effect of bile acid sequestrants is fat malabsorption.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 53-year-old man with hyperlipidemia comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. His home medications include acetaminophen and atorvastatin. Serum studies show elevated total cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations. A drug that activates the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha is added to his existing therapy. This patient is most likely to develop which of the following drug-related adverse effects?

answer_choices.C: Pruritus and flushing of the skin

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's hyperlipidemia is not adequately controlled with atorvastatin alone, so a fibrate (eg, gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) is added to his regimen. Fibrates are agonists of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-alpha), a nuclear transcription factor expressed in the liver and brown adipose tissue. Activation of PPAR-alpha upregulates genes involved in lipid metabolism, reducing levels of triglycerides and increasing levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol.

Fibrates can cause a variety of adverse effects, including gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhea), myopathy, and hepatotoxicity. In addition, fibrates can displace warfarin from plasma albumin, potentiating its anticoagulant effect and increasing the risk of bleeding. However, this patient is not taking warfarin, so this is not a concern.

The most likely adverse effect in this patient is reddish-brown discoloration of the urine due to cholelithiasis. Fibrates can increase cholesterol excretion into the bile, leading to cholesterol gallstones.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: Three weeks after starting a new medication for hyperlipidemia, a 54-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain and swelling in his left great toe. Examination shows swelling and erythema over the metatarsophalangeal joint of the toe. Analysis of fluid from the affected joint shows needle-shaped, negatively-birefringent crystals. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the drug he is taking?

answer_choices.B: Inhibition of intestinal bile acid absorption

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of acute monoarticular joint pain and swelling, along with the finding of needle-shaped, negatively-birefringent crystals in the joint fluid, are consistent with gout. Gout is caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in the joints due to hyperuricemia. The hyperuricemia can be due to overproduction or underexcretion of uric acid.

The patient's gout attack was likely precipitated by the initiation of a new medication for hyperlipidemia. The most likely medication is niacin (also known as nicotinic acid), which is known to cause hyperuricemia. Niacin inhibits hepatic VLDL synthesis, which leads to decreased LDL levels. However, it can also cause hyperuricemia by increasing the renal reabsorption of uric acid, leading to decreased uric acid excretion.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 14-year-old boy comes to the physician for a follow-up after a blood test showed a serum triglyceride level of 821 mg/dL. Several of his family members have familial hypertriglyceridemia. The patient is prescribed a drug that increases his risk of gallstone disease. The expected beneficial effect of this drug is most likely due to which of the following actions?
few_shot.explanation:
Familial hypertriglyceridemia is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by increased serum triglycerides due to impaired lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity. LPL is responsible for hydrolyzing triglycerides in chylomicrons and very low-density lipoproteins (VLDLs). The most effective agents for lowering triglyceride levels are the fibric acid derivatives (eg, gemfibrozil, fenofibrate). These drugs act as agonists for peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-α), a transcription factor expressed in the liver, heart, and skeletal muscle. When activated, PPAR-α upregulates LPL, leading to increased VLDL clearance. It also inhibits the synthesis of apolipoprotein C-III, an inhibitor of LPL. The net effect is decreased plasma triglyceride levels.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's LDL cholesterol level is significantly elevated. The first-line treatment for elevated LDL cholesterol is a statin. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step in cholesterol synthesis in the liver. This leads to upregulation of LDL receptors and increased clearance of LDL from the circulation. Statins have been shown to decrease mortality in patients with and without known coronary artery disease.

The most common side effects of statins are hepatotoxicity and myopathy. Hepatotoxicity usually manifests as asymptomatic elevation in aminotransferase levels, which is reversible upon discontinuation of the drug. Rarely, statins can cause severe liver injury, liver failure, and death. Myopathy due to statins can range from myalgia without creatine kinase (CK) elevation to life-threatening rhabdomyolysis with very high CK levels, electrolyte disturbances, and acute kidney injury.

few_shot.question: A 10-year-old boy who recently immigrated to the United States from Africa with his family is brought to the emergency department by his mother for a progressively worsening ulcerative lesion on his jaw. His mother reports that her son’s right jaw has rapidly enlarged over the past few months. He says that it is very tender though he doesn’t recall any trauma to the site. In addition, the mother says her son hasn’t been himself the past few months with intermittent fever, weakness, and fatigue. Physical exam reveals a large, ulcerating right jaw mass that is draining serous fluid and painless cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Laboratory results are notable for an elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase. A biopsy of the right jaw mass is shown in the photograph. Which of the following chromosomal translocations is most likely to be found in this patient’s lesion?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of a rapidly enlarging jaw mass, B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), and painless lymphadenopathy in a child from an endemic region (Africa) is suggestive of endemic Burkitt lymphoma. Burkitt lymphoma is a high-grade B-cell neoplasm that is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and a characteristic chromosomal translocation, t(8;14). This translocation results in the juxtaposition of the MYC oncogene from chromosome 8 to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene locus on chromosome 14. The constitutive high-level expression of MYC results in unregulated cell growth and proliferation. The "starry sky" appearance on biopsy is characteristic and results from a high proliferation rate with scattered benign macrophages that have ingested apoptotic debris.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: An 11-year-old boy who recently emigrated from Nigeria is brought to the physician for evaluation of jaw swelling. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. This patient's presentation of a rapidly growing mass in the jaw region, associated with significant cervical lymphadenopathy, is suggestive of Burkitt lymphoma. It is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection, especially in patients from equatorial Africa, where Burkitt lymphoma is the most common malignancy in children. The characteristic histologic finding is the "starry sky" appearance, which is due to sheets of monomorphic, medium-sized lymphocytes interspersed with tingible body macrophages that have abundant cytoplasm and round, open nuclei.

Burkitt lymphoma is associated with a translocation involving the MYC gene on chromosome 8 and the immunoglobulin heavy chain region on chromosome 14 [t(8;14)]. This translocation results in overexpression of the MYC oncogene, which leads to increased cell proliferation.

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old woman presents to the medicine clinic with swelling around the right side of her chin and neck (Image A). She reports pain when moving her jaw and chewing. The most common pathogens in acute bacterial parotitis are Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus viridans. Risk factors include dehydration, poor oral hygiene, and sialolithiasis. This patient's recent surgery likely resulted in dehydration and subsequent decreased salivary flow, leading to bacterial ascent into the parotid gland. Treatment is with intravenous antibiotics (eg, nafcillin, cefazolin) and maintenance of hydration.

CSD is a common cause of chronic lymphadenopathy in children and young adults. The disease is usually self-limited, but it can become severe in immunocompromised patients. The organism is difficult to culture, and diagnosis is usually made by serology or PCR. Warthin-Starry silver stain can also be used to visualize the organism.

question: A 52-year-old man presents to the physician because of ongoing shortness of breath, which is more prominent when he lies down. Occasionally, he experiences palpitations, especially during strenuous activities. In addition to this, he has been experiencing difficulty in digestion and often experiences regurgitation and dysphagia. He reports that he emigrated from Mexico 20 years ago and visits his hometown twice a year. The vital signs include: blood pressure 120/75 mm Hg, respiratory rate 19/min, and pulse 100/min. The physical examination shows jugular vein distention along with pitting edema in the ankles. Bilateral basilar crackles and an S3 gallop are heard on auscultation of the chest. A chest X-ray is taken. An electrocardiogram (ECG) shows no significant findings. What is the most likely explanation for this patient’s physical and diagnostic findings?

few_shot.question: A 50-year-old man comes to the physician for the evaluation of recurrent palpitations and a feeling of pressure in the chest for the past 6 months. He also reports shortness of breath when walking several blocks or while going upstairs. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. He does not smoke. He has a 30-year history of drinking 7–10 beers daily. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. There are jugular venous pulsations 9 cm above the sternal angle. Crackles are heard at both lung bases. Cardiac examination shows an S3 gallop and a displaced point of maximum impulse. There is pitting edema below the knees. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in the management of the underlying cause of this patient's current condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of heavy alcohol use, along with findings of jugular venous distention, crackles at the lung bases, an S3 gallop, and lower extremity edema, suggest a diagnosis of alcoholic cardiomyopathy. Alcoholic cardiomyopathy is a type of dilated cardiomyopathy that can occur in patients with long-term heavy alcohol use (ie, >10 years of >5-6 standard drinks daily for men, >3-4 standard drinks daily for women). The exact mechanism by which alcohol damages the myocardium is not known, but several theories exist, including direct toxic effects of alcohol or its metabolites, nutritional deficiencies (eg, thiamine), and increased oxidative stress.

The most important intervention in alcoholic cardiomyopathy is complete abstinence from alcohol. Abstinence can lead to significant improvement in cardiac function, even in patients with severe heart failure. Nutritional supplementation, particularly thiamine, may also be beneficial.

Therefore, the answer is [A].
