few_shot.question: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for a 1-week history of worsening shortness of breath. The symptoms occur when he climbs the stairs to his apartment on the 3rd floor and when he goes to bed. He gained 2.3 kg (5 lbs) in the past 5 days. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, alcoholic steatosis, and osteoarthritis. He received surgical repair of a ventricular septal defect when he was 4 months old. He started taking ibuprofen for his osteoarthritis and simvastatin for his hyperlipidemia one week ago. He drinks 2–3 beers daily after work. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), his pulse is 114/min, and his blood pressure is 130/90 mmHg. Physical examination reveals jugular venous distention and 2+ pitting edema in his lower legs. On cardiac auscultation, an additional, late-diastolic heart sound is heard. Bilateral crackles are heard over the lung bases. Echocardiography shows concentric hypertrophy of the left ventricle. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, along with physical examination findings of jugular venous distention, an S4 heart sound, and bilateral crackles, are consistent with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). HFpEF, also known as diastolic heart failure, is characterized by signs and symptoms of heart failure in the setting of a normal left ventricular ejection fraction. The most common cause of HFpEF is long-standing hypertension, which leads to pressure overload, left ventricular hypertrophy, and, eventually, impaired ventricular relaxation and elevated diastolic filling pressures. The S4 heart sound heard on examination is due to a stiff, noncompliant left ventricle that results in forceful atrial contraction against a high resistance to ventricular filling.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and fatigue. His symptoms began insidiously and progressively worsened over the course of a month. He becomes short of breath when climbing the stairs or performing low-intensity exercises. He also needs to rest on multiple pillows in order to comfortably sleep. A few weeks ago he developed fever, malaise, and chest pain. Medical history is significant for hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, type II diabetes, and bariatric surgery performed 10 years ago. He is taking lisinopril, atorvastatin, and metformin. He drinks alcohol occasionally and does not smoke. He tried cocaine 3 days ago for the first time and has not used the illicit drug since. Physical exam is significant for bibasilar crackles, an S3 heart sound, and a laterally displaced cardiac apex. He has normal muscle tone throughout, 2+ reflexes, and an intact sensory exam. Which of the following is most likely the cause of this patient's symptoms
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, malaise, and chest pain followed by signs of heart failure (eg, dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, bibasilar crackles, S3 heart sound, displaced cardiac apex) is suggestive of myocarditis. Myocarditis is most commonly due to viral infection, with enteroviruses (eg, coxsackievirus) being the most common cause. Other causes include infection with adenovirus, parvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and human immunodeficiency virus. Noninfectious causes include autoimmune diseases (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis), drugs, and toxins. Although cocaine use can cause myocardial ischemia and infarction, the time course is usually within 1-3 hours of use, not 3 days later. In addition, cocaine use does not typically present with a preceding febrile prodrome.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 32-year-old man who recently emigrated from Colombia comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of shortness of breath and fatigue. Physical examination shows jugular venous distention and an additional late diastolic heart sound. Crackles are heard at the lung bases bilaterally. Cardiac catheterization is performed and left ventricular pressures are obtained. The left ventricular pressure-volume relationship compared to that of a healthy patient is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's heart failure?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's presentation of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) in the setting of recent immigration from Latin America is suggestive of Chagas disease. Chagas disease is caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, which is transmitted by the reduviid (kissing) bug. The disease has an acute phase characterized by fever and malaise, which is usually not recognized. After a latent period that can last up to 20-30 years, approximately 30% of infected individuals develop chronic disease, which can manifest as cardiomyopathy, megaesophagus, or megacolon.

Chagas cardiomyopathy is the most common cause of nonischemic cardiomyopathy in Central and South America. It is characterized by a dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm and mural thrombus, arrhythmias, and HFpEF. HFpEF is characterized by symptoms of heart failure, a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, and evidence of diastolic dysfunction. The pressure-volume loop in this patient shows a decreased rate of left ventricular pressure decline in diastole and an increased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, indicative of impaired ventricular relaxation and decreased compliance, respectively.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of nausea and upper abdominal and substernal chest pain radiating to his lower jaw. He vomited several times before arriving at the hospital. His last visit to the primary care physician was 6 months ago during which he complained of fatigue, ‘slowing down’ on his morning walks, and abdominal pain that exacerbated by eating spicy food. His current medications include atorvastatin, metformin, insulin, omeprazole, aspirin, enalapril, nitroglycerin, and metoprolol. Today, his blood pressure is 95/72 mm Hg in his right arm and 94/73 in his left arm, heart rate is 110/min, temperature is 37.6°C (99.6°F), and respiratory rate is 30/min. On physical examination, he is diaphoretic and his skin is cool and clammy. His cardiac enzymes were elevated. He is treated appropriately and is admitted to the hospital. On day 5 of his hospital stay, he suddenly develops breathlessness. His blood pressure drops to 80/42 mm Hg. On examination, bibasilar crackles are heard. Cardiac auscultatory reveals a high pitched holosystolic murmur over the apex. Which of the following most likely lead to the deterioration of this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.A: Scarring of mitral valve as a complication of childhood illness
answer_choices.B: Age-related fibrosis and calcification of the aortic valve
answer_choices.D: Papillary muscle rupture leading to reflux of blood into left atrium

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute-onset dyspnea, hypotension, and a new holosystolic murmur at the apex following an acute myocardial infarction (MI) is suggestive of acute mitral regurgitation (MR) due to papillary muscle rupture. The papillary muscles, which attach to the mitral valve leaflets via the chordae tendineae, contract during systole to prevent the valve from prolapsing into the left atrium. Rupture of a papillary muscle is a mechanical complication of MI that typically occurs 2-7 days after the event. The posteromedial papillary muscle is most commonly affected due to its single blood supply from the right coronary artery (vs dual supply for the anterolateral muscle). Sudden rupture leads to severe MR with resultant pulmonary edema (eg, dyspnea, hypoxia, crackles) and cardiogenic shock (eg, hypotension, cool extremities). This is a surgical emergency, and patients require immediate stabilization with vasodilators (eg, nitroprusside) and intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation, followed by valve replacement.

question: A 37-year-old primigravid woman at 12 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of vaginal bleeding and dull suprapubic pain for 3 hours. She has had spotting during the last 3 days. Her medications include folic acid and a multivitamin. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 89/65 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a dilated cervical os and a uterus consistent in size with an 11-week gestation. Ultrasonography shows an embryo of 4 cm in crown-rump length and no fetal cardiac activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

few_shot.question: A 36-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of vaginal bleeding and mild suprapubic pain 1 hour ago. The bleeding has subsided and she has mild, brown spotting now. Her medications include folic acid and a multivitamin. She smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 10 years and drank alcohol occasionally but stopped both 6 weeks ago. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 116/77 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a closed cervical os and a uterus consistent in size with an 8-week gestation. Ultrasonography shows an intrauterine pregnancy and normal fetal cardiac activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with threatened abortion, which is defined as vaginal bleeding before 20 weeks' gestation with a closed cervical os. It is a common complication of early pregnancy, occurring in up to 25% of pregnancies. The majority of these patients will continue their pregnancies without intervention. The most important risk factor for threatened abortion is advanced maternal age. Other risk factors include cigarette smoking, alcohol use, cocaine use, and trauma. The diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasonography, which shows an intrauterine pregnancy with evidence of fetal cardiac activity. The most appropriate management is expectant, with reassurance and follow-up ultrasonography to ensure appropriate interval growth.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 26-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a prenatal visit. Pregnancy was confirmed by an ultrasound 3 weeks earlier after the patient presented with severe nausea and vomiting. The nausea and vomiting have subsided without medication. She has no vaginal bleeding or discharge. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 10-week gestation. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a gestational sac with a mean diameter of 23 mm and an embryo 6 mm in length with absent cardiac activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's transvaginal ultrasound shows an embryo with a crown-rump length (CRL) >7 mm and no cardiac activity, which is diagnostic of embryonic demise (ie, "missed abortion"). Embryonic cardiac activity can be seen on transvaginal ultrasound when the CRL is >5 mm. Therefore, absence of cardiac activity in an embryo with a CRL >5 mm is not compatible with a viable pregnancy. Management options for embryonic demise include expectant management, medical management, or surgical evacuation. Medical management with misoprostol is typically used for patients who desire noninvasive treatment but wish to avoid the uncertainty of expectant management. Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analogue that causes cervical ripening and uterine contractions, facilitating passage of the products of conception.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 1, at 22 weeks gestation visits her physician for a prenatal visit. She feels well. Her current pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She has attended many prenatal appointments and followed the physician's advice about screening for diseases, laboratory testing, diet, and exercise. The patient’s previous pregnancies were complicated by preterm labor at 24 weeks gestation in one pregnancy and spontanious abortion at 22 weeks in the other. She takes a multivitamin with folate every day. At the physician’s office, her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), and blood pressure is 109/61 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation. Fetal heart sounds are normal. An ultrasound shows a short cervix, measured at 20 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient has a history of spontaneous preterm birth and a short cervix on transvaginal ultrasound, which are both risk factors for preterm birth. The most appropriate next step in management is placement of a cerclage, a stitch placed in the cervix to keep it closed. This is typically done between 12 and 24 weeks gestation and is removed around 37 weeks gestation. Cerclage is recommended in women with a history of spontaneous preterm birth and a short cervix (<25 mm) on transvaginal ultrasound.

few_shot.question: A 22-year-old primigravid woman at 12 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of several hours of abdominal cramping and passing of large vaginal blood clots. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.3°F), pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 110/65 mmHg. The uterus is consistent in size with a 12-week gestation. Speculum exam shows an open cervical os and blood clots within the vaginal vault. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty gestational sac. The patient is worried about undergoing invasive procedures. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of abdominal cramping and passing of large vaginal blood clots, along with an open cervical os and an empty gestational sac on ultrasound, is consistent with an incomplete abortion. Incomplete abortion is defined as the passage of some, but not all, of the products of conception. The patient may present with heavy bleeding and an open cervical os. The uterus is usually enlarged and boggy, and products of conception may be felt in the cervical os.

Management of incomplete abortion includes expectant management, medical management with misoprostol, or surgical management with suction curettage. Expectant management is appropriate for hemodynamically stable patients without signs of infection who can reliably follow up. It involves waiting for the products of conception to pass spontaneously, which usually occurs within 1-2 weeks. If the products of conception do not pass, or if the patient develops heavy bleeding or signs of infection, medical or surgical management should be pursued.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 35 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department for the evaluation of lower abdominal and back pain and vaginal bleeding that started one hour ago. She has had no prenatal care. Her first two pregnancies were uncomplicated and her children were delivered vaginally. The patient smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years; she reduced to half a pack every 2 days during her pregnancies. Her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. The uterus is tender, and regular hypertonic contractions are felt every 2 minutes. There is dark blood on the vulva, the introitus, and on the medial aspect of both thighs bilaterally. The fetus is in a cephalic presentation. The fetal heart rate is 158/min and reactive with no decelerations. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of painful vaginal bleeding in the third trimester is concerning for placental abruption, a premature separation of the placenta from the uterus. Risk factors include maternal hypertension, trauma, smoking, cocaine use, and a history of abruption. The classic presentation is painful bleeding, uterine tenderness, and hypertonic uterine contractions. However, the amount of vaginal bleeding does not correlate with the severity of abruption because blood can be concealed behind the placenta. Fetal heart rate abnormalities (eg, late decelerations, bradycardia) are common and are due to uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxemia. Maternal and fetal mortality and morbidity are increased due to hemorrhage, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and preterm labor.

Management of placental abruption depends on gestational age, severity of abruption, and maternal and fetal status. In a hemodynamically stable patient at term with reassuring fetal status, as in this patient, a vaginal delivery is usually appropriate. An emergent cesarean delivery is indicated if there is evidence of fetal compromise (eg, nonreassuring fetal heart tracing, fetal death) or if labor fails to progress.

So, the answer is [A].

question: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of difficulty falling asleep for the past 2 months. She wakes up frequently during the night and gets up earlier than desired. She experiences discomfort in her legs when lying down at night and feels the urge to move her legs. The discomfort resolves when she gets up and walks around or moves her legs. She has tried an over-the-counter sleep aid that contains diphenhydramine, which worsened her symptoms. She exercises regularly and eats a well-balanced diet. She admits that she has been under a lot of stress lately. Her brother has similar symptoms. The patient appears anxious. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A complete blood count and iron studies are within the reference range. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient's symptoms?

few_shot.question: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-month history of insomnia. She frequently experiences leg discomfort when trying to fall asleep that is relieved temporarily by movement. Her husband tells her that she frequently flexes her ankles upward when she sleeps. She appears fatigued and anxious. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies including a complete blood count and iron studies are within the reference range. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of leg discomfort at night relieved by movement are consistent with restless legs syndrome (RLS). RLS is a common sensorimotor disorder that is characterized by an urge to move the legs, often accompanied by uncomfortable sensations. Symptoms typically occur at rest, worsen in the evening, and are relieved by movement. RLS can lead to significant sleep disturbance and impaired quality of life. The pathophysiology of RLS is not completely understood, but it is thought to involve central nervous system iron and dopamine dysfunction. 

First-line treatment for RLS is with a dopamine agonist such as pramipexole or ropinirole. In patients who cannot tolerate dopamine agonists, gabapentin or a low-potency opioid can be used.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old woman presents with complaints of difficulty sleeping due to discomfort in her legs for the past 6 months. She is unable to describe the discomfort, but says it is an unpleasant, creeping and crawling feeling that is not painful. She feels an irresistible urge to move her legs to decrease the discomfort. The unpleasant sensation in her legs often occurs at night when she is lying in bed. She is recently divorced and lives alone. She denies any changes in appetite, weight loss, low mood, or suicidal thoughts. The physical examination is unremarkable except for signs of mild pallor. Laboratory test results show microcytic anemia with hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL and decreased serum iron and ferritin levels. Apart from correcting her anemia, which additional drug would you prescribe for her symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of an unpleasant sensation in her legs, an irresistible urge to move her legs, and worsening of symptoms at rest (especially at night) are suggestive of restless legs syndrome (RLS). RLS is a common sensorimotor disorder that often disrupts sleep. The pathophysiology of RLS is not well understood, but it is thought to involve central nervous system iron insufficiency and dopamine dysregulation. Iron deficiency is a known secondary cause of RLS, and iron replacement is indicated in patients with iron deficiency anemia.

The treatment of RLS involves nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic measures. Nonpharmacologic measures include maintaining good sleep hygiene, regular exercise, and avoidance of caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol. Pharmacologic treatment is indicated for patients with significant sleep disturbance or impaired quality of life. First-line pharmacologic treatment options include dopamine agonists (eg, pramipexole, ropinirole) and α2δ calcium channel ligands (eg, gabapentin, pregabalin).

few_shot.question: A 59-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for trouble sleeping. The patient states that when she goes to bed at night she has an urge to get up out of bed and walk around. The patient often wakes her husband when she does this which irritates him. She states that there is a perpetual uneasiness and feeling of a need to move at night which is relieved by getting up and walking around. The patient denies symptoms during the day. She works as a mail carrier and is nearing retirement. She has a past medical history of anxiety, depression, irritable bowel syndrome, and dysmenorrhea. She is not currently taking any medications. Her temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 157/98 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals 5/5 strength in the upper and lower extremities, 2+ reflexes in the upper and lower extremities, a stable gait pattern, and normal sensation. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams are within normal limits. Which of the following is the best initial step in management?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of an urge to move her legs at night, which is relieved by movement, are suggestive of restless legs syndrome (RLS). RLS is a common condition that is often associated with iron deficiency, even in the absence of anemia. Therefore, the first step in management is to check iron studies (serum ferritin, iron, total iron-binding capacity, transferrin saturation) to evaluate for iron deficiency. If iron deficiency is present, oral iron supplementation is the treatment of choice. If iron studies are normal, treatment with a dopamine agonist (eg, pramipexole, ropinirole) or a calcium channel alpha-2-delta ligand (eg, gabapentin, pregabalin) can be considered.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question: A 53-year-old woman presented to her PCP with one week of difficulty falling asleep, despite having good sleep hygiene. She denies changes in her mood, weight loss, and anhedonia. She has had difficulty concentrating and feels tired throughout the day. Recently, she was fired from her previous job. What medication would be most helpful for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's difficulty falling asleep, daytime fatigue, and difficulty concentrating are suggestive of insomnia. Insomnia is a common condition that can be caused by many factors, including stress, medical conditions, medications, and poor sleep hygiene. In this patient, the recent job loss is likely a significant stressor contributing to her insomnia.

The first-line treatment for insomnia is good sleep hygiene, which includes regular sleep schedule, a quiet sleep environment, and avoidance of caffeine and stimulating activities before bedtime. If sleep hygiene measures are not effective, short-term pharmacologic treatment can be considered. The nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotics (eg, zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone) are considered first-line pharmacologic treatment for insomnia. These drugs bind to the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor complex and have a shorter half-life and less tolerance and dependence compared with benzodiazepines.

few_shot.question: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of poor sleep for the past 8 months. She has been gradually sleeping less because of difficulty initiating sleep at night. She does not have trouble maintaining sleep. On average, she sleeps 4–5 hours each night. She feels tired throughout the day but does not take naps. The patient asks for a sleeping aid but does not want to feel drowsy in the morning because she has to drive her daughter to kindergarten. Short-term treatment with which of the following drugs is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient's symptoms?

This patient's difficulty initiating sleep, decreased total sleep time, and daytime fatigue are consistent with insomnia disorder. Insomnia is a common condition that can be associated with significant distress and impairment. It is often comorbid with psychiatric disorders, especially anxiety disorders, as seen in this patient.

Benzodiazepine receptor agonists (BzRAs) are commonly used for the short-term treatment of insomnia. BzRAs enhance the action of GABA, the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, and facilitate sleep. Triazolam is a short-acting BzRA that is especially effective for sleep-onset insomnia due to its rapid absorption and short half-life (2-5 hours). It is less likely to cause residual daytime sedation or next-day psychomotor impairment ("hangover effect") compared to longer-acting BzRAs (eg, flurazepam).

question: A 26-year-old man presents to his physician with a history of diarrhea and vomiting for the past 24 hours. few_shot.question: A 32-year-old man recently visiting from Thailand presents with diarrhea and fatigue for the past 6 days, which began before leaving Thailand. The patient denies any recent history of laxatives, nausea, or vomiting. His vital signs include: blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg, heart rate 105/min, and temperature 37.7°C (99.8°F). On physical examination, the patient is pale with dry mucous membranes. A stool sample is obtained for culture, which is copious and appears watery. Which of the following is the correct categorization of this diarrheal disease?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with secretory diarrhea, which is characterized by large-volume, watery stools that persist despite fasting. This type of diarrhea is caused by bacterial enterotoxins (eg, Vibrio cholerae, enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli), laxatives (eg, magnesium hydroxide, castor oil), and certain rare tumors (eg, vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting tumors). The enterotoxins stimulate the secretion of anions (eg, chloride) into the intestinal lumen, which is followed by water. The large volume of fluid overwhelms the absorptive capacity of the colon, leading to diarrhea.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question:
A 41-year-old man presents to urgent care with a 1-week history of severe diarrhea. He says that he has been having watery stools every 2-3 hours. The stools do not contain blood and do not float. On presentation, he is observed to have significant facial flushing, and laboratory tests reveal the following:

Serum:
Na+: 137 mEq/L
K+: 2.7 mEq/L
Cl-: 113 mEq/L
HCO3-: 14 mEq/L

A computed tomography scan reveals a small intra-abdominal mass. Staining of this mass would most likely reveal production of which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's severe, watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome) suggest the diagnosis of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)oma. VIPomas are rare neuroendocrine tumors that most commonly originate in the pancreas. They secrete VIP, a hormone that stimulates intestinal water and electrolyte secretion, inhibits gastric acid secretion, and causes vasodilation. The diagnosis is confirmed by elevated serum VIP levels. Treatment is with surgical resection, but somatostatin analogs can be used to control symptoms by inhibiting the release of VIP.

few_shot.question: A 55-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with diarrhea. She states that it has persisted for the past several weeks and has not been improving. She also endorses episodes of feeling particularly flushed in the face. Her temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 125/63 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Physical exam is notable for wheezing on pulmonary exam. The patient is discharged with medications for her symptoms. She returns 2 weeks later with symptoms of diarrhea, dry skin, a non-specific rash, and a notable decline in her memory. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s most recent presentation?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia is suggestive of pellagra, which is caused by niacin deficiency. Niacin, also known as vitamin B3, is a component of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP), which are involved in many metabolic processes, including glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and the electron transport chain. Deficiency in niacin can lead to a variety of symptoms, including the classic triad of diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia. If left untreated, it can be fatal.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

Answer: [D] > [C] > [B] > [A].

few_shot.question:
A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of diarrhea. During this period, he has had about 10 bowel movements per day. He states that his stools are light brown and watery, with no blood or mucus. He also reports mild abdominal pain and nausea. Over the past year, he has had 6 episodes of diarrhea that lasted several days and resolved spontaneously. Over this time, he also noticed frequent episodes of reddening in his face and neck. He returned from a 10-day trip to Nigeria 3 weeks ago. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for the past 13 years. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes. The abdomen is tender with no rebound or guarding. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show:
Na+ 136 mEq/L
Cl- 102 mEq/L
K+ 2.3 mEq/L
HCO3- 22 mEq/L
Mg2+ 1.7 mEq/L
Ca2+ 12.3 mg/dL
Glucose (fasting) 169 mg/dL
Nasogastric tube aspiration reveals significantly decreased gastric acid production. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?"

answer_choices.D: Transmural inflammation of the intestinal walls

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's chronic diarrhea, facial flushing, and hypokalemia are suggestive of VIPoma, a rare neuroendocrine tumor that originates from the non-β islet cells of the pancreas. These tumors secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), which inhibits gastric acid secretion and stimulates secretion of water and electrolytes in the small bowel. This leads to large-volume secretory diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome). VIP also causes vasodilation, which can lead to flushing and hypotension. Hyperglycemia and hypercalcemia can also occur due to VIP's glycogenolytic and bone-resorbing effects, respectively.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

Answer: [B] > [C] > [A] > [D].

few_shot.question:
A 59-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of worsening nausea and reduced urine output for the past 3 days. One week ago he had a 4-day episode of abdominal pain, vomiting, and watery, nonbloody diarrhea that began a day after he returned from a trip to Mexico. He has not been able to eat or drink much since then, but the symptoms resolved 3 days ago. He has a history of tension headaches, for which he takes ibuprofen about 10 times a month. He also has gastroesophageal reflux disease and benign prostatic hyperplasia. His daily medications include pantoprazole and alfuzosin. He appears pale. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Examination shows dry mucous membranes. The abdomen is soft without guarding or rebound. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL
Platelet count 250,000/mm3
Serum
Na+ 147 mEq/L
Cl- 102 mEq/L
K+ 4.7 mEq/L
HCO3- 20 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen 109 mg/dL
Glucose 80 mg/dL
Creatinine 3.1 mg/dL
Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's laboratory findings?"
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recent diarrhea, reduced urine output, and physical examination findings of dry mucous membranes and tachycardia suggest hypovolemia. The laboratory findings of hypernatremia, increased blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine are consistent with prerenal azotemia due to volume depletion. The BUN/creatinine ratio is typically >20:1 in prerenal azotemia, as seen in this patient. This is because BUN reabsorption is increased in the setting of low renal perfusion, whereas creatinine reabsorption remains relatively constant.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

question: A previously healthy 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after sustaining burns over 45% of her body in a house fire. On arrival, she is in acute distress but is fully oriented. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun and the patient is transferred to the intensive care unit of a burn center. 20 hours later, she has several large, tarry black stools and develops hypotension and tachycardia. Despite appropriate lifesaving measures, she dies. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of the patient's tarry black stools?

answer_choices.C: Bacterial colonization of the gastric antrum

few_shot.question: A 80-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department from a senior living home with a chief complaint of acute onset and severe abdominal pain with 5 episodes of bloody diarrhea. She has a history of having chronic constipation, and postprandial abdominal pain which subsides after taking nitroglycerin. The abdominal pain that she is currently experiencing did not subside using her medication. A week ago, she had a percutaneous intervention for an inferior wall STEMI. On physical examination, the patient looks pale and confused. The vital signs include: blood pressure 80/40 mm Hg, heart rate 108/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and temperature 35.6°C (96.0°F). The patient receives an aggressive treatment consisting of intravenous fluids and vasopressors, and she is transferred to the ICU. Despite all the necessary interventions, the patient dies. During the autopsy, a dark hemorrhagic appearance of the sigmoid colon is noted. What is the most likely pathology related to her death?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of chronic constipation, postprandial abdominal pain, and recent myocardial infarction, along with her presentation of severe abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea, are suggestive of ischemic colitis. Ischemic colitis is a condition characterized by inflammation and injury of the colon resulting from inadequate blood supply. It can be caused by a variety of conditions, including atherosclerosis, thromboembolic disease, and low-flow states such as shock or sepsis. In this case, the patient's history of atherosclerosis and recent myocardial infarction suggest that she likely had significant atherosclerotic disease, which could have led to a decrease in blood flow to the colon.

The dark hemorrhagic appearance of the sigmoid colon on autopsy is consistent with a transmural infarction, which involves the full thickness of the bowel wall. This is the most severe form of ischemic colitis and can lead to bowel necrosis, perforation, and death.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: An 80-year-old man comes to the office for evaluation of anemia. His medical history is relevant for end-stage renal disease and aortic stenosis. When questioned about his bowel movements, the patient mentions that he has occasional episodes of loose, black, tarry stools. His heart rate is 78/min, respiratory rate is 17/min, temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pale skin and conjunctiva and orthostasis upon standing. A complete blood count shows his hemoglobin is 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit is 27%, and mean corpuscular volume is 76 μm3. A colonoscopy is obtained. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s current condition?
few_shot.explanation:
Angiodysplasia is a common cause of lower gastrointestinal bleeding in the elderly. It is characterized by dilated, thin-walled blood vessels in the cecum and right colon. The exact cause is unknown, but it is thought to be due to age-related degeneration of the blood vessels. The bleeding is usually slow and chronic, but can occasionally be acute and severe. The bleeding is often painless and presents as melena or hematochezia. The diagnosis is made by colonoscopy, which shows dilated, tortuous blood vessels in the mucosa and submucosa.

This patient's history of aortic stenosis is also relevant, as angiodysplasia is associated with aortic stenosis through a poorly understood mechanism known as Heyde syndrome.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of black, tarry stools. He has also had upper abdominal pain that occurs immediately after eating and a 4.4-kg (9.7-lb) weight loss in the past 6 months. He has no history of major medical illness but drinks 3 beers daily. His only medication is acetaminophen. He is a financial consultant and travels often for work. Physical examination shows pallor and mild epigastric pain. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy shows a bleeding 15-mm ulcer in the antrum of the stomach. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing factor for this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is a common condition that can cause upper abdominal pain and gastrointestinal bleeding. The most common cause of PUD is infection with Helicobacter pylori, a gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the stomach. H. pylori infection is associated with both gastric and duodenal ulcers. Other risk factors for PUD include use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), smoking, and, to a lesser extent, alcohol consumption. However, H. pylori infection is the strongest risk factor for PUD in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 46-year-old woman from Ecuador is admitted to the hospital because of tarry-black stools and epigastric pain for 2 weeks. The epigastric pain is relieved after meals, but worsens after 1–2 hours. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Fecal occult blood test is positive. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy shows a bleeding duodenal ulcer. Microscopic examination of a duodenal biopsy specimen is most likely to show which of the following?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's epigastric pain that is relieved by meals and recurs 1-2 hours after eating is suggestive of a duodenal ulcer. The most common cause of duodenal ulcers is infection with Helicobacter pylori, a gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the stomach and duodenum. H. pylori is a curved, flagellated rod that is able to survive in the acidic environment of the stomach by producing large amounts of urease, which breaks down urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. The ammonia neutralizes gastric acid, allowing H. pylori to survive and establish infection.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 52-year-old Caucasian male presents to your office complaining of black, tarry stool. Which of the following possible causes of this patient's presentation is LEAST associated with the development of carcinoma?
few_shot.explanation:
The patient's presentation of black, tarry stool is indicative of melena, which is usually due to bleeding in the upper gastrointestinal tract. The causes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding include Barrett's esophagus, adenomatous polyps, gastric ulcers, and duodenal ulcers.

Barrett's esophagus is a condition in which the normal squamous epithelium of the esophagus is replaced by metaplastic columnar epithelium. This condition is associated with chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and is a risk factor for the development of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Adenomatous polyps are benign neoplasms of the colon that have the potential to progress to colorectal carcinoma. The risk of malignant transformation is related to the size of the polyp and the presence of villous features or high-grade dysplasia.

Gastric ulcers can be benign or malignant. Malignant gastric ulcers are usually due to gastric adenocarcinoma. Even benign gastric ulcers can be associated with an increased risk of gastric cancer.

Duodenal ulcers, on the other hand, are usually benign and are not associated with an increased risk of cancer. They are most commonly due to infection with Helicobacter pylori or the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

Therefore, the answer is [D].

question: A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation comes to the physician for shortness of breath with mild exertion, progressive weakness, and a dry cough that has persisted for 6 months. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years. His medications include warfarin, enalapril, and amiodarone. His pulse is 85/min and irregularly irregular. Physical examination shows enlarged fingertips and markedly curved nails. A CT scan of the chest shows clustered air spaces and reticular opacities in the basal parts of the lung. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's dyspnea?

answer_choices.D: Excess collagen deposition in the extracellular matrix of the lung

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old patient comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of persistent dry cough and shortness of breath with mild exertion. He reports feeling too weak to leave the house on most days. He has a history of hypertension and chronic atrial fibrillation. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years. His medications include warfarin, enalapril, and amiodarone. His temperature is 36.1°C (97°F), pulse is 85/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 148/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows enlargement of the fingertips with increased curving of the nail. Inspiratory crackles are heard over both lung bases. Spirometry shows decreased vital capacity. A CT scan of the chest shows clustered air spaces and reticular opacities in the basal parts of the lung. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's dyspnea?

answer_choices.A: Excess collagen deposition in the extracellular matrix of the lung
answer_choices.D: Increased pressure in the pulmonary arteries

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, persistent dry cough, dyspnea, and inspiratory crackles on lung examination are suggestive of interstitial lung disease (ILD). The CT scan findings of clustered air spaces (honeycombing) and reticular opacities are consistent with usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), the most common form of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). UIP is characterized by excess collagen deposition in the extracellular matrix of the lung, leading to fibrosis and destruction of the lung parenchyma. This results in decreased lung compliance and impaired gas exchange, causing dyspnea and hypoxemia. Clubbing, as seen in this patient, is common in IPF and is thought to be due to the release of platelet-derived growth factor from the lungs.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 75-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department for increasing shortness of breath for the last 8 months. He also complains of a dry cough for the last 6 months. Initially, his shortness of breath occurs with exertion, but now he feels it at rest as well. He has no other complaints. He has a sedentary lifestyle and had a hip replacement surgery recently. The past medical history is significant for hypertension for which he is taking lisinopril. The patient is a lifetime non-smoker. The blood pressure is 135/85 mm Hg, pulse rate is 85/min, and the temperature is 36.6°C (97.9°F). Physical examination reveals fine inspiratory crackles and digital clubbing. A chest X-ray reveals peripheral reticular opacities associated with traction bronchiectasis predominantly at the lung bases. The pulmonary function test results reveal a decreased FEV1, a decreased FVC, and a preserved FEV1/FVC ratio. High-resolution CT scan of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's clinical presentation and imaging findings are consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). IPF is a specific form of chronic, progressive, fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause that occurs primarily in older adults. It is associated with the histopathologic and/or radiologic pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia. The most common symptoms of IPF are dyspnea and nonproductive cough. Physical examination may reveal inspiratory crackles and digital clubbing. Pulmonary function tests typically show a restrictive pattern (ie, decreased total lung capacity) with decreased diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide. The diagnosis of IPF requires the exclusion of other known causes of interstitial lung disease (eg, drug toxicities, environmental exposures, connective tissue diseases) and either a surgical lung biopsy or a characteristic radiologic pattern on high-resolution CT scan of the chest. The CT scan in this patient shows peripheral, predominantly basal, reticular opacities associated with traction bronchiectasis and honeycombing, which are characteristic of usual interstitial pneumonia.

So, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician for shortness of breath and chest discomfort that is becoming progressively worse. He has had increasing problems exerting himself for the past 5 years. He is now unable to walk more than 50 m on level terrain without stopping and mostly rests at home. He has smoked 1–2 packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. He appears distressed. His pulse is 85/min, blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, and respirations are 25/min. Physical examination shows a plethoric face and distended jugular veins. Bilateral wheezing is heard on auscultation of the lungs. There is yellow discoloration of the fingers on the right hand and 2+ lower extremity edema. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of heavy smoking, progressive exertional dyspnea, and wheezing is suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is characterized by chronic bronchitis (ie, cough and sputum production) and/or emphysema (ie, destruction of alveolar walls). Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as a cough with sputum production for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years. Emphysema is defined pathologically as abnormal, permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis. The most common cause of COPD is smoking.

Patients with severe COPD can develop pulmonary hypertension due to hypoxic vasoconstriction, destruction of the pulmonary vascular bed, and hyperinflation of the lungs with compression of the pulmonary vasculature. Pulmonary hypertension can lead to cor pulmonale (right ventricular hypertrophy and eventual failure due to pulmonary disease). Signs of cor pulmonale include exertional dyspnea, signs of right heart failure (eg, jugular venous distension, lower extremity edema), and loud P2 on cardiac examination.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 53-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a persistent cough and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He has had these symptoms for several weeks and used to only become breathless during exercise but now has breathing difficulty while at rest. The patient says that he has mild-to-moderate respiratory distress and fatigue for months. Past medical history is significant for lymphoma, treated with several rounds of chemotherapy, now in remission. Additionally, he takes a baby aspirin every day and a multivitamin. He smokes cigarettes and cigars and has smoked at least a half of a pack of cigarettes every day for the past 30 years. Family history is significant for 1 uncle with a lung problem but he does not know what it was. On physical exam, the vital signs include: heart rate 101/min, respiratory rate 23/min, blood pressure 125/85 mm Hg, and temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F). On cardiopulmonary examination, diffuse crackles are auscultated over all lung fields during inspiration. Mild digit clubbing is observed. A preliminary diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is established. Which additional finding is also expected in this patient?

answer_choices.C: Reversal of symptoms with smoking cessation
answer_choices.D: Cystic airspaces in the lung interstitium on CT scan

few_shot.explanation:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive lung disease of unknown etiology that primarily affects older adults. It is characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung parenchyma, leading to irreversible loss of lung function. The most common symptoms of IPF are nonproductive cough and exertional dyspnea. Physical examination often reveals end-inspiratory crackles and finger clubbing. The diagnosis is suggested by high-resolution CT scan of the chest, which shows reticular opacities, honeycombing (ie, cystic airspaces in the lung interstitium), and traction bronchiectasis. Lung biopsy is usually not necessary if the clinical and radiographic findings are typical for IPF.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 65-year-old male engineer presents to the office with shortness of breath on exertion and a dry cough that he has had for about a year. He is a heavy smoker with a 25-pack-years history. His vitals include: heart rate 95/min, respiratory rate 26/min, and blood pressure 110/75 mm Hg. On examination, he presents with nail clubbing and bilateral and persistent crackling rales. The chest radiograph shows basal reticulonodular symmetric images, with decreased lung fields. The pulmonary function tests show the following: diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is 43% and reference SaO2 is 94% and 72%, at rest and with exercise, respectively. What is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive, fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause that occurs primarily in older adults. It is associated with the histopathologic and/or radiologic pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia. The diagnosis of IPF requires exclusion of other known causes of interstitial lung disease (eg, certain drug toxicities, environmental exposures, and connective tissue diseases) and the presence of a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern on high-resolution computed tomography in patients not subjected to surgical lung biopsy. Patients with IPF often have a history of cigarette smoking. The most common symptoms are dyspnea and nonproductive cough. Clubbing is present in about half of patients. Bibasilar inspiratory crackles are a typical finding on physical examination. Pulmonary function tests show a restrictive pattern with decreased lung volumes and reduced DLCO. The prognosis is poor, with a median survival of 2-3 years after diagnosis.

So, the answer is [D].

question: A 68-year-old male comes to the physician for evaluation of right flank pain. He has a history of diabetes and peripheral artery disease. His blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows abdominal tenderness and right flank tenderness. An ultrasound shows dilation of the right ureter and renal pelvis. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

few_shot.question: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of hematuria and bilateral flank pain. He has passed urinary stones twice before and has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. He reports no recent trauma. His father had a history of kidney failure and underwent a kidney transplant. His temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 155/98 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows palpable, bilateral flank masses. Results of a complete blood count are within the reference range. His serum creatinine concentration is 2.9 mg/dL. Which of the following findings is most likely to be associated with this patient's condition?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of recurrent urinary tract infections, hematuria, and bilateral flank masses, along with a family history of kidney failure, is suggestive of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). ADPKD is characterized by the development of numerous fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys, leading to progressive renal failure. Extrarenal manifestations of ADPKD include hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse, and intracranial aneurysms. The latter can rupture, leading to subarachnoid hemorrhage, a life-threatening condition. Therefore, patients with ADPKD should be screened for intracranial aneurysms, especially if they have a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

So, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 53-year-old male presents to your office for abdominal discomfort. The patient states he first noticed pain on his right flank several months ago, and it has been gradually getting worse. For the past week, he has also noticed blood in his urine. Prior to this episode, he has been healthy and does not take any medications. The patient denies fever, chills, and dysuria. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history. Vital signs are T 37 C, HR 140/90 mmHg, HR 84/min, RR 14/min, O2 98%. Physical exam is unremarkable. CBC reveals a hemoglobin of 17 and hematocrit of 51%, and urinalysis is positive for red blood cells, negative for leukocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of flank pain, hematuria, and a smoking history is concerning for renal cell carcinoma (RCC). RCC is the most common primary renal malignancy and is associated with smoking, obesity, and hypertension. The classic triad of RCC is flank pain, hematuria, and a palpable abdominal mass, but this is seen in less than 10% of patients. More commonly, patients present with more vague symptoms such as weight loss, anorexia, and malaise. Paraneoplastic syndromes are also common in RCC and can manifest as hypercalcemia, hypertension, and polycythemia, as seen in this patient.

Therefore, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of right flank pain that started 3 days following a procedure. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows right costovertebral angle tenderness. An intravenous pyelogram shows a dilated renal pelvis and ureter on the right with a lack of contrast proximal to the ureterovesical junction. This patient most likely recently underwent which of the following procedures?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of right flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness, along with the finding of a dilated renal pelvis and ureter on the right, is suggestive of hydronephrosis. The most likely cause of her hydronephrosis is ureteral injury, which is a known complication of pelvic surgery. The ureters are at risk of injury during hysterectomy due to their close proximity to the uterus and other pelvic structures. Ureteral injury can lead to urinary extravasation and subsequent ureteral obstruction, which can cause hydronephrosis.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician because he has been having flank and back pain for the last 8 months. He said that it started after he fell off a chair while doing yard work, but it has been getting progressively worse over time. He reports no other symptoms and denies any weight loss or tingling in his extremities. His medical history is significant for poorly controlled hypertension and a back surgery 10 years ago. He drinks socially and has smoked 1 pack per day since he was 20. His family history is significant for cancer, and he says that he is concerned that his father had similar symptoms before he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma. Physical exam reveals a painful, pulsatile enlargement in the patient's abdomen. Between which of the following locations has the highest risk of developing this patient's disorder?

answer_choices.C: Renal arteries and common iliac arteries
answer_choices.D: Superior mesenteric artery and common iliac arteries

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's history of smoking, hypertension, and a painful, pulsatile abdominal mass is suggestive of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). AAAs are most commonly located between the renal arteries and the aortic bifurcation into the common iliac arteries. Risk factors for AAA include age >60, smoking, male sex, and a family history of AAA. Hypertension is also a risk factor, but it is more strongly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms.

Therefore, the answer is [C].

few_shot.question:
A 54-year-old man with lymphoma presents to his oncologist with severe abdominal pain and flank pain. He says that the pain started 2 days ago and has gotten worse over time. He has also not been able to urinate over the same time period. On presentation, his temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 110/72 mmHg, pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 12/min. Physical exam reveals bilateral flank tenderness. Labs results are shown below:

Blood urea nitrogen: 34 mg/dL
Creatinine: 3.7 mg/dl
Urine osmolality: 228 mOsm/kg

Renal ultrasonography shows dilation of the kidneys bilaterally with a normal-sized bladder. Which of the following would most likely be beneficial in treating this patient's condition?

answer_choices.B: Bilateral stenting of the renal arteries

few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of acute renal failure, severe flank pain, and bilateral hydronephrosis is suggestive of postrenal acute kidney injury (AKI) due to bilateral ureteral obstruction. The most common cause of bilateral ureteral obstruction in adults is malignancy. In men, prostate cancer is the most common malignancy to cause bilateral ureteral obstruction. However, given this patient's history of lymphoma, it is likely that retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy is causing the bilateral ureteral obstruction.

The initial management of postrenal AKI due to bilateral ureteral obstruction involves relieving the obstruction. This can be accomplished by placement of bilateral ureteral stents or percutaneous nephrostomy tubes.

So, the answer is [C].

question: A 74-year-old man has been treated for prostate cancer for the past 6 months. He is on an experimental drug (drug X) that is used to reduce the action of testosterone by blocking the androgen receptor. Since the initiation of therapy, the growth of the cancerous tissue has slowed. This medication is known to be excreted by the kidneys at the current dose that he is taking. The patient has no significant complaints, except for excessive sweating at times. On physical examination, a small area of tissue around his nipples is enlarged bilaterally. No other abnormal findings are present. Which of the following drugs most likely belongs to be the same class as drug X?

few_shot.question: A 69-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of urinary urgency, nocturia, and progressive pain in his lower back. The pain is worse at night and does not respond to ibuprofen. Rectal examination shows an enlarged, asymmetric prostate with a nodular surface. Prostate-specific antigen concentration is 11 ng/ml (N < 4). A biopsy of the prostate shows a high-grade adenocarcinoma. A CT scan of the pelvis shows multiple osteoblastic lesions of the lumbar spine. The patient is started on a drug that competes with androgens for interaction with the testosterone receptors. Treatment with which of the following drugs was most likely initiated in this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's symptoms of urinary urgency, nocturia, and lower back pain, along with the physical examination findings of an enlarged, asymmetric prostate with a nodular surface, are concerning for prostate cancer. The elevated prostate-specific antigen concentration and biopsy findings confirm the diagnosis. The presence of osteoblastic lesions in the lumbar spine on CT scan indicates metastatic disease.

Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is the mainstay of treatment for metastatic prostate cancer. This can be achieved through surgical castration (bilateral orchiectomy) or medical castration using a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist (eg, leuprolide) or antagonist (eg, degarelix). However, these therapies can lead to an initial surge in testosterone levels (with GnRH agonists) or a profound testosterone deficiency, both of which can exacerbate the symptoms of prostate cancer.

To prevent these complications, patients are often started on an antiandrogen medication (eg, flutamide, bicalutamide) prior to treatment with a GnRH agonist or antagonist. These drugs work by competing with circulating androgens for binding to the androgen receptors in the prostate cells, thereby inhibiting the effects of testosterone on the prostate.

few_shot.question: A 75-year-old male is diagnosed with advanced metastatic prostate cancer. After further evaluation and staging, the patient is started on flutamide therapy. Addition of which of the following medications to this patient’s medication regimen would be of greatest benefit in the treatment of this patient’s condition?
few_shot.explanation:
Flutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen that competitively inhibits androgen receptors, thereby decreasing the effects of circulating androgens. It is used in the treatment of advanced prostate cancer, usually in combination with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analog such as leuprolide. Leuprolide is a GnRH analog that ultimately downregulates GnRH receptors in the pituitary gland, leading to decreased production of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). This results in decreased production of testosterone by the testes. The combination of flutamide and leuprolide is known as total androgen blockade or combined androgen blockade, and it is more effective than either agent alone in the treatment of advanced prostate cancer.

few_shot.question: A 76-year-old male presents to his primary care physician because he is concerned about changes in urination. Physical exam reveals a uniformly enlarged and non-tender prostate. Lab tests showed that the prostate specific antigen (PSA) was within normal limits. The patient did not tolerate an alpha blocker due to episodes of syncope so another medication is prescribed that affects testosterone metabolism. Which of the following disorders can also be treated with the medication most likely prescribed in this case?

This patient's symptoms of urinary frequency and difficulty initiating and stopping urination are suggestive of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). BPH is a common condition in older men and is caused by an increase in the number of prostatic cells. The prostate gland is dependent on dihydrotestosterone (DHT) for growth, and DHT is synthesized from testosterone by the enzyme 5-alpha reductase. Therefore, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride, dutasteride) are commonly used in the treatment of BPH. These drugs decrease the conversion of testosterone to DHT, leading to decreased prostate size and improvement in symptoms.

5-alpha reductase inhibitors are also used in the treatment of male pattern baldness (androgenetic alopecia). This condition is characterized by hair follicle miniaturization in a specific pattern on the scalp, and is also dependent on DHT. Therefore, decreasing DHT levels can slow the progression of hair loss.

Finasteride is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor that decreases the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). DHT is a potent androgen that stimulates prostate growth, so reducing its levels can help to shrink the prostate and relieve BPH symptoms. few_shot.question: A 70-year-old man presents to an urgent care clinic with bilateral flank pain for the past 2 days. BPH is a common condition in older men and is caused by proliferation of both the glandular and stromal cells in the prostate. This patient's bilateral flank pain and palpable kidneys suggest urinary retention with bilateral hydronephrosis, a complication of BPH.

The treatment of BPH involves two classes of medications: alpha-1-adrenergic antagonists (eg, tamsulosin) and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride). Alpha-1-adrenergic antagonists work by relaxing smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck, leading to improved urinary flow. These drugs work quickly and are typically first-line therapy for symptomatic BPH.

5-alpha reductase inhibitors work by blocking the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone in the prostate. This leads to a decrease in prostate size. These drugs take several months to reach full effect and are typically used in patients with larger prostates (>40 g) or in those who fail or cannot tolerate alpha-1-adrenergic antagonists.

This patient's developmental delay, self-mutilation, and hyperuricemia are suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). The classic presentation of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome includes motor dysfunction (eg, dystonia, spasticity, choreoathetosis), intellectual disability, and self-mutilation (eg, lip and finger biting). The self-mutilation is thought to be due to a combination of decreased nociception and a compulsive behavior to self-harm.

few_shot.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. He started walking at 20 months of age. He can use a cup to drink but cannot use silverware. This patient's findings of tall stature, long and slender fingers, high-arched palate, and bilateral inferior lens dislocation are suggestive of Marfan syndrome. Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene (FBN1) on chromosome 15. Fibrillin is a major component of microfibrils, which provide strength and flexibility to connective tissue throughout the body. Deficiency of fibrillin-1 leads to increased transforming growth factor-beta signaling, which results in excessive growth of the long bones and laxity of the skin, ligaments, and blood vessels.

The most serious complications of Marfan syndrome involve the cardiovascular system. These include aortic root dilation, aortic dissection, and mitral valve prolapse with or without regurgitation. Therefore, patients with Marfan syndrome should have regular follow-up with echocardiography to monitor for these complications.

Normally, the paternal genes in this region are expressed, while the same region on the maternal chromosome is imprinted (and therefore silenced). In PWS, the paternal genes are deleted or unexpressed, which leads to the features of this syndrome.

PWS is characterized by severe hypotonia and feeding difficulties in early infancy, followed in early childhood by excessive eating and gradual development of morbid obesity. Other findings may include hypogonadism, global developmental delay, and characteristic facial features with almond-shaped eyes and a thin upper lip.

Alendronate is a bisphosphonate that is used as first-line therapy for osteoporosis. It is typically taken once weekly on an empty stomach with a full glass of water. The patient must remain upright for at least 30 minutes after taking the medication to reduce the risk of esophageal irritation and ulceration. 

Raloxifene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, is typically used as a second-line therapy for osteoporosis. It can cause hot flashes, flu-like symptoms, and peripheral edema.

She travels to Latin America every winter. Two weeks ago, she traveled to Brazil and spent most of her time outdoors. She is restless. The temperature is 38.0℃ (100.4℉), the pulse is 110/min, the respiration rate is 33/min, and the blood pressure is 90/70 mm Hg. Conjunctival suffusion is seen. The extremities are cold. A maculopapular rash covers the trunk and extremities. Ecchymoses are observed on the lower extremities. The lung bases reveal absent sounds with dullness to percussion. The abdomen is distended. The liver edge is palpable and liver span is 15 cm. Shifting dullness is present. The laboratory studies show the following:
Laboratory test
Hemoglobin 16.5 g/dL
Leukocyte count 3500/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 55%
Lymphocytes 30%
Platelet count 90,000/mm3
Serum
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 75 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 70 U/L
Total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL
Direct bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's presentation of fever, retro-orbital pain, severe myalgias, and rash is suggestive of dengue fever. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness common in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. The illness is characterized by high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgias/arthralgias, and a maculopapular rash. Minor bleeding phenomena (eg, petechiae, ecchymoses, gingival bleeding) are also common due to thrombocytopenia and increased capillary fragility. In severe cases, dengue can cause a transient shock syndrome and/or a characteristic plasma leakage syndrome due to increased capillary permeability. Manifestations of plasma leakage include hemoconcentration, pleural effusions, ascites, and hypoproteinemia. Patients typically worsen around the time of defervescence (fever lessening), which usually occurs 3-7 days after symptom onset.

This patient's fever, fatigue, and leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes after a hiking trip in Alabama are suggestive of ehrlichiosis. Ehrlichiosis is a tick-borne illness caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, which is transmitted by the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum). It is most commonly found in the southeastern and south-central United States. After a bite from an infected tick, the organism infects monocytes within the human host, forming intracytoplasmic morulae. Clinical manifestations typically occur 1-2 weeks following the tick bite and most commonly include fever, malaise, headache, and myalgias. Laboratory abnormalities often include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated aminotransferases. Diagnosis is typically clinical, but can be confirmed with PCR or immunofluorescence assay. Treatment is with doxycycline.

few_shot.question:

VHFs are a group of illnesses caused by four families of viruses: arenaviruses, bunyaviruses, filoviruses, and flaviviruses. The most common VHFs in Africa are caused by Ebola and Marburg viruses (filoviruses), Lassa virus (an arenavirus), Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (a bunyavirus), and yellow fever virus (a flavivirus). 

Ebola virus is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms. Ebola virus disease is characterized by fever, severe headache, myalgias, and maculopapular rash, followed by vomiting, diarrhea, and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. The incubation period is 2-21 days. The virus is transmitted to humans from wild animals (eg, fruit bats, monkeys, apes) and then spreads in the human population through human-to-human transmission via direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected people, and with surfaces and materials (eg, bedding, clothing) contaminated with these fluids.

question: A 38-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for her yearly exam. Her only complaint is difficulty losing weight. Her BMI is 34 kg/m^2. few_shot.question: A 43-year-old woman presents to her primary care provider for follow-up of her glucose levels. At her last visit 3 months ago, her fasting serum glucose was 128 mg/dl. At that time, she was instructed to follow a weight loss regimen consisting of diet and exercise. Her family history is notable for a myocardial infarction in her father and type II diabetes mellitus in her mother. She does not smoke and drinks 2-3 glasses of wine per week. Her temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 131/78 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 17/min. Her BMI is 31 kg/m^2. On exam, she is well-appearing and appropriately interactive. Today, despite attempting to make the appropriate lifestyle changes, a repeat fasting serum glucose is 133 mg/dl. The patient is prescribed the first-line oral pharmacologic agent for her condition. Which of the following is the correct mechanism of action of this medication?

answer_choices.B: Closure of potassium channels in pancreatic beta cells
answer_choices.C: Inhibition of alpha-glucosidase in the intestinal brush border

few_shot.explanation:
The patient's fasting serum glucose levels are consistent with a diagnosis of type II diabetes mellitus (DM). The first-line oral pharmacologic agent for type II DM is metformin. Metformin primarily works by inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis and improving peripheral glucose uptake and utilization. It also decreases intestinal glucose absorption. Metformin is the only oral hypoglycemic agent that has been shown to reduce macrovascular complications and mortality in patients with type II DM. It is also weight neutral, making it a good choice for overweight or obese patients.

Therefore, the answer is [D].

few_shot.question: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. One week ago, an oral glucose tolerance screening test showed elevated serum glucose levels. She has complied with the recommended diet and lifestyle modifications. Over the past week, home blood glucose monitoring showed elevated fasting and post-prandial blood glucose levels. Which of the following describes the mechanism of action of the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient?
few_shot.explanation:
This patient's elevated fasting and postprandial blood glucose levels despite diet and lifestyle modifications are consistent with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). GDM is defined as carbohydrate intolerance that begins or is first recognized during pregnancy. It is associated with an increased risk of fetal macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, and maternal preeclampsia. 

Insulin is the preferred treatment for GDM when lifestyle modifications are insufficient to maintain euglycemia. Insulin does not cross the placenta and has an excellent safety profile. Insulin binds to tyrosine kinase receptors, leading to autophosphorylation and activation of the receptor. This initiates a cascade of events that ultimately promotes glucose uptake and utilization, glycogen synthesis, and lipogenesis, while inhibiting gluconeogenesis.

Therefore, the answer is [B].

few_shot.question: A 21-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine physical examination. She feels well. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 20.3 kg/m2. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Her fasting serum glucose concentration is 132 mg/dL. Serum insulin concentration 30 minutes after oral glucose administration is 20 mIU/L (N: 30–230). Her hemoglobin A1C concentration is 7.1%. After a thorough workup, the physician concludes that the patient has a chronic condition that can likely be managed with diet only and that she is not at a significantly increased risk of micro- or macrovascular complications. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's condition?

answer_choices.A: Defect in expression of glucokinase gene

few_shot.explanation:
This patient has mild fasting hyperglycemia and impaired glucose tolerance, as evidenced by a low insulin response to glucose challenge. However, she is not overweight and has no evidence of microvascular (eg, retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) or macrovascular (eg, coronary, cerebrovascular, peripheral vascular disease) complications. These findings are consistent with maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY), an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by impaired insulin secretion. MODY is often mild, can be managed with diet alone, and is not typically associated with the long-term complications seen in type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

The most common form of MODY is caused by a mutation in the glucokinase gene. Glucokinase is the glucose sensor of the beta cell. It phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, the first step in glucose metabolism. This process is critical for insulin secretion because metabolism of glucose leads to an increase in the ATP/ADP ratio, closure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels, depolarization of the beta cell, and insulin release. A defect in glucokinase decreases the ability of the beta cell to sense glucose, leading to a higher glucose concentration being necessary for insulin secretion.

So, the answer is [A].

few_shot.question: A 51-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of fatigue and increased thirst. She has no history of serious medical illness and takes no medications. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 72 kg (160 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m2. Her fasting serum glucose concentration is 249 mg/dL. Treatment with an oral hypoglycemic agent is begun. The first-line treatment for T2DM is lifestyle modification (eg, diet, exercise, weight loss). If lifestyle modifications are insufficient or if the patient is significantly hyperglycemic at presentation (as in this patient), pharmacologic therapy should be initiated. Metformin is the initial drug of choice for the treatment of T2DM. It primarily works by decreasing hepatic gluconeogenesis and improving peripheral glucose uptake and utilization. Metformin has been shown to decrease mortality in patients with T2DM and is weight neutral, making it an excellent choice for overweight or obese patients.

The first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus is lifestyle modification (eg, diet, exercise, weight loss) and metformin. question: Twelve hours after undergoing an exploratory laparotomy for a perforated duodenal ulcer, a 36-year-old man has shortness of breath. He has asthma well controlled with an albuterol inhaler.
